concepts/command-of-the-sea.title: Command of the Sea
concepts/command-of-the-sea.content:
Command of the Sea
Command of the sea was the strategic doctrine on which British defence and empire rested: the capacity, in war, to destroy or securely blockade an enemy fleet so that the national frontier, for the purpose of that war and that purpose only, was carried to the enemy’s coast. It was not a claim of peacetime sovereignty over the high seas beyond the gunshot of the shore—such claims England had once made, and other states had at times acquiesced in for the suppression of piracy—but a military condition that made invasion of Britain impossible and invasion of the enemy possible, and that kept open the oceanic routes of trade and empire. Halford Mackinder put the office of sea power in a single image: the navy was Britain’s shield and the army her spear; the final office of command was freedom to choose the point of land attack.
Development
Mackinder’s definition and the nineteenth-century margin
In Britain and the British Seas Mackinder stated the doctrine in geographical terms. A Power has command of the sea against another with which it is at war when it has destroyed the enemy’s fleet or securely blockaded it. Had Britain obtained that command in a war with France, the British frontier would be carried to the French coast and the Channel added to the sphere within which the commanding Power prepared attack; France would be liable to invasion, England safe from it. Had France obtained command, the conditions would reverse. Neutral rights would still limit even complete command against the enemy; but the strategic contrast was absolute.
Viewed from that standpoint, the defence of Britain resolved into three problems: first, retention of the command of the sea—or rather of the power of taking that command when occasion demanded it; second, the defence of Great Britain should command be temporarily lost; third, the separate defence of Ireland in the same contingency, for under such a condition the prompt reinforcement of the army in Ireland would not be practicable. Practically, owing to the limited fuel radius of modern fleets, the regions most threatened were those about the continental angle and the Channel entries; the position of the Metropolis magnified that danger. The chief bases—Chatham, Sheerness, Portsmouth, Devonport—lay within Metropolitan England, opposite the Rhine mouths, Cherbourg, and Brest; harbours of refuge stood at Portland, Dover, and Harwich; Pembroke and Queenstown covered the ocean roads into the St. George’s and Bristol Channels. Mackinder left the chapter as written in 1902, noting only that the growth of the German Fleet and the increased coal-storage of larger battleships opened Britain to invasion, should she lose command, at all points and not merely on either hand of Dover—so that none but a great and efficient army would suffice against a dominant sea-power basing itself on a peninsula such as Cornwall or Fife.
For most of the nineteenth century the Royal Navy’s margin over any likely combination of rivals made the doctrine almost a habit. The Naval Defence Act of 1889 enshrined the two-power standard: the British fleet should equal the combined strength of the next two navies. Against France and Russia that standard rested on a fleet of some fifty pre-dreadnought battleships. Langer’s account of the “new navalism” placed British maritime supremacy as the condition that made England and the Empire almost unassailable while other powers, under Mahan’s teaching on high-seas battle-fleets, turned to naval programmes of their own. Imperial expansion and the scramble for markets sharpened the stake; command of the sea kept the British world-system open.
Tirpitz, risk theory, and the Navy Laws
The German challenge after 1897 turned habit into race. Admiral Alfred von Tirpitz, appointed Secretary of State for the Navy in June 1897, returned from the East Asian cruiser squadron convinced that Germany’s economic expansion, commercial rivalry with Britain, and lack of overseas bases made a cruiser war of little use: the only decisive factor would be a battle-fleet in the North Sea. His “risk theory” (Risiko-Gedanke) held that Germany need not equal Britain ship for ship; she needed a fleet powerful enough that even a British victory would cost Britain so heavily as to risk her global position—“a maritime fighting force of such strength that it could not be overcome without much ado even by one of the larger naval forces.” Germany’s position athwart British trade routes would magnify the threat, forcing Britain to recall squadrons from the Mediterranean and elsewhere; rather than pay that price, Tirpitz believed, Britain would accommodate German ambitions.
Tirpitz organised a publicity bureau at the Ministry of Marine, arranged the translation of Mahan’s The Influence of Sea Power upon History, and collaborated with the Pan-German League and the newly formed Navy League (Flottenverein). The First Navy Law, passed by the Reichstag on 28 March 1898, authorised eleven battleships, five first-class cruisers, and seventeen smaller cruisers by 1905—presented as a minimum to lift the German fleet above a quantité négligeable, but revolutionary in legislating construction years ahead of annual budgets. The Second Navy Law of 14 June 1900, riding the nationalist surge of the South African War, doubled authorised strength to thirty-eight battleships, twenty large cruisers, and thirty-eight smaller cruisers—a permanent “risk fleet” that would make attack by even the strongest naval power “a risky undertaking for the aggressor.” Novellen in 1906, 1908, and 1912 accelerated size, pace, or capital-ship numbers. By 1908 the German Navy League claimed 1,018,590 members and a monthly journal, Die Flotte, of 375,000 circulation; nearly seven hundred lectures and exhibitions in seventy-eight towns drove public agitation. Tirpitz later told the Reichstag, as the Annual Register recorded, that the Navy Laws had supplied the only possible method of creating, with the funds at their disposal, the sea power they had created.
Fisher, Dreadnought, and redistribution
Britain answered under Sir John Fisher, First Sea Lord from October 1904. He scrapped scores of obsolescent vessels that “had no fighting value,” introduced a nucleus-crew system that kept reserve ships manned at about forty per cent of complement ready for instant mobilisation, and concentrated British naval power in home waters, shifting the centre of gravity from the Mediterranean toward the North Sea. By 1907 the preponderant might of the British Navy lay in and around the North Sea—the Home Fleet with sixteen fully commissioned battleships and eight in reserve, the Atlantic Fleet relocated toward Dover.
Fisher’s most dramatic stroke was HMS Dreadnought—the first all-big-gun battleship—laid down in October 1905 and commissioned in December 1906 after little more than a year. Armed with ten 12-inch guns against the four heavy guns of a typical pre-dreadnought, turbine-powered and capable of 21 knots, she rendered every existing battleship obsolete at a stroke. The gamble nullified Britain’s overwhelming pre-dreadnought superiority, but Fisher calculated that British industrial capacity would outbuild any rival in the new class. For a few years he was proved right: in 1906–07 Britain’s naval superiority still far exceeded the requirements of the two-power standard. Germany’s Novelle of 1906 was modest; that of 1908, after the second Moroccan crisis and the Daily Telegraph affair, accelerated replacement and authorised the first German dreadnoughts—Nassau, Westfalen, Rheinland, and the large cruiser Blücher among them. The Navy League pressed for a seventeenth battleship and for ships equal in power to those of other nations.
The 1909 scare, conversations, and the approach to war
The Anglo-German naval race entered its most acute phase in 1908–09. Early in 1908 Berlin revamped goals toward a grand total of fifty-eight battleships instead of the thirty-eight of 1900; Admiralty intelligence then reported secret acceleration of dreadnought construction. Estimates predicted Germany with seventeen—or even twenty-one—dreadnoughts by 1912 against Britain’s eighteen; the two-power standard “would be swept away, and possibly Britain with it.” Fisher and the Board demanded six new dreadnoughts for 1909–10 instead of the usual four. The radical wing of the Liberal government—David Lloyd George as Chancellor and Winston Churchill as President of the Board of Trade—resisted, arguing that the intelligence was exaggerated and the cost unaffordable. For months the government was racked by a major crisis; Fisher leaked to the Conservative press; the opposition and public took up the slogan “We want eight and we won’t wait!” Asquith’s government finally capitulated. As Churchill later recorded in The World Crisis: the Admiralty had demanded six; the economists offered four; “we finally compromised on eight”—four laid down at once, four “contingent” later in the year. The 1909 estimates were the largest in British history to that point; the margin was reaffirmed in practice if not in name.
Naval conversations with France, the Haldane mission to Germany, and intermittent “naval holiday” proposals—Churchill’s later advocacy among them—failed to arrest the competition. By 1914 the High Seas Fleet forced concentration of British strength in the North Sea; the doctrine of command had become a two-power struggle with one principal rival. When the July crisis broke, the Fleet that had been concentrated for a test mobilisation was held at war stations. On Churchill’s instruction Prince Louis of Battenberg told the ships not to disperse; a public communiqué under the heading “British Naval Measures” announced that the First Fleet at Portland would not disperse for manœuvre leave. On 30 July the Fleet passed the Dover Straits by night to its war stations. At eleven on the night of 4 August—midnight German time—the war telegram “Commence hostilities against Germany” flashed to ships and establishments under the White Ensign worldwide. The outbreak of the Great War found British command of the sea already disposed for the North Sea struggle that the race had made inevitable.
Dogger Bank, Jutland, blockade, and armistice
In war the doctrine was tested by fleet action and by distant blockade. On 24 January 1915, about the Dogger Bank, Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty’s battle-cruiser force brought Rear-Admiral Hipper’s German battle cruisers to action—the first engagement in which Dreadnought-type capital ships fought one another with heavy guns at long range. The armoured cruiser Blücher was sunk; the German battle cruisers, damaged and on fire, escaped; Beatty’s flagship Lion was crippled. Signalling confusion after Lion was disabled turned the squadron onto Blücher and let Hipper’s heavy ships get clear—an incomplete victory that nonetheless, as Corbett judged, demonstrated the efficacy of the new Grand Fleet distribution after the Yorkshire coast raid. Churchill told the House that Dogger Bank had established the superiority of British guns and shooting.
On 31 May and the night following, off Jutland, the Grand Fleet under Admiral Sir John Jellicoe and the High Seas Fleet under Vice-Admiral Scheer met in the greatest naval battle since Trafalgar. Beatty and Hipper opened the action; the main fleets closed in evening mist; Scheer, finding himself face to face with the whole Grand Fleet, extricated himself by practised battle-turns under destroyer smoke and forced a passage home. No second Trafalgar followed. Yet when Sir Julian Corbett summed the purely strategical result, Scheer had failed to cut off and overwhelm part of the British advanced forces, and Jellicoe had increased the Grand Fleet’s margin of superiority as a combative force, a defence against invasion, and an instrument of blockade. British control of the North Sea remained unbroken. Command need not mean the annihilation of every enemy ship; it meant that the enemy could not use the sea for invasion or for breaking the economic cordon, while Britain could move armies and sustain the island and the empire. The Battle of Jutland left the strategic condition of command intact.
Through 1917–18 the same condition underwrote the land war. Newbolt’s naval history insisted that the final collapse of Central Europe was mainly the fruit of command of the sea and economic strangulation, of which the Allied counter-offensive was the last expression. When the Armistice of 11 November 1918 was signed, its naval conditions consummated that grip: surrender of all submarines, fifty destroyers, eight light cruisers, six battle-cruisers, and ten battleships; the High Seas Fleet transferred into Allied custody—surface ships to the Forth and then Scapa Flow, submarines off Harwich. The terms were tantamount to complete surrender at sea as on land. The cost of the long doctrine had been fiscal and diplomatic: dreadnought estimates, German enmity, subordination of other stations to the North Sea, and the political crises of 1909 and after. Yet for a state whose food, raw materials, and imperial communications all moved by water, no alternative strategy presented itself. From Mackinder’s shield and spear through Tirpitz’s risk fleet, Fisher’s redistribution, the race to 1914, and the tests of Dogger Bank and Jutland to the Armistice naval clauses, command of the sea remained the condition of British survival as a world power.

concepts/constitutional-monarchy.title: Constitutional Monarchy
concepts/constitutional-monarchy.content:
Constitutional Monarchy
Constitutional monarchy in late Victorian and Edwardian Britain meant a Crown that reigned as the symbol of national unity and continuity while ministers exercised the surviving royal prerogatives and the sovereign stood aloof from party. Influence replaced command. Popularity rested on neutrality, private virtue, and public ceremonial rather than on the old politics of “the King’s friends.” The Crown remained the pledge of national continuity, tempering the evils of absolute party government; such prerogatives as were not dead were carried out by ministers, while royal influence still ran through every branch of the State.
Development
Victoria and the doctrine of aloofness
The transformation was under way when Victoria came to the throne. William IV in 1830 had feared a hostile London demonstration at the Mansion House; his death in 1837 evoked no national mourning. Victoria, unknown to the people at her accession, had Lord Melbourne’s political advice in the early years of the reign. Her marriage in 1840 brought the Prince Consort, who studied the politics of the day with great industry, spoke openly to ministers on all subjects, and saw quickly that if monarchy was to rise in popularity it could only be by the sovereign leading a good life and keeping quite aloof from party. The days of a profligate court and of royal partisanship were past; the royal influence was to succeed the royal prerogative.
The Prince Consort did for the Crown what Wellington did for the House of Lords. Just as the Duke saw that the Lords must give up setting themselves against the national will strongly expressed, so the Prince saw that the Crown could no longer exercise those legal rights for which George III had fought. Like the Lords, the Crown became a checking and regulating, rather than a moving, force. It remained the pledge and symbol of the unity and continuity of the national life, tempering the evils of absolute party government. Such of the royal prerogatives as were not dead must be carried out by ministers. That doctrine—aloofness from partisanship, private virtue in place of court intrigue, ceremonial presence without party command—became the working theory of the Victorian monarchy and the inheritance of her successors.
Party government under the Crown
The Crown’s neutrality mattered because government itself had become party government. The orator who could sway multitudes was checked by the superior power of party organisation; yet the party organiser and political “boss” could as easily become a curse to representative institutions. Patronage became a method for keeping a party in power; the promise of rewards and spoils enabled an opposition to defeat the Government and obtain office. In England it had become practically impossible for a man to take any serious part in politics except by becoming part of the machine: an independent attitude meant isolation. A troublesome critic might be bought with office, a legal appointment, or a peerage. When public interest sank to “backing your candidate,” or lower still to mercenary calculation, the danger was the indifference of the average honest citizen—the warning John Stuart Mill had given against leaving politics to the politicians.
The Crown did not break that machine; it tempered its absolutism. Great as royal influence might be in the social life of the wealthier classes, it did not operate in the casting of votes at parliamentary elections. No one seriously suspected the King of desiring Liberal or Tory victories; that neutrality was the surest guarantee of continued popularity. The permanent Conservative majority in the Lords acted on the assumption that a Liberal ministry did not represent the will of the people—at variance with democratic theory and in contradiction to the constitutional practice of the Crown. The sovereign’s role was not to choose a party programme but to stand outside the spoils system.
Republicanism, Jubilee, and popular pageantry
Republicanism had a brief working-class Radical vogue in the late 1870s and early 1880s. Charles Bradlaugh was its chief exponent; Joseph Chamberlain and Sir Charles Dilke were regarded as Republicans before they entered Gladstone’s ministry in 1880. The movement waned before Bradlaugh’s death; he came to feel that agitation for an ideal form of government was less fruitful than agitation against class privilege, and in his last dozen years his work went mainly to reforms within the Constitution. With the rise of Socialism in England in 1884–5 and the Queen’s Jubilee in 1887, republicanism became utterly moribund. Nothing save an attempt by the sovereign to take a definite side in party politics, or a notorious lapse from the morals required of persons in office of State, seemed likely to revive it.
The Jubilee of 1887 marked the beginning of the popular revival in pageantry and official ceremonial—a parallel to the earlier ritual revival in the Church of England and the processions of revived Roman Catholicism. By gratifying the common human instinct for spectacle the monarchy gained the popular affections. The Whigs had scoffed at pageants; the earlier Puritans had proscribed ceremonial as idolatry. In the latter half of the nineteenth century England began to throw off the shackles of Puritanism and to lose all interest in Whiggery. The new democracy was neither coldly Deist nor austerely Republican. It showed no inclination to inaugurate a reign of “pure reason,” but boldly adopted symbolism and pageantry. Modern democracy did not desire that kings or priests should rule; it did require that on State occasions they should be clad in kingly and priestly robes.
Edward VII and the opening of the crisis
Victoria’s successors maintained that aloofness. Under Edward VII the Crown continued as a social and ceremonial presence of great weight among the wealthier classes, without operating as a party force at the polls. The fiscal and constitutional storm of 1909–10 tested the residual prerogative without overturning the Victorian settlement. Parliament opened on 16 February 1909 under Edward with a Speech already warning that old-age provision and the Navy would raise expenditure. Asquith insisted that finance must be the first business of the session. The Finance Bill introduced by David Lloyd George on 29 April—the People’s Budget—was rejected by the Lords on 30 November 1909 by 350 to 75, the first rejection of a finance measure since 1860. Lord Loreburn held that rejection was “legal, but not constitutional”: supply was the exclusive function of the Commons, and rejection invaded their privilege and the powers of the Crown.
The January–February 1910 general election left a hung Parliament—Liberals 275, Unionists 273, Labour 40, Irish Nationalists 82—with a united majority of about 124 for the ministry dependent on Irish and Labour votes. The Finance Bill then passed and was accepted by the Lords in April. The constitutional question—the Lords’ veto—now became the central issue. The death of Edward VII in May cast a temporary hush over party warfare. The lying-in-state and funeral (17–20 May) occupied the nation; Parliament paid its tributes; even industrial disputes were postponed. The Crown’s popularity as national symbol was displayed in mourning as in festival.
George V, Conference, and the peerage-creation guarantee
George V succeeded in the midst of deadlock. On 17 June 1910 the Constitutional Conference opened—an attempt by leading men from both sides to compose the differences between the Houses. On 23 June the Duke of Cornwall was created Prince of Wales and Earl of Chester. On 21 August a Royal Proclamation announced that the Coronation should take place in June 1911; on 26 August the King reviewed the Fleet in Torbay. The Accession Declaration Bill modified the form of Declaration required of a new Sovereign so as to remove offence to Roman Catholics while safeguarding the Protestant Succession. The Conference failed without public disclosure. The December 1910 election left the balance substantially as before (united majority about 126). The Liberal–Irish–Labour coalition now had a renewed mandate to reform the House of Lords through the struggle known as the People’s Budget and Parliament Act crisis.
Parliament was opened in state for the first time in the new reign by George V on 6 February 1911. Before delivering his Speech the King read and signed the Accession Declaration as established by the Act of 1910. Proposals would be submitted without delay “for settling the relations between the two Houses of Parliament, with the object of securing the more effective working of the Constitution.” The Parliament Bill embodied the Commons resolution of June 1907 (carried 432 to 147): that within a single Parliament the final decision of the Commons should prevail. Money Bills not passed unamended by the Lords within a month were to receive the Royal Assent notwithstanding; other bills passed by the Commons in three successive sessions were to become law in the third without the Lords’ assent; the maximum duration of a Parliament was cut from seven years to five. Leave to introduce was given on 22 February by 351 to 227. On 22 June 1911 the Coronation exhibited the ancient British Monarchy as the most popular and democratic: for three or four days party strife was suspended. The Imperial Conference received the King and the Dominion Premiers; the Royal visit to Scotland in July called forth a demonstration of loyalty.
When the Lords returned the measure with amendments the Commons refused, Asquith announced—as Grey and others had obtained from William IV in 1832—that he had received guarantees from the Crown that peers would be created in numbers sufficient to pass the Bill if it were again rejected. Behind the scenes the King’s pledge on peer creation was the residual prerogative used to resolve a deadlock between the Houses. Lord Midleton and the Earl of Rosebery pressed for a clear statement as to the “guarantees.” To avoid the making of some three or four hundred Liberal peers—in 1831 forty creations might have sufficed; by 1911 about four hundred were said to be required—Lord Lansdowne, following Wellington’s example, advised Conservative peers to refrain from opposition. Unionist peers divided between those who counselled surrender and the “die-hards” or “Halsburyites,” led by the Earl of Halsbury (100–150). On 10 August 1911 the Bill passed the Lords by 131 to 114; some 300 Unionist peers stayed away. The Royal Assent followed on 18 August. The threat, not the mass creation, had sufficed. The sovereign had acted on ministerial advice to make parliamentary government possible; he had not chosen a party programme. The permanent Conservative majority above the bar had long contradicted the Crown’s own practice of neutrality; the Parliament Act brought the second chamber into line with the constitutional monarchy that Victoria’s generation had defined—checking and regulating, not moving, when the national will was strongly expressed through the elected House.
War kingship
The same Crown that had underwritten the Parliament Act stood as the focus of national unity when European war broke in 1914. The spring of that year had already shown how thin was the line between constitutional agitation and force in Ireland: the Curragh incident, the Larne gun-running, and the Buckingham Palace Conference had divided Cabinet and Army while Europe moved toward war. Within twelve days the Cabinet that on 24 July was still debating Fermanagh and Tyrone found itself at war with the German Empire. On 2 August there was a patriotic demonstration before Buckingham Palace; a partial Moratorium was decreed by Royal Proclamation. The King held a Council at 4.30 p.m.; the Government took control of all wireless telegraphy; and the Admiralty called out the Naval Reserves. On the announcement of that last step a crowd of some 6,000 marched up the Mall to Buckingham Palace and sang the national anthems of Great Britain and France. On 3 August Cowes Regatta was abandoned by special desire of the King; Royal Proclamations authorised the Admiralty to requisition British ships and forbade the export of warlike stores. On 4 August an Order in Council placed the railways under Government control; British Army mobilisation was ordered by Proclamation; measures empowered the Crown to impose restrictions on aliens. At eleven o’clock at night—midnight by German time—the ultimatum to Germany expired. Along the Mall an immense concourse was singing “God save the King.” As the first stroke of Big Ben boomed out, the war telegram—“Commence hostilities against Germany”—was flashed to the ships and establishments under the White Ensign all over the world. The outbreak of the Great War found the constitutional monarchy not as a party arbiter but as the ceremonial and legal centre through which proclamations, Orders in Council, and the symbols of national resolve ran. Lord Kitchener’s acceptance of the War Office—not as a politician, his acceptance identifying him with no set of political opinions—illustrated the same settlement: the Crown and non-party national service standing above party rivalry while ministers exercised the prerogatives of mobilisation.
From Melbourne’s advice and the Prince Consort’s doctrine of aloofness, through the Jubilee revival of pageantry and the extinction of republicanism, through Edward VII’s death in the Budget crisis and George V’s peer-creation guarantee that broke the Lords’ absolute veto, to the Mall crowds of August 1914, the Crown’s path was consistent. Influence succeeded prerogative; neutrality secured popularity; residual prerogative was used, on ministerial advice, only to make parliamentary government work when the Houses deadlocked or the nation went to war. That was the constitutional monarchy of 1865–1919.

concepts/financial-administration.title: Financial Administration
concepts/financial-administration.content:
Financial Administration
Financial administration was the public counterpart of the private money-market: the machine by which the Crown, the Treasury, the House of Commons, the Banks of England and Ireland, the Paymaster-General, and the Comptroller and Auditor General turned revenue into authorised spend and spent money into audited accounts. Estimates, appropriation, custody, issue, accounting, and audit were treated as one chain. The document that bound needs, prior grants, and resources into a single plan for a future year was the Budget — a definite proposal for financing the business of the state on both sides of the account.
Development
Until 1854 England ran three financial years at once (estimates, appropriations, accounts). By 17 & 18 Vict. c. 94 s. 2 the year became 1 April–31 March for all purposes. Books closed on a cash basis at year-end: prompt treasury figures, less scientific cost information than the French accrual practice of keeping years open until all accruals were collected and paid. No expenditure was lawful except under parliamentary authority — annual appropriation or permanent statute. Commons had first controlled the total the Crown might take in tax, not the detail of spend; discretion in expenditure remained a Crown prerogative long after 1688. The modern principle that Parliament may determine purposes and manner of spending was complete by the late nineteenth century, yet the most characteristic English feature was how much discretion was still left to the Executive. Minute specification was refused because the Crown was thought better placed to decide details.
Two reforms made a general appropriation system possible. The Civil List separated the sovereign’s personal revenues from those of the state. William III’s grant with a £700,000 ceiling first put a Civil List on the statute book; George III surrendered most hereditary revenues for £800,000 a year; since William IV the sovereign received a salary covering personal and court expenses. The 1913–14 Finance Accounts showed a Civil List of £470,000 (privy purse £110,000; household salaries £125,800; household expenses £193,000; works £20,000; royal bounty £13,200; unappropriated £8,000), a permanent charge on the Consolidated Fund like debt interest and judges’ salaries. The Commissioners of Public Accounts in 1785 condemned earmarking — seventy-four charges on Customs, militia on the land tax, hereditary annuities on the Post Office — and recommended one fund into which every stream of revenue should flow and from which every service should be supplied. The Consolidated Fund Act of 1787 (27 Geo. III c. 13) created that fund; Irish revenues were similarly treated in 1816 and the two funds united.
The Fund stood to the credit of the Exchequer at the Bank of England and the Bank of Ireland (Scotch banks received and remitted in rotation). In 1834 revenues were ordered paid into the two banks to the Exchequer account. The banks were mere bankers of the Government: they received and paid to officers charged with settling obligations, taking the place of the old Teller and the three-lock chest.
No tax or expenditure was considered unless recommended from the Crown. Standing Orders 66 and 68 (early eighteenth century) barred petitions or motions for grants unless so recommended, and barred compounding Crown debts without official certificate. Members might not move to increase the Crown’s demand. The rare exception was an Address asking a special grant (monument, reward for service), still voted in committee. Permanent charges were Consolidated Fund Services; annually voted charges were Supply Services. Estimates, accompanying tables, and appropriation accounts covered only Supply. The 1913–14 Finance Accounts recapped Consolidated Fund issues of about £37.3 million against total Exchequer issues of £239.8 million — roughly one-sixth. Critics such as Harold Cox pointed out that public-office annuities, Queen’s Colleges, Irish land purchase, and Indian Army Pension Deficiency were split between the Fund and Supply votes, so estimates understated the total cost of particular services. Supply, when voted, was still paid from the Consolidated Fund.
Every appropriation rested on a formal estimate — both a calculation of need and a formulated demand of the Executive on Parliament. Estimates were the act of the Ministry as a whole. Except Army and Navy (presented by those departments only after Treasury approval), they were submitted by the Treasury. In disputes the Treasury decided, subject to rare Cabinet appeal on large policy (social reform, army or navy increase). About 1 October the Treasury issued an Estimates Circular to accounting officers of the civil services (the 1912–13 circular of 2 October 1911, signed C. Hobhouse, is the specimen). Forms were due by 1 December, latest 13 January; if detail would be late, an approximate total by 15 December so the Chancellor could foresee the aggregate. Even an estimate no larger than last year’s had to be justified; “the habit of regarding each year’s estimate as the starting point for the next” was singled out for vigilance. Departmental estimates were largely a summation of items already approved by the Treasury during the year.
Estimates were classified into Army, Navy, Civil Services, and Revenue Departments. The Treasury itself was treated as a civil service. Civil Services fell into seven historical classes: Public Works and Buildings; Salaries and Expenses of Civil Departments; Law and Justice; Education, Science and Art; Foreign and Colonial Services; Non-effective and Miscellaneous; Old-age Pensions, Labour Exchanges, Insurance, etc. Revenue Departments were Customs and Excise, Inland Revenue, and the Post Office. Appropriations were by votes — 15 Army, 15 Navy, 120 Civil, 3 Revenue, 153 in all. Classification was by organisation unit, one appropriation per branch, United Kingdom/England distinguished from Scotland and Ireland, effective from non-effective. Quarters, buildings, stationery, and printing were centralised in the Office of Works and the Stationery Office. Vote totals (except Army and Navy) could not be exceeded without Parliament; subhead allotments might be transferred with Treasury sanction (virement). Army and Navy might transfer even between votes. T. Gibson Bowles attacked army and navy vote transfers as defeating appropriation and creating a “huge pooled fund”; the reply was that without virement departments would pad every vote. Safeguards were Treasury authority, visible accounts, report to Commons, and Public Accounts Committee review.
“Appropriations in aid” assigned miscellaneous extra receipts of a service — fees, fines, sale of property, and, in a special case, War Office recoveries from Indian, colonial, and Egyptian governments of over £2½ million — as an aid to the formal grant from the Consolidated Fund. Extra receipts so treated did not pass through Exchequer receipt and issue accounts, though they were rigidly accounted for. Estimated extra receipts were the maximum usable; excess was surrendered as miscellaneous Consolidated Fund income. Where receipts exceeded needs (the Mint), only enough was appropriated in aid to cover expenditure, plus a token vote of £10 or £100 so the estimate still came before Parliament. The present form dated from Public Accounts Committee observations of 1881 and the Public Accounts and Charges Act 1891. Applied first to Army and Navy, then gradually to civil votes, the device avoided overstating revenue and expenditure (the Treasury in 1881 put the inflation at more than £4 million a year) and gave departments credit for realising receipts. Gross expenditure and appropriations in aid both appeared in the estimates. American observers still treated the practice as a breach of Consolidated Fund unity: net figures hid activity.
Financial power now resided wholly in the Commons. The Lords’ claim to amend money bills ended in the crisis over Lloyd George’s Budget of 1909 and the Parliament Act 1911. A Money Bill, certified by the Speaker, if sent up at least a month before the end of the session and not passed unamended within a month, was presented for Royal Assent without Lords consent. “Money Bill” covered taxation, charges on the Consolidated Fund or money provided by Parliament, supply, appropriation, receipt, custody, issue or audit of public money, and loans — not local rates. The Speaker’s certificate was conclusive and not questionable in any court. The People’s Budget struggle had shown how fiercely the financing of social reform and naval power could divide the constitution; the machinery of estimates and supply then ran on Commons rules alone.
Committees of Supply and Ways and Means were appointed at the beginning of the session (committee of the whole, not a select committee). Supply was first order on Thursdays. Not more than twenty days before 5 August were allotted to annual army, navy, and civil estimates including votes on account. On the last day but one the chairman put remaining class totals; on the last day the Speaker put outstanding reports. Authorization of expenditure (voting of supply) was distinguished from appropriation of funds (ways and means). Committee of Supply approved votes by resolution; the House agreed; Committee of Ways and Means voted the funds; only then was a bill drafted. Money was not available until the appropriation bill was signed, except votes on account (credit for use after 1 April while the session continued). Excess votes regularised overspending after the fact; votes of credit covered war or unforeseen large needs. The House in practice adopted estimates as submitted. Supply days were the opposition’s opportunity to debate policy and administration, not to recast figures; closure at twenty days forced remaining grants. The 1902–03 Select Committee on National Expenditure, barred from criticising policy, found Supply discussion partisan and more apt to urge increase than decrease. In 1912 a Select Committee on Estimates was established — scrutiny of detail without sharing ministerial responsibility for the programme of work.
Legislative control required a guardian of issues. Under the old Exchequer the Auditor held one of three keys; in 1811 Lord Grenville as Auditor refused a £500,000 issue despite five Lords of the Treasury, for want of Crown authority during George III’s incapacity. In 1834 Clerk of the Pells and Auditor were abolished and a Comptroller General of the Receipt and Issue of the Exchequer created. The Exchequer and Audit Departments Act 1866 consolidated issue-control and audit in one officer: Comptroller and Auditor General. The Treasury first obtained “credits” on the Exchequer. For Consolidated Fund services two Lords of the Treasury requisitioned the C&AG, who if satisfied granted credit by warrant. For Supply a royal order had to precede the requisition, because supply was granted to the Sovereign. Credit did not move cash. Issues went only to principal accountants: the Comptroller of the National Debt and the chief cashiers of the two banks (debt service); the accountants-general of the revenue departments; and the Paymaster-General, general paymaster for military and civil services. Principal accountants requisitioned the Treasury, which ordered the banks to transfer from credits to their accounts. The C&AG did not intervene at this second stage.
The Paymaster-General was banker, not accounting officer: he paid orders drawn by departmental accounting officers, satisfied as to form and supporting documents. He kept a separate book account for each civil vote and consolidated Army and Navy accounts, but one cash balance. Pay offices were consolidated 1830–56 to reduce idle balances. A Treasury minute of 21 February 1885 described his sources: extra receipts as appropriations in aid; Treasury Chest Fund; Civil Contingencies Fund; departmental deposit funds; and daily Consolidated Fund issues. He exhausted outside cash before drawing the Fund. Departmental accounting officers examined and settled claims and drew on the Paymaster. They were personally liable and were not bonded.
Expenditure of appropriations was not mandatory. Money was granted to the Crown and placed at ministers’ disposal; statute did not say “You shall spend so much.” The Treasury was the organ through which the Crown decided how far to use the grant. Theoretically every expenditure needed Treasury sanction. Normal continuing spend was taken as sanctioned unless the Treasury ordered retrenchment; any new clerk, new work, or departure required express sanction even if already in the printed estimate. Passing an estimate did not authorise an increased establishment; the Audit Office would not pass the spend without a separate Treasury letter. Control was over incurring liabilities — programme, plant, organisation, personnel, equipment — not over individual vouchers. The Treasury was technically a board. The Lord High Treasurer’s office had been put in commission in 1714; real authority passed to the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The First Lord was often Prime Minister and did not manage the office. The Chancellor was assisted by a Permanent Secretary and a Permanent Financial Secretary, both remaining through changes of ministry. The financial secretary’s staff grouped departments into seven divisions, each under a principal clerk who lived with those departments’ papers all year.
Civil works were concentrated in the Office of Works and Public Buildings: planning and construction of civil buildings at home and of diplomatic and consular buildings abroad; alteration, maintenance, and repair; royal palaces, parks, ancient monuments; renting, fixtures, furniture, fuel. No building was authorised except on the demand of the using service, presented not to Parliament but to Works, which decided whether to proceed after Treasury scrutiny — a single works programme. Estimates showed for each work original total, revised total, probable spend to date, amount voted this year, further amount to complete, and amount asked for next year. Military and naval works stayed with War Office and Admiralty. His Majesty’s Stationery Office supplied stationery and printing to all departments, military and naval as well as civil. It originated in Burke’s Administrative Reform Act of 1782. By 1914 it was a purchasing, contracting, distributing, and selling department with a turnover of £897,670. Departments submitted no stationery estimates. A single vote (1914–15 net £1,069,272 after £168,000 appropriations in aid) was accounted for under sixteen subheads. Until recently the lump under each subhead was available to all services; the Controller recommended, and the 1911 Select Committee on Publications adopted, allotment to departments on the basis of past spend, not to be exceeded without Treasury approval.
For a hundred and sixty years Commons had laboured under the illusion that it could control expenditure by putting checks upon issue from the Exchequer instead of ascertaining how the money had been spent. Tudor–Stuart Exchequer audit “limped leisurely” — in 1782 accounts twenty and thirty years old, some back to William III, were still open. Pitt created a Board of Audit that reported to the Treasury. Sir James Graham at the Admiralty in 1831 obtained an annual Navy Appropriation Account — the model of later appropriation accounts. The Public Monies Committee of 1856–57 “knocked on the head once for all” issue-watching as sufficient control. A standing order of 1861 (Gladstone) created the Committee of Public Accounts; the 1866 Act created the independent auditor. The C&AG was an officer of Parliament, appointed by the Crown, holding during good behaviour, removable only on address of both Houses, salary a Consolidated Fund charge — the same securities as judges. Yet the Treasury appointed his clerks and prescribed how accounts were kept and rendered. He audited appropriation accounts, might disallow items, and was expected to comment on unwise or extravagant expenditure, not merely legality. The Standing Committee of Public Accounts (originally eleven members, later fifteen; chairman by usage from the Opposition) examined those accounts. C&AG and a principal Treasury officer always attended. Functions extended to wisdom, faithfulness, and economy, to receipts as well as issues, and to the form of estimates. Committee recommendations had no force until the Treasury answered in a minute. The 1911 Epitome of the Reports from the Committees of Public Accounts 1857 to 1910 was the working code of accounting method.
Parliament received two sets of figures: Exchequer receipts and issues, and audited receipts and expenditure. Finance Accounts of the United Kingdom dated from 1802. From 1802 to 1866 the House learned only issues (imprests), not departmental expenditure. The 1913–14 volume was a compact cash statement of 101 small-octavo pages (ordered printed 25 May; the principal table as a special return 27 April). That return was the basis of the Chancellor’s budget proposals. The 1913–14 income-and-expenditure account showed tax and non-tax income totalling £198,242,897 against Consolidated Fund and Supply issues totalling £197,492,969, surplus £749,928. Appropriation Accounts were the C&AG’s audited statements of spend against votes, available many months later. There was no single general report that brought the two families of figures into one surveyed statement.
A budget was not a separate operation but the means of surveying both sides of the account together so that deficit or surplus was visible. Since the Revolution an annual statement “partaking of the nature of a budget” had been made; the phrase that the Chancellor “opens the budget” was in force soon after 1750 (from French bougette, a leather bag of papers). For 1914–15 three documents did the work: the Financial Statement 1914–1915 as laid before the House when the Chancellor opened the Budget on 4 May 1914 (seven pages — “in effect the real budget”); the Budget Speech of that day; and a six-page statement explaining rate changes. Tables compared 1913–14 estimated versus issued expenditure (Consolidated Fund £37.3 million issued; Supply £160.2 million; grand total issues £197.5 million; plus £4.4 million chargeable to capital — telegraphs, telephone transfer including National Telephone purchase, Post Office London Railway, Land Registry — total State responsibility £201.9 million); 1913–14 revenue versus budget (taxes £163.0 million against £160.0 million estimated; non-tax £35.2 million; total £198.2 million); and 1914–15 estimated expenditure (Supply up £9.9 million, of which Navy +£5.2 million, Civil +£2.1 million, Post Office +£1.8 million; total £206.0 million plus £5.3 million capital).
Ten working principles summarised the machine: a budget considering all needs at once; executive preparation of the plan; opposition opportunity to force answers in committee of the whole; residual responsibility remaining with the executive (Commons rules forbade motions to increase); no spend until Parliament approved, then rigid accounting; parliamentary audit by a C&AG with judicial tenure; a Public Accounts Committee chaired from the opposition; a Treasury not coordinate with spending departments but superior, acting as Parliament’s agent; distinction of votes, subheads, and supporting details, with virement under Treasury and audit safeguards; appropriations not mandatory — spend only on Treasury authorisation.

concepts/free-trade-and-tariff-reform.title: Free Trade and Tariff Reform
concepts/free-trade-and-tariff-reform.content:
Free Trade and Tariff Reform
Free trade was the mid-Victorian orthodoxy of British commercial policy: the open import of food and manufactures without protective duties, and the belief that cheap bread and open markets served both the industrial nation and the consumer. Tariff reform was Joseph Chamberlain’s challenge to that orthodoxy—a programme of imperial preference and, if need be, retaliatory duties—which split the Unionist party, dominated electoral politics from 1903 to the Liberal landslide of 1906, and returned as the Unionist alternative to Free-Trade finance in the years of the People’s Budget and the struggle with the Lords.
Development
Cobdenite free trade had become almost a national creed after the repeal of the Corn Laws. By the early twentieth century, however, Germany and the United States had risen as protected industrial competitors, while self-governing Colonies offered preferential rates to British goods and asked for reciprocity. The orthodoxy that forbade Britain either to favour her Colonies or to retaliate when foreign Powers penalised them for doing so was still the “established fiscal policy of this country”—and it was precisely that policy which the Colonial Secretary set out to reopen.
On 15 May 1903 Chamberlain, Colonial Secretary and the most formidable Radical-turned-Imperialist of his generation, told his Birmingham constituents that his mind ran more on the future of the Empire than on smaller domestic controversies. The time had come, he said, deliberately to adopt or reject a policy of imperial unification. Preferential tariffs were the Colonies’ chosen instrument. A South African colonial conference had recommended a 25 per cent preference on dutiable goods; Australia and New Zealand had accepted the principle; Canada, already giving 25 and then 33⅓ per cent preference without equivalent, was ready to go further if Britain allowed a drawback on the shilling corn duty. Germany, treating Canada as a separate country, had penalised Canadian goods to deter other Colonies from following Canada’s example. Britain faced two alternatives: maintain “in all its severity” the interpretation of Free Trade placed on Cobden and Bright by a “small remnant of Little Englanders of the Manchester school,” and so remain precluded from favouring or protecting the Colonies; or refuse any purely technical definition of Free Trade, seek free interchange with the world, and yet “recover our freedom, resume that power of negotiation and, if necessary, retaliation whenever our own interests or our relations between our Colonies and ourselves are threatened by other people.” Make a mistake in Imperial policy, he warned, and it was irretrievable. He believed in a British Empire self-sustaining against the competition of all its rivals—not in a Little England dependent on the mercy of those who envied its prosperity.
The same day Arthur Balfour, Prime Minister, was defending the repeal of the corn duty to a deputation led by Henry Chaplin. He denied that the duty had ever been intended as protective; a preferential scheme was not yet possible, and until the mass of the people moved, a trifling food duty would only be the shuttlecock of opposing parties. The simultaneous appearance of these two positions—the Colonial Secretary calling for a revolution in fiscal policy while the Prime Minister dismantled the very tax that might have been its starting point—produced in the public mind “a condition of astonishment and perplexity bordering on stupefaction.” Chamberlain’s prestige as an Imperial statesman had never stood higher after his South African tour; yet within the Unionist party the divisions were immediate. Theoretical Protectionists, moderate “fiscal reformers,” and Free Traders separated at once. Vigorous sections discerned the danger of perpetual food taxes and the taint of Protection. The Spectator emerged as an energetic opponent; Liberals and the Liberal press opposed with almost complete unanimity. Rival fiscal organisations formed; Free Trade Unionist M.P.s met; Balfour refused a general fiscal discussion in the Commons.
The fissure proved irreparable. In September 1903, after Cabinet councils, Balfour’s pamphlet, and the Fiscal Blue-book, Chamberlain resigned to campaign openly, as did Mr. Ritchie and Lord George Hamilton; the Duke of Devonshire, Liberal Unionist leader, also left the Cabinet. Balfour’s Sheffield declarations and new appointments left the Unionists openly divided into three factions: Chamberlainite Tariff Reformers, Balfourite moderates who favoured a flexible but undefined “fiscal reform,” and Unionist Free Traders—later organised as the Unionist Free Food League and the Unionist Free Trade Club—who adhered to orthodox Cobdenite principles. Chamberlain threw himself into a nationwide speaking tour of extraordinary intensity: Glasgow and Greenock, Newcastle, South Wales, and, closing his first campaign on 18 January 1904 at the Guildhall in London, where four thousand hearers admitted by ticket drowned a band struggling to perform the National Anthem. Free imports, he argued, were not free exchange; Germany and the United States were rising as exporters while commercial powers that lost their industrial base—Holland, Venice, the Hanseatic cities—had decayed. The Tariff Reform League, founded in 1903, became a formidable propaganda machine; Devonshire, the Spectator, and Free Trade Unionists fought back. Asquith, Ritchie, Lord Spencer, Austen Chamberlain, and Rosebery filled the platforms on both sides. The fiscal question engrossed the public mind through 1904–5 “to such an extent as very perceptibly to draw off interest from” other questions, and reunited Liberals who had been disunited for twenty years on Home Rule. By-elections told against any tampering with free trade in food and raw materials: at Stalybridge in January 1905 the Liberal majority rose from 81 in 1900 to 951, a result attributed in cotton Lancashire to the conviction that free trade in the great industry would be prejudicially affected. Chinese labour in the Transvaal—denounced as “Chinese slavery”—the Education Act of 1902, and Irish embarrassments after Wyndham’s resignation compounded Unionist weakness. By the autumn of 1905 articles in the Times and the Daily Telegraph pointed to the Premier’s resignation.
On 4 December 1905 Balfour resigned. The King invited Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman to form a government, which he did by 10 December: Asquith at the Exchequer, Grey at the Foreign Office, Haldane at the War Office, Lloyd George at the Board of Trade, Morley at the India Office, and John Burns—the first working-class man to enter a British Cabinet—at the Local Government Board. The election campaign that followed was judged the most exciting and startling since 1880, if not since 1832. The late Ministers were arraigned for reckless extravagance, misjudgment of South African affairs, Chinese labour, the endowment of denominational education, and “crude and self-contradictory ‘fiscal reforms.‘” Liberals claimed to be the real Free Traders and apostles of economic progress. Among issues the fiscal question was probably the most important, especially in rural constituencies; next came Chinese labour; then modification of the Education Act of 1902. Devonshire, writing on 29 December 1905 to the Unionist Free Trade Club, declared the Tariff Reform League’s proposals “indistinguishable from pure Protection,” and that Free Trade Unionists should support Free Trade candidates irrespective of party. Chamberlain attacked the new ministry as a Home Rule and Little Englander Government which must exist, if at all, by Irish votes. Campbell-Bannerman declared that “Protection was immoral, oppressive and corrupting.” At Derby on 3 January Chamberlain claimed a million able-bodied male paupers under Free Trade—a misuse of the poor-law figures which Free Trade economists immediately challenged. Asquith at Perth insisted Ministers could not take steps that would raise the cost of food and lower the standard of living.
Polling for the general election of 1906 began on 12 January and ended on 13 February with Orkney and Shetland. Manchester and Salford were swept clear of Unionists; Balfour himself was defeated in East Manchester, for which he had sat since 1885, by 6,403 to 4,423. London, Tyneside, the West Riding, Glasgow (five of seven divisions), and the agricultural districts all swung against the Unionists. Lyttelton fell at Leamington; Chaplin at Sleaford; Brodrick at Guildford; Sir W. Hart Dyke, “Father of the House,” at Dartford to a Labour candidate. Birmingham alone among great industrial centres held solid for Unionism. In Greenwich and King’s Lynn the Unionist vote split between Free Trader and Tariff Reformer; Lord Hugh Cecil came bottom of the poll at Greenwich. Final results: Liberals 377, Labour 53 (29 from the Labour Representation Committee sitting as an independent party), Nationalists 83—Ministerialist total 513—against Conservatives 132 and Liberal Unionists 25, Opposition 157. The Liberal and Labour majority over all others was 134; the prediction that the Government would depend on Nationalist votes was falsified. Within the Opposition a Times analysis counted about 109 Chamberlainite Tariff Reformers, 32 Balfourites, and only 11 Unionist Free Fooders (later revised by Devonshire to 102, 36, and 16). Wales returned no Unionist; Scotland became predominantly Liberal. Campbell-Bannerman reaffirmed Free Trade as the settled doctrine of the Government; Asquith, as Chancellor, warned that a 2s. corn duty would mean a rise of about 2½d. on the four-pound loaf.
Free trade thus remained the commercial policy of the new Parliament, and the victory cleared the way for a decade of Liberal social legislation financed under Free-Trade assumptions—old-age pensions, progressive taxation, national insurance—while Tariff Reform survived as the chief item in the Conservative programme. Clayton, writing while these measures were still new, observed that legislative proposals for social reform were treated as non-party questions, and that Tariff Reform “was adopted and is advocated mainly as a social reform, a cure for industrial evils, and the misery of unemployment.” The two paths of Edwardian betterment stood in competition: Free-Trade finance taxing great incomes and land values for pensions and the Navy, versus imperial preference and duties on foreign manufactures framed as a remedy for industrial distress.
That competition returned with full force when Lloyd George introduced the Finance Bill of 1909—the People’s Budget—to fund old-age pensions and naval construction. Austen Chamberlain, moving rejection on 7 June, indicated that the Opposition alternative was Tariff Reform. Lord Curzon at Leeds in October called the Budget’s socialistic feature its intention to “side-track” Tariff Reform. When the House of Lords rejected the Bill by 350 to 75 on 30 November 1909, the constitutional crisis joined the financing of pensions and the Navy to free trade against Tariff Reform and to the Irish demand that Home Rule no longer be blocked by an hereditary chamber. The January 1910 election was fought with unexampled vigour—about 250 meetings by Peers in five weeks; the Tariff Reform League and Free Trade Union spending lavishly—and turned on the Lords’ rejection, Tariff Reform versus Free Trade, and Home Rule. The result was a hung Parliament—Liberals 275, Unionists 273, Labour 40, Irish Nationalists 82. The Finance Bill then passed and was accepted by the Lords in April 1910. Through the Constitutional Conference Free Trade Unionists urged that food taxes be postponed; the Morning Post ranked Tariff Reform above the constitutional issue. At Mile End on 21 November Lloyd George put the popular case: the Government needed money for defence and social reforms by taxing great incomes, while the Lords demanded that the burden fall on the bread and meat of the people. The Attorney-General warned that Tariff Reform, once imposed, could never be repealed if the Lords controlled finance. The December 1910 election left the balance substantially unchanged; the Parliament Act of 1911 stripped the Lords of absolute veto; Free-Trade finance and social reform advanced under Asquith and Lloyd George while Unionism retained Tariff Reform as its unfinished imperial and industrial programme.
By the outbreak of the Great War the electorate of 1906 had long since refused food taxes and a general tariff, yet the argument between open markets and imperial preference had not been settled inside the Unionist party or as a permanent settlement of commercial policy. Free trade remained the settled practice of Liberal government and the commercial face of mid-Victorian orthodoxy; Tariff Reform remained the commercial cement of Empire in the minds of Chamberlain’s followers, and the competing social cure for unemployment on the Unionist benches. The fiscal question that opened on 15 May 1903 thus framed a decade of party realignment, electoral upheaval, and the financing of the social state—without ever wholly leaving the unfinished business of Edwardian politics.
J. A. Hobson, writing Imperialism: A Study before Chamberlain’s 1903 campaign had yet remade Unionist politics, already treated protection and imperialism as allies rather than alternatives. Part I, chapter V—“Imperialism based on Protection”—argued that increased military and naval outlay was best read as insurance premiums for existing colonial markets and as current outlay on new ones. Any considerable, calculable increase of revenue by indirect taxation meant the abandonment of Free Trade: duties on necessaries and prime conveniences of life and trade had a protective effect whether or not they were labelled revenue. Imperialist finance was not yet prepared to admit the name; preparatory steps found other names—a countervailing duty on beet-sugar posing as an instrument of Free Trade, a tax on prison-made goods followed by protection against all “sweated” foreign industry, export duties on coal, military necessity as the most formidable mask (home food supply and a rural recruiting stock), bounties in the shipbuilding trade, and, above all, “Free Trade within the Empire,” a protectionist tariff masquerading as an Imperial Zollverein. Chamberlain’s attempt of 1897 was already named as a witness; the South African war merely precipitated the policy. “In many ways it thus appears that Protection is the natural ally of Imperialism.”
The economic root, stated in the following chapter as the taproot of Imperialism, was the desire of organised industrial and financial interests to secure, at the public expense and by the public force, private markets for surplus goods and surplus capital. Everywhere appeared excessive powers of production and capital in search of investment: more goods than could be sold at a profit, more capital than could find remunerative employment at home. Surplus savings that could not assist current consumption either lay idle or sought speculative use abroad “under the protection of the Government.” If the consuming public had raised its standard of consumption with every rise of productive power, there would have been no excess of goods or capital clamorous to use Imperialism in order to find markets. A Liberal party committed to militant Imperialism, Hobson added, was in a hopeless dilemma: it had neither the pluck nor the principle to renounce Imperialism or to insist that the classes who sought to benefit by it should pay for it by direct taxation on property. Protection thus fed imperialism, and imperialism fed protection—the two policies locking surplus capital into protected fields overseas and into a fiscal system that would hide its exclusive side under imperial loyalty.

concepts/house-of-lords.title: House of Lords
concepts/house-of-lords.content:
House of Lords
The House of Lords was the hereditary second chamber of the United Kingdom Parliament: a body of peers whose power to amend or reject Commons bills had long coexisted with the convention that money bills belonged to the Lower House. In the decades after 1865 that balance became the central constitutional problem of British politics whenever a Liberal ministry commanded the Commons but faced a permanent Conservative majority above the bar. The chamber stood as a hereditary check on the elected House—revising, delaying, and, when a Liberal government was in power, destroying measures that the electors had returned a majority to pass. Great Britain remained unique in combining democratic forms with a second chamber of hereditary legislators; the democratic grievance against it was not merely hereditary membership but one-sided use of the veto.
Development
Liberal conflicts before the Edwardian crisis
Conflict between the Houses was not new. Over Irish Church disestablishment in 1869 a compromise was found and the Lords, on the whole, gave way. In 1871, when the Lords proposed to amend the Army Reform Bill abolishing purchase of commissions, Gladstone advised the Crown to cancel the royal warrant that made purchase legal and issue a new warrant ending the sale—so that rejection would only deprive officers of the compensation the bill awarded. The device completely worsted the Lords. In 1884 the Lords refused the rural labourers’ enfranchisement bill unless redistribution accompanied it; Gladstone yielded, and franchise and redistribution passed together as the Third Reform Act.
The most consequential pre-Edwardian collision was over Home Rule. Gladstone’s Second Home Rule Bill of 1893 passed the Commons by 301 to 267—the first Home Rule measure ever to clear the Lower House—and was rejected by the Conservative-dominated Lords by 419 to 41. With no statutory means of overriding the absolute veto, the bill was dead. Home Rule entered a decade of eclipse, and the Upper House became part of the Irish question itself: so long as peers could kill a Commons-passed Irish measure, Nationalist support for any Liberal ministry would demand not only a bill but a remedy for the chamber that had killed its predecessor.
One-sided veto after 1906
After the Liberal landslide of 1906—the election-1906-tariff-reform that returned a majority swollen by Labour and Irish Nationalist support—the Upper House rejected or heavily amended a series of Liberal measures. Education and licensing bills felt the weight of revision; there was no pretence of revising Conservative measures with the same severity. The permanent and overwhelming Conservative majority acted on the assumption that a Liberal ministry did not represent the will of the people—an assumption at variance with democratic theory and with the constitutional practice of the Crown. In June 1907 the Commons resolved, by 432 to 147, that the power of the other House to alter or reject bills must be so restricted by law that within a single Parliament the final decision of the Commons should prevail. That resolution was the seed of the Parliament Bill; between its adoption and the Act of 1911 came the Budget rejection, two general elections, and a failed joint conference.
The Budget of 1909 and the breach of convention
The crisis broke over finance. Parliament opened on 16 February 1909 under King Edward VII with a Speech already warning that old-age provision and the Navy would raise expenditure. Asquith insisted that finance must be the first business: social-reform had to be paid for, and the Old Age Pension Act was only the first instalment. On 29 April David Lloyd George, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, introduced the Finance Bill that became the People’s Budget—a “War Budget” against poverty. It proposed a 20 per cent tax on the unearned increment of land when sold; a halfpenny in the pound on the capital value of undeveloped land; a 10 per cent reversion duty on a landlord’s interest at lease expiry; increased death duties; and a super-tax on incomes above £5,000—proceeds to fund pensions and naval construction amid accelerating Anglo-German rivalry. Balfour declared that the force behind the Budget was “really Socialism.” Austen Chamberlain, moving rejection on second reading, indicated that the Opposition alternative was Tariff Reform.
By October independent Unionist peers were making the case for rejection. Lord Curzon at Leeds insisted that the Lords had only waived, never abandoned, the right to amend a Finance Bill, and had never waived the right of rejection—whether for tacking, as mischievous, or to refer principles to the people. After five months of Commons debate the Finance Bill went up to the Lords. On 30 November 1909, by 350 to 75, the House rejected it—the first rejection of a finance measure since 1860, and a breach of the convention, standing since the seventeenth century, that the Lords did not interfere with money bills. The Earl of Crewe, moving second reading, faced a resolution from the Marquess of Lansdowne asserting the Lords’ right to reject a Money Bill; Lansdowne argued that Commons privileges were now interpreted strictly, that “tacking” had increased, and that the Budget would merely be reserved for the approval of the people. The Lord Chancellor (Lord Loreburn) replied that rejection was “legal, but not constitutional”: supply was the exclusive function of the Commons, and rejection was a direct invasion of their privilege and the powers of the Crown. The conflict, he warned, could only end ultimately in one way.
Two elections and the Constitutional Conference
The Lords’ rejection forced a dissolution. The January–February 1910 election turned on the constitutional struggle opened by rejection of the Finance Bill, on Tariff Reform versus Free Trade, and on Home Rule. The result was a hung Parliament—Liberals 275, Unionists 273, Labour 40, Irish Nationalists 82—leaving the ministry dependent on Irish and Labour votes, with a united majority of about 124. The Finance Bill was passed promptly by the new Commons and accepted by the Lords in April 1910—the Peers having, as they claimed, referred it to the people and now bowed to the electoral result on that measure alone.
The constitutional question—the Lords’ veto—now became the central issue. Opposition speakers declared that there had never been a deadlock between the House of Lords and the country, and that Veto resolutions would reduce the Upper House to legislative impotence. The Attorney-General (Sir W. Robson) replied that if the Lords controlled finance they could control the Administration and force dissolutions; they would have unlimited power without responsibility; Tariff Reform, once imposed, could never be repealed if the Lords could stand in the way. The death of Edward VII in May cast a temporary hush over party warfare. On 17 June the Constitutional Conference opened—an attempt by leading men from both sides to compose the differences between the Houses without a further appeal to the constituencies. An influential section of Unionist Peers held that if they were to be deprived of their powers it should be done by the constituencies and not by a conference. Rumours later attributed the final disruption to Lords Lansdowne and Cawdor and to the numerical strength of majorities required on bills sent back after rejection. The Conference continued through summer and early autumn without public disclosure; its failure was welcomed by advanced Liberals, Labour, and the main body of the Nationalists.
On 18 November Asquith insisted that Dissolution was best got over at once: Liberal legislation did not get a fair chance, and the Lords only forced a Dissolution when Liberals were in office. Lloyd George, addressing 5,000 men at Mile End on 21 November, said the crisis had been precipitated by rejection of the Budget: the Government needed money for defence and social reforms by taxing great incomes, while the Lords demanded that the burden fall on the bread and meat of the people. The December 1910 election left the balance of parties substantially as before—a united majority of about 126. Unionist speakers insisted that the Parliament Bill was a dodge to smuggle through Home Rule. The Liberal–Irish–Labour coalition now had a renewed mandate to reform the House of Lords.
The Parliament Act, 1911
King George V opened his first Parliament on 6 February 1911 with a Speech promising proposals “for settling the relations between the two Houses of Parliament, with the object of securing the more effective working of the Constitution.” The Parliament Bill embodied the 1907 resolution. It declared that a Money Bill sent up by the Commons, if not passed unamended by the Lords within a month, should receive the Royal Assent without them; that any other bill passed by the Commons in three successive sessions should become law in the third session without the Lords’ assent; and that the maximum duration of a Parliament should fall from seven years to five. After two days’ debate, leave was given on 22 February by 351 to 227 to introduce the Bill.
In the Lords, Committee began on 28 June. The Earl of Cromer moved to transfer the decision on money bills from the Speaker to a Joint Committee; supported by Lansdowne and the Archbishop of Canterbury, it was carried by 183 to 44, but the Government refused it. Unionist peers divided between those who counselled surrender and the “die-hards” or “Halsburyites,” led by the Earl of Halsbury and numbering between 100 and 150 peers determined to reject or emasculate the Bill. When the Lords returned the measure with unacceptable amendments, Asquith announced—as in 1832—guarantees from the Crown that peers would be created in numbers sufficient to pass it. Lord Midleton and the Earl of Rosebery pressed for a clear statement as to the “guarantees.” To avoid some three or four hundred Liberal creations, Lansdowne—following the Duke of Wellington’s example—advised Conservative peers to refrain from opposition. On 10 August 1911 the Bill passed the Lords by 131 to 114; some 300 Unionist peers stayed away rather than vote against their leadership or join the die-hards. The Royal Assent followed on 18 August. Thereafter the Lords might delay ordinary legislation for two sessions, but not destroy it if the Commons persisted; money bills they could delay for a month only.
Peerage inflation and the permanent majority
The size of the House made packing difficult: in 1831 the creation of forty peerages might have sufficed against Tory opposition to the Reform Bill; by 1911 some four hundred were said to be needed for a Liberal working majority. Every Prime Minister from Melbourne onward added with generous hand—Melbourne forty-four (1835–41); Disraeli twenty-three across his ministries besides his own earldom; Gladstone fifty in four premierships; Campbell-Bannerman twenty in less than two years (1905–7); Asquith thirteen in his first year. Yet only a small minority of Liberal peers retained their allegiance: many whose titles were not more than six years old already voted with the Conservatives. Social popularity of titles endured even among those who denounced hereditary legislation.
Effect on Home Rule and the constitution
The Parliament Act permanently altered the British constitutional-monarchy. No Act of Parliament had been required to abolish the veto of the Crown on statutes; democratic public opinion had not proved strong enough to end the Lords’ veto on Liberal Commons bills, and therefore statute was required. Conservatives after 1911 preferred to reform the composition of the Upper House and make it a stronger and more representative assembly; Liberals preferred that its power of veto stay curtailed. The Act cleared the path for Home Rule, Welsh Church disestablishment, and other Liberal measures—including National Insurance—that the unreformed Lords would have blocked. The absolute veto that had killed the 1893 bill became a suspensory veto of two sessions. That change—itself won with Irish votes in the majorities of 124–126—made a Home Rule statute possible over the head of the Upper House and bound the Liberals, dependent on the Irish Party, to deliver it. The Third Home Rule Bill, introduced by Asquith on 11 April 1912, passed the Commons in each of the sessions 1912, 1913, and 1914 under the Parliament Act provisions; the real drama then unfolded outside Parliament, as Ulster Unionist resistance, the Covenant, the Ulster Volunteer Force, and mutual arming drove the irish-home-rule-crisis toward civil conflict until European war suspended the unfinished settlement. Finance, once the exclusive preserve of the Commons, had been the weapon that broke the hereditary veto—and the instrument by which social reform and free-trade finance were secured against a second chamber that had never accepted either.
Belloc and Cecil Chesterton, in The Party System, refused to read that struggle as a genuine feud between Houses. The two Front Benches were “not two but one”; their essential aim was maintenance of the Party System. Agreement between them was “the normal method of governing the country,” and the 1910 Constitutional Conference was “only one of the hundred conferences” of leaders, Whips, and official paymasters. The Conference, they wrote, “did not fail. It did exactly what it was intended to do. It saved for a moment the life of the moribund Party System.” They predicted that after “ridiculous sham demagogy” from the Treasury Bench and “sham indignation” from relatives across the table, Lords’ powers would be altered so that the Upper House could not stop measures concerted between the two Front Benches, yet could stop end-of-Parliament “swing of the pendulum” bills: the Second Chamber turned into “a machine subservient to the bi-party system.” In the Commons the same group allotted the time-table: five-sixths or more of time at the Government’s disposal under Standing Orders; Opposition protest “merely ceremonial”; no opposed private member’s Bill becoming law without ministerial facilities. The reconstituted Lords, they added, would drop the country squires “who are in one sense really representative of England” and keep purchasers of peerages, professional politicians, and bishops—new elements “nominees of the machine, or, as the pretty phrase goes, ‘of the Crown.’”
