concepts/imperialism.title: Imperialism
concepts/imperialism.content:
Imperialism
Imperialism, in the late-Victorian and Edwardian sense used by observers of the “scramble,” was the deliberate extension of European—and especially British—political control, commercial privilege, and strategic position beyond the older settled empire into Africa, Asia, and the Pacific. It was not merely the inheritance of colonies, but a movement: a concentrated outburst of annexation, partition, and protectorate-making that remade the map between roughly 1880 and 1914. Langer treated it as a world-policy phenomenon in which rivalry overseas became, in the last years of the century, “every whit as important, and perhaps more important, than the shifting trends of purely European diplomacy.”
Development
Drivers of the late-Victorian outburst
Britain already ruled the largest overseas empire when the new phase began. India, the self-governing Dominions, and scattered crown colonies formed a system whose defence rested on sea power and the routes to the East. The opening of the Suez Canal and the occupation of Egypt after 1882 bound that system to the Mediterranean and the Nile. With the Franco-Russian grouping complete by 1894, the old European issues fell into something like deadlock; that fact, together with growing economic pressure and intensifying competition for markets, stimulated and facilitated the overseas expansion Langer called the “tremendous, almost epic outburst of European interest in affairs that lay beyond the frontiers of Europe.” Industrial rivals sought markets and raw materials; prestige and ideology supplied language for expansion; and because so much of the globe was already an English preserve, Britain tended to become the object of attack for both continental groupings even as she advanced claims to regions still unappropriated. Maritime supremacy made England and the Empire almost unassailable; navalism elsewhere became bound up with designs hostile to the British world-system.
Contemporaries framed the movement in more than economic terms. Imperial federation, the literature of action, the popular press, evolutionary theories of society, and a democratic suffrage that cheered Jubilees and colonial wars all entered the climate in which Rhodes, Chamberlain, and Liberal Imperialists such as Rosebery spoke of markets, mission, and special fitness for empire. “Little Englander” became the term of abuse for those who put domestic reform or pure free trade above imperial consolidation. Rudyard Kipling gave the age its most resonant verse of imperial duty; the same democracy that filled music-halls with imperial song also, in time, returned free-trade Parliaments and paid for social reform from a free-trade Exchequer.
The economic measure and taproot
J. A. Hobson, writing in 1902 as the South African War closed, treated the same outburst as a measurable policy rather than a destiny. Quibbles about the word, he held, were best resolved by the last thirty years of annexation and asserted sway. Britain had added some 4,754,000 square miles and an estimated 88,000,000 people in a generation; taking Giffen’s empire (with Egypt and the Sudan) at about 13,000,000 square miles and 400–420 million inhabitants, a third of the area and a fourth of the population had been acquired since 1870. The full impetus came only in the mid-eighties: from about 1884 the method of wholesale partition assigned great African tracts, and a compiled list for 1884–1900—New Guinea, Nigeria, Bechuanaland, Upper Burma, British East Africa, Rhodesia, Uganda, Ashantee, Wei-hai-wei, the Sudan, the Transvaal and Orange River Colony among them—ran to some 3,711,957 square miles and 57 million people. The novelty was not British peculiarity but competing empires: France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Russia, and, after 1898, the United States. The new lands were tropical or sub-tropical, thinly settled by whites, and held by protectorate, charter, or paramountcy rather than genuine colonisation. Imperialism was nationalism overflowing its banks to absorb reluctant and unassimilable peoples; colonialism in the best sense—migration carrying self-government, as in Canada and Australasia—was a genuine expansion of nationality. The scramble recast European policy and produced a sliding diplomatic vocabulary of hinterland, sphere, suzerainty, protectorate, lease, and concession.
The commercial case failed on the figures. National income was about £1,700,000,000; 1898 trade at a liberal 5 per cent. profit yielded a little over £38,000,000, about one forty-fifth of income. There was no natural necessity for external markets: with everything produced a corresponding power to consume was created. In the three decades of conscious struggle for markets, external trade had not kept pace with internal trade; value of external trade per head had actually shrunk. Trade did not follow the flag: the share with British possessions was virtually the same in 1855–59 and 1895–98, while colonial trade among themselves grew faster than trade with the United Kingdom. The most profitable commerce remained with rival industrial nations; recent tropical acquisitions were poor and precarious markets. Nor was the new empire an outlet for surplus population. Net emigration was modest; the great majority of outward passengers went to the United States; no substantial settlement of Britons was taking place on areas acquired since 1870 except the Transvaal and Orange River Colony. A few soldiers, officials, engineers, missionaries, and overseers held temporary posts. The new empire was even more barren for settlement than for profitable trade.
If the policy was a business blunder for the nation, it was rational for sectional interests that usurped control of national resources. Direct beneficiaries included armament firms drawing a peacetime bill of some £60,000,000, export manufacturers, shipping claiming subsidies, the services, and colonial posts that James Mill had called outdoor relief for the upper classes. By far the most important factor was investment. Identified foreign income nearly doubled from 1884 to 1900; by the century’s end foreign and colonial holdings could not be set below £2,000,000,000. Interest on investments enormously exceeded profits on ordinary external trade and grew far faster: modern foreign policy was primarily a struggle for profitable markets of investment. Britain was becoming a nation living upon tribute from abroad. More dangerous still were the financiers for whom stocks were material for speculation—banking, broking, loan-floating, company-promoting: parasites upon patriotism, carried on the side of Imperialism by public debts and fluctuating values.
Logical Imperialism repudiated Free Trade and rested on Protection. The markets forced were small, unprofitable, and subject to diminishing returns; the open door was an advantage, not a necessity. The economic taproot lay deeper than any particular annexation. Productive power had outstripped consumption; over-saving—rents, monopoly profits, and other unearned or excessive income—flooded production because consuming power was mal-distributed. Imperialism was the endeavour of the great controllers of industry to broaden the channel for surplus wealth by seeking foreign markets and foreign investments they could not use at home. Divert that excess to wages or to the community as taxes, and there would be no need to fight for foreign markets; the home market was capable of indefinite expansion. Imperialist finance used government machinery to secure those private gains: ordinary expenditure rose sharply from the late eighties; roughly three-quarters of revenue went to naval and military charges and military debts. The classes who formed the economic core extracted these sums to improve investments and open new fields, while the people paid, preferably without knowing they paid—hence the bias toward indirect taxation, cheap drink, and “Mafficking.”
Politically the new empire enlarged the unfree proportion of British subjects. Of some 367 million outside the British Isles, not more than ten million had any real self-government; where British government was real it did not carry freedom, and where it carried a measure of freedom it was not real. India and Egypt were in essential features Crown colonies; government of the vast majority rested on the will of imperial officials, not the consent of the governed. The scientific defence—Pearson, Demolins, Kidd, Giddings—rested on “social efficiency” as capacity to beat other races, a natural-history struggle dressed as a mission of civilisation. Moral and sentimental factors furnished protective colour: a genuine wish to spread Christianity and diminish cruelty was utilised by selfish forces; Egypt occupied for military and financial reasons was afterwards said to have been entered for the fellah. Aggressive Imperialism was virtually confined to those weaker and incapable of effective resistance. Intensive tightening of control over “lower races” in Africa and Asia was as important as extensive growth; if interference were ever justified it must be for the world and the inhabitants, internationally sanctioned, and not destructive of self-development. Asia was the great test: a century of able Indian administration had not materially warded off chronic famine, and China threatened partition of concessions rather than trusteeship. Imperial federation of the self-governing colonies collided with the tropical policy: those colonies would not share the cost of ruling unassimilable millions for City investments; a white federation that excluded the coloured majority would not be the Empire, one that included it would not be free. The outcome, if the policy were not destiny, required repudiation of the claim that any subject venturing person or property abroad could call the nation’s force to his aid, and a genuine democracy directing external policy. To term Imperialism a national policy was, on this showing, an impudent falsehood; every tropical enlargement was a distinct enfeeblement of true British nationalism.
The scramble for Africa
The Scramble for Africa was the most visible theatre of the movement. The Berlin Conference of 1884–85, convened by Bismarck after Leopold II’s claims in the Congo and coastal rivalries, did not itself divide the continent. Fourteen nations produced the General Act of Berlin: free trade in the Congo Basin, freedom of navigation on the Congo and Niger, and above all the principle of effective occupation—a power could keep a claim only by administration, military presence, or treaties with local rulers. Once that rule was set, powers raced to plant flags and posts. Bilateral bargains followed: Anglo-German spheres in East Africa (1886), Anglo-French lines in West Africa (1889), and the Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty of 1890, by which Salisbury ceded Heligoland for a clearer British sphere north of a line from Lake Victoria toward Lake Tanganyika, securing Uganda against Karl Peters’s German treaties and the threat, as The Times put it in April 1890, of Germans on the Nile.
British advance ran along three great axes. In East Africa the Imperial British East Africa Company (chartered 1888 under Sir William MacKinnon), Stanley’s relief of Emin Pasha, and the race for Uganda preceded the protectorate of 1894 and the Uganda Railway (1896–1901). In West Africa the Royal Niger Company under Sir George Goldie secured the lower Niger and Benue against French and German rivals; its charter was revoked in 1899 and the territories became the Protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria (unified 1914). Ashanti was annexed after the wars of 1873–74 and 1895–96; the Benin Expedition of 1897 followed the massacre of a British mission. Further south, Harry Johnston, subsidised by Rhodes, planted posts between Lakes Nyasa and Tanganyika; Bechuanaland, made a protectorate in 1885, kept open the “road to the north” between the Transvaal and German South-West Africa. An ultimatum to Portugal in January 1890 broke the “rose-coloured map” that would have linked Angola to Mozambique.
Egypt, the Sudan, and Fashoda
The Egyptian and Sudan campaigns were the strategic hinge of British African imperialism. Dual Control of Egyptian finance by Britain and France, the nationalist cry “Egypt for the Egyptians,” and the rise of Ahmed Arabi produced the Alexandria crisis of June–July 1882. After the French fleet withdrew, Sir Beauchamp Seymour bombarded the forts (11 July); John Bright resigned from Gladstone’s Cabinet; Sir Garnet Wolseley crushed Arabi at Tel-el-Kebir. Though Granville had written that Her Majesty’s Government had “a strong objection to the occupation by themselves of Egypt,” the troops stayed. McCarthy put the irony plainly: English statesmanship had first meant only to secure the Canal and the highway to India—and then occupied alone. Langer judged the occupation the “initial impetus to British imperialism in the last years of the century.” After France and Russia blocked the projected Anglo-Turkish convention of 1887, “the chances of evacuation rapidly diminished.”
From Egypt Britain was drawn into the Sudan. Muhammad Ahmad, the Mahdi, annihilated Hicks’s Egyptian army (1883) and in January 1885 took Khartoum two days before Wolseley’s relief; General Charles Gordon died on the palace steps. The Ministry survived votes of censure only to fall on Childers’s budget in June 1885. For more than a decade the Sudan remained under the Khalifa Abdallahi. Sir Evelyn Baring (Lord Cromer) denied any serious idea of reconquest; yet fear for Egypt’s water supply—Milner in England in Egypt (1892) called regular Nile water a question of life so long as the upper reaches were uncontrolled—drove policy back toward the river. After Italy’s disaster at Adwa (1896), Salisbury authorised an advance from Wadi Halfa toward Dongola, “to plant the foot of Egypt farther up the Nile.” Sir Herbert Kitchener, Sirdar of the Egyptian army, built railway across desert, destroyed Mahmoud at the Atbara, and on 2 September 1898 at Omdurman broke a Dervish host of over 60,000 with Maxim guns and Lee-Metfords—some 11,000 dead against fewer than fifty British and Egyptian killed. Gordon was “avenged”; the Sudan became an Anglo-Egyptian condominium (1899). The same Nile thrust met a French expedition at Fashoda: the crisis of 1898 brought Britain and France to the edge of war before French withdrawal cleared the way for later colonial bargain.
Rhodes, Cape-to-Cairo, and the Boer War
Cecil Rhodes was the most energetic empire-builder of the southern advance—“the great imperialist” ready to take over anything in central Africa between the Zambezi and the White Nile. The Cape-to-Cairo vision of continuous British territory and railway from Egypt to the Cape, first aired by Sir Edwin Arnold in 1876, became his life’s work. The British South Africa Company received a Royal Charter in autumn 1889 with “almost unlimited rights and powers of government” north of the Transvaal and west of the Portuguese, without fixed northern limit. Southern and Northern Rhodesia took his name. The Chartered Company wrote “a new volume of history with a big pen, sometimes… dipped in very red ink,” conquering Ndebele and Shona while Rhodes, Cape Premier (1890–96) and master of De Beers and the Gold Fields, combined mining capital with territorial ambition.
Gold on the Rand filled the Transvaal with Uitlanders who outnumbered Boers yet were denied the franchise by President Paul Kruger. “Sooner or later,” McCarthy wrote, “the influence of President Kruger and the influence of Mr. Cecil Rhodes must come into collision.” On 29 December 1895 Dr. Leander Starr Jameson rode from Bechuanaland into the Transvaal; the High Commissioner ordered him stopped; he pressed on, was defeated, and was sent to England for trial. A Parliamentary Committee found that Rhodes, controlling Chartered Company, De Beers, and Gold Fields, “directed and controlled the combination which rendered such a proceeding as the Jameson Raid possible.” The Kaiser’s telegram to Kruger inflamed Anglo-German feeling; Rhodes fell as Cape Premier; race feeling was embittered.
The road to the South African War ran through Sir Alfred Milner’s High Commissionership, the failed Bloemfontein Conference of May 1899, and Chamberlain’s pressure for a five-year Uitlander franchise. On 9 October 1899 the Transvaal issued an ultimatum; war followed on 12 October. Black Week (Stormberg, Magersfontein, Colenso, 10–17 December 1899) shattered expectations of a short campaign. Lord Roberts and Kitchener reorganised; Cronje surrendered at Paardeberg (27 February 1900); Bloemfontein and Pretoria fell; both republics were annexed. Guerrilla war under Botha, De Wet, and de la Rey then stretched across country “nearly equal to the area of Continental Europe.” Blockhouses, farm clearances, and concentration camps—denounced by Emily Hobhouse and by Campbell-Bannerman as methods of “barbarism”—became the political cost of reconquest. The Treaty of Vereeniging (May 1902) ended the war. Chamberlain had staked imperial paramountcy in South Africa; the conflict exposed continental hostility, strained isolation, and left reconstruction and Union (1910) as unfinished imperial business. Gandhi’s South African years belonged to the same settler empire the war had secured.
Free-trade empire and tariff preference
Imperialism was also a domestic and fiscal politics. For most of the Victorian age the commercial face of empire was free trade: open imports, cheap food, and the belief that British industry needed no protective wall. The self-governing Colonies, however, offered preference to British goods and asked reciprocity; Germany and the United States rose as protected competitors. Colonial federation and closer commercial union became Chamberlain’s programme after his years at the Colonial Office (1895–1903). Preferential tariffs were offered as the economic cement of empire—the alternative to a “Little England” dependent on the mercy of rivals.
On 15 May 1903, at Birmingham, Chamberlain opened the campaign for Tariff Reform and imperial preference: recover freedom to negotiate and, if necessary, retaliate; bind the Empire by duties that favoured colonial produce; fund social reform from new revenue if need be. The Unionist party split among Chamberlainite reformers, Balfourite moderates, and Unionist Free Traders. The general election of 1906 returned an overwhelming Free-Trade majority; Campbell-Bannerman and Asquith kept Cobdenite finance as the basis of Liberal social legislation. Yet Tariff Reform remained the chief Unionist imperial programme through the People’s Budget and the Lords crisis—the commercial argument of Empire against the free-trade Exchequer that still paid for navy and pensions. Free-trade empire and preference empire thus competed inside the same imperial state.
Sea power, isolation, and pre-war diplomacy
Strategic geography governed what annexation could hold. The Cape route, the Canal, coaling stations, and command of the sea made a scattered empire defensible; Mackinder’s Imperial Britain was a maritime system whose heart was the British Isles and whose unity depended on oceanic communication. The Naval Defence Act of 1889 had enshrined the two-power standard. Tirpitz’s Navy Laws after 1897 and Fisher’s redistribution and Dreadnought revolution turned that standard into the Anglo-German naval race—the fiscal underside of late imperialism, in which South African war feeling, Navy League agitation, and the 1909 dreadnought scare (“We want eight and we won’t wait!”) bound empire, taxes, and German enmity together.
Diplomatically, the Boer War shattered complacency about “splendid isolation.” Chamberlain told Baron Eckardstein that if alliance with Germany proved impossible, England would have to reach an understanding with France and Russia even at far-reaching cost. The Anglo-Japanese Alliance (30 January 1902) was the first formal breach; Lansdowne discarded “musty formulas or old-fashioned superstitions.” The Entente Cordiale of 8 April 1904 was “essentially colonial in inspiration and results” yet possessed European significance: France recognised the British position in Egypt; Britain recognised French special interests in Morocco; Newfoundland, Siam, Madagascar, and the New Hebrides were settled. Diplomatic support in Morocco pulled Britain into continental crises at Tangier and Algeciras; staff talks followed. Colonial bargains had become the road out of isolation and into the alignment that faced Germany in 1914.
By 1914 the map of Africa was almost entirely coloured in European claims. The British share was vast—from Egypt and the Sudan through East and West Africa to the Cape and the Rhodesias—but so were the costs and the enmities. Imperialism had enlarged the empire, entangled Britain in continental rivalries through colonial bargains, forced naval concentration in the North Sea, and left Ireland and the Dominions as unfinished problems of self-government within a system still styled “Empire.”

concepts/irish-home-rule.title: Irish Home Rule
concepts/irish-home-rule.content:
Irish Home Rule
Home Rule was the claim that Ireland should manage her own domestic affairs through a legislature in Dublin while remaining within the United Kingdom under the supreme authority of the Imperial Parliament. It was at once a constitutional design, a party schism, and the dominant Irish demand of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries—distinct from repeal of the Union on the one hand and from simple remedial land or church legislation on the other. From Gladstone’s conversion in 1885–86 through the Parliament Act path of 1911–14, the question remade Liberal politics, bound the Irish Nationalist party into the arithmetic of every Liberal majority, and finally armed both Ulster and the South before European war suspended a settlement that the Easter Rising then challenged from outside the constitutional tradition.
Development
Gladstone’s meditation and the franchise
Isaac Butt’s Home Rule motion in the 1870s found Gladstone unconvinced: neither England nor Ireland, he then held, had made up its mind on the principle; but if the principle were once recognised, the difficulty of machinery would not be insuperable. For years he studied the question without committing himself. McCarthy records that at least five years before 1885 Gladstone had suggested to a friend that review articles might put the case fairly before the English reading public—still without professing himself a convert. He saw two imperial obstacles. First, could a scheme give Ireland the management of her own affairs and still secure the supreme and final control of the Imperial Parliament? Second, did the great majority of the Irish people desire Home Rule?
Until the Reform measures of 1884–85—the Third Reform Act and redistribution—the Irish representation lay largely with landlords and the wealthy trading class. The most ardent advocate could not deny that a majority of Irish MPs were either opposed or lukewarm. After popular suffrage the genuine Home Rule party returned about eighty-two strong out of 103 Irish seats (the figure of eighty-six for Parnell’s Nationalists holding the balance after the 1885 election marks the same landslide). Tory and Orange seats in the North largely held; the “nominal Home Rulers,” as Gladstone had called them, disappeared from Parliamentary life. One of Gladstone’s difficulties was gone. Ireland, at least, was by its vast majority resolute for national self-government; and Gladstone’s own earlier declaration—that he could not think much of any statesmanship incapable, under such conditions, of framing a measure—now pointed toward conversion.
1885–86: adoption, bill, and Liberal split
In December 1885 mysterious club and newspaper rumours reported that Gladstone had made up his mind to adopt Home Rule if he returned to office. Former colleagues denied them; Gladstone himself did not—a silence that some observers took as confirmation. He did not at first take all leading colleagues into confidence; John Morley was among those consulted. The 1885 election had left Liberals and Conservatives nearly level, with Parnell’s Nationalists holding the balance. When Gladstone formed his third ministry in February 1886, secession was already expected: Lord Hartington would never adopt the policy; many still doubted that Joseph Chamberlain would refuse office, though he too soon revolted. Even while the ministry was forming, talk turned on who would not hold office if Gladstone persevered.
On 8 April 1886 Gladstone moved for leave to introduce his bill for the better government of Ireland. Members queued from five or six in the morning; chairs filled the floor from bar to table; his speech of nearly three and a half hours was heard in breathless silence. The scheme had two essential principles: Ireland was to have a Parliament of its own, and Ireland was to have no representation at Westminster—Grattan’s Parliament restored without the narrow suffrage and religious conditions of the eighteenth century. Parnell and his colleagues, after consideration, assented. The Irish legislature was to consist of two orders, either of which might demand separate voting and so veto legislation until the next dissolution or for at least three years: a first order of twenty-eight representative peers and seventy-five members elected for ten years on a £25 yearly / £200 property qualification; a second order of the existing 103 Union members plus 101 elected for five years. A great land-purchase measure for buying out Irish landlords was declared essential to the scheme’s success. Ireland was to contribute one-fifteenth of public expenditure instead of one-twelfth. Radical critics asked whether this was not taxation without representation; federalists preferred an American-style arrangement in which Ireland managed local affairs and remained represented at Westminster for common business. George Trevelyan resigned on that ground (he later returned when the 1893 bill retained Irish members). Chamberlain withdrew, citing the land scheme even more than Home Rule itself, though he had by then discovered complete opposition to Home Rule; his own earlier local-government scheme for Ireland—dismissed by Irish members as “Popkin’s plan”—had failed because the Irish people would not accept mere county self-government in place of a recognition of nationality.
A new Unionist coalition formed against the bill. At a great Opera-house meeting Lord Cowper presided; Hartington, Lord Salisbury, and Goschen spoke; some reputed Radicals shared the platform. The most damaging secession was John Bright’s: lifelong friend of Irish land reform and of governing Ireland “according to Irish ideas,” he had never favoured a separate Parliament, and his public opposition carried weight far beyond that of aristocratic Liberals. On 7–8 June 1886 the second reading fell by 343 to 313, Liberal secessionists holding the fate of the measure. Gladstone dissolved at once. The July election returned Conservatives and Liberal Unionists at 393 against 275 Radicals and Home Rulers—a Unionist majority of 118. The Cabinet resigned without waiting for a Commons vote. The Liberal split endured: Liberal Unionists under Chamberlain and Hartington gradually merged with the Conservatives, and Liberals would not again hold an independent majority until 1906.
Parnell’s fall and the second bill (1890–93)
Parnell’s zenith after the Special Commission’s vindication of the forged Times letters was followed by ruin. Captain O’Shea’s divorce suit, undefended, named Parnell; Nonconformist pressure and Gladstone’s insistence that continued Parnellite leadership would cost Home Rule its English majority split the Irish party in Committee Room No. 15. A majority elected a new chairman; a minority held to Parnell. After a wild campaign over Ireland—Kilkenny the first major anti-Parnellite victory—Parnell died at Brighton on 6 October 1891, aged forty-five. The split and scandal discouraged many British supporters even while most stood by the principle.
Gladstone’s fourth ministry after 1892 depended on the divided Irish vote. On 13 February 1893 he introduced a measure “to amend the provision for the government of Ireland.” Essential difference from 1886: a National Parliament in Dublin while retaining eighty Irish members at Westminster under existing conditions—the change that brought Trevelyan and others back. Two Irish chambers were proposed: a Legislative Council elected by £20 rating voters, and a Legislative Assembly on the ordinary parliamentary franchise. Irish Nationalists wanted any bill affirming the principle, leaving emendation to later time; thoughtful Irishmen feared that a second Liberal failure would return the movement to the “party of action” from whom Parnell had wrested control. The bill passed the Commons by 301 to 267—the first Home Rule measure ever to clear the Lower House. Asquith’s second-reading speech made a great impression. The Lords read it a first time on 2 September 1893 and rejected the second reading by 419 to 41. In practical politics a Commons-passed, Lords-killed measure was thought on the road to eventual success; but Gladstone neither dissolved on Home Rule nor made the Lords’ veto the sole issue of a dissolution. The administration dragged on discouraged; he resigned in March 1894. Home Rule entered a decade of eclipse, and the absolute veto of the House of Lords became part of the Irish question itself.
Parliament Act path and the third bill (1906–14)
After the Liberal landslide of 1906—and still more after the elections of 1910 left Liberals dependent on Labour and Irish Nationalist votes—Home Rule returned as the price of Irish support. The crisis over Lloyd George’s 1909 Budget and the two elections of 1910 produced the Parliament Act of 1911: money bills could become law without the Lords after one month; other bills passed by the Commons in three successive sessions became law in the third without Lords’ assent; the maximum duration of a Parliament fell from seven years to five. The Lords’ absolute veto, which had killed the 1893 bill, became a suspensory veto of two sessions. That constitutional change—itself won with Irish votes in the majority of 124–126—made a Home Rule statute possible over the head of the Upper House.
Asquith introduced the Government of Ireland Bill on 11 April 1912. It proposed a bicameral Irish Parliament for domestic affairs, with imperial reservations (Crown, defence, foreign policy, and related powers) and continued Irish representation at Westminster (forty-two members in the final design). In committee the Government conceded exemptions and safeguards: Trinity College and the Queen’s University, Belfast, were taken out of the Irish Parliament’s reach; religious endowments were protected; children in state-aided schools were shielded from compulsory religious instruction. Amendments seeking Imperial control of labour conditions, an English-only official language, or further religious-equality wording were rejected, usually by majorities over one hundred. Asquith in Dublin offered to strengthen Ulster safeguards if shown insufficient, but insisted that a minority had no right, on mere suspicion of injury, to thwart the constitutional demand of a vast majority of fellow-countrymen; he did not believe civil war was at hand.
Ulster crisis, war suspension, and the radical alternative
Unionist resistance, especially in Ulster, moved from parliamentary opposition to extra-parliamentary organisation. Churchill’s Belfast visit had to leave the Ulster Hall for a tented meeting; Orange demonstrations and shipyard expulsions of Catholic and Protestant Home Rule workers marked the summer of 1912. On Ulster Day, 28 September 1912, mass signing of the Covenant bound men to use “all means which may be found necessary” to defeat Home Rule and, if it were imposed, to refuse recognition of a Dublin parliament. The Ulster Volunteer Force drilled openly; by 1913 it claimed tens of thousands of volunteers backed by large private guarantees. Nationalist Irish Volunteers formed in response. By March 1914 the bill stood on the Parliament Act path toward the statute book. Asquith offered provisional county-option exclusion for six years from the first meeting of the Dublin legislature—automatic inclusion thereafter unless Westminster decided otherwise—after “Home Rule within Home Rule” and permanent exclusion had failed to bridge the gap with Bonar Law and Carson. The Curragh incident, Larne and Howth gun-runnings, and mutual arming made civil conflict seem near.
European war suspended the unfinished settlement. The Home Rule Act was placed on the statute book but its operation deferred for the duration; Redmond pledged Nationalist support to the Empire. Constitutional Home Rule thus remained the Liberal–Nationalist programme—franchise reform in Ireland, the Liberal–Unionist schism of 1886, the destruction of the Lords’ absolute veto, and an uncompleted Ulster bargain. In Easter week 1916 a rising in Dublin, identified with Sinn Fein and republican proclamation rather than with devolution under the Crown, offered a radical alternative to the suspended parliamentary settlement. Suppression, executions, and the subsequent collapse of the old Nationalist monopoly transformed the politics that Gladstone and Asquith had framed as Home Rule within the United Kingdom. The concept’s arc—from Gladstone’s two difficulties through three bills and a constitutional revolution in the Lords—ends, within this period, not in working devolution but in war delay and a challenge from arms. Detail of the armed crisis of 1912–14 and of the 1916 rising belongs to the event narratives; the concept is the demand itself and the successive designs by which British parties tried, and failed before 1919, to meet it.

concepts/labour-representation.title: Labour Representation
concepts/labour-representation.content:
Labour Representation
Labour representation meant the election of working men—trade-union secretaries, municipal leaders, miners’ agents—to the House of Commons, and the organisation of those members into a distinct parliamentary force. It was the political counterpart of franchise reform: once the workman had the vote, he sought men of his own class to sit for industrial seats and to press legislation that would ease working-class life. Enfranchisement to secure representation for the redress of grievances guided English advance toward democracy; middle class and working class alike used the vote to obtain seats, and the return of a Labour party of some forty members marked the political arrival of organised labour within the constitution.
Development
The Acts of 1867 and 1884 made the entry of the workman into Parliament inevitable. The Reform Bill of 1867 enfranchised all male householders in boroughs and male lodgers paying £10 a year for unfurnished rooms, raising the electorate from about a million to two million and giving the town workman the vote as 1832 had given it to the middle-class man. Gladstone’s third Reform Act of 1884 extended household suffrage to the country districts, enfranchising the agricultural labourer; the Redistribution of Seats Act of 1885 created single-member equal electoral districts on a basis of roughly 54,000 inhabitants and fixed the membership of the Commons at six hundred and seventy. With that double extension the change in the personnel of the House became marked. The richer middle class had entered in force after 1832; after 1867 and 1884 the workman followed.
Miners were the first to send Labour representatives to Westminster, and their members came to outnumber those of any other trade. From 1892 industrial constituencies—chiefly in Yorkshire, Lancashire, South Wales, and the mining districts—steadily elected and re-elected working-class representatives, trade-union secretaries and officers for the most part. Parallel to that electoral growth ran the organisation of independent labour politics. The Independent Labour Party, formed in 1892, professed Socialism yet aimed rather at returning labour members to Parliament and local councils than at converting the working class to dogmatic social democracy. Behind it lay the Socialist revival of the mid-1880s: the Social Democratic Federation founded by H. M. Hyndman in 1884, which never won trade-union confidence yet trained many future Labour leaders; and the Fabian Society of the same year, which educated opinion toward State interference in the conditions of life and labour. The Independent Labour Party and its offspring, the Labour Party in the Commons, became the effective parliamentary instrument.
The formation of a National Labour Representation Committee in 1900 gathered these representatives into a separate organisation. After 1906 they sat as the Labour Party. The general election of January–February 1906, climax of the Tariff Reform crisis and the Liberal landslide, returned Labour as a distinct parliamentary force rather than a mere wing of Liberalism. The Annual Register recorded fifty-three Labour members among the Ministerialist majority of five hundred and thirteen—twenty-nine of them from the Labour Representation Committee, sitting as an independent party—beside three hundred and seventy-seven Liberals and eighty-three Irish Nationalists, against one hundred and fifty-seven Unionists. When the new Parliament assembled on 13 February, J. W. Lowther was re-elected Speaker on the motion of Sir Edward Grey, seconded by Keir Hardie, who thus marked Labour’s arrival as a separate force. The King’s Speech promised legislation on Trade Disputes, Workmen’s Compensation, Merchant Shipping, and Education. At subsequent general elections some forty Labour members returned to Westminster; by the years just before the war more than forty workmen sat in the Commons.
Those members had almost all served apprenticeship in municipal and trade-union office. Northumberland, Durham, Yorkshire, Lancashire, Stafford, South Wales, Glasgow, Dundee, Leicester, Norwich, and London all returned Labour members. Preference fell on men who had proved honesty and capacity as municipal councillors or union leaders: G. N. Barnes, for ten years general secretary of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers; J. R. Clynes, long district secretary of the Gas Workers’ and General Labourers’ Union; Will Thorne, general secretary of that union since 1889 and a West Ham councillor for more than sixteen years; George Lansbury and Will Crooks, known for work on the London County Council, borough councils, and boards of guardians. All the miners’ representatives were tried and experienced men. In the House they were grave, business-like, and undemonstrative—respecting the rules and dignity of the assembly because public business required order and because they were there to get legislation for their constituents. When Victor Grayson, in youthful passion against the misery of the poor, made a scene and was expelled, Labour members disapproved: disorder alienated sympathy, was not helpful in debate, and was not popular with the electors.
Belloc and Cecil Chesterton, writing the party-system as this wiki names Clayton on the rise of democracy, treated that expulsion as something larger than a breach of manners. The two Front Benches were, they said, one Governing Group—a self-elected corporation filling vacancies by co-option—and the “kindly tolerance” politicians congratulated themselves upon was extended only to those who played the game. It was not extended to Parnell, and it was not extended to Mr Victor Grayson. Labour’s absorption, in their account, was not caused by the Tone of the House but by a definite compact with the Executive: places, advantage in moving motions, and ultimately, perhaps, Cabinet rank as the price of compromise. The real grip was secret Party Funds, the control of elections, and the choice of candidates. An independent member who asked a question or moved a motion affecting the machine was reminded that his ability to fight his seat again depended upon a secret Caucus and the money that kept it going. Once pledged to do nothing that might injure the party, a candidate could cheerfully pledge himself to almost anything else, knowing that if the measure was inconvenient to the Front Benches he would have no chance of voting on it, or his vote would be rendered harmless by the subsequent shelving of the question. Only three types normally entered Parliament: local rich men who dominated the local organisation; rich men from outside who had suborned the central organisation; and comparatively poor men willing, for a seat and the chances of material gain, to become the obedient servants of the caucus.
The Old Age Pensions Bill of 1908 was their chosen farce of representation. They first describe a supposed Distress Relief Bill whose Committee stage is consumed in verbal amendments—seven lines of the bill “debated” in a day, nothing changed—until the Front Benches closure the rest before the vital clause is reached and “the people of the West Riding are left without relief.” Substitute, they write, destitute people over seventy for South Lancashire, the Old Age Pensions Bill for the Distress Relief Bill, and destitute old people between sixty-five and seventy for the West Riding, “and you have an exact and literal account of what took place” in Committee in the summer of 1908. The one thing that most mattered to the destitute was dealt with “precisely as a despotic monarchy would deal with it,” without a despot’s moral right: “the procedure of the House had been used simply to cheat the people.”
F. W. Jowett, Labour M.P., they treat as an outsider proposing to smash that machinery. In the penny pamphlet What is the Use of Parliament? he would abolish the Ministry with its collective responsibility and substitute departmental committees of the House, like those of local councils, on which all parties would sit and to which the permanent officials would be responsible. The Minister would remain as chairman and might be outvoted; neither that nor a reversal by the House would produce a “crisis.” Belloc and Chesterton called the exposure lucid and the examples typical, and allowed that if freely and honestly carried out, with duration of Parliament fixed by law so that Front Benches could not force a dissolution, the scheme would smash the Party System and give a free deliberative assembly its machinery. As things stood they saw little chance of honest working: committees packed with partisans; independent members kept off the particular committees where they might be dangerous. Grayson had told the world how he applied to sit on a Committee of Social Reform and was immediately appointed to the Irish Linen Marks Bill—“no insignificant indication” of what Jowett’s plan would become in a House still dominated by the Party System.
The House itself proved more orderly and industrious than a century earlier. It asked of a new member not birth or wealth but awareness of the honour of membership, modesty of bearing, and readiness to catch the tone of the chamber. A labourer or the son of a belted earl was indifferent so long as parliamentary manners were good. Labour’s presence increased rather than diminished that good behaviour and compelled a volume of social legislation—Workmen’s Compensation, old-age pensions, the Trade Disputes Act, and kindred measures—that members of fifty years earlier would have thought impossible. Once in Parliament or on city councils, Labour men became absorbed in practical legislation and administration; the return of so many of them damped the fires of scientific Socialism by placing the ablest working-class leaders in positions of authority. Social Reform took the place of social democracy as the conscious programme of democratic politics.
Three working-class leaders stood out in contemporary politics: John Burns, Keir Hardie, and J. Ramsay MacDonald. Two of an earlier generation—Thomas Burt and Henry Broadhurst—had held under-secretaryships in the Liberal ministry of 1892–5; Burns was the first trade unionist to sit in the Cabinet. He might have taken an under-secretaryship then, but decided that if he was fit for that place he was fit for the Cabinet. At the close of 1905 Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman offered him the Local Government Board; at forty-seven he accepted, and the workman first took his place in the Cabinet. His robust egoism was largely class pride: whatever John Burns did, that the working class did in the person of their representative. He had polled as a Social Democratic candidate at West Nottingham in 1885; been charged with seditious conspiracy after an unemployed riot in 1886 and acquitted; suffered six weeks’ imprisonment with Cunninghame Graham for free speech in Trafalgar Square in 1887; led the London dockers with Mann and Tillett in 1889; and been returned by Battersea to the London County Council in 1889 and to the Commons in 1892. The Liberal Party offered a wider sphere than the Socialists; political isolation was barren; and Burns passed from the trade-union movement to the Treasury Bench. Socialist convictions of early manhood mellowed under responsibility, yet he still held that the working class must work out its own salvation rather than leave affairs to a benevolent bureaucracy.
Hardie, a Lanarkshire miner and active trade unionist, embodied independent Labour politics. To him, more than to any other man, the existence of the Independent Labour Party and of the Parliamentary Labour Party—the latter consisting of the Independent Labour Party and the trade unions—was due. Political independence of an organised working class was the one great idea of his public life. Both he and Burns entered the House in 1892. From 1895 to 1900 Hardie was out of Parliament, rejected by South West Ham; nothing turned him from independence. Merthyr Tydvil re-elected him in 1900 at the very time he was denouncing the South African War. He would never take office in a Liberal ministry; sturdy republicanism kept him from court functions and the dinner parties of the rich. Visionary, with a religious temperament that treated political work as a solemn calling, he recruited the Independent Labour Party considerably from Nonconformists with Puritan traditions, and lived to see an independent Labour Party of forty members and to serve as its accredited leader.
MacDonald, elected leader of the Labour Party and its secretary since its formation, was for the working class but, though born of labouring people and educated in a Scotch board school, had long ceased to be of them. Never a workman and never associated with a trade union, he went from school teaching to journalism and a political private secretaryship, settled into the habits of the ruling middle class, and by marriage removed fear of poverty. He entered the Commons only in 1906, at forty; as leader of the Labour Party he was already a distinguished parliamentary figure. Native prudence had restrained him from pioneering, but once Hardie’s Independent Labour Party promised an effectual means of political work he joined it. He studied politics as others study art or science; by indefatigable industry he became controlling power first in the Independent Labour Party and then in the National Labour Party. Contemporaries expected him as a Cabinet Minister—even as Prime Minister—in a Liberal-Labour Government: a “safe” man without taint of fanaticism. Burns and Hardie remained, in their own and the public eye, representatives of the working class; MacDonald adapted himself to the life and manners of the wealthier professional classes and moved without constraint in the social world of high politics.
David Lloyd George, though of the industrious Nonconformist middle class rather than the workshop, illustrated the same opening of the highest offices to men neither wealthy nor of distinguished family. He entered Parliament in 1890 at twenty-seven; with Burns he entered the Cabinet at the Liberal revival of 1905, and government by aristocracy was ended. From the Board of Trade he passed to the Exchequer; the Budget of 1909 and National Insurance made his name the most loudly spoken in the country. The Cabinet had ceased to be an aristocratic committee.
Labour representation was tested again in the years of the great labour unrest of 1911–1914. On the Address in 1912 Ramsay MacDonald moved a Labour amendment ascribing industrial trouble to insufficient wages amid expanding national wealth and rising living costs: of some 7,300,000 wage-earners, he said, sixty per cent had incomes of less than thirty shillings a week; a minimum wage, begun experimentally by the Trade Boards Act of 1910, must go on. J. R. Clynes seconded. When the national coal stoppage of March 1912 forced Asquith’s government to legislate a district minimum wage, Labour members spoke for the miners’ claim that a minimum for abnormal places must have legal sanction. In the railway crisis of August 1911 Arthur Henderson sat on the Special Commission that investigated the 1907 conciliation scheme; MacDonald attacked the Home Office for a “reckless display of force” even as settlement came through Board of Trade channels. Parliamentary Labour thus stood between the industrial army outside and the Liberal ministry inside—pressing social claims, criticising the use of troops, yet remaining a constitutional force within the House.
War completed the transformation. In May–June 1915, when shells, drink, and the Admiralty rupture made pure party government impossible, Asquith reconstructed his administration as the First Coalition. Unionists and Labour sat on the Treasury Bench with Liberals; both Houses reassembled on 3 June for the first sitting of the Coalition, and the old party geography of the chamber was visibly altered. Labour accepted a place in national government for the duration of the emergency. The franchise settlement that followed closed the long sequence of parliamentary reform. The Representation of the People Act 1918, shaped by a Speaker’s Conference and carried through the critical stages of 1917, wrote women into the electorate at thirty, secured the vote of soldiers and sailors, redistributed seats toward industrial and urban centres, and produced the greatest single extension of the parliamentary franchise in British history. By 26 February 1918, when the Labour Party met in resumed Annual Conference at the Central Hall, Westminster, the party adopted a new constitution transforming itself from a federation of societies into a national democratic political organisation open to every worker who laboured “by hand or by brain.” The change marked the determination of the party leaders to seize the opportunity of the widened electorate and the enfranchisement of women. The first general election under the new register returned Labour candidates with nearly two and a half million votes. The electoral foundation of modern labour representation was completed at last by statute.

concepts/money-market.title: The Money Market
concepts/money-market.content:
The Money Market
The money market—named by Walter Bagehot after the street where it lived, Lombard Street—was the concrete machinery of short-term credit, bank reserves, and the Bank of England’s central position in Victorian and Edwardian London. It was not an abstract force but a set of institutions: the Bank of England, joint-stock and private banks, bill brokers, the separation of the Bank’s Issue and Banking departments under Peel’s Act of 1844, and the national habit of concentrating ultimate cash in Threadneedle Street. “Money will not manage itself,” Bagehot wrote.
Development
Bagehot opened Lombard Street (1873) to dispel the notion that the Money Market could be spoken of only in impalpable terms. It was as real as anything else, and could be described in plain words. He deliberately set aside the long controversy over Peel’s Act of 1844—the “cast iron” separation of the Issue Department from the Banking Department—except for its experienced effects. Half the supposed difficulty of the subject, he held, had arisen from abstract disputes about that statute. A quarter-century of material progress and almost marvellous banking development had intervened since 1844; he therefore sought to isolate the “Post-Peel” agencies rather than re-argue the note issue.
The briefest and truest description of Lombard Street was that it was by far the greatest combination of economical power and economical delicacy the world had seen. Money was economical power; England was the greatest moneyed country, with more immediately disposable and ready cash than any other. Known bank deposits published at the turn of 1872–73 illustrated the scale: London about £120,000,000; Paris £13,000,000; New York £40,000,000; the German Empire £8,000,000—and London’s unpublished private deposits were greater still. Concentration of money in banks, not mere national wealth, made the English market so rich: a million in a single banker’s hands was a great power; the same sum scattered through a nation was no power at all. Civilised governments could borrow in Lombard Street at a price; English bankers advanced on foreign stocks “with a margin.” Domestically, trade was carried on upon borrowed capital to an extent few foreigners imagined. A merchant with £10,000 of his own who borrowed £40,000 by discounts could undersell the rich man trading only on his own capital. Modern English business thus placed a steady bounty on trading with borrowed capital; the rough, “democratic” structure of commerce—new men created by bank discounts—kept English trade awake.
Lombard Street was the great go-between between quiet saving districts and active employing districts. Savings from agricultural counties such as Somersetshire and Hampshire lodged in local banks, travelled to London bankers or bill brokers, and were employed in discounting the bills of Yorkshire and Lancashire. English capital ran as surely toward profitable trades as water finds its level: when the iron trade slackened, iron bills thinned; when corn became profitable, corn bills multiplied and were discounted.
The objects grouped about Lombard Street were the Bank of England, the private banks, the joint-stock banks, and the bill brokers. In continental language the Street was an organisation of credit; the cardinal question was soundness—whether the promises to pay would be kept. For banking purposes the practical test was legal tender on demand: gold and silver coin (silver for small amounts only) and Bank of England notes. The attainable note issue was limited by the Act of 1844, which divided the Bank into two halves. The Issue Department issued notes only: by the late-1860s specimen return Bagehot printed (week ending 29 December 1869), notes issued stood at £33,288,640, of which £15,000,000 rested on government debt and other securities and £18,288,640 on gold coin and bullion. The Banking Department conducted ordinary banking with proprietors’ capital, the “rest,” public and private deposits, and a reserve of notes and coin—on that day liabilities of about £27,235,000 against a cash reserve of £11,297,000.
A crucial distinction ran through the system. Cash in the till for daily business was stock-in-trade, not the true reserve. The safety-fund was the special reserve held against extraordinary and unfrequent demands. Broadly, no bank held any considerable sum in hard cash or legal tender above daily needs except the Banking Department of the Bank of England. All London banks kept their principal reserve on deposit there. Bill brokers did much the same: they lent most of their money and deposited the remnant with the Bank or a London banker. Country bankers retained only the minimum cash for local business and sent spare money to London; Scotch and Irish practice was similar. You always came back to the Bank of England at last. The banking reserve of the Banking Department—some £10,000,000 on an average of years when Bagehot wrote, formerly much less—was therefore all that was held against the liabilities of Lombard Street, of all London, and of England, Ireland, and Scotland.
That single-reserve system was both strength and danger. In quiet times it economised capital; in crisis a run on the system became a run on one institution. Three times Peel’s Act had been suspended because the Banking Department was empty: before the breach the reserve had fallen to about £1,994,000 in 1847, £1,462,000 in 1857, and £3,000,000 in 1866. The danger was not merely artificial. In 1825, when only coin was legal tender and the Bank was undivided, the reserve had been reduced to £1,027,000 and the Bank was within an ace of stopping payment. Since the Franco-German war London had become to a much larger extent the banker of Europe; with specie payments at the Bank of France suspended, international cash payments centred more and more on Threadneedle Street. Foreign deposits were delicate: after the panic of 1866, and especially after foreigners confounded suspension of Peel’s Act with suspension of cash payments, large foreign money had been withdrawn. On the wisdom of the directors of that one joint-stock company, Bagehot insisted, it depended whether England should be solvent or insolvent.
Yet the Bank had never by corporate act distinctly acknowledged the public duty of keeping the ultimate reserve. Some directors denied it. Mr. Hankey wrote that the Banking Department did not differ, as far as he was aware, from any well-conducted London bank—though published figures showed it holding 30 to 50 per cent of liabilities in notes and coin while other banks kept only a bare till minimum. No resolution of Parliament, no report of a committee, no remembered speech of a responsible statesman had enforced the duty; authorities from Sir Robert Peel to Mr. Lowe had often taught that the Banking Department was only a joint-stock bank looking to the proprietors’ dividend. Two pressures pulled the Court opposite ways: national and City opinion, taught by panics, demanded a large reserve; shareholders pressed to diminish idle cash. Directors were rich City merchants, not trained bankers; three times since 1844 the Banking Department had needed assistance, yet popular faith held that the Bank could not fail and that the Government stood close behind it.
The liability structure of Lombard Street had grown with startling speed. In 1844 the liabilities of the four great London joint-stock banks had been about £10,637,000; by Bagehot’s day they exceeded £60,000,000. The collapse of Overend, Gurney, and Co.—a house that ten years earlier had stood next the Bank of England in the City—showed that long-established credit was no guarantee. When Overends failed in 1866, the Bank did not flinch: it made advances that would hardly be credited, advanced half its reserves before any Treasury authority to exceed the statutory note issue could arrive, and refused no legitimate application backed by adequate security—an admission that the Bank kept the sole real banking reserve of the country.
Two kinds of drain required opposite remedies, often at once. An unfavourable foreign exchange emptied the Bank till; the holders of the reserve ought at the very beginning of such a drain to raise the rate of interest, so as to stop further diminution and to replenish the reserve by imports of bullion. A rise in the discount rate acted at once on trade: prices fell, imports diminished, exports increased, and bullion was more likely to return. Between resumption of cash payments in 1819 and 1857 the Bank’s management of foreign drains had been, in Bagehot’s judgment, a miserable history; the panic of 1857 first taught the directors sound principles, though policy remained defective. A domestic drain—internal discredit—was different. The instinct was to hoard the reserve; the right course was to lend freely. Discredit meant an opinion that you had no money; to dissipate it you must employ money for the public benefit so that the public may know you have it. The time for accumulation was before the panic. Holders of the cash reserve must advance most freely for the liabilities of others—merchants, minor bankers, “this man and that man”—whenever the security was good. One failure made many; the way to stop derivative failures was to arrest the primary failure. In 1825 Mr. Harman for the Bank had described the classical treatment: the Bank lent by every possible means and in modes never adopted before—took stock on security, purchased and advanced on Exchequer bills, discounted outright, advanced on bills of exchange to an immense amount, and was “not on some occasions over-nice.” After a day or two the City was calm. When foreign drain and internal panic coincided, the rule was clear: raise the rate as high as necessary for the foreign drain; at that raised rate lend freely. Very large loans at very high rates were the best remedy for the worst malady of the money market.
Historically the monarchical form of Lombard Street was an accident of growth, not deliberate design. The Bank of England was founded in 1694 as a Whig finance company to lend to a government desperate for money; its charter privileges made it the only joint-stock bank permitted in England until 1826, and within the London radius until 1833. Bill brokers evolved from agents into principals who borrowed from banks at call and re-lent by discounting commercial bills. Joint-stock and private banks found it convenient to keep balances at the Bank; the practice ossified—“not so much a matter of law or of deliberate arrangement as the result of a growth which no one planned and no one could now reverse.”
The Chancellor of the Exchequer stood in a special relation to the market. In theory banking was a trade and government should let the Money Market take care of itself; but a modern government was the richest corporation in the country. If it deposited its immense income at a bank, it became interested in that bank’s welfare: it could not pay the interest on the National Debt, salaries, or miscellaneous expenses if the bank failed when the money was wanted. Public deposits—Exchequer, Savings Banks, Commissioners of the National Debt, dividend accounts—fluctuated with revenue: taxes coming in reduced the banking reserve; government payments returned money to the market. The published “Public Deposits” mixed the home Budget account with others, including the Secretary for India in Council and Chancery and Savings Bank balances. In peace the government account was calculable; in war it became among the most uncertain of all accounts.
Bagehot’s categories—reserve, legal tender, the Bank as holder of last resort, the money market as a concrete street of firms—remained those in which Englishmen understood financial crisis down to 1914. When the European crisis of late July 1914 broke upon London, the machinery he had described was tested at once. On 31 July the London Stock Exchange was closed and the Bank rate raised to 8 per cent; on 1 August the rate advanced to 10 per cent, the National Penny Bank suspended payment, and a partial moratorium was decreed; a moratorium of a month was established for certain bills of exchange. The fiscal state that free trade and later social expenditure had shaped still rested on the credit of Lombard Street: the People’s Budget struggle of 1909–11 had shown how fiercely the financing of social-reform and naval power could divide the constitution, yet the short-term market remained the daily barometer of confidence. On the outbreak of war the Commons cheered a Vote of Credit of £100,000,000 for naval and military operations, food supplies, trade, distress, and war expenses.
Exchequer cash at the Banks
Bagehot’s “public deposits” were the market’s view of the same balances that financial-administration treated as Exchequer cash. The 1917 Willoughby report, written from interviews and papers collected in London in July–August 1914, described the public side that touched Threadneedle Street without confusing it with the banking reserve. The Consolidated Fund stood to the credit of the Exchequer—the public treasury—at the Bank of England and the Bank of Ireland; Scotch banks received and remitted in rotation. Since 1834 revenues had been paid into those two banks to the Exchequer account. The banks were “mere bankers of the Government”: they received and paid to officers charged with settling obligations, and they took the place of the old Teller. They did not hold the market’s last legal-tender reserve in Bagehot’s sense; they kept the Crown’s cash chest.
Legislative control required a guardian of issues. The Exchequer and Audit Departments Act 1866 consolidated that guardianship with audit in one officer: Comptroller General of the Receipt and Issue of Her Majesty’s Exchequer and Auditor General of Public Accounts—the Comptroller and Auditor General. Funds at the two banks were subject to Parliament. The Treasury first obtained “credits” on the Exchequer. For Consolidated Fund services two Lords of the Treasury requisitioned the C&AG, who if satisfied granted credit by warrant. For Supply a royal order had to precede the requisition, because supply was granted to the Sovereign, who was under no legal duty to use it until he signified that wish. Credit did not move cash. Issues went only to “principal accountants”: the Comptroller of the National Debt and the chief cashiers of the two banks (debt service); the accountants-general of the revenue departments; and the Paymaster-General, general paymaster for military and civil services. Principal accountants requisitioned the Treasury, which ordered the banks to transfer from credits to their accounts. The C&AG did not intervene at that second stage; he had already granted the credit.
The Paymaster-General was banker, not accounting officer. He paid orders drawn by departmental accounting officers, satisfied as to form and supporting documents. He kept a separate book account for each civil vote and consolidated Army and Navy accounts, but one cash balance, and could pay any in-form order so long as the general balance sufficed. Pay offices had been consolidated between 1830 and 1856 to reduce idle balances; the 1856–57 Committee on Public Monies endorsed the single-balance system. A Treasury minute of 21 February 1885 (the Chancellor answering W. H. Smith) listed his sources: extra receipts as appropriations in aid; the Treasury Chest Fund (expenditure abroad); the Civil Contingencies Fund; departmental deposit funds; and daily Consolidated Fund issues. He exhausted outside cash before drawing the Fund, so daily Exchequer-issue returns did not equal expenditure except at prescribed adjustments—monthly, fairly accurate quarterly, and as close as possible at 31 March to the C&AG’s audited expenditure nine or ten months later.
Parliament therefore received two sets of figures: Exchequer receipts and issues, and audited receipts and expenditure. The Finance Accounts remained a compact cash statement of Exchequer income and issues and of year-end resources and liabilities at the two banks. For 1913–14 they showed tax and non-tax income of about £198.2 million against Consolidated Fund and Supply issues of about £197.5 million; Part II opened with balances at the Bank of England and the Bank of Ireland. Those balances were public cash awaiting authorised issue, not the Banking Department’s reserve against Lombard Street’s liabilities. Bagehot’s Chancellor mattered because government payments and tax inflows moved the market reserve; Willoughby’s Comptroller, credits, and Paymaster-General mattered because no shilling left the Exchequer accounts at the two banks until statute, royal order, and warrant had opened the chest.
