concepts/parliamentary-reform.title: Parliamentary Reform
concepts/parliamentary-reform.content:
Parliamentary Reform
Parliamentary reform in the United Kingdom between the mid-Victorian decades and the end of the Great War meant the successive widening of the franchise and the remaking of the electoral map so that the House of Commons might answer to a larger share of the adult population. It was not a single doctrine of abstract rights, but a practical programme: who might vote, on what qualification, in what constituencies, and under what conditions of open or secret poll. Each great Act settled one generation’s demand and left the next unfinished—until wartime necessity, in 1918, forced something close to mass democracy.
Development
Inheritance: 1832 and Chartism
The industrial revolution had already shifted wealth and population toward the manufacturing North and Midlands before the period opened. Towns that sent no members to Parliament grew rich; agricultural southern seats retained old weight. The Reform Act of 1832 had enfranchised the middle-class householder and broken many pocket boroughs, yet left the town workman and the agricultural labourer outside the pale. Power passed from the landed aristocracy to the middle class; the working class remained, in the language of the day, still unrepresented.
Chartism (1838–1850) kept the demand alive. The People’s Charter asked for universal (male) suffrage, vote by ballot, annual Parliaments, equal electoral districts, abolition of the property qualification for members, and payment of members. The movement failed through divided leadership, but the desire for enfranchisement never died out. Palmerston, “Tory chief of a Radical Cabinet,” gave no encouragement to reform from 1855 to 1865; his death left the Liberal Party to Earl Russell’s premiership, with Gladstone as leader in the Commons. Reform was now inevitable.
The Second Reform Act, 1867
In 1866 a mild Liberal bill—£7 rental qualification in the boroughs—fell to a combination of Conservatives and Whig dissentients (the “Adullamites”). It was too moderate to provoke enthusiasm and hateful to those who objected to any working-class enfranchisement. Reform Leagues and Reform Unions revived. On 23 July 1866 the London Reform Union’s attempt to hold a meeting in Hyde Park met closed gates; crowds pressed the railings until half a mile of iron went down and the people poured into the park. The disturbance was no revolution—the Guards were cheered, not fired upon—but it convinced ministers that reform could not be postponed.
A Conservative ministry under Lord Derby, with Disraeli leading the Commons, took office. Disraeli told his followers that a party of mere resistance to change was impossible in a progressive country. The parliamentary drama of 1867 was intricate. An abortive “Ten Minutes’ Bill” was withdrawn; Cranborne (afterwards Lord Salisbury) and others resigned rather than accept household suffrage; a “Tea-Room Party” of advanced Liberals forced successive concessions. By August the measure had passed both Houses. Derby called the policy a “leap in the dark.”
The Reform Act of 1867 established household suffrage in the boroughs: every male householder rated for the poor, and every male lodger paying £10 a year for unfurnished rooms. The town workman was enfranchised as the middle-class man had been in 1832. John Stuart Mill’s amendment to include women was defeated (73–196). Eleven small boroughs were disfranchised; thirty-five with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants became single-member constituencies; additional members went to Chelsea, Hackney, Leeds, Liverpool, Manchester, Salford, Glasgow, Birmingham, Dundee, and Merthyr. The electorate rose toward about two million. Household suffrage in the boroughs made it plain that middle-class county constituencies could not last much longer.
The Ballot Act, 1872
Open voting had long exposed the tenant and the workman to the landlord, the employer, and the patron. Chartism had listed the ballot among its six points; after 1867 the new borough electors made secrecy a practical necessity. Gladstone’s first ministry carried the Ballot Act of 1872. The secret ballot put an end to an enormous amount of corruption and almost altogether extinguished the illegitimate influence of landlord, employer, and patron. In a debate on women’s suffrage in 1871 Gladstone had already observed that if the ballot were once introduced there would be no harm done by allowing women to vote—an admission that secrecy would alter the conditions of the controversy by removing the duty of going up to the open poll. The Ballot Act thus completed the 1867 settlement on the side of electoral method, even as the county franchise and the sex bar remained for later generations.
The Third Reform Act and redistribution, 1884–85
The Third Reform Act, carried by Gladstone in 1884, extended household suffrage to the counties and created a service franchise for those qualified neither as householders nor lodgers. The agricultural labourer entered the electorate. The Lords refused the rural franchise bill unless redistribution accompanied it; Gladstone yielded, and franchise and redistribution passed together—the Upper House using the leverage that would later define its conflict with Liberal ministries over the House of Lords veto.
The Redistribution of Seats Act of 1885 adopted, in the main, single-member districts on a basis of about 54,000 inhabitants. Membership of the Commons rose from 658 to 670. Only twenty-three boroughs, the City of London, and the Universities of Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin retained double-member representation. The principle of equal electoral districts—long a Chartist demand—entered the statute book in practical form. The franchise remained, as fixed in 1885, occupation and ownership giving the right to vote.
Unfinished business: plural voting and the party machine
What remained unsettled after 1885 was the tangle of plural voting. No elector might give more than one vote in any constituency, yet a man with property in various places might vote in each; some men thus gave as many as a dozen votes at a general election. Liberals pressed “one man, one vote”; Conservatives answered with “one vote, one value” and redistribution, especially the alleged over-representation of Ireland under the Act of Union. A bill for the abolition of plural voting passed the Commons in 1906 but was rejected by the Lords. There was also a wide feeling for simplifying registration—three months’ residence instead of a year from one July to the next—and a limited demand for adult male suffrage, usually bound up with the question of votes for women.
Enfranchisement transformed party organisation. Larger electorates required registration agents, constituency associations, and disciplined machines. Clayton warned that the party organiser and political “boss” could raise (or lower) the simple business of choosing a representative into the art of electioneering, and make patronage the method of keeping a party in power. In England it became practically impossible for a man to take any serious part in politics except by becoming part of the machine; an independent attitude meant isolation. John Stuart Mill had already warned that representative institutions were of little value when electors sold their votes or voted at the beck of someone who controlled them. The Ballot Act reduced open intimidation; it did not abolish the party machine. Democracy after 1867 and 1884 was mass politics organised by Liberal, Unionist, and—later—Labour structures.
Working-class representation
With the extension of the franchise the change in the personnel of the Commons became marked. The Acts of 1867 and 1884 made the entry of the workman inevitable. Miners were the first to send Labour representatives; industrial constituencies in Yorkshire, Lancashire, South Wales, and the mining districts steadily elected trade-union secretaries and officers. The National Labour Representation Committee of 1900 organised these members into a separate force—the Labour Party after 1906. Enfranchisement to secure representation for the redress of grievances guided the English people toward democracy: middle class and working class alike used the vote to obtain seats. labour-representation was the political counterpart of franchise reform—the workman, once enfranchised, sought men of his own class to sit for industrial seats.
Women’s suffrage and the last disability
One disability remained after the religious barriers of the century had fallen—the sex disability that denied the parliamentary franchise to women. Mill’s amendment of 1867 had opened the controversy; Chorlton v. Lings (1868) closed the judicial route; municipal franchise from 1869 and eligibility for county and borough councils from 1907 made the parliamentary exclusion increasingly anomalous. The constitutional campaign and the militant suffragette-movement kept the demand before the country until war suspended peacetime methods. The full story belongs to womens-suffrage; for parliamentary reform the decisive point is that the sex bar survived 1867 and 1884 and fell only in 1918, and then only for women of thirty.
The Representation of the People Act, 1918
War completed the cycle. Soldiers and sailors abroad could not be left off any wartime register; from that narrow necessity the path led through a failed select-committee expedient in July 1916, a Speaker’s Conference on electoral reform, and a full reconstruction of the franchise. Many members declared that the experiences of the conflict had shown that the conscious co-operation of women in the activities of the nation was a source of strength and not of weakness.
The Representation of the People Act 1918—the largest franchise measure of the age—received the Royal Assent early in 1918. Its main provisions were exact. Men qualified at twenty-one years of age with six months’ residence or occupation of business premises. Women qualified at thirty years of age, and either as a local-government elector or as the wife of one. University franchise extended to a man or woman within those age-limits who had taken a degree (in England and Wales); a woman was also qualified for a university that did not admit women to degrees if she had fulfilled the conditions for a man’s degree. Naval and military voters were to be registered for the constituencies for which they would have been qualified but for their service; male voters who had served in the war were qualified at nineteen. Dual voting was limited to two constituencies at a general election. Conscientious objectors were temporarily disqualified; the receipt of poor relief ceased to be a disqualification. Two registers a year were ordered. Membership of the Commons rose to 707 (England 492, Wales 36, Scotland 74, Ireland 105). Redistribution added seats to industrial and urban centres—Greater London 101, Lancashire 66, Birmingham and environs 41, Glasgow and environs 32—while Irish redistribution remained unresolved under the Speaker’s Conference bargain.
On 19–20 June 1917 the Commons fixed the women’s age-limit at thirty; the women’s clause was carried by 214 to 17. In the Lords the clause enfranchising women passed on 10 January 1918 by 134 to 71. The scale was unprecedented. While the Reform Act of 1832 enfranchised some 500,000 new voters, that of 1867 one million, and that of 1884 two million, the Act of 1918 enfranchised eight million—six million being women, of whom five million were married, and two million being men. Full adult equality of age with men still lay in the future, but the sex bar on the parliamentary franchise had been broken. Later in 1918 the Parliament (Qualification of Women) Act removed the bar on women standing for the Commons. Labour rewrote its constitution to exploit the widened electorate; nearly 2,500,000 Labour votes at the first election under the new register measured how far the enlarged nation had already shifted party competition.
Arc and meaning
The long Victorian and Edwardian sequence thus ran in a single line: 1832 transferred power to the middle class; 1867 enfranchised the borough workman and Disraeli’s Conservatives “dished the Whigs”; 1872 made the vote secret; 1884–85 brought in the agricultural labourer and single-member districts; party machines organised the new masses; Labour members entered as the political fruit of working-class enfranchisement; 1911 curtailed the Lords’ absolute veto; 1918, under wartime pressure, established manhood suffrage (with residual dual-vote and university anomalies) and admitted women of thirty. Enfranchisement and representation remained the two chosen instruments of democratic government. What began as a practical settlement of who might vote ended as something close to mass democracy—still short of equal adult suffrage for both sexes, but unrecognisable as the narrow, open-poll electorate of Palmerston’s last years.

concepts/party-system.title: The Party System
concepts/party-system.content:
The Party System
The Party System was the machinery by which, after the enlargement of the electorate, two Front Benches in the House of Commons acted as one Governing Group: they filled ministries by co-option, allotted the time-table of the House, selected candidates and programmes through the caucus, and financed elections from unaudited secret funds. Representation, in the democratic sense of laws the mass desired, did not exist; the assembly had been rendered null, and the public, still taking sides as at a boat-race, mistook a sham contest for self-government.
Development
Democracy is government by the general will: wherever the laws the people desire are passed and those they dislike rejected, there is democracy; wherever the laws have no relation to that desire, there is none. Votes, elections, and assemblies are only machinery. Pure democracy is the elders under the village tree; representation is the indirect substitute, and it requires free selection of members, strict responsibility to constituents, and independence of the Executive. None of those conditions obtained. A member who voted opposite to Bethnal Green was merely an oligarch. The force that turned the assembly into an engine of oligarchy was the Party System. The “Will of the People” dispute of the two elections of 1910 reduced itself to whether that will was best represented by the Duke of Sussex or by his son-in-law, the Right Honourable James Blagg.
The public that the machine exploited was still, in the main, honest. A Conservative leader had to denounce land taxes his followers sincerely detested, even if he had no intention of repealing them. Enthusiasts remained: Conservatives who thought the Liberal Government was held from spoliation only by the Opposition; Liberals who saw Asquith and Churchill as tribunes of a people struggling to be free. Single-issue men—Tariff Reformers, churchmen, teetotalers, the Irish to whom nothing mattered but nationality—counted at elections. The mass took sides year after year as crowds take Oxford or Cambridge, with no control of the crew. An uneasy minority noticed laws they detested passed by both parties, desired measures never mentioned, the Jameson Raid inquiry stifled by both Front Benches, Balfour’s hesitations on Tariff Reform, and the meaningless Conference of 1910. They blamed Asquith for being too Whiggish or Balfour for being weak, not seeing that Balfour was strong in the traditions of party and the net of relationships that covered English politics.
The system had not always been the organised imposture of 1911. Seventeenth-century conflict was real because men were willing to fight. 1689 was made not only by but for wealthy intrigues with a mainly financial object; more than six million acres of common land were enclosed after Hanover. Parliament then represented a narrow class, but within that class Pitt and Fox did not speak to each other and did not, like Asquith and Balfour, belong to the same set. Direct bribery of the legislature ceased, perhaps because of the growing impotence of the Commons rather than virtue. Industrial wealth and French Revolutionary ideas produced 1832; later Reform Acts enlarged the electorate while power silently passed from the Commons to the Cabinet. Unreal issues, defined neither by the people nor by Parliament but by the politicians, gave a semblance of reality to an empty competition.
After the house-of-lords threw out Lloyd George’s Budget in 1909, Asquith at the Albert Hall pledged he would neither assume nor retain office without guarantees that the veto would be limited. He won the January 1910 election, assumed office, retained office, and produced no guarantees. Instead he entered a conference with his alleged opponents, six months supposedly spent bridging an “unbridgable gulf.” Both sides then announced that the Conference had failed, and another election was declared necessary, though there was nothing to vote about. The Conference did not fail: it saved for a moment the life of the moribund Party System. The 1906 mandate had been squandered—Chinese Labour, the Licensing Bill, the collapse and absorption of the Labour Party. “Down with the Lords!” rallied supporters, then was smothered when a handful of Radicals demanded fulfilment. The Opposition’s refusal to attack the broken Albert Hall pledge was evidence of collusion: practically every move was arranged beforehand by the confederates on the two Front Benches. Governments abandoned causes because they consulted the sense of the Governing Group; Oppositions tolerated the abandonment because they wished to preserve the system that would, by the connivance of those rivals, bring them office in turn.
Ministers were not nominated by the Crown or by Parliament: they nominated themselves. They formed a self-elected body, filling vacancies by co-option. The two Front Benches were one close oligarchical corporation. Admission cost complete surrender of independence. Recruits fell into Relations (blood and marriage—not to be confused with the old privileges of the Great Houses), Private Secretaries (sons of the new rich or of party subscribers; Montagu and Herbert Samuel, related to Lord Swaythling), and make-weights (lawyers, an ex-workman, anyone who had given annoyance while independent). Asquith in 1892 was unconnected by any direct tie; by 1911 he and his were connected by a dozen such ties. Office, unlike the kingdom of heaven, was not taken by storm.
The kinship list made the imposture visible: Norfolk as Conservative Postmaster-General; Austen Chamberlain inheriting rank from his father; the Prime Minister’s brother-in-law Tennant on the Treasury bench; Churchill with a double right; Selborne, son-in-law of Salisbury, governing South Africa while first cousin Arthur Balfour was Prime Minister and brother Gerald enjoyed office and pension; Liberal Whip Sir John Fuller brother-in-law of Hobhouse, both grandchildren by blood or marriage of Conservative Chancellor St Aldwyn; Masterman nephew by marriage of Conservative Colonial Secretary Lyttelton; Asquith and Lyttelton married sisters; Churchill cousin of Marlborough and his successor as Under Secretary for the Colonies. If Lady Capulet were a born Montague, Lady Montague first cousin of old Capulet, Mercutio nephew of a Capulet and brother-in-law of a Montague, the feud at Verona would be kept up mainly for the entertainment of the people. Tolerance was extended only to those who “played the game,” not to Parnell or Victor Grayson. Concealment of the relationships was sound moral proof that their motive was imposture.
The Placeman was as prominent as in Walpole’s day, only more decently veiled. He voted as the Whips dictated, tabled blocking motions, or played at independence without ever touching what was inconvenient to both Front Benches. Masterman, independent critic of Burns and of the Education Bill, voted for the Labour Right to Work Bill on 13 March 1908; in May he accepted office at £1,200 (later £1,500); on 20 April 1909 he voted against the same Bill. He was regarded as a man of exceptionally high ideals. Barristers abounded because prizes were in the gift of the group; Buckmaster moved the amendment that shelved secrecy of the Party Funds. Those funds, unaudited, were immediately withdrawn from any member who voted against the Government.
“Discipline” was a military word fatal to criticism. Rank and file were held under a rigidity nothing short of civil war could justify, while commanders concocted their plan of campaign in concert. The 1910 Conference was only one of a hundred conferences of leaders, secretaries, Chief Whips, confidential hangers-on, and principal official paymasters. Agreement was the normal method of governing the country. Three cases of halted victory showed the alliance: the Jameson Raid committee, always on the verge of a startling revelation, stopped like a newspaper serial because Harcourt, Campbell-Bannerman, and Ellis were Front Benchers as eager as any Tory to hush the Colonial Office; Chinese Labour, the issue of 1906, not followed by immediate repatriation—anxious negotiations to propitiate the South African Jews, 1,300 Chinese admitted after the change of government, and the new House not allowed to divide on the question; the Conference itself, which openly branded as a farce the rhetoric of five months before.
A prediction followed as a test. After sham demagogy and sham indignation, Lords’ powers would be altered so that the Lords could not stop measures concerted between the two Front Benches, and could stop end-of-Parliament “swing of the pendulum” bills. The reconstituted House would drop the country squires who were in one sense really representative of England and keep purchasers of peerages, professional politicians, and bishops; new elements would be nominees of the machine, or, as the pretty phrase went, “of the Crown.” Each Front Bench wanted the prizes of office, but that aim was subordinate to the essential aim of both: the maintenance of the Party System. Speaker and Chairman of Committees, impartial because they knew the fight was sham, supported them when they agreed. This governing group allotted the time of the House and what might be said.
Five-sixths or more of time was at the Government’s disposal under Standing Orders; closure ended discussion automatically. Opposition protest was merely ceremonial; Balfour showed a disposition to drop it. Private members had one afternoon a week, insecurely held; no opposed private member’s Bill had in recent years become law without ministerial facilities. After consultation with the Opposition Front Bench, officials approached Buckmaster to nullify the debate on secrecy of the Party Funds; his amendment confined the evil to the Tariff Reform League; Unionists moved a twin amendment on the Free Trade Union; the division became an ordinary party division. The “blocking motion”—notice of a motion never moved—prevented anyone else discussing the subject (Rees in the 1906 Parliament, especially India). Adjournment on a matter of urgent public importance required forty members; with Front Benches united this was hard to find, the House usually attended by a dozen or twenty. Foreign affairs got a few hours a year. Question time allowed nothing but a bare answer, which might be refused.
The repressive machinery was most infrequent—applied only to rare revolts—which is why the public did not see it. There could be all the sham fight desired upon the sham issues the bosses had arranged, but no initiative on the part of the electorate. A concrete example made the cheat exact: a supposed Distress Relief Bill of 1910, verbal amendments occupying pages of Hansard, the vital clause never reached, closure by the Front Benches. Substitute destitute people over seventy for South Lancashire, the Old Age Pensions Bill of 1908 for the Bill, and destitute people between sixty-five and seventy for the West Riding, and the account of the summer of 1908 was literal. The procedure had been used simply to cheat the people.
The tone of the House was stupid and rather degraded, much lower than that of the House of Lords, death to rhetoric, an air in which it was much easier not to bother. It was a far smaller factor than visitors supposed. A dozen determined men could have broken the Front Bench arrangements from within. Labour’s absorption was not caused by Tone but by a definite compact with the Executive by which places, advantage in moving motions, and ultimately perhaps Cabinet rank should be the price of compromise. That compact was the parliamentary fate of labour-representation. The real grip was secret Party Funds, the control of elections, and the choice of candidates.
The most important fact about English politics was the fact that nobody mentioned. Two huge war-chests were secretly subscribed and secretly disbursed. Light on collection came from the Honours List; on expenditure, from the division list. They were subscribed by rich men who wanted some advantage, financial or social, from the Government, and spent in paying the expenses of members—in other words, in corrupting the legislature. Organisers proclaimed perennial penury and issued bogus appeals to working men; there would be no lack of funds so long as the supply of peerages and baronetcies was unchecked. Expenditure was Walpole’s Secret Service, refined: instead of buying votes after election, the gang ensured that no one should be elected who was not prepared so to vote, eliminating the chance of an incorruptible member. The member answered to the caucus that paid him. Not one man in thirty knew that there were such things as Party Funds.
There was a market for peerages in Downing Street as there was a market for cabbages in Covent Garden. A peerage conveyed not only dignity but legislative power: a Peer was a Senator. Among ten creations in twenty years, a few (Peel, Kitchener, Curzon, Morley, Fisher) fit the senatorial idea. The 1910 Liberal Birthday Honours, issued while the Government denounced the Peers, created seven peers: Causton (Southwark), Foster (Ilkeston), Kearley (Devonport), Pearson (Cowdray), Holland (Rotherham), Freeman-Thomas (Willingdon), Furness. Ilkeston, President of the National Liberal Federation, was elevated mainly because he gave up a safe seat for Colonel Seely. Causton, unpaid Paymaster, rejected at Southwark in January 1910, received a consolation prize that was a right to make and unmake laws. Furness, unseated on petition, promptly received a coronet. Holland was an enormously rich cotton-owner. Pearson’s contracting company had recently articled Lloyd-George junior. Conservatives were no cleaner; some families paid both chests. The Guests received Wimborne in 1880, crossed in 1904, and in 1909, just when the politicians were loudest in denunciation of the Peers, Ivor Guest became Lord Ashby St Ledger. A Conservative Government made Alfred Harmsworth Lord Northcliffe; a Liberal Government gave a brother a baronetcy.
Worse than the sale of honours was traffic in policies. Cecil Rhodes’s letters to Schnadhorst offered sums running into tens of thousands on condition Egypt remain British and the Cape-to-Cairo railway be viewed favourably. Money was paid; Gladstone, publicly for evacuation, did not evacuate. In 1903 Dr Rutherfoord Harris announced publicly that he had sent £10,000 to the Conservative Party Funds; shortly afterwards a Conservative Government sanctioned Chinese labour on the Rand. Liberals, winning 1906 on the issue, still refused a division and negotiated so that Chinese stayed until they had done their work in reducing the wages of the Kaffirs. Drink was the standing case. The public never heard municipalisation or free trade in liquor; the only choice was Balfour’s Licensing Bill (endowment of brewing and distilling firms out of public funds) versus Asquith’s (irritating restrictions leading logically to ultimate prohibition). Conservatives needed brewers of tied houses; Liberals needed cocoa manufacturers, grocers who sold drink retail, and rich faddists who would prohibit. The people chose between the brewer and the cocoa-manufacturer, and usually preferred the brewer.
The Central Office was not representative of the people nor even of active party members. National Liberal Federation and National Union of Conservative Associations passed resolutions that had the smallest effect until ratified by the Central Office. The Office was the hinge between the Front Bench group and local organisations, themselves largely dominated by the local rich men and too democratic to be trusted with the reality of political power. Its head, nominated by the Governing Group, held the purse-strings of the secret sums and made arrangements with subscribers of which the Leader was conventionally supposed to know nothing.
Free local choice of candidates did not happen. Either the richest local man paid the local organisation and was confirmed by the machine, or an outsider approached Central Office: a rich man put down a subscription and the seat’s safety varied with the amount; a poor man fought hopeless seats as a useful gladiator, preferably via a private secretaryship, especially if a lawyer. The Fortunatus Purse of the Party Funds was placed unreservedly at his disposal if he sacrificed freedom and honour. Independents lacked money; there was no second ballot; electors feared to waste votes. Only three types normally entered: local rich men, outside rich men who had suborned the centre, and poor men willing to be obedient servants of the caucus.
An election was decided first by salaried officials: purchasers first; university speakers; heredity (a Cecil, a Howard, a Churchill, or a Rothschild); poor advocates sent first to seats safe for the other colour. The test was willingness to defend not only the existing brief but any future decision. Locally there was no Westminster collusion: prominent Liberals really differed in type from prominent Conservatives. The official organisation was a few dozen men—never a hundred, often twenty or thirty—who sent one to London to fetch someone on the list. In ninety-nine cases they accepted the nominee. Pledges made under popular excitement were expected to be broken always in the spirit and even, if necessary, in the letter. Nomination required cash equivalent to a well-paid skilled artisan’s yearly income; avowed expenses averaged £1,000 and came in reality to nearly double. Winning by 10 per cent of the electorate was enormous; by 2 per cent was not even close. The winner went to Westminster to vote for anything whatsoever that the machine might order.
Two programmes were drawn up by the politicians, usually after consultation with each other. Framing the question was to go a long way towards framing the answer. Free Trade in the 1840s was forced on the legislature by a popular demand; Tariff Reform began when a Cabinet Minister declared for Protection and professional politicians who had never doubted Free Trade converted overnight. Drink and Education Bills were framed for sectarian and trade subscribers, not for parents. In November 1910 the Front Benches agreed the Osborne Judgment should not be an electoral issue and that payment of members should side-track the demand of the workers; the Labour Party of course gave way. The Unemployed were not allowed to vote on the Right to Work Bill. “Non-controversial measures” meant all violently unpopular proposals for the oppression of the poor which happened in no way to affect the professional politicians (Children’s Bill, Prevention of Crimes Bill). Licensing clauses of the People’s Budget, certainly unpopular, would be continued by Conservatives when by mutual arrangement their turn of office came. Irish-home-rule and Protection, launched against the rules, were turned by digestion into unreal issues. Legislation had passed to that Standing Committee of Professional Politicians called in the House of Commons the Two Front Benches.
Beneficiaries said states were organic; Britain had unbroken institutional continuity; under the Party System England had recently been the wealthiest and almost the strongest nation; leave well alone unless a concrete alternative existed. Every question had a yes and a no; an unchecked Executive was worse; two salaried teams arguing Protection versus Free Trade produced open discussion; the system supplied an alternative government without violence. The last argument rested on ignorance and vanity. Britain no longer had the offensive strength, economic position, or social condition it claimed; continental peoples regarded the English poor with pity and horror. The old Whig/Tory philosophical division was real into the last quarter of the nineteenth century; by 1911 not the memory, not the savour of a real distinction remained. Between wage-earners for Jones and for Smith there was no line, not even the vaguest dotted line. The system could not supply an alternative government for a vital change, because it depended upon the conception that there could not be any vital change. Not one great national issue since the repeal of the Corn Laws had had genuine party debate; real disagreement produced stalemate, because a permanent victory would be the death of the system by which both sets of politicians obtained their bread-and-butter. Because it was no longer a real contest of ideals, it could not register or resolve the conflicts that actually pressed—poverty at home, foreign insult abroad.
Scholarship would say an institution in this condition was past praying for. Yet nothing was appearing that could take the place of Parliament. Most statutes were the work of permanent officials; the Commons, fallen into a universally recognised decay, was still the only instrument for making laws. Franchise extension would only drill twenty thousand where ten thousand were drilled now. Abolishing plural voting would be met by a new cry to rebalance the teams. Payment of official election expenses would leave the independent disadvantaged against the Fortunatus fund; payment of members would not stop larger future bribes. Auditing party funds would spawn a second secret fund. A short, indissoluble Parliament of four years at most would be more to the purpose: a vote of censure would not dissolve the House, so members could vote freely. Even an adumbration of independent voting had forced Campbell-Bannerman to give way on the Trades Disputes Bill. Jowett’s proposal to replace collective Cabinet responsibility with departmental committees would still fail in a packed House without a fixed term. Primaries would be valuable but hard to graft. Balfour’s Referendum was obviously insincere unless joined to Initiative. Machinery failed unless the democracy refused party hacks. The first need was exposure; the second, pledges inside the machine—not vague promises, but a pledge to vote against whatever Government unless scheduled measures passed the Commons by a date. Had members in 1906 been pledged to vote against the Government unless the first Chinese left by 1 March 1906 and the last by 31 December, the politician would have been caught. If the mass would not organise, the law-making institution of England was done with. The body would jerk, perhaps—it would not revive. Until a successor organ appeared, the country faced one of those evil spaces, subject to foreign insult and domestic misfortune, when nations lose grip over their own destinies.
Compared with Germany (the Emperor choosing responsible heads in public view), France (ministries satisfying a fluctuating Chamber, with no automatic dissolution and no standing compact of two Front Benches), and the United States (a President personally choosing heads excluded from congressional party rigidity), Britain vested recruitment in a dozen or so who co-opted continuously. Parliament had no actual check. Today it was impossible to conceive of any appointment, however monstrous, which would lead to remonstrance from the drilled voting machine.
Collusion was not the absence of all conflict. What the opponents preserved was the conditions under which they and their clique should retain the opportunities for large salaries. They prevented division on the sale of honours, connections between antagonists, procedure, private members’ time, salaries, public committees. No one important policy for fifteen years had been allowed to form a clear division, with the exception of Women’s Suffrage—and even that reached law only if the Front Benches permitted; they leaned toward a well-to-do franchise, not adult women’s suffrage. Administration, especially where great financiers and some cosmopolitan banker in Egypt or Ceylon were concerned, was concerted. Notes were tossed across the table; Whips conferred openly to prevent majority decisions.
The daily press was more devoted to the Party System than any part of the State except the professional politicians themselves. Liberal advocacy: Star, Daily News, Manchester Guardian, Westminster Gazette. The other team: Times, Daily Telegraph, Birmingham Daily Post, Pall Mall Gazette. Writers on a “Conservative” paper might be Socialists; a “Free Trade” paper might be owned by a Protectionist. The politicians’ only regular lever was honours to proprietors, now rather a matter of routine. The attitude was not wicked, it was merely stupid. Reformers should attack the parliamentary game, that machine for grinding wind, not expect to purify newspapers first. The Press had long ceased to affect opinion on party; it still affected it by selection of foreign news.
Parliamentary-reform that merely widened the drilled electorate, and social measures such as pensions and the People’s Budget that the two Benches could close or chew into unreal issues, left the oligarchy intact. The Party System was the name of that oligarchy.

concepts/servile-state.title: The Servile State
concepts/servile-state.content:
The Servile State
The Servile State is the arrangement of society in which so considerable a number of families and individuals are constrained by positive law to labour for the advantage of other families and individuals as to stamp the whole community with the mark of such labour. It is the stable condition toward which industrial capitalism, with the means of production owned by a few and the mass proletarian, is tending: not Collectivism, and not the restoration of widely distributed property, but compulsory labour of non-owners for owners, in exchange for sufficiency and security. The epigraph of the thesis is exact: if the institution of property is not restored, the institution of slavery cannot be escaped; there is no third course.
Development
Definitions
Man lives by transforming his environment. That conscious transformation is the production of wealth; without wealth he cannot exist; to control its production is to control life. Labour is human energy applied to nature; land is material and natural force; capital is wealth reserved for future production. The means of production are land and capital combined. A man master only of his labour, without useful control of land or capital, is proletarian; a considerable class of such men is a proletariat. Property is the legal vesting of control of land and of wealth made from land in a person or corporation, to use or to withhold. Private property is distinguished because the owner may exercise control to his own advantage, not as a trustee for society.
A society in which political officers hold the means of production in trust is Collectivist (Socialist in that special sense). A society in which private ownership is confined to a number of free citizens not large enough to determine the social mass, the rest proletarian, is Capitalist. Its two marks are political freedom of the citizen and restriction of ownership to a section markedly less than the whole. Labour is servile when it is undertaken not in fulfilment of contract but under the compulsion of positive law, attaching to the status of the labourer and performed for the benefit of others under no such compulsion. The free man can refuse his labour and use that refusal as a bargain; the slave has no such instrument. Servile does not mean oppressive: a man guaranteed against insecurity and insufficiency, with subsistence in old age, might be better off than a free man lacking those things. The test is withdrawal of free choice to labour or not, here or there, and compulsion by law to labour for others who do not fall under the same compulsion. Ownership of the slave by a particular master is not essential. A week’s contract of service is not slavery; a life-contract at bare subsistence is.
Pagan origin and Christian dissolution
European civilisation sprang from a purely servile conception of production. Two thousand years ago and upward, slavery was the fundamental institution of Mediterranean city-states, Celtic tribes, and German hordes—everywhere present, nowhere disputed. The Greek had a Greek slave, the Latin a Latin slave; human equality was recognised between master and slave; poverty made the slave, and the slave bred the slave. There were no martyrs for freedom against slavery. Slavery was of the stuff of Europe until the Faith.
The Church included no attack upon the institution as immoral; emancipation was a good work, as among pagans. Over close upon a thousand years the villa transformed the slave. Custom limited dues; surplus was left as an implied bargain; sale of men became exceptional. By the ninth century the estate divided into domain, land in villenage, and common waste with remembered rights. The servus became serf, then nearly a peasant: bound in theory, in practice inheriting a holding, buying, selling, building to his own profit. Town industry organised in guilds of private owners of capital, designed to check competition, safeguard the division of property, and prevent a proletariat. The Middle Ages conceived the Distributive State: the normal family should own. Collectivism did not replace slavery; common land was guarded by personal proprietors.
English failure
That consummation was destroyed, more particularly in Britain, not by machinery but by the deliberate action of men. The Industrial System proceeded from Capitalism; it was not machinery that lost freedom but the loss of a free mind. At the close of the Middle Ages England was economically free. Monastic lands—well over a fifth of agricultural communities, the Church lord of something over a quarter—were seized intending to vest them in the Crown and passed instead to an already wealthy section. Had the Crown kept them, the State might have used economic power against the wealthier classes. Large owners added a new fifth to their third and became at a blow owners of half the land. Clerical landlords had been customary; the new owners were strictly competitive. Howards, Cavendishes, Cecils, Russells, and fifty other new families rose upon the ruins of religion. By 1630–40 an oligarchy of large owners overshadowed a dwindled monarchy. By 1700 more than half the English were dispossessed: England had already become capitalist. That, and not the later so-called Industrial Revolution, accounts for the social condition of the present. Newcomen, Watt, Hargreaves, Darby, and Kay’s shuttle came upon a people already largely without economic freedom; capitalisation had to come from the class that monopolised accumulations. Common rights were destroyed of set purpose. There is not an example of so-called social-reform which is not directed to the further entrenchment of a society in which a few shall own and the majority live at a wage under them.
Instability of capitalism
Capitalism is a transitory phase between two stable states. As it grows perfect it grows unstable. First, law still presupposes free citizens—property as normal, contract as free, punishment as the sanction—while property as experience is unknown to nineteen out of twenty. The vast bulk of free contracts are leonine: one party may take or leave, the other faces starvation. Most men fear the loss of employment more than legal punishment; the true master of the Englishman is the Capitalist. Second, capitalism destroys security. Labour of the non-owner fetches nothing in sickness or despair. A perfect capitalist state cannot exist: left completely free there would be so heavy a mortality from starvation as would dry up labour. It must keep the masses alive by non-capitalist methods—Elizabeth’s Poor Law, the Poor Law of 1834, and a hundred others. Competitive anarchy makes employment precarious; understandings and secret political forces restrict competition. England is no longer possessed of the absolute political freedom true capitalism demands.
Three solutions; why Collectivism slides
There are but three social arrangements that can replace capitalism: slavery, socialism, and property. To solve capitalism one must get rid of restricted ownership, or of freedom, or of both. The only alternative to freedom is legal compulsion to work. Leaving freedom untouched, property must go into the hands of many (the Distributive State) or of none (Collectivism: vesting as a trust in political officers). Direct re-establishment of slavery would be a true solution and is the probable goal, but surviving Christian tradition forbids open advocacy.
The capitalist state breeds a Collectivist theory which in action produces the Servile State. Restoration of property works against the grain: confiscation and redistribution raise insoluble injustices; slow building of small savings must reverse the economy of interest; the proletarian mass thinks in terms of employment, not property. Collectivism works with the grain. Buying out a railway or municipalising gas does not disturb any fundamental thing; creating many small shareholders would leave owners free to sell again to a few. Collectivism promises employment, pensions, promotion, security vastly increased because the State guarantees it. To owners it is an enemy with whom they can treat: a business proposition. The State’s greater credit can seemingly “buy out”—an illusion: it is impossible by any jugglery to buy out the universality of the means of production without confiscation. If you desire to confiscate, you must confiscate. Actual “Socialist” measures fund new official salaries or hand proceeds to another set of capitalists: death duties become palings under an Inebriates Bill, or pass to Prudential shareholders under the Insurance Act.
Reformers, the mass, and the beginning of compulsion
Three interests make for the change: the Socialist (the confiscator who cannot confiscate, and the lover of tables and a vast bureaucracy who fathers servile regulation without trenching on privilege); the Practical Man, who cannot define first principles and gloats on every new detail in the building up of the Servile State; and the proletarian mass—about nineteen-twentieths in England, excluding Ireland, where reaction against capitalism is already successful. The generation of the Education Acts has grown up hopelessly proletarian. Offered a life-contract of service at the usual full wage, very few would refuse. That is the key. What the mass most fears is not the Courts but the sack. After the long terrors of a freedom unaccompanied by property, they see, at the expense of a mere legal freedom, the prospect of having enough and not losing it. The Servile State is, in industrial England, no longer a menace but something in actual existence; the corner-stone is already laid.
Factory laws that bind the citizen as citizen are not an origin. The first servile legislation on the statute book is the present form of Employers’ Liability: it admits status—the worker as inferior claiming protection from a superior. Later measures fall into three categories: relief of proletarian insecurity through the employing class or the proletariat under compulsion; compelling the employer to give not less than a certain minimum; compelling a man lacking the means of production to labour though he has made no contract.
The Insurance Act follows in every particular the lines of a Servile State. Its criterion is employment: compulsion if exchanging services for goods below a certain amount, or being a vulgar fellow working with his hands. It excludes the educated and therefore powerful classes and those earning enough to be economically free. The duty of seeing the law obeyed is put not upon the proletariat but upon the Capitalist class. The future historian will fix upon that point as the cardinal landmark: two categories, the lower man compelled to registration and a tax, the upper man the instrument in enforcing that registration and collecting that tax. Registration of the proletariat—name, address, movement, illness, supposed malingering, drink, domestic habits, employment—is very nearly complete, imposed by the wealthier classes who are the actual gatherers of the poll tax. Labour exchanges will register every proletarian as a worker, his tendencies to rebellion against capital, whether and when he has refused service. Insurance sums are not in the hands of a society he can control: refuse work at twenty-five shillings and he shall not have a right to the money he has been compelled to put aside. No man, once so registered and known, can escape.
Minimum wage as a statutory sum had not entered the laws as of September 1912, but mining had legal sanction for a hypothetical minimum arrived at by local boards—wages boards in one great industry, shortly in more. Parliamentary debate on the miners did not turn on their owning the mines or the State owning them, but on the minimum wage at a satisfactory level. Both parties were agreed upon that fundamental change. A sliding scale according to prices and profits is easy and natural: capital gets guarantee against disturbance; labour sufficiency and security. The proletarian loses the power to refuse his labour and thus to aim at putting himself in possession of the means of production. Two and a half millions guaranteed against unemployment at a weekly sum related to estimated earnings is a short step to statutory sums in employment. A minimum wage involves compulsory labour: courts must constrain either party to a ratified bargain; habit over years makes it compulsory labour. The man who cannot produce the minimum must be made to work; the labour colony—a prison so called because euphemism is necessary to every transition—will crown the edifice. Compulsory arbitration is the obvious bludgeon, twice brought forward as a Bill; no civilised European state has yet succumbed.
Municipalisation and nationalisation proceed by loan, not confiscation. Interest is continued surplus values; sinking fund the instalments. Capitalism is a winner and not a loser by this form of sham Socialism. Translation of the means of production from private owners to public officials is nowhere being attempted.
The Old Age Pensions Act belongs to the same body of organised reform that labour-representation pressed and that ran parallel to the great-labour-unrest-1911-1914: security without property, regulation without confiscation. The community left to itself settles upon that servile basis which was its foundation before the Christian faith, from which that faith slowly weaned it, and to which in the decay of that faith it naturally returns. Mere capitalist anarchy cannot endure. Theoretical Collectivism, now so plainly failing, will not inform a living society. Societies that broke with Christian continuity in the sixteenth century—roughly North Germany and Great Britain—tend to the re-establishment of a servile status. Ireland has decided for a free peasantry; France has contemptuously rejected registration and insurance of artisans as a separate category. The tide making for the Servile State in Prussia and in England may be modified, checked, perhaps defeated in war, by those freer societies upon its flank.
In the Sources

concepts/social-reform.title: Social Reform
concepts/social-reform.content:
Social Reform
Social reform was the programme of state action—pensions, insurance, labour regulation, and progressive taxation—by which late-Victorian and Edwardian governments sought to mitigate poverty without the common ownership demanded by Socialism. In the years after 1906 it became the central domestic work of the Liberal ministries, financed by Free-Trade revenue, opposed by the house-of-lords, and pressed forward under the pressure of labour-representation and industrial unrest.
Development
In the late seventies and early eighties republicanism still claimed many ardent working-class Radicals; Charles Bradlaugh was its chief exponent, and both Joseph Chamberlain and Sir Charles Dilke had been suspected of republican leanings. But the rise of Socialism in the eighties diverted republican enthusiasm into social channels. Robert Owen’s utopian Socialism had flourished and died, as Chartism flourished and died. Marx’s “scientific” Socialism claimed to emancipate the workers from wage slavery and insisted that the change was inevitable. On the Continent Social Democracy gained enormous working-class support. In England the Social Democratic Federation (later the Social Democratic Party), founded in 1884 by H. M. Hyndman, never won the sympathy of the trade unions nor the confidence of the working-class electorate; yet John Burns and many another Labour leader passed through its ranks, and a social conscience was made sensitive to the miseries of the poor. The Fabian Society, also founded in 1884, made no proposal for a separate Socialist party; its influence showed mainly in statistical knowledge and State interference in the conditions of life and labour. The Independent Labour Party (1892) professed Socialism yet aimed rather at returning labour members to Parliament and local councils than at converting the working class to dogmatic social democracy. Often frankly opportunist, the ILP and its offspring, the Labour Party in the Commons, followed the national custom of attacking and redressing evident evils—with considerable success. That success was the institutional foundation of modern labour-representation.
While Socialists made social reform the chief concern of all politicians, the idea of a social democracy steadily receded. Socialist workmen in Parliament found themselves absorbed in practical legislation, with neither leisure nor outlet for revolutionary propaganda. The return of so many Labour members damped down the fires of Socialism by placing the ablest leaders in positions of authority. John Burns might be denounced as a renegade by Socialist critics, but a working-class electorate returned him; Cunninghame Graham and Victor Grayson might be applauded for consistency, but working-class constituencies were loth to return such representatives. As Socialism became a dim and remote possibility of the future, Social Reform took its place. In Britain, where practical politics had always prevailed over theory, the old Liberal doctrines of laissez faire, unrestricted competition, and the personal liberty of the subject were as dead as the Stuart doctrine of divine right. Hostility to State interference and compulsory social legislation melted away. Lord Cromer and Harold Cox still repeated the ancient watch-words of Victorian Liberalism—and were regarded as strange survivals, but no popular echo followed. Pensions for the aged, better provision for the sick and infirm, the well-being of children, national health, some cure for destitution, and some remedy for unemployment—these were the matters a Liberal Government was concerned about. Conservatives were no less sincere; legislative proposals for social reform were treated as non-party questions, and Tariff Reform was advocated mainly as a social reform, a cure for industrial evils and unemployment. Thus the debate over free-trade-and-tariff-reform was itself framed, on the Unionist side, as a competing path of social betterment.
The two ideals stood in clear contrast. Socialism proposed the abolition of poverty and the common ownership of land and the means of production, distribution, and exchange. Social Reform proposed to mitigate the hardships of life for the multitude and, while leaving land and capital in private hands, to compel by taxation provision for the wants of the people. Its aim was the abolition of destitution by State assistance to voluntary effort and the gradual raising of the standard of life—not the removal of the cause of poverty. It promised a living wage, decent housing, insurance against unemployment, and security in old age, and left national or private ownership to posterity. Alongside both ideals ran Henry George’s Single Tax: Progress and Poverty (1879) became the bible of land reformers as Marx’s Capital was (or had been) of Socialists. George’s visits in 1881, 1884, and 1889 strengthened the movement for taxing land values; Liberals were won over—if not to twenty shillings in the pound, at least to a tax on land values—and principal municipalities petitioned Parliament in its favour.
The Liberal landslide of 1906—the election-1906-tariff-reform that broke Tariff Reform at the polls and returned a majority swollen by Labour and Irish Nationalist support—put the condition of the people at the centre of the parliamentary programme. Free-Trade finance was to carry social legislation without food taxes. Under Campbell-Bannerman, and then under Asquith, the statute book received Workmen’s Compensation, the Trade Disputes Act, regulation of sweated trades, and the first great social-security statute of the ministry.
The Old Age Pensions Act of 1908 created a non-contributory state pension for persons over seventy, paid from the Exchequer and subject to tests of means, character, and poor-relief history. On 15 January 1908 Asquith, still Chancellor, promised at Lancaster that a scheme would be begun. Lord Cromer, five days earlier at Glasgow, had condemned any such scheme as developing “demoralising dependence on the State.” The Speech from the Throne on 29 January promised proposals “for making better provision for old age”; Lansdowne condemned “the assumption of the colossal liability of old-age pensions.” After Campbell-Bannerman’s death in April, Asquith became Prime Minister and David Lloyd George succeeded him at the Exchequer. Moving the second reading on 16–17 June, Lloyd George said contributory schemes had been abandoned by most reformers, including Chamberlain; they would exclude women; and the failure of friendly societies’ superannuation schemes had shown the contributory plan impracticable. Of 1,262,632 persons over seventy, 572,000 were estimated pensionable; annual cost £7,500,000, with £6,000,000 for the first year—“the most liberal scheme yet proposed in any old country.” The Bill imposed a qualified character test and disqualified persons who had received poor relief (other than medical relief) since 1 January 1907. Friendly societies regretted the absence of thrift encouragement; labour organisations treated the measure as only an instalment. Harold Cox condemned expenditure by “arbitrary standards of age, income and character”; O’Grady for Labour declared the Bill “hopelessly inadequate.” Haldane replied that it embodied the poor-law principle since Elizabeth—that the prosperous must relieve the necessitous. By early 1909 some 490,000 had established claims, with about 130,000 more probable. Asquith insisted that Free-Trade finance would “stand the strain of social reform,” and that the Act was “only the first instalment.”
That instalment forced the financial crisis of 1909. Parliament opened under King Edward VII with a Speech warning that old-age provision and the Navy would raise expenditure. Asquith told the Commons that finance must be the first business: social reform had to be paid for. On 29 April Lloyd George introduced the Finance Bill that became the People’s Budget—a “War Budget” against poverty. It proposed a 20 per cent tax on the unearned increment of land when sold; a halfpenny in the pound on the capital value of undeveloped land; a 10 per cent reversion duty on a landlord’s interest at lease expiry; increased death duties; and a super-tax on incomes above £5,000—proceeds to fund pensions and naval construction amid accelerating Anglo-German rivalry. Balfour declared the force behind the Budget “really Socialism.” Austen Chamberlain, moving rejection, indicated that the Opposition alternative was Tariff Reform. The Lord Advocate answered that land owed its value to the community and that the Budget was “a great and democratic Budget.” After five months of Commons debate the Lords, on 30 November 1909, rejected the Bill by 350 to 75—a breach of the convention that the Upper House did not interfere with money bills. The constitutional crisis that followed—two general elections in 1910, a broken Constitutional Conference, and the Parliament Act of 1911 stripping the Lords of absolute veto—joined the financing of pensions and the Navy to social reform, free trade against Tariff Reform, and the Irish demand that Home Rule no longer be blocked by an hereditary chamber. At Mile End in November 1910 Lloyd George put the issue in popular form: the Government needed money for defence and social reforms by taxing great incomes, while the Lords demanded that the burden fall on the bread and meat of the people. The People’s Budget struggle made progressive taxation for social expenditure inseparable from the remaking of the constitution.
Once the Parliament Act had broken the absolute veto, the Government could press social measures the Lords could no longer kill outright. When King George V opened his first Parliament, the Speech named, as the only Bills specifically promised, removal of the pauper disqualification for old-age pensions and “insurance against sickness, invalidity, and (in special trades) unemployment.” Asquith had already, at Glasgow in April 1909, sketched labour exchanges and unemployment insurance as “the next stage of social reform after old-age pensions and debt reduction.” Lloyd George’s visit to Germany in August 1908 to study workmen’s insurance had given him a continental model of contributory provision that the non-contributory pension scheme had deliberately rejected. The National Insurance Act of 1911 established compulsory insurance against sickness and invalidity for the mass of employed persons, and against unemployment in selected trades. Contributions were shared among worker, employer, and the State; benefits ran largely through approved friendly societies, with a provisional Post Office scheme for those outside. Separate Commissioners covered Ireland, Scotland, and Wales. Sick pay was set at 10s. per week for men and 7s. 6d. for women for twenty-six weeks; maternity benefit extended to the wife of an insured person; persons earning less than 9s. a week paid no contribution. Labour opposition was not to insurance in principle but to the Bill’s treatment of casuals, sweated workers, and “poor lives.” Keir Hardie’s proposal to give maternity benefit to unmarried mothers was defeated 207 to 95; yet when the great strikes of August estranged Labour and some advanced Liberals, the Government had “gained in popularity, apparently, by the Insurance Bill.” “Joy Day,” 15 July 1912, was the day the Act came into force: of 13,000,000 persons compulsorily insurable, 9,500,000 had already joined approved societies. Medical resistance over panel terms continued; Bonar Law answered “Certainly” when asked whether he would repeal it if he became Prime Minister—then qualified the admission in the press.
Social reform did not quiet the workshops. The great-labour-unrest-1911-1914 of seamen, dockers, railwaymen, miners, and transport workers ran parallel to the Insurance Act, the aftermath of the People’s Budget, and the deepening Irish crisis. Bonar Law, at Leeds in autumn 1911, blamed the Budget campaign of 1909 for intensifying working-class unrest, of which the labour disturbances were “the fruit,” and pointed to a rise of nearly 10 per cent. in the cost of living without a corresponding rise in wages; the Government’s method, he said, was to take from the rich by taxation and give to the poor in doles. The coal strike of March 1912 forced a district minimum-wage statute; Ramsay Macdonald, on the Address of 1912, ascribed labour troubles to insufficient wages amid expanding national wealth—of 7,300,000 wage-earners, 60 per cent. under 30s. a week. Social reform had fixed pensions and insurance on the statute book; it had not abolished the industrial conflict that Socialism had once promised to end by reconstruction.
Belloc, writing while the same statutes were still new, refused that middle ground. In The Servile State he argued that social reform which registered the proletariat, erected wages boards, mapped men through labour exchanges, and levied insurance contributions did not restore the Institution of Property and did not confiscate the means of production for the community. It established security and sufficiency without ownership: the wage-earner kept his legal freedom only so long as he remained unregistered and uncompelled; once the State defined him by employment, collected a poll-tax through his master, and accumulated a dossier of work refused, he slid toward status and compulsory labour. Collectivism, Belloc held, was the ideal reformers named; the servile-state was the third thing their statutes actually produced—owners confirmed, the mass constrained, and the path of confiscation made more remote with every “positive economic reform.” The national-insurance-1911 was his cardinal instance: compulsion attached to the employed, not to the citizen as citizen; the Capitalist class enforced registration and gathered the tax.
Clayton, writing while these measures were still new, listed old-age pensions with Workmen’s Compensation and the Trade Disputes Act among the labour legislation of the previous twenty years that demonstrated “the value of parliamentary representation to the working class.” Social reform thus occupied the middle ground between laissez faire and collectivism. It assumed free trade and a solvent Exchequer; it used the newly widened franchise and the presence of Labour members to compel legislation that the Commons of fifty years earlier would have thought impossible; and it left private property standing while taxing it more heavily for public ends. Socialism proposed the abolition of poverty by reconstruction; social reform proposed its reduction by statute. The years 1906–14 were the high season of the second path—interrupted by war before a full reckoning with either ideal could be made.
In the Sources

concepts/womens-suffrage.title: Women's Suffrage
concepts/womens-suffrage.content:
Women’s Suffrage
Women’s suffrage was the claim that women should share the parliamentary franchise on terms that already qualified men—or on closely related occupation and household qualifications—and thereby sit, through their chosen representatives, within the constitution that taxed them, bound them by statute, and increasingly admitted them to local government. It was the last great sex disability in a century of parliamentary-reform that had already opened Parliament and public life to Catholics, Jews, Nonconformists, freethinkers, and working men. Enfranchisement and representation were, in the language of the movement itself, the two chosen instruments of democratic government.
Development
Medieval exemption and modern exclusion
Medieval practice had excused women from parliamentary attendance and from juries without treating their powers and privileges as landowners as shortened by sex. The modern exclusion was judicial and statutory. The Reform Act of 1832, by writing “male person” into the parliamentary franchise, fixed in statute what custom had left ambiguous. Thereafter the path to the vote ran only through Parliament—or through the courts, which in 1868 closed the judicial route.
Mill’s amendment, 1867
During the discussions on the Reform Bill of 1867, John Stuart Mill introduced an amendment to admit women who were registered occupiers as well as men to the franchise—in other words, to make the qualification one of occupation only, without reference to sex. The majority of the House were at first disposed to regard the proposition as something merely droll, and to deal with it only in the spirit of pleasantry; but the debate proved a very interesting, grave, and able discussion, and it was the opening of a momentous chapter of political controversy. Mill got seventy-three members to follow him into the lobby; 196 voted the other way. The amendment that women should not be excluded from the franchise was defeated. The borough franchise that emerged from the Act established household suffrage for male householders and £10 male lodgers, and left sex as an express barrier. From that time supporters of women’s suffrage were always present in the Commons. Henry Fawcett, the radical Liberal who married Millicent Garrett Fawcett, was remembered as “a most ardent advocate of women’s claims to the legislative suffrage.”
Chorlton v. Lings and the local-government franchise
In 1868 the test case Chorlton v. Lings was brought. The judges decided that women householders were not to be registered as electors; it was left to Parliament to pass a Women’s Enfranchisement Bill. The parliamentary door closed; the municipal door opened almost at once. Since 1869 women who were householders enjoyed the municipal franchise, and as Poor Law guardians and members of school boards they were freely elected to sit side by side with men. Local government became the practical school of female citizenship while the national franchise remained closed. In 1907 Parliament declared women eligible for membership on county and borough councils, and for the chairmanship of county councils and the mayoralty of boroughs. Women entered the councils of great cities—Manchester and Liverpool among them—and were chosen as mayors in several towns. The contrast sharpened the grievance: women ratepayers and councillors still stood outside the House that levied the taxes and made the laws they administered.
Constitutional campaign, bills, and Conciliation
A Women’s Suffrage Bill introduced in 1870 passed its second reading in the Commons by 124 to 91 but was later blocked by the government. During a debate on women’s suffrage in 1871, Gladstone stated that if the ballot were once introduced there would be no harm done by allowing women to vote—an admission that the secret ballot would alter the conditions of the controversy, removing the duty of going up to the open poll. Another bill reached a second reading in 1884, during the passage of the Third Reform Act, but Gladstone refused to include women’s suffrage in the government’s franchise measure, arguing that the question was not ripe for settlement. The Act of 1884, which extended household suffrage to the counties, confined the vote to male householders.
Throughout the 1880s and 1890s the constitutional wing grew. In 1897 the many local and regional women’s suffrage societies were federated into the National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies (NUWSS) under the presidency of Millicent Garrett Fawcett. The NUWSS pursued parliamentary lobbying, petitioning, public meetings, and the education of opinion. By the turn of the century the organisation represented some 300,000 women; successive governments still declined to bring forward a franchise bill. Only the refusal of the Government to give time for discussion of the Bill in Committee prevented a Woman’s Enfranchisement measure, which on several occasions received a second reading, from passing the Commons.
Women were not asking for adult suffrage, but were willing to receive enfranchisement on the terms that qualified men as electors. The Conciliation Bill—so called because members of every political party agreed to make it their Bill—would have placed on the roll of electors rather more than a million women voters. The demand rested on the old constitutional ground of the Parliamentarians of the seventeenth century—that those who are directly taxed by Government must have some political control of the public expenditure—and it was supported by A. J. Balfour, then leader of the Conservative Party, on the ground that government can only be carried on in England by consent of the governed. Campbell-Bannerman stated that personally he warmly supported the enfranchisement of women: they were taxed without direct representation, and had to obey laws they did not make. The agitation for “Votes for Women” became one of the most conspicuous public movements of the age—parallel, in the minds of its advocates, to the earlier certainty of middle-class men and workmen that Parliament would not understand popular grievances until they chose their own representatives. Enfranchisement and representation were the instruments women sought; the same instruments underlay the rise of labour-representation for working men.
The militant movement
Frustration with the slow pace of constitutional methods produced a schism that became the suffragette-movement. In 1903 Emmeline Pankhurst and her daughter Christabel founded the Women’s Social and Political Union (WSPU) in Manchester, adopting the motto “Deeds, not words.” The first militant phase began in 1905 when Christabel Pankhurst and Annie Kenney disrupted a Liberal meeting in Manchester, courting arrest for publicity. The Annual Register for 1906 recorded that the agitation by the extreme supporters of women’s suffrage, popularly known as the “suffragettes,” had caused a good deal of disturbance both in Liberal meetings and in the House of Commons itself. In June 1906 a deputation attempted to force its way to the Prime Minister’s house in Cavendish Square; one leader assaulted a police sergeant and was sentenced after refusing to recognise courts “on the ground that laws were made exclusively by men.”
In 1907 nearly thirty women’s suffrage societies, representing some 300,000 women, held a conference under Mrs. Fawcett and passed resolutions that neither sex nor marriage should disqualify for the franchise. The WSPU escalated: in 1908 suffragettes chained themselves to the railings of 10 Downing Street; by 1909 prisoners in Holloway broke windows, assaulted wardresses, and adopted the “hunger strike.” The government’s response—forcible feeding—provoked intense public controversy. After 1910, when a promised Conciliation Bill that would have enfranchised women householders was abandoned by the government of Asquith, the WSPU answered with systematic attacks on property—letterboxes set alight, windows smashed, unoccupied houses burned (Ascot, Clevedon, Kew among them). In April 1913 the Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Bill—the “Cat and Mouse Act”—allowed hunger-striking prisoners to be released on licence when health was endangered and rearrested when recovered; it did nothing to moderate the agitation. On 4 June 1913 Emily Wilding Davison ran onto the course at the Epsom Derby, was struck by the King’s horse Anmer, and died four days later. By the spring of 1914 militancy had reached its peak—churches burned, paintings slashed at the National Gallery and Royal Academy, a deputation toward Buckingham Palace leading to the arrest of sixty-six women. WSPU receipts for the year ending February 1914 amounted to nearly £37,000.
War, suspension, and the Reform Act of 1918
The outbreak-of-the-great-war transformed the situation. On 10 August 1914 the government announced a general amnesty for suffragist prisoners. Both the non-militant and the militant groups of the suffrage societies provisionally abandoned their agitation and organised themselves for the relief of women and children sufferers by the war. Admirable work was done by the National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies and by the Women’s Emergency Corps; Christabel Pankhurst, on her return from Paris, spoke at meetings designed to encourage recruiting for the “new Army.” Women filled factory jobs—particularly in munitions—served as nurses, drove ambulances, worked on the land, and replaced men in civilian occupations. By 1918 they had demonstrated capacity for labour previously considered the exclusive domain of men.
The need for a new franchise became practical before it became comprehensive. Soldiers and sailors abroad could not be left off any wartime register; from that narrow necessity the path led to a Speaker’s Conference on electoral reform and a full reconstruction of the franchise. Many members declared that the experiences of the conflict had shown that the conscious co-operation of women in the activities of the nation was a source of strength and not of weakness. On 19–20 June 1917 the Commons fixed the women’s age-limit at thirty; Sir George Cave opposed lowering it, and the women’s clause was carried by 214 to 17. The age of thirty was the price of carrying the principle: it kept the women’s electorate short of a majority of the whole, and held together a wartime coalition of suffragists and cautious converts that a more sweeping clause might have broken.
The Representation of the People Act 1918—the largest single extension of the franchise in British history—received the Royal Assent on 6 February 1918, at the close of the third war session. Its main women’s provisions were exact. Men qualified at twenty-one years of age with six months’ residence or occupation of business premises. Women qualified at thirty years of age, and either as a local-government elector or as the wife of one. The qualification for the local-government franchise was six months’ ownership or tenancy of land or premises; lodgers in furnished rooms were not qualified. University franchise extended to a man or woman within those age-limits who had taken a degree (in England and Wales), and a woman was also qualified to vote for a university that did not admit women to degrees if she had fulfilled the conditions for the admission of a man to a degree. Naval and military voters were to be registered for the constituencies for which they would have been qualified but for their service; male voters who had served in the war were qualified at nineteen. Dual voting was limited to two constituencies at a general election; the receipt of poor relief ceased to be a disqualification.
In the House of Lords the clause which enfranchised women was passed on 10 January 1918 by 134 votes to 71—a majority of sixty-three. A particularly powerful plea for woman suffrage was made by Lord Selborne, who declared that the enfranchisement of women would bring strength and fresh power to the country and the Empire. The Archbishop of Canterbury also strongly supported the measure.
The scale of the Act was unprecedented. While the Reform Act of 1832 enfranchised 500,000 new voters, that of 1867 one million, and that of 1884 two million, the Act of 1918 enfranchised eight million new voters—six million being women, of whom five million were married, and two million being men. Full adult equality of age with men still lay in the future, but the sex bar on the parliamentary franchise had been broken. Later in 1918 the Parliament (Qualification of Women) Act, passed on 23 October, removed the bar on women standing for election to the Commons (carried by 274 to 25). Under the Coalition that Lloyd George led into the post-armistice election, the duty of removing remaining legal inequalities between men and women entered the programme of reconstruction; the franchise Act had opened the gate.
In the Sources
