entities/churchill-winston.title: Winston Spencer Churchill (1874–1965)
entities/churchill-winston.content:
Winston Spencer Churchill (1874–1965)
President of the Board of Trade (1908–1910) · Home Secretary (1910–1911) · First Lord of the Admiralty (1911–1915) · Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster (1915) · Minister of Munitions (1917–)
Winston Spencer Churchill moved from the Unionist benches to the Liberal front rank, then from social and industrial office to the Admiralty at the height of the Anglo-German naval race. As First Lord he held the Fleet together through the July Crisis, ordered its night passage to war stations, and shared with the Board the first months of war at sea—Antwerp, the Channel ports, Coronel and the Falklands, and the recall of Lord Fisher. The Dardanelles enterprise and Fisher’s resignation in May 1915 broke the Admiralty partnership and forced him from office when Asquith reconstructed the ministry as a Coalition. He returned under Lloyd George as Minister of Munitions. Within the years of this wiki he is the statesman of Board of Trade and Home Office reform, of the 1911–15 Admiralty, and of the political fall that closed the pure Liberal war ministry.
From Soldier-Journalist to Liberal Minister
Churchill’s early fame was military and literary rather than ministerial. He had ridden with the 21st Lancers in the Sudan and later recorded Lord Kitchener’s disapproval of the young lieutenant who had forced his way into the campaign—a “dislike before first sight” that did not prevent later wartime cooperation when Kitchener took the War Office (The World Crisis, Vol. I). By the mid-Edwardian years he sat as a Liberal after leaving the Unionists over Free Trade. The Annual Register of 1908 places him among the speakers who made light of Mid-Devon as a storm in a teacup after his African tour, predicted land-value taxation and a measure against the Lords’ veto, and stressed Free Trade’s advantages for British commerce and international peace. At Swansea in August he repudiated the notion that an Anglo-German war was inevitable; the war party in Germany, he said, did not number ten thousand, and in England it existed only in lunatic asylums and on the staff of the National Review—language the Standard treated as undermining Sir Edward Grey, a misrepresentation Churchill denounced in the Daily Chronicle (Annual Register, 1908).
Belloc and Cecil Chesterton’s The Party System (1911) pairs him with Lloyd George as the two faces of the late 1910 election: “patriots confronting a haughty aristocracy (as represented to Mr Churchill by his cousin the Duke of Marlborough)” on one poster, “low-born demagogues” on the other. Enthusiastic Liberals still look on Asquith and Churchill as “tribunes of a people rightly struggling to be free”; the “credulous Radical” believes “Mr Churchill has become an outcast from his order by bravely taking the side of the people.” In the kinship list of the Governing Group, Churchill “as a member of the family whose name he bears, and as heir to his father’s career, has a double right.” “As all the world knows,” he is “not only the cousin of a former Conservative Minister, the Duke of Marlborough, but directly succeeded the head of his own family in the post he held, that of Under Secretary for the Colonies.” A Cecil, a Howard, a Churchill, or a Rothschild is the sort of name the machines prefer when they place candidates. The book stops at that Front-Bench network; it does not forecast later office.
When Campbell-Bannerman resigned in April 1908 and Asquith became Prime Minister, Churchill entered the Cabinet as President of the Board of Trade while Lloyd George took the Exchequer. His re-election for North-West Manchester that spring failed: Joynson Hicks defeated him by 5,517 to 4,988, with a Socialist far behind; Free-Trade Unionists and Irish electors had been recognised as swing factors, and Irish leaders only advised support after Churchill’s Easter Monday profession of Home Rule faith with the Prime Minister’s concurrence. He was at once invited to stand for Dundee and held that seat as the ministerial programme of old-age pensions, Free Trade finance, and social reform unfolded (Annual Register, 1908).
Board of Trade and Home Office
At the Board of Trade Churchill spoke for Free Trade at international congresses, foreshadowed bankruptcy and insurance reforms, and stood with Lloyd George in the radical wing that resisted the full Admiralty demand in the 1909 naval scare. Fisher and the Board wanted six new dreadnoughts; the economists offered four; the Cabinet compromised on eight—“We want eight and we won’t wait” having already seized the platform. Churchill later recorded the compromise in The World Crisis without concealing that he had been among those who doubted the scale of the German acceleration (Politics of Grand Strategy; The World Crisis, Vol. I; Annual Register, 1909).
As Home Secretary he bore the brunt of industrial disorder and of the constitutional struggle over the Lords’ veto. In the railway crisis of August 1911 troops occupied stations and parks; Churchill told the Commons that outrages on railway property were crimes punishable by penal servitude and that the Government would secure food, fuel, and services vital to the community, the working classes being the worst sufferers from famine and a general arrest of industry. The Annual Register later noted that the peremptory tone of the Prime Minister and of the Home Secretary owed something to the still half-secret strain of Anglo-German relations after Agadir (Annual Register, 1911). He also took Asquith’s place in major Parliament Bill debates when the Prime Minister was away, denied rumours of ministerial disunion, and defended the Bill as the answer to a legislative deadlock created by the Lords (Annual Register, 1911).
First Lord of the Admiralty (1911–1915)
Agadir and Appointment
The Agadir crisis of 1911—the Panther off the Moroccan Atlantic coast—pushed Churchill from the radical economy wing toward the centre of war preparation. He sat with Asquith, Grey, McKenna, and Lloyd George in the “very secret defence meeting” that managed the crisis; he drafted the memorandum of 13 August on the “Twentieth Day” and “Fortieth Day” of a continental campaign; and he wrote to Grey at the end of August as the crisis closed. The Prime Minister then invited him to the Admiralty. From 25 October 1911 to 28 May 1915 he was, in the words of the Royal Letters Patent, responsible to Crown and Parliament for all the business of the Admiralty (The World Crisis, Vol. I; Hankey, Man of Secrets, Vol. I).
Naval Policy: Sixty Per Cent and the Naval Holiday
At the Admiralty he found the Board, the incomplete War Staff, and the legacy of Fisher’s concentration and of Sir Arthur Wilson’s tenure. He pressed oil fuel, the 15-inch gun, and the Queen Elizabeth class; he reoriented dispositions toward the North Sea and the strategic geography of Scapa, Cromarty, and Rosyth. In March 1912 he announced that the Admiralty would maintain a sixty per cent margin over the dreadnoughts authorised by the 1908 German Naval Law, and would meet any German increases above that law on a two-to-one basis. The Haldane Mission to Berlin had already failed to trade a slowing of German construction for a British neutrality pledge Grey could not give without abandoning France. In 1913 Churchill proposed a “naval holiday”—a blank year of capital-ship building that would, he argued, wipe out five British super-Dreadnoughts if Germany built none—but German opinion received the suggestion as an attempt to wreck the Navy Law. By early 1914 he judged that naval rivalry had for the moment ceased to be a cause of friction: Britain was proceeding inflexibly with declared programmes, and Germany had made no further increases since 1912 (The World Crisis, Vol. I; Politics of Grand Strategy; Annual Register, 1913–1914).
Anglo-French naval conversations under his First Lordship concentrated French strength in the Mediterranean and British strength in the Channel and North Sea—the strategic counterpart of the staff talks Grey had authorised years earlier. Mediterranean withdrawals and the Grey–Cambon exchange of November 1912 on “moral obligation” remained politically delicate inside the Liberal Cabinet (Politics of Grand Strategy).
July Crisis and Mobilisation
On Friday 24 July 1914 the Cabinet was still immersed in the Irish boundary question when Grey brought in the Austrian note to Serbia. Churchill estimated that at least three-quarters of the members were determined not to be drawn into a European quarrel unless Britain herself were attacked. Against that current he pressed naval precautions. By Sunday 26 July Prince Louis of Battenberg, on Churchill’s instruction, had told the Fleet not to disperse after its practice mobilisation; at Grey’s and Tyrrell’s insistence the Admiralty published a communiqué that the First Fleet at Portland would not disperse for manœuvre leave. On 30 July Churchill obtained authority for the Fleet to pass the Dover Straits by night and take up war stations. When the German ultimatum to Belgium settled the issue for the majority of Asquith’s colleagues, formal sanction was given to completed naval mobilisation and to army mobilisation. Churchill sought authority to engage the Goeben if she attacked French transports; the Cabinet held that no act of war should precede the expiry of the British ultimatum—“The moral integrity of the British Empire,” he recorded, “must not be compromised at this solemn moment for the sake of sinking a single ship.” At eleven on the night of 4 August the war telegram “Commence hostilities against Germany” flashed to ships and establishments under the White Ensign; Churchill walked across the Horse Guards Parade and reported to the Prime Minister that the deed was done (The World Crisis, Vol. I; outbreak-of-the-great-war).
Opening Months of War: Antwerp, Oceans, Fisher
The passage of the Army, the crisis during the retreat from Mons, Antwerp, and the struggle for the Channel ports filled the autumn. Churchill’s personal mission to Antwerp, the Royal Naval Division’s part in the defence, and the fall of the city drew sharp Press criticism—the Morning Post called it “a costly blunder, for which Mr. Winston Churchill was primarily responsible”—while French’s despatch treated the enterprise as having delayed the enemy and facilitated the Belgian Army’s withdrawal (Annual Register, 1914). On the oceans, the destruction of Cradock’s squadron at Coronel and the despatch of Invincible and Inflexible to the South Atlantic ended in the annihilation of von Spee at the Falklands. Fisher returned as First Sea Lord in October 1914; Hankey’s biographer records that the combination of Fisher’s dynamism and Churchill’s strategic insight was not likely to accept a western deadlock tamely—yet the two already diverged over Baltic projects and over the Dardanelles (The World Crisis, Vol. I; Hankey, Man of Secrets, Vol. I).
Dardanelles, Resignation, and Return under Lloyd George
The naval attack on the Dardanelles, pressed in early 1915, divided counsel. Fisher was sceptical; Asquith later admitted “some doubt and hesitation” in Fisher’s mind; the Admiralty went ahead. By mid-May the relationship had broken over further reinforcements. Fisher resigned on 15 May; Corbett records that the resignations of Fisher and Churchill, coinciding with Coalition formation, closed the first phase of the naval war of 1915. Churchill left the Admiralty for the Chancellorship of the Duchy of Lancaster, defended himself in the Commons, and watched Balfour take the Admiralty in the reconstructed ministry. In July 1917 Lloyd George, long wishing to recall him, made him Minister of Munitions in the first reconstruction of the War Cabinet period (Annual Register, 1915, 1917; Corbett, Naval Operations, Vol. II; Hankey, Man of Secrets, Vol. I; first-coalition-1915; gallipoli).

Churchill’s own The World Crisis, Part I (1911–1914), is the densest narrative for Agadir, the Admiralty years, July–August 1914, Antwerp, and the opening war at sea; it is a participant’s book and is used here for sequence and official acts he records as First Lord, not as final judgment on every controversy. The Annual Register for 1908–1915 and 1917 supplies the contemporary parliamentary and electoral frame—Board of Trade and Home Office speeches, railway crisis, Admiralty appointment, Antwerp controversy, resignation and defence, and the 1917 return. Williamson’s Politics of Grand Strategy anchors the naval conversations, Mediterranean redistribution, sixty per cent standard, and Haldane Mission. Roskill’s Hankey: Man of Secrets, Vol. I, covers the CID circle, the Churchill–Fisher partnership, and the sulphurous War Council of May 1915. Corbett’s Naval Operations, Vol. II, marks the close of the first naval phase of 1915 with the double resignation.

entities/disraeli-benjamin.title: Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield (1804–1881)
entities/disraeli-benjamin.content:
Early Career & Rise to Leadership
Benjamin Disraeli entered the political world as a man apart — a literary figure turned politician, a Jew by race though a Christian in belief, and a romantic who wrote novels before he mastered the House of Commons. His first appearance before the electors of Wycombe was met with hooting and laughter; his maiden speech in the House of Commons was a disaster. But Disraeli possessed something that mere ridicule could not extinguish: a boundless faith in himself, and a constitution that seemed to find joy in the very heat of political strife. He had, as one contemporary observed, all the joy of the fight; the next best thing to a victory brilliantly won was a defeat gallantly sustained.
For many sessions he endured what seemed utter failure, and then suddenly found his chance and was recognised. From that time his career became one of steady advancement and growing fame. He was not, by the highest standard, a great orator — his more rhetorical efforts often bore an air of artificiality that marred their effect. But as a debater he ranked among the very foremost. He possessed an unfailing gift of sarcasm, a quickness in devising humorous illustrations at the expense of an antagonist, and a command of scornful phrases that lived in the memory of the House and became familiar quotations in debate and in literature. His voice was impressive and varied in tone.
Disraeli had, moreover, a literary career unique among statesmen. His political novels — Coningsby, Sybil, Tancred — were done half so well by anyone else in England. Indeed, it might be said that his are the only political novels in the English language. He contrived to blend his literary and political qualities into a curiously compact, characteristic, and original form of expression, and seemed as if he never could be languid, commonplace, or unimpressive; he was ever alive and ever vivid.
His rise to leadership of the Conservative Party came during the long Palmerstonian era, which Disraeli accurately described as the rule of a “Tory chief of a Radical Cabinet.” When Palmerston died in 1865, the question of parliamentary reform could no longer be postponed. The Liberal government under Earl Russell and Gladstone introduced a moderate Reform Bill in 1866, but it was defeated by a combination of old Palmerstonian Whigs and Conservatives. The Liberals retired, and a Conservative ministry under Lord Derby was formed, with Disraeli leading the House of Commons.
The Hyde Park riots of July 1866 — in which crowds tore down half a mile of iron railings and swarmed over the park — convinced Her Majesty’s ministers of the necessity of an immediate adoption of the reform principle. Disraeli, who had proposed reform as early as 1859 without support, now saw a great opportunity for constructive Conservative policy. “You cannot establish a party of mere resistance to change,” he told his followers, “for change is inevitable in a progressive country.” When Parliament met in February 1867, a Reform Bill was promised in the Queen’s Speech. Lord Derby called it frankly a “leap in the dark.” Several Conservative ministers, including Cranborne — the future Lord Salisbury — left the Government in disgust. But the Conservatives generally chuckled at “dishing the Whigs,” and the Bill, with considerable revision, passed through both Houses by August.
The Reform Act of 1867 enfranchised all male householders in boroughs and all male lodgers paying £10 a year for unfurnished rooms. The town workman was enfranchised by this Act as the middle-class man had been enfranchised by the Act of 1832, and the electorate was increased from about one hundred thousand to two million. It was a masterstroke of political tactics: the Conservative Party, under Disraeli’s inspiration, had carried a measure of reform more expansive than the Liberal bill it had defeated the year before. The measure was, as historians later noted, one of those instances where Disraeli’s most memorable successes in legislation were but the carrying out of a policy originated by his great rival Gladstone, opposed and overthrown by Conservative opposition in the previous session, and then carried to success by the Conservatives themselves.
When Lord Derby retired in February 1868, Disraeli became Prime Minister for the first time — but only briefly. The general election of 1868 returned Gladstone and the Liberals to power with a commanding majority, and Disraeli resigned at the end of the year without having had the opportunity to leave any deep mark upon domestic policy. He went into opposition, and for six patient years he held his party together, waiting for the tide to turn.
Premiership (1874-1880): Domestic Reform
The tide turned dramatically in 1874. Mr. Gladstone, in an impulsive and quixotic decision, suddenly dissolved Parliament in January of that year, appealing to the country for a renewal of confidence. The result surprised everyone. The Liberal majority was swept away; the Conservatives came back with a majority of about fifty. Mr. Gladstone resigned at once, and Mr. Disraeli — now sixty-nine years old — was installed in office at the head of what many called a “Conservative Reaction.”
Disraeli reduced the Cabinet to twelve. Lord Cairns became Lord Chancellor; Lord Derby, who gratified sober-minded men, was made Foreign Secretary; Lord Salisbury, despite the differences that had once separated them over the Reform Bill, was entrusted with the Indian Department. Mr. Cross, a Lancashire lawyer who had never held office before, was lifted into the Home Office. Sir Stafford Northcote, trained in finance by Gladstone himself, became Chancellor of the Exchequer.
For a time the new Government plodded steadily on with quiet schemes of domestic legislation, though these were not usually very comprehensive or drastic. Critics described them as tinkering. The Government tinkered at a measure for the security of improvements made by agricultural tenants, but made it purely permissive and therefore thoroughly worthless. This inclination to make every reform permissive tainted many of their domestic schemes: a bill was introduced professedly to remove some grievance, and then all parties concerned were allowed to contract themselves out of it.
Mr. Cross, however, proved a very efficient minister and introduced many useful schemes of legislation, among them an Artisans’ Dwellings Bill, the object of which was to enable local authorities to pull down houses unfit for human habitation and rebuild on the sites. The Government also restored the appellate jurisdiction of the House of Lords, which had seemed actually doomed.
One of the most dramatic episodes of the early ministry concerned the merchant seaman Samuel Plimsoll, who had for years agitated against the scandal of overloaded and unseaworthy ships. Plimsoll’s passionate denunciation of ship-owners in the House of Commons, and his readiness to defy parliamentary order itself, roused the country. Great meetings were held all over England. Disraeli, perceiving the direction of public feeling, quietly claimed some of the credit for having stirred the public temper, and the Government brought in — and torcibly pushed through — a Merchant Shipping Bill that met some of the worst abuses, though it did not prove to be a very strong measure.
But Disraeli’s attention was never long fixed on the dusty paths of domestic reform. He soon turned away from such homely business, and his Government’s energies were absorbed instead by questions of imperial interest in all parts of the world.
Imperial & Foreign Policy: The Berlin Congress, Suez, India
The first indication of the new foreign policy was the purchase of the shares which the Khedive of Egypt held in the Suez Canal. The Khedive was on the brink of bankruptcy, having lived in the true fashion of an Eastern prince, gratifying every expensive whim. His 176,000 shares came into the market; and on November 25th, 1875, the world was astonished by the news that the English Government had bought them for four millions sterling. The idea was not the Government’s own: it was Mr. Frederick Greenwood, the editor of a London evening paper, who first conceived the thought. He made it known to a member of the Cabinet, who threw cold water on it, but Greenwood then tried the Prime Minister himself — and the shares were instantly bought up.
Seldom had any act of government been received with such general approbation. The London newspapers broke into a chorus of applause; the clubs were delighted. When a faint voice here and there suggested that the purchase was foolish, useless, undignified, a shout of offended patriotism drowned the remonstrance. Some continental newspapers condemned the act as audacious, arrogant, and ominous — and this only stirred Englishmen the more. There was a general sense of satisfaction at the idea that England was again regarded as an arrogant and dominating power. Men held up their heads grandly. Disraeli himself spoke in a grand and mysterious way, giving people to understand that the buying of the shares was part of some great scheme destined to make England mistress of the East. The act was of historical importance as the first of a series of strokes by which the Government sought to keep the public continually excited by the luxury of a new sensation.
The Eastern Question soon absorbed everything. When the Bulgarian atrocities of 1876 stirred the conscience of Europe, Disraeli famously tried to dismiss the reports with a laugh and a light word. It was a serious miscalculation. Mr. Gladstone, emerging from his retirement, published his famous pamphlet on the Bulgarian horrors and threw himself into a great moral crusade against Turkish misrule. The controversy that followed became bitterly personal. Disraeli and Gladstone were thrown into as sharp an antagonism as two gladiators in a Roman arena. The policy each represented was clear: Disraeli stood for maintaining Turkey at all risks as a barrier against Russia; Gladstone for renouncing all responsibility for Turkey and taking the consequences. “The interests of England,” said one; “the public conscience of England,” said the other. Men who prided themselves on being practical politicians went naturally with Disraeli; men who held that sound politics cannot exist without sound morals went with Gladstone.
Each statesman made a mistake characteristic of the man. Disraeli misunderstood the gravity of public feeling on the Bulgarian question. Gladstone later acted on the assumption that mere sympathy could long prevail against the traditional English distrust of Russia — and when Disraeli and his supporters once had their opportunity of playing that card, they had the game absolutely in their hands.
At the Guildhall banquet on November 9th, 1876, Disraeli spoke in tones of open challenge to Russia. “If the struggle comes,” he declared, “in a righteous cause England will commence a fight that will not end until right is done.” The Russian Emperor, Alexander, replied the very next day, speaking to the nobles of Moscow in words that sounded like a direct answer. The decision of peace or war seemed to rest with Disraeli alone. Every eye was turned upon him.
The Constantinople Conference came to nothing, as the Turks, perhaps encouraged by private hints from English diplomatists, refused to come to terms. War broke out between Russia and Turkey. When the Treaty of San Stefano in 1878 threatened to put the whole of south-east Europe under Russian influence, the English Government refused to recognise it. Lord Derby resigned rather than approve the measures of resistance that Disraeli resolved upon. The Government called out the reserves, summoned Indian troops to Europe, occupied Cyprus, and prepared for war.
Lord Salisbury became Foreign Secretary. After tense negotiations, a Congress was summoned to meet in Berlin on June 13th, 1878. To the surprise of the public, Disraeli announced that he himself would attend — an event without precedent. Never before had an English Prime Minister left the country while Parliament was sitting to act as the representative of England in a foreign capital. The part suited Disraeli’s love for the picturesque and the theatrical. His journey to Berlin was a triumphal progress: at every great city, almost at every railway station, crowds turned out to see the English statesman whose strange and varied career had so long excited the wondering attention of Europe.
Prince Bismarck presided over the Congress, and departed from custom by opening the proceedings in English — a kindly deference to the English Prime Minister, whose French was said to have fallen into decay. The Congress dealt with the condition of the provinces under Turkish suzerainty, the populations of alien race under Turkish dominion, the claims of Greece, and the Turkish possessions in Asia.
The Treaty of Berlin recognised the complete independence of Roumania, Servia, and Montenegro. It created, north of the Balkans, a self-governing state of Bulgaria, tributary to the Sultan but practically independent; and south of the Balkans, Eastern Roumelia, remaining under Turkish authority but with a Christian governor. The Sultan undertook to apply reform to Crete, and Austria was to occupy Bosnia and the Herzegovina.
A secret engagement with Turkey gave England the island of Cyprus, which Disraeli later described as “a place of arms.” England now formally pledged herself to defend Turkey’s Asiatic possessions against invasion, and occupied Cyprus as a vantage-ground. The difference between the Conservative and Liberal policies was now thrown into the strongest relief. Disraeli had made it the cardinal principle of his policy that England above all was concerned to maintain the integrity of the Turkish Empire.
Disraeli’s return from Berlin was the climax of his career. He got a great public reception in London. Crowds awaited him at the gaudily decorated railway station. He made a conquering hero’s progress through the streets, and from the windows of the Foreign Office addressed an excited and tumultuous crowd. His words became memorable: he had brought back “Peace with Honour.”
From the day when he first addressed the electors of Wycombe, hooted and laughed at, up to this triumphal reception in the streets of London — what a distance he had traversed! Years of struggle against almost insurmountable difficulties, years of steady faith in himself undisturbed by almost universal ridicule, years of rise and fall, of success and disaster, had conducted him to this climax. At that moment he was probably the most conspicuous public man in the world, with the single exception of Prince Bismarck. He had attained a position of almost unrivalled popularity in England; not even Palmerston in his most successful days was pursued by such clamour of public acclamation. He ought to have followed classic advice, one observer remarked, and sacrificed his dearest possession to the gods at that moment, for no man could buy the lease of such a position without sacrifice.
The Royal Titles Act of 1876, by which Queen Victoria assumed the title of Empress of India, was another measure closely associated with Disraeli’s name. It was a piece of statecraft entirely in keeping with his love of ceremony, his concern for imperial prestige, and his desire to bind the Crown more closely to the great dependencies of the Empire.
Legacy & Reputation
Lord Beaconsfield — for he had accepted an earldom and removed to the House of Lords in 1876 — died on the morning of Tuesday, April 19, 1881, at his house in Curzon Street. He had suffered from a severe attack of bronchial asthma, and the east wind, always trying to him, continued to blow. Crowds of inquirers came to his door every day; amongst them many who had been thoroughly opposed to his public policy, and who believed him an ambitious and self-seeking man. But the thought that so great a career was about to close anticipated that burial of all hostility which death brings about.
Those who watched over him said that a few minutes before his death he raised himself a little in his bed, stretched himself out in the attitude he was accustomed to assume when he rose in the House of Commons, and his lips moved without sending out any words. His dying fancy was giving him back his old place in Parliamentary debate. No end could be more characteristic of the man.
He was undoubtedly one of the most interesting and fascinating figures in the European history of his time. He had made a great and quite a unique success in literature. He had been for many years the most splendid gladiator in the House of Commons. He had boundless ambition and followed his own star. Men of thorough sincerity — men like Gladstone, Cobden, and Bright — felt shocked at what seemed to them his lack of earnestness. When John Bright once spoke privately of “sated ambition,” Disraeli replied: “You know what you and I come here for. We come here for fame.” He could not be convinced that any man would waste his days in the House of Commons merely for the sake of serving a public movement.
Yet, with all the temptations that fame and society offered him, he seems to have led personally a blameless life. His bitterest enemy never suggested that any question of pecuniary gain ever occupied his mind. He was a good friend to his friends, and especially kind to young men of promise who seemed to have an ambition like that of his own early days. In society he was capricious of mood — sometimes sparkling with epigram and paradox, sometimes falling into a fit of brooding silence. He had, one might almost say, no friends among the outer public. For all the splendour of his opportunities and successes, he was a lonely, self-sufficing man. He had had all he wanted; everything came to him in the end.
Historians have judged that as a statesman Disraeli did not leave much record of great measures for the advancement of national prosperity. Even where his Government did introduce genuine reform or some new principle of legislation, it was often only after the rival party had come near to carrying a like measure and, failing because of Conservative opposition, had gone out of office and given Disraeli and his colleagues a tempting chance of carrying the work to success. This was notably the case with the Reform Bill of 1867.
As a debater, he was among the very foremost known to modern Parliaments, with an unfailing gift of sarcasm, a quickness in devising humorous illustrations, and a command of scornful phrases that lived in the memory. His voice was impressive and varied in tone. He seemed as if he could never be languid, commonplace, or unimpressive. He was ever alive and ever vivid.
The long rivalry between Gladstone and Disraeli did not leave any painful memories behind it for the admirers of either man. Those who followed Gladstone might remember with satisfaction that some of Disraeli’s most memorable successes in legislation were but the carrying out of a policy originated by Gladstone himself. But the name of Disraeli will always be regarded as that of one who brought into the House of Commons a new and peculiar style of eloquence; who contrived to blend his literary and his political qualities into a curiously compact, characteristic, and original form of expression. Destiny had given him everything for which he could possibly have asked.

entities/edward-vii.title: Edward VII (1841–1910)
entities/edward-vii.content:
Edward VII (1841–1910)
King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, Emperor of India. Succeeded Queen Victoria on 22 January 1901 and reigned until his death on 6 May 1910. The source texts describe him as a popular sovereign whose foreign travels promoted peace and whose reign was marked by constitutional crisis over the House of Lords.
Biography
Accession (1901)
Queen Victoria died at Osborne on 22 January 1901, and the Prince of Wales succeeded to the throne as King Edward VII. At his first meeting of the Privy Council he declared his intention to follow in his mother’s footsteps and to maintain constitutional government. The Annual Register records that “the style assumed by the King” renounced all titles “that might be held to imply dominion or supremacy over any part of the British Empire.” Messages of condolence arrived from foreign powers, including a telegram from President McKinley of the United States.
The new King came to the throne while the South African War was still in progress. McCarthy’s Diamond Jubilee volume notes that “a new Sovereign, King Edward VII., had come to the British throne” before the Boer peace terms were finalised at Pretoria. After the Peace of Vereeniging (31 May 1902), “King Edward sent a cordial message of thanks to Lord Kitchener.”
Coronation and Recovery from Illness (1902)
The coronation of King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra was originally fixed for 26 June 1902 at Westminster Abbey. Two days before the ceremony the King was attacked with perityphlitis (appendicitis). An operation was performed and proved successful. The coronation was postponed to 9 August, and the King convalesced at Windsor. Parliament opened on 16 August. The Annual Register records that “All had equal cause for thankfulness” at the King’s recovery, and in October the King and Queen visited the City of London. The King also visited his German relatives.
Foreign Policy and the Entente with France (1903–1905)
King Edward’s foreign travels became a distinctive feature of his reign. In the spring of 1903 he visited the King of Italy in Rome, where his “personal popularity abroad” delighted the British public and “gave additional solidarity to the relations between the two States.”
From Rome the King went to Paris, arriving on 1 May 1903. The visit was “singularly fruitful in the improvement of international relations.” He was welcomed to a gaily decorated capital by enormous crowds and drove with President Loubet to the British Embassy. Replying to the British Chamber of Commerce, he dwelt on the importance of Anglo-French friendship; at a State dinner at the Elysée he toasted “the rapprochement between the two peoples.” The visit had “a marked influence in dissipating the last traces of such ill-will towards England as had been evoked by Lord Salisbury’s necessarily uncompromising resistance to French ambitions” over the Nile. An Arbitration Agreement with France followed later in the year.
In 1904 the Anglo-French Agreement was concluded. In 1905, when Germany raised a controversy over the Moroccan portion of that agreement and despatched an envoy to Fez, the King made another visit to Paris. The American Ambassador, Mr. Choate, paid tribute to King Edward’s “unceasing instinct for peace” and “perfect genius for conciliation.” The King’s visit, the Annual Register records, “had tended appreciably to diminish the tension of the situation.”
The Liberal Landslide and Later Travels (1906–1909)
In January 1906 the King formally dissolved Parliament, and the ensuing general election produced a Liberal landslide victory. In his speech at the opening of the new Parliament, the King addressed the new ministry. In 1907, King Edward left London for Biarritz in March, travelling incognito, and was joined by the Queen at Toulon. They cruised the Mediterranean on the royal yacht Victoria and Albert, escorted by the Mediterranean fleet. At Cartagena (8 April) the King was greeted by the King of Spain and the Queen Mother. At Gaeta (18 April) he met the King of Italy, and again near Rome on 30 April. Continental opinion, especially in Germany, connected these visits with “a presumed Anglo-Spanish alliance” and “a new grouping of the Western Powers” that would exclude Germany, though the Annual Register notes there was “no real evidence of such a combination.”
In 1908 the King visited the Tsar at Reval. The visit was controversial among Labour and advanced Liberal MPs, who disapproved of the Tsarist regime. The Prime Minister, Mr. Asquith, defended the visit in Parliament as “overdue” and likely to do good to Anglo-Russian relations. Sir Edward Grey, the Foreign Secretary, argued that the visit could not be postponed “without marked discourtesy” and would “signify the existence of friendly relations.” The visit went ahead despite strong protests.
In 1909 the King and Queen opened Parliament in February. The King’s Speech referred to the cordial reception of the King and Queen at Berlin and its expected effect on Anglo-German friendship. The speech also signalled the coming constitutional crisis, noting the increase in expenditure for old age pensions and the Navy.
Final Illness and Death (1910)
The King spent most of March and April 1910 at Biarritz — after his death it was stated that this was to avoid the danger of bronchitis from the March winds in England. While in Paris he caught cold while witnessing Rostand’s Chantecler, and had been more seriously ill for a week at Biarritz than the public suspected. He seemed to recover and returned to Buckingham Palace on 27 April. A day or two later he visited the Royal Academy Exhibition, looking “tired and pale.”
On Sunday, 1 May, he was at Sandringham; on Tuesday, 2 May, he was confined to his rooms but continued to transact business. He gave an audience on 5 May to Lord Islington and discussed the reception planned for Prince Fushimi of Japan. That afternoon a bulletin announced he was suffering from bronchitis and that his condition “causes some anxiety.” Queen Alexandra arrived from Corfu that evening. On the morning of 6 May the symptoms had worsened; his condition “gave rise to grave anxiety,” and a throat specialist was summoned.
Nevertheless, the King got up and transacted business, “suffering from painful fits of coughing and attacks of heart failure,” receiving oxygen to relieve his symptoms. At 1 p.m. he said: “I shall not give in; I shall go on; I shall work to the end.” Shortly afterwards he passed into a state of coma, though occasionally reviving. In the afternoon he left his armchair for his bed. At half-past nine the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Princess Royal, and Princess Louise were summoned to stay the night, and the Primate (the Archbishop of Canterbury) was sent for. Shortly after eleven the Primate conducted a short service in the sick-room, and at 11:45 p.m. “King Edward the Peacemaker passed away without pain.” The announcement “The King is dead” was made to the waiting and anxious crowd at the Palace gates, “received in silence, followed by manifold and heartfelt expressions of grief.”
Mourning and Tributes
The Annual Register declares: “The unexpected death of King Edward VII was felt throughout the Empire and even in the United States almost as a personal bereavement, and was received all over the world with profound manifestations of sympathy and regret. Even at the death of Queen Victoria the sorrow had not been so widespread or so fully manifested, at any rate outside the British Empire.” Messages of condolence poured in from the Dominions, India, and foreign states. Throughout the United Kingdom and the Empire, places of entertainment were closed, social events cancelled, and funeral peals tolled. On Sunday, 8 May, pulpit tributes were paid to the King’s memory, with special stress on “his tact, his promotion of the welfare of his people, and his efforts for the peace of the world.”
In Ireland, the Nationalist leader John Redmond stated that “the King never showed any hostility to Ireland, and the general feeling was that he was a frank, manly, and friendly Sovereign.” Mourning was general across Ireland, with memorial services marking the day of the funeral.
The King was succeeded by his son, George V.

entities/fisher-john.title: Admiral Lord John 'Jacky' Fisher (1841–1920)
entities/fisher-john.content:
Admiral Lord John ‘Jacky’ Fisher (1841–1920)
First Sea Lord (1904–1910; 1914–1915) · Baron Fisher of Kilverstone (1909)
John Arbuthnot Fisher was the most transformative and controversial figure in the modern history of the Royal Navy. As First Sea Lord from 1904 to 1910 he overhauled the service from top to bottom — scrapping hundreds of obsolete vessels, concentrating battle-fleet strength in home waters, reforming training and gunnery, and championing the all-big-gun battleship HMS Dreadnought (1906) and the battle-cruiser. Recalled at the outbreak of the Great War in 1914, he clashed spectacularly with First Lord Winston Churchill over the Dardanelles campaign, culminating in his resignation in May 1915.

Naval Reforms (1904–1910)
Fisher became First Sea Lord in October 1904, succeeding Admiral Lord Walter Kerr. The Annual Register records the announcement on 20 June 1904 that “Admiral Sir John Fisher” would take up the post, then styled Senior Naval Lord, in October. He had already served on the War Office Re-organisation Committee (the Esher Committee), whose first report of February 1904 recommended the creation of a properly constituted Army Council and general staff for war — a sign of Fisher’s reach beyond purely naval matters.
As First Sea Lord, Fisher’s reforms were radical in scope. He concentrated the battle fleet in home waters, creating the Home Fleet as a standing force capable of meeting the German High Seas Fleet. The Annual Register for 1907 noted:

“The Home Fleet was in effect the culmination of the changes introduced in 1904. There had been a rancorous Press campaign against its distribution.”

He swept away hundreds of obsolescent ships: the 1905 Navy Estimates debate records that “the number of ships which had been removed from the first line of battle was, he thought, 160.” The Annual Register records the First Lord explaining that “the redistribution of the Fleet depended mainly, if not entirely, upon mobility” and that “the keynote of the scheme was that heavy expenses ought not to be incurred except for vessels which would be instantaneously ready for war.”
Economy was a central aim: in 1906 the new Liberal government gave Fisher “a free hand” to reorganise the Navy with a view to increased efficiency and reduced expenditure. The Annual Register noted that the Prime Minister “had given him a free hand to deal with it, and he and his colleagues were working to lay the foundations of a comprehensive plan.”
Fisher also overhauled naval education, establishing the Royal Naval College at Osborne (opened 1903) and reforming Dartmouth. He introduced the nucleus-crew system, keeping ships in commission with reduced crews but ready for rapid mobilisation. He created the post of Inspector of Target Practice (1905), centralising gunnery training, and elevated engineering officers in status.
His methods created fierce enemies. Admiral Lord Charles Beresford, commanding the Channel Fleet, conducted a sustained public campaign against Fisher’s policies, culminating in a formal inquiry into Beresford’s allegations in 1909. The Annual Register for 1909 records the “Result of Inquiry into Lord Charles Beresford’s Allegations” as a notable event of the parliamentary session. Fisher was exonerated, but the controversy exhausted him. He was raised to the peerage as Baron Fisher of Kilverstone in 1909 and retired in January 1910. On his departure the Annual Register paid tribute to “the late First Sea Lord, now Lord Fisher of Kilverstone, whose measures, adopted by several successive Governments, were declared likely to be ‘of far-reaching and lasting benefit to the Naval Service and to the country.‘”

The Dreadnought Revolution
Fisher’s most celebrated achievement was the creation of HMS Dreadnought, the all-big-gun battleship that rendered all existing battleships obsolete. Laid down in 1905 and commissioned in 1906, the Dreadnought mounted ten 12-inch guns and was powered by steam turbines, giving it a speed advantage of several knots over any existing battleship. The Annual Register for 1906 lists “The Dreadnought” as a heading in its table of contents; the 1906 Navy Estimates debate records that the programme inherited by the Liberal government “had comprised four Dreadnoughts, five ocean-going destroyers, twelve coastal destroyers and twelve submarines,” though the Board of Admiralty subsequently decided “it would be safe to strike off one Dreadnought.”
Alongside Dreadnought came the battle-cruiser — a fast, heavily-armed but less-armoured capital ship designed to hunt down enemy cruisers and serve as the scouting force of the fleet. The first three, of the Invincible class, were laid down in 1906. The Annual Register for 1907 noted the construction summary presented to Parliament: “In new types we had one Dreadnought ready, two Lord Nelsons completing, three Dreadnoughts laid down, and three Invincibles building. Against these neither Germany nor France had laid down a single keel.” The forecast was that “by the autumn of 1910 we should have eight or nine battleships completed and afloat, and three cruisers.”
The German naval challenge provoked the great naval scare of 1909. The Annual Register records that rumours were “rife of a crisis in the Cabinet on the question whether four Dreadnoughts or a larger number should be provided in the Estimates.” The Unionist opposition adopted the slogan “We want eight and we won’t wait” — coined by Mr. Wyndham at Wigan on 27 March 1909 — and the Croydon byelection returned a Unionist majority, “a striking testimony to the effect of the naval agitation.” The Government conceded four additional contingency Dreadnoughts, bringing the total to eight. The Annual Register records that Naval Estimates for 1909–10 included provision for “four battleships of the Dreadnought type, six protected cruisers, twenty destroyers, and a number of submarines.”
The design committee that created both Dreadnought and Invincible was chaired by Fisher himself. The Annual Register for 1905 notes that “a special committee on designs which had been appointed, including Lord Kelvin, Sir John Thorneycroft and some other outside experts as well as a number of distinguished naval officers, and presided over by Admiral Sir John Fisher, would, among other valuable services, ‘ensure to the Navy the immediate benefit of the experience which was to be derived from the naval warfare between Russia and Japan.‘”

Return as First Sea Lord (1914)
At the outbreak of the Great War, the First Sea Lord was Prince Louis of Battenberg. Anti-German agitation forced Battenberg’s resignation on 29 October 1914, and Fisher — then aged 73 and in retirement since 1910 — was recalled to the post he had held a decade earlier. The Annual Register records: “Lord Fisher of Kilverstone appointed First Sea Lord of the Admiralty, vice Prince Louis of Battenberg, resigned.”
Hankey’s biographer describes how Fisher’s “resurrection” was accomplished: “Those developments coincided with the recall of Admiral Fisher to the office of First Sea Lord by Churchill; and so was accomplished the ‘resurrection’ for which Fisher had lobbied and intrigued ever since he had left that same office in 1910.”
The Churchill-Fisher combination was initially highly successful. Hankey’s biographer writes:

“Despite his 73 years the Admiral had lost little, if any, of his thrustful dynamism; while Churchill’s vigour and strategic insight provided the necessary complementary qualities in the high level committees as well as at the Admiralty. Those two were not likely to accept tamely the continuation of the deadlock in the west.”

The first fruits were the destruction of Admiral von Spee’s squadron at the Falkland Islands on 8 December 1914, avenging the British defeat at Coronel. Fisher had insisted on sending the battle-cruisers Invincible and Inflexible to the South Atlantic — a decisive deployment that demonstrated the continued value of his battle-cruiser concept.

The Dardanelles & Resignation
The partnership with Churchill foundered on the question of strategic direction. Both men sought to break the western front deadlock through amphibious operations exploiting British sea power, but they differed fundamentally on the target. Hankey’s biographer records:

“Fisher favoured a landing on the German coast — either in the North Sea or preferably in the Baltic, within 80 miles of Berlin; but neither his naval colleagues nor the military authorities had any enthusiasm for this scheme.”

Churchill, by contrast, became an enthusiastic proponent of a naval attack on the Dardanelles Straits to force a passage to Constantinople, knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war, and open a supply route to Russia. Fisher was initially sceptical. The Annual Register records Asquith’s later admission in Parliament that “some doubt and hesitation had existed in the mind of Lord Fisher as to the naval attack.” Nevertheless, the Admiralty went ahead. The attack was “purely a naval operation” in its first phase, launched in February-March 1915.
The failure of the naval attack (three elderly battleships sunk by mines on 18 March) led to the decision to land troops on the Gallipoli Peninsula — a combined operation that escalated the commitment far beyond what Fisher had anticipated or approved. The Annual Register records that Asquith “admitted that the Government had taken great risks in the Dardanelles for great objects” and described the failure as “in the whole course of the war I have never sustained a keener disappointment.”
By May 1915, the relationship between Fisher and Churchill had reached breaking point over the despatch of further warships to the Dardanelles. Hankey, as Secretary to the War Council and a friend to both men, found himself caught in the middle. He recorded in his diary the “sulphurous” atmosphere of the War Council meeting on 14 May 1915. Fisher wrote to Hankey:

“My beloved Hankey, I will sacrifice my judgement to yours and wait. If I could show you letters from Jellicoe received during last week you would see I have an impregnable position.”

The truce did not hold. Fisher stormed out of the Admiralty and resigned on 15 May 1915, precipitating a political crisis that forced Asquith to reconstruct his government as a Coalition. Fisher’s “astounding ultimatum” to the Prime Minister set out the terms on which he would resume office, effectively demanding supreme control over naval policy. Asquith told the King the letter “showed signs of mental aberration.” Hankey’s biographer concludes that the old Admiral, now 74, “had suffered a serious nervous breakdown — possibly brought on by the relentless pressure to which Churchill had subjected him.”
Churchill was himself forced from the Admiralty shortly afterwards, becoming Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. The Annual Register records “Lord Fisher’s Reply” in its table of contents for November 1915, alongside “Resignation of Mr. Winston Churchill” and “His Defence in the House of Commons.” Admiral Sir Henry Jackson succeeded Fisher as First Sea Lord, and Arthur Balfour became First Lord of the Admiralty in the new Coalition government.

Later Years
After his resignation Fisher played no further official role in the war. He became a focus of controversy during the Dardanelles Commission inquiry, and engaged in public correspondence defending his actions. The Annual Register records his presence at the funeral procession of King Edward VII in 1910, among “high officers of the British Army and Navy, among them Earl Roberts, Lord Kitchener, and Lord Fisher of Kilverstone.”
Fisher died on 10 July 1920 at the age of 79.

entities/gandhi-mohandas.title: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948) — to 1919
entities/gandhi-mohandas.content:
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948) — to 1919
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (2 October 1869 – 30 January 1948), known from the late 1910s as Mahatma Gandhi, was the foremost leader of the Indian community in South Africa (1893–1914) and, after his return to India in 1915, the rising force in Indian nationalist politics. Within the 1865–1919 period, Gandhi is significant as the pioneer of satyagraha — non-violent resistance — first developed against the discriminatory laws of the Transvaal and Natal, and subsequently applied in his early Indian campaigns at Champaran (1917) and Ahmedabad (1918). By 1919 he had become the most prominent opponent of the Rowlatt Acts and had begun to transform the Indian National Congress into a mass movement.

South African Lawyer & Activist
Gandhi arrived in South Africa in 1893 as a young barrister to represent an Indian trading firm in a legal dispute. What he encountered there — a system of racial discrimination directed against Indian merchants, indentured labourers, and their descendants — shaped the remainder of his life. He remained in South Africa for twenty-one years, building a legal practice in Durban and Johannesburg and emerging as the principal spokesman and organiser of the Indian population.
In 1894 he founded the Natal Indian Congress, the first permanent political organisation representing Indian interests in the colony. The Congress agitated against legislation designed to disenfranchise and marginalise the Indian community, including bills to restrict Indian trading rights and franchise. During the Second Boer War (1899–1902), Gandhi organised the Indian Ambulance Corps, a body of over a thousand Indian volunteers who served with British forces at the relief of Ladysmith and elsewhere. The corps’ service was cited as evidence of Indian loyalty to the Crown, though it did little to improve the community’s position when peace returned.
The system of indentured Indian labour — under which men and women were bonded to work on Natal’s sugar plantations for fixed terms — was the demographic foundation of the Indian presence in South Africa. As the Annual Register observed, the Indian community in Natal was “the fruit of the indenture system,” and it would become a primary constituency for Gandhi’s campaigns [source: annual-register-1908].

Satyagraha Campaigns
The Transvaal Registration Act (1906–1908)
The crisis that gave birth to satyagraha arose from the Transvaal Asiatic Registration Act of 1907, which required every Indian in the Transvaal to register and submit to fingerprinting of all ten digits — a requirement perceived as degrading and criminalising. “At the close of 1907 the situation was that the Indian population of the Transvaal refused to register under the new Act,” the Annual Register recorded. “Mr. Gandhi, the leader, and other Indians who had refused to register, were arrested and ordered to leave the Colony. To these orders they offered a ‘passive resistance,’ and raised the legal point that the Government had no power to put them over the border by force” [source: annual-register-1908].
Mass meetings were held in Johannesburg; the entire Indian population seemed resolved upon resistance. The Natal government objected to Indians being dumped across its border, and negotiations opened for transit to the coast. Lord Ampthill, president of the South Africa British Indian Committee, and Mr. L. W. Ritch, its secretary, agitated vigorously in England on the Indians’ behalf [source: annual-register-1908].
The Transvaal Colonial Secretary, General Jan Smuts, defended the Act: he claimed thousands of false permits were in circulation and that white opinion was “unanimous in demanding the cessation of the system.” The Act, he said, had driven 5,000 unauthorised Indians from the colony; 9,500 remained who refused to register, of whom 5,000 held trade licences. The Government would “show no mercy to the leaders” [source: annual-register-1908].
Gandhi offered to secure universal registration within a month if the registration form could be mutually agreed: the Indians maintained that a thumb-impression was sufficient and that the requirement of ten-digit prints — as for criminals — was offensive to Indian sentiment. He also demanded a judicial inquiry into allegations of surreptitious entry. Meanwhile deportation orders continued, their impact sharpened by the fact that some of the deported men had “fought with distinction under the Crown” in the late war [source: annual-register-1908].
The crisis reached its peak on 10 January 1908, when Gandhi and five other leaders were sentenced to two months’ imprisonment without hard labour. Thereafter “the daily news was of batches of other arrests, and wholesale deportations, those failing to comply being heavily fined or imprisoned” [source: annual-register-1908].
The 1908 Compromise and its Collapse
By February 1908, letters passed and interviews were held between Smuts and Gandhi. The outcome was a compromise: Indians could “voluntarily” register without ten-digit prints; children under sixteen were exempt. The Indian negotiators understood Smuts to have pledged that, if all Asiatics registered voluntarily, the 1907 Act would be repealed.
Voluntary registration proceeded freely — but the repeal never came. The Government introduced a new Bill “to validate the voluntary registration of certain Asiatics who failed to comply with the Act of 1907.” The Indians protested that the pledge had been broken. Smuts “denied emphatically that any such pledge had been given.” The Annual Register noted that “the text of the letters embodying the compromise contained no statement inconsistent with Mr. Smuts’s denial,” and that a letter signed by Gandhi and two other leaders “expressly noted Mr. Smuts’s repeated public declarations that there was no likelihood of the repeal of the Act” [source: annual-register-1908].
Smuts then added a further condition: the 1907 Act could be repealed only if the Immigrants Restriction Act were simultaneously amended to exclude all future Indian immigration — a policy that implied “in the long run the elimination of the Indian community.” The amended Act passed the Transvaal Legislature in a single day’s sitting. Lord Crewe, the Colonial Secretary, declined to advise the Crown to disallow it, accepting the view that the Act represented “the deliberate policy of the white community, which had been vested with the power of self-government” [source: annual-register-1908].
Renewal (1911)
Passive resistance was suspended in April 1911 after a fresh arrangement between Smuts and Gandhi. In return for abandoning resistance to the 1907 registration law, the Indians obtained an undertaking to repeal it. New legislation would rest on “equality to all immigrants, but differential treatment by the application of a language test” — the Australian model. The Indians reluctantly accepted a language test and gave Gandhi “a free hand in negotiating over the new Bill.” Concessions included the right of thirty deported Asiatics to return from India, the annual admission of six educated Indians without registration, and exemption from thumb-prints for educated Indians of repute. General Botha “reminded Asiatics of the determination of the Union not to admit further Indians except those specially coming under this settlement.” The settlement appeared to have “worked satisfactorily” for the remainder of 1911 [source: annual-register-1911].
The Final Campaign (1913)
The peace was short-lived. In 1913 the Union Government’s refusal to modify the racial bar in immigration legislation provoked a renewal of passive resistance. Mr. G. K. Gokhale, the Indian leader then visiting South Africa, complained that the Government had not carried out understandings he had reached with Ministers earlier in the year, and appealed to the Government of India to intervene [source: annual-register-1913].
In October the movement intensified. Early in November, Gandhi led 2,500 Indians through Laing’s Nek and past Majuba Hill towards Volksrust, where a vigilance committee had been formed to prevent his entry into the Transvaal by force. He was arrested on 6 November and sentenced at Dundee (Natal) to a month’s imprisonment for inducing Indians to leave the Province. A strike had broken out among Indian colliery workers, and for abetting this Gandhi was sentenced to nine months’ imprisonment. He received a further three months at Volksrust for violating the Immigration Act [source: annual-register-1913].
At the Volksrust court, Gandhi explained his strategy: he knew his actions meant “great risk and personal suffering for those who acted with him, but, after mature consideration and twenty years’ experience of South Africa, he had concluded that nothing short of suffering would move the conscience of the Government and of the people of the Union.” He claimed to be a law-abiding citizen [source: annual-register-1913].
The strike spread from the collieries to the sugar plantations of Natal, with serious disturbances at Ladysmith — the police were “roughly handled until they were provided with rifles and reinforced by citizens with revolvers and shot guns.” Simultaneously, 5,000 Indian workers in Durban went on strike. The Indians demanded the remission of the £3 annual poll tax on those whose indentures had expired, and the right to bring in one wife. Plantations in the Durban district were fired. By 19 November, 116 free and indentured Indians had been sentenced to seven days’ imprisonment, and fifty-four to fines [source: annual-register-1913].
This final wave of resistance, with its combination of labour strikes, mass marches, and coordinated civil disobedience, forced the Union Government to negotiate. The result was the Indian Relief Act of 1914, which abolished the £3 poll tax, recognised Indian marriages, and removed the most objectionable features of earlier legislation. Gandhi considered the campaign a qualified success and, his South African work concluded, left for England and then India in July 1914.

Return to India
Gandhi arrived back in India in January 1915, after twenty-one years abroad. He was welcomed as a hero by G. K. Gokhale and the moderate wing of the Indian National Congress, who saw in him a disciplined organiser capable of bridging the gap between the educated elite and the rural masses. He spent his first year travelling the country, studying conditions, and establishing Sabarmati Ashram near Ahmedabad, his base of operations for the next decade and a half.
The Indian political landscape he returned to was in flux. The Indian National Congress had renewed its declarations of loyalty in 1915 as the war continued [source: annual-register-1915]. By July 1917 the Congress and the Moslem League had jointly demanded that the Imperial Government “pledge itself to the policy of making India a self-governing unit in the Empire” [source: annual-register-1917]. Annie Besant, the Irish-born advocate of Indian Home Rule, had been imprisoned for her agitation, and her release became a rallying cause. It was into this environment — of rising nationalist expectation constrained by imperial wartime security — that Gandhi began to assert his leadership.

Champaran & Ahmedabad
Champaran (1917)
Gandhi’s first major intervention in Indian politics was the Champaran indigo protests of 1917. In the Champaran district of Bihar, European planters had long compelled tenant farmers to grow indigo on a portion of their land under a system of exploitative contracts (tinkathia). Gandhi was invited by local peasants to investigate their grievances. Despite official attempts to have him expelled from the district, he refused to leave, accepted service of a summons, and pleaded guilty to a charge of disobeying orders to depart. His willingness to face imprisonment electrified the region. The Viceroy’s government, unwilling to create a martyr, eventually appointed a commission of inquiry — with Gandhi as a member — which found in favour of the peasants and led to the abolition of the tinkathia system.
Champaran established the template for Gandhi’s method: careful factual investigation of grievances, non-cooperation with unjust orders, a willingness to suffer imprisonment, and the mobilisation of public opinion through the press and mass meetings.
Ahmedabad (1918)
In February–March 1918, Gandhi took up the cause of cotton-mill workers in Ahmedabad who were demanding a 35 per cent wage increase to cope with wartime inflation. When the mill-owners refused to arbitrate, Gandhi led the workers in a hunger strike — his first use of this weapon in India — and fasted until the mill-owners agreed to a compromise settlement of a 35 per cent increase. The strike cemented his bond with the industrial working class and added another instrument to the Gandhian repertoire.
Later in 1918, Gandhi undertook a recruiting campaign for the British Indian Army in Kheda district (Gujarat), where he urged peasants to volunteer for service in the belief that such loyalty would be rewarded with post-war reforms. The campaign was a failure — few volunteered — and Gandhi later acknowledged it as a misjudgment.

Rowlatt & Post-War Politics
The Rowlatt Acts (1919)
The turning point in Gandhi’s relationship with the British Raj came with the Rowlatt Acts (the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919), which extended wartime emergency powers into peacetime — permitting trial without jury, internment without trial, and press censorship. Gandhi saw the Acts as an intolerable violation of civil liberties and a betrayal of the reformist promises contained in the Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918), which had proposed gradual Indian self-government.
Gandhi organised a nationwide hartal — a general strike and day of fasting and prayer — for 30 March 1919 (later rescheduled to 6 April). The response was unprecedented: shops closed, markets were deserted, and processions filled the streets of Bombay, Delhi, Lahore, Ahmedabad, and Calcutta. Gandhi declared the beginning of satyagraha against the Rowlatt Acts, the first all-India campaign of non-violent resistance against British rule.
Jallianwala Bagh & the Aftermath
The hartal was largely peaceful in most places, but in the Punjab it sparked serious disturbances. In Amritsar, violence erupted on 10 April 1919 when a crowd, protesting the arrest of local leaders, clashed with troops and set fire to banks and government buildings. Five Europeans were killed. The authorities summoned Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer, who imposed a strict ban on public meetings.
On 13 April 1919, the day of the Baisakhi festival, thousands of unarmed men, women, and children gathered in the Jallianwala Bagh — a walled garden with a single narrow entrance — for a peaceful protest. Dyer arrived with fifty Gurkha and Baluchi riflemen and, without warning, ordered them to open fire. They continued firing for ten to fifteen minutes until the ammunition was nearly exhausted. Official estimates placed the dead at 379, though Indian sources put the figure much higher; over 1,200 were wounded. Dyer later stated he had acted to produce a “moral effect” throughout the Punjab.
News of the massacre spread rapidly despite censorship, and it produced a profound rupture between Indian public opinion and the Raj. Gandhi was staggered by the violence. He suspended the satyagraha campaign in mid-April, declaring that the movement had been disfigured by acts of mob violence that he could not countenance. He undertook a three-day fast as penance. But the damage was done: the Jallianwala Bagh massacre convinced Gandhi that the British Empire was fundamentally unreformable, and it set him on the path towards the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–22.
The Government of India Bill, enacting the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms (limited elected councils and Indian participation in provincial government), was passed in December 1919 — overshadowed and hollowed out by the events of April.

Legacy (to 1919)
By the close of 1919, Gandhi had completed a remarkable transformation. From a South African lawyer and community organiser, he had become the most recognisable mass leader in India. He had developed and tested the techniques — passive resistance, the hunger strike, the hartal, the disciplined march — that would define Indian nationalism for the next three decades. He had given the Indian National Congress a method that could mobilise peasants, workers, and the urban middle class alike. And he had arrived at the conviction, forged in Champaran and hardened at Jallianwala Bagh, that the Empire could not be reformed from within — that it would have to be confronted.
The Annual Register of 1915 had noted simply that “the Indian National Congress met again at the very end of December and renewed its declaration of loyalty.” Within four years, that loyalty had been shattered. The Gandhi who emerged from 1919 was no longer a petitioner for imperial justice; he was the architect of a movement that would, within a generation, end British rule in India.

In the Sources

annual-register-1911 — The 1911 settlement between Smuts and Gandhi, suspension of passive resistance, language-test immigration legislation.
annual-register-1913 — Renewal of passive resistance, Gandhi’s march of 2,500 Indians through Laing’s Nek, his arrest and sentences, colliery strikes, disturbances in Natal.

Note: The source corpus available for this period does not contain detailed contemporary accounts of Gandhi’s early legal career in South Africa (1893–1905), the founding of the Natal Indian Congress (1894), his Boer War ambulance service (1899–1900), the Champaran indigo campaign (1917), the Ahmedabad mill strike (1918), the Rowlatt satyagraha (1919), or the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919). These sections rely on the broader historical record beyond the immediate source files.
