entities/george-v.title: George V (1865–1936)
entities/george-v.content:
George V (1865–1936)
King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, Emperor of India. Succeeded his father Edward VII on 6 May 1910 and reigned through the Parliament Act crisis, the Great War, and the post-war settlement.
Accession (May 1910)
King George V ascended the throne upon the death of his father, King Edward VII, on 6 May 1910. The Annual Register records that “King George V. was proclaimed with the customary picturesque ceremonial” on Monday morning, 9 May. At St. James’s Palace, the Duke of Norfolk, the Earl Marshal, the Kings-at-Arms, and the four Pursuivants appeared on a balcony in their official robes with the state trumpeters, and “four of the King’s children” were present [source: annual-register-1910].
King George V held his First Council and made a Declaration to the Privy Council. A letter was published from King George to his people, and messages were despatched to the Navy and Army and to the Government of India [source: annual-register-1910]. The King then took the oath of accession.
The King had seen a good deal of service in the Navy, and his professional background distinguished him from his predecessors. The public mood at the accession was recorded as one of confidence and respect, with “King George’s exemplary life and high-minded desire” widely acknowledged [source: annual-register-1910].
The Constitutional Crisis & Parliament Act (1911)
The new King inherited a constitutional crisis of the first magnitude. The Liberal Government of Mr. Asquith, having secured its mandate in the two General Elections of 1910, was determined to curtail the veto power of the House of Lords. The Parliament Bill, which sought to strip the Lords of their power to reject money bills and reduce their veto on other legislation to a suspensory period of two years, dominated the political landscape.
The constitutional deadlock placed the King in a delicate position. The Liberal Government sought from the new Sovereign a guarantee that he would create sufficient Peers to force the Parliament Bill through the House of Lords should the Upper House resist. The threat of a mass creation of peerages — a step not taken since Queen Anne’s reign — hung over the proceedings throughout 1910 and 1911.
In the House of Commons, Mr. Churchill confirmed that the King had been “fully acquainted with the political situation and all the matters in dispute.” The Unionist Opposition, led by Mr. Balfour, accused the Government of unconstitutionally drawing the Crown into party politics. Lord Hugh Cecil denounced the Government’s threat and declared he would be glad to see the Prime Minister punished for high treason. Sir Edward Carson condemned the Prime Minister’s letter as a “blackmailing letter.”
After months of fierce debate and manoeuvring, the House of Lords finally surrendered. In August 1911, by a narrow majority — the famous “Peers’ Surrender” — the Lords accepted the Parliament Bill, and the Royal Assent was given. The Parliament Act of 1911 fundamentally altered the British constitution, establishing the supremacy of the House of Commons. King George V had remained scrupulously constitutional throughout, but his willingness to create Peers as a last resort had been a decisive factor [source: annual-register-1911].
The Coronation & Indian Durbar (1911)
King George V and Queen Mary were crowned at Westminster Abbey on 22 June 1911 amid great national rejoicing. The Coronation was celebrated with enthusiasm throughout the Empire. Special music was composed for the service by Sir Hubert Parry, Sir Charles Stanford, and Sir Edward Elgar. The Coronation was followed by a naval review at Spithead and a Festival of Empire at the Crystal Palace [source: annual-register-1911].
Later that year, the King and Queen departed for India — the only reigning British monarch to visit India as Emperor. The King formally announced his departure “for the purpose of celebrating in his Indian Dominions the solemnity of the Coronation,” appointing four Counsellors of State — Prince Arthur of Connaught, the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord Chancellor, and the Lord President of the Council — to transact business in his absence. Their independent powers did not extend to the dissolution of Parliament, the conferring of titles, or action in matters beyond prescribed limits [source: annual-register-1911].
The Imperial Durbar was held at Delhi in December 1911, where the King-Emperor appeared in person before the assembled princes and peoples of India — a spectacle of imperial grandeur that demonstrated the Crown’s direct connection with its Indian Empire.
The Great War (1914–1918)
When war came in August 1914, King George V played a vital role as the symbolic head of the nation and Empire. His reign was immediately defined by the conflict.
In April 1914, the King had paid a State Visit to Paris, cementing the Entente Cordiale. The visit was received with great enthusiasm and was widely seen as a demonstration of the solidarity between the two nations in the face of the rising German menace [source: annual-register-1914].
The King took an active constitutional role in the transition to coalition government in May 1915, following the shells scandal and the resignation of Lord Fisher as First Sea Lord. The formation of the First Coalition under Mr. Asquith brought Unionists and Labour into the Ministry for the first time. The King’s support for the coalition helped stabilise the Government during a moment of national crisis [source: annual-register-1915].
In October 1915, the King paid a historic visit to the Army in France, passing a day at Havre inspecting the English camps. He met the President of the French Republic, reviewed British troops at the front, and paid a visit to the French Armies. On his departure, he addressed to the soldiers of France an expression of his admiration for their military virtues. At the conclusion of his tour, an unfortunate accident occurred: the King’s horse, frightened by the cheers of the men, reared and fell, and His Majesty was severely bruised. Although the injuries were not such as to leave any permanent disablement, the King was obliged to go to bed and abandon the remainder of his tour in France [source: annual-register-1915].
Throughout the war, the King and Queen made frequent visits to hospitals, munitions factories, and military camps. The King maintained a close interest in the conduct of the war and in the welfare of his troops, corresponding regularly with his commanders and visiting the Grand Fleet and the armies in the field.
The House of Windsor (1917)
As the war raged on and anti-German feeling intensified in Britain, the King took a momentous decision. On 17 July 1917, the King “abandoned all German titles for himself and family; and issued a proclamation that his House and Family should henceforth be known as the House and Family of Windsor” [source: annual-register-1917]. The House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha — the German name of the dynasty — was formally changed to the House of Windsor. The King’s German relatives were stripped of their British honours. This act of symbolic patriotism did much to cement the monarchy’s bond with the British people during the war’s darkest hours.
Post-War (1919)
The signing of the Peace Treaty on 28 June 1919 was received throughout Great Britain with great rejoicings. A notable demonstration was made outside Buckingham Palace by large crowds. The King and Queen, their three sons, and Princess Mary appeared on the balcony and were enthusiastically greeted [source: annual-register-1919].
On the same day, the King issued a message for publication, expressing his “deep thankfulness” that the war had been brought to its concluding stages and that “the victory of the ideals of freedom and liberty” had been manifested. He shared his people’s “joy and thanksgiving,” and earnestly prayed “that the coming years of peace may bring to them ever-increasing happiness and prosperity” [source: annual-register-1919].
The formal Proclamation of Peace took place on 2 July at St. James’s Palace and in the City of London according to tradition. The King’s Proclamation was first read from the balcony of St. James’s Palace, with a Guard of Honour formed by the Welsh Guards. The procession moved to Charing Cross, then to Temple Bar, where the Lord Mayor with many members of the Corporation was waiting to give the heralds leave to pass. The Proclamation was read at Cheapside and from the steps of the Royal Exchange [source: annual-register-1919]. Peace Celebrations followed in July, with Marshal Foch visiting London and the King reviewing the troops.
Legacy
King George V reigned through one of the most turbulent periods in British history. His reign saw the passage of the Parliament Act of 1911, which fundamentally altered the British constitution; the cataclysm of the Great War, during which he served as a unifying symbol of the nation and Empire; and by changing the royal name to Windsor, aligned the monarchy definitively with British identity. He was a constitutional monarch in the strictest sense, acting on the advice of his Ministers while maintaining a steady and visible presence as head of the nation. His reign witnessed the rise of Labour, the extension of the franchise, the transformation of the British Empire into the Commonwealth, and the establishment of the modern model of constitutional monarchy.

entities/gladstone-william-ewart.title: William Ewart Gladstone (1809–1898)
entities/gladstone-william-ewart.content:
William Ewart Gladstone
William Ewart Gladstone (29 December 1809 – 19 May 1898) was the dominant figure of late Victorian British politics, serving four times as Prime Minister over a span of more than a quarter of a century. No statesman of his time performed a greater part in history, nor won so high a place in the admiration and affection of the living world. A titan of the Liberal Party, Gladstone was at once a great orator, a profound student of history and literature, a philanthropist of the purest order, and a parliamentary combatant of unsurpassed energy and eloquence. His career was the story of a man whose one impassioned desire was “to see the right, and to follow it whithersoever it might lead.”

Early Career & First Ministry (1868–1874)
Gladstone’s rise to the leadership of the Liberal Party came amidst a shifting of the political guard. With the death of Lord Palmerston, the Queen invited Lord Russell to form a government, and Mr. Gladstone became leader of the House of Commons. He and Benjamin Disraeli were now brought directly face to face — one led the House, the other led the Opposition. Gladstone had what Condorcet happily called “an impatient spirit,” and it was to many a problem of deep interest whether his genius would prove equal to the trying task of leadership under circumstances of peculiar difficulty. As McCarthy records, Gladstone’s “admirers were the most extreme of the Liberals,” while he was “distrusted and dreaded by all of Conservative instincts.”
The Great Ministry
When the general election of 1868 returned the Liberals to power with a commanding majority, the Queen sent for Mr. Gladstone. What followed was one of the most remarkable reforming administrations in British history. McCarthy captures the astonishing legislative energy of these years:

“The organising energy which had accomplished such marvels during three or four resplendent years had spent itself and was out of breath.”

The first great measure was the Irish Church Disestablishment Act (1869), which severed the connection between the Anglican Church and the state in Ireland — a long-standing grievance of the Catholic majority. This was followed by the Irish Land Act of 1870, which began the process of reforming the landlord-tenant system that had for centuries been a source of Irish misery.
In the same burst of reform, Mr. Forster’s Education Bill (1870) established a national system of elementary education in England. As McCarthy notes, “The Government undertook a great and a much-needed work when it set about establishing a national system of elementary education” — a system that had been scandalously neglected compared to other European nations.
The Ballot Act of 1872 introduced the secret ballot, a reform of immense consequence. McCarthy observes that the Ballot Act “put an end to an enormous amount of corruption, and it may be said to have almost altogether extinguished the illegitimate influence of the landlord, the employer, and the patron.”
Cardwell’s Army reforms and the Licensing Act of Mr. Bruce were further planks in this extraordinary legislative programme. The Treaty of Washington (1871) and the subsequent Geneva arbitration on the Alabama claims marked a triumph for Gladstone’s commitment to international arbitration over the angry demands of the jingo press.
The Fall
The great ministry met its nemesis in the Irish University Bill of 1873. Gladstone’s gallant effort to reconcile the conflicting claims of Irish education was a measure that satisfied none of the contending parties — Protestants, Catholics, and Nonconformists alike condemned it. As McCarthy movingly records:

“Mr. Gladstone was the first English Prime Minister who had ever really sacrificed place and popularity to serve the interests of Ireland; it seemed a cruel stroke of fate which made his fall from power mainly the result of the Irish vote in the House of Commons.”

The bill was defeated by a majority of three — 287 against 284. Though Disraeli declined to form a government, and Gladstone returned reluctantly to office, the administration’s authority was shattered. In January 1874, Gladstone suddenly dissolved Parliament. The country was taken utterly by surprise, and the result was a Conservative majority of about fifty. Mr. Gladstone resigned at once.

“So sudden a fall from power had not up to that time been known in the modern political history of the country. The great Liberal Administration had fallen as suddenly as the French Empire; had disappeared like Aladdin’s palace.”

In March 1875, Gladstone announced his intention of retiring from the leadership of the Liberal Party. The party reeled under the blow, seeming for a moment not only without a leader, but even without a policy or a motive for existence. McCarthy records the bitter murmurs among Liberals who contrasted his abandonment of them with Disraeli’s unwearying perseverance through long years of opposition.

The Midlothian Campaign & Second Ministry (1880–1885)
The Challenge to Beaconsfield
Gladstone did not remain in retirement. During the Eastern Crisis of 1876, he emerged to denounce the “Bulgarian horrors” committed by the Turks, publishing a pamphlet that sold in tens of thousands and electrified the nation. But it was the Midlothian Campaign of 1879–1880 that transformed British politics. In a series of epic speeches delivered from railway carriages, in great halls, and to vast open-air crowds, Gladstone held the Disraeli government — then led by Lord Beaconsfield — to account for its “imperialist” adventures in Afghanistan, South Africa, and the Near East.
As McCarthy describes, the 1880 general election was a cataclysm for the Conservatives:

“With the very first day of the elections it was evident that the Conservative majority was already gone. Each succeeding day showed more and more the change that had taken place in public feeling. Defeat was turned into disaster. Disaster became utter rout and confusion. When the elections were over it was found that the Conservative party were nowhere. A majority of some hundred and twenty sent the Liberals back into power.”

The Queen sent for Lord Hartington, then for Lord Granville — but everyone knew in advance who was to come into power at last:

“Mr. Gladstone had stood up against Lord Beaconsfield for some years and fought him alone. He had dragged his party after him into many a danger. Now, at last, the battle had been given to his hands, and it was a matter of necessity that the triumph should bring back to power the man whose energy and eloquence had inspired the struggle.”

The Second Gladstone Ministry
Gladstone’s second administration (1880–1885) inherited a host of foreign entanglements from its Conservative predecessors — troubles in Western Asia, in Egypt, and in South Africa. There were wars as yet unfinished, and as McCarthy noted, “some of the men who were most necessary to a strong Liberal Administration were in their hearts utterly opposed to any policy which aimed at the extension of territory.”
The early years were plagued by the Bradlaugh Affair — the atheist MP for Northampton being denied the right to take his seat — which consumed vast amounts of parliamentary time. In Ireland, the agricultural depression and the rise of the Land League under Charles Stewart Parnell created a crisis that demanded action. The Land Act of 1881 granted the “three Fs” (fair rent, fixity of tenure, free sale), but coercion and the imprisonment of Parnell at Kilmainham were followed by the Kilmainham Treaty, a compromise that alarmed the Whig wing of the Liberal Party.
Egypt and the Sudan
The most fateful foreign entanglement was Egypt. In 1882, the Gladstone government bombarded Alexandria and sent Sir Garnet Wolseley to defeat the nationalist forces of Arabi Pasha at Tel el-Kebir, leading to the British occupation of Egypt. As the Langer volume notes, “There can be little or no doubt that Gladstone intended to withdraw again from Egypt as soon as possible” — yet the occupation would last for decades.
The Sudan crisis proved even more disastrous. The government sent General Charles George Gordon to Khartoum to evacuate Egyptian forces from the Sudan, where the Mahdi’s rebellion was sweeping all before it. Gordon instead became besieged at Khartoum. McCarthy vividly describes the agonising delay:

“There was a strange, and to this day an unaccountable, delay about the measures to be taken for Gordon’s rescue. People said that the Government had no hope of being able to do anything to save him; and a Government is in sore straits when people believe that there is something that it ought to do and cannot even try to do.”

The relief expedition under Wolseley arrived two days too late. Khartoum had fallen; Gordon was dead. The news struck England like a thunderbolt. Though the ministry survived a vote of censure, the moral authority of the government was deeply wounded.
The Third Reform Act
Despite these disasters, Gladstone’s government achieved one great constitutional reform. The Franchise Bill of 1884 extended the household suffrage enjoyed by borough voters to the counties, enfranchising millions of agricultural labourers. The Redistribution Act of 1885 redrew constituency boundaries to reflect population. As Gladstone declared when introducing the Franchise Bill:

“I take my stand upon the broad principle that the enfranchisement of capable citizens, be they few or be they many — and if they be many, so much the better — is an addition to the strength of the State.”

The government fell in June 1885 on a budget amendment, narrowly defeated. Lord Salisbury formed a minority Conservative administration.

Home Rule & the Liberal Split (1886)
The general election of 1885 returned a hung parliament, with Parnell’s Irish Nationalists holding the balance of power. Gladstone, by now convinced that justice for Ireland demanded a measure of self-government, became converted to the cause of Home Rule.
His conversion was not sudden. As early as the 1870s, when the Home Rule movement first emerged under Isaac Butt, Gladstone had shown an anxious desire to understand the new agitation. McCarthy records that while many English voices cried out that Home Rule must be “simply brushed away as a nuisance,” Gladstone “was not a man to deal with political questions in that sort of way. He showed an anxiety to understand the new agitation and its objects.”
Gladstone returned to office in February 1886 at the head of his third administration. On 8 April 1886, he introduced the First Home Rule Bill, a measure to create a separate Irish parliament for domestic affairs while reserving imperial questions to Westminster. The Bill split the Liberal Party. Joseph Chamberlain and Lord Hartington — Gladstone’s most formidable colleagues — led the secession of the Liberal Unionists, who allied themselves with the Conservatives in opposing the measure.
The Bill was defeated in the House of Commons on 8 June 1886, with 93 Liberals voting against their own government. McCarthy writes:

“Gladstone’s first Home Rule Bill was rejected by the House of Commons. His second Home Rule Bill passed safely through the House of Commons and was rejected only when it came for the first time into the House of Lords.”

The general election that followed returned a massive Conservative and Liberal Unionist majority. The Liberal Party was shattered. Gladstone resigned, and Lord Salisbury formed his second government. For a decade, the Liberal Party would remain a broken force, divided between Gladstonian Home Rulers and Liberal Unionists.

Final Ministry & Legacy (1892–1894)
Despite his advancing years — he was now in his eighties — Gladstone led the Liberal Party to a narrow victory at the general election of 1892. His fourth and final administration was formed with the support of the Irish Nationalists. The great object was to pass Home Rule once more.
The Second Home Rule Bill was introduced in 1893. It passed the House of Commons after a titanic struggle, but was overwhelmingly rejected by the House of Lords. McCarthy records the significance of this moment:

“Gladstone, in the last speech which he ever delivered to the House of Commons, had dwelt upon this important fact, and had impressed upon the House that the hereditary chamber had done with the Home Rule Bill just what it had done at first with every important measure brought forward in the cause of political advancement. If Gladstone had been but a few years younger, or could have retained his health and strength for a few years more, he would in all human probability have compelled the House of Lords to accept his measure.”

But age and infirmity had finally caught up with the Grand Old Man. He resigned the premiership in March 1894, succeeded by Lord Rosebery. In his retirement, he was not idle. As McCarthy notes, “Again and again some great public question, such as that which was created by the sufferings of the Armenians under Turkish rule, had aroused him into active appeals on behalf of the side for which the claims of justice and mercy were combined.”

Death and Apotheosis
William Ewart Gladstone died at his beloved home, Hawarden Castle, on Ascension Day, 19 May 1898. McCarthy’s narrative of his final hours is poignant:

“On that day William Ewart Gladstone breathed his last. He died in his Hawarden home — passed away from the ever-loving and ever-devoted ministrations of the wife to whom he had been so tenderly attached and who had always been his most trusted and most affectionate companion.”


“When the inevitable came at last and was made known, a profound shock passed through all civilised nations. No statesman of the time had performed a greater part in history than Gladstone had done, or had won so high a place in the admiration and affection of the living world. Every one felt that he had left no equal behind him.”

Both Houses of Parliament gave generous expression to the national grief. In the House of Lords, the Prime Minister, Lord Salisbury — his greatest political opponent — delivered a speech at once eloquent, sincere, and heartfelt, noting “the universal agreement of all persons, classes, and schools of thought in doing honour to the memory of a man who had been engaged more continually in political conflict than probably any other man of his generation.”
Gladstone’s wish for simplicity was respected. He was buried in Westminster Abbey, near the graves of Sir Robert Peel and Lord Beaconsfield. His grave lies close to that of his old rival — the rivals whom the poet might have said were joined in death as “drop upon Fox’s grave a tear, ‘twill trickle to his rival’s bier.”

“Those whose political faith made them followers of Gladstone might have remembered with satisfaction that some of Disraeli’s most memorable successes in legislation were but the carrying out of the policy originated by Gladstone and opposed and for the time even overthrown by his most powerful political opponent.”

Character and Oratory
McCarthy’s voluminous tribute to Gladstone’s personal qualities is worth quoting at length:

“As a Parliamentary orator and debater Gladstone never had a superior in the splendid record of British Parliamentary eloquence. He had a magnificent voice, a splendid delivery, a fluency which never faltered yet never failed to find the most appropriate words, and he showed a rare and happy gift of humour heightened with touches of sarcasm which were none the less successful because they never carried the sting of malignity with them.”


“He was a most delightful talker, and there was hardly a subject in the range of human reading on which he could not converse with readiness and with full appreciation. He was filled, too, with an intense desire to increase his stock of knowledge from every available source.”

The ways and artifices common to statesmanship had never been moving influences with him. “Even his most unyielding political opponents never believed him guilty of adopting any course for the sake of mere party interests or of taking up any cause for the reason that it was popular.”
The Liberal Inheritance
Gladstone’s retirement from public life, followed so soon by his death, left the Liberal Party in a peculiar position. There was no man who could claim to be his rightful successor. As McCarthy observes:

“It must happen from time to time to every great political party to lose a leader of supreme ability whose loss it may appear just then hardly possible to repair.”

The Liberal Party was not only leaderless but divided. Some influential Liberals had formally withdrawn from the party over Home Rule. A section of Liberal opinion believed that “the policy of Home Rule for Ireland lay buried in that statesman’s grave.” Yet McCarthy himself perceived the flaw in this reasoning:

“The reflective and impartial reader may find it hard to understand how this idea came into existence, seeing that Mr. Gladstone’s measure of reform for Ireland had passed through just the same stages of progress which had to be accomplished by almost every great measure of reform for England.”


Historical Assessment
William Ewart Gladstone bestrode the late Victorian world like a colossus. He had been a great statesman, one of the greatest known to modern times; an orator entitled to rank among the highest of all ages; a profound student of history and literature, a lover of poetry and all the arts; a man who understood and appreciated the discoveries and influences of modern science; and a philanthropist of the purest order.
His life was fortunate in its biographer. As McCarthy notes, John Morley’s Life of Gladstone remains “the authentic and authoritative record of that life of unsurpassed activity and on the whole of superb success.” In its pages, “we see how his many-sided nature came to realise the demands of each new claim made upon his attention, and to seek the best way of bringing each cause to full success when once it had secured his adhesion.”
Gladstone was, in the most profound sense, the author of modern Liberalism. The reforms of his first ministry — disestablishment of the Irish Church, the secret ballot, national education, land reform — transformed the relationship between the state and the citizen. The Midlothian Campaign created a new model of popular political engagement. The Home Rule crusade, though it failed in his lifetime, defined the Irish question for a generation.
He passed from the stage leaving behind him the enduring conviction — expressed in the closing passages of his last parliamentary speech — that the cause for which he fought was not dead, but sleeping; that “the hereditary chamber had done with the Home Rule Bill just what it had done at first with every important measure brought forward in the cause of political advancement.”

Sources

entities/grey-edward.title: Sir Edward Grey (1862–1933)
entities/grey-edward.content:
Sir Edward Grey (1862–1933)
Parliamentary Under-Secretary, Foreign Office (1892–1895) · Foreign Secretary (1905–1916)
Sir Edward Grey held the Foreign Office from the formation of Campbell-Bannerman’s Liberal government in December 1905 until the fall of Asquith in December 1916—the longest continuous tenure of any British Foreign Secretary in the period of this wiki. He inherited the Entente Cordiale with France, authorised the military staff conversations that grew from the first Moroccan crisis, concluded the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907, managed the Bosnian and Agadir crises and the London Ambassadors’ Conference of the Balkan Wars, and on 3 August 1914 stated the case for war to the House of Commons before the British ultimatum on Belgian neutrality expired. Contemporaries credited him with force of character, elegance of expression, and a liberal moral view of obligation; critics on the radical left and among Unionists charged that the entente system had entangled Britain without the safeguards of a formal alliance. By 1907, in the judgment of The Politics of Grand Strategy, preservation of the Entente Cordiale had become the cardinal feature of his diplomacy.
Liberal Imperialist and Accession (1905–1906)
Grey belonged to the Liberal Imperialist wing associated with Asquith and Haldane—the group that had parted from the main stream of Liberal opinion over the South African War yet returned to office under Campbell-Bannerman. Before the 1906 landslide he spoke against Unionist fiscal fog, for amendment of the Education Act, and for continuity of foreign engagements. In October 1905, already regarded as the next Foreign Secretary, he told J. A. Spender that Britain was “running a real risk of losing France and not gaining Germany,” and in a City speech outlined the main tenets of future Liberal foreign policy: the Japanese alliance and friendship with the United States first, then the maintenance of the French understanding (Politics of Grand Strategy; Annual Register, 1905).
When he took office the Algeciras Conference was in its throes. Campbell-Bannerman authorised him to support France strongly and, almost as a first act of an era of Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform, the beginning of military conversations between the British and French General Staffs. Churchill later stressed the profundity of that step: the minds of the military men were turned into a particular channel; mutual trust grew in one set of relationships and mutual precautions in the other (The World Crisis, Vol. I). Williamson records Grey’s letter to Haldane of 8 January 1906 that a situation might arise in which popular feeling would compel help to France, and Fisher was ready to drive the German fleet off the sea; Grey wanted the War Office preparing an answer. Official staff talks followed—Grierson and Huguet, then wider channels—while Grey insisted that the conversations created no formal alliance obligation (Politics of Grand Strategy).
Grey was the first Foreign Secretary to sit in the Commons since Lord Stanley in 1868. He arranged to answer questions on Tuesdays and Thursdays, to attend whenever foreign business was before the House, and to leave other days to a parliamentary under-secretary—an informal adjustment to combine office with the chamber (Annual Register, 1906). He told the country that the Government intended to keep, in letter and spirit, the engagements entered into by its predecessor, and he defended the refusal to aid Chinese labour recruiting under improper conditions as a moral limit on the use of diplomatic machinery (Annual Register, 1906).
Entente Consolidation and the Triple Understanding (1906–1908)
Through 1906–1907 Grey held the French entente against intermittent hopes of better relations with Berlin. Anti-German direction in the Foreign Office, strengthened by Eyre Crowe’s promotion, and French protests against any Anglo-German flirtation drove him closer to Paris; he assured Cambon that if a subject like Algeciras arose again, French support would be as firm as before (Politics of Grand Strategy). He had long wanted a settlement with Russia—to restore or overturn the balance against Germany, to check the Kaiser’s flirtations with the Tsar, and to quiet German intrigues in Persia and the Near East. The Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 divided Persia into spheres, recognised Afghanistan as outside the Russian sphere, and affirmed Chinese suzerainty over Tibet. Grey defended the Agreement in the Commons as a measure that would “make for peace”: without it Anglo-Russian relations must have got worse; an opportunity had been seized which might not have returned (Annual Register, 1908). The Dual Alliance, the Entente Cordiale, and the Convention of 1907 formed the triangle later called the Triple Entente—understandings, not a formal triple alliance.
Crises: Bosnia, Agadir, and the Naval Entente (1908–1912)
Bosnia-Herzegovina (1908–1909)
Austria-Hungary’s annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina tested the new alignment. Grey laboured to restrain Serbia, pacify Turkey, and give full diplomatic support to Russia while making clear that Britain would not be drawn into war on a Balkan quarrel. The crisis ended when Germany insisted that Russia advise Serbia to give way and the Powers recognised the annexation without a conference. The Annual Register recorded that the attitude of Germany and Austria-Hungary and the recalcitrance of Servia seemed to portend a great European war and emphasised the need of British attention to national defence. Grey had already, on 5 November 1908, alerted the Admiralty to prepare in case Germany sent France an ultimatum and the Cabinet decided that Britain must assist France (The World Crisis, Vol. I; Politics of Grand Strategy; Annual Register, 1909; eastern-question-balkans).
Agadir (1911)
The Panther’s arrival at Agadir in July 1911 transformed the Moroccan question into an international crisis. The Cabinet resolved to remain faithful to the 1904 obligations to France and to oppose German demands for tripartite negotiations, but firmly refused to send a British ship to Morocco. Grey stood between the Foreign Office’s pro-French pressure and the radical caution of Loreburn, Morley, and others—patient, wary, and persistently evasive in Williamson’s phrase, trying to bridge Cabinet and Office. Lloyd George’s Mansion House speech of 21 July, aligned with the opposite wing of the Government on foreign policy, was the “thunder-clap” that convinced Berlin Britain would stand by France. When Count Metternich demanded that Lloyd George be turned out of the Government, Grey replied that if that was the request the conversation must end. The secret defence meetings of Asquith, Grey, McKenna, Lloyd George, and Churchill managed the crisis; by November Asquith, Grey, and Haldane had resolved in principle to aid France if Germany attacked—Haldane telling Asquith that if Britain failed France he would not give ten years’ purchase for the British Empire (Politics of Grand Strategy; Hankey, Man of Secrets, Vol. I; The World Crisis, Vol. I).
Naval Conversations and Grey–Cambon Letters
From 1911–1912 Anglo-French naval staff conversations complemented the military talks: French concentration in the Mediterranean, British guard of the Channel and North Sea. The exchange of letters between Grey and Cambon in November 1912 defined consultation and “moral obligation” without converting the Entente into a formal alliance—language that remained central when war came. Grey’s management of the diplomatic consequences of the naval race sought detente without sacrificing France; he could not accept a German demand for unconditional British neutrality as the price of slowing Tirpitz’s programme (Politics of Grand Strategy).
Balkan Wars and the London Conference (1912–1913)
During the Balkan Wars Grey chaired the Ambassadors’ Conference of the Great Powers in London (December 1912–August 1913), working to localise the conflict, prevent a general European war, and secure an independent Albania that would deny Serbia an Adriatic port Austria-Hungary was determined to prevent. British policy, he stated, was to consolidate Turkish authority in Asiatic dominions behind the Enos-Midia line, resting on sound finance, reforms, and the consent of the Powers. The Earl of Crewe praised his reputation for straightforwardness and candour as a diplomatic asset. He worked with France and Russia while maintaining communication with Germany and Austria—the Concert method under Entente conditions (Annual Register, 1913; eastern-question-balkans).
July 1914 and British Entry into the War
The July Crisis found the Cabinet still deep in the Irish boundary question when Grey brought the Austrian ultimatum to Serbia into the room on 24 July. He held two fixed points: the obligation involved in Belgian neutrality, and the danger if France were left to face Germany alone. With Tyrrell he pressed the Admiralty communiqué that held the Fleet together. On 3 August, after the German ultimatum to Belgium, he made his statement in the Commons; that afternoon, outside the Chamber, Churchill asked what would happen next. “Now,” Grey said, “we shall send them an ultimatum to stop the invasion of Belgium within 24 hours.” Asquith later moved the Vote of Credit with tribute to Grey’s unremitting efforts for peace, quoting the German Chancellor’s appeal for British neutrality as infamous. The war, Asquith said, had been forced upon Britain—to fulfil a solemn international obligation and to vindicate the principle that small nationalities were not to be crushed by arbitrary power (The World Crisis, Vol. I; Annual Register, 1914; outbreak-of-the-great-war).
Grey remained Foreign Secretary through the first Coalition and the early war years, corresponding through the United States Ambassador on the treatment of submarine prisoners and other wartime diplomacy, until Asquith’s fall in December 1916 ended the ministry in which he had served for eleven years (Annual Register, 1915–1916).
Domestic Voice
Though foreign affairs were his office, Grey spoke on the industrial unrest of the pre-war years. At Darlington in October 1910 he ascribed restlessness among wage-earners to great hopes combined with consciousness of power, and thought foreign politics would not be the main consideration of the twentieth century as economic interdependence increased. In 1912 he wound up for the Government on the Minimum Wage Bill: the House faced a new demand that the miner be paid a fair wage when he failed to earn it from causes beyond his control; carried to its extreme, the strike meant starvation and the destruction of national life (Annual Register, 1910, 1912). His 1911 speech on Anglo-American arbitration was cordially received on both sides of the Atlantic (Annual Register, 1911).

Sources
Williamson’s The Politics of Grand Strategy is the structural guide to Grey’s role in military and naval conversations, Entente consolidation, Agadir, and the Grey–Cambon letters. Churchill’s The World Crisis, Vol. I, supplies the Cabinet and Admiralty vantage on Algeciras, Agadir, and the July days, including the exchange outside the Commons on the Belgian ultimatum. The Annual Register year by year records his public defences—Anglo-Russian Convention, arbitration, Balkan conference line, 3 August 1914, and wartime FO business. Roskill’s Hankey places him in the CID and secret defence circle. Langer’s diplomacy volumes frame the Eastern Question inheritance against which Grey’s Balkan management is read.

entities/haig-douglas.title: Haig, Douglas
entities/haig-douglas.content:
Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig (1861–1928)
Commander, First Army (1914–1915) · Commander-in-Chief, British Expeditionary Force (1915–1919) · Field Marshal (1917) · 1st Earl Haig (1919)

Command of First Army
When the British Expeditionary Force deployed to France in August 1914, Sir Douglas Haig commanded I Corps, the senior of the two corps in the original BEF. During the Retreat from Mons, his corps was heavily engaged south and east of Maroilles. The Annual Register recorded that “mainly through his skill, and with the assistance of two French reserve divisions, it was extricated in the night and resumed its march at dawn.” (Annual Register 1914)
During the First Battle of Ypres (October–November 1914), Haig’s I Corps played a decisive role. The Annual Register noted that the Corps “gained positions on that day by ‘skilful, bold, and decisive’ action which alone enabled the British forces to maintain their foothold on the north bank during three weeks’ severe fighting.” (Annual Register 1914) Haig was instructed on 19 October to advance through Ypres north-eastwards towards Thorout.
Following the expansion of the BEF, Haig was appointed to command the newly formed First Army. His leadership was noted in the Battle of Neuve Chapelle (March 1915), where Sir John French brought “to Your Lordship’s special notice the valuable services of General Sir Douglas Haig, K.C.B., K.C.I.E., K.C.V.O., A.D.C., Commanding the First Army.” (Annual Register 1915) In the operations around La Bassée in December 1914, Haig took over command from Sir James Willcocks and stabilised the front.
Maurice Hankey, visiting the front in April 1915, recorded after a long conversation with Haig that he was “a most charming personality, and a great man I think.” (Hankey, Man of Secrets)

Commander-in-Chief of the BEF
In December 1915, Sir John French, “under severe and incessant strain, relinquished at his own request the command of the British Armies in Flanders, and was succeeded by General Sir Douglas Haig, who had been in command of the first army corps.” (Annual Register 1915) Haig was promoted to full General and took command of the BEF at a critical juncture, when the British Army was expanding from a small professional force into a mass citizen army.
The consequent changes in higher command saw General Sir Charles Monro take over the First Army, and Major-General L. Kiggell appointed as Haig’s Chief of the General Staff. Sir William Robertson, who had been Haig’s Chief of Staff in the First Army, was recalled to London as Chief of the Imperial General Staff — establishing a close partnership between the Commander in the Field and the CIGS that would prove important in the strategic debates of 1916–1917.
In 1916, Haig’s standing was publicly affirmed. Lord Derby declared in the House of Lords: “We have a combination of Sir Douglas Haig, Commander in the Field, and Sir William Robertson, Chief of the General Staff, which cannot be equalled and much less improved.” (Annual Register 1916) He was awarded the G.C.V.O. in September 1916 and was unanimously nominated for the Rectorship of St. Andrews University.
Haig’s relationship with Prime Minister Lloyd George became increasingly strained. Hankey’s biographical note records that Haig served as C-in-C “despite Lloyd George’s mistrust of his strategy and attempts to have him replaced.” (Hankey, Man of Secrets) In February 1917, Haig gave an interview to the Havas Agency that deepened the political tension, declaring that “there could be no peace without complete victory” and predicting that “the decision must come upon the Western Front” — statements that Lloyd George considered exceeded a commander’s proper role. (Annual Register 1917)
He was promoted to Field Marshal on 1 January 1917.

The Somme (1916)
The Somme offensive, launched on 1 July 1916, was Haig’s first great offensive as Commander-in-Chief. The Annual Register noted that the offensive “was mainly a British movement. The French co-operated, but they were allotted a minor part.” The position was the reverse of the previous September, “when much the more important operations had been allotted to the French troops.” (Annual Register 1916)
The battlefront chosen by the Franco-British commanders “began several miles south of Arras, but north of the river Ancre, and extended to several miles south of the Somme.” The object in its first stage “was to smash the German front lines, drive the enemy back into the Ardennes about Maubeuge, thus reconquering the greater part of that important industrial district of France.” (Annual Register 1916)
The assault along the whole selected line was launched at 7:30 a.m. on 1 July — the bloodiest single day in British military history. South of the Somme the French were fortunate in finding the Germans relatively unprepared, the enemy having deemed the French army incapable of any serious offensive after Verdun. The Annual Register recorded that “the first French assault, which gained ground, took the enemy somewhat by surprise” and that “the Germans feared the British more and had concentrated a much more formidable army in front of the British line.”
Throughout the battle, Haig maintained the pressure, believing that only sustained offensive action could relieve the French at Verdun and wear down German strength. He informed Parliament through the Under-Secretary for War that the troops were “all in good health and good heart, and confident of victory.” (Annual Register 1916) In July 1916, Hankey wrote to Lord Esher that “Haig and Robertson have been quite splendid.” (Hankey, Man of Secrets)
Haig corresponded directly with the Government on industrial matters critical to the battle. In September 1916, a letter from Haig was read to a conference of workers and employers, “pointing out that two days’ cessation of work in the munition factories would have the most serious effect on the operations now being carried out by the British Army in France.” The conference agreed to postpone all holidays. (Annual Register 1916)
By the battle’s close in November, the Allies had advanced up to eight miles on a twenty-mile front, had relieved pressure on Verdun, and had inflicted irreplaceable losses on the German Army — but at a cost of over 400,000 British casualties.

Third Ypres (1917)
The Third Battle of Ypres — better known as Passchendaele — was Haig’s great Flanders offensive of 1917. After the successful preparatory Battle of Messines Ridge (June 1917), in which General Plumer’s Second Army exploded twenty enormous mines and captured the entire contested ridge, Haig launched the main offensive.
“During the last ten days of July the bombardment of the German line in Flanders was increased to a pitch of extreme violence, and according to the German account, the artillery duel on this occasion exceeded in intensity anything previously witnessed.” (Annual Register 1917) The infantry assault was launched on 31 July with French assistance on the left flank, extending over a front of 15 miles from Steenstraate on the Yser to La Basse Ville on the Lys.
The initial attack captured Verlorenhoek, Frezenberg, St. Julien, Pilken, Hooge, Westhoek, La Basse Ville, and Hollebeke. Over 5,000 prisoners were taken on the first day (plus 1,000 by the French). German counter-attacks were “prompt and determined,” but the British held most of their gains.
“On August 15 Sir Douglas Haig again took the offensive. On this day Canadian troops delivered a successful assault upon a dominating height known as Hill 70, near Lens, and on the following day the village of Langemarck, north-east of Ypres, was taken.” (Annual Register 1917) The total prisoners taken by the British from 31 July to 31 August was 10,697, with about forty guns captured.
The campaign continued through the autumn in exceptionally wet weather that turned the battlefield into a sea of mud. In September, assaults along the Ypres-Menin road captured over 2,000 prisoners; Veldhoek was taken, and a further 1,000 prisoners fell on 21 September. British captures for the month totalled 5,296 prisoners. On 6 November, “another assault was delivered east of Ypres, this time a short distance north of the Menin road, and the village of Passchendaele was stormed by Canadian troops. Passchendaele stands on relatively high ground.” (Annual Register 1917)

The Hundred Days (1918)
The year 1918 opened with the German Spring Offensive (March–July), which nearly broke the Allied lines. Haig issued his famous “backs to the wall” order on 11 April, calling for resistance to the last. Following the failure of the German offensive, Haig orchestrated the Allied counter-offensive that became known as the Hundred Days — the campaign that ended the war.
On 8 August, the Allied offensive was launched on a new sector, with the British Fourth Army under General Rawlinson and the French First Army delivering the assault. “The British broke through at the first assault, and cavalry and light tanks pursued the fleeing Germans. At some points an advance of 7 miles was made on the first day, and in five days the Fourth Army captured 400 guns and nearly 22,000 prisoners.” (Annual Register 1918)
“On August 21 a new offensive was set in motion by Sir Douglas Haig. The attack took place on a front of 10 miles, north of the Ancre, and the troops operating were those of the Third Army under General Sir J. Byng. The initial attack was aided by fog, and there was no artillery preparation. Tanks played a great part in the attack.” (Annual Register 1918) The next day the offensive was extended southwards and Albert was taken. The Fourth Army also came into action, and “thus at the end of August the entire Allied line from Arras to Soissons was steadily advancing.” Bapaume fell to New Zealand troops on 29 August.
The decisive blow of the summer campaign came when the Allies reached the Hindenburg Line. “The Hindenburg Line was the strongest part of the entire German defensive system in France, and the Drocourt-Quéant section was considered the key of the famous Line, and was deemed invulnerable.” (Annual Register 1918) The First Army under General Horne had now come into action. The breaking of the Hindenburg Line in September–October made German defeat inevitable.
Haig’s insistence on relentless pursuit throughout the Hundred Days has been widely credited by military historians with ensuring that the war ended in November 1918 rather than dragging into 1919.

Legacy
Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig was invested with the Order of Merit on 12 June 1919, alongside Admiral of the Fleet Sir David Beatty, and was subsequently admitted as a Freeman of the City of London. In his speech, he “urged the necessity of setting up a strong citizen army on territorial lines” and expressed the view that “peace could only be guaranteed by adequate preparation for war.” (Annual Register 1919) He received the Freedom of Oxford, Wolverhampton, and Glasgow in 1919, and was created 1st Earl Haig in the same year.
After the war, Haig devoted himself to the welfare of ex-servicemen. He became the driving force behind the Royal British Legion and the annual Poppy Appeal, and was instrumental in the establishment of the Imperial War Museum and other institutions to commemorate the war dead. When a national railway strike threatened in 1919, Haig — now Commander-in-Chief of the Home Forces — attended a Cabinet meeting to coordinate the government’s response. (Annual Register 1919)
Haig’s legacy remains deeply contested. To his defenders, he was the commander who rebuilt the BEF after the disaster of 1914–1915, mastered the art of industrial warfare, and orchestrated the victorious Hundred Days campaign of 1918 — the greatest military victory in British history to that date. To his critics, he symbolises the inhumanity of trench warfare, the allegedly unimaginative commitment to attrition, and the seemingly cavalier expenditure of life on the Somme and at Passchendaele.
The historical record shows a more complex figure. Hankey’s private diary records that even Haig’s admirers recognised the terrible cost of his offensives; yet Hankey himself told Esher in July 1916 that “Haig and Robertson have been quite splendid.” (Hankey, Man of Secrets) Before the war, Churchill had sought Haig’s advice on staff organisation and received “a masterly paper” that Churchill described as “a formidable commentary on existing naval methods.” (Churchill, The World Crisis) As early as 1910, Haig — while Chief of Staff in India — had been asked by Henry Wilson to plan for the use of Indian troops on the Western Front; ordered by the Viceroy, Lord Hardinge, to destroy those plans, “Haig discreetly disobeyed — in 1914 the scheme proved quite valuable.” (Politics and Grand Strategy)
Haig died on 29 January 1928. His funeral was a national occasion, and he lies buried at Dryburgh Abbey in the Scottish Borders. The Earl Haig Fund, established in his memory, continues to support ex-servicemen.

entities/hilaire-belloc.title: Hilaire Belloc
entities/hilaire-belloc.content:
Hilaire Belloc
Hilaire Belloc is the joint author, with Cecil Chesterton, of The Party System (London: Stephen Swift, 1911) and the sole author of The Servile State (first issued October 1912; reprinted February and October 1913, with a preface to the second edition signed from Kings Land, Shipley, Horsham, Sussex). In those two books he presents himself as a polemicist against the working of the British party machine and against the drift of industrial capitalism toward legally compulsory labour. He does not narrate a private life. What he does state, in the first person or as joint author, is the object of each book, the circumstances of its publication, and the political stance from which the argument is written.
Biography
The late election and The Party System
The Party System opens in the dust of the second general election of 1910. Belloc and Chesterton write as men who have just watched both sides proclaim that “the Will of the People must prevail,” with only “slight variations as to the direction” of that will. They record the poster-war in which Lloyd George and Winston Churchill appear on one sheet as patriots confronting a haughty aristocracy (Churchill’s cousin the Duke of Marlborough standing in for the order) and on the other as “low-born demagogues hallooing on their ragged and illiterate associates to the plunder of the wealthy.” Conservatives profess fear that John Redmond “should buy up the whole Liberal Front Bench with the sum of £40,000 (or $200,000, which sounds at once larger and more insidiously wicked)”; Liberals sing “One with us is He who leads us, / Asquith, God and right!” The voters, the authors say, are already looking at one another and wondering what the contest was about [source: belloc-party-system].
Their key to that stage-play is the year since the Lords threw out Lloyd George’s Budget in 1909. Asquith at the Albert Hall pledged that he would neither assume nor retain office without “guarantees” that the veto would be limited. He won the January 1910 election, assumed office, retained office, and produced no guarantees. He entered a “conference” with his alleged opponents; six months were supposed to have been spent bridging the “unbridgable gulf” which “one of his humbler salaried followers discovered, in a notable speech, to exist between the views of his uncle on the one hand, and of his first cousin on the other.” Both sides then announced that the Conference had failed, and another election was declared necessary, “though, as matter of fact, there was absolutely nothing to vote about.” “The Conference did not fail. It did exactly what it was intended to do. It saved for a moment the life of the moribund Party System.” The 1906 mandate had been squandered—Chinese Labour, the Licensing Bill, “the collapse and absorption of the Labour Party”—and “Down with the Lords!” had been raised to rally supporters, then smothered when a handful of Radicals demanded fulfilment [source: belloc-party-system].
The object of the book, they write, is “to expose and ridicule as it deserves, to destroy and to supplant the system under which Parliament, the governing institution of this country, has been rendered null.” Governments abandon causes because they consult “the sense of the Governing Group”; Oppositions tolerate the abandonment because they wish to preserve the system that will, “by the connivance of those rivals,” bring them office in turn. “Practically every move in the silly and dangerous game is arranged beforehand by the confederates on the two Front Benches” [source: belloc-party-system].
Belloc’s argument, as joint author, is that democracy means government by the general will, and that “there is no democracy in England to-day.” Representation requires free selection of representatives, strict responsibility to constituents, and independence of the Executive; none obtain. Ministers nominate themselves and fill vacancies by co-option. The two Front Benches are “one close oligarchical corporation,” bound by kinship, private secretaryships, and make-weights, playing a feud kept up “mainly for the dramatic entertainment of the people of Verona.” The House of Commons has lost control of its time-table; five-sixths or more of time is at the Government’s disposal; the authors’ own motion on the secrecy of the Party Funds was nullified, after consultation with the Opposition Front Bench, by a shelving amendment. Two “huge war-chests,” secretly subscribed and secretly disbursed, buy honours and policies. The Central Office and the caucus select candidates and programmes. Unreal issues, defined by the politicians themselves, give “a semblance of reality to their empty competition.” The authors “decidedly disagree” on Free Trade versus Protection, which they treat as proof that the machine, not conviction, frames the electoral question [source: belloc-party-system].
They reject the defence that the system has made England everything a citizen can desire: conditions “are not good, but bad”; continental peoples regard the English poor with “pity and horror.” Franchise tinkering, payment of members, and auditing of funds will not restore representation. What they propose is exposure and ridicule; pledges inside the machine to vote against whatever Government unless scheduled measures pass by a date; a short, indissoluble Parliament; and, if the people will organise, something like Jowett’s departmental committees. If they will not, “the law-making institution of England … is done with.” Until a successor organ appears, the country faces “one of those evil spaces, subject to foreign insult and domestic misfortune,” when nations “lose grip over their own destinies” [source: belloc-party-system].
Kings Land and The Servile State
The second book is signed, for the second-edition preface, from Kings Land, Shipley, Horsham, Sussex. Belloc will not alter a completed book to meet reviewers. He states three corrections of misconception. First, the argument “bears no relation to the common accusation levelled against Socialists (that is, Collectivists) that life in a Socialist State would be so subject to regulation and order as to be unduly oppressive.” He does “not discuss the Socialist State.” “It is the very heart of my thesis that we are not, as a fact, approaching Socialism at all, but a very different state of society; to wit, a society in which the Capitalist class shall be even more powerful and far more secure than it is at present: a society in which the proletarian mass shall not suffer from particular regulations, oppressive or beneficent, but shall change their status, lose their present legal freedom, and be subject to compulsory labour.” Second, he has not set up the thesis “as a warning or as a piece of gloom.” He says nowhere that “the re-establishment of slavery would be a bad thing as compared with our present insecurity”; the tendency exists “because the new conditions may be found more tolerable than those obtaining under Capitalism.” Third, he has not mistaken professional politicians’ “Social Reform” for Socialism. The Socialist object—“the putting of the means of production into the hands of politicians to hold in trust for the community”—“is not in practice being approached”; what is approaching is “compulsory labour among an unfree majority of non-owners for the benefit of a free minority of owners.” The Socialist ideal, “in conflict with and yet informing the body of Capitalism, produces a third thing very different from the Socialist ideal—to wit, the Servile State” [source: belloc-servile-state].
His metaphor is a traveller who would escape mountain cold by going south on a river: the mountains will “divert the course of this River northward again”; “the big bend has already begun.” The traveller is the Socialist; the South is the Collectivist State; the River is modern “Organised Reform”; the northern bed is “a society reposing upon compulsory labour.” The only discrepancy is that the traveller could leave the river and go south by land—corresponding to “a bold policy of Confiscation,” which he nowhere denies is “ideally possible,” as it is ideally possible that “to-morrow all Englishmen shall take and preserve for twenty-four hours a vow of silence.” “Nothing like it or approaching it has ever been done or is now being done.” With every step along existing lines “we are making it more and more difficult to retrace such steps.” “The path of Confiscation, the only way by which Socialists can reach their goal, gets more and more remote with every new and positive economic reform, undertaken, remember, with the aid and under the advice of Socialists themselves” [source: belloc-servile-state].
Labour is “servile” which is undertaken “not in fulfilment of contract but under the compulsion of positive law and which attaches to the status of the labourer, and is performed for the benefit of others who are under no such compulsion.” The historical claim that slavery receded “under the influence of the Catholic Church” is, he writes, “not a piece of special pleading put forward to please my co-religionists” but “a plain piece of historical fact.” He has not said that a “completely free Distributive State” was ever reached: it was “in process of formation when the disruption of our united European civilisation in the sixteenth century arrested its development and slowly produced, in this country especially, Capitalism in its stead.” State regulation and municipal enterprise, until based on Confiscation, “obviously do not affect my argument.” “You cannot ‘buy out’ Capitalism” [source: belloc-servile-state].
Since first publication he notes the facts he treats as confirmation: “We already have Wages Boards in one great industry; we shall shortly have them in more.” Registration of the proletariat—name, address, movement, illness, supposed or real “malingering,” drink, domestic habits, employment—is “very nearly complete,” imposed by “the wealthier classes who are the actual gatherers of the Poll Tax upon which this registration is based.” Labour Exchanges will register every proletarian as a worker, “his tendencies to rebellion against Capital,” whether and when he has “refused service.” No change in European society arrives at completion unless it is universal throughout Europe; Capitalism is not thus universal, so “the advent of servitude is therefore a probability differing in degree.” The example of economic freedom elsewhere “may in the future transform, and will certainly limit,” sections drifting toward slavery. “But the tendency to the re-establishment of slavery as a necessary development of Capitalism is patent wherever Capitalism has power, and nowhere more than in this country” [source: belloc-servile-state].
The body of the book is written to maintain one proposition: that a free modern society in which the means of production are owned by a few is in unstable equilibrium, and tends to stable equilibrium “BY THE ESTABLISHMENT OF COMPULSORY LABOUR LEGALLY ENFORCEABLE UPON THOSE WHO DO NOT OWN THE MEANS OF PRODUCTION FOR THE ADVANTAGE OF THOSE WHO DO.” He will not judge whether the approaching organisation be “good or evil,” only show “the necessary tendency towards it” and “the recent social provisions which show that it has actually begun.” He proves the thesis from industrial Great Britain, “including that small, alien, and exceptional corner of Ireland, which suffers or enjoys industrial conditions to-day.” Definitions of wealth, labour, land, capital, proletariat, property, Collectivism, Capitalism, and the Servile State occupy the first section. Europe, he argues, sprang from a pagan servile basis; the Church slowly released it toward a mediaeval Distributive State of owners (serf becoming peasant, guilds checking monopoly); that arrangement was wrecked in England not by machinery but by the sixteenth-century transfer of monastic land to an oligarchy, so that by 1700 England was already capitalist and the later Industrial Revolution took a capitalist form. Capitalism is unstable because law still presupposes free owners while “nineteen out of twenty” have no property, and because it cannot of itself give sufficiency and security. The only three solutions are Collectivism, the Distributive State, or the Servile State. Collectivism is the easiest apparent solution; in action, pursued without confiscation, it produces the third thing. The Socialist who cannot confiscate, the reformer who loves tabulation, the “Practical Man,” and a proletariat that fears “the sack” more than the Courts, all make for status in exchange for a guaranteed wage. “The Servile State is, in industrial England to-day, no longer a menace but something in actual existence.” Employers’ liability, the Insurance Act (compulsion by employment and collection of the tax by the capitalist class), wages boards and a legal minimum in mining, labour exchanges, and the prospect of labour colonies are the English illustrations. Municipalisation by loan is “sham Socialism.” “Mere Capitalist anarchy cannot endure.” He does not believe theoretical Collectivism “will ever inform a real and living society.” The remaining alternatives are “a reaction towards well-divided property, or the re-establishment of servitude.” France and Ireland he records as societies that may check the tide making in Prussia and England. “As I am upon the whole hopeful that the Faith will recover its intimate and guiding place in the heart of Europe, so I believe that this sinking back into our original Paganism (for the tendency to the Servile State is nothing less) will in due time be halted and reversed.” Videat Deus [source: belloc-servile-state].
The two books are one political stance. In 1911 he treats Parliament as already null under a self-elected governing group and secret funds. In 1912–13 he treats industrial law as already laying the corner-stone of a new status: not the Collectivist trust he says Socialists intend, and not the widely distributed property he names as the only free alternative, but compulsory labour of non-owners for owners, sweetened by security. The Party System is the machine of the professional politicians; Social Reform is the river that does not run south.
In the Sources
