entities/jellicoe-john.title: Jellicoe, Sir John
entities/jellicoe-john.content:
Admiral Sir John Rushworth Jellicoe (1859–1935)
Commander-in-Chief, Grand Fleet (1914–1916) · First Sea Lord (1916–1917) · Admiral of the Fleet (1919) · 1st Earl Jellicoe of Scapa (1925)

Command of the Grand Fleet
John Rushworth Jellicoe was appointed Second Sea Lord in 1912, where he “vehemently pressed for very large increases” in oil-fuel reserves, recognising the strategic importance of petroleum for the fleet. (Churchill, The World Crisis Vol. 1) In June 1914, Winston Churchill — then First Lord of the Admiralty — arranged for Jellicoe to become Second-in-Command of the Home Fleet under Sir George Callaghan, with Churchill writing privately that Jellicoe “is not yet sufficiently in command of the confidence of the Sea Service, to justify what would necessarily be a very startling promotion” but that the appointment would “see what fitness he will develop for the succession.” (Churchill, The World Crisis Vol. 1) The appointment passed Jellicoe “over the heads of four or five of the most important senior Admirals on the active list” and made him “virtually designated for the supreme command.” (Churchill, The World Crisis Vol. 1)
On the eve of war, Vice-Admiral Sir John Jellicoe was appointed Second-in-Command of the Home Fleet on 31 July 1914. Corbett’s official history records that “to strengthen the staff of the Fleet, Vice-Admiral Sir John R. Jellicoe had been appointed Second in Command,” with Rear-Admiral Charles E. Madden as Chief of the Staff. (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. I)
When war broke out, Admiral Callaghan was relieved and Jellicoe succeeded to the supreme command with the acting rank of Admiral. Corbett notes that Callaghan had brought the Fleet “to the high state of efficiency it was showing” but “it was thought better to commit the arduous work ahead to a younger officer.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. I) The Annual Register recorded that “Admiral Sir John Jellicoe was appointed to the supreme command of the Home Fleets, with Rear-Admiral C. E. Madden as his Chief of Staff.” (Annual Register 1914)
When Admiral Jellicoe took over the Grand Fleet, it “consisted of twenty Dreadnoughts, eight King Edwards, four battle cruisers, two squadrons of cruisers and one of light cruisers.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. I) He received notice of the ultimatum at sea on 4 August and immediately commenced the precautionary movements laid down for covering the passage of the British Expeditionary Force. By 5 August he had completed his sweep of the North Sea and was directed to keep his fleet to the northward to hold the entrance to the North Sea. (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. I)
Jellicoe established his headquarters at Scapa Flow in the Orkney Islands, the principal wartime base of the Grand Fleet. The base was still being fortified when war began, and Jellicoe repeatedly pressed for improved defences. In November 1914, “Admiral Sir John Jellicoe was instructed to return the twelve detached destroyers as soon as the Scapa defences were secure.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. II) The insecurity of the northern anchorages “continued in some measure to cramp Admiral Jellicoe’s freedom of action” in the early months of the war. (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. II)
Throughout 1915 and early 1916, Jellicoe maintained the deterrent posture on which British grand strategy rested. He urged the creation of “special flotillas” for hunting submarines, pressed for more trawlers for minesweeping ahead of the fleet, and faced constant demands on his destroyer force. In the summer of 1915, King George V visited the Grand Fleet, “under the command of Admiral Sir John Jellicoe,” expressing “his pride and admiration at the splendid aspect of the Navy.” (Annual Register 1915) Jellicoe was promoted G.C.B. in the same year. (Annual Register 1915)

Battle of Jutland
The Battle of Jutland (31 May – 1 June 1916) was the only major fleet action of the war. Jellicoe commanded the Grand Fleet’s battle squadrons while Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty led the Battle Cruiser Fleet in advance. The German High Seas Fleet under Admiral Scheer had sortied in an attempt to cut off and destroy a portion of the British forces.
Corbett’s official history of the battle (Volume IV) describes the outcome from the strategic perspective: “Admiral Scheer had failed in his object of cutting off and overwhelming part of our advanced forces, and had found himself unexpectedly entrapped into meeting the Grand Fleet. From this encounter he had succeeded in extricating himself at considerable expense, but, on the other hand, both before and after the main action he had inflicted upon us more serious losses than he could ever have contemplated.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. IV)
The critical assessment recorded by Corbett was that “Admiral Jellicoe had outmanœuvred and surprised the High Seas Fleet, and for him the net result of the action had been to increase the Grand Fleet’s large margin of superiority as a combative force, a defence against invasion, and an instrument of blockade. The control of the North Sea remained in our hands, and any expectation that this control might be weakened or taken from us had been finally dissipated.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. IV)
Jellicoe’s battle fleet returned to Scapa Flow between 10.30 a.m. and noon on 2 June. By 9.45 p.m. that evening, Jellicoe reported to the Admiralty that “the Grand Fleet was at its base, re-fuelled, with steam at four hours’ notice, and ready for sea.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. IV) This rapid return to readiness drew admiration from neutral observers: “The Dutch naval officers were reported to be ‘filled with admiration for the speed with which Jellicoe was ready for action again.‘” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. IV) A German naval commentator wrote that “Jellicoe did not for an instant surrender the command of the sea.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. IV)
Almost immediately upon return to harbour, Jellicoe “appointed committees of gunnery, torpedo and signalling experts to report upon the manner in which the fleet material had stood the test.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. IV) His tactical caution — the decision to decline night action against the retiring German fleet — became the subject of lasting debate, but reflected his understanding of the strategic stakes: he commanded the margin of British naval supremacy, and its destruction in an ill-timed engagement could have been catastrophic for the Allied cause. The contemporary view, as summarised by Winston Churchill, was that Jellicoe was “the only man on either side who could lose the war in an afternoon.”

First Sea Lord & Convoy System
In November 1916, as the strain of command and the mounting threat of unrestricted submarine warfare demanded fresh leadership at the Admiralty, Jellicoe was appointed First Sea Lord. The Annual Register recorded the announcement: “Admiral Sir John Jellicoe would become First Sea Lord in place of Admiral Sir Henry Jackson. Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty had already assumed command of the Grand Fleet in succession to Sir John Jellicoe.” (Annual Register 1916) Balfour stated that “the decision involving these appointments was taken some time previously, but that for military reasons the announcement had been delayed.” (Annual Register 1916)
Jellicoe’s appointment came at a critical moment. Maurice Hankey, Secretary of the War Cabinet, had noted a “marked strain of pessimism in Jellicoe’s character” and recorded that “Lloyd George, Beaverbrook and Dr. Thomas Jones all expressed opinions identical to Hankey’s on this matter; yet Jellicoe was appointed First Sea Lord in succession to Admiral Jackson in the following December.” (Hankey, Man of Secrets Vol. I)
The submarine crisis was the overriding problem. As early as October 1916 — while still C-in-C of the Grand Fleet — Jellicoe had written to the Prime Minister “expressing anxiety with regard to the danger to the Allied cause from submarine attacks on merchant ships, which with notable prescience he anticipated would increase in the following spring.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. V) At the War Committee meeting on 2 November 1916, Jellicoe was asked by Lloyd George if he had any plan against German submarines. Corbett records that “Sir John Jellicoe said that he had not” and that when Lloyd George suggested a convoy system with a dozen ships escorted by three warships, Jellicoe replied “that they would never be able to keep merchant ships sufficiently together to enable a few destroyers to screen them.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. V)
Corbett’s history provides careful context: “It was, however, probable that the view put forward by Sir John Jellicoe on this occasion was more the Admiralty’s than his own. He was at this time commanding the Grand Fleet and had not studied the question of the protection of ocean trade.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. V) When he became First Sea Lord, Jellicoe “was bound to give great weight and consideration to Admiralty opinion as he found it; and, since the November Conference, opinion had not changed at all. Indeed, it had hardened.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. V) An official Admiralty pamphlet issued in January 1917 stated “quite emphatically, that a convoy system was not a sound measure of trade defence.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. V)
Nevertheless, Jellicoe himself was “still clear and decided on one point: that if the existing system of trade defence needed reinforcing and supplementing, then this could only be done by instituting some kind of convoy system. One of his earliest minutes was a warning to the Staff that they might be obliged to place some of the Atlantic trade under convoy.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. V) The practical difficulties were formidable: destroyer resources were stretched to breaking point, and Jellicoe “was constantly held back by the reflection that the destroyer forces required for convoy work would have to be collected from commands both at home and abroad.” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. V)
In April 1917, following the Longhope Conference on the Scandinavian trade, Jellicoe “endorsed the findings of the Conference and gave orders that the ‘system was to be tried, and a report sent fortnightly on its working.‘” (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. V) The experimental convoy on the Scandinavian route proved successful, and the system was gradually extended to Atlantic and Mediterranean trade. The convoy system is widely regarded as the decisive strategic innovation that defeated the U-boat offensive in 1917–1918.
Jellicoe also co-operated with the reorganisation of the Admiralty’s War Staff in May 1917, when “Sir John Jellicoe, as Chief of the Staff, was freed of all administrative detail in order that he might give his undivided attention to questions of policy and strategy.” (Annual Register 1917)
Jellicoe’s tenure as First Sea Lord ended abruptly. In December 1917, Sir Eric Geddes (the new First Lord) dismissed him. Hankey’s account records that Geddes asked Admiral Sir Rosslyn Wemyss “whether he would be prepared to step into Jellicoe’s shoes,” and “on the evening of Monday 24th Jellicoe found on his desk a letter of dismissal.” (Hankey, Man of Secrets Vol. I) The Sea Lords threatened resignation, and “a somewhat heated correspondence followed.” (Hankey, Man of Secrets Vol. I) The King conferred a peerage on Jellicoe, and Wemyss succeeded him as First Sea Lord. (Annual Register 1917) Hankey wrote privately to Jellicoe expressing his admiration for “the way you have tackled the difficult problems with which you were confronted, and literally put a new face on the submarine warfare.” (Hankey, Man of Secrets Vol. I)

Later Career
Jellicoe was promoted to Admiral of the Fleet on 3 April 1919, alongside Sir David Beatty. (Annual Register 1919) He was raised to the peerage as Viscount Jellicoe of Scapa in 1918 and later created 1st Earl Jellicoe of Scapa in 1925.
In 1919, Jellicoe published The Grand Fleet: 1914–16, described by the Annual Register as “one of the most important books published during the year” and “of the first historical importance.” (Annual Register 1919) The work dealt with “the whole period of his command, from the beginning of the war down to his return to the Admiralty in 1917.” It gave “a very interesting account of the Battle of Jutland — ‘the first Fleet action since Trafalgar, if we except the action in the Russo-Japanese War’” and described “the defects in the material of the Fleet,” noting that “in many respects the Germans had the advantage.” (Annual Register 1919)
Jellicoe undertook an extended naval mission to India and the Dominions (1919–1920), advising on post-war naval organisation and imperial defence. He remained a prominent public figure and an authoritative voice on naval affairs until his death on 20 November 1935.
His papers were preserved in the British Museum, and his official correspondence was later edited by A. Temple Patterson and published by the Navy Records Society as The Jellicoe Papers (1966–1968). (Hankey, Man of Secrets Vol. I; Politics and Grand Strategy)

Assessment: Jellicoe commanded the Grand Fleet at its moment of maximum responsibility, from the outbreak of war through the Battle of Jutland — the only major fleet engagement between dreadnought battleships. His strategic caution at Jutland reflected a clear understanding that the destruction of the Grand Fleet meant the loss of the war. As First Sea Lord, he presided over the Admiralty during the most dangerous phase of the unrestricted submarine campaign and laid the groundwork for the convoy system that ultimately defeated the U-boat. His dismissal in December 1917 was a brutal end to a pivotal wartime career, but the convoy measures set in motion under his tenure proved decisive in the final year of the war.

entities/kipling-rudyard.title: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936)
entities/kipling-rudyard.content:
Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936)
Rudyard Kipling was the foremost literary exponent of British imperialism — poet, short-story writer, and novelist whose work captured the ethos of the British Empire at its zenith, who chronicled the lives of common soldiers and colonial administrators, and who articulated the ideological underpinnings of imperial expansion. Born in Bombay in 1865 and educated in England, Kipling returned to India as a journalist and established himself as the voice of British India. His later years were shadowed by the death of his only son, John, in the Great War.
Early Life & Indian Writing
Joseph Rudyard Kipling was born on 30 December 1865 in Bombay, India, where his father John Lockwood Kipling served as curator of the Central Museum and principal of the Mayo School of Art at Lahore [source: annual-register-1911]. After a harsh English boarding-school education (later fictionalised in Stalky & Co.), Kipling returned to India in 1882 at age sixteen to work as a journalist in Lahore on the Civil and Military Gazette.
His early work consisted of short stories and verses capturing Anglo-Indian life, published in Departmental Ditties (1886) and Plain Tales from the Hills (1888). These established his reputation for sharp observation, colloquial vigour, and intimate knowledge of the British-Indian world. His first book in England appeared in 1890, and his popularity increased so rapidly that by the end of the century “no other writer of his time had so profoundly swayed the English mind” [source: langer-diplomacy-imperialism-vol1].
From this period came The Jungle Book (1894) and Kim (1901), works that demonstrated his extraordinary sympathy for Indian life and landscape. Mackinder’s lectures on India reference the building Kipling “spoke of as the Moulmein Pagoda” and mention “Kim in Rudyard Kipling’s book” in connection with the Zamzamah gun at Lahore [source: mackinder-eight-lectures-india].
Imperial Poet & Empire Writing
From the 1890s onward, Kipling became the voice of the New Imperialism, what his contemporaries called “the banjo-bard of Empire” [source: langer-diplomacy-imperialism-vol1]. His Barrack-Room Ballads (1892) and army stories stimulated interest in British activity overseas and appealed to the fighting instincts of the nation. Hostile critics accused him of exalting brutality and giving “a picture of unmitigated barbarism, drunken, swearing, coarse-minded, vulgar hooliganism” while admirers saw him as “the man who saved the Empire” who “roused the sleeping nerve centres of Imperialism” [source: langer-diplomacy-imperialism-vol1].
Kipling’s two most famous poems of the imperial period appeared in 1897 and 1899. “Recessional” — written for Queen Victoria’s Diamond Jubilee in 1897 — struck a sombre note of imperial humility (“Lest we forget”) that contrasted sharply with the jubilee’s triumphalism. “The White Man’s Burden” (1899), addressed to the United States on the occasion of its acquisition of the Philippines, articulated the doctrine of imperial trusteeship — the belief that Western powers had a duty to govern “lesser breeds without the Law.”
By the early 1900s, a reviewer of Kipling’s collection The Five Nations (1903) noted that while Kipling’s earlier work had been “songs and tales dealing with the humours of Anglo-Indian life,” he had lately cultivated “a sort of Christian Imperialism mingled with no small share of militarism.” It was not true that his verse produced the war fever, but “he certainly voiced the self-satisfied optimism with which Englishmen surveyed the rest of the world.” However, “such poems as the ‘White Man’s Burden’ and the ‘Recessional’ go far to redeem the present volume from the charge of unchecked jingoism” [source: annual-register-1903].
The literary historian Langer described the cultural moment: “It was such a ‘tidal mood of mankind’ which carried Kipling to unprecedented literary success in the decade following 1890.” W. T. Stead wrote at the time of Kipling’s illness (1899) that he stood revealed “as the man who most of all has impressed the popular mind, fired the popular imagination, interpreted the popular consciousness” [source: langer-diplomacy-imperialism-vol1]. In the larger sense, his popularity reflected the impatience of the average Englishman with Pre-Raphaelite poetry and the decadents — “the young Englishman, it has been said, yawned and longed to go out and shoot something he could understand” [source: langer-diplomacy-imperialism-vol1].
Boer War & Journalism
During the South African War (1899–1902), Kipling became the unofficial poet laureate of the conflict, producing verses that were “sung at every music-hall in the country, and aroused raptures of applause wherever they were heard.” Yet McCarthy, writing shortly after the war, offered a more sceptical assessment: “the more judicious of Mr. Kipling’s admirers wished that he had not gone quite so far out of his way in the endeavour to sound such a trumpet.” He concluded that the Boer War verses of Kipling and Newbolt sounded as if they had been composed “not by the genuine inspiration of their authors, but rather in obedience to that traditional impulse of the author’s pen, the request of friends — ‘You really must give us a poem about this war, the public are looking for it, the music-halls want it, and you will be thought unpatriotic if you do not rise to the occasion’” [source: mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol2].
Kipling visited South Africa during the war, where he edited a newspaper, The Friend, in Bloemfontein alongside fellow journalists after the British occupation. His poem “The Islanders” (1902), published in The Times on 4 January 1902, “severely satirised the British people for their excessive devotion to field sports and other pleasures, and their unwillingness to face the sacrifices necessary for national security” [source: annual-register-1902]. In the same year, he opened a covered rifle range at Lower Sydenham for the employees of Dr. Jaeger’s Sanitary Woollen System, reflecting his practical commitment to national preparedness [source: annual-register-1902].
In 1907, Kipling was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature. The award was noted as somewhat ironic: “his selection from the ranks of British writers by a body of trustees who were understood to reflect the pacific wishes of the founder of the fund, seemed somewhat strange, Mr. Kipling having done more than any writer to fan the military spirit of his countrymen into the flame which made the South African War inevitable” [source: annual-register-1907].
His political interventions extended beyond poetry. In 1911, Kipling published a verse in the Morning Post opposing the Declaration of London, part of the controversy over naval prize law. The verse ran: “The light is still in our eyes / Of Faith and Gentlehood, / Of Service and Sacrifice, / And it does not match our mood / To turn so soon to your sophistries / That starve our land of her food” [source: annual-register-1911]. In 1912, during the Home Rule crisis, his bitter verse in the Morning Post (8 July) “condensed the hostile feeling of ‘loyal Ulster’” [source: annual-register-1912]. And in March 1914, he was among the eminent signatories of the British Covenant, which declared that if the Home Rule Bill were passed without a general election, the signatories would “hold themselves justified in taking or supporting any action that might be effective to prevent it from being put into operation” [source: annual-register-1914].
Great War & Personal Loss
The Great War of 1914–1918 was the great turning point in Kipling’s personal and literary life. His only son, John (Jack) Kipling, was commissioned into the Irish Guards and was killed at the Battle of Loos on 27 September 1915, aged eighteen. John’s body was never identified; Kipling spent years searching for him. The loss devastated Kipling and transformed his writing.
During the war, Kipling produced propaganda writing and visited the front. He served on the Imperial War Graves Commission, where he helped choose the phrase “Their Name Liveth For Evermore” for the Stone of Remembrance and wrote the epitaphs for war cemeteries. His volume A Diversity of Creatures (1917) collected short stories published during the war period, including tales that showed “Mr. Kipling’s serious method” and gave “a beautiful and vivid picture” of soldiers at war [source: annual-register-1917].
Kipling’s most profound poetic response to the war was “Epitaphs of the War” (1919), a cycle of short epitaphs covering the dead of the Great War from every service and perspective — from the poignant “If any question why we died / Tell them, because our fathers lied” (“Common Form”) to individual epitaphs for sailors, airmen, and soldiers. These epitaphs are among the most powerful war poetry in the English language, stripped of the triumphalism of his earlier work and marked instead by grief, irony, and elegiac restraint.
Legacy
Kipling’s reputation underwent dramatic shifts in the decades after his death in 1936. At his peak (c. 1890–1910), he was by far the most popular writer in the English-speaking world — translated into every major language, read by the masses and respected by literary figures like Henry James and Edmund Gosse. The Nobel Prize in 1907 confirmed his international standing.
The rise of anti-colonial nationalism after the Second World War, and the critical reassessment of imperialism, led to a sharp decline in his literary reputation. Critics condemned the jingoism, militarism, and racial assumptions embedded in his work. Later scholarship, however, recovered the complexity of his achievement — the technical mastery of his verse, his deep knowledge of Indian life, his sympathy for the common soldier, and the genuine anguish of his later war poetry. T. S. Eliot’s selection of Kipling’s verse (1941) attempted to reclaim him as a serious poet.
Kipling’s influence on the language remains permanent: phrases he coined — “The White Man’s Burden,” “Recessional” (“Lest we forget”), “the law of the jungle,” “never the twain shall meet,” “a first-class fighting-man” (used approvingly in the House of Commons in 1903 [source: mccarthy-1903-1905]) — have become part of the common vocabulary. His memorial in Westminster Abbey’s Poets’ Corner stands near the graves of the writers he influenced and those he outlived. As Langer’s analysis concluded, Kipling “reflects the diverse ideas that went under the general term of imperialism” [source: langer-diplomacy-imperialism-vol1] — and for that reason, his work remains indispensable to understanding the British Empire and the mental world of the age that created it.
See also: imperialism, scramble-for-africa, command-of-the-sea

entities/kitchener-horatio.title: Kitchener, Horatio Herbert
entities/kitchener-horatio.content:
Field Marshal Lord Horatio Herbert Kitchener (1850–1916)
Commander of the Nile Expedition (1896–1898) · Chief of Staff, South Africa (1899–1900) · Commander-in-Chief, India (1902–1909) · Secretary of State for War (1914–1916) · Field Marshal (1909) · 1st Earl Kitchener of Khartoum (1914)

Sudan Campaign & Omdurman
Kitchener’s greatest military achievement before the Great War was the reconquest of the Sudan and the destruction of the Dervish power. As Sirdar (Commander-in-Chief) of the Egyptian Army, he meticulously prepared for a campaign to avenge the death of General Charles Gordon at Khartoum in 1885.
Early in 1898, Sir Herbert Kitchener, “the keenest observer of events within his sphere, believed he had good reason to know that the Dervishes were cautiously but steadily making preparations for a disturbing movement.” (McCarthy, Diamond Jubilee, Vol. 1) He sent for large reinforcements from Cairo, and “before many weeks he had organised a powerful military force on the banks of the Nile.” The Sudan Railway aided British movements, and in early April 1898 the Anglo-Egyptian army attacked the entrenched camp of the Dervishes, which held a force numbering nearly 10,000 men. Kitchener’s army “killed at least 3,000 Dervishes, captured 3,000 more, and made the leader of the Dervish band, Mahmoud, a prisoner.” (McCarthy)
This victory spurred Kitchener to prepare for the final confrontation. He resolved to make Khartoum “the point of his final attack.” The Khalifa’s forces numbered more than 60,000, “including in their mass some of the most warlike tribes known to that region, and were, it was said, well supplied with artillery.” The English troops numbered only some 23,000 men. (McCarthy)
On 2 September 1898, the decisive Battle of Omdurman was fought. The Dervishes came out to meet the British troops, but “after more than one long and desperate fight the skill and tactics of the British force, with an unfailing discipline and unbroken courage, accomplished a complete success over their enemies.” The Dervish force underwent “a complete defeat, and had to disperse and fly from the scene of action. The flight soon became an utter rout.” (McCarthy)
Kitchener entered Omdurman a triumphant conqueror, and on Sunday, 4 September, a thanksgiving service was held within Khartoum, where “the British and the Egyptian flag were displayed side by side over the shattered citadel where Gordon had closed his gallant and devoted life.” The victory was accepted in England as “the destruction of the Dervish power and the re-conquest for civilisation of the whole of the Egyptian Soudan.” (McCarthy)
Winston Churchill, who was present as a young lieutenant in the 21st Lancers, later recalled that he had been sent back “to report verbally to the Commander-in-Chief the position of the advancing Dervish Army.” Kitchener, Churchill wrote, “had disapproved of me severely in my youth, had endeavoured to prevent me from coming to the Sudan Campaign, and was indignant that I had succeeded in getting there. It was a case of dislike before first sight.” (Churchill, World Crisis, Vol. 1)
Following his victory, Kitchener proceeded up the Nile to Fashoda, where he confronted Captain Jean-Baptiste Marchand’s French expedition. “Lord Kitchener acted with his usual promptitude” and “at once went up the Nile with a flotilla of gun-boats and a military force,” informing Marchand that the territory belonged to Egypt. The confrontation brought Britain and France to the brink of war before the French government backed down. (McCarthy; Politics & Grand Strategy)
Kitchener returned to England to a national welcome “which was only in proportion with the splendid services he had rendered, his marvellous foresight, his patient organisation of details, and the efforts he had always made that there should be as little waste of human life on either side as was possible.” He received from Queen Victoria the title of Lord Kitchener of Khartoum. He also raised £100,000 to found the Gordon Memorial College in Khartoum, “the noblest and the most appropriate monument to the memory of the hero Gordon.” (McCarthy)

South African War & Indian Service
When the South African War broke out in 1899, Kitchener was appointed Chief of Staff to Field Marshal Lord Roberts, who became Commander-in-Chief in South Africa in December 1899. After Roberts’s recall in 1900, Kitchener succeeded him as Commander-in-Chief in South Africa, overseeing the difficult final phase of the war against Boer guerrilla resistance. (McCarthy, Diamond Jubilee, Vol. 2) His implementation of the scorched earth policy and the establishment of concentration camps remain deeply controversial aspects of his career.
From 1902 to 1909, Kitchener served as Commander-in-Chief in India, where he undertook a thorough reorganisation of the Indian Army. In 1907, the Committee of Imperial Defence declined to rule upon Indian defence needs “without the opinion of Lord Kitchener, head of British forces in India,” and Prime Minister Asquith ordered the Indian Secretary to sound Kitchener on the military situation. (Politics & Grand Strategy) His reforms created an army capable of contributing significantly to the Great War effort.
He was promoted to Field Marshal in 1909 and served as Agent and Consul-General in Egypt from 1911 to 1914. During this period, he “made a tour of the Sudan in January” 1914, and his report, written “with fresh knowledge,” surveyed the state of the territory he had conquered sixteen years earlier. (Annual Register 1914)

Secretary for War (1914–1916)
At the outbreak of the Great War, Prime Minister Asquith was also serving as Secretary of State for War but “could not possibly be burdened with the continuous flow of inter-departmental work.” He therefore “invited Lord Kitchener to undertake ministerial charge of the War Office, and the Field-Marshal, who had certainly not sought this post in any way, had no choice but to accept.” (Churchill, World Crisis, Vol. 1)
Churchill noted that “my relations with Lord Kitchener had been limited” before the war. “I was glad when he was appointed Secretary of State for War, and in those early days we worked together on close and cordial terms. He consulted me constantly on the political aspects of his work, and increasingly gave me his confidence in military matters.” (Churchill)
“The appointment of Earl Kitchener as a non-political War Minister” was noted as a significant departure, and “was followed by rumours of the impending establishment of a coalition Government.” (Annual Register 1914) In his maiden speech in the House of Lords on 26 August 1914, Kitchener declared that “as a soldier, he had no politics, and his term as War Secretary was that of the new Army — for the war, but not for longer than three years.” He reported that mobilisation “had taken place without a hitch” and that the Expeditionary Force “proved itself wholly efficient, thoroughly well equipped, and immediately ready to take the field.” (Annual Register 1914)

The New Armies
Kitchener’s most transformative contribution was the creation of the New Armies (popularly known as “Kitchener’s Armies” ). Almost alone among British leaders, he foresaw a long war requiring mass armies. Churchill recorded that when Kitchener joined the Cabinet:

“Lord Kitchener now came forward to the Cabinet, on almost the first occasion after he joined us, and in soldierly sentences proclaimed a series of inspiring and prophetic truths. Every one expected that the war would be short; but wars took unexpected courses, and we must now prepare for a long struggle. Such a conflict could not be ended on the sea or by sea-power alone. It could be ended only by great battles on the Continent. In these the British Empire must bear its part on a scale proportionate to its magnitude and power. We must be prepared to put armies of millions in the field and maintain them for several years.” (Churchill, World Crisis, Vol. 1)

Churchill believed that had Kitchener “proceeded to demand universal national service, his request would have been acceded to.” However, Kitchener “proposed to content himself with calling for volunteers, and in the first instance to form six new regular divisions.” The new Secretary of State “had little knowledge of and no faith in the British territorial system,” having witnessed the failure of French Territorial troops during the Franco-Prussian War. (Churchill)
“He set himself to create the cadres first of six, then of twelve, and ultimately of twenty-four ‘Kitchener Army’ divisions, at the same time that the recruits were pouring in upon him by the hundred thousand. That this vast feat of improvisation was accomplished must certainly rank among the wonders of the time.” (Churchill, World Crisis, Vol. 1)
The famous recruiting poster featuring Kitchener’s pointing finger and the words “YOUR COUNTRY NEEDS YOU” became one of the enduring images of the war. Within months, hundreds of thousands of volunteers flocked to the colours. By August 1915, Lord Kitchener could inform the House of Commons that “the results of recruiting during the last few months had been most satisfactory; and that the numbers were being maintained with surprising regularity.” (Annual Register 1915)

The Shell Crisis
By early 1915, the immense scale of modern industrial warfare had exposed critical shortages in munitions. The “Shell Crisis” of May 1915 forced a political crisis that led to the formation of the first Coalition Government under Asquith.
In the Army Estimates debate, Lord Kitchener made the frank admission that “the output is not equal to our necessities.” (Annual Register 1915) This statement caused deep alarm, with critics in Parliament charging that the Government had “proclaiming our shortage of munitions from the housetops” and calling for better news management: “Let the country know of reverses as well as successes; people can stand the truth.” (Annual Register 1915)
A few days after this debate, a War Office Armaments Output Committee was appointed, consisting of Lord Kitchener; Major-General Sir Stanley B. von Donop; Sir Herbert J. Walker, Chairman of the Railways Executive Committee; Sir Algernon Firth; Mr. George M. Booth; and Mr. Allan M. Smith. “The functions of the Committee were to arrange for the increase in the production of armament and munitions of war.” (Annual Register 1915)
The crisis contributed to the formation of a Ministry of Munitions under David Lloyd George, which removed responsibility for arms production from the War Office. Kitchener’s authority was effectively diminished as a result, though he remained Secretary of State for War. In a War Council meeting at 10 Downing Street on 29 October 1915, Kitchener, Asquith, Lloyd George and Balfour met with General Joffre to discuss strategic coordination. (Annual Register 1915) Kitchener also undertook a mission to the Eastern Mediterranean in November–December 1915, and visited Athens in November 1915 “as an official emissary of the British Government” to warn King Constantine of Greece against pro-German neutrality. (Annual Register 1915)

Death at Sea
By June 1916, Kitchener’s public standing remained immense despite the political eclipse of his authority. Accepting an invitation from Tsar Nicholas II to visit Russia for consultations, he embarked on the evening of 5 June 1916 from the north of England aboard H.M.S. Hampshire.
The Annual Register recorded the disaster:

“On June 5 there occurred what was perhaps the greatest disaster suffered by the country in the course of the year. Lord Kitchener, on the invitation of the Tsar of Russia, left the north of England on that day in H.M.S. Hampshire. At about 8 o’clock in the evening, the Hampshire struck a mine to the west of the Orkneys and sank. She had been accompanied on her voyage by two destroyers up to about an hour before the explosion occurred, but they had then been detached owing to the very heavy seas which were running. The ship sank within ten minutes. Destroyers and patrol vessels were immediately despatched to the scene, but in spite of every measure that could be taken, the boats which put off from the Hampshire were wrecked and lost, and only twelve survivors reached the shore on a raft.” (Annual Register 1916)

“The death of Lord Kitchener was deeply felt by all parties and persons throughout the Empire.” On 13 June, a memorial service was held at St. Paul’s Cathedral, at which the King and Queen were present, with other services at Westminster Abbey and across the country. “On the re-opening of Parliament the first concern of both Houses was to place on record their sense of the great loss which the country had sustained.” In the House of Lords, Lord French “related Lord Kitchener’s unsparing efforts to supply all his demands while he was Commander-in-Chief of the Army in France. So high was his estimate of Lord Kitchener as a soldier that when he was originally selected for the chief command in the field, he had urged Lord Kitchener to see the Prime Minister and arrange to take his place, Lord French himself acting as Chief-of-the-Staff.” In the House of Commons, a resolution was moved by Asquith and seconded by Bonar Law “that a national monument be erected to Lord Kitchener.” (Annual Register 1916)
Churchill, reflecting on Kitchener’s death, wrote poignantly:

“Both these two men were marked for death at the hands of the enemy, the young Minister grappling with his adversary in the high air, the old Field-Marshal choking in the icy sea.” (World Crisis, Vol. 1 — referring to Kitchener and Lord Lucas)


Legacy
Lord Kitchener was the most iconic British military figure of the first half of the Great War. His face, staring from recruiting posters with the command “Your Country Needs You,” became the visual symbol of national mobilisation. His strategic foresight in anticipating a war of years rather than months, and his creation of the New Armies of volunteers, laid the foundations for the mass citizen army that would ultimately win the war.
McCarthy’s contemporary account captured the national sentiment: Kitchener’s “marvellous foresight, his patient organisation of details, and the efforts he had always made that there should be as little waste of human life on either side as was possible” earned him “a national welcome which was only in proportion with the splendid services he had rendered.” (McCarthy, Diamond Jubilee, Vol. 1)
His tenure as Secretary of State for War was marked by immense achievements — the raising of thirty divisions of volunteer soldiers — and by equally immense strains: the shell crisis, the Dardanelles controversy, and the growing tension between his autocratic style and the demands of democratic war-making. Hankey’s committee work during the early 1900s had already revealed the tensions between the War Office and the Admiralty that would mark the first two years of the war. (Hankey, Man of Secrets, Vol. 1)
Lord Curzon, in a House of Lords debate on the voluntary system, noted the pressure on the War Office and urged “preliminary steps with a view to preventing chaos if it should become necessary later on to institute compulsory service.” (Annual Register 1915) Kitchener remained committed to voluntarism throughout his time at the War Office, resisting full conscription until the Military Service Act of 1916 was forced upon the Government.
His sudden death removed from the direction of the war the one figure whose prestige could command unquestioning public trust. The shock of his loss — a Field Marshal and War Minister drowned on a mission to Russia — sent reverberations through British society and remains one of the most dramatic single events of the war. The uncertainty surrounding the sinking of the Hampshire — whether it struck a drifting mine or was deliberately targeted by a U-boat — fuelled conspiracy theories that persist to this day.

entities/lloyd-george-david.title: Lloyd George, David
entities/lloyd-george-david.content:
David Lloyd George (1863–1945)
Chancellor of the Exchequer (1908–1915) · Minister of Munitions (1915–1916) · Prime Minister (1916–1922) · Leader of the Liberal Party

Early Career & the People’s Budget (1890–1911)
David Lloyd George entered Parliament in 1890 at the age of twenty-seven, not as a labour representative but as “the chosen mouthpiece of the working middle class, enthusiastic for Welsh nationalism.” A product of the industrious Nonconformist middle class, he came from a background untouched by wealth or distinguished family. In youth, full of the fervour of Mazzini’s democratic teaching, he dreamed of Wales as a nation, even a republic, with himself perhaps as its first president. Welsh nationalism could not breed a Home Rule party as Irish nationalism had done, however, and Lloyd George found greater scope for his talents in the Liberal Party. During the ten years of Conservative ascendancy (1895–1905) he fought his way into the front rank of the party, pitting himself more than once against Joseph Chamberlain and winning general acknowledgment for his powers as a parliamentary debater. (Clayton, The Rise of the Democracy)
With his entry into the Cabinet in 1905, alongside John Burns, government by aristocracy was effectively ended. When Lloyd George went from the Board of Trade to the Chancellorship of the Exchequer in 1908, “startling changes were predicted in national finance” — predictions that were fulfilled in the Budget of 1909. (Clayton)
The “People’s Budget” of 1909 was the great engine of the constitutional crisis that followed. It was described in the Annual Register as a Budget that “took a step” towards systematic social reform through radical taxation — including super-tax on high incomes, land value duties, and increased death duties. The House of Lords, dominated by Unionists, considered the financial proposals so revolutionary that it took the unprecedented course of rejecting the Bill, thus precipitating the dispute between the two Houses of Parliament. Winston Churchill later observed that the Lords’ rejection of the Budget in November 1909 was “a constitutional outrage and political blunder almost beyond compare,” which “led directly to the two General Elections of 1910, to the Parliament Act, and to the Irish struggle.” (Churchill, The World Crisis)
The crisis was brought to a satisfactory end by the Parliament Act of 1911, which stripped the Lords of their veto over money bills and reduced their power over other legislation to a suspensory veto of three sessions. The Act was the culmination of the struggle that Lloyd George’s Budget had ignited.
Belloc and Cecil Chesterton’s The Party System (1911) opens on the same election dust. On one poster Lloyd George and Winston Churchill appear as “patriots confronting a haughty aristocracy (as represented to Mr Churchill by his cousin the Duke of Marlborough)”; on the other as “a pair of low-born demagogues hallooing on their ragged and illiterate associates to the plunder of the wealthy.” The Lords’ rejection of “Mr Lloyd George’s Budget” is the first move of the stage-play that, in their account, the two Front Benches then manage by Conference and a second poll. They do not assign him a separate psychology; he is one of the paired election figures of the Governing Group. In the chapter on secret funds they instance the 1910 Liberal Birthday Honours: Sir Weetman Pearson (Lord Cowdray), “head of a great contracting company, to which Mr Lloyd-George, junior, son of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, has recently been articled. He is a very rich man, and there is an end of it.” The sale-of-policies pages name Rhodes, Schnadhorst, and Rutherfoord Harris, not the Chancellor. Later they write that it is “quite incredible” that such men as Asquith and Lloyd George, Balfour and F. E. Smith, could under any other circumstances give expression to the “imbecilities” of platform speech — again a Front-Bench type, not a private diagnosis. Belloc’s Servile State treats the Insurance Act and wages boards as marks of status compulsion; it does not name Lloyd George or attach those measures to his office.

Social Reform: The National Insurance Act 1911
With the constitutional question settled, Lloyd George turned to the ambitious programme of social reform that defined his Chancellorship. The National Insurance Bill of 1911 was his signature achievement. The Annual Register records that the Bill was “three years in the building” and affected millions of working people. Lloyd George advocated the Bill at Birmingham on 10 June 1911 to an audience of three thousand — though applications for tickets had numbered seventy thousand. He pointed to the existence, side by side, of “extreme wealth and extreme poverty,” dealing eloquently with the difficulties and efforts of the poor, and presenting the Bill as “a means of keeping up national efficiency.” In great cities, he said, half the outdoor pauperism was due to sickness, and the Bill aimed to break that cycle.
The National Liberal Federation at its annual meeting in Bath eulogised “the National Insurance Bill and Mr. Lloyd George’s services to it.” Lloyd George himself described the Bill as “swimming through a murky flood of misrepresentation,” predicting that its opponents would ultimately discover its advantages. The Bill provided for compulsory health insurance for workers, covering medical treatment and sick pay, and laid the groundwork for unemployment insurance. The scheme applied to some 2,400,000 workers initially and was financed by contributions from workers, employers, and the State. (Annual Register 1911)
Clayton, writing in 1911, observed that Lloyd George’s Budget and his speeches in its support had already made his name familiar to the people of Great Britain, and that “in the eager discussion on his Bill for National Insurance, that name is still more loudly spoken. Hated by opponents and praised by admirers, denounced and extolled, Mr. Lloyd George enjoys the tumult he arouses. His passionate speeches for the poor provoke the sympathy of the working class; his denunciations of the rich stir the anger of all who fear social revolution.”

The Agadir Crisis: The Mansion House Speech (1911)
In July 1911, the German gunboat Panther appeared at the Moroccan port of Agadir, precipitating a major international crisis. The German Government had assumed that Lloyd George would head the “peace party” in the British Cabinet and that British action would be neutralised. They were profoundly mistaken.
Lloyd George, whose foreign policy alignment had hitherto been uncertain, made a decisive intervention. As Churchill described it: “The accession of Mr. Lloyd George in foreign policy to the opposite wing of the Government was decisive.” On 21 July 1911, speaking at the Mansion House, the Chancellor of the Exchequer declared:

“I believe it is essential in the highest interests not merely of this country, but of the world, that Britain should at all hazards maintain her place and her prestige amongst the Great Powers of the world… If a situation were to be forced upon us in which peace could only be preserved by the surrender of the great and beneficent position Britain has won by centuries of heroism and achievement… then I say emphatically that peace at that price would be a humiliation intolerable for a great country like ours to endure.”

The speech was, in Churchill’s words, “a thunder-clap to the German Government.” The German Ambassador, Count Metternich, protested in acrid terms, and the German Government was forced to realise that Britain would stand by France. The crisis subsided, and the negotiations that followed resulted in colonial compensations for Germany rather than war. The speech marked Lloyd George’s emergence as a force in foreign policy and confirmed the Anglo-French Entente at a critical moment. (Churchill, The World Crisis; Politics and Grand Strategy)

Minister of Munitions & War Organisation (1915–1916)
By the spring of 1915, the scale of the war had exposed a catastrophic shortage of artillery shells and other munitions. The “Shells Scandal” brought down the Liberal government and forced the creation of the First Coalition in May 1915. Lloyd George was appointed the first Minister of Munitions, tasked with transforming the nation’s industrial output for war. Hankey recorded that before Lloyd George’s appointment, the deplorable state of munitions production had been known and pressing; Ottley had urged the appointment of “an official with plenary powers to commandeer the entire manufacturing potentialities of the Empire” as early as September 1914, but “nothing was done until May 1915 when Lloyd George was appointed Minister of Munitions in the First Coalition government.” (Hankey, Man of Secrets)
The Munitions of War Bill, introduced in June 1915, gave the new minister sweeping powers. Lloyd George declared that the Central European Powers were turning out 250,000 shells a day and insisted that Britain could surpass that output if organised properly. He secured “some of the best business brains of the country,” adopted a policy of decentralisation into ten munition areas each run by local business committees, and took measures to mobilise labour: no strikes or lock-outs, compulsory arbitration, suspension of trade union restrictions on output, and limitation of employers’ profits. (Annual Register 1915)
The Bill provoked fierce debate. Critics charged that it gave the Minister of Munitions “power to socialise labour,” and one member warned of “a slave-driver with absolute power to imprison by his warrant any man who he thought took too many glasses of whisky or refused to work overtime.” Nonetheless, the Bill passed, and under Lloyd George’s direction munitions output soared. When he reported on the Ministry’s work later, he could point to a transformation in Britain’s capacity to wage industrial war.
Lloyd George was also deeply involved in strategic questions. In November 1916, before the War Committee, he pressed the Admiralty on the question of convoy protection against German submarines, suggesting that a dozen ships be convoyed by three warships, though the naval leadership remained sceptical at that stage. (Corbett, Naval Operations Vol. V)

Premiership (1916–1922)
The Fall of Asquith and Formation of the War Cabinet
By December 1916, dissatisfaction with Asquith’s conduct of the war had reached a crisis. Lloyd George, then Minister of Munitions, presented a plan for a small War Committee to direct the war that effectively sidelined the Prime Minister. Asquith demurred at serving under Bonar Law, and after a Buckingham Palace conference on 5–6 December, the King turned to Lloyd George. Within twenty-four hours, Lloyd George had formed a new government. As one source records, “Asquith declined to serve in a subordinate post,” and the new administration was “principally, though not exclusively, Unionist, and no Liberal member of the late government (except Lloyd George himself) joined it.” (Asquith entity)
Lloyd George’s most immediate innovation was the creation of a small War Cabinet of four or five members, freed from all departmental duties. As Corbett’s Naval Operations records:

“On assuming office, he at once altered the existing machinery by creating a small War Cabinet of four or five members, freed of all departmental duties; and also by creating new ministries for the rapid despatch of the vast mass of additional business which resulted from the complete mobilisation of the nation’s resources. The first War Cabinet was composed of the Premier, Lord Curzon, Lord Milner, Mr. Bonar Law, and Mr. Arthur Henderson… this new War Cabinet was no longer an inner committee taking decisions which must be referred… its rulings, taken after consultation with the naval and military authorities, were absolute and final.”

Hankey was appointed Secretary of the War Cabinet, a body that would hold 650 meetings before its dissolution in October 1919. (Hankey, Man of Secrets)
War Direction (1917–1918)
Lloyd George’s War Cabinet governed with unprecedented executive authority throughout 1917 and 1918. In July 1917, Lloyd George carried out his first Cabinet reconstruction: Sir Edward Carson retired from the Admiralty to join the War Cabinet without portfolio, and Churchill — whom Lloyd George had long wished to recall to office — became Minister of Munitions. The War Cabinet at this time consisted of Lloyd George, Lord Milner, Lord Curzon, Carson, Bonar Law, George Barnes, and General Smuts. (Annual Register 1917)
In a major speech at Glasgow in July 1917, Lloyd George defined Britain’s peace terms with unprecedented clarity. He declared that Belgium and Serbia must be restored and compensated, that Mesopotamia and Armenia must be freed from Turkish rule, that the wishes of inhabitants of German colonies must be the dominant factor in their future, and that the war’s guarantee lay in “the destruction of Prussian military power, or better still from the democratisation of the German Government.” The Russian Revolution, he argued, had postponed victory but made it “more sure and of a better quality.” (Annual Register 1917)
The year 1918 opened with Lloyd George issuing a New Year’s appeal for sacrifice: “The road is clear before you; follow it, and it will lead ere long to safety for our people and victory for our cause.” The winter was the coldest on record; food queues formed; German air raids killed scores of civilians. Lloyd George introduced the last Man-Power Bill of the war, extending military service to meet the crisis of the German spring offensive. Compulsory rationing was introduced for meat and other staples. (Annual Register 1918)
The Peace Settlement
Lloyd George was the dominant British figure at the Paris Peace Conference of 1919, representing Britain alongside President Wilson and Clemenceau. Hankey served as secretary to the Council of Four, the inner body that shaped the peace. (Hankey, Man of Secrets)
At home, Lloyd George led a Coalition Government that faced the enormous task of demobilisation and transition from war to peace. The Annual Register for 1919 records that the year was “dominated by the conclusion of peace and the labour disputes that followed the war,” with waves of strikes across British industry. Lloyd George addressed a Joint Industrial Committee as a “Peace Congress,” warning that since “Russia had gone to pieces, and Germany showed symptoms of going to pieces also, it might fall upon this country — not for the first time — to save civilisation.” He insisted that “employers must take the long view” and that “Britain could not save civilisation by the triumph of any one class.” (Annual Register 1919)

Character and Reputation
Contemporaries saw in Lloyd George a figure of extraordinary energy, ambition, and talent, but also of danger. Clayton’s portrait of 1911 captures the ambivalence:

“A supreme self-confidence carries him along, and the spur of ambition is constantly pricking. Political co-operation is difficult for such a man, and an indifference to reforms that are not of his initiation, and a willingness to wreck legislation that cannot bear his name, are a weakness in Mr. Lloyd George that may easily produce a fall.”

Neutral minds, Clayton wrote, doubted whether Lloyd George “is sufficiently well-balanced for the responsibilities of high office,” and expressed misgivings “lest the era of social reform be inaugurated too rapidly.” Yet he concluded: “In this year of grace 1911, Mr. Lloyd George, incarnation of the hard-working middle class, is a very distinct personality in the government of the country, and his presence in the Cabinet a fact in the history of democracy.”
Churchill, who knew Lloyd George intimately, captured in his account of the Agadir crisis the qualities that made him formidable: his unpredictability, his decisiveness, his willingness to break with expectation. Until a few hours before the Mansion House speech, Churchill wrote, “his colleagues did not know. Working with him in close association, I did not know. No one knew. Until his mind was definitely made up, he did not know himself.”

Legacy
David Lloyd George was the most consequential British statesman of the early twentieth century after Asquith. As Chancellor of the Exchequer, his People’s Budget of 1909 destroyed the absolute veto of the House of Lords and inaugurated the modern system of progressive taxation. As the architect of the National Insurance Act 1911, he laid the foundations of the British welfare state. As Minister of Munitions, he organised Britain for industrial war and solved the shell crisis that had threatened the war effort. As Prime Minister from 1916, he created the War Cabinet system that directed the war to victory and was the principal British architect of the post-war settlement.
Yet the same ambition and independence that drove his achievements also isolated him from the Liberal Party he had once led. The Coalition he formed in 1916 had few Liberals in it; the party split and never recovered its former position. The pages of political history, as Clayton wrote in 1911, “are strewn with the stories of high careers wrecked in a feverish haste for fame.” Lloyd George’s career did not end in wreck, but neither did it reach the heights his early promise had suggested. He remained Prime Minister until 1922, but never held office again.

entities/queen-victoria.title: Queen Victoria (1819–1901)
entities/queen-victoria.content:
Queen Victoria (1819–1901)
Queen Victoria reigned as Sovereign of Great Britain and Ireland for sixty-four years, until her death on 22 January 1901 [source: annual-register-1901]. During the period 1865–1901 covered by this wiki, she exercised her constitutional role through successive ministries [source: mccarthy-history-vol4], presided over the expansion of the British Empire while the colonies looked up to her as their Queen-Mother [source: mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol1], and became the object of profound public reverence and affection, especially during her Golden and Diamond Jubilees [source: mccarthy-history-vol5-extended][source: mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol1].
Biography
Constitutional role and ministerial changes (1865–1880)
When Lord Russell’s Liberal ministry collapsed in June 1866 after the defeat of their Reform Bill, Russell and his colleagues tendered their resignation to the Queen, and after a little delay and some discussion the resignation was accepted. “The Queen, of course, sent for Lord Derby. There was no one else to send for. Somebody must carry on the Queen’s government” [source: mccarthy-history-vol4]. Lord Derby consented to relieve the sovereign and the country from difficulties by accepting the office of Prime Minister.
When Lord Derby later became gravely ill and determined to retire from office, he tendered his resignation, “and it was accepted by the Queen” [source: mccarthy-history-vol4].
In 1866, after the successful laying of the Atlantic telegraph cable, the Queen exchanged messages of congratulation with the President of the United States. The Queen congratulated the President upon “the successful completion of the great international work,” and was convinced that “the President will unite with her in fervently hoping that the electric cable which now connects Great Britain with the United States will prove an additional link between the nations whose friendship is founded in their common interest and reciprocal esteem” [source: mccarthy-history-vol4].
The Diamond Jubilee (1897)
The celebration of the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee in London in 1897 attracted great public attention. Unlike the Golden Jubilee procession of 1887, where “the Sovereigns and Princes of Europe and Asia were the most conspicuous figures,” the Diamond Jubilee procession was used “to show that semi-independent colonies and far-distant settlements in all parts of the globe looked up to the Sovereign of Great Britain as their Queen-Mother whose care and protection they cheerfully and loyally acknowledged.” After the “Empress Queen herself, the eyes and acclamations of the crowds which lined the route were directed to the Colonial Premiers, the Colonial troops, and the dark auxiliaries from our Asiatic and African dependencies” [source: mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol1].
Assessment of the reign (1897)
Looking back at her reign at the time of the Diamond Jubilee, McCarthy wrote that “the reign so far has given its measure, and no one can deny that on the whole it has been a reign of great success,” especially productive “of reform in political, in economical, and in social life,” with domestic reform and domestic advancement being particularly successful. “Never once during her time has the strength of the monarchy been shaken, or even threatened,” while many monarchies and republics abroad had fallen. “The monarchical system of Great Britain has not been seriously threatened in the slightest way since Queen Victoria came to the throne.” Though this was not “owing to any inspiration or any effort of the Queen herself,” it may be assumed “that the wisdom with which, as a constitutional sovereign, she discharged her duties, and acted in the end on the advice of her ministers, has had much to do with the stability of the Empire and the rule.” McCarthy concluded: “it would be unjust even to the history of the time not to give a word of praise to the steady, constitutional action of the sovereign” [source: mccarthy-history-vol5-extended].
Visit to Ireland (1900)
A memorable event in the closing years of Queen Victoria’s reign was her visit to Ireland in April 1900—the first in forty years. The visit “was projected by the Queen entirely of her own motion, and did not come from the promptings of any among her recognised official advisers,” who were disposed on the whole to discourage the project, fearing hostile demonstrations. “The Queen appeared to have made up her mind.” It seemed “that the Queen felt at heart a regret for the long estrangement between her and the Irish people.” To make the visit she gave up her annual visit to the South of France, taken to recruit her health in a climate which especially suited her [source: mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol2].
Her visit was preluded by the announcement of the Queen’s desire that on St. Patrick’s Day Irish soldiers in her service should wear the emblematic shamrock, “welcomed as a graceful act on the part of the Sovereign and as a recognition of the national feeling.” The Queen was received in Dublin “with every sign of respect, and even with a general expression of popular welcome.” She declared she had come “to this fair country to seek change and rest, and to revisit scenes which recall to my mind, among the thoughts of the losses which years must bring, the happiest recollection of a warm-hearted welcome given to me and my beloved husband and children” [source: mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol2].
No hostile demonstration interfered with the visit’s success. While the Irish National party leaders did not take part in the welcome, feeling they could not identify with demonstrations “to a ruler who, whatever her own personal feelings, was the representative of a power which had of late only made itself known in Ireland by the enforcement of exceptional penal laws,” there was “no hostile feeling to the Queen in person among the whole Irish population.” The visit “may, under all the circumstances, be regarded as a success,” creating throughout the country “a common and sincere desire that the Queen might again come to Ireland” [source: mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol2].
Final months (1900–1901)
In the early months of 1901, the opening of the new century was “clouded by a national sorrow altogether exceptional, alike in its intensity and in its diffusion.” The Queen’s “keen and watchful sympathy with the joys and sorrows, the cares and the hopes of all parts of” the Empire were “as vividly realised in the first few days of the new age as at any former period in her prolonged and gloriously eventful reign.” In a brief message of “characteristic simplicity and directness,” she conveyed through Lord Hopetoun her “heartfelt interest” in the inauguration of the Australian Commonwealth on 1 January 1901, and her “earnest wish that, under Divine Providence, it might ensure the increased prosperity and well-being of her loyal and beloved subjects in Australia” [source: annual-register-1901].
During 1900, the intensity of her participation in the South African anxieties of the nation, “the pains she took to show herself on many occasions to large numbers of the people, and the spirit in which she conceived” her role, further enhanced the hold she possessed upon the reverence and affection of her people [source: annual-register-1901].
In the closing weeks of her life, Lord Roberts, returning from South Africa, visited the Queen at Osborne, and she conferred upon him an earldom and the Order of the Garter [source: annual-register-1901].
Illness and death (January 1901)
The German Emperor travelled from the celebrations of the two-hundredth anniversary of the foundation of the Prussian Monarchy “as quickly as possible to reach the bedside of his Royal grandmother at Osborne.” The whole civilised world “seemed, and indeed was, united with the British race in their passionate craving for the preservation of the life of the venerable Monarch, whose influence was universally recognised as having been directed for sixty years and more, with a single eye, to the good of her own vast dominions, and through them to that of mankind at large.” The “slight rally” was not maintained. By four o’clock on Tuesday afternoon, 22 January, the Queen was announced to be sinking, having earlier in the day recognised the several members of her family, including the German Emperor, and at half-past six that evening she passed away [source: annual-register-1901].
“It is quite impossible to exaggerate the sense of bereavement which oppressed the whole British nation and Empire. To her subjects of every rank Queen Victoria’s death meant the removal of what had appeared an essential feature in the framework of life.” The feeling of forlornness which pervaded the country in its diffusion and depth was “of a kind such as has not been known in England since the death of King Alfred a thousand years before.” A beneficent and inspiring presence had disappeared, “one which seemed to come nearer to the British people of every grade individually and in their families than any personality outside their own immediate circles” [source: annual-register-1901].
The funeral pageant
The Queen’s body lay at Osborne, then was taken by gun-carriage to Trinity Pier at Cowes, placed aboard the Alberta, which slowly steamed through an avenue of British and foreign men-of-war to Portsmouth Harbour. The body was conveyed by train to London, then on a khaki-coloured gun-carriage in a great procession “by Buckingham Palace, St. James’s Street, Piccadilly and Hyde Park to Paddington,” lined by over 30,000 troops, with a column “representative of every branch of the land and sea forces of the Crown” stretching a mile or more. Behind the coffin rode the King in field-marshal’s uniform, with the German Emperor on his right. From Paddington the body was conveyed to Windsor, and the funeral service performed in St. George’s Chapel [source: annual-register-1901].
Accession of King Edward VII
The day after the Queen’s death, the King left Osborne for London, held his first Council at St. James’s Palace, and a proclamation was approved declaring the accession of King Edward VII, bearing ninety-one signatures. The King delivered a declaration: “My first and melancholy duty is to announce to you the death of my beloved mother the Queen… I need hardly say that my constant endeavour will be always to walk in her footsteps” [source: annual-register-1901].
Tributes
President McKinley of the United States ordered the flag on the White House half-masted and addressed a telegram expressing “the profound sorrow” with which the President had received the death of her Majesty the Queen, “whose noble life and beneficent influence have promoted peace and won the affection of the world” [source: annual-register-1901].
Ex-President Harrison of the United States affirmed that “no other death could have excited such general sorrow” [source: annual-register-1901].
Lord Salisbury, the Prime Minister, moving an address in the House of Lords, said the late Queen reigned “by sheer force of character and by the lovableness of her disposition over the hearts of her subjects, and exercised a greater influence in moulding their destinies than she could have done even if she had been invested with the most despotic power. She had been a great instance of government by example, by esteem, and by love.” As a Constitutional Monarch, “her Majesty always maintained and practised a rigorous supervision over public affairs, giving to her Ministers her frank advice, and warning them of danger if she saw there was danger ahead. She had an extraordinary power of divining what her people, and especially, Lord Salisbury thought, those of the middle classes, would think. Yet she never adhered to her own conception obstinately, but, on the contrary, she was full of concession and consideration.” Lord Salisbury concluded that future historians “will look to the Queen’s reign as the boundary which separates the two states of England” and recognise “that we have undergone” great change “so peaceably, so easily, and with so much prosperity and success” [source: annual-register-1901].
Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman alluded to “a certain homely sincerity of character and life and purpose” in Queen Victoria “which, amid all the pomp and dignity of her august position, seemed to make the whole world kin.” Between the Queen and her people existed “a friendly, tender, almost familiar mutual understanding, which it is almost impossible to put into words.” He held the Queen’s reign to have been “the most beneficent that had been seen in any nation and in any age of the world” [source: annual-register-1901].
Lord Rosebery said: “Probably every subject in Great Britain realises that he has lost his greatest and his best friend. But they do not understand of what enormous weight in the councils of the world we are deprived by the death of our late Sovereign. She gave to the councils of Great Britain an advantage which no talents, no brilliancy, no genius, could supply. She had reigned for sixty-three years. For sixty-three years she had known all that was to be known about the political condition of her country. For sixty-three years she had been in communication” [source: annual-register-1901].
The King’s message to Parliament stated: “Her devotion to the welfare of her country and her people and her wise and beneficent rule during the sixty-four years of her glorious reign will ever be held in affectionate memory by her loyal and devoted subjects throughout the dominions of the British Empire” [source: annual-register-1901].
Imperial and worldwide mourning
Within the English-speaking parts of the British Empire, grief manifested was of the profoundest quality. “Reverent devotion to the person of the Queen had been one of the main welding influences by which the self-governing Colonies, as they grew in population, wealth and importance, were drawn into increasingly close touch with the mother country.” Remarkable also were manifestations of respectful sorrow exhibited “by the various non-British communities within the allegiance of the British Crown. Certain it is that among the French Canadians, among the Cape Dutch, and even the Boer prisoners, among the peoples of India, of the most diverse creeds and races, among the Maoris of New Zealand, and many other tribes of Asiatic, African and Polynesian blood, the signs of mourning bore every mark of genuineness.” “One pulse of sorrow seemed to be uniting the whole Empire” [source: annual-register-1901].
