events/armistice-1918.title: The Armistice (1918)
events/armistice-1918.content:
The Armistice (1918)
The armistice that ended the Great War on the Western Front was signed at 5 a.m. on Monday, 11 November 1918, and came into force at 11 a.m. French time the same day. It closed the continuous Allied advance that had run from Foch’s counter-stroke of 18 July and Rawlinson’s breakthrough of 8 August — the Allied counter-offensive that reversed the German Spring Offensive — and imposed terms which the Annual Register judged tantamount to complete surrender. Germany was defeated and surrendered; the surrender was not quite unconditional, being framed on President Wilson’s Fourteen Points with two Allied qualifications, but the German Government did not negotiate as equals. At home the signal was the sound of maroons over London; for the British army the last act of the war was the Canadian entry into Mons and, as the Register records, shots fired by King Edward’s Horse a few minutes before eleven. The Coalition under Lloyd George turned at once to demobilisation, Rhine occupation, and the December “coupon” election under the franchise of the Representation of the People Act.
Approach to Surrender
The capitulation of Bulgaria and Turkey, and the surrender of the Austro-Hungarian Government together with the dissolution of the Dual Monarchy, caused the German Government — now led by Prince Max of Baden — to decide to accept a peace on the lines of President Wilson’s Fourteen Points and to seek an armistice on that basis. The German Government inquired of the American Government whether the European Allies also agreed to accept the Fourteen Points as a basis of peace. On 4 November it was announced on behalf of Great Britain, France, and Italy that those Powers accepted the Fourteen Points subject to a reservation on the so-called “freedom of the seas” and to a second reservation on exacting reparation from Germany for damage done in invaded territory. With these two qualifications, therefore, President Wilson’s dicta were formally accepted by all parties as the basis of the future treaty of peace. This point having been settled, it only remained to arrange the armistice.
The terms were decided by the Associated Governments and communicated to Marshal Foch and Admiral Sir Rosslyn Wemyss, who were authorised to convey them to the Germans. The Register is explicit that the Allies could have enforced unconditional surrender within a few months, probably within a few weeks, but did not deem it necessary to incur the extra sacrifice of life, since the terms Germany was already willing to accept — the Wilson policy with the two qualifications — provided the foundation for a just and enduring peace.
The German Delegation and Foch’s Terms
A German delegation, headed by Herr Erzberger and General von Gündell, approached the French lines on 7 November. They were conducted through the French lines, and on the following day they formally applied for an armistice from Marshal Foch. The latter read out the terms which had been drawn up, and the Germans were given seventy-two hours in which to accept or reject them — the Chronicle of Events recording that the conditions were to be accepted by 11 a.m. on 11 November. Herr Erzberger declared himself astonished at their severity and asked to be allowed to communicate with the German headquarters, which were then at Spa. The member of the delegation used as courier, Captain Helldorf, was delayed on his journey to Spa by a misunderstanding on the part of the German High Command regarding arrangements for a cease-fire along the route he was to travel; hence the armistice was not actually signed until 5 a.m. on Monday, 11 November. It came into force at 11 a.m. (French time) on that day.
Before that hour Canadian troops captured the town of Mons, so that, from the British point of view, the war may be said to have ended at the spot where it began. In the meantime it was announced on 9 November that the Emperor William had abdicated. Prince Max of Baden issued a decree stating that the Kaiser had abdicated; Herr Ebert became Imperial Chancellor in place of Prince Max. On most parts of the front fighting continued during the six hours’ interval between the signing of the armistice and the moment at which it came into operation. It was said that the last shots of the war were fired by a troop of King Edward’s Horse, who were proceeding to capture a field-gun a few minutes before 11 o’clock. They shot two of the gun crew and were about to rush the gun when the officer in charge, watch in hand, stopped the operation — for it was 11 o’clock.
Terms: Military, Territorial, Naval
The terms of the armistice, given in full in the Register’s Public Documents, stipulated for the immediate evacuation of the invaded territories — Belgium, France, Luxemburg, and (the Register notes) Alsace-Lorraine — and for the surrender by the Germans of 5,000 guns (2,500 heavy and 2,500 field), 30,000 machine-guns, 3,000 flame-throwers, and 2,000 aeroplanes. Further, all Germany west of the Rhine was to be evacuated in thirty-one days, and the principal bridge-heads at Mainz, Coblenz, and Cologne were to be occupied by the Associated Powers. The naval conditions included the surrender of all submarines, fifty destroyers, eight light cruisers, six battle-cruisers, and ten battleships. The duration of the armistice was to be thirty-six days, but provision was made for possible (and probable) extension.
It will be seen that the terms imposed were tantamount to complete surrender. The victory was complete. Germany was defeated and surrendered. It was true, however, that the surrender was not quite unconditional. The German Government did not in any sense enter into negotiations as equals — they surrendered; but they surrendered not unconditionally, but to certain terms: President Wilson’s Fourteen Points, with two qualifications. Newbolt’s naval history underlines the same point from the sea: the naval clauses stripped Germany of the means of renewing submarine or surface war and transferred the High Seas Fleet into Allied custody pending the peace treaty — the consummation of command of the sea that had constrained Central Europe throughout the war.
11 November in London: Maroons and the Lord Mayor’s Banquet
At 11 in the morning on Monday, 11 November, London was stirred by the sound of maroons. It was the long-expected signal that Germany had signed the armistice terms. The announcement had been awaited all the previous week, and even as late as Saturday evening (9 November) at the Lord Mayor’s banquet Lloyd George, one of the principal speakers, commenced his speech by saying he had no news for them. The Chronicle records that at that same banquet the Prime Minister announced the abdication of the Kaiser. The Lord Mayor’s Show on 9 November had itself been a pageant of the nation’s war effort — naval and military detachments, Women’s Auxiliary Corps, tanks, captured guns, colonial and Allied troops — celebrated in accordance with time-honoured custom while the German plenipotentiaries were already inside the French lines.
The Register’s English History chapter “Peace” opens on the maroons and the public recognition that the long struggle was over. The same hours saw the last naval loss of the war recorded in the Chronicle: H.M.S. Britannia torpedoed in the western entrance to Gibraltar Straits on 9 November, thirty-nine officers and 673 men being saved. On the front, Maubeuge had fallen to the Guards and the 62nd Division on 8 November; Sedan had been occupied by the Americans on the 6th; Valenciennes by the British on the 3rd. Hostilities ceased on all fronts at 11 a.m. on the 11th.
Preceding Armistices: Bulgaria, Turkey, Austria-Hungary
The German armistice was the last of a chain. Bulgaria, after the Salonika offensive of mid-September and the French entry into Uskub on 29 September, applied to General Franchet d’Esperey; the armistice was granted on severe terms — immediate evacuation of Greek and Serbian territory, demobilisation, surrender of arms, munitions, vehicles, and horses, restitution of Greek Fourth Army Corps material, and the treatment as prisoners of Bulgarian troops of the Eleventh German Army north and west of Uskub. King Ferdinand abdicated and retired to Germany; the Crown Prince Boris became King.
Turkey followed after the fall of Bulgaria. In mid-October Taalat and Enver resigned; Izzet Pasha became Grand Vizier and immediately entered into negotiations for an armistice, utilising General Townshend (the hero of Kut) as intermediary in the preliminary negotiations. Vice-Admiral Calthorpe acted for the Allied Powers. The armistice was signed at Mudros on 30 October and came into operation the following day; its terms provided for the opening of the Dardanelles and the occupation of the Bosporus forts. Calthorpe was appointed British Commissioner at Constantinople.
Austria-Hungary signed an armistice with General Diaz on 3 November; it came into operation at 3 p.m. on 4 November. Italian troops landed at Trieste on the 3rd. Between 24 October and 4 November the Allied armies on the Italian front — including Lord Cavan’s mixed Italian–British Tenth Army on the Piave — had taken 300,000 prisoners and 5,000 guns. The Dual Monarchy dissolved as it surrendered.
Aftermath into 1919
The conditions of the armistice were carried out in a quiet and orderly manner. The British occupied Cologne and Bonn; the Americans were stationed in Coblenz; the French took over Mainz. The British occupied the furthest points — the Cologne bridge-head — on 12 December, the river being formally crossed that day; on the following day the Americans crossed the Rhine at Coblenz.
The German warships were surrendered in batches, the first ships leaving the German ports for that purpose on 20 November and the remainder following during the next few days. The submarines surrendered off Harwich. The surface warships surrendered in the Forth and were then sent to Scapa Flow, where they were to remain until the treaty of peace decided their final fate — the naval counterpart, in Newbolt’s account, of the military occupation of the Rhine bridge-heads.
After the termination of hostilities certain provisional statistics of casualties were published. The total British (including Dominion and Indian) military casualties were given provisionally as 3,050,000. The total of “killed” reported up to 10 November was 658,704, but many soldiers reported “missing” were no doubt killed. The Admiralty report of total casualties was stated to be complete: officers and men together, 39,766 (dead 33,361; wounded 5,183; missing 47; prisoners 1,175). These totals included a certain number of merchant seamen serving temporarily in a naval capacity. In addition, no fewer than 14,661 officers and men of the mercantile marine lost their lives through enemy action whilst following their ordinary vocations, and 3,295 were captured and held as prisoners of war. A provisional estimate of German casualties published in December stated that the dead numbered 1,600,000 and the total casualties 6,385,000, with wounded given as over 4,000,000.
Politically the Armistice opened the path to the Peace Conference and to the domestic settlement of 1919. The Coalition manifesto and the December election, fought on the enlarged register of the Representation of the People Act, translated military victory into a parliamentary majority pledged to “make Germany pay” and to reconstruct at home. The thirty-six-day armistice was extended as expected; the formal treaty of peace, and the fate of the fleet at Scapa, belonged to the following year. For Britain the war that had opened in 1914 closed under Haig’s armies on the old Mons ground, under Foch’s supreme command, and under a Coalition whose naval and economic grip — command of the sea — the Register and Newbolt alike treat as the condition of the land surrender of 11 November.

events/boer-war.title: The Boer War (1899–1902)
events/boer-war.content:
The Boer War (1899–1902)
The South African War, commonly called the Boer War, was the struggle between the British Empire and the two Dutch republics — the South African Republic (Transvaal) and the Orange Free State — arising from the collision of imperial expansion with Boer resistance. The war passed through three distinct phases: a conventional campaign in which the Boers besieged British garrisons and inflicted a series of shocking defeats; a British counter-offensive that captured the republican capitals and led to the formal annexation of both territories; and a protracted guerrilla struggle that dragged on for nearly two years more before the Treaty of Vereeniging brought peace in May 1902.
Origins and Prelude
The roots of the conflict lay in the long encounter between the British Empire and the Boers — descendants of Dutch Protestants and French Huguenot exiles who had settled in South Africa generations before. The Boers had repeatedly moved their settlements inland to escape British authority, establishing themselves in the Transvaal and the Orange Free State. As McCarthy observes, the Boer “lives apart and unto himself… His one great terror was of English domination. Wherever he set up for himself, it seemed to him that England was determined to follow him, to surround him, and to prevent him from carrying on the sort of life that suited him best.”
The discovery of gold in the Transvaal transformed this encounter into a crisis. Adventurers and settlers from all over the world — the Uitlanders, or Outlanders — flooded into the region, rapidly outnumbering the Boer population even within the Transvaal itself. The Outlanders demanded citizenship rights and a voice in the government of the Republic, but President Paul Kruger, a Boer of the Boers — “undoubtedly a man of great ability, of absolute integrity, firm as a rock” — regarded them with deep suspicion, identifying their demands with English designs on the country.
The antagonism was personified in two great figures. Paul Kruger stood for the old Boer order — religious, stubborn, self-sufficient. On the other side stood Cecil Rhodes — “above all things an adventurer by temperament and by career” — who had risen to become Prime Minister of Cape Colony, founder of the Chartered Company, and the driving force behind British expansion in southern Africa. “Sooner or later,” writes McCarthy, “the influence of President Kruger and the influence of Mr. Cecil Rhodes must come into collision.”
The Jameson Raid (1895)
On 29 December 1895, Dr. Leander Starr Jameson, the administrator of the Chartered Company in South Africa, led a raid from Bechuanaland across the Transvaal frontier with the avowed purpose of compelling President Kruger to do justice to the Outlanders’ claims. A small force of mounted men, including some officers in regular British service, crossed into the Transvaal. The British Government, through the High Commissioner Sir Hercules Robinson, telegraphed instructions to stop the invasion; Jameson refused and pressed on. He was swiftly defeated by Boer forces, and he and his officers were taken prisoner.
President Kruger acted with “wise clemency” — the lives of all the invaders were spared, and the leaders were sent to England for trial. Jameson became for a time a popular hero among certain classes in England, though a Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry later found that Cecil Rhodes, in his capacity as controller of the British South Africa Company, De Beers Consolidated Mines, and the Gold Fields of South Africa, “directed and controlled the combination which rendered such a proceeding as the Jameson Raid possible.”
The Raid had far-reaching consequences. The German Emperor Wilhelm II sent a telegram of congratulation to President Kruger on the defeat of the raiders — a message widely regarded in England as “a compliment to President Kruger and a snub to the English Government.” This Kruger Telegram inflamed Anglo-German relations and became a lasting symbol of German hostility.
The Road to War (1896–1899)
After the Raid, relations between Britain and the Transvaal worsened steadily. In April 1897 the two governments were on the verge of war. Sir Alfred Milner was sent out as High Commissioner; his estimate of the situation led him to recommend a strong policy. Milner and Kruger met at Bloemfontein at the close of May 1899 to discuss the Outlander franchise. Kruger offered some concessions but would not accept the terms Milner demanded. The Bloemfontein Conference broke up without agreement.
Negotiations continued through the summer of 1899. Joseph Chamberlain, the Colonial Secretary, pressed for a five-year franchise for the Outlanders. Kruger ultimately withdrew his qualified offer and reverted to his original seven-year residence requirement. Simultaneously, Boer troops began massing along the frontier; Outlanders started leaving the Transvaal; and the Boer government stopped trains and confiscated gold belonging to Outlander capitalists.
On 9 October 1899, the Transvaal issued an ultimatum demanding that British troops be withdrawn from the borders. The British government rejected the terms, and on 12 October 1899 war was declared.
Conventional Phase (1899–1900)
The war opened with a general advance of the Boer forces. They invaded Natal and laid siege to the British garrisons at Ladysmith, Mafeking, and Kimberley. The British public, McCarthy records, expected a short, sharp campaign: “The general impression amongst these was that the war would be very short, not very sharp, and promptly decisive.” This confidence was founded on a profound misunderstanding of the enemy. The Dutch Boers were “descended from the race who held out so long against Spain” and had shown at Majuba Hill (1881) that “in fighting capacity they were not unworthy of their heroic Dutch ancestors.”
General Sir Redvers Buller arrived in Natal on 25 November 1899. In December, Lord Roberts was appointed Commander-in-Chief in South Africa, with Lord Kitchener as his Chief of Staff; Buller remained in command of the Natal Army, with Sir Charles Warren leading the Fifth Division under him.
Black Week (December 1899)
The week of 10–17 December 1899 became known as “Black Week” for the British. At Stormberg, at Magersfontein, and at Colenso, the British suffered three consecutive defeats in the space of a few days. At Colenso on 15 December, Buller’s attempt to cross the Tugela River failed disastrously; Lord Roberts’s son was mortally wounded while trying to save the guns. The Boers, fighting on ground they knew, from behind rocks with rifles they had used since boyhood, proved far more formidable than the British command had anticipated. As McCarthy acknowledges, “it very soon became apparent that the Boers, however limited their numbers, were well prepared for the war, and that they were animated by a spirit of desperate resistance.”
The British Counter-Offensive
The British responded by mobilising on a massive scale. The obstacles — “rivers and mountain ranges, and the apparently limitless stretches of country” — were such as could be overcome only by commanders of the highest gifts. Lord Roberts and Lord Kitchener reorganised the British forces and launched a counter-offensive. Cronje’s army was surrounded and forced to surrender at Paardeberg on 27 February 1900. On 13 April Roberts entered Bloemfontein, the capital of the Orange Free State.
Relief of the Besieged Towns
The sieges of Ladysmith, Kimberley, and Mafeking became the focus of intense public emotion in Britain. When the relief of Ladysmith and, above all, the relief of Mafeking were “successfully and brilliantly accomplished by the British forces, there was an outburst of national enthusiasm which could not have been exceeded if the success on the British side had been that of another Waterloo.” The word “Mafeking” itself entered the English language as a term for exuberant patriotic celebration.
Annexation of the Transvaal and Orange Free State
On 28 May 1900, the Orange Free State was formally annexed and renamed the Orange River Colony. At the end of the same month, President Kruger fled from Pretoria. Lord Roberts entered Pretoria and hoisted the British flag there on 5 June 1900. The Transvaal was also annexed to the British Crown.
A very general impression prevailed in England that the war was substantially at an end. “Yet the war was by no means at an end,” McCarthy notes. “It was for the most part a guerilla warfare on the side of the Dutch and of the Orange Free State, and such a war might be carried on for an almost indefinite time even after all the strongholds of the invaded States had been occupied by the enemy.”
Guerrilla Phase (1900–1902)
After the capture of Pretoria, the war entered a new and more difficult phase. The Boer commandants, led by able and determined commanders — Louis Botha, Christiaan De Wet, and Koos de la Rey — dispersed into the vast countryside and carried on a mobile guerrilla war. “De Wet,” writes McCarthy, “had a positive genius for sudden surprises, unexpected attacks, and instantaneous disappearances, and had given immeasurable trouble to the British Commanders by the mere fact that they never knew where to have him.”
The Boers were ideally suited to this kind of warfare. “The Boers were men trained from their early boyhood to just that kind of work… The Boers had to make their living in great measure by the pursuit of game, and every one was trained to the use of the rifle.” The British forces, by contrast, included many new levies who had to learn a completely unfamiliar style of campaigning.
The guerrilla phase stretched across an area “nearly equal to the area of Continental Europe.” The British commanders adopted a strategy of relentless pursuit, building a network of blockhouses to control the countryside and restrict Boer movement. By 1902, Mr. Brodrick could report in Parliament that “the blockhouse system had had excellent results” — the safety of the railways was now practically secured, and large portions of the country had been freed from the ravages of war. The remaining Boer forces in the field — perhaps 2,000 men each under De Wet, Botha, and Delarey — were steadily pressured by Kitchener’s columns.
Concentration Camps
As the guerrilla war continued, Lord Kitchener adopted a policy of clearing the countryside. Farms were destroyed to deny supplies to the Boer commandos, and the women and children of the Boer population — as well as black Africans — were gathered into camps established along the railway lines. These were originally described as “places of refuge for those willing to submit,” to which “burghers may take themselves, their families, and their stock for protection.”
This was, as the Annual Register records, “the beginning of the concentration camps, of the conditions of life and the mortality in which much was to be heard later in the year.” Terrible conditions in the camps led to a humanitarian outcry. In the House of Commons debate of June 1901, the camps were denounced as “an outrage against humanity.” Emily Hobhouse’s narrative of conditions in the camps moved public opinion profoundly. Campbell-Bannerman, the Liberal leader, denounced the “barbarous” system of the concentration camps, and the issue became one of the great political controversies of the war. The camps remained a deeply controversial aspect of Kitchener’s command, with high mortality rates from disease, particularly among children.
Peace and Aftermath
The Treaty of Vereeniging
By the spring of 1902, the Boer leadership recognised that further resistance was hopeless. The Boer “Governments” — the acting government of the Transvaal under Schalk Burger and the Orange Free State government under President Steyn — entered into negotiations with Lord Kitchener and Lord Milner. A peace conference was held on 15–16 May 1902 at Vereeniging, where sixty delegates from the two republics gathered under safe-conduct from the British military authorities.
The Boer delegates initially sought to preserve some form of independence — proposing a British protectorate with the surrender of foreign relations — but Kitchener and Milner refused to negotiate on any basis that admitted the question of independence. The British terms, as revised by Mr. Chamberlain, were presented for a “Yes” or “No” vote.
The terms of surrender were signed at Pretoria on 31 May 1902 by Lord Kitchener and Lord Milner on behalf of the British Government, and by the representatives of the two Boer Governments — including Generals Botha, Delarey, and De Wet. The terms included: the absorption of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State into the British Empire; no death penalty for Boers who had fought for their country; the use of the Dutch language in law courts where necessary; and a liberal grant of £3,000,000 and loans to enable Boer farmers to re-establish themselves.
The End of the War
When the terms were signed, Lord Kitchener congratulated the Boers on “the stout and gallant struggle they had made” and welcomed them in their position as citizens of the British Empire. General De Wet, in his later book Three Years’ War, dedicated the volume “To my fellow-subjects of the British Empire.” The thanks of the King and Parliament were voted to the army, navy, Indian and Colonial forces, and to Lord Kitchener, who “had dealt with ninety mobile Boer columns over an area nearly as large as the European Continent.” Kitchener sailed for England on 23 June 1902, and the three years’ war was at an end.
Hobson: measure and type
J. A. Hobson’s Imperialism: A Study, dated August 1902, does not narrate the campaigns recorded above by McCarthy, the Annual Register, and Langer. It uses South Africa as a measure of the new Imperialism and as a type of costly annexation. “Quibbles about the modern meaning of the term Imperialism are best resolved by reference to concrete facts in the history of the last thirty years.” His compiled table for 1884–1900 includes Rhodesia under the British South Africa Charter (1889: 750,000 square miles) and the Transvaal and Orange River Colony (1900: 119,139 and 48,826 square miles). For so small a nation to add in one generation some 4,754,000 square miles is “a historical fact of great significance”; one-third of the Empire by area has been acquired within that generation. The new lands are tropical or sub-tropical, thinly settled by whites, held by protectorate, charter, or paramountcy rather than genuine colonisation. “No substantial settlement of Britons is taking place upon any of the areas of the Empire acquired since 1870, excepting the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony.”
If the Imperialism of the last three decades is “clearly condemned as a business policy” — “enormous expense” for “a small, bad, unsafe increase of markets” — it remains “rational enough from the standpoint of certain classes.” Financiers who gained from the Jameson Raid recouped themselves, in his account, by war contracts and by “freezing out” smaller Transvaal interests; they “are essentially parasites upon patriotism.” Hicks-Beach estimated the wars in South Africa and China in the three years to 31 March 1902 at £165,034,000, of which some £119,614,000 was added to the Debt. “The enormous expenditure upon the South African war” would be followed by a demand for a large permanent increase of army and navy outlay. “The South African war, openly fomented by gold speculators for their private purposes, will rank in history as a leading case of this usurpation of nationalism.” The “abnormally rapid swelling of financial needs due to the disastrous policy in South Africa” would, he thought, precipitate an Imperial Zollverein dressed as federation, exploiting colonial loyalty shown in the war. This diagnosis sits beside, and does not replace, Langer’s diplomatic origins and McCarthy’s military narrative.
Consequences
The war had profound consequences for the British Empire. The Canadian and Australian colonies had rendered “splendid service” throughout the conflict, and the war brought about “closer and more cordial relations between the Colonies and the mother country” — a significant step on the road toward Imperial federation and Dominion status.
But the war also left deep scars. Its policy “and many of its conditions” had provoked “serious doubts and misgivings” among many Englishmen. The concentration camps controversy, the immense cost in blood and treasure — at its peak the war cost £5,500,000 a month — and the revelation of British military unpreparedness all made the Boer War a turning point in British politics and military reform. The ex-President Kruger and President Steyn went into exile; the Boer leaders Botha and De Wet later visited England, where they were received by King Edward VII and presented by Lord Kitchener to Mr. Chamberlain at Southampton in August 1902, though they subsequently endeavoured in correspondence to reopen various points of the Vereeniging Agreement, particularly the amnesty for Cape rebels.

events/dogger-bank-1915.title: The Dogger Bank Action (24 January 1915)
events/dogger-bank-1915.content:
The Dogger Bank Action (24 January 1915)
On the morning of Sunday, 24 January 1915, in the grey waters of the North Sea about the Dogger Bank, the battle-cruiser force of Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty brought Rear-Admiral Hipper’s German battle cruisers to action. The chase that followed was the first fleet engagement in which Dreadnought-type capital ships fought one another with heavy guns at long range. The armoured cruiser Blücher was sunk; the German battle cruisers, damaged and on fire, escaped into their own waters; Beatty’s flagship Lion was crippled and had to be towed home. The action confirmed the new distribution of the Grand Fleet after the Yorkshire coast raid of December 1914, reduced the chance of another military raid on the English coast, and, four days later, stood behind the final decision to attack the Dardanelles. It was a sharp episode in the long contest for command-of-the-sea that had run from the Anglo-German naval race into the war, and a dress-rehearsal for the greater meeting of battle cruisers that would come at jutland.
After Scarborough: Redistribution and Temptation
The German raid on the Yorkshire coast in mid-December 1914 had left the British public angry and the Admiralty restless. Hipper’s battle cruisers — Seydlitz, Moltke, Von der Tann, Derfflinger, and the armoured cruiser Blücher — had struck and withdrawn; Ingenohl had stretched the Kaiser’s permission by bringing out battle squadrons in support. Corbett records the post-Christmas restlessness in German ports and the expectation that the apparent impunity of the Yorkshire raid would tempt a repeat.
On the British side the Home Fleets had been redistributed. After the loss of the Bulwark, Beatty had been moved from Cromarty to Rosyth with the 3rd Battle Squadron and 3rd Cruiser Squadron. Jellicoe, after the loss of the Formidable and the disabling of the Conqueror in collision with the Monarch, could count only some eighteen Dreadnoughts against seventeen German; Beatty had five battle cruisers against Hipper’s four (Queen Mary was docking; Invincible was preparing for distant service). Ship for ship the British were more powerful — Lion, Tiger, and Princess Royal with 13.5-inch guns against Derfflinger’s 12-inch and Seydlitz and Moltke’s 11-inch; New Zealand and Indomitable with 12-inch against Blücher’s 8.2-inch. The intercepting dispositions were designed so that Hipper should not get back unscathed.
Intelligence and the Sortie of 23–24 January
On 23 January intelligence set the whole North Sea machinery in motion. A coastal raid was feared. The German object, as later claimed, was to clear the Dogger Bank of fishing vessels and patrols used for observation. Hipper put to sea with Seydlitz (flag), Moltke, Derfflinger, and Blücher, the light cruisers Stralsund, Rostock, Kolberg, and Graudenz, and a strong destroyer force.
Early on the morning of the 24th, about fourteen miles east-south-east of Beatty’s battle-cruiser squadron, a patrolling flotilla of British destroyers sighted the German force steering westward, apparently making for the English coast. As soon as they were discovered they turned and made for home. Pursuit was ordered at once. Beatty’s squadron consisted of Lion, Tiger, Princess Royal, New Zealand, and Indomitable. The Germans had Derfflinger, Seydlitz, Moltke, and Blücher. With the possible exception of Derfflinger, the British ships could attain a somewhat higher speed. After working up to 28 and 29 knots they began to fire at about 18,000 yards and to hit at about 17,000.
The Chase and the Gun Action
Lion made her first hit on Blücher, the fourth ship in the German line. Tiger opened fire; the range of the leading ship was 17,500 yards at 9.35 a.m. New Zealand came within range of Blücher, which had already dropped somewhat astern. By about 9.45 the situation was clear: Blücher showed signs of having suffered severely; the leading German ship and No. 3 were also on fire. Lion engaged No. 1, Princess Royal No. 3, New Zealand No. 4; Tiger, second in the British line, fired first at their No. 1 and, when interfered with by smoke, at their No. 4.
The enemy destroyers emitted vast columns of smoke to screen the battle cruisers. Under cover of that smoke the German heavy ships appeared to alter course northward to open the range; the rear ships hauled out on the port quarter of their leader. Beatty ordered the battle cruisers to form a line of bearing north-north-west and to proceed at utmost speed. When the German destroyers showed signs of an attack, Lion and Tiger opened fire on them and drove them back. The British light cruisers held an excellent position on the port quarter of the enemy line, able to observe, keep touch, or fall on any ship that dropped out.
At 10.48 Blücher, well astern, hauled out to port, steering north with a heavy list, on fire, and apparently defeated. Beatty ordered Indomitable to attack the enemy breaking northward. At 10.54 submarines were reported on the starboard bow; Beatty personally observed the wash of a periscope and turned to port. At 11.03 an injury to Lion was reported as incapable of immediate repair — a shot had damaged a feed-tank and stopped the port engine. He directed Lion to shape course north-west. At about 11.20 he called the destroyer Attack alongside, shifted his flag to her at about 11.35, and raced to rejoin the squadron.
Signals, the Turn on Blücher, and Hipper’s Escape
The crucial half-hour after Lion was disabled decided the fate of the German battle cruisers. Lion’s wireless was out of action; she had only two signal halyards left. Beatty, dropping astern and no longer able to act as guide, hoisted two short signals: first, “Attack the enemy’s rear”; second, Nelson’s last word at Trafalgar, “Keep closer to the enemy.” The wind blew the flags end-on to the other three battle cruisers. The first signal seems to have been hoisted before the compass signal “Course N.E.” had been hauled down. Rear-Admiral Moore, and the Tiger and Indomitable with him, concluded that the Chief was ordering the squadron to “attack the enemy’s rear bearing N.E.” — the meaning of the flag groups as they were seen and logged. The final signal, “Keep closer to the enemy,” was taken in by none of the battle cruisers.
Blücher bore about north-east from New Zealand. She was therefore taken as the objective indicated by the eight-point turn and the signals. Tiger and Princess Royal ceased firing on Derfflinger and Moltke and edged off to starboard to circle round Blücher. The German battle-cruiser squadron, half beaten as it was, was left alone. The luck that had snatched the Germans from the British grasp at the time of the Scarborough raid stood by them again.
Moore had no difficulty in finishing Blücher. Commodore Goodenough’s light cruisers were hitting her at 14,000 yards; she could fire with only two turrets. A Zeppelin that tried to intervene was driven off. Arethusa and the “M” class destroyers closed; Meteor was hit forward and put out of action, but the others claimed hits, and Arethusa fired two torpedoes that were claimed to have taken effect. The battle cruisers poured in salvoes until Blücher was a mass of smoke and flame. For three hours she had been the focus of an overwhelming concentration of fire and had never ceased to reply — an example of discipline and fighting spirit that Corbett places among the rarest in naval war. At 11.45 Commodore Tyrwhitt signalled that she appeared to have struck. Moore ceased fire and turned to resume the chase, but the three flying battle cruisers were now over twelve miles away and still apparently doing their full 25 knots. Two hours would be needed to get into effective range again; by then they would be close to Heligoland. A signal had been intercepted that the High Seas Fleet was coming out. Nothing could be got from Lion. Moore decided to retire in her direction and leave the light cruisers to rescue survivors.
Tyrwhitt closed the burning ship in Arethusa. She was in a pitiable condition — upper works wrecked, fires raging between decks through enormous shot-holes, a heavy list to port, some three hundred men clustered on the upper deck and net shelves. At 12.10, as Arethusa got within a hundred yards, Blücher suddenly capsized, floated a few minutes bottom upwards, and disappeared. With the help of the destroyers 260 survivors were picked up. More might have been saved, but a seaplane came up and began to bomb the rescuers; it was driven off by gunfire, not before killing some of the men still in the water. A Zeppelin approached on a similar errand. Tyrwhitt had to call off boats and destroyers. Corbett calls the attack on the rescuers a grave violation of the old courtesies of war upon the sea.
Beatty Rejoins; Lion Towed Home
Of all this Beatty knew nothing while he raced in Attack. When at noon he came in sight of the squadron they were coming back towards him. He transferred his flag to Princess Royal about 12.20. Captain Brock reported that Blücher had been sunk and that the enemy battle cruisers had continued eastward in a considerably damaged condition; a Zeppelin and a seaplane had tried to bomb the vessels rescuing Blücher’s survivors. Beatty’s first hope was that at least one of the three flying ships had been sunk; even before he learned that all three had been suffered to carry on homewards he signalled to turn after them. Further inquiry convinced him that no more could be done. The crucial half-hour had been missed. He re-formed the squadron and went back to cover Lion. Indomitable took her in tow by 5 p.m. under difficult circumstances; the good seamanship of both captains brought the flagship into port. No British ship had been sunk. Casualties were few. In Berlin it was claimed for a time that a British battle-cruiser had been sunk; only gradually did the Germans recognise the scale of their reverse.
The Annual Register notes that Blücher, an armoured cruiser of 15,550 tons, was the largest vessel hitherto destroyed by gun-fire in naval warfare, and that the fight was of special interest as the first in which Dreadnoughts had taken part. Beatty reported two other enemy battle cruisers very heavily on fire and seriously damaged. Later in the session Mr. Churchill told the House that the action off the Dogger Bank had established the superiority of British guns to those of the Germans and shown that British shooting was at least as good; it had also shown that the Germans did not venture to fight when they were in a minority of four to five, and that if they had fought they would unquestionably have been destroyed.
Aftermath
Corbett judges that the action demonstrated the efficacy of the new distribution of the Grand Fleet and reduced the chances of another military raid on the British coast. The Kaiser, after Dogger Bank, tightened control over High Seas Fleet sorties. Four days later, on 28 January, the final decision was taken to attack the Dardanelles — Carden’s plan accepted though still unsettled, with a Salonica and Balkans alternative still live and a Greek reply of 27 January in play. The first phase of the naval war of 1915 would close only with the resignations of Fisher and Churchill and the formation of the Coalition Government in May; the Lusitania sinking of 7 May would overshadow the check at the Dardanelles. Dogger Bank itself remained a victory incomplete: Blücher gone, the German battle cruisers mauled but home, signalling confusion written into the lessons that Beatty and the battle-cruiser force would carry forward to jutland.
Chronology

events/easter-rising-1916.title: The Easter Rising (1916)
events/easter-rising-1916.content:
The Easter Rising (1916)
In the week after Easter 1916 a rising broke out in Dublin that the Annual Register ranked among the outstanding events of the year, with the two Military Service Acts and the later reconstruction of the Government. Armed men identified with the Sinn Fein movement seized the General Post Office and other public buildings, proclaimed an Irish Republic, and held the centre of the city against British troops until the last days of April. The rebellion was suppressed under martial law; its leaders were tried by court-martial and shot; Sir Roger Casement, landed from a German submarine on the eve of the outbreak, was later convicted of high treason and sentenced to death. The rising did not overturn British rule in Ireland, but it transformed the politics of irish-home-rule that had been suspended for the duration of the war after the Home Rule crisis of 1912–14, and it forced the Coalition under Mr. Asquith into a new and bitter Irish settlement debate.
Background: Home Rule Suspended and Sinn Fein
Before the outbreak of the Great War Ireland had stood on the edge of civil conflict over the third Home Rule Bill. The irish-home-rule-crisis had armed Ulster and the Nationalist volunteers alike; the Curragh incident and the gun-runnings had shown how thin was the line between constitutional agitation and force. When war came, the Home Rule Act was placed on the statute book but its operation was suspended for the duration. John Redmond pledged Nationalist support to the Empire; recruiting in Ireland became a test of that pledge.
By early 1916 another current was running. As early as 4 March The Times published an article drawing attention to the growth of the Sinn Fein movement and commenting on the neglect of the Government to take strong measures against the disaffection brewing in the country. Military authorities had already, by the middle of 1915, represented to the Government that their recruiting efforts were being frustrated by the hostile activities of Sinn Fein supporters. In February 1916 they pointed out on their own initiative the general danger of the situation; the warning, the Royal Commission later found, fell on unheeding ears. The Chief Secretary, Mr. Birrell, and the system of Irish executive government — a political Chief Secretary in the Cabinet, a largely ceremonial Lord-Lieutenant — would be held primarily responsible for the lawlessness that had been allowed to grow up unchecked.
Casement and the German Arms Ship
On the Tuesday after Easter the Secretary of the Admiralty announced that during the night of 20 April an attempt had been made to land arms and ammunition in Ireland by a vessel disguised as a neutral merchant ship but in reality a German auxiliary, acting in conjunction with a German submarine. The auxiliary was sunk and a number of prisoners were made, among them Sir Roger Casement, who had already acquired an unenviable notoriety since the outbreak of the war by endeavouring to seduce Irish prisoners in Germany from their loyalty to the British Crown. The attempt to land arms was evidently a preconcerted signal for a general rising.
Dublin, 24 April: Outbreak
On 24 April serious disturbances broke out in Dublin. A large body of men identified with the Sinn Feiners, mostly armed, occupied St. Stephen’s Green and took forcible possession of the Post Office, where they cut the telegraphic and telephonic wires. Houses were also occupied in Stephen’s Green, Sackville Street, Abbey Street, and along the quays. In the course of the day soldiers arrived from the Curragh, and fighting immediately began. The rebels made a half-hearted attack on Dublin Castle which was not pressed through. They held up troops on their way from barracks and fired on them from the windows of houses; by the following day they had been driven out of Stephen’s Green with a number of casualties, though they remained in occupation of various important buildings, including the Post Office, the City Hall, and the Law Courts.
A proclamation issued in the name of a “Provisional Government” announced that the new Irish Republic was a sovereign independent State. The signatories pledged their lives and the lives of their comrades in arms to the cause of its army, its welfare, and its exaltation among the nations. The Republic claimed the allegiance of every Irishman and Irishwoman, guaranteed religious and civil liberty, equal rights and equal opportunities to all citizens, and declared the intention of establishing a permanent national government representative of the whole people of Ireland and elected by the suffrages of all her men and women. Until success of arms made such a government possible, civil and military affairs were to be administered by the Provisional Government on whose behalf the proclamation was issued, signed by seven of its members.
Suppression and Martial Law
Reinforcements speedily arrived from Belfast and from England and established a cordon round the centre of the town on the north bank of the river, entirely enclosing the area of the rebellion. By 26 April Liberty Hall, the headquarters of the citizen army and formerly of Mr. Larkin, had been wholly or partially destroyed and occupied by the military. Field guns from the south bank of the Liffey and a gun from the patrol ship Helga attacked Liberty Hall; fires broke out in the Sackville Street quarter which the fire-brigade could not reach because it was fired on by the rebels. By that time the troops had suffered casualties to the extent of about nineteen killed and twenty-seven wounded. Risings of a far less serious character took place in other parts of Ireland — notably at Ardee in County Louth, and at Swords and Lusk near Dublin. On 25 April German warships again crossed the North Sea and bombarded Lowestoft and Yarmouth for about half an hour, doing very little damage; the purpose of the raid was no doubt to cause the British Government to hesitate before sending large numbers of troops over to Ireland.
On 27 April the situation seemed sufficiently serious to justify the Irish Executive in proclaiming martial law over the whole of Ireland. Sir John Maxwell left London that day with plenary powers over the whole country; the Irish Executive placed themselves at his disposal to carry out his instructions. In the Commons Mr. Butcher expressed the view that the Government were stamping out the rebellion with all possible vigour and promptitude. Sir Edward Carson affirmed his satisfaction and said he would gladly join with Mr. Redmond in everything that could be done to put down the rebels. Redmond himself asked leave to express, on behalf of the Nationalist party and, he believed, of the overwhelming majority of the people of Ireland, the feeling of detestation and horror with which they regarded the recent proceedings; he joined with Carson in the hope that no attempt would be made to use the rising as a political weapon against any party.
At midnight on 28–29 April an official communiqué described the progress of suppression. The organised forces of the rebels in Dublin were confined to a few localities, the principal one being the Sackville Street district where they had established their headquarters in the General Post Office. The cordon of troops was gradually drawn closer, though outside it there was not infrequent sniping from houses in various parts of the city.
Surrender
Owing to considerable opposition at barricades, especially in North King Street, it was not until 9 a.m. on 29 April that the Four Courts area was completely surrounded. Throughout that morning the squeezing out of the surrounded areas was vigorously proceeded with. Infantry were greatly assisted by a battery of field artillery under Major Hill, who used his guns against the buildings held by the rebels with such effect that a Red Cross nurse brought in a message from the rebel leader P. H. Pearse asking for terms. The reply was that only unconditional surrender would be accepted. At 2 p.m. Pearse surrendered himself unconditionally and wrote and signed notices ordering the various “Commandos” to surrender. During the evening the greater part of the rebels in the Sackville Street and Four Courts area did so.
Early on 30 April two Franciscan monks informed the military that the rebel leader MacDonagh, declining to accept Pearse’s orders, wished to negotiate. He too was told that only unconditional surrender would be accepted; at 3 p.m., when all preparation for an attack on Jacob’s Biscuit Factory (which he held) had been made, MacDonagh and his band surrendered. In the St. Stephen’s Green area Countess Markievicz and her band surrendered and were taken to the Castle. These surrenders practically ended the rebellion in the city of Dublin. Through the night of 30 April–1 May isolated rebels continued to snipe the troops; during 1 May they were gradually cleared out, and a systematic house-to-house search for rebels and arms proceeded in conjunction with the police. Disquieting reports had come from many counties — Dublin, Meath, Louth, Galway, Wexford, Clare, Kerry — and small detachments had been sent to reinforce exposed points.
Executions, Birrell, and Asquith
By 3 May three of the seven signatories of the Republican proclamation — P. H. Pearse, T. J. Clarke, and Thomas MacDonagh — had already been sentenced to death by court-martial and shot, and from day to day for some time afterwards further executions were announced. When the House of Commons was at last able to discuss the question at length, on 3 May, the sitting was chiefly devoted to Mr. Birrell’s apology for his share of responsibility. He confessed frankly that he had made an untrue estimate of the Sinn Fein movement — not of its character, numbers, localities, or frequent disloyalties, but of the possibility of disturbances of the kind that had broken out, of the mode of fighting pursued, and of the desperate folly displayed by the leaders and their dupes. As soon as the insurrection was over (on 1 May) he had placed his resignation in the hands of the Prime Minister, who had accepted it, “no other course being open to me or to him.” He had subordinated everything in order to maintain unbroken the front of Ireland towards the enemies of the Empire, and in that work he had been gallantly assisted by Mr. Redmond. The insurrection, he said, had been no Irish rebellion, and he hoped it would not be associated with past rebellions in the minds of the Irish people. The House listened with emotion.
Asquith, defending General Sir John Maxwell and the troops, reminded the House that only thirteen rebels had been executed. Apart from one execution for murder, it was only the leaders of the rising who had been subjected to the extreme penalty; two more such leaders were awaiting death, and that would complete the tale of the condemned insurrectionists. In any other case of murder there would be a public trial. He suggested that the rank and file would be “given an opportunity of redeeming what was in their case a venial and more or less pardonable error.” He announced his intention of going to Ireland that same evening to consult the civil and military authorities with a view to some arrangement for the future government of the country.
Casement’s Trial
Sir Roger Casement, whom the Annual Register calls the main instigator, was placed upon his trial in the civil courts. The preliminary hearing of the charge of high treason opened at Bow Street on 15 May; beside him in the dock was a soldier of the Royal Irish Rifles, Daniel Julian Bailey, alleged to have joined the “Irish Brigade” raised in Germany and to have accompanied Casement on the expedition to the coast of Kerry. The two were committed for trial on 17 May; a Grand Jury in the High Court found a true bill on the indictments of high treason. Casement’s trial began on 26 June. The indictment charged him with “adhering to the King’s enemies elsewhere than in the King’s Realm, to wit, in the Empire of Germany.” After a trial of four days he was convicted of high treason and sentenced to death. From the beginning there never could be any doubt as to his guilt, though he was defended with conspicuous ability by Serjeant A. M. Sullivan, K.C., of the Irish Bar. It was not denied that he had gone to Germany and that, with the connivance and assistance of the German authorities, he had endeavoured to seduce from their allegiance the King’s Irish soldiers who were prisoners of war.
Royal Commission and Political Aftermath
A Royal Commission inquired into the causes of the outbreak and into the conduct and degree of responsibility of the civil and military executive in Ireland. It found that the main cause of the rebellion appeared to be that lawlessness had been allowed to grow up unchecked, and that Ireland for several years past had been administered on the principle that it was safer and more expedient to leave law in abeyance if collision with any faction of the Irish people could thereby be avoided — a policy which was “the negation of that cardinal rule of Government which demands that the enforcement of the law and the preservation of order should always be independent of political expediency.” The Commissioners acquitted the Lord-Lieutenant (Lord Wimborne) of responsibility and held the Chief Secretary (Mr. Birrell) primarily responsible for the situation that was allowed to arise and for the outbreak. They remarked, however, that the policy of the Chief Secretary was the policy of the British Government as a whole. Sir Matthew Nathan, the Under-Secretary, was credited with complete loyalty to that policy but was thought not to have sufficiently impressed on Birrell the need of more active measures against sedition. If the Government were convicted of weakness before the rebellion, no such charge could be brought against the action they took after the outbreak.
The political sequel was an attempt, under the Coalition, to find a wartime Irish settlement. Lloyd George was charged with negotiating; proposals involving the exclusion of Ulster and the retention of Irish members at Westminster became the subject of bitter dispute. By late July the negotiations had hopelessly broken down. Redmond denounced any Bill framed at variance with the Lloyd George agreement; Asquith stated that the Government could not agree to the retention of the Irish members in undiminished numbers after the next election, and would not introduce any Bill unless the parties were substantially agreed. Martial law, Asquith later said, proclaimed as a precautionary measure, had not been enforced in practice, and he hoped it might be possible before long to discard even the form of it. Mr. Duke, K.C., Unionist Member for Exeter, was appointed Chief Secretary; the office of Lord-Lieutenant was for the time being not filled up — a restoration of “Dublin Castle with a Unionist Executive” that Redmond said would outrage the feelings of Ireland. He appealed to Englishmen not to let their natural indignation at the wicked outbreak of some two thousand men in Dublin lead them to forget the hundred and fifty thousand Irishmen fighting on the battlefields of France.
The Rising thus left Ireland under a military imprint and a failed settlement, with Home Rule still on the statute book and still in suspense, and with Sinn Fein transformed from a neglected faction into the central fact of Irish politics. The Annual Register’s year-list placed the Irish Rebellion beside the Military Service Acts and the Reconstruction of the Government as the defining domestic events of 1916.

events/eastern-question-balkans.title: The Eastern Question and the Balkans (1875–1913)
events/eastern-question-balkans.content:
The Eastern Question and the Balkans (1875–1913)
Overview
The “Eastern Question” — the diplomatic problem posed by the progressive decay of the Ottoman Empire and the competing ambitions of the Great Powers to inherit its territories — was the most persistent and dangerous theme in European diplomacy throughout the nineteenth century. For British foreign policy, it was a question of survival: the security of the route to India, the balance of naval power in the Mediterranean, and the fate of Constantinople and the Straits all hung upon the management of Ottoman decline. As Justin McCarthy observed, the Eastern Question was that “perennial source of modern trouble” which repeatedly brought Europe to the brink of war.
Between 1875 and 1913, the Eastern Question went through a series of acute crises — the Great Eastern Crisis (1875–1878), the Armenian Massacres (1894–1896), the Bosnian Crisis (1908–1909), and the Balkan Wars (1912–1913) — each of which tested British diplomacy under successive leaders. Lord Salisbury, the dominant figure in Conservative foreign policy from 1878 to 1902, approached the problem with a hard-headed realism, while Sir Edward Grey, Liberal Foreign Secretary from 1905 to 1916, sought to manage Balkan crises through the Concert of Europe. Through it all, the fate of the Balkan peoples — Bulgarians, Serbs, Greeks, Albanians, Macedonians, and Armenians — was shaped and reshaped by the rivalries of the Great Powers.

The Great Eastern Crisis (1875–1878)
Origins: Revolt in the Balkans
The crisis began with an uprising of Christian peasants in Herzegovina in July 1875, which quickly spread to Bosnia. The Ottoman authorities responded with brutal repression, but the revolt drew in Serbia and Montenegro and, behind them, Russia. The European Powers attempted diplomatic intervention: the Andrassy Note (December 1875) demanded administrative reforms, the Berlin Memorandum (May 1876) proposed an armistice and more far-reaching measures. Britain under Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli (Lord Beaconsfield) refused to associate itself with the Berlin Memorandum, suspicious of Russian intentions and determined to uphold the Ottoman Empire as a bulwark against Russian expansion towards Constantinople and the Mediterranean.
The Bulgarian Atrocities (1876)
In May 1876, Ottoman irregular troops (bashi-bazouks) suppressed a Bulgarian uprising with horrifying savagery. An estimated 12,000 to 15,000 Bulgarians were massacred in the district of Philippopolis (Plovdiv). When the news reached England, it provoked a political earthquake. William Ewart Gladstone, then in retirement, published his famous pamphlet “The Bulgarian Horrors and the Question of the East” in September 1876, denouncing the Turks as “the one great anti-human specimen of humanity” and demanding that they be expelled “bag and baggage” from the provinces they misgoverned.
The Bulgarian atrocities shattered the traditional British policy of pro-Turkish neutrality. Gladstone’s moral crusade mobilised Nonconformist opinion and split the Liberal Party from the Conservatives, who under Disraeli continued to support the Ottoman Empire as a strategic necessity. The atrocity propaganda — as Langer notes — created a template that would be repeated during later crises: “the outcry that went up after the Bulgarian atrocities of 1876” was the model for subsequent humanitarian campaigns over Armenia and Macedonia.
The Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878)
Despite a conference of the Great Powers at Constantinople in December 1876–January 1877, the Sultan refused to implement meaningful reforms. In April 1877, Russia declared war on Turkey, ostensibly to protect the Christian populations of the Balkans. The war was bitterly fought. After initial Turkish resistance at Plevna (July–December 1877), the Russians crossed the Balkans in January 1878 and advanced to within a few miles of Constantinople. The British Mediterranean Fleet was ordered to the Dardanelles; war between Britain and Russia seemed imminent.
The Treaty of San Stefano (March 1878)
The Russians imposed the Treaty of San Stefano on the defeated Turks in March 1878. Its key provision was the creation of a “Big Bulgaria” — a vast, autonomous principality stretching from the Danube to the Aegean and incorporating most of Macedonia. This state was to be occupied by Russian troops for two years and would in practice be a Russian satellite.
The Treaty of San Stefano was a diplomatic bombshell. As Langer records, the Treaty “incorporated most of Macedonia in the great new Bulgaria” — precisely what Britain and Austria had feared. To Disraeli and his Foreign Secretary, Lord Salisbury (who had succeeded Lord Derby in March 1878), this was unacceptable. A “Big Bulgaria” would give Russia dominant influence in the Balkans and threaten British interests in the Eastern Mediterranean and the route to India. The British demanded that the treaty be submitted to a European congress for revision, and mobilised Indian troops to Malta as a demonstration of force.
The Cyprus Convention (June 1878)
To strengthen Britain’s strategic position before the Congress, Salisbury negotiated the Cyprus Convention with the Sultan on June 4, 1878. By its terms, Britain agreed to defend Turkey’s Asiatic possessions against Russia in return for the right to occupy and administer Cyprus as a naval base. The Convention also required the Sultan to undertake reforms in Anatolia for the protection of Christian subjects — a provision aimed at the Armenians.
As Langer notes, the Cyprus Convention was driven less by concern for the Armenians than by strategic calculation: “From the negotiations preceding the conclusion of the Convention it is perfectly clear that the English government was much less concerned with the Armenians than with the country they inhabited. They were interested in bolstering up the Turkish rule in northeastern Anatolia.” The acquisition of Cyprus gave Britain a key naval station in the Eastern Mediterranean and a foothold in the Levant, and it became a cornerstone of Salisbury’s policy of defending the Ottoman Empire’s Asiatic territories while accepting the loss of most of its European provinces.

Congress of Berlin (1878)
The Congress of Berlin (June 13–July 13, 1878), presided over by Otto von Bismarck as “honest broker,” was the most important European diplomatic conference between the Congress of Vienna (1815) and the Paris Peace Conference (1919). Disraeli and Salisbury represented Britain; Prince Gorchakov and Count Shuvalov represented Russia; Count Andrássy represented Austria-Hungary.
Terms of the Treaty of Berlin
The Congress radically revised the Treaty of San Stefano:


Bulgaria was divided into three parts: a small autonomous principality north of the Balkan Mountains (a vassal of the Sultan); Eastern Roumelia, a semi-autonomous province under a Christian governor appointed by the Porte; and the remainder — including most of Macedonia — returned to direct Turkish rule.


Bosnia and Herzegovina were placed under Austro-Hungarian occupation and administration, though remaining nominally under Ottoman suzerainty. This provision, a key goal of Andrássy, planted the seed of the Bosnian Crisis thirty years later.


Serbia, Montenegro, and Romania were recognised as independent states, with some territorial gains.


Russia recovered Southern Bessarabia (lost in 1856) and gained Batum, Kars, and Ardahan in the Caucasus.


Article LXI engaged the Porte to undertake reforms in the Armenian provinces and to report periodically to the Powers — a promise honoured mostly in the breach.


The Cyprus Convention was accepted as a fait accompli.


British Achievements at Berlin
The Congress of Berlin was Disraeli’s greatest diplomatic triumph. He returned to London proclaiming “peace with honour.” The British had achieved their core objectives: the “Big Bulgaria” was dismantled, Russian influence in the Balkans was checked, and Britain acquired Cyprus. Salisbury, who had done much of the detailed negotiation, emerged as a statesman of European stature.
Yet the settlement contained deep flaws. The return of Macedonia to Turkish rule condemned that region to three decades of misrule, insurgency, and inter-ethnic violence that would culminate in the Balkan Wars. The occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina by Austria-Hungary, without annexation, created a legal ambiguity that poisoned Austro-Serb relations. And the Armenian reform clause was a dead letter from the start. As Langer records, the Berlin Congress came as “a thundering blow” to the Bulgarians, who resolved to use the new principality as “an organ for the whole of the nation” — meaning the irredentist recovery of Macedonia.

The Armenian Question and Decline of the Sick Man
The Armenian National Movement
The Armenians of the Ottoman Empire, concentrated in six eastern vilayets (provinces), had experienced a cultural and political revival from the mid-nineteenth century. A constitution for the Armenian millet was adopted in 1860, and the Armenian patriarchate became a focal point for reform. But as Langer notes, “there was no thought of breaking away from the Empire” — the Armenian movement was initially a movement for reform within the Ottoman system.
The Treaty of Berlin (Article LXI) and the Cyprus Convention raised Armenian hopes, but the promised reforms never materialised. “Bulgaria was freed by the intervention of Russia, why not Armenia with the help of England?” became a common refrain. Armenian revolutionary committees — the Hunchakian (Social Democrat) and the Dashnagtzoutian (Armenian Revolutionary Federation) — were formed in the 1880s and 1890s, advocating armed resistance.
The Hamidian Massacres (1894–1896)
Sultan Abdul Hamid II responded to Armenian agitation with systematic violence. Between 1894 and 1896, an estimated 100,000 to 300,000 Armenians were massacred across the eastern provinces. The worst outbreaks occurred at Sasun (1894), where 25 villages were destroyed and 10,000–20,000 Armenians killed; throughout Zeitun and the southern provinces (1895–96); and a mass pogrom in Constantinople itself (August 1896) that left 6,000 dead.
When news of the massacres reached England, there was “a repetition of the outcry that went up after the Bulgarian atrocities of 1876” (Langer). The Anglo-Armenian Committee and the Evangelical Alliance mobilised public opinion. Gladstone, in his last great public campaign, thundered against the Sultan — “the great assassin” — and demanded intervention. Lord Salisbury’s Conservative government was deeply conflicted: humanitarian sentiment demanded action, but strategic realities constrained it. As Langer notes: “Thoughtful Englishmen realized that British policy in the past (especially the Cyprus Convention) had ingrained suspicion of British designs so deeply among the peoples and governments of other nations that any effort to act single-handedly would almost certainly have resulted in war.”
The Powers did nothing effective. Britain, France, and Russia — the “Armenian Triplice” — had presented reform proposals to the Sultan in 1895, but Abdul Hamid played them off against each other. The massacres continued unchecked. The Armenian Question was, for the time being, submerged, but the moral failure of the Powers left deep scars.
The Greco-Turkish War (1897) and the Cretan Question
The Armenian crisis fed into a wider Balkan instability. The Cretan insurrection of 1896–97 pitted Greek Christians against the Ottoman authorities, leading to the Greco-Turkish War of April–May 1897. Greece was decisively defeated, and only the intervention of the Powers — including a British admiral who bombarded the town of Canea — prevented a massacre of Christians on the island. Crete was granted autonomous status under a Greek high commissioner, moving gradually towards union with Greece (formalised in 1913).
The Macedonian Problem
By the late 1890s, Macedonia had become the focal point of Balkan tensions. The three Turkish vilayets of Salonika, Monastir (Bitola), and Kosovo were a tangled mosaic of Slavs, Greeks, Vlachs, Jews, and Albanians. The Treaty of Berlin had returned Macedonia to Turkish rule with promises of reform that were never kept. Bulgarian, Serbian, and Greek propaganda, church, and guerrilla organisations competed for the loyalty of the population. Bulgarian comitadjis (the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organisation, IMRO) waged an armed campaign against Turkish rule, provoking brutal reprisals.
The Ilinden-Preobrazhenie Uprising (August 1903) was crushed with savage ferocity. Austria and Russia intervened diplomatically, drawing up the Mürzsteg Reform Programme (October 1903), which provided for European financial control and gendarmerie reorganisation in Macedonia. But reform was half-hearted and obstructed by both the Porte and the Great Powers.
As the Annual Register for 1908 observed, the Balkan Committee repeatedly drew attention to the “chronic international scandals of Macedonia,” warning that “the existing anarchic degeneration could hardly end except in a violent catastrophe.” That catastrophe was delayed by the Young Turk Revolution of July 1908, but only momentarily.

The Bosnian Crisis (1908–1909)
The Young Turk Revolution and Austrian Opportunism
The Young Turk Revolution (July 1908) forced Sultan Abdul Hamid II to restore the constitution of 1876 and re-establish the Ottoman Parliament. This sudden revival of Turkish vigour alarmed Austria-Hungary, whose position in Bosnia and Herzegovina — occupied since 1878 but legally still Ottoman — seemed vulnerable.
Baron von Aehrenthal, the Austro-Hungarian Foreign Minister, decided to act. At a meeting with the Russian Foreign Minister Alexander Izvolsky at Buchlau in Moravia on September 15, 1908, Aehrenthal secured Russian acquiescence to the annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in return for Austrian support for Russian demands on the Straits. On October 5, 1908, Bulgaria — acting in coordination with Austria — declared its complete independence from the Ottoman Empire. Two days later, on October 7, the Emperor Francis Joseph issued a proclamation announcing the annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, promising constitutional institutions and “a higher level of political life” for the inhabitants.
The Crisis
The annexation provoked fury in Serbia, which had regarded Bosnia as the natural nucleus of a future Serbian state (the “Greater Serbia” idea). The Serbian government demanded territorial compensation or the restoration of the status quo and mobilised its army. Montenegro supported Serbia. Russia, humiliated by Izvolsky’s failure to secure the opening of the Straits, backed the Serbian position.
The crisis quickly escalated. Austria-Hungary mobilised troops on the Serbian frontier. Sir Edward Grey, the British Foreign Secretary, attempted to mediate, proposing a European conference to legalise the annexation while addressing Serbian grievances. As the Annual Register for 1909 recorded: “The attitude of Germany and Austria-Hungary, and the recalcitrance of Servia, seemed to portend the outbreak of a great European war, and emphasised the need of British attention to questions of national defence.”
Germany intervened decisively on Austria’s side. On March 21, 1909, the German ambassador in St. Petersburg delivered an ultimatum: Russia must recognise the annexation and abandon support for Serbia, or Germany would fight. Russia, weakened by the 1905 revolution and not yet recovered militarily, capitulated. Serbia was forced to follow suit on March 31, issuing a humiliating statement that its rights had not been infringed.
Consequences
The Bosnian Crisis was a profound humiliation for Russia and Serbia and a victory for Austrian expansionism. As the Annual Register for 1912 observed in retrospect: the annexation “drew upon her [Austria] the hostility of Russia and Servia, set Italy the example of another defiance of treaties and of European public opinion in the attack on Turkey in Tripoli, and taught the smaller Balkan States that it was only by united action and in disregard of the great Powers, that they could achieve their national aims.” The pattern was set for the Balkan Wars — and ultimately for the Great War of 1914.
For Britain, the crisis demonstrated the fragility of the European balance and the limits of Grey’s policy of conciliation through the Concert of Europe. The Bosnian annexation also strengthened the Anglo-Russian Entente (signed in 1907), as both powers saw the need for closer cooperation against Austro-German assertiveness in the Balkans.

The Balkan Wars (1912–1913)
The Formation of the Balkan League
The lesson of the Bosnian Crisis was not lost on the Balkan states. If they were to achieve their national ambitions — principally the partition of Macedonia — they would have to act together and in defiance of the Powers. The Balkan League was formed under Russian auspices in 1912, bringing together Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece, and Montenegro. As the Annual Register noted: “For the first time in history the populations of these countries, which for five hundred years had been in constant conflict with each other, were now united against the Turk, and the union was a formidable one, for it had at its disposal a combined military force of 790,000 men.”
The immediate catalyst was the Turco-Italian War (1911–1912), which had stripped away Tripoli and the Dodecanese from the Ottomans and revealed Turkish military weakness. Meanwhile, massacres of Christians in Macedonia — notably at Kotchana (August 1912), where Bulgarian villagers were slaughtered in the streets — inflamed Balkan opinion beyond the point of restraint.
The First Balkan War (October 1912 – May 1913)
Montenegro declared war on Turkey on October 8, 1912, and the other Balkan allies followed within ten days. The war was a stunning military success for the League:


The Bulgarians shattered the main Turkish army in Eastern Thrace, advancing to the Tchataldja Lines, within thirty miles of Constantinople, and laying siege to Adrianople (Edirne).


The Serbians won decisive victories at Kumanovo (October 23–24) and Monastir (November 16–18), driving the Turks out of most of Macedonia.


The Greeks captured Salonika on November 8, just hours ahead of the Bulgarian advance, seized Yanina (Ioannina) in March 1913, and their navy dominated the Aegean.


The Montenegrins besieged Skutari (Shkodër) on the Adriatic coast.


By December 1912, the Ottoman Empire had lost virtually all its European territories except Constantinople, the Gallipoli peninsula, and the narrow strip behind the Tchataldja Lines. An armistice was signed on December 3, 1912 (Greece continued operations in Epirus).
The London Peace Conference
A peace conference opened in London in December 1912, conducted simultaneously as a meeting of the Balkan belligerents and an Ambassadors’ Conference of the Great Powers, chaired by Sir Edward Grey. The key questions were:


The fate of Adrianople: Bulgaria insisted on its cession; Turkey refused.


Albania: The Powers insisted on the creation of an independent Albanian state (proclaimed at Avlona on November 28, 1912), denying Serbia an Adriatic seaport, which Serbia regarded as essential for economic independence.


The Aegean Islands: Greece claimed the islands of the Eastern Aegean; Turkey resisted.


The Treaty of London was finally signed on May 30, 1913. Turkey ceded all territory west of the Enos-Midia line (a line drawn from the Aegean Sea at Enos to the Black Sea at Midia), renounced Crete in favour of Greece, and recognised the independence of Albania. The treaty was a triumph for the Balkan League — but its provisions satisfied no one fully, and the victors promptly fell out over the division of the spoils.
The Second Balkan War (June–July 1913)
The division of Macedonia was the casus belli of the Second Balkan War. Bulgaria, which had done the most fighting, felt cheated by the territorial settlement imposed by Russia’s arbitration after the First War. On the night of June 29–30, 1913, Bulgarian forces attacked their former allies Serbia and Greece in Macedonia without a declaration of war.
This was a catastrophic miscalculation. Serbia and Greece fought back effectively; Romania, which had remained neutral in the First War, invaded Bulgaria from the north to seize the Dobrudja; and even Turkey took the opportunity to recapture Adrianople under Enver Bey (July 20, 1913). In less than a month, Bulgaria was defeated on all fronts.
The Treaty of Bucharest (August 10, 1913) redrew the Balkan map:


Serbia acquired most of northern and central Macedonia (including Monastir and the Vardar valley).


Greece took southern Macedonia (including Salonika), Epirus, and Crete.


Romania obtained the southern Dobrudja.


Turkey recovered Adrianople and Eastern Thrace west to the Enos-Midia line (later revised).


Bulgaria was left with only a small, landlocked western corner of Macedonia and a narrow outlet to the Aegean at Dedeagach (Alexandroupoli).


British Diplomacy and the Balkan Wars
Sir Edward Grey played a central role in managing the international dimensions of the Balkan Wars, particularly through the London Ambassadors’ Conference (December 1912 – August 1913). Grey’s objectives were to localise the conflict, prevent a general European war, and secure the creation of an independent Albania to deny Serbia a port on the Adriatic (which Austria-Hungary was determined to prevent).
As the Annual Register for 1913 recorded, Grey stated that British policy was “to consolidate the authority of Turkey in her Asiatic dominions” behind the Enos-Midia line, resting on “sound finance and reforms” and the “consent and goodwill of the Powers.” He worked closely with France and Russia (the Triple Entente) while maintaining communication with Germany and Austria (the Triple Alliance). His personal reputation for “straightforwardness and candour” (as the Earl of Crewe put it) was a diplomatic asset of great value.
The Balkan Wars left a deeply unstable settlement. Serbia had doubled its territory and emerged as the dominant power in the Western Balkans, emboldening its ambition to unite all South Slavs — including those still under Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia. Bulgaria burned with revanchist fury, determined to recover Macedonia. The Ottoman Empire, humiliated but recovering, looked to a future of military reorganisation under German tutelage. The stage was set for the assassination at Sarajevo in June 1914.

Summary
The Eastern Question, which had dominated European diplomacy for a century, reached its climactic phase between 1875 and 1913. Through the Great Eastern Crisis, the Congress of Berlin, the Armenian massacres, the Bosnian Crisis, and the Balkan Wars, British policy — shaped successively by Disraeli, Salisbury, and Grey — sought to preserve the Ottoman Empire as a barrier to Russian expansion while managing the irresistible pressures of Balkan nationalism. The settlements imposed by the Great Powers — at Berlin (1878), at London (1913), and at Bucharest (1913) — each contained the seeds of future conflict. The Eastern Question was not resolved; it was merely transformed into the powder keg that would ignite the First World War.
