events/egypt-sudan-campaigns.title: The Egyptian and Sudan Campaigns (1882–1898)
events/egypt-sudan-campaigns.content:
The Egyptian and Sudan Campaigns (1882–1898)
Overview
The British involvement in Egypt and the Sudan between 1882 and 1898 represents one of the most significant episodes in Victorian imperial history. What began as a reluctant military intervention to suppress a nationalist revolt against the Khedive’s regime evolved into a permanent occupation, a disastrous attempt to extricate Egyptian garrisons from the Sudan that ended in the death of General Gordon, and ultimately a reconquest of the Sudan under Kitchener that brought Britain to the brink of war with France at Fashoda. Through it all, the British maintained what Alfred Milner famously described as a “veiled protectorate” over Egypt — ruling indirectly through the Khedive while keeping the country formally part of the Ottoman Empire.

The Occupation of Egypt (1882)
The Egyptian National Movement and Arabi Pasha
By the early 1880s, Egypt was reeling under the weight of enormous foreign debt and the intrusive Dual Control exercised by Britain and France over its finances. European officials filled every government bureau, railway station, and telegraph office. As Justin McCarthy observed: “The inevitable Englishman, with his unwelcome comrade, the equally inevitable Frenchman, could be seen in every bureau and every railway station and every telegraph office.”
A nationalist movement crystallised around the slogan “Egypt for the Egyptians,” finding its leader in Ahmed Arabi (Arabi Bey, later Arabi Pasha), an army colonel who emerged from the “insurrection of the colonels” — a bloodless army revolt. Arabi became Minister for War and de facto master of the Egyptian administration. The winter of 1881–82 saw his popularity at its zenith. Tourists at Shepheard’s Hotel watched him ride past on his white horse, and noted that “the people ran after him as they did not run after the Khedive.” The Khedive Tewfik himself initially coquetted with the movement.
The Alexandria Crisis and Bombardment
Tensions escalated through the spring of 1882. British and French ironclads were ordered to Alexandria. When Arabi and his colleagues resigned office in protest at demands they should leave the country, the Khedive failed to form a new ministry, and the army declared against him.
On June 11, 1882, a riot erupted in Alexandria between natives and Europeans. The English consul was dragged from his carriage and severely wounded; several British and French subjects were killed. Though no deliberate massacre had been planned, the disturbance provided the casus belli.
France, under the ministry of de Freycinet, declined to intervene actively. On the night of July 10, the French fleet steamed away for Port Said, effectively ending the Dual Control. The British admiral, Sir Beauchamp Seymour (later Lord Alcester), was ordered to prevent further fortification of Alexandria’s defences. At 7 a.m. on July 11, 1882, the British fleet — eight ironclads and five gunboats with over 100 guns — opened fire on the Egyptian forts. The bombardment lasted two days. Egyptian gunners fought bravely, with women and children helping to serve the guns. Arabi and his troops withdrew from the fortifications, and Alexandria descended into chaos — “fire, plunder and murder raged in unchallenged possession of the historic and beautiful city” for two days, with an estimated 2,000 Europeans killed.
The bombardment prompted John Bright’s resignation from Gladstone’s Cabinet. Bright declared the action a violation both of international law and of the moral law. He had delayed his resignation out of personal devotion to Gladstone but could no longer remain.
Tel-el-Kebir and the End of the Revolt
With the Canal secured, Sir Garnet Wolseley was sent to command operations with about 11,000 bayonets, 2,000 sabres, and 60 guns. Arabi entrenched his forces at Tel-el-Kebir. Wolseley’s advance was so swift and well-timed that the Egyptians were taken by surprise. “After the first bayonet charge of the English all was practically over.” Arabi was captured, pleaded guilty to rebellion, was sentenced to death, and had his sentence commuted to perpetual banishment in Ceylon — a leniency reflecting the Khedive’s own earlier sympathy with Arabi’s cause.
The Occupation Begins
Though the government had repeatedly declared its objection to a British occupation — Lord Granville had written in January 1882 that “Her Majesty’s Government have a strong objection to the occupation by themselves of Egypt” — the troops did not withdraw. The Dual Control vanished, and England occupied Egypt on her own account.
McCarthy summarised the irony: “English statesmanship had in the first instance no other purpose than that of securing the Canal and the whole highway to India… Down to the very latest moment, the English Government was altogether opposed to an English occupation of Egypt.”

Gordon and Khartoum (1884–1885)
The Mahdi Rising
After the British occupation of Egypt, the Sudan — under Egyptian administration — fell into chaos. In 1881, a religious movement of extraordinary force erupted under Muhammad Ahmad, who proclaimed himself the Mahdi (“the Guided One”). The Mahdist revolt swept through the Sudan, annihilating an Egyptian army under General Hicks in 1883. By 1884, the Mahdi’s forces controlled much of the country.
Gordon’s Mission
The Gladstone government decided to abandon the Sudan entirely, resolving to withdraw the Egyptian garrisons and restore the territory to some form of native independence. To accomplish this, the government turned to General Charles George Gordon — “Chinese Gordon” — a man of legendary courage, deep religious conviction, and immense public popularity.
Gordon was sent to Khartoum in January 1884 with instructions to evacuate the Egyptian garrisons. He understood the government’s decision to be irrevocable. Gladstone himself would later refer to the Mahdi’s followers as “a people struggling to be free, and rightly struggling to be free.” Gordon, however, soon concluded that evacuation was impossible without first establishing some form of stable government, and he began instead to organise the defence of Khartoum. By March 1884, the Mahdi’s forces had surrounded the city.
Delay and the Relief Expedition
For months, the government hesitated. As McCarthy records: “There was a strange, and to this day an unaccountable, delay about the measures to be taken for Gordon’s rescue. People said that the Government had no hope of being able to do anything to save him; and a Government is in sore straits when people believe that there is something that it ought to do and cannot even try to do.”
At last, a relief expedition was assembled under Sir Garnet Wolseley. It was perhaps a half-hearted enterprise at best. The public had full confidence in Wolseley — the hero of the Red River expedition and the Egyptian campaign against Arabi — but the difficulties were immense. Wolseley had to fight his way step by step up the Nile. Colonel Fred Burnaby, the beloved and chivalrous soldier of gigantic stature, was among the first to fall — a dark omen.
The Fall of Khartoum
On January 26, 1885, after a siege of nearly eleven months, Khartoum fell. Gordon was killed on the palace steps, two days before the relief force arrived. In a cruel irony, Punch had published a cartoon depicting the gladsome meeting of Wolseley and Gordon at Khartoum — on the very day the news of Gordon’s death arrived.
Gordon’s death was a terrible blow to the Liberal Government. “Gordon was an ideal hero; and an Administration of saints and sages could not have been saved from reproach.” Yet the Ministry did not immediately fall. It survived votes of censure until the budget of the Chancellor, Mr. Childers — proposing increased taxes on income, spirits, and beer — was defeated by a majority of twelve on June 8, 1885. Lord Randolph Churchill danced on the benches of the House of Commons in wild excitement as the Gladstone administration fell.

The Reconquest of Sudan (1896–1898)
The Long Interval
For over a decade after Gordon’s death, the Sudan remained under the rule of the Mahdi’s successor, the Khalifa Abdallahi. Egypt — and her British administrators — lacked both the funds and the political will for reconquest. Sir Evelyn Baring (later Lord Cromer), the British Agent and Consul-General in Egypt, wrote in 1888: “There is not now, and since the destruction of General Hicks’ army there never has been, any serious idea of deliberately adopting a policy involving the reconquest of the Soudan by force of arms.”
The fear, however, that another European power might seize the Upper Nile and control Egypt’s water supply — the legendary fear of Nile manipulation dating back to medieval times — gradually drove British policy toward reconquest. As Lord Milner wrote in his influential book England in Egypt (1892): “It is an uncomfortable thought that the regular supply of water by the great river, which is to Egypt not a question of convenience and prosperity but actually of life, must always be exposed to some risk, as long as the upper reaches of that river are not under Egyptian control.”
The Decision to Advance
The immediate catalyst came in early 1896. The Italians had suffered a catastrophic defeat at Adwa in Abyssinia, and the Dervish forces were concentrating near Kassala. Lord Salisbury’s cabinet, concerned both to assist the Italians and to plant “the foot of Egypt farther up the Nile,” authorised an advance from Wadi Halfa toward Dongola. Salisbury wrote to Cromer that the decision was “inspired specially by a desire to help the Italians at Kassala, and to prevent the dervishes from winning a conspicuous success which might have far-reaching results. In addition, we desired to kill two birds with one stone, and to use the same military effort to plant the foot of Egypt farther up the Nile.”
Kitchener’s Campaign
The advance was placed under the command of Sir Herbert Kitchener, the Sirdar (Commander-in-Chief) of the Egyptian army. Kitchener — a man of remarkable organisational ability, foresight, and patience — methodically built up his forces and extended the railway across the desert. In the spring of 1898, he attacked and destroyed the entrenched Dervish camp at the Atbara River, killing at least 3,000 men and capturing the Dervish leader Mahmoud.
The Battle of Omdurman (2 September 1898)
Kitchener’s final objective was Khartoum itself. The Khalifa had assembled a force of over 60,000 men, including the most warlike tribes of the region, well supplied with artillery. The British and Egyptian troops numbered some 23,000.
On September 2, 1898, the two forces met at Omdurman, just north of Khartoum. The Dervishes attacked with desperate bravery, charging again and again into the concentrated fire of Kitchener’s army — armed with modern rifles, machine guns, and artillery. Maxim guns and Lee-Metford rifles mowed down the advancing Mahdist forces. By the end of the day, some 11,000 Dervishes lay dead and 16,000 wounded, against fewer than 50 British and Egyptian killed.
Kitchener entered Omdurman in triumph. On September 4, a thanksgiving service was held in Khartoum, and the British and Egyptian flags flew side by side over the shattered citadel where Gordon had died. As McCarthy observed: “The feeling was that Gordon had at last been avenged, and that the place which had seen his murder had now become the scene of the vengeance inflicted for that murder.”
Kitchener’s Reward
Kitchener returned to England to a hero’s welcome. The Queen created him Lord Kitchener of Khartoum. At a banquet at the Mansion House, he invited the British public to raise £100,000 for a college at Khartoum to be built as a memorial to Gordon — a task he completed before returning to Egypt.

Fashoda Crisis
The Marchand Expedition
Even before the battle of Omdurman, Kitchener received intelligence that a European force was in occupation of Fashoda, a point on the White Nile far south of Khartoum, and that the French flag was flying there. This was the expedition of Major Jean-Baptiste Marchand, who had crossed Africa from the French Congo with a small force of Senegalese soldiers, reaching Fashoda in July 1898 after an epic two-year journey.
Kitchener’s Confrontation with Marchand
Kitchener acted with characteristic promptness. He steamed up the Nile with a flotilla of gunboats and a military force. Finding Marchand in occupation and the French flag flying, he informed the French officer that Fashoda was Egyptian territory under British protection, and firmly — but politely — invited him to withdraw.
Marchand replied that he was there on the orders of the French Government and could not leave without instructions from Paris. The two commanders exchanged courtesies: Kitchener is said to have offered whisky and water; Marchand responded with champagne of the best brand. Kitchener established a Sudanese garrison at Fashoda under an English officer and left the diplomatic settlement to London and Paris.
The Crisis Deepens
The British Government published the despatches on October 10, 1898, revealing a serious international crisis. It emerged that as early as December 1897, Sir Edmund Monson, the British Ambassador in Paris, had warned the French Government that no other power could claim to occupy any part of the Nile Valley. In 1895, Sir Edward Grey, then Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs, had declared that a French advance into the Nile Valley would be regarded as “an unfriendly action” — diplomatic language for a threat of war.
For weeks, the two nations stood on the brink of conflict. The French Foreign Minister, Delcassé, argued that France was only following England’s example of expansion. Lord Salisbury directed the French Government to be told that the Fashoda region was now subject, by right of conquest, to British and Egyptian authority.
The French Back Down
A remarkable display of national unity emerged in Britain. Lord Rosebery and the Liberal leaders joined the Conservatives in declaring that England’s claims must be maintained — by war if necessary. “The strong feeling thus manifested through England had its effect on the hesitating action of the French Government.”
In early November 1899, the Marchand expedition was recalled. Fashoda was evacuated in December. A profound sense of relief was felt in both countries. The crisis had tested the new alignment of European powers and demonstrated Britain’s determination to control the entire Nile Valley from source to sea.

The Veiled Protectorate
An Occupation Without a Name
From 1882 onward, Britain exercised effective control over Egypt, yet the country remained nominally part of the Ottoman Empire, with the Khedive as the Sultan’s vassal. This arrangement — neither outright annexation nor genuine independence — came to be known as the “veiled protectorate.” The term was popularised by Alfred Milner in his 1892 book England in Egypt, which made a deep impression on the British public.
The British ruled through a British Agent and Consul-General — Sir Evelyn Baring (created Lord Cromer in 1892) held this post from 1883 to 1907. Cromer was effectively the ruler of Egypt, though he operated behind the facade of the Khedivial government. As McCarthy noted, writing in 1897: “Since then, of course, the Dual Control has vanished, and England has occupied Egypt on her own account. There can be no doubt that the British occupation has brought great material benefit to the people of the country. Taxation has been reduced and equalised, forced labour has been abolished, and something like justice has been done in the courts of law.”
The Paradox of the Occupation
Yet the occupation remained paradoxical. As McCarthy observed: “No English statesman could possibly pretend, or ever did pretend, that British diplomacy had any such purpose when it planted a more or less firm foot on the banks of the Nile… English statesmanship had in the first instance no other purpose than that of securing the Canal and the whole highway to India.”
After 1887, when France and Russia blocked a convention between England and Turkey for evacuation, the chances of withdrawal rapidly diminished. By 1892 it was clear the occupation would last indefinitely, and Cromer settled down with renewed confidence to the work of reconstruction.
The Results of the Protectorate
Cromer’s regime brought considerable material progress: irrigation works expanded, the tax burden was rationalised, and the judicial system reformed. But the veiled nature of British control created constant tension. France remained unreconciled to British dominance in Egypt. The occupation drew Britain deeper into African affairs, leading to the reconquest of the Sudan and nearly to war with France at Fashoda. As McCarthy presciently concluded: “The problem is, how to keep what we have already got, and thus far the idea of statesmanship, whether Liberal or Tory, seems to be that of an extension of territory and frontier southwards… Expedition after expedition has been sent out to extend the Egyptian frontier, nominally for the Khedive, but really for the English occupation, and some of the expeditions have been ghastly failures, while others have been at least temporary successes.”
The veiled protectorate lasted until 1914, when Britain declared Egypt a formal protectorate at the outbreak of the First World War.

events/election-1906-tariff-reform.title: The General Election of 1906 & Tariff Reform
events/election-1906-tariff-reform.content:
The General Election of 1906 & Tariff Reform
The general election of January–February 1906 produced one of the most decisive Liberal landslides in British electoral history, returning a government with a majority of 134 over all opposition groups combined. The contest was the climax of a three-year political crisis triggered by Joseph Chamberlain’s campaign for Tariff Reform, which split the Unionist party, drove the reunited Liberals back to power, and cleared the way for a decade of social reform legislation.
The Tariff Reform Split
The rupture within the Unionist party began on May 15, 1903, when Joseph Chamberlain, the Colonial Secretary and the most formidable Radical-turned-Imperialist of his generation, delivered a speech at Birmingham that, as the Annual Register recorded, produced “a condition of astonishment and perplexity bordering on stupefaction” in the public mind. Chamberlain proposed that Britain abandon unilateral free trade and adopt a system of imperial preference — reciprocal tariffs with the self-governing Colonies — to consolidate the Empire commercially. If the Colonies offered to favour British goods, Britain must be free to reciprocate: “We will, nevertheless, recover our freedom, resume that power of negotiation and, if necessary, retaliation whenever our own interests or our relations between our Colonies and ourselves are threatened by other people.”
On the very same day, Prime Minister Arthur Balfour was defending the repeal of the corn duty to a deputation led by Henry Chaplin. Balfour denied that the duty had ever been intended as protective, declared that a preferential scheme was not yet possible, and treated Chamberlain’s proposals as a “remote and very doubtful contingency.” The simultaneous appearance of these two contradictory positions — the Colonial Secretary calling for a revolution in fiscal policy while the Prime Minister dismantled the very tax that might have been its starting point — left the country bewildered.
The Annual Register noted that Chamberlain “was widely held to possess a unique claim on the respectful attention of his countrymen,” but within the Unionist party the divisions were immediate and severe. Among Conservatives there was “a considerable prevalence of theoretical Protectionist opinion,” but vigorous sections — especially among younger Conservatives and Liberal Unionists — discerned “the social and economic danger of perpetual food taxes and the taint of Protection.” The Spectator, the principal weekly organ of thoughtful Unionism, emerged as an energetic opponent. The Liberal party and Liberal press threw themselves “with almost complete unanimity” into opposition.
Chamberlain remained in the Cabinet for several more months, but the fissure proved irreparable. On September 9, 1903, he resigned from the government to campaign publicly for his fiscal programme. The Duke of Devonshire, the Liberal Unionist leader, also left the Cabinet. The Unionist party was now openly divided into three factions: Chamberlainite Tariff Reformers, Balfourite moderates who favoured a flexible but undefined “fiscal reform,” and Unionist Free Traders who adhered to orthodox Cobdenite principles.
Chamberlain’s Campaign (1903–1905)
Chamberlain threw himself into a nationwide speaking tour of extraordinary intensity. His first campaign closed on January 18, 1904, at the Guildhall in London. The Times reported that “he intermits [his campaign] now on the highest level he has yet reached.” Four thousand hearers were admitted by ticket; the enthusiasm of his welcome “was immense, drowning a band which was struggling to perform the National Anthem.”
In his Guildhall speech, Chamberlain argued that free imports — as distinct from genuine free exchange — had not produced the promised benefits. “We had never had free exchange; we had had free imports instead, which was a very different thing.” He pointed to the rising exports of Germany and the United States, the decline of British industrial supremacy, and the imperative need to maintain the Empire as a commercial unit. He drew historical parallels with Holland, Venice, and the Hanseatic cities — commercial powers that had decayed when they lost their industrial base.
The Tariff Reform League, founded in 1903, became a formidable propaganda machine, organising demonstrations, publishing literature, and pressing candidates to commit to the cause. The Unionist Free Traders, led by the Duke of Devonshire and the Spectator, fought back through the Unionist Free Trade Club. The Annual Register of 1904 recorded that the Liberal party, “disunited for twenty years” on the Home Rule question, now found a unifying cause in opposition to Protection. The fiscal question “engrossed the public mind to such an extent as very perceptibly to draw off interest from” other questions.
By-elections told a consistent story. Liberal candidates made steady gains, and even in constituencies where Unionists held on, the reduced majorities reflected the accumulating discontent. The Stalybridge by-election of January 1905 saw the Liberal majority increase from 81 in 1900 to 951 — a result the Annual Register attributed “apart from the discontents accumulating against the Government” to Lancashire’s conviction that “the interests of that great industry would be prejudicially affected by any tampering with” free trade in cotton.
Through 1905, the Unionist government staggered from crisis to crisis. The Chinese labour controversy in the Transvaal — the importation of indentured Chinese coolies to work the Rand gold mines under conditions that Liberals denounced as “Chinese slavery” — became a powerful moral rallying cry. The Education Act of 1902 had alienated Nonconformists. The government’s Irish policy was in disarray after the resignation of George Wyndham as Chief Secretary. By the autumn, as the Annual Register noted, “articles pointing to the Premier’s resignation” appeared in the Times and the Daily Telegraph.
The 1906 Election
On Monday, December 4, 1905, Arthur Balfour resigned the premiership. The King invited Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman to form a government, which he did by December 10. The new Cabinet was remarkable: H. H. Asquith at the Exchequer, Sir Edward Grey at the Foreign Office, Richard Haldane at the War Office, David Lloyd-George at the Board of Trade, John Morley at the India Office, and John Burns — the first working-class man to enter a British Cabinet — at the Local Government Board. The Annual Register observed that the composition of the new ministry “was favourably regarded by public opinion.”
The election campaign began at once. The Annual Register described it as “the most exciting and startling since 1880, if not since 1832.” The reversal of roles was complete: the Opposition (the departing Unionists) were now “arraigned on charges of reckless extravagance, misjudgment of South African affairs, the introduction into the Transvaal of ‘Chinese slavery,’ the endowment of denominational education, and the propounders of crude and self-contradictory ‘fiscal reforms.‘” The Liberals, formerly the party of criticism, now posed as reformers, “claiming to be the real Free Traders and apostles of economic progress.”
The fiscal question was probably the most important single issue, especially in rural constituencies, with “Chinese slavery” next, and then the modification of the Education Act of 1902. The Duke of Devonshire, in a letter to the Unionist Free Trade Club, declared that the Tariff Reform League’s proposals were “indistinguishable from pure Protection.” Chamberlain attacked the new ministry as “essentially a Home Rule and Little Englander Government which must exist, if at all, by Irish votes.” Balfour, in his address to Manchester, denounced the Liberal programme as “surrounded with obscurity” and warned that Home Rule, Disestablishment, and the destruction of voluntary schools “had lost none of their ancient charm for Radical lawmakers.”
Campbell-Bannerman’s address contained no specific programme and no mention of Home Rule. He attacked the Unionist record — wars and adventures abroad, reckless finance, confused Army reorganisation — and declared that “Protection was immoral, oppressive and corrupting.”
The campaign was notable for its intensity. The Churches issued special prayers; the Free Church Council sent ministers travelling through the country by motor car delivering Liberal speeches; full-page newspaper advertisements defended Chinese labour; cartoons, “especially those against Chinese labour, aroused lively indignation.”
The Liberal Landslide
Polling began on January 12, 1906, and the scale of the Unionist defeat was apparent from the first returns. The Annual Register recorded the results as they came in:

London: Unionists lost heavily, including five seats on a single day (January 16). Cheltenham, Brighton, two divisions of Liverpool, Wednesbury, and West Bromwich fell to the Liberals.
Key defeats: Mr. Lyttelton, the former Colonial Secretary, was defeated at Leamington; Mr. Chaplin, the venerable Protectionist, at Sleaford; Mr. Brodrick at Guildford; Sir W. Hart Dyke, the “Father of the House,” at Dartford — the last to a Labour candidate.
Glasgow: Five of seven divisions passed to Liberal or Labour candidates.
Tyneside and the West Riding: Heavy Liberal gains in precisely the industrial districts to which Chamberlain had appealed.
Birmingham: Alone among industrial centres, Birmingham held solid for the Unionists, generally with increased majorities.

In two seats — Greenwich and King’s Lynn — the Unionist vote was split between a Free Trader and a Tariff Reformer, with the Free Trade Unionist (Lord Hugh Cecil in Greenwich) coming bottom of the poll.
The election ended on February 13, 1906, with the declaration of the result for Orkney and Shetland. By January 30, 666 of the 670 results were already known.
Final results as recorded by the Annual Register:

















































PartySeatsMinisterialistsLiberals377 (or 401 including Labour-allied)Labour53 (29 from the Labour Representation Committee, sitting as an independent party)Nationalists (Irish Parliamentary Party)83Total Ministerialists513OppositionConservatives132Liberal Unionists25Total Opposition157Liberal/Labour/Nationalist majority over all others134
Within the Unionist party, according to a Times analysis, 109 members were Chamberlainite Tariff Reformers, 32 adhered to Balfour’s more moderate programme, and only 11 were returned as Unionist Free Fooders. Wales did not return a single Unionist. Scotland was again “predominantly Liberal.” The House contained 157 Nonconformists — the largest number since Cromwell’s day — and 16 Jewish members.
The prediction that the Liberal government would be dependent on Irish Nationalist votes was decisively falsified: the Liberal and Labour majority alone was overwhelming.
Significance
The 1906 election was one of the most consequential in modern British history. It settled, for a generation, the fiscal question that had dominated politics since Chamberlain’s 1903 speech: Tariff Reform was decisively rejected at the polls, and the free-trade orthodoxy that had prevailed since the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 was reaffirmed. The Unionist party emerged from the contest deeply divided — the leadership question unresolved between Balfour and Chamberlain, the fiscal question still open within the party.
For the Liberals, the landslide represented the reunion of a party that had been fractured by the Boer War and the Home Rule crisis of 1886. Campbell-Bannerman, who had held the party together through its years in the wilderness, was vindicated. The new government commanded an independent majority and could legislate without bargaining for Irish or Labour votes.
The election was also the breakthrough of the Labour Representation Committee, which returned 29 members committed to independent political action. Keir Hardie, the new chairman of the Labour party, seconded the election of the Speaker — a symbolic recognition of Labour’s arrival as a parliamentary force.
Social reform, which the Clayton Rise of Democracy records had received “neither time nor inclination” under the outgoing government, now moved to the centre of the agenda. The King’s Speech of February 1906 promised legislation on Trade Disputes, Workmen’s Compensation, Education, Merchant Shipping, and the reform of Irish government. Old Age Pensions, though not yet funded, were discussed with deputations from the Trades Union Congress. The Annual Register noted that “the social and economic conditions of the rural districts in Great Britain” were to receive “careful consideration,” and the new Parliament included a generation of legislators — Labour members, Nonconformists, Radicals — committed to the active use of state power for social improvement.
The Chinese labour controversy, which had done so much to sway the election, continued to reverberate. The new Colonial Secretary, Lord Elgin, announced that no further Chinese would be imported into the Transvaal pending the establishment of representative government there. The system was gradually brought to an end.
In the longer perspective, the 1906 Liberal government — sustained by the largest majority in a generation — would go on to enact the Trade Disputes Act (1906), the Workmen’s Compensation Act (1906), the Education Act (1906, though blocked by the Lords), old age pensions (1908), labour exchanges (1909), and the Parliament Act (1911) that finally curbed the veto of the House of Lords. The election of 1906 was the political precondition for all of this — a decisive popular verdict that ended the long Conservative ascendancy and opened the Edwardian era of social reform.
Chronology

May 15, 1903 — Joseph Chamberlain’s Birmingham speech proposing imperial preference; Balfour simultaneously defends repeal of the corn duty.
September 1903 — Chamberlain resigns from the Cabinet to campaign for Tariff Reform. Duke of Devonshire also resigns.
1903–1904 — Chamberlain’s nationwide speaking tour; Tariff Reform League founded; Unionist Free Trade Club formed; Liberal party reunites in opposition to Protection.
1904–1905 — By-elections show steady swing against the government; Chinese labour controversy intensifies; Wyndham resigns over Irish policy.
December 4, 1905 — Balfour resigns as Prime Minister.
December 5–10, 1905 — Campbell-Bannerman forms the Liberal government.
January 12 – February 13, 1906 — General election polling.
January 30, 1906 — 666 of 670 results declared.
February 13, 1906 — Final result (Orkney and Shetland); Parliament opens.
February 19, 1906 — King’s Speech outlines social reform programme.

events/entente-cordiale.title: The Entente Cordiale and the Alliance System (1904–1914)
events/entente-cordiale.content:
The Entente Cordiale and the Alliance System (1904–1914)
The Entente Cordiale was the series of diplomatic agreements signed between Britain and France on 8 April 1904 that resolved a century of colonial rivalry and laid the foundation for the Anglo-French alliance that fought the First World War. The agreements marked the end of Britain’s policy of “splendid isolation” and inaugurated the broader entente system — a network of understandings with France, Japan, and Russia that eventually confronted the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy. The transformation from aloof isolation to continental commitment was neither sudden nor deliberate: it was forged in successive crises over Morocco and the Balkans that hardened the alliances into rigid, armed camps.

Splendid Isolation and the Anglo-Japanese Alliance
For most of the nineteenth century, British foreign policy rested on the premise that no continental combination could seriously threaten an island empire commanding the world’s strongest navy. This stance — dubbed “splendid isolation” — was a point of pride for Lord Salisbury, who as late as the turn of the century remained “still wedded to the idea of splendid isolation,” convinced that “the much-discussed continental coalition was a chimera and that England was safe so long as she commanded the Channel.” (Langer, Diplomacy of Imperialism, Vol. II)
The Boer War (1899–1902) shattered this complacency. The war exposed Britain to a storm of continental hostility; Germany made little secret of its sympathy for the Boers, and the European press united in denouncing Britain. “The days of splendid isolation were over,” Chamberlain told Baron Eckardstein; if an alliance with Germany proved impossible, England would have to “reach an understanding with France and Russia, even at the cost of far-reaching concessions.” (Langer) Sir Charles Beresford declared that the time for splendid isolation “was very useful for Noah, but it is not suitable for the present time.” (Langer)
The Search for Allies
The first breach in the policy came in October 1900, when the Boxer Rebellion in China persuaded Chamberlain, Balfour, and Lansdowne to persuade Salisbury to accept an Anglo-German accord on the integrity of China. (Politics & Grand Strategy) More significant was the arrival of Lord Lansdowne as Foreign Secretary in November 1900. Lansdowne “ensured a more dynamic policy, one more to the tastes of the younger men in the Cabinet.” (P&GS) He explored an alliance with Germany through 1901, but Berlin’s reluctance — and the Kaiser’s suspicion that Britain wanted only to drag Germany into a war with Russia — brought the talks to nothing.
The Anglo-Japanese Alliance (1902)
The search for allies turned eastward. “The conclusion of the Anglo-Japanese alliance opened a new era in British foreign policy,” writes Samuel R. Williamson. “Despite recent contentions to the contrary, the alliance was a significant step away from the tradition of splendid isolation.” (P&GS) The treaty, signed on 30 January 1902, was Lansdowne’s first great achievement. By it, he “committed Britain to a course of action which he hoped would discourage further Russian adventures in Manchuria; yet he also had to face the prospect of honouring this commitment if Russia forced the issue.” (P&GS)
The alliance recognised Japan’s “special interests” in Korea and Britain’s in China, and stipulated that if either party went to war with a single power, the other would remain neutral; if either faced two or more powers, the other would come to its aid. Lansdowne explained in the House of Lords that “the old arguments would no longer hold good. The nations were now joined in groups and were heavily armed. War might break out very suddenly, and England therefore had to be prepared.” He hoped the House would not be swayed “by any musty formulas or old-fashioned superstitions.” (Langer)
The reaction in Britain was mixed. William T. Stead found the text “entirely too vague”; others complained that Lansdowne had “exchanged splendid isolation for splendid complication.” (Langer) The French were “most disagreeably surprised” — Cambon spoke “pretty frankly to Lansdowne about the danger of England’s being dragged into war with Russia by Japan.” (Langer) Yet the alliance served its purpose: Japan went to war with Russia in 1904, Britain remained benevolently neutral, and Japan’s victory checked Russian expansion in the Far East.

The Entente Cordiale (1904)
The Anglo-Japanese alliance indirectly advanced the rapprochement with France. “The signing of the Anglo-Japanese alliance presented a profound challenge to French foreign policy,” Williamson notes. “In the first place it necessitated an apparent extension of the Dual Alliance to cover the Far East. Then, because of Russia’s ambitions in the Orient, the new alliance increased the possibility of an Anglo-French conflict.” (P&GS) Deleassé, the French Foreign Minister, had long sought an understanding with Britain, and the new strategic realities gave him his opportunity.
Negotiations and Terms
Anglo-French negotiations, conducted between Lansdowne and the French ambassador Paul Cambon, began in earnest in 1903. King Edward VII’s visit to Paris in May of that year — a personal triumph that melted French suspicion — smoothed the diplomatic path. By early 1904 the two sides had reached agreement on a comprehensive colonial settlement.
The treaties signed on 8 April 1904 comprised several agreements:

Egypt: France recognised Britain’s predominant position in Egypt, accepting the British occupation and administration. In return, Britain recognised France’s special interests in Morocco.
Newfoundland: France surrendered its ancient fishing rights on the “French Shore” of Newfoundland, receiving financial compensation and territorial concessions in West Africa.
Siam: The two powers agreed on spheres of influence in Siam — the Menam valley remaining a buffer state — resolving a long-running source of friction in Southeast Asia.
Madagascar: Britain recognised France’s protectorate over Madagascar and dropped objections to French tariffs on the island.
New Hebrides: The two powers agreed to joint administration of the New Hebrides (the Anglo-French Condominium), ending a dispute that had dragged on for decades.
Morocco: In public clauses, both powers promised mutual diplomatic support for their respective positions in Morocco and Egypt. Secret clauses, which would later cause great controversy, contemplated the eventual partition of Morocco, with Spain receiving the northern coast opposite Gibraltar.

Lansdowne had been careful to safeguard British strategic interests in the Mediterranean. The final accord declared that “to secure free passage of the Straits of Gibraltar” neither power would permit fortifications between Melilla and the River Sebou. In a secret clause, France agreed that this same territory would go to Spain if Morocco were ever partitioned. (P&GS)
Significance
The agreements were “essentially colonial in inspiration and results,” but they “possessed European significance.” (P&GS) By obligating Britain to support France’s position in Morocco, the “diplomatic support” clause increased the chances of Anglo-German friction and inadvertently pulled Britain into the orbit of European power politics. “In subsequent years this provision would become the most important aspect of the entire Anglo-French accord, for diplomatic support could only be meaningful if backed by military and naval force.” (P&GS)
The Entente was not a military alliance. No mutual defence commitment was undertaken, and the Balfour government “demonstrated a naive unawareness of the European aspects of the Moroccan problem” when it accepted the obligation of diplomatic support. (P&GS) But the French ambassador, Paul Cambon, understood what the British public did not: that diplomatic support in a serious crisis would require military backing — and that the logic of the entente would drive Britain inexorably toward continental commitment.

The First Moroccan Crisis
The first test of the Entente Cordiale came sooner than expected. The German government, led by Chancellor von Bülow and the scheming Friedrich von Holstein of the Foreign Office, resolved to test the strength of the Anglo-French understanding by challenging French ambitions in Morocco. The instrument they chose was the Sultan of Morocco himself.
The Kaiser’s Visit to Tangier (1905)
On 31 March 1905, Kaiser Wilhelm II landed at Tangier during a Mediterranean cruise. Escorted by German diplomats, he delivered a speech in which he declared that Germany recognised the Sultan as an independent sovereign and expected the open door for German commerce. He refused to meet the French legation and implied that Germany would not accept a French protectorate over Morocco.
The Kaiser’s visit was a deliberately provocative act. Berlin’s objective was to force Deleassé’s resignation, humiliate France, and demonstrate that the Entente Cordiale was worthless — that Britain would not support France in a serious confrontation.
The Crisis Deepens
Germany demanded an international conference on Morocco, invoking the Madrid Convention of 1880. Deleassé, the architect of the Entente Cordiale, refused to yield. Throughout April and May 1905, the crisis intensified. The French government grew anxious; the army was unprepared for war, and Russia — France’s ally — was hopelessly entangled in the Russo-Japanese War.
The British response was cautious but crucial. Lansdowne warned Germany that Britain would view any attempt to humiliate France as a matter of concern. In April and May 1905, he exchanged notes with Deleassé about Morocco’s ports — exchanges that the French later interpreted as a British pledge of military support. The actual commitment fell short of a promise, but it was enough to stiffen French resistance.
Deleassé’s Fall and the Algeciras Conference
On 6 June 1905, under intense German pressure and abandoned by his own Cabinet colleagues (especially the cautious Premier Rouvier), Deleassé resigned. Rouvier opened direct negotiations with Berlin and agreed to the international conference Germany had demanded. The German press exulted; the entente appeared shattered.
The Algeciras Conference met from January to April 1906. To Germany’s dismay, the conference proved a diplomatic disaster for Berlin. “The fiction of Moroccan independence was preserved but France and Spain took control of the police in eight Moroccan ports,” Williamson records. “Berlin had only succeeded in reducing, not preventing French and Spanish encroachments in Morocco, and this at a very high political cost: German pressure had consolidated and reinforced the Entente Cordiale.” (P&GS)
Britain’s new Liberal Foreign Secretary, Sir Edward Grey, who had taken office in December 1905, firmly supported France throughout the conference. “Grey was inclined to be conciliatory toward Berlin on occasion,” but “he firmly supported French demands on the key question of who controlled the police in the Moroccan ports.” (P&GS) He wrote to Haldane that “if this expectation is disappointed the French will never forgive us. There would also I think be a general feeling in every country that we have behaved meanly and left France in the lurch.” (P&GS)
The Military Conversations
The first Moroccan crisis also produced a more concrete result: the beginning of Anglo-French military staff talks. In January 1906, even before the Algeciras conference opened, General Grierson (the British Director of Military Operations) and Colonel Huguet (the French military attaché) began confidential discussions about how Britain could assist France in the event of a German attack. The talks were authorised by Haldane, the War Secretary, and tacitly approved by Grey and the Prime Minister, Campbell-Bannerman.
These conversations remained secret — most of the Cabinet was not informed — but they “henceforth had government approval and patronage.” (P&GS) They established a pattern that would deepen over the following years: informal military co-ordination that created expectations and obligations far exceeding the formal terms of the entente.

The Anglo-Russian Entente (1907)
If the entente with France resolved Britain’s colonial disputes in Africa and Asia, the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 aimed to remove the last great source of imperial friction: the rivalry with Russia along the northern frontiers of India.
Grey’s Vision
Sir Edward Grey had long wanted a settlement with Russia. He “wanted Russian help in restoring, or perhaps overturning, the balance of power against Germany; he feared the Kaiser’s periodic flirtations with the Tsar; he suspected German intrigues in Persia and elsewhere in the Near East.” (P&GS) Satisfactory relations with St. Petersburg, Grey believed, would remove these dangers.
The Russian defeat by Japan in 1905 had made St. Petersburg more amenable to compromise. Russia was also increasingly preoccupied with the Balkans and less inclined to pursue an aggressive policy in Asia.
The Convention of August 1907
Prolonged negotiations conducted by Sir Arthur Nicolson, the British ambassador to Russia, led to the signature of the Anglo-Russian Convention in August 1907. The convention addressed the three zones of Anglo-Russian rivalry:

Persia: The country was divided into three zones — a Russian sphere in the north, a British sphere in the southeast (adjacent to India), and a neutral buffer zone in between. Britain recognised Russia’s special interests in the north; Russia recognised Britain’s in the south. The arrangement, Grey told the Commons, did not restrict Persian independence, but it effectively partitioned the country into spheres of influence.
Afghanistan: Russia recognised Afghanistan as outside its sphere of influence and agreed to enter into no direct relations with the Ameer. Britain retained its existing treaty relationship with Afghanistan, described as a “buffer state.” Grey insisted that “the Agreement did not restrict the Ameer’s right to develop his own country.” (Annual Register, 1908)
Tibet: Both powers recognised the suzerainty of China over Tibet and agreed to respect Tibetan territorial integrity, refraining from interference in Tibetan internal affairs.

The convention was defended by Grey in the Commons as a measure that would “make for peace.” If “there had been no Agreement, Anglo-Russian relations must have got worse; an opportunity had been seized which might not have returned.” He trusted that “good feeling and confidence would grow up between the two countries.” (Annual Register, 1908)
The Triple Entente
The Anglo-Russian convention completed the triangle of understandings — France with Russia (the Dual Alliance of 1894), France with Britain (the Entente Cordiale of 1904), and now Britain with Russia (the Convention of 1907). These three understandings came to be called the Triple Entente, though they were not a formal alliance. “By 1907 preservation of the Entente Cordiale had become the cardinal feature of Grey’s diplomacy.” (P&GS)
The convention also had strategic implications. “The pressure on India was further eased by Russia’s new concern over the troublesome Balkans.” (P&GS) But it also deepened the division of Europe: the improvement in Anglo-Russian relations “was not duplicated in Anglo-German affairs.” (P&GS) The consolidation of the entente system was matched by growing German suspicion and hostility.

The Crises that Hardened the Alliances
The years 1908–1911 saw a succession of international crises that transformed the loose understandings of the entente system into a rigid structure of opposing alliances, each crisis binding Britain more tightly to France.
The Bosnian Crisis (1908–1909)
In October 1908, Austria-Hungary unilaterally annexed the Ottoman provinces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which it had administered since the Congress of Berlin (1878). The annexation outraged Russia, which considered itself the protector of the Slav peoples of the Balkans, and enraged Serbia, which aspired to unite the South Slavs under its own leadership.
The crisis brought Europe to the brink of war. Russia, weakened after its defeat by Japan, sought diplomatic support from France and Britain, but received only tepid encouragement. In March 1909, Germany delivered an ultimatum to St. Petersburg: recognise the annexation or face war with Austria-Hungary and Germany. Russia, unprepared for war, capitulated. “Not until the Bosnian crisis of 1908–1909 was there a significant modification in the alliance’s laissez-faire approach to military planning,” with the Austrian and German chiefs of staff opening direct correspondence in January 1909. (P&GS)
The Bosnian humiliation had lasting consequences. It convinced Russian statesmen that the Triple Entente needed to be strengthened into a more effective counterweight to the Central Powers. It also emboldened Austria-Hungary, creating a pattern of German-backed Austrian aggression in the Balkans that would repeat itself in July 1914.
The Casablanca Incident (1908–1909)
Even before the Bosnian crisis subsided, a further Franco-German confrontation erupted. In September 1908, the German consul at Casablanca attempted to conceal deserters from the French Foreign Legion. The French arrested the Germans, and a diplomatic crisis ensued.
The international situation, “already tense because of Vienna’s annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, grew dangerous.” (P&GS) Grey, though cautious, secretly prepared for war. On 5 November 1908 he alerted the Admiralty to “make preparations in case Germany sent France an ultimatum and the Cabinet decided that we must assist France.” (P&GS) By mid-November, Grey, Haldane, and Asquith had resolved in principle to aid France. “Haldane told Asquith that if we failed France, he would not give ten years’ purchase for the British Empire.” (P&GS)
The crisis ended with a German retreat in early 1909, but it revealed the depth of Britain’s commitment. The Casablanca dispute was settled by arbitration, and a Franco-German declaration on Morocco was signed in February 1909, recognising Morocco’s independence while affirming France’s “special political interests.” Hardinge called it “a complete vindication of the Anglo-French ‘entente.’ The Germans have thrown up the sponge.” (P&GS)
The Second Moroccan Crisis / Agadir (1911)
The most dangerous pre-war crisis began in April 1911, when French forces, ostensibly to protect European lives, occupied Fez, the Moroccan capital. The French action violated the Act of Algeciras, which had guaranteed Moroccan independence.
Germany, under Foreign Secretary Alfred von Kiderlen-Wächter, decided to exact compensation. On 1 July 1911, the German gunboat Panther — soon joined by the light cruiser Berlin — appeared off the Atlantic port of Agadir. The “Panther’s leap” startled the world. “The coup d’Agadir transformed the Moroccan question into an international crisis.” (P&GS)
The British Response
The Panther’s arrival “completely surprised the three-day-old Caillaux government.” (P&GS) De Selves, the French Foreign Minister, wanted to send a French warship to Mogador, but the British Cabinet refused to co-operate. On 4 July, the Cabinet resolved to remain faithful to the 1904 obligations to France, to oppose German demands for tripartite negotiations over Morocco, and to propose instead four-power talks including Spain. But it “firmly refused to send any ship to Morocco.” Grey was ordered to remind the French “that they must recognise that largely by their own action, a return to the status quo ante has become difficult.” (P&GS)
Grey’s position was complicated by divisions within the British government. Sir Arthur Nicolson and Eyre Crowe at the Foreign Office pressed for a strong pro-French stance. Lord Loreburn, Lord Morley, and the radical wing of the Cabinet urged caution. The man caught between these approaches was Grey — “patient, wary, and persistently evasive,” he “tried to bridge the gulf between the Cabinet and the Foreign Office.” (P&GS)
The Crisis Peaks
Through July and August 1911, Europe stood on the edge of war. The critical moment came in July 21, when David Lloyd George, the radical Chancellor of the Exchequer and a man generally regarded as pro-peace, delivered the Mansion House speech. He declared that Britain’s interests were directly engaged in Morocco and that peace at any price was not a policy for a great nation. The speech shocked Germany and signalled that Britain would stand by France.
Negotiations between France and Germany dragged on through the summer, with Germany demanding the entire French Congo as compensation for abandoning Morocco. In November, a settlement was finally reached: Germany recognised a French protectorate over Morocco in return for a strip of the French Congo (about 100,000 square miles). The British, whose interests in Morocco were safeguarded, raised no objection.
Consequences of Agadir
“The Moroccan crisis of 1911 exerted a profound impact upon Anglo-French relations. The jolt of the Agadir incident prompted both governments to reconsider every facet of the entente relationship — diplomatic, military, naval.” (P&GS) The crisis produced three crucial outcomes:


Anglo-French naval conversations: In 1912, Britain agreed to concentrate its battle fleet in the North Sea, while France concentrated its fleet in the Mediterranean. This redistribution meant that Britain became responsible for defending the French Channel coast, and France for defending British interests in the Mediterranean. It was, in effect, a naval alliance.


Anglo-Belgian staff talks revived: The British General Staff renewed its planning for continental operations, now envisaging the rapid dispatch of the British Expeditionary Force to the left wing of the French army.


Hardening of attitudes: Agadir “deepened anti-German feeling in Britain and convinced many in the Cabinet that the entente must be maintained at all costs.” As Hankey later recorded (Hankey, Man of Secrets, Vol. I), the crisis prompted the formation of a special “very secret defence meeting” attended by Asquith, Grey, McKenna, Lloyd George, and Churchill — the inner circle that would effectively manage British strategy in 1914.


The Hardening of the Alliances (1912–1914)
By 1912 the entente system had been transformed. The loose understandings of 1904–1907 were now underpinned by detailed military and naval planning, joint strategic preparations, and the expectation — on both sides of the Channel — that Britain and France would fight together in any major European war.
The Anglo-French naval agreement of 1912 was the decisive step. When the Committee of Imperial Defence met on 23 August 1911, in the aftermath of Agadir, it heard the General Staff and the Admiralty present conflicting views on Britain’s continental strategy. The outcome was a compromise that in practice committed Britain to the defence of France. “Henceforward the preservation of the entente became a question not merely of diplomatic convenience but of national strategy.”
Grey’s critics — and there were many on the radical left and among the Unionist opposition — argued that the entente system had entangled Britain in dangerous commitments without the safeguards of a formal alliance. Grey himself insisted that Britain remained free to decide its own course. But when war came in August 1914, the decision was never seriously in doubt. The entente system had created the strategic, diplomatic, and psychological conditions for British intervention.

Assessment
The abandonment of “splendid isolation” and the construction of the entente system was the most consequential transformation in British foreign policy of the pre-war period. The Anglo-Japanese Alliance (1902) was the first breach; the Entente Cordiale (1904) established the principle of colonial co-operation with France; the Anglo-Russian Convention (1907) completed the diplomatic alignment; and the crises of 1905–1911 welded these understandings into a de facto alliance.
The entente system achieved its immediate purpose — it ended the dangerous isolation that the Boer War had revealed and checked German ambitions on the Continent. But it also locked Britain into continental politics, created expectations that could not easily be renounced, and made a general European war more, not less, likely. As Samuel R. Williamson observed, the Entente Cordiale “began as a colonial settlement” but “ended as a military commitment that would send the British Expeditionary Force to France in 1914 to fight alongside the French army.”

events/first-coalition-1915.title: The First Coalition Government (1915)
events/first-coalition-1915.content:
The First Coalition Government (1915)
In the late spring of 1915 the pure Liberal ministry that had carried the United Kingdom into the Great War came to an end. Nine months of fighting on the Western Front, the opening of the Dardanelles enterprise, a public agitation over shells and drink, and a rupture at the Admiralty between Lord Fisher and Mr. Churchill made the continuation of single-party government impossible. Mr. Asquith remained Prime Minister, but he reconstructed his administration as a Coalition in which Unionists and Labour sat on the Treasury Bench with Liberals. The change did not settle the war; it marked the moment when party government, as peacetime Britain had known it, yielded to a wartime national ministry whose first great domestic instrument was the Ministry of Munitions under Mr. Lloyd George.
Drink, Shells, and the Spring Crisis
By the spring of 1915 the country was already deep in the industrial and social strain of a long war. The Annual Register records that the daily cost of the war had risen above three and a half millions sterling, and that recruiting for 1916, blockade policy, and the partial application of the Declaration of London were under constant public scrutiny. Into this atmosphere the Government thrust a second controversy — drink.
On 29 April Lloyd George brought before the House proposals framed as a clearing of the road to munitions output. Production of shells and war material, he insisted, was “life for the Empire.” The drink trade was presented as an obstacle to that production; restriction of the liquor traffic was therefore urged not as a temperance crusade but as a munitions measure. The same weeks saw a fierce Press campaign, led by The Times and the Daily Mail, on the shortage of high-explosive shell at the front. The Northcliffe papers hammered the War Office and the Government; the cry for a Ministry of Munitions became a political force that no Cabinet could ignore.
Lord Kitchener remained Secretary of State for War, the great figure of voluntary recruiting and of the New Armies. The War Office, however, was increasingly identified in the public mind with the shell shortage. The munitions agitation and the drink proposals together destroyed the atmosphere in which a purely Liberal Cabinet could claim unchallenged authority over the conduct of the war.
Fisher, Churchill, and the Breaking of the Liberal Ministry
At the Admiralty the strain took a different form. The Dardanelles enterprise, pressed through the early months of 1915 as a naval and then a combined operation, had divided counsel. Corbett records that the resignations of Lord Fisher and Mr. Churchill, coinciding with the formation of a Coalition Government, closed the first phase of the naval war of 1915. Fisher’s departure as First Sea Lord made the position of the existing Liberal ministry, already under fire over munitions, untenable. The Annual Register treats the reconstruction of the Government as the political consequence of that double crisis — shells and Admiralty — rather than as a sudden conversion to the principle of coalition for its own sake.
Asquith did not resign the Premiership. He reconstructed. The Unionist leaders, who had given patriotic support since the outbreak of war, were brought into office; Labour accepted a place on the Treasury Bench. The new Unionist members of the Cabinet required, under the existing law, re-election on taking office, and an emergency Bill was prepared to deal with that inconvenience. The King, George V, remained the constitutional centre of the reconstruction; the party truce of August 1914 was converted into a formal sharing of power.
The Coalition Meets: 3 June 1915
Both Houses reassembled on 3 June for the first sitting of the Coalition. The Commons presented a novel appearance. Unionists and Labour sat on the Treasury Bench with Liberals; the old party geography of the chamber was visibly altered. The Annual Register marks the occasion as the opening of a new political chapter: not the end of party, but its suspension for the duration of the war emergency.
The reconstructed ministry retained Asquith at its head and Kitchener at the War Office. Lloyd George left the Exchequer to take the newly constituted Ministry of Munitions — the institutional answer to the shell crisis and to the Press campaign of the spring. The Admiralty passed into new hands after Fisher’s and Churchill’s resignations. The Coalition was thus, from the first day of its parliamentary life, a munitions ministry as much as a war ministry: its domestic priority was the organisation of national output for the armies in France and for the expedition at gallipoli.
Summer and the Unsettled Year
Through the summer of 1915 the Coalition governed under the continuous pressure of war news — Zeppelin raids, the air war, the second anniversary of the war marked by patriotic meetings on 4 August, and the successful campaign to place cotton on the absolute contraband list. The Ministry of Munitions began its work of concentrating and expanding shell and war-material production. The Northcliffe Press continued to criticise Ministers on munitions, compulsion, and the general conduct of the war; collision between Press and Cabinet became a standing feature of the Coalition’s first half-year.
At the close of 1915 the Annual Register records that National Service had “not escaped” public discussion though it remained unsettled. Recruiting for 1916 was already a source of anxiety. The blockade and the partial Declaration of London were under scrutiny. Compulsory military service was left as the chief internal question for the new year — a question the Coalition would meet in 1916 with the Military Service Acts, after the Derby Scheme had shown the limits of voluntary attestation. The first Coalition had been formed to win the war and to produce the munitions the war required; it had not yet decided how far the State would go in compelling men as well as organising shells.
Aftermath
The Coalition of May–June 1915 ended the last purely Liberal government of the long reform era that had run from the People’s Budget through the Parliament Act and the Irish Home Rule crisis. It did not end Asquith’s Premiership; that would wait until the further reconstruction of December 1916. It did, however, fix the pattern of wartime British politics: multi-party government, a Ministry of Munitions under Lloyd George, Kitchener still at the War Office, and a public argument over compulsion that would dominate the following year. The Easter Rising of 1916 and the military-service legislation would test the Coalition on Irish and recruiting ground; the gallipoli evacuation would close the Eastern enterprise that had helped to break the old Admiralty. For the moment, in the summer of 1915, the achievement was simpler and more constitutional: the war would be fought by a national ministry, not by a single party.
