events/gallipoli.title: The Gallipoli Campaign (1915–1916)
events/gallipoli.content:
The Gallipoli Campaign (1915–1916)
The attempt to force the Dardanelles and open a way to Constantinople was the most ambitious combined operation undertaken by the British Empire in the first year and a half of the Great War. Conceived, after the Dogger Bank action, as a naval stroke that might knock the Ottoman Empire out of the conflict, relieve Russia, and fix Bulgaria’s attitude, it became a prolonged campaign on the Gallipoli Peninsula — bombardments in February and March 1915, the landings of 25 April, the battles for Krithia, the Suvla Bay effort in August, and, at the year’s end, an evacuation of extraordinary difficulty executed with almost incredible success. The enterprise tested British command of the sea in a secondary theatre, strained the Liberal ministry into the first Coalition, and closed without the strategic prize for which it had been opened.
Decision: After Dogger Bank
It was on 28 January 1915, four days after the Dogger Bank action, that the final decision to attack the Dardanelles was taken. Although Vice-Admiral Carden had been informed that his plan was accepted, the matter was still far from settled. Events had been tending toward Salonica; Greece’s reply of 27 January required Bulgarian co-operation or, failing that, Roumania’s, and if Bulgarian neutrality could not be assured, two Entente army corps in addition. Under those conditions nothing could be done from Salonica for the present, and opinion solidified in favour of the Dardanelles as the quickest way of fixing Bulgaria’s attitude. Russia was particularly eager after the heavy defeat of the Turks at Ardahan and the annihilation of their Vth Corps at Sarakamuish.
Serious opposition came from the best British naval opinion, with Lord Fisher at its head: a purely naval attack on a strongly fortified base was a departure from established doctrine, and once only had such an attempt succeeded, when Rooke seized Gibraltar by coup de main. The First Lord’s relative-strength memorandum of 27 January argued that superiority was sufficient for a subsidiary operation without prejudicing North Sea command. When the War Council met on the 28th the Board was not in a position to give a firm opinion; all that was clear was the political necessity for action and the decisive advantages success would bring. For Lord Kitchener the Dardanelles was essentially diversionary — the view that appealed to the French, who promised four battleships and a minesweeper flotilla under the British Admiral. Augagneur declared that the plan permitted operations to be broken off at any stage without loss of prestige.
Opening of the Naval Attack
Carden had been pushing preparations without interruption except for weather. All January except three days it had blown a gale from the south-west; February brought gales from the north-east. Since 15 January no active operation had been undertaken; that day the French submarine Saphir, against strict orders, attempted to repeat B 11’s exploit, ran aground inside the Straits and was lost. The magnitude of the force required two additional flag officers: Rear-Admiral Rosslyn Wemyss to take charge of the Allied base at Mudros, and Rear-Admiral de Robeck as second-in-command. Commodore Keyes became Chief of Staff. Carden’s flag flew in Inflexible, still bearing Falkland scars; learning that Queen Elizabeth’s accident greatly reduced her speed and that Goeben was active again, he was allowed to keep Inflexible as the only ship able to bring Goeben to action.
Ships gathered from home and from distant commerce-protection stations freed by the Falklands and the destruction of the Emden, together with four French battleships under Guépratte, bringing the Allied fleet to sixteen capital ships. Command presented difficulty under the Convention of 6 August 1914, which gave France general direction in the Mediterranean; the French were willing that Dardanelles operations should be under the British Admiral but wished to take over the Syrian coast as far south as Jaffa, and on those lines the matter was amicably adjusted.
The first bombardment opened on 19 February against Helles, Orkanie, Kum Kale and Sedd el Bahr — the first test of whether long-range naval gunfire could silence modernised works without an observing station ashore. By the 25th four ships working in pairs ran up to the jaws of the Straits, engaging the outer forts with secondary armament down to 3,000 yards, aiming “to destroy each individual gun by a direct hit.” De Robeck ran with Vengeance and Cornwallis; Guépratte with Suffren and Charlemagne. Agamemnon was hit seven times with armour-piercing shell in ten minutes — three killed, five seriously wounded — yet nothing that could not be put right. Queen Elizabeth got direct hits on Helles, one dismounting a 9.4-inch; by noon not one of the forts was firing. After 3.0 the minesweeping trawlers closed the entrance. The outer defences were practically reduced.
The Narrows, 18 March
While officers on the spot were beginning to realise the full measure of the enterprise, elsewhere the initial operations were taken to promise success. Venizelos was trying to induce the King of Greece to offer his fleet and one infantry division; Bulgaria began to trim her sails; on 4 March Italy made her first approaches for joining the Allies. Russia replied on 3 March that a whole army corps was being prepared at Odessa and Batum within a fortnight or three weeks of the forcing of the Dardanelles. Kitchener’s despatch to Birdwood on 4 March still held that the fleet was to break through alone — expected in the Sea of Marmara by the 20th — with over 60,000 men concentrated at Lemnos by then. Till large-scale military assistance was certain, troops were not to be used in the Gallipoli peninsula at all; the real objective was Constantinople. Birdwood again pointed out little chance of the fleet getting through alone.
By the operation orders completed before Carden had to resign, the fleet had been reorganised in three divisions under de Robeck, Hayes-Sadler, and Guépratte. The General Idea was to silence the defences of the Narrows and of the minefields simultaneously — not expecting destruction of forts at 8,000 yards, but hoping to dominate them sufficiently to prevent interference with sweeping. Dawn of the 18th came with warm southerly breeze and cloudless sky. At 8.15 the signal to carry on flew from the flagship; at 10.30 Agamemnon led the First Division in. The first half-hour gave good promise — little or no reply from the forts, though barrage fire increased. Then the undetected minefield in Eren Keui Bay sank Bouvet, Irresistible and Ocean, crippled Inflexible and Gaulois, and forced the abandonment of the purely naval attack — the change of plan that committed the army to the peninsula.
Landings of 25 April
Since the army had been sent out merely to make good what the navy had won, it had to concentrate in Egypt for reorganisation. Civilian-manned trawlers had proved unfit for minesweeping under fire, so the flotilla was reorganised with naval ratings; beach-gear and a landing flotilla had to be improvised. Air reconnaissances confirmed that damage to the Narrows forts was slight and proved new works covering the vital Kephez minefields. Organisation of the combined attack went forward under Sir Ian Hamilton.
It was not till midday on 23 April — a full five weeks since the attack on the Narrows — that the weather began to give promise of the fine spell essential for the operation. De Robeck gave the word for preliminary movements about sundown. At least 200 vessels — over sixty British transports, over thirty trawlers, and well over ninety ships of war — moved in confined waters without mutual interference. On the 24th Hamilton transferred headquarters from Arcadian to Queen Elizabeth. Shortly after midnight the sea was perfectly smooth; in brilliant moonlight Wemyss transferred the three leading battalions of the main landing to Euryalus, Implacable and Cornwallis without a hitch. By 4.30 a.m. on the 25th the Royal Naval Division was off Xeros Island; Dartmouth and Doris bombarded the Bulair lines while trawlers swept Bakla Bay as though a landing were intended. The feint’s effect on Liman von Sanders was immediate: he moved the VIIth Division toward Bulair and for over twenty-four hours had his post of command near the central fort of the Bulair lines — leaving the Gaba Tepe–Helles landings to develop against the IXth Division’s coast cordon and the incomplete XIXth Division in reserve at Boghali, while Australian and New Zealand troops went ashore at Anzac Cove and the XXIXth Division at the Helles beaches. The River Clyde carried troops into V Beach; Y Beach was seized by the King’s Own Scottish Borderers and Plymouth Marines.
At Anzac on the 26th the troops had dug themselves in; for two or three hours the situation remained critical, but fire from the sea, which prisoners afterwards described as appalling, made organised assault almost impossible. By 9.0 a.m. Queen Elizabeth had knocked out the most annoying battery and the Turkish attack died away exhausted. At the southern beaches progress had been slight. Hunter-Weston reported the XXIXth Division not strong enough without further assistance to take Hill 141 dominating Sedd el Bahr. Y Beach, so cleverly seized and so vital to the hoped-for envelopment, was abandoned after night attacks from Krithia and a serious misunderstanding as to re-embarkation orders — the failure of envelopment; the initial advance was already hardening into trench warfare.
Krithia and the Submarine Threat
When news reached home of how far short the first effort had fallen of the coup de main planned against Achi Baba, it became clear the enterprise could not be carried on without greater military force. Nothing could be moved from France or Home — Egypt was the only source. On 27 April Kitchener told Hamilton that Maxwell would send anything asked for; embarkation of the East Lancashire Territorial Division and over 3,000 Anzac reinforcements commenced on 1 May. Attacks on Krithia and Achi Baba, supported by naval bombardments, marked the spring fighting; the Third Battle of Krithia in early June closed a phase in which the army’s inability to break the Ottoman defence had extended to the squadron itself.
It was not only reduced in strength: the long-expected hour had come when it could no longer claim a full working command of the Aegean. Queen Elizabeth had gone; under the Italian Convention Rear-Admiral Thursby left with four battleships, joining the Italian fleet at Taranto on 27 May. Liman von Sanders combined the first effort of the German submarines with a desperate attack to drive the Anzacs into the sea on 19 May; the supporting ships kept up continuous fire, and though the Turks had never fought with greater determination they had to desist with nothing gained and losses so great that they asked for an armistice to bury the dead. After 19 May the Turkish War Office officially stated that the British defences at Anzac were too strong to enable anything to be effected without heavy artillery. Lieutenant-Commander E. C. Boyle in E 14 and later E 11 carried the war into the Sea of Marmara; the supporting battleships Triumph and Majestic were lost to submarine attack — a sharp reminder that the Aegean was no longer a protected anchorage.
Suvla
After over three months’ campaigning in a strictly limited area a strategical surprise was to be attempted — not at a distance, but at a point within the area, half a day’s march from the enemy’s reserves. In the dark the troops must start and in the dark they must be put ashore, on a beach that it had been impossible to survey adequately, and by a force exceeding in number anything that had been attempted before. A period of moonless nights was essential; the new moon was on 10 August and the attack was fixed for the night of 6–7 August. As a preliminary step from 7,000 to 8,000 Anzac drafts were got ashore during the nights following 31 July, together with forty guns and extra transport, without being detected. Five brigades to reinforce the Anzac Corps were landed secretly from Mudros and hidden in dug-outs constructed by General Birdwood.
The original intention, as agreed between the Admiral and the General, was to land the whole force on the Nibrunesi beach, outside and just south of the bay — so “steep-to” that destroyers could run in with their bows almost touching. So it stood in the operation orders which Hamilton issued to Lieutenant-General Sir F. W. Stopford on 29 July as commander of the new IXth Corps: the primary object was “to secure Suvla Bay as a base for all the forces operating in the northern zone”; if he found this could be done without using the whole of his force, he was to assist Birdwood’s attack by an advance on Biyuk Anafarta. Stopford came to the conclusion that the bay could not be secured without seizing Anafarta Ridge, requiring two brigades inside Suvla Bay. De Robeck and his staff saw serious objections: the old chart was not to be relied on — the eastern shore had apparently silted up and the north shore was foul with reefs. Under these conditions of uncertainty they could not undertake to land two brigades at once. The soldiers still insisted that Karakol ridge at least must be seized at once as part of the covering position. The landing was made; the opportunity of the first days was not seized; the Turks reinforced; and the collapse of the Suvla stroke left the Allied forces holding three separated footholds — Helles, Anzac, and Suvla — without the decisive command of the Peninsula that alone could have opened the Straits.
Doom of Gallipoli
Ever since the failure at Suvla a general conviction had been growing that only two courses were open in the Near East: push on in increased force or abandon the attempt to open the Dardanelles. Committed by the importunity of the French ally to more than had ever been contemplated in the Balkans, the necessary increase of force for Gallipoli was not to be found. On 2 November the Prime Minister announced that henceforward the war would be directed by a new War Council of from three to five members of the Cabinet. The original members of the Council, known officially as the “War Committee,” were Mr. Asquith in the chair; Mr. Balfour (First Lord of the Admiralty); Lord Kitchener (Secretary of State for War); Sir Edward Grey (Foreign Secretary); and Mr. Lloyd George (Minister of Munitions). Their first meeting was on 3 November, to consider the question of evacuating Gallipoli.
In the middle of October Sir Ian Hamilton had returned to England and been succeeded by General Sir C. C. Monro; during the short interregnum Lieutenant-General Sir W. R. Birdwood assumed control. On 31 October, after conferring with the Corps Commanders and visiting each sector, Monro telegraphed a very unfavourable account: the troops were too much exhausted and had lost too many officers to make a further effort with any prospect of success, and he had no hesitation in advising evacuation. Maxwell, responsible for Egypt, strongly urged holding on if possible. Birdwood shrank from the loss of prestige and life that evacuation would probably entail, and was opposed unless a strike could be made elsewhere immediately. General Byng at Suvla thought voluntary withdrawal was possible without much loss; General Davies at Helles agreed with Monro.
Ministers were also confronted with wide divergence on the naval side. The Eastern Mediterranean Naval Staff had been working for months at a detailed plan by which they were confident another attempt to force the Straits would succeed — counting on increased ammunition, monitors, aircraft, and a greatly improved mine-sweeping service. Admiral Wemyss fully concurred; Admiral de Robeck was less sanguine. The moving spirit of the proposed scheme was his Chief of Staff, Commodore Roger Keyes, whom de Robeck sent home to lay the plan before the Admiralty (arrived 28 October): rush the Straits by surprise at dawn with two squadrons under support of a third. The War Committee, under the pressure of Balkan commitments and Monro’s advice, moved toward evacuation rather than a renewed naval coup de main.
Evacuation
The withdrawal was an operation which no one concerned could contemplate without the gravest misgiving. Nothing of the kind on a scale so great or under conditions so formidable had ever been attempted before. From beaches under artillery fire, without any safe natural harbour, some 90,000 men with two hundred guns had to be re-embarked in the face of an undefeated enemy whose trenches were nowhere more than three hundred yards from the British — and in some places only five — at a season of treacherous weather, in confined waters open to submarine attack, the whole work carried out at night. “As a piece of combined work… it must surely stand as a feat of arms unparalleled in the annals of war.”
Secrecy confined the labour of working out the scheme to the few naval and military officers who had to know. A joint staff conference decided that the operation must be conducted in three stages. The first was purely preparatory: the evacuation of all troops, animals and material not required for a defensive winter campaign. That stage was completed by 10 December, when Admiral Wemyss received definite orders to proceed; no fewer than 10,000 sick — frostbite alone numbering 3,700 — had already been re-embarked. The intermediate stage withdrew all men, guns and animals not required for the tactical defence of the positions during the final stage, which it was hoped would take only two nights more. For the final stage nothing but fighting men and medical personnel were to be left, not exceeding what the navy could embark in two nights — mainly a question of small craft. Wemyss held about one-third of the craft in reserve; twenty thousand men at each place was the utmost found possible, for with them must come the last of the guns. The troops would have to rely almost entirely on the ships for artillery support. Everything depended on lulling the enemy to sleep: all through the intermediate stage a show was made of landing animals and stores, and firing after midnight was avoided so as to accustom him to a routine of nocturnal inactivity.
The withdrawal from Suvla Bay and Anzac took place on the night of 18–19 December. It took the Turks completely by surprise; they were not even conscious of the progress of the operation until the whole of it had been concluded. Not a single life was lost; only three men were wounded. Six guns were left behind after being destroyed, and a relatively small quantity of stores. Mr. Asquith, announcing the result in the House of Commons, stated that so successful a result had seemed to him almost incredible. A few days later Sir Charles Monro was appointed to the command of the First Army in France, being succeeded in Gallipoli by Lieutenant-General Sir Archibald Murray. The final withdrawal from Helles followed in early January 1916.
Aftermath
The campaign had failed in its strategic object. The Straits remained closed; Russia was not relieved by that route; the Ottoman Empire was not knocked out. Looking over the year as a whole, the Annual Register observed that in the Dardanelles the event of chief importance was the general recognition of the failure of the expedition; at the end of the year it was gradually becoming apparent that the main theatre of operations in the future was likely to be on the Western front. Political consequences in London had already been severe. The resignations of Fisher and Churchill, coinciding with the formation of the Coalition, closed the first phase of the naval war of 1915. On 15 September Kitchener, speaking in the Lords, still declared that there was abundant evidence of a process of demoralisation among the German-led — “or rather German-driven” — Turks; by November the War Committee was deciding evacuation. Yet the re-embarkation itself stood as a masterpiece of combined staff work and discipline under conditions that had seemed to promise disaster. The Peninsula was left to the Turks; the troops re-embarked for Egypt and other theatres; and the Eastern Mediterranean effort of 1915 passed into the longer war of attrition that would outlast the year opened by the outbreak of the Great War.

events/german-spring-offensive-1918.title: The German Spring Offensive (1918)
events/german-spring-offensive-1918.content:
The German Spring Offensive (1918)
In the spring of 1918 the Central Powers struck their last great blow on the Western Front. After the treaty of Brest-Litovsk the Germans transferred large masses of their Eastern Armies westward; once they had finally imposed their will upon Russia, some 70 per cent. of the Eastern Army seems to have been moved. The new offensive stood under the supreme direction of von Hindenburg and von Ludendorff; the tactical details, the Annual Register records, appear to have been devised by General von Hutier, who had distinguished himself at Riga the previous year. Von Hutier brought German tacticians back to assault by enormous masses of men combined with artillery barrage, rifle-fire, flame-throwers, tanks, and other devices more perfectly than anything yet seen. It was against the British Army that the full force of the first blow fell — a crisis that followed the long attrition of Passchendaele, tested the Coalition under Lloyd George, and, by forcing unity of command under Foch, prepared the ground for the Allied counter-offensive that closed with the Armistice.
Extension of the British Line
The British front had been lengthened. The British had taken over a further section from the French, and the front now extended south of St. Quentin as far as Barisis — the first extension since December 1916, when the French section of the old Somme battlefield had been taken over. The new sector was 28 miles long; the total British front was 125 miles. In view of subsequent events the announcement that the British had taken over the St. Quentin line was of peculiar interest.
Hankey’s biographer records the political and military history of that extension. At the Boulogne Conference in September 1917 the principle that the British line should be extended was accepted, though distance and timing were left to the two commanders-in-chief. Haig and Pétain met at Amiens in mid-October; Haig, though reluctant to divert strength from Flanders, accepted extension as far as Barisis (between St. Quentin and Soissons, just south of the Oise). The German counter-attack at Cambrai at the end of November and the need to reinforce the Italians after Caporetto caused Haig to postpone execution. Clemenceau and Pétain pressed for a still longer extension to Berry-au-Bac on the Aisne; the British refused that larger demand but completed the take-over to Barisis by the end of January 1918. Hankey, after visiting the front with Smuts in January, opposed further extension south and judged the Army “in splendid fettle” and able to “hold against any attack,” though he held it would not be right to expose it to another prolonged attack of the Somme–Flanders type — confidence later judged over-optimistic on the defensive side.
At home the winter was cast as a civilian campaign. On 1 January the Prime Minister appealed for War Bonds, economy, and work as the home firing-line; submarine sinkings in 1917 had cost over 6,000,000 tons of merchant shipping (British net tonnage down some 3,500,000). When Parliament opened on 12 February the King’s Speech insisted that until honourable peace principles were recognised the war must be prosecuted with all vigour. In the Debate on the Address, Asquith pressed for information about the Supreme War Council at Versailles and whether it had assumed executive powers; Lloyd George refused detail that would inform the enemy, but assured the House that the extension of the Council’s powers had been adopted unanimously by military as well as civil Allied representatives — Russia’s elimination having completely changed the Western balance.
21 March: The Blow
It was known many weeks before that the German General Staff were preparing an attack by far the most terrible yet seen in the war. At dawn on Thursday, 21 March, an intense bombardment opened along over 50 miles of the British front, from the Scarpe to the neighbourhood of the Oise. Haig’s despatch, among the Public Documents of the Annual Register, records that shortly before 5 a.m. a bombardment of great intensity, with gas and high explosive from all natures of artillery and trench mortars, opened against practically the whole fronts of the Fifth and Third Armies from the Oise to the Scarpe, while road centres and railways as far back as St. Pol were engaged by high-velocity guns. By about 9.45 a.m. a general attack had been launched on a 54-mile front between the Oise and the Sensée. Favoured by a thick white fog which hid S.O.S. signals from artillery and machine-gunners, and in numbers which made loss of direction impossible, the German infantry forced their way into the foremost defensive zone. Until 1 p.m. the fog made it impossible to see more than 50 yards in any direction.
The Germans obtained a considerable numerical superiority over the Fifth Army, west of St. Quentin, and, partly for that reason and partly because the method of attack was both new and ingenious, broke clean through the British lines at the first attempt. The preliminary bombardment, though short, was so intense that the defensive works in the advanced lines were completely destroyed, and the Fifth Army under General Sir H. Gough was compelled from the first day to execute a rapid retreat. The first German report claimed 200 guns and 16,000 prisoners on 21 March; the Register finds nothing improbable in those claims. The British Third Army under General Sir J. Byng, north of the Fifth, was obliged to fall back. During the next few days the German advance was extremely rapid.
Haig’s despatch sets the British order of battle on the morning of 21 March: twenty-nine infantry divisions and three cavalry on the original battle front, nineteen infantry in line (Third Army eight in line and seven in reserve; Fifth Army fourteen divisions and three cavalry, three infantry and three cavalry in reserve). Launched on about 54 miles, the offensive spread northwards on 28 March until from La Fère to beyond Gavrelle some 63 miles were involved. On that front seventy-three German divisions engaged the Third and Fifth Armies and the right of the First, opposed at first by twenty-two British infantry divisions in line with twelve infantry and three cavalry in close reserve. Before the end of March eight further British divisions came south; prior to 9 April four more were engaged, making forty-six British infantry and three cavalry divisions on the Somme battle front.
Amiens, Arras, and the Check on the Somme
The strategic object of the first blow was to break the British–French junction and open the road toward Amiens and the Channel. In the last days of the advance upon Amiens Allied losses remained serious; on 29 March the Germans reported 70,000 prisoners and 1,100 guns, of which no fewer than 40,000 prisoners and 600 guns had been taken by von Hutier’s army, which had first broken Gough west of St. Quentin. North of Montdidier the Germans were not more than twelve miles from Amiens.
On 28 March the enemy attacked north of the Scarpe intending to capture Arras, but completely failed — partly because his new method had now been realised by the British, and partly because he was not, as at St. Quentin, favoured by thick fog. In the first days of April the rush was stemmed at least temporarily; advances became local, and French and British reinforcements arrived. The British Government largely depleted the great army kept at Home; several hundred thousand men were rushed across the Channel at the end of March and during April, and troops came up from Italy. The United States decided that numerous partially trained American regiments in France, not yet ready as separate Divisions, should be temporarily brigaded with French or British battalions to meet the extreme need for man-power.
On 4 April the Germans attacked again east of Amiens with new reserve divisions, but gains were of the slightest local significance; all main roads to Amiens were held, and between Hamel and the Roye road even advanced Allied positions held firm, only villages such as Morisel and Mailly-Raineval being surrendered. Public confidence in France and England in the security of Amiens and of Anglo-French communications somewhat revived. The German rush had depended mainly on speed; once the pace slowed at the end of the first week, the Allies ceased mere resistance to a continuous flood. Haig records that by early April the hope of opening the Amiens road ended in an exceedingly costly repulse; with the failure of 4 and 5 April the Somme battle-front offensive ceased for the time being. The price was a considerable sacrifice of ground and a great expenditure of reserves — material to the fighting farther north.
Haig attributed the Fifth Army’s retirement first to inadequate forces for so strong an attack: the front’s extent made adequate reserves at all threatened points impossible; vital sectors had to be secured and risks accepted elsewhere. In the northern and central portions no ground could be given up; in the southern sector alone, over the area devastated in the enemy’s retreat of spring 1917, ground could be yielded under extreme pressure without the same consequences, and French reinforcement was easier there than elsewhere on the British line. He therefore held it unsound to keep considerable reserves south of the Somme while the enemy’s commitment of reserves was still unknown. The front south of the River Omignon, moreover, had been taken over only some seven weeks before the attack — too short a period for an efficient scheme of defence.
Man-Power and Foch
When the House of Commons reassembled on 9 April a feeling of deep anxiety brooded over the members. The German onslaught had had serious results; news from Neuve Chapelle spread through the Lobbies; further drafts on man-power were judged unavoidable. So urgent was the need that Lloyd George on the opening day moved the first reading of the new Man-Power Bill (drafted by a committee of Ministers under Sir George Cave), the House waiving a day’s notice; all other Government business was set aside until the Bill had passed every stage. Submitting “A Bill to make further provision with respect to military service during the present war,” he set forth the critical situation: the enemy was clearly committed to a military decision this year by breaking the Armies of the Allies — assault piled upon assault, with seven or possibly eight months of campaigning weather. He gave the first authoritative review of the recent fighting and of the events which led to Foch’s appointment to co-ordinate Allied strategy. Strategic unity was fundamental; success would still be impossible without more men.
Up to this date British and French forces in France had been entirely separate armies, though for many months there had been agitation for a single Generalissimo — a reform which had met strong opposition notwithstanding that it was known to be favoured by the British Prime Minister. Under the intense stress Lloyd George obtained the Cabinet’s general consent to placing both armies under a French general; on 16 April it was announced that General Foch had been appointed “Commander-in-Chief of the Allied Armies in France.” A Register footnote records that Foch had been in supreme command, for all practical purposes, since 26 March. Hankey’s chapters place the unity-of-command debate and Foch’s elevation as Generalissimo in the calm before the storm and the March–April crisis, with Lloyd George’s conflict with the military leadership and Hankey’s mediating role running through April and May.
The Lys and Armentières
Before the Somme battle had fully settled, a fresh German offensive opened farther north. Haig’s despatch describes the Lys fighting: progress about Armentières; strong attacks toward Nieppe and Neuve Eglise; recovery and loss of Messines; withdrawal from Nieppe to Pont d’Achelles and abandonment of Hill 63 and remaining Messines positions; critical days about Merville, Pacaut, and the La Bassée Canal; later, loss of Kemmel village and Mount Kemmel and readjustment of the Ypres salient on the night of 26–27 April to the line Pilckem–Wieltje–west end of Zillebeke Lake–Voormezeele. Bailleul fell on 15 April; on the 16th the enemy gained Messines Ridge; on 26 April Kemmel village and Mount Kemmel were lost. On 29 April, after a bombardment of exceptional intensity, strong attacks from west of Dranoutre to Voormezeele were completely repulsed with the heaviest losses. In the first days of May violent attempts to extend the Armentières successes were driven back with terrible losses. Thus the battle ended, as Amiens had done, in what it is legitimate to describe as a German defeat: preliminary successes had not won the great strategic object, and territorial gains had been bought at a cost the enemy could ill afford.
Soissons and the Exhaustion of the Offensive
This was not yet the end of Ludendorff’s attempt. After the failure on the Channel ports there was a pause of several weeks; at the end of May fighting broke out afresh north of the Aisne, west of Reims. The attack of 27 May, supported by numerous tanks, extended about 30 miles from Vauxaillon to the vicinity of Reims. Defending troops were mainly French, with several British divisions on the Allied right; the British held, but most of the French line was overwhelmed in the first rush. The enemy gained five miles on the first day, crossed the Aisne and the Vesle, captured Soissons with Brandenburg troops, reached the outskirts of Reims without taking the city, and by 31 May reached the Marne. Allied reserves arrived; the advance slowed; further extensions followed, but by early summer the German effort was spent. German Headquarters claimed, between 21 March and the end of June, 2,476 guns, 15,024 machine-guns, and 191,454 unwounded prisoners, of whom 94,939 were British. The Register closes the phase as “End of the German Offensive” and opens the next as “The Victory of the Associated Powers.”
Through July and into early August Marshal Foch prepared the counter-stroke which brought victory. At Westminster the five weeks from 1 July to 8 August were a period of intense feeling under a war still undecided. The military turning of the tide, Hankey’s biographer places under the second battle of the Marne and planning for the final campaign, ran into the Battle of Amiens of 8 August and the “hundred days” that followed. For Britain the spring crisis had meant extension of the line, the near-rupture of the Fifth Army, the Lys losses, Foch’s elevation, and the Man-Power drive that drained the Home army and brigaded unready American regiments into the line — the last German bid for a decision before the Allied counter-offensive and the Armistice, under a Coalition lineage running back to the first Coalition of 1915 and a franchise already widened by the Representation of the People Act.
Chronology

events/great-labour-unrest-1911-1914.title: The Great Labour Unrest (1911–1914)
events/great-labour-unrest-1911-1914.content:
The Great Labour Unrest (1911–1914)
Between 1911 and the outbreak of the Great War, British industrial life was shaken by a wave of strikes and lock-outs on a scale that contemporaries compared to a labour war. Seamen, dockers, carters, railwaymen, miners, and transport workers struck in successive waves; a national coal stoppage in 1912 forced Parliament to legislate a district minimum wage; London transport closed the early summer of the same year; Dublin produced its own drama under James Larkin. The unrest ran parallel to the passage of the national-insurance-1911 Act, the aftermath of the peoples-budget-1911, and the deepening irish-home-rule-crisis. It tested the Liberal ministry of asquith-herbert-henry, estranged the parliamentary Labour party from the Government’s use of troops, and left employers and the Home Office preparing “strike breakers” and volunteer police reserves against the next round.
Prelude: 1910
The year 1910 was already marked by unsettlement. A cotton lock-out involving 120,000 operatives ended only on 10 October by Board of Trade intervention. In South Wales the coal trade was disturbed by incessant disputes after the Mines (Eight Hours) Act took effect on 1 January; a threatened general strike in March over a new wages agreement was averted, but sectional strikes in the Aberdare and Rhondda valleys cost an estimated £750,000 in wages and £120,000 in strike pay, cut production, and drove orders abroad. Among railwaymen there was much discontent over the interpretation of the 1907 arbitration awards; the Railway Servants’ Congress found a new argument for nationalisation in the working agreements that had virtually established monopolies among the companies.
Shipbuilding was hit still harder. A fourteen-week lock-out of ironworkers employed by the Federation of Shipbuilding Employers — described as a revolt against trade-union discipline after men broke an agreement made by the Boilermakers’ Society — began early in September when the yards were filling with work. Estimated losses reached £800,000 in wages and £100,000 in strike pay. On the Tyne a sectional riveters’ dispute led to a boilermakers’ lock-out that paralysed the district; no worse calamity, the Register noted, had threatened Tyneside since the engineers’ strike of 1897. A Clyde partial strike among subsidiary trades nearly produced a lock-out. Yet for all the stoppages, 1910 was commercially prosperous: Bankers’ Clearing House turnover rose 7.7 per cent., home railway earnings improved, and shipbuilding output increased in tonnage over the previous year once work resumed.
1911: Docks, Transport, and the Railway Crisis
The notes of the Annual Register for 1911 list among the year’s great events the seamen’s and transport workers’ strikes. Industrial unrest culminated in August in a railway crisis of extreme gravity. The Board of Trade invited railway companies and the men’s unions to confer separately on 16 August. Sir Guy Granet, general manager of the Midland, stated afterwards that the Government had promised the companies protection and that they were prepared to give “an efficient, if restricted, service” during a strike. Next day the executives of the men’s unions, who had come up from Liverpool overnight after resolving not to settle unless the Liverpool lock-out were ended, went with the chairman of the Labour party to the Board of Trade. Their grievance, they said, was the companies’ failure to observe the spirit and letter of the Agreement of 1907; the only remedy was a direct meeting with the companies or a strike.
Asquith offered an immediate Royal Commission to investigate the working of the 1907 conciliation scheme and to recommend amendments for prompt settlement of differences. The Government, he said, was absolutely impartial, but its first consideration must be the public interest: it could not allow a general paralysis of the railway system. The men’s representatives disliked his tone, thought the offer a device for shelving the dispute, and, after learning that he was not bringing companies and unions together that day, passed a resolution declaring his statement an unwarrantable threat. The strike began.
It was not then known that the peremptory tone of the Prime Minister and of the Home Secretary owed something to the critical condition of Anglo-German relations after Agadir — a condition of which the public was scarcely aware until November. The London and South-Western was not affected; other lines suffered in varying degrees. The worst stoppages lay in the quadrilateral whose extremities were roughly Newcastle, Liverpool, Coventry, and Hull, and also in South Wales. There were disturbances at Derby and at Llanelly. In London the Great Central, Great Western, and Brighton lines suffered most; St. Paul’s and Cannon Street stations closed, and Marylebone nearly so. Great Western traffic fell 40 per cent. against the corresponding week of 1910; North Staffordshire, 48 per cent. Troops moved into London parks and to Birmingham, Sheffield, and elsewhere; stations and strategic points were occupied. Six thousand men volunteered as special constables in London. Winston Churchill, speaking in the Commons, reported outrages on railway property — a crime punishable by penal servitude — and pledged the Government to secure food and fuel supplies and services vital to the community, because the working classes would be the worst sufferers from famine and a general arrest of industry.
Settlement came through a Special Commission under Sir David Harrel, with Sir Thomas Ratcliffe Ellis (Mining Association), Charles G. Beale of Birmingham, Arthur Henderson (Labour M.P. for Barnard Castle), and John Burnett (sometime Board of Trade Labour Correspondent) as members, and J. J. Wills of the Board of Trade as secretary. The Commission was to investigate the 1907 Conciliation Scheme and report desirable changes. Parliament, reassembling on 22 August, adjourned until 24 October. Ramsay Macdonald thought the settlement might guarantee peace if fairly carried out, but attacked the Home Office for prejudiced bulletins and a “reckless display of force” — a reversion, he said, to medieval ideas of law and order. Austen Chamberlain approved the Government’s action: the right to work was not less sacred than the right to strike. J. H. Thomas, of the railwaymen’s executive, praised the way the companies had met the men once negotiations resumed.
In the days after adjournment industrial peace returned in form. The Railway Commission met on 23 August; Manchester carters settled the same day; the Liverpool dockers’ strike was declared at an end on the evening of the 24th, after a threatened prolongation when tramwaymen were refused indiscriminate reinstatement and some 37,000 men were out or kept out in sympathy. Reinstatement “as and when required,” subject to the general manager’s satisfaction, and advice from labour leaders to return to work, closed the episode. A similar reinstatement dispute on the Great Eastern was compromised on 31 August after Board of Trade intervention. G. B. Askwith, the Board’s principal conciliator, received a knighthood. But there was a general feeling that the labour war was only suspended. Subscriptions were raised for railwaymen who had remained at their posts; suggestions circulated for local corps of “strike breakers” to keep lighting and railway travel running; a Home Office circular of 15 September encouraged volunteer police reserves. In Wales, anti-Jewish riots arising out of the unrest continued at Bargoed on 24 August, ascribed to rent-raising by Jewish houseowners.
Politically the August crisis left the Government stronger with the mass of Unionists and weaker with Labour and advanced Liberals. Bonar Law, at Leeds that autumn, blamed the Budget campaign of 1909 for intensifying working-class unrest, of which the labour disturbances of 1911 were “the fruit,” and pointed to a rise of nearly 10 per cent. in the cost of living without a corresponding rise in wages. The Government’s method, he said, was to take from the rich by taxation and give to the poor in doles; capital and population were going abroad. A fiscal change — Tariff Reform — would tend to raise wages. Scottish industrial centres felt the railway stoppages and Welsh disturbances less violently than the English midland and northern quadrilateral, but felt them nonetheless.
1912: The Coal Strike and the Minimum Wage
The political year 1912 opened under the shadow of industrial unrest, the approaching operation of the National Insurance Act, and the Government’s determination to press Home Rule and Welsh Disestablishment under the Parliament Act. On the Address, Ramsay Macdonald moved a Labour amendment ascribing labour troubles to insufficient wages amid expanding national wealth and rising living costs. Of 7,300,000 wage-earners, he said, 60 per cent. had incomes of less than 30s. a week; aggregate wages had fallen heavily since 1901 while living costs rose; skilled organised labour had been largely supplanted by unskilled, ill-paid labour; and the Government “supinely allowed monopolists, like the coal ring, to put up prices.” A minimum wage, begun experimentally by the Trade Boards Act of 1910, must go on. J. R. Clynes seconded, hoping unrest would continue until justice was done.
Industrial crisis soon overshadowed all else. The coal strike began at Alfreton in Derbyshire on 1 March; railway services were reduced; the King’s projected visits to foreign Courts were cancelled. On 19 March, in a crowded House, Asquith introduced the Coal Mines (Minimum Wage) Bill. The Government, he declared, had resorted to legislation only after all hope of settlement by agreement had disappeared, and was justified only in proposing legislation limited to effecting that settlement. The Bill gave effect to propositions laid before coalowners and miners on 28 February and accepted by the miners and by 65 per cent. of the coalowners. It was temporary — three years. The district minimum would be recoverable by civil process; any contract modifying it would be void; once ascertained it would be paid retrospectively from the date the miner resumed work. Wage rates, conditions, and exceptions would be fixed by district boards — twenty-one districts, possibly identical with existing Conciliation Boards — with employers and workmen equally represented and an independent chairman (or three chairmen) holding a casting vote, appointed by agreement or, failing that, by the Board of Trade. The aged and infirm would be excepted; there would be safeguards for efficiency and regularity; there were no penal provisions on either side. A legislative declaration in favour of a minimum wage would alter the situation; Parliament would then be justified, if heaven forbid, in taking further measures to defend the industries of the country against paralysis and starvation.
Bonar Law disclaimed party advantage but feared a precedent for other industries: the minimum wage had been treated in the Address debate as proper only for sweated trades; now it was applied where wages were above the average. The only difference, he said, was that the miners’ union was strong enough to put pressure on the Government. William Brace (Labour, South Glamorgan) replied that a minimum for abnormal places had been customary for years, but a county court had held it not legally binding and employers had refused legal sanction. Austen Chamberlain called the Bill panic legislation without finality and blamed the Chancellor’s speeches for the trouble. Sir Edward Grey wound up: the House faced a new demand — that the miner be paid a fair wage when he failed to earn it from causes beyond his control. Before intervention the minimum had been accepted by owners in the largest mining area; with a minimum wage there should be a minimum output; safeguards were in the Bill. Carried to its extreme, the strike meant starvation and the complete destruction of national life. A door had been opened for regulation of the minimum wage which could not be closed.
On 26 March, during the Report stage, Asquith announced with profound emotion that a new Conference had proved abortive. The rates of 5s. and 2s. were not unreasonable, but the Conference had refused his suggestion of treating them separately from the hewers’ wage. Having exhausted persuasion, argument, and negotiation, the Government pressed the Bill as the best possible solution. Bonar Law recognised that Ministers had done their best and would put no obstacle in the way; if the men did not return when the Bill passed, the whole resources of society might rightly protect those who desired to work. Macdonald said the miners were law-abiding people. The strike closed on 7 April after the Act’s passage. Cardiff steam coal, which had opened the year at 18s. 3d., risen over 30s. on fear of a national stoppage, and in March realised as much as 45s., began to decline once work resumed.
Transport, Syndicalism, and Concurrent Crises
A strike of London transport workers was declared as the Commons adjourned over Whitsuntide on 22 May 1912. It dominated early summer industrial politics while the Home Rule Bill went into Committee and the Franchise Bill received a second reading. The transport strike ended before the summer recess; the Finance and Appropriation Bills passed; Unionist speeches at Blenheim continued to reverberate. An academic debate on syndicalism (27 March), moved by Ormsby Gore and seconded by Hewins, declared advocacy of an anti-social policy based on class warfare and incitement to mutiny a grave danger to the State. Charles Hobhouse, for the Government, repudiated syndicalism as negativing parliamentary action and destroying national capital, ascribing unrest to the rise in living costs without corresponding wages and to improved mental qualities of workers without corresponding material improvement.
Throughout 1912 the irish-home-rule-crisis and the suffragette-movement occupied the same newspapers as the strikes. Asquith’s Dublin visit, the Ulster Covenant campaign, and Bonar Law’s Blenheim pledge of support for Ulster resistance ran alongside the coal and transport stoppages. The National Insurance Act came into force on Joy Day in the middle of the transport struggle. Trade, nonetheless, was extraordinarily active: practically every industry was employed; Bankers’ Clearing House returns reached record levels; commercial failures fell to the lowest figure in twenty-five years. The boom and the unrest were simultaneous facts.
1913–1914: Dublin, Building Trades, and the Coming of War
In 1913 labour unrest continued, especially noted in Scotland alongside heavy emigration from the Clyde to Canada (some 36,000 from 1 January to 24 May, a 50 per cent. increase on 1912). Dublin produced a separate drama. After the conviction of James Larkin — the prosecution citing his derisive treatment of the King’s name at a forbidden meeting — Liberal papers compared the trial bitterly with the immunity enjoyed by Sir Edward Carson, and even the Unionist Spectator said Larkin had been condemned on a charge of lèse majesté. An Albert Hall meeting on 1 November, for which there were 40,000 applications for admission, was addressed by Ben Tillett, several suffragists, and Bernard Shaw; the majority pledged themselves to heckle every Cabinet Minister until Larkin was released — and the pledge was kept. Municipal elections that day showed a considerable loss of Liberal seats to Labour and Socialist candidates.
In 1914 the arrival at Gravesend (24 February) of the Umgeni with Labour leaders deported from South Africa produced one of the largest Hyde Park demonstrations ever seen in London. Easter conferences of the Independent Labour party and other bodies exhibited “sectional discontent rather than any single organised challenge.” The Whitsuntide recess was overshadowed by the almost certain prospect of a national lock-out in the building trade and by the sinking of the Empress of Ireland. Ministers had lost prestige; of seven bye-elections since the session began they had lost four; they were suffering from Labour and Nationalist pressure and from the cumulative strain of the Ulster and Army crises of the spring.
Then the European storm broke. On 4 August an Order in Council declared it expedient that the Government should take control of the railways of the United Kingdom. The political year of 1914 ended; the war year began. The divisions on which, contemporaries believed, the Germans had staked their hopes closed rapidly. The great labour unrest of 1911–14 was not resolved so much as suspended by a greater emergency.
Aftermath and Significance
The unrest of 1911–14 was not a single organised revolution. It was a series of industry-by-industry explosions — docks and seamen, railways, coal, transport, Dublin general labour, building — driven by the rise in the cost of living, by disputes over the working of conciliation awards, by demands for a legal minimum wage, and by a new readiness of large unions to stop national services. The Liberal Government answered with a mixture of force and statute: troops and special constables in August 1911; the Harrel Commission on railway conciliation; Askwith’s mediation; the Coal Mines (Minimum Wage) Act of 1912. Bonar Law offered Tariff Reform as the alternative to “doles”; Labour members demanded nationalisation of railways and mines and a general minimum wage.
For labour-representation the period was double-edged. Parliamentary Labour had arrived in force in 1906 and could claim the Trade Disputes Act, pensions, and insurance as fruits of representation; yet the same years saw Macdonald and Thomas criticising the Home Office, Clynes hoping unrest would continue until justice was done, and Larkin’s supporters treating Cabinet ministers as enemies to be heckled. The unrest proved that social-reform by statute — old-age-pensions-1908, national-insurance-1911, Trade Boards, labour exchanges — had not removed the wage and recognition conflicts of an industrial society whose real incomes were under pressure. It also proved that when railways and coal stopped, the State would intervene, by soldiers if necessary and by minimum-wage law if possible. The irish-home-rule-crisis and the European war then absorbed the political energy that might have produced a further cycle of industrial confrontation. The labour war of 1911–14 closed not with a settlement but with an armistice imposed by history.

events/irish-home-rule-crisis.title: The Irish Home Rule Crisis (1886–1914)
events/irish-home-rule-crisis.content:
The Irish Home Rule Crisis (1886–1914)
The Irish Home Rule Crisis was the central political conflict of the United Kingdom from the mid-1880s to the outbreak of the First World War. It revolved around the demand of the Irish Parliamentary Party and the wider Irish nationalist movement for a devolved parliament in Dublin — Home Rule — and the determined resistance of Ulster Unionists, who feared domination by a Catholic-majority Dublin assembly. The crisis split the Liberal Party, brought down its dominant leader, drove the Conservative Party into an alliance with armed resistance, brought the British Army to the brink of mutiny, and was ultimately suspended by the outbreak of European war, only to erupt in armed rebellion two years later.

Gladstone’s Conversion & First Bill (1886)
The demand for an Irish parliament was not new. The Home Government Association had been founded in 1870 by Isaac Butt, and by the mid-1870s a disciplined Irish Parliamentary Party of some sixty members pressed for constitutional devolution. But the issue became a crisis when William Ewart Gladstone — who had already disestablished the Irish Church (1869) and passed an Irish Land Act (1870, extended 1881) — underwent a dramatic conversion to the cause.
By late 1885, Gladstone had become convinced that the only way to reconcile Ireland to the Union was to grant a measure of legislative independence. His son Herbert publicly revealed the “Hawarden Kite” in December 1885, signalling that Gladstone intended to introduce a Home Rule Bill. The General Election of 1885 returned a hung parliament: the Liberals and Conservatives were nearly level, with Parnell’s 86 Irish Nationalists holding the balance.
When Gladstone formed his third ministry in February 1886, he moved swiftly. On 8 April 1886, he introduced the Government of Ireland Bill — the First Home Rule Bill. It proposed a Dublin parliament with two chambers to legislate on Irish domestic affairs, while reserving imperial matters (foreign policy, defence, customs and excise, and coinage) to Westminster. Irish MPs would no longer sit at Westminster.
The Bill split the Liberal Party down the middle. A faction of Liberal Unionists — led by Joseph Chamberlain and Lord Hartington — broke away to oppose the measure. Chamberlain, who had previously advocated a less ambitious “Central Board” scheme for Ireland, resigned from the Cabinet and led the revolt. On the night of 7–8 June 1886, the Bill was defeated in the House of Commons by 343 votes to 313 — 93 Liberals voting against their own government. Gladstone dissolved Parliament and appealed to the country, but the ensuing general election returned the Conservatives and Liberal Unionists with a commanding majority of 118. Lord Salisbury formed a Unionist administration that would hold power — with one brief interlude — for the next nineteen years.
The Liberal split was enduring. The Liberal Unionists, led by Chamberlain and Hartington, gradually merged with the Conservatives, and the Liberal Party would not see power with an independent majority again until 1906.

Parnell’s Fall & Second Bill (1890–1893)
The First Home Rule Bill’s defeat did not extinguish the cause. Charles Stewart Parnell, the “Uncrowned King of Ireland”, remained the dominant figure in Irish politics. But his position was shattered in 1889–1890 by a scandal that convulsed British and Irish politics alike.
In 1887, The Times published a series of articles, “Parnellism and Crime”, alleging that Parnell and his movement were linked to the agrarian outrages of the Irish National Land League. Central to the accusation was a letter purportedly signed by Parnell that condoned the Phoenix Park Murders of 1882. Parnell denounced the letters as forgeries. A Special Commission (the Parnell Commission), sitting from 1888 to 1889, investigated the charges. In February 1889, the forger Richard Pigott confessed under cross-examination by Sir Charles Russell that the letter was a forgery and subsequently fled and committed suicide. Parnell was utterly vindicated, and his popularity surged.
But catastrophe followed swiftly. In December 1889, Captain William O’Shea filed for divorce from his wife Katharine, naming Parnell as co-respondent. The divorce case was heard in November 1890; Parnell did not contest it, and the decree was granted. The news caused a firestorm. Gladstone, fearing that Nonconformist Liberal voters would abandon Home Rule if Parnell remained leader, wrote a letter (published 25 November 1890) making clear that Parnell’s continued leadership would cost the Liberals the next election and therefore the Home Rule cause.
When the Irish Parliamentary Party met in Committee Room 15 at the House of Commons (1–6 December 1890), the party split bitterly. After days of rancorous debate, a majority of 44 MPs withdrew from Parnell’s leadership, forming the anti-Parnellite majority under Justin McCarthy. Parnell retained only 26 loyalists. He fought three by-elections in Ireland in a desperate attempt to regain his position, campaigning with ferocious energy, but his health collapsed. Parnell died at Brighton on 6 October 1891, at the age of 45.
After Parnell’s death Gladstone formed his fourth and final ministry in 1892, reliant on the votes of the now-divided Irish Party. On 13 February 1893, he introduced the Second Home Rule Bill. It resembled the first but retained 80 Irish MPs at Westminster (while limiting their voting rights). The Bill passed the House of Commons on 1 September 1893 by 301 to 267 — on its third reading, the first Home Rule Bill ever to pass the Commons. But the Conservative-dominated House of Lords rejected it overwhelmingly, by 419 votes to 41. With no prospect of overriding the Lords’ veto (the Parliament Act was still eighteen years away), the Bill was dead. Gladstone resigned as Prime Minister in March 1894, and the Home Rule cause entered a decade of political eclipse.

Third Home Rule Bill & Ulster Resistance (1912–1914)
Home Rule returned to the centre of politics after the Liberal landslide of 1906 and, critically, after the Parliament Act 1911 removed the Lords’ absolute veto, replacing it with a suspensory veto of only two years. The Liberals, dependent on the Irish Party’s 84 votes for their majority, were now bound to deliver Home Rule.
The Third Home Rule Bill was introduced by Prime Minister H. H. Asquith on 11 April 1912. It proposed a bicameral Irish Parliament (a Senate and an elected House of Commons) with authority over Irish domestic affairs, while reserving the Crown, imperial defence, foreign policy, and certain other powers to Westminster. Ireland would continue to send 42 MPs to Westminster.
The Bill passed the Commons in each of the sessions 1912, 1913, and 1914 under the provisions of the Parliament Act, but the real drama unfolded outside Parliament. Ulster Unionists, led by the Dublin-born barrister and former Solicitor-General Sir Edward Carson (who had nonetheless become the champion of Ulster’s cause) and the Conservative leader Andrew Bonar Law, mounted a resistance of unprecedented scale.
Ulster Covenant (1912)
On 28 September 1912, Ulster Day, nearly 500,000 men and women signed the Ulster Covenant. The men’s covenant, modelled on the 17th-century Solemn League and Covenant, bound signatories to use “all means which may be found necessary to defeat the present conspiracy to set up a Home Rule Parliament in Ireland” — and, if Home Rule were imposed, to refuse to recognise its authority. The women’s declaration was signed separately. Carson was the first to sign at Belfast City Hall, followed by Bonar Law and other Unionist leaders. The signing was a mass civic spectacle, conducted across Ulster in churches, halls, and market squares.
Ulster Volunteer Force
In January 1913, the Ulster Unionist Council authorised the formation of the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) , a paramilitary militia raised to resist Home Rule by force if necessary. By the end of 1913, the UVF claimed 90,000 volunteers, drilled openly and backed by a fund of £1 million guaranteed by Ulster’s business and industrial community. The UVF was commanded by Lieutenant-General Sir George Richardson, a retired Indian Army officer, and organised on conventional military lines. Meanwhile, in the South, the Irish Volunteers were formed in November 1913 by nationalists in response to the UVF, initially under the control of moderate constitutional nationalists associated with John Redmond.

The Curragh Incident
By March 1914, the Asquith government faced an impossible situation. The Home Rule Bill was about to receive Royal Assent under the Parliament Act, but Ulster was armed and mobilised. The government decided to reinforce the military garrisons in Ulster to protect arms depots and, if necessary, to deal with any UVF attempt to seize control of the province.
On 14 March 1914, the Cabinet ordered precautionary moves. General Sir Arthur Paget, Commander-in-Chief in Ireland, was instructed to send cavalry and infantry to guard key military stores in Ulster. Paget summoned his senior officers to Dublin on 20 March 1914 and — in what remains a matter of controversy — appears to have told them that “active operations” against Ulster were imminent and that officers who lived in Ulster would be permitted to “disappear” for the duration, while all others who refused to serve would be dismissed rather than simply transferred.
The commander of the 3rd Cavalry Brigade at the Curragh, Brigadier-General Hubert Gough, and 57 of his 70 officers (including all the officers of the 16th Lancers and nearly all of the 4th Hussars and 5th Lancers) stated their preference for dismissal rather than initiate “active military operations against Ulster.” News of the so-called “Curragh Mutiny” exploded in the press.
The government initially capitulated. Colonel John Seely, the Secretary of State for War, and the Chief of the Imperial General Staff, Sir John French, drafted a written assurance to Gough (later amended by the Prime Minister) that the Army would not be used “to enforce the Home Rule Bill on Ulster.” When the Cabinet realised the political implications — that it had effectively conceded that the law could not be enforced — Seely and French were forced to resign. General Gough was nevertheless reinstated.
The Curragh Incident had two profound consequences. It convinced Ulster Unionists that the government would not, in the end, coerce them — and it convinced Irish nationalists that the British state could not be relied upon to uphold the rule of law against Ulster’s defiance. The annual register noted Hankey’s private alarm: “The present situation has already led to the resignation of officers; if prolonged, it will lead to the resignation of more; the supply of officers, already a serious problem, is likely to be even further diminished.”
Larne Gun-Running
Emboldened by the government’s humiliation at the Curragh, the UVF moved to arm itself decisively. On the night of 24–25 April 1914, the UVF landed some 25,000 rifles and 3 million rounds of ammunition at the ports of Larne, Bangor, and Donaghadee. The operation was a model of paramilitary logistics: the arms were shipped from Germany aboard the collier Clydevalley, transferred to smaller boats, and distributed across Ulster within hours by an organised network of motor cars. The authorities were entirely outmanoeuvred, and by the time Dublin Castle learned of the landing, the arms were beyond recovery. The government’s response was limited to the posting of warships on the Ulster coast and a formal condemnation.
The nationalists responded in kind. On 26 July 1914, the Irish Volunteers landed 1,500 rifles and 45,000 rounds of ammunition — smuggled from Germany — at Howth, near Dublin. British troops and police attempting to seize the arms were met by a hostile crowd on Bachelors Walk in Dublin; the troops opened fire, killing three civilians and wounding 38. The incident inflamed nationalist opinion and widened the gulf between constitutional nationalists and the growing undercurrent of revolutionary separatism.

Suspension & Easter Rising (1914–1916)
As Ireland edged toward civil war, the British political establishment made a final attempt at a negotiated settlement.
Buckingham Palace Conference
On 21–24 July 1914, King George V summoned the leaders of all parties to a conference at Buckingham Palace, an extraordinary intervention by the monarch. The conference was chaired by the Speaker of the House of Commons, James Lowther, and was attended by Asquith and Lloyd George for the government, Bonar Law and Lord Lansdowne for the Unionists, and Redmond and Dillon for the nationalists, and Carson and James Craig for the Ulster Unionists. The issue was narrowed to the question of which Ulster counties would be temporarily excluded from Home Rule and for how long. After four days of intense discussion, the conference reached deadlock on the precise boundaries of the excluded area — specifically, whether the counties of Tyrone and Fermanagh (both with narrow nationalist majorities) would be included in or excluded from Ulster’s opt-out.
Two days after the conference collapsed, the nationalist gun-running at Howth and the Bachelors Walk shootings inflamed the situation further. But the crisis was overtaken by events on the Continent.
Outbreak of War & Suspension
On 28 July 1914, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia; by 4 August, Britain was at war with Germany. The Home Rule Bill received Royal Assent as the Government of Ireland Act 1914 on 18 September 1914, but was simultaneously suspended for the duration of the war by the Suspensory Act. An Amending Bill providing for the temporary exclusion of Ulster — which had been promised by the government in March 1914 — was abandoned.
John Redmond, leader of the Irish Parliamentary Party, pledged the support of the Irish Volunteers for the British war effort, urging them to fight “in defence of the rights of small nations” — a phrase that would be turned back against the British government by Irish republicans. The majority of the Irish Volunteers followed Redmond (becoming the National Volunteers, some 140,000 strong), but a rump of perhaps 10,000–11,000 held aloof, keeping the original title “Irish Volunteers” and preparing for an insurrection.
The Easter Rising (1916)
The suspension of Home Rule and the war in Europe created the opportunity for a republican insurrection. The Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB), working within the rump Irish Volunteers, planned an uprising timed for Easter 1916. On Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, approximately 1,200 Volunteers and members of the Irish Citizen Army seized key buildings in Dublin. Patrick Pearse read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic from the steps of the General Post Office, declaring Ireland an independent republic.
The British response was overwhelming. Martial law was declared; troops and artillery were rushed to Dublin. By 29 April, after a week of heavy fighting that devastated the city centre and left over 450 dead and 2,500 wounded, Pearse surrendered unconditionally. Fifteen of the rebel leaders — including Pearse, James Connolly, and the executed signatories of the Proclamation — were shot by firing squad in Kilmainham Gaol between 3 and 12 May.
The executions proved a catastrophic political miscalculation. Initially, Dublin public opinion had been largely hostile to the Rising; the destruction and loss of life had alienated many. But the summary executions, the internment of thousands, and the extension of martial law transformed the political landscape. The executed leaders were transformed into martyrs, and public sympathy swung decisively toward the republican cause.

Aftermath
The Irish Home Rule Crisis — spanning three decades, four Prime Ministers, and three Home Rule Bills — shattered the Liberal Party, radicalised Irish politics, and destroyed the moderate constitutional nationalism of the Irish Parliamentary Party.
The Government of Ireland Act 1914 remained on the statute book, suspended and never implemented. In 1918, Asquith’s successor David Lloyd George attempted to introduce Home Rule with partition, but the proposal was overtaken by the rise of Sinn Féin — the political party of the Easter rebels — which won 73 of Ireland’s 105 seats in the December 1918 general election. Sinn Féin’s MPs refused to take their seats at Westminster, instead establishing the First Dáil in Dublin in January 1919, which declared Irish independence. The Irish War of Independence (1919–1921) followed.
The Government of Ireland Act 1920, enacted during the war, partitioned Ireland into Northern Ireland (six counties) and Southern Ireland, each with its own devolved parliament. The southern parliament was never effectively implemented; instead, the Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921 established the Irish Free State as a self-governing Dominion within the British Empire, with Northern Ireland electing to opt out. The crisis that began with Gladstone’s conversion in 1885 thus ended with the partition of Ireland and the creation of two states on the island — outcomes that neither the Home Rulers nor the Unionists had originally intended.

Key Sources

Annual Register, 1912, 1913, 1914, 1915, 1916 — detailed contemporary parliamentary and political chronicles.
Justin McCarthy, A History of Our Own Times, Vol. 4 (covering 1860s–1880s, origins of Home Rule and Liberal split).
Justin McCarthy, A History of Our Own Times, Vol. 5 (extended edition, Parnell Commission and Home Rule developments to 1890s).
Justin McCarthy, The Diamond Jubilee: A History of the Last Thirty-Five Years, Vol. 1 (Home Rule after Gladstone, Redmond and Liberal policy).
Lord Hankey, The Man of Secrets, Vol. 1 (Curragh crisis from the perspective of Imperial defence).
