events/jutland.title: The Battle of Jutland (1916)
events/jutland.content:
The Battle of Jutland (1916)
On 31 May and the night following, in the North Sea off the coast of Jutland, the Grand Fleet under Admiral Sir John Jellicoe and the High Seas Fleet under Vice-Admiral Scheer met in the greatest naval battle since Trafalgar. The battle-cruiser forces of Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty and Vice-Admiral Hipper opened the action; the main fleets closed in the evening mist; Scheer, finding himself face to face with the whole Grand Fleet, extricated himself by practised battle-turns under destroyer smoke; and through the short northern night he forced a passage home across the British wake. No second Trafalgar followed. Yet when Sir Julian Corbett summed the purely strategical result, Scheer had failed in his object of cutting off and overwhelming part of the British advanced forces, and Jellicoe had increased the Grand Fleet’s large margin of superiority as a combative force, a defence against invasion, and an instrument of blockade. British control of the North Sea remained unbroken. Public judgment, fed by a candid first communiqué and by German claims that reached neutrals first, was another matter.
Strategic Setting and the Eve
The Lowestoft–Yarmouth raid of late April came with something of a shock after the enemy’s long inactivity. Faith in the navy was scarcely shaken, but the Admiralty thought a reassuring pronouncement desirable. It took the form of a letter from Mr. Balfour, First Lord, to the Mayors of Lowestoft and Yarmouth: home forces were about to be redistributed so as to make a repetition of such a raid highly dangerous. Earlier it had been necessary to keep the main fleet in northern waters, able to concentrate against invasion but not to intercept raids; now new construction allowed important forces to be brought south without imperilling preponderance elsewhere.
A redistribution of that character had been under consideration since the beginning of the year. On 17 February, at a meeting of the War Committee which Jellicoe came down to attend, the whole strategical aspect of the naval situation was investigated. The Committee explored a naval offensive on the lines of Lord Fisher’s still-born plan — seizing a German coastal island as an aircraft and submarine base, a landing on the Schleswig coast, or in Denmark if the enemy should violate Danish neutrality, with as ultimate objective the coast of Pomerania within a hundred miles of Berlin. Fisher’s special fleet had been eaten away by the Dardanelles; no troops were available; mines and submarines made Baltic supply harder than ever. The conclusion was to preserve the old expectant attitude, while persevering to goad the High Seas Fleet into the open sea.
On the German side Scheer, since his accession to command, had worked to produce a situation of exceptional tactical advantage — using battle cruisers and light forces to entice similar British units within reach of his battle fleet. The stress of the British blockade had come to be severely felt in Germany. Scheer’s object was not a direct general engagement between entire forces: it was to take the British fleet in detail if possible, destroy a portion of it, and retreat to the protection of the German coasts. The Imperial Admiralty entertained no illusion that the chance was anything but very small; the risks were grave, yet the naval and economic situation had become such that those risks had to be taken.
Battle-Cruiser Action, 31 May
On 31 May Beatty, leading the 1st Battle Cruiser Squadron (Lion, Princess Royal, Queen Mary, Tiger), had been zigzagging at nineteen knots towards the Jutland bank. Eight miles ahead light cruisers were spread in pairs; the 2nd Battle Cruiser Squadron (New Zealand and Indefatigable) was three miles on his port bow; Rear-Admiral Evan-Thomas with the “Queen Elizabeths” (Barham, Valiant, Warspite, Malaya) was five miles astern. At 2.0, believing himself only ten miles short of his assigned position (in fact over fifteen), he signalled for the fleet to turn northward at 2.15.
Hipper, with five battle cruisers (Lützow flag, Derfflinger, Seydlitz, Moltke, Von der Tann), five light cruisers and thirty-three destroyers, had left the Jade at 2.0 a.m. and was about fifty miles east of the Lion. Following him, over fifty miles astern, was Scheer with his two Dreadnought squadrons and the pre-Dreadnought “Deutschlands.” As yet Scheer had no suspicion of the Grand Fleet’s presence. It looked as though Jellicoe’s dispositions were exactly what was needed — if nothing incalculable happened Scheer would have little chance of avoiding the battle for which the British had so long been striving. But the incalculable did happen.
Contact opened through the light cruisers. The Galatea’s signals began to reach Jellicoe about 2.20; Beatty, nearer the scene and much faster than the main battle fleet, came up with Hipper long before the battleships. The run to the south followed — Beatty engaging Hipper’s five battle cruisers while Evan-Thomas’s four fast 15-inch battleships came into the fight. In that phase the Queen Mary and the Indefatigable were destroyed. When Scheer’s battle fleet was sighted, Beatty turned north, drawing the High Seas Fleet after him toward Jellicoe — the “run to the north” that converted Scheer’s intended partial stroke into a meeting with the main British force. The four “Queen Elizabeths” fought a rearguard against superior numbers; the Warspite was badly damaged. The Annual Register called Beatty’s earlier stand an action in keeping with the most dashing traditions of the British Navy.
Fleet Contact and the Main Battle
When at 5.30 the firing died away Jellicoe was twenty-three miles to the northward, with his three Dreadnought squadrons in divisions in line ahead disposed abeam. Rear-Admiral Hood with the 3rd Battle Cruiser Squadron (Invincible, Inflexible, Indomitable) was 21 miles ahead. Spread in advance were the 1st Cruiser Squadron (Defence, Warrior, Duke of Edinburgh, Black Prince) under Rear-Admiral Arbuthnot and the 2nd under Rear-Admiral Heath. Without counting Evan-Thomas’s four ships, Jellicoe had twenty-four Dreadnoughts against Scheer’s sixteen and six older pre-Dreadnoughts. The Germans had no gun heavier than 12-inch, while British main armament ranged from 12-inch to 15-inch; German ships were better protected and carried more submerged torpedo tubes. Jellicoe’s best chance was a smashing blow with his main weapon; Scheer would naturally seek to avoid such a blow, or at least to weaken it.
As reports grew more serious Jellicoe ceased zigzagging, increased speed, signalled prepare for action, and altered course toward Horn Reefs. Urgent messages from the Lion reported that Beatty was engaging. As the battle fleets closed, Hood entered the fray not far in advance of the main body, fell into line with Beatty, and within a few minutes the Invincible — veteran of Heligoland Bight and the Falklands — sank with the famous admiral on board. Arbuthnot’s armoured cruisers pressed into the zone of heavy fire; the Defence was destroyed and the Warrior disabled (later abandoned). The action was fought at about 9,000 to 12,000 yards in misty evening light; during the junction the British battleships had to exercise the greatest care not to mistake, at long range, British for German ships.
The explosion in which the Invincible perished heralded a new phase. A period of manœuvring ensued comparable with Howe and Villaret-Joyeuse in 1794 — but now a tactical contest of days was condensed into hours. Scheer had come suddenly upon his enemy in the act of deployment; instead of throwing him into confusion, he found his own van being enveloped by a superior force ready for action. Persuaded by submarine reports that the Grand Fleet had been split up, he did not as yet realise that he was face to face with the whole of it. Out of the mist fire was coming from about eight points of the compass. Nearly all British ships were firing and getting hits, while they themselves suffered not at all. The Lützow was completely disabled; Hipper was about to board a destroyer to shift his flag. The Derfflinger, with masts and rigging cut to shreds and water pouring through a large hole in her bows, was little better off. So boldly had Captain Heaton-Ellis in the Inflexible led on past the wreck that the rest of the German battle cruisers swerved away to the westward about 6.35.
Completely out-manœuvred, Scheer had no choice but to get his neck out of the noose. To retire in succession was not to be thought of — the turning-point would be a deathtrap. In the German tactical manuals the simultaneous withdrawal was the Gefechtskehrtwendung (battle turn-away), practised so that an inferior fleet could disengage at any moment. The only means of preventing escape was a resolute immediate chase; to baffle pursuit the Kehrtwendung was made under cover of a destroyer attack and a smoke screen.
It soon appeared to Jellicoe that the enemy must have turned away. An immediate turn by divisions to follow was out of the question: it would have placed the fleet open to long-range torpedoes from the enemy capital ships — a danger then new and unmeasured — and would have brought German destroyers directly ahead. A turn in succession would have led the fleet into waters the enemy had occupied, and German capital ships were all believed to carry mines. Scheer retreated south-east as night fell and left the British in possession of the scene of action.
Night and Morning, 1 June
At 9.14 — three minutes before Jellicoe gave directions for night cruising order — Scheer signalled the main body to maintain course S.S.E. ¼ E. at 16 knots, the rallying course toward Horn Reefs. Shortly after 9.30 the van began to lead round to port on that course. Foiled once if not twice in his attempt to get by to the eastward, he could no longer delay another determined effort to cross the enemy’s wake.
The courses of the two fleets converged. Scheer’s advanced-guard cruisers struck the destroyer rear guard where the Castor with the 11th Flotilla had taken station, Commodore Hawksley at the head. Scheer altered a point to starboard at 10.6, but that proved insufficient. Commodore Goodenough with the 2nd Light Cruiser Squadron, keeping touch with the Marlborough (torpedoed, limited to 16 knots), met the 4th Scouting Group (Stettin, München, Frauenlob, Stuttgart, Hamburg) on a converging course. Against the faint glow that still tinged the western horizon the silhouettes of five cruisers took shape, very close. Recognition lights and a sudden close action followed. Throughout the night British light cruisers and destroyers harried the retreating Germans; the pre-Dreadnought Pommern was torpedoed and sunk; the light cruisers Elbing and Rostock met their fate; British destroyers Tipperary, Turbulent, Fortune, Sparrowhawk and Ardent were among those lost. Scheer held the course for Horn Reefs.
High up in the North Sea summer nights are short. All eyes strained to know if there was to be another First of June. As Lord Howe made sure he had the enemy fairly to leeward, so Jellicoe had little doubt he was between them and their bases. If there was any misgiving it was mistrust of the weather: the mists began to thicken again, and a wind was getting up that promised anything but a fine summer day. Away to the northward Hipper’s shattered flagship Lützow was being abandoned, as were Elbing and Rostock.
The only flotilla that could still bar the way was the 12th, forced eastward and northward until nearly thirty miles from the battle fleet. Captain Stirling in the Faulknor led twelve powerful 34-knot destroyers. At 1.45, as the first streaks of dawn woke the black horizon, he made out a line of large ships on a south-easterly course; closing, he recognised German battleships, ordered the 1st Division to attack, and signalled the Commander-in-Chief. The enemy turned away together to avoid the attack. The 12th Flotilla’s torpedoes claimed their share, but Scheer’s main body was not brought to a renewed fleet action. When full day came the High Seas Fleet was no longer in a position from which a general action could be forced.
Communiqués and Public Reception
Jellicoe’s Battle Fleet reached Scapa between 10.30 a.m. and noon on 2 June. That evening he reported the Grand Fleet re-fuelled, at four hours’ notice, and ready for sea. Beatty, answering an inquiry on the night of 3 June, reported New Zealand, Indomitable and Inflexible ready and Lion, Tiger and Princess Royal available if necessary. Merchant vessels that had been lying up put to sea on 2 June without hesitation. Control of the North Sea remained in British hands.
It was not from the purely strategical point of view that a general action could at the moment be judged by either nation. Britain had looked for a decisive encounter that would mark a turning-point and give spectacular proof of maritime supremacy; Germany, without experience of naval war, was moved by ambition and apprehension. A second Trafalgar was, among possible results, the only one which could not have surprised either side; what actually happened was unexpected by both. In the German navy the marked feeling among officers was relief at having met the Grand Fleet and escaped without complete destruction.
Guidance of public opinion differed greatly. German censorship and propaganda were practised with premeditation and mechanical efficiency; British practice treated candour as the most effective influence in the long run. Admiral von Holtzendorff’s dictum that “in life it is not things as they are which decide, but the images people make of them” stands against the First Lord’s first communiqué of the evening of 2 June. That announcement, written by Balfour, reported a naval engagement off Jutland: the brunt had fallen on the Battle Cruiser Fleet and supporting forces, with heavy losses; the German battle fleet, aided by low visibility, had avoided prolonged action with the main British forces and returned to port after severe damage. The battle cruisers Queen Mary, Indefatigable and Invincible, and the cruisers Defence and Black Prince, were sunk; the Warrior was disabled and later abandoned; five named destroyers were lost. No British battleships or light cruisers were sunk. Enemy losses were serious: at least one battle cruiser destroyed; one battleship reported sunk by destroyers; two light cruisers disabled and probably sunk.
Looking back, Corbett judged the announcement candid, accurate and restrained. Yet it caused dismay and even indignation, because it disappointed high hopes without offering any estimate of success or of the resulting naval position. Only six hours later the Admiralty claimed three German capital ships sunk instead of two — substantially true: besides the Pommern and the Lützow, the Seydlitz had sunk in shallow water on the way home and was only raised some days later. But the German Official Report, dated 1 June and published on the 2nd, reached neutral countries at least a whole day before English news. It claimed successful heavy engagements between Skagerrak and Horn Reefs, including the destruction of the battleship Warspite (only damaged), and admitted only Wiesbaden and Pommern lost. Corbett notes the overestimates and the deliberate concealments: nothing of the grounding of Seydlitz, nor of the abandonment of Elbing, Rostock and Lützow. British newspaper comment was at first a chorus of disappointment, moderated by responsible voices pointing to the enemy’s retreat. On 5 June a further Admiralty report stated that a very brief period of contact had sufficed to compel the severely punished High Seas Fleet to seek refuge in protected waters.
Aftermath
On returning to London after the action, Maurice Hankey stressed to Balfour a rather pessimistic letter from Jellicoe about German gunnery and night-fighting arrangements. “Rather discouraging,” commented Hankey, “but Jellicoe is always rather a pessimist.” On 24 June, as the Somme bombardment opened, Hankey lunched with the Asquiths and they compared notes on Jellicoe’s Jutland despatch. Asquith called it “the worst despatch I have ever read” and “everything a despatch ought not to be.” Hankey was commissioned to get it amended at the Admiralty. He saw Balfour, who sent for Admirals Jackson and Jellicoe; as soon as his criticisms were accepted he reported to Asquith — “who was much amused.” On his way out he called on Hall, the Director of Naval Intelligence, who agreed in every detail; the Admiralty, Hankey wrote, had never consulted Hall. Thus did Hankey’s waning confidence in the Balfour–Jackson régime suffer a further decline.
When Jellicoe visited the Admiralty late in June to discuss Jutland, the conference agreed that dispositions had stood the test; disasters were attributed to technical faults of material and design — amounting practically to a vote of confidence in the Commander-in-Chief. Three days after the fleet’s return, on 5 June, Lord Kitchener, bound for Russia, lunched with Jellicoe at Scapa and embarked in the cruiser Hampshire. In a north-easterly gale she struck mines laid by U 75 on the night of 28–29 May — one of the submarines watching British bases during the German sortie before Jutland — and sank with almost all hands. The strategic result of the battle and the political shock of Kitchener’s death fell upon the country within the same week.
Scheer had failed and been unexpectedly entrapped into meeting the Grand Fleet; he extricated himself at considerable expense, yet both before and after the main action he had inflicted more serious losses than he could ever have contemplated. Jellicoe had outmanœuvred and surprised the High Seas Fleet; the net result was to increase the Grand Fleet’s large margin of superiority. After Jutland the High Seas Fleet was for some months unequal to covering a serious attack on the Dover Straits; Scheer’s and von Holtzendorff’s opinions brought the official decision restricting fleet action to support of the submarine campaign. When first reports vanished, Corbett observed, the true result was as clear as a well-drawn balance sheet: the High Seas Fleet had inflicted loss on a battle-cruiser squadron and escaped with its life, but control of the sea was irrevocably in British hands. Jutland had ended one stage of the naval war and defined the form of the final struggle — from the outbreak of the Great War through the Dogger Bank action of 1915 into the long attritional struggle for command of the sea, while the armies locked on the Western Front prepared the Somme offensive.

events/military-service-acts-1916.title: The Military Service Acts and Conscription (1916)
events/military-service-acts-1916.content:
The Military Service Acts and Conscription (1916)
The Military Service Acts of 1916 ended the British tradition of a purely voluntary army in the greatest of modern wars. After a year and a half of recruiting by appeal, attestation, and the last great voluntary canvass known as the Derby Scheme, the Coalition under asquith-herbert-henry redeemed its pledge and brought unmarried men of military age under compulsion. A second Act, debated through the spring almost to the end of May, placed recruiting upon a still broader compulsory basis. The passage of the two measures ranked, with the Irish Rebellion and the reconstruction of the Government, among the outstanding domestic events of the year.
The Strain on Voluntary Recruiting
From the first months after the outbreak-of-the-great-war, the War Office had lived upon the extraordinary flood of volunteers. By early 1915 that flood was no longer enough. When the House of Lords re-assembled on 6 January 1915 to hear kitchener-horatio, the Secretary of State for War could still report that recruiting at home had proceeded on “normal lines,” and that over 218,000 names of persons willing to serve had been registered by the Parliamentary Recruiting Committee; the shortage of officers had been made good by more than 29,000 appointments. The language was reassuring, and deliberately unspecific.
By mid-September the tone had changed. Parliament re-assembled on 14 September with National Service uppermost in members’ minds. asquith-herbert-henry refused Captain Guest a day for discussion and would say only that compulsory service had “not escaped the attention of the Government.” John Dillon declared strong opposition unless an overwhelming case were made out, and criticised officers who had published in The Times a manifesto for compulsion. The Prime Minister begged officer-members to remember that they did not sit as representatives of the Army.
The next day, 15 September, Kitchener told the Lords that provision for the forces in the field during 1916 had caused him anxious thought, owing to the recent falling off in the numbers coming forward to enlist. A large addition to the recruit supply would be needed, and he hoped for an early solution of the problem. On the same day in the Commons the Prime Minister asked for a further Vote of Credit of £250,000,000 — the seventh since the outbreak of war, bringing the seven together to £1,262,000,000 — and noted that the average daily net expenditure was running rather over £3,500,000. The war was consuming men and money at a rate that made voluntary recruiting alone look increasingly precarious.
The autumn also saw open collision between Ministers and the Northcliffe Press, whose papers had combined criticism of the Government with advocacy of compulsory service and had led the agitation that helped produce the Ministry of Munitions. Sir John Simon, then Home Secretary, denounced in the Commons a Daily Mail map of 11 October, “The Road to India,” as a dangerous instrument in enemy hands — a railway sketched from Berlin through Vienna to Constantinople and Asia, finger-posted “to Suez and India,” already reproduced in a German newspaper for propaganda. The year closed with National Service still unsettled though “not escaped,” with recruiting for 1916 already a source of anxious thought to the Secretary of State for War, with the daily cost of the war over three and a half millions sterling, and with the solution of compulsory military service left as by far the most important subject of internal settlement for 1916.
The Derby Scheme and the Unattested Residue
The last great voluntary effort was Lord Derby’s canvass. The Scheme ran from 23 October to 15 December 1915. The understanding was explicit: if any considerable proportion of unmarried men remained unattested when it closed, Compulsory Service would follow. The report of the result, issued with the New Year, showed that the unattested residue could by no means be called a “negligible quantity.”
The grand total of men of military age in the country was estimated at 5,011,441. Of these, attested, enlisted, and rejected men amounted to 2,829,263, leaving an unaccounted residue of 2,182,178, of whom 1,029,231 were set down as unmarried. Deducting 378,071 as an estimated figure for badged, reserve, and indispensable men, the number of single men left over amounted to 651,160. On all hands it was agreed that the first business of Parliament must be to redeem the pledge given by Asquith and introduce Compulsory Military Service.
Sir John Simon’s Resignation and the First Act
The end of 1915 left the country in considerable ferment over compulsion. Prophecies of a revolutionary movement among the working classes, and of an internal condition more unsettled than for a very long time past, had been freely made. Those anticipations were altogether dissipated by the reception accorded to the measure on its introduction at the beginning of the year.
The only dissentient member of the Cabinet was Sir John Simon. His resignation was announced on 1 January 1916. When the House of Commons met on 4 January, Asquith officially confirmed that Simon had resigned the office of Home Secretary. The greater part of that day, however, was occupied by lloyd-george-david, then at the Ministry of Munitions, defending his department from criticism, including the suppression of the newspaper Forward.
The first Military Service Act thus came in as the redemption of a public pledge, not as a sudden conversion. It dealt first with the unmarried men whose failure to attest had broken the Derby Scheme’s bargain. The country that had dreaded industrial revolt found, in the event, that the measure was accepted as a necessity of war. Compulsion arrived not as a party triumph of the Northcliffe campaigners of 1915, but as the Coalition’s reluctant fulfilment of a condition that Asquith himself had attached to the last voluntary canvass.
Tribunals, Hardship, and the Working of the Act
Acceptance in principle did not mean smooth administration. On the last day of February 1916, on the third reading of the Consolidated Fund Bill, the House returned to the difficulties and misunderstandings that had already gathered round the Act. Simon opened the debate by complaining that the Local Tribunals had failed to give effect to the Government promise that young men who were the sole support of their mothers should not be sent into the Army. He declared that, notwithstanding War Office undertakings, excepted men were still being bluffed into attesting. The muddle, he argued, had arisen out of Mr. Tennant’s statement that single young men rejected under the Derby Scheme must be re-examined. He quoted cases in which rejection certificates had been torn up by Recruiting Officers, and others in which the certificates had never been delivered at all. Mr. Pringle adduced further instances of the same character.
Tennant admitted that his earlier answer had been unfortunate. The Recruiting Offices had not kept lists of the rejected since 14 August, and for that reason the “Yellow Form” had been sent out indiscriminately to all men of the prescribed qualifications. Every endeavour was being made, he said, to transfer married men liable to service into reserved occupations so that single men might be set free for military duties. Mr. Long assured the House that he would do everything in his power to prevent hardship to widowed mothers and other dependants of single young men.
The Tribunals were attacked from the opposite direction as well. On 2 March Lord Derby told the House of Lords that the charge against them was that they had given altogether an unnecessary number of exemptions to attested single men. Between the complaint of over-harshness and the complaint of over-leniency, the new machinery of compulsion settled uneasily into the life of the home front.
Wimbledon, Secret Sessions, and the Second Act
Political pressure for a still broader measure continued into the spring. The last event recorded before Easter was the Wimbledon bye-election. The Coalition candidate, Sir Stuart Coats, supported by both great party organisations, was opposed by Mr. Kennedy Jones, standing as an Independent in general opposition to the Government with the cry “Do it now” against “Wait and see.” The seat, long held by Mr. Chaplin with immense majorities, returned Coats on 20 April by a majority of only 1,811. The result was taken to imply a weakening of the Government’s position in the country; there could be little doubt that hesitation on compulsory military service had cost support even in this traditionally Conservative constituency. The Government soon found itself unable any longer to resist the obvious feeling of the country. The most important business of Parliament after Easter was that of placing the whole subject of recruiting upon a new basis.
The Easter holidays were no sooner over than matters of the utmost importance came before the public. On 25 April the first announcement was made of the outbreak in Dublin — the easter-rising-1916 — and on the same day Secret Sessions were held in both Houses of Parliament to inform members of the facts and figures underlying the problem of recruiting. When the Commons met that day, Asquith called the Speaker’s attention to the presence of strangers, who were ordered to withdraw. In the Lords a Secret Session had already been provided for by an order of the Lord Great Chamberlain excluding all strangers. No report of the proceedings could of course be given; but an official account was afterwards communicated to the Press, in which the proposals of the Government were embodied under three headings.
Before turning fully to the Irish Rebellion, the contemporary record concluded the account of the final adoption of conscription, the discussion of which was carried on in Parliament almost to the end of the month of May. The second Military Service Act completed what the first had begun, extending compulsion beyond the unmarried residue that the Derby Scheme had failed to bring in. Together the two Acts transformed the British Army’s relation to the civil population and made man-power a permanent subject of parliamentary and administrative struggle for the rest of the war.
Sacrifice, Resolution, and Later Man-Power
Looking back from the end of 1916, the outstanding historical events of the domestic year were judged to be the passage of the two Military Service Acts, the Irish Rebellion, and the Reconstruction of the Government. Most classes of the community had been called upon to bear sacrifices little anticipated at the commencement of the war. That those sacrifices would be increased in the new year seemed beyond question: reference was made especially to the scheme for introducing universal national service, and to the plans for reducing the consumption of food. The prospect of these further sacrifices appeared quite powerless to modify the national resolution to prosecute the war to a successful conclusion.
The pressure of prices had already shown how closely man-power and the civilian economy were bound together. The increase in the price of food had given rise to discontent among railway workers, who demanded a 10s. advance in wages; South Wales railwaymen threatened to stop work unless the demand were conceded within a week; and only Board of Trade intervention produced a settlement on 20 September 1916 that raised the previous war bonus of 5s. to 10s. Compulsion of men and regulation of the home front advanced together.
The logic of military compulsion did not end in 1916. In 1917 critics still argued that full advantage was not being attained from the Military Service Acts because they were applied only to a section of the population. The proposed scheme for universal national service, already prominent at the end of 1916 and intended to secure a better utilisation of the man-power of the nation for both military and industrial purposes, remained in the experimental stage through the following year. In the spring of 1918, under the shadow of the german-spring-offensive-1918, the need for fighting men became again acute. When the House of Commons reassembled on 9 April 1918, a feeling of deep anxiety brooded over members. The German onslaught on the Western Front had had serious results for the Allies; the news from Neuve Chapelle spread through the Lobbies some time before the rising of the House; and it was generally agreed in the country that further drafts on man-power would be unavoidable. So urgent was the need considered that lloyd-george-david, now Prime Minister, moved on the opening day the first reading of a new Man-Power Bill — “A Bill to make further provision with respect to military service during the present war” — drafted by a committee of Ministers with Sir George Cave as Chairman. The House waived the customary day’s notice; all other Government business was set aside until the Bill had passed through all its stages. The enemy, the Prime Minister told the House, was committed to an attempt to secure a military decision that year by breaking the Armies of the Allies; seven or possibly eight months of campaigning weather remained; strategic unity under General Foch was a fundamental condition of victory, but success would be impossible without a further supply of men. Several hundred thousand men were rushed across the Channel at the end of March and during April from the great army hitherto kept at Home; British troops were also brought up from Italy, and American regiments were temporarily brigaded with French or British battalions to meet the extreme need of the next few weeks.
Thus the Acts of 1916 were not a single legislative episode but the beginning of a man-power regime that lasted until victory. What had begun as the redemption of Asquith’s Derby pledge became, under the successive pressures of the Irish rising, the reconstruction of the Government, and the German spring offensive, the organising principle of the British home front in total war.
Chronology

1915, 6 January: Kitchener addresses the Lords; recruiting still described as proceeding on normal lines.
1915, 14–15 September: National Service uppermost in the Commons; Kitchener warns of the falling off in recruits for 1916.
1915, 23 October–15 December: Derby Scheme in operation.
1916, 1 January: Sir John Simon resigns; Derby Scheme results published; 651,160 single men left over after deductions.
1916, 4 January: Asquith announces Simon’s resignation as Home Secretary; first Military Service measure the first business of Parliament.
1916, end of February: Commons debate on tribunal grievances and the working of the Act.
1916, 2 March: Lord Derby on exemptions granted by Local Tribunals.
1916, 20 April: Wimbledon bye-election; Coalition majority reduced to 1,811.
1916, 25 April: Announcement of the Dublin outbreak; Secret Sessions on recruiting in both Houses.
1916, to end of May: Final adoption of conscription; second Military Service Act.
1918, 9 April: Lloyd George introduces further Man-Power Bill under the spring crisis in France.

Sources

Annual Register, 1915. English History chapters on the National Service debate of mid-September, Kitchener’s statement on the recruiting shortfall for 1916, the Northcliffe Press collision, and the year-end judgment that compulsory military service remained the chief unsettled internal question.
Annual Register, 1916. Chapter I (end of the session / new session material) for the ferment over compulsion, Derby Scheme figures, Simon’s resignation, introduction of the Military Service Act, and February–March tribunal grievances; Chapter III (summer months) for Wimbledon, the 25 April Secret Sessions concurrent with the Dublin outbreak, and the final adoption of conscription through May; year-end summary ranking the two Military Service Acts among the outstanding events of 1916.
Annual Register, 1918. Chapter II on the Man-Power Bill of 9 April and Lloyd George’s statement of the spring military crisis, showing the later continuation of the conscription regime.

events/national-insurance-1911.title: The National Insurance Act 1911
events/national-insurance-1911.content:
The National Insurance Act 1911
The National Insurance Act of 1911 was the second great pillar of Liberal social-reform, following the non-contributory old-age-pensions-1908 and the financial and constitutional settlement of the peoples-budget-1911. Introduced by lloyd-george-david as Chancellor of the Exchequer while the Parliament Bill still occupied the centre of the session, it established compulsory insurance against sickness and invalidity for the mass of employed persons, and insurance against unemployment in selected trades. Contributions were shared among worker, employer, and the State; benefits were delivered largely through approved friendly societies and, for those outside societies, through a provisional Post Office scheme. The Act became law in the autumn of 1911 and came into force on “Joy Day,” 15 July 1912, amid medical resistance, Unionist obstruction, and the concurrent drama of the great-labour-unrest-1911-1914.
From Pensions to Insurance
Asquith had already, at Glasgow in April 1909, sketched labour exchanges, the reduction of boy labour, and unemployment insurance as “the next stage of social reform after old-age pensions and debt reduction.” Lloyd-George’s visit to Germany in August 1908 to study workmen’s insurance had given the Chancellor a continental model of contributory provision that the non-contributory pension scheme of 1908 had deliberately rejected. The constitutional crisis of 1909–11 delayed legislation; once the Parliament Act had broken the absolute veto of the house-of-lords, the Government could press social measures that the Upper House could no longer kill outright.
When george-v opened his first Parliament, the Speech from the Throne promised, as the only Bills specifically named, measures removing the pauper disqualification for old-age pensions and providing “insurance against sickness, invalidity, and (in special trades) unemployment.” The National Insurance Bill was brought forward as the principal social measure of the session. From the outset its details were closely scrutinised by friendly societies, the Labour party, and employers. Concurrently the Parliament Bill ground through Committee; the Coronation of 22 June suspended party strife for a few days; and industrial unrest on the docks, railways, and in transport trades rose toward the August climax.
Structure of the Bill: Health and Unemployment
The Bill had two main parts. The health (or national health insurance) part covered sickness, invalidity, maternity, and — through sanatorium benefit — consumption. The unemployment part applied only to special trades. Administration was to rest on approved societies — predominantly the great friendly societies — with a residual “Post Office” contributor class for those who did not join a society. Separate Commissioners were provided for Ireland, Scotland, and Wales. Local Health Committees, later renamed Insurance Committees, were given enlarged numbers and powers.
Committee stage was, in the Register’s phrase, “kaleidoscopic,” though most of the hundreds of amendments were verbal or consequential. The chief substantive changes fixed the shape of the Act as it left Parliament. Sick pay was set at 10s. per week for men and 7s. 6d. for women, and was to continue for twenty-six weeks instead of the original thirteen. Maternity benefit was extended to the wife of an insured person even if she herself was insured. Sanatorium benefit for consumption might be extended to the dependants of the insured consumptive. Married women might come in during their husband’s lifetime as voluntary contributors with reduced payments, receiving sickness and disablement benefit. Soldiers, sailors, naval men, and mercantile seamen might come in under special provisions; so might fishermen co-partners under regulations adapted to local custom.
Where it was the custom for the employer to pay full wages during sickness — especially for agricultural labourers and clerks — contributions of both employer and employed might be reduced, and sickness benefit likewise, if the employer agreed to pay wages for six weeks of illness. Persons earning less than 9s. a week paid no contribution; those between 9s. and 12s. paid 1d. per week less than under the original Bill — a provision of particular importance to women outworkers and to Scottish rural and industrial populations. The Post Office part of the Bill was made distinctly provisional. For Ireland the employer’s contribution was reduced to 2½d. a week; migratory labourers and outworkers whose work was done in leisure time were exempted; medical benefit was withdrawn in view of the existing dispensary system; and the constitution of Health Committees was adapted to Irish conditions.
Labour Criticism and the Weakest Classes
Labour opposition was not to insurance in principle but to the Bill’s treatment of the weakest. Broadly, the measure was thought to do too little for casuals, sweated workers, “poor lives,” and the strugglers generally. On 17 July 1911 attempts were vainly made to extend full medical benefit to persons entitled to maternity benefit; to extend maternity benefit to unmarried mothers (Keir Hardie’s proposal, defeated by 207 to 95); and to make sick pay run from the first day of illness — as the friendly societies desired — instead of from the fourth day as the Bill provided. The next day Lloyd-George appealed to members not to seek popularity by voting away safeguards they knew to be proper. On the day following, Lees Smith (Liberal, Northampton) moved to exempt insured persons who had fallen into arrears through unemployment from having to pay up the employer’s arrears as well as their own before recovering benefits. The amendment was defeated only by 163 to 116, after the Chancellor warned that its success might involve the defeat of the Bill. The arrears clause as amended was carried by 210 to 77. Rejection of these amendments intensified Labour denunciations; at pending bye-elections Unionists made much of the Bill’s defects.
Yet when the great strikes of August had estranged the Labour party and some advanced Liberals from the Ministry, the Register recorded that the Government had “gained in popularity, apparently, by the Insurance Bill.” Firmness against industrial paralysis had mitigated Unionist hostility; the social measure remained a popular asset.
Passage, Misrepresentation, and Medical Resistance
The Bill completed its progress in the autumn of 1911. Hundreds of amendments had been absorbed; separate national Commissioners were in place; Irish medical benefit had been withdrawn; low-wage contribution relief had been written in. The Act received the Royal Assent as the session closed. Implementation, however, was another battle. Through the winter of 1911–12 and the spring of 1912, Unionists attacked the measure in Parliament and misrepresented it in the country; a Liberal Insurance Committee was formed to answer those misrepresentations. In the Address debate of February 1912, Asquith asked whether Mr. Bonar Law, if he became Prime Minister, would repeal the Act. Bonar Law answered “Certainly” — then wrote to the press that he meant repeal only if Unionists took office before the Act became operative; otherwise they would amend it drastically. Ministers treated the admission as a gift.
Medical resistance was the most serious practical obstacle. Doctors objected to the terms of service under the panel system. On Joy Day itself Lloyd-George told a great meeting at the Kennington Theatre that six shillings per member had been set aside for the doctors, who would have an interest in keeping patients well and no bad debts; if they would not come to terms, the £4,000,000 set aside for them would go back to the members, and actuarial report showed that large additional benefits could then be given. The doctors asked for 11s. per member — an extra £4,000,000 a year, or roughly 1d. on the income tax and ¾d. on tea. Sir William Plender’s report showed that in Dundee doctors’ incomes worked out at 4s. 2d. per head, including guinea patients. The Chancellor was not afraid of the “squalid resistance” to paying 3d. a week that opponents encouraged, but he warned that the beginning of law-breaking was full of menace.
Joy Day and the Working of the Act
“Joy Day,” 15 July 1912, was the day the Act came into force. Through hot weather, or through the efforts of opponents, it was not extensively celebrated; but Lloyd-George at Kennington worked the meeting to high enthusiasm. Of 13,000,000 persons compulsorily insurable, 9,500,000 had already joined approved societies; in three weeks or a month, he predicted, there would be 12,000,000, and 500,000 Post Office contributors would be in societies as well. Friendly societies, previously at a standstill and hard put to keep solvent, would start solvent with a margin; those joining were making additional payments for higher benefits. Critics said the Government could not deliver the benefits — “wait and see.” The money for the sanatoria was there, but “the Act was not an Aladdin’s lamp”; already eleven tuberculosis doctors had been appointed for the whole of Wales out of fifty-seven applicants.
By late autumn Lloyd-George was claiming at Kirkcaldy that the Insurance Act was “working like clockwork.” At Port Sunlight, Asquith linked Old Age Pensions and Insurance as benefits secured under the Parliament Act, which Ministers would have betrayed their trust not to use for the declared wishes of the electorate. The Act thus closed the legislative arc opened by the 1906 majority: from non-contributory pensions financed by the People’s Budget, through the curbing of the Lords, to compulsory contributory insurance administered by the voluntary societies of the working class itself.
Aftermath and Significance
National Insurance did not end industrial unrest; the coal strike of March 1912 and the transport strike of the early summer ran alongside the Act’s first months. It did not satisfy Labour critics who wanted more for casuals and sweated workers. It did not immediately reconcile the doctors. But it created a permanent machinery of contributions, approved societies, Insurance Committees, and State subsidy that transformed the relationship between the British State and the wage-earning population. Clayton’s contemporary survey of democracy already treated the labour legislation of the previous twenty years — including pensions and the wider social programme of which insurance was the climax — as proof that parliamentary representation could deliver material gains to the working class.
Belloc, in The Servile State, treated the Act as the registration of the wage-earning class. Compulsion attached to employment below a certain income, or to “a vulgar fellow working with his hands,” not to the citizen as citizen; the educated and the economically free were excluded. The duty of seeing the law obeyed was laid on the Capitalist class, who gathered what he called a Poll Tax and completed the map of name, address, illness, and supposed malingering. Labour exchanges already recorded the worker, his refusals of service, and his “tendencies to rebellion against Capital.” Insurance money, once compelled, was not even in a society he could control: refuse work at a stated wage and “you certainly shall not have a right to the money you have been compelled to put aside.” For Belloc the Act followed “in every particular the lines” of the servile-state — security purchased by a change of status, not by restoration of property.
Politically, the Act was Lloyd-George’s personal monument within the Asquith ministry: a measure he had prepared since the German journey of 1908, defended through the constitutional crisis, forced through Committee against Labour amendments and Unionist hostility, and launched on Joy Day against medical and partisan resistance. It completed, with old-age pensions, the Edwardian experiment in using Free-Trade finance and a reformed parliamentary constitution for social-reform — even as the great-labour-unrest-1911-1914 and the irish-home-rule-crisis tested how far statute could contain the conflicts of an industrial and multi-national kingdom.

events/old-age-pensions-1908.title: The Old Age Pensions Act 1908
events/old-age-pensions-1908.content:
The Old Age Pensions Act 1908
The Old Age Pensions Act of 1908 was the first great social-security statute of the Liberal ministry returned in the landslide of election-1906-tariff-reform. It created a non-contributory state pension for persons over seventy, paid from the Exchequer and subject to tests of means, character, and poor-relief history. The measure announced that Free-Trade finance could carry the cost of social-reform without Tariff Reform, and it opened a legislative path that would run through the peoples-budget-1911 to the national-insurance-1911 Act three years later.
The Liberal Programme after 1906
The Liberal majority returned in 1906, swollen by Labour representation and Irish Nationalist support, put the condition of the people at the centre of the parliamentary programme. By 1908 trade was turning down: throughout the year there was grave industrial depression; on the Clyde, shipbuilding, which had reached maximum output in 1907, fell to the level of 1894; cotton spinning and weaving, jute, linen, steel and iron, and building all suffered.
On 15 January 1908, speaking at Lancaster, asquith-herbert-henry — still Chancellor of the Exchequer under campbell-bannerman-henry — promised that an old-age pension scheme would be begun. Lord Cromer, addressing Unionist Free Traders at Glasgow five days earlier, had already condemned any such scheme as developing “demoralising dependence on the State.” When the King opened Parliament on 29 January, the Speech from the Throne promised proposals “for making better provision for old age,” together with licensing and education Bills, mines hours, housing and town planning, valuation reform, Irish universities and land purchase, a Port of London authority, and the consolidation of the law on children and juvenile offenders. The Marquess of Lansdowne, replying in the Lords, condemned “the assumption of the colossal liability of old-age pensions” as one of the Government’s most dangerous commitments.
Campbell-Bannerman’s health was already failing. After his death in April, Asquith became Prime Minister and lloyd-george-david succeeded him at the Exchequer. The pensions Bill, foreshadowed in the Budget, now became the Chancellor’s principal social measure of the session. Winston Churchill, fighting and losing North-West Manchester in April, still promised that old-age pensions would be “in existence before the year was out.”
The Bill: Non-Contributory, Means-Tested, at Seventy
The Bill as printed on 2 June differed from the Budget forecast. It imposed a qualified character test; it disqualified persons who had received poor relief (other than medical relief) since 1 January 1907; and it extended the married-persons limitation to other relatives living in the same house. The scheme was deliberately non-contributory. Moving the second reading on 16–17 June, Lloyd-George told the House that so-called contributory schemes had been abandoned by most reformers, including chamberlain-joseph; that they would exclude women; and that the failure of friendly societies’ superannuation schemes had shown the contributory plan to be impracticable.
The numbers were carefully stated. Of 1,262,632 persons over seventy in the United Kingdom, 572,000 were estimated to be pensionable. The annual cost was put at £7,500,000, with £6,000,000 for the first year. Lloyd-George claimed it as “the most liberal scheme yet proposed in any old country.” Friendly societies, for their part, expressed dissatisfaction that the Bill gave no encouragement to thrift; labour organisations treated it as only an instalment. At a National Liberal Club banquet on 12 June, Asquith defended the measure against both advocates of a contributory scheme and Liberal and Labour critics, explaining that the exclusion of persons in receipt of poor relief was only for the current year, pending the report of the Poor Law Commission.
Opposition in the Commons was sharp but not united. Harold Cox moved an amendment condemning the expenditure of taxpayers’ money on persons selected by “arbitrary standards of age, income and character,” and commended the German contributory model. Lord Robert Cecil discerned Socialistic elements and cited United States pension lists as a warning. For the Labour party, Mr. O’Grady advocated universal pensions as a right and declared the Bill “hopelessly inadequate.” Richard Haldane replied that the Bill embodied the principle of the English poor law since Elizabeth — that the prosperous must relieve the necessitous — and that it formed part of a larger class of reforms to follow the Poor Law review. The second reading was carried; the Bill proceeded through Committee and the Lords and became law in the course of the session.
Cost, Finance, and the Stock Market
The financial burden was the Opposition’s strongest point and the City’s immediate anxiety. On the Stock Exchange, Consols were depressed by the difficulty of providing means for old-age pensions, by the prospect of a large issue of Irish Land Stock, by falling revenue, and by competition from other gilt-edged securities. Trade depression made the revenue outlook still more uncertain. Asquith, speaking at the International Free-Trade Congress dinner in August, conceded that Britain was entering a period of comparative depression and might have to suspend debt reduction and impose fresh taxation, but insisted that Free-Trade finance would “stand the strain of social reform” and that none of the yield of taxation would be diverted to privileged interests.
The Act came into operation at the turn of the year. Claims immediately exceeded expectation. By early 1909 Asquith had reckoned on about 500,000 pensioners; some 490,000 had already established their claims, and an addition of about 130,000 seemed probable. The Annual Register for 1909 opened with the revenue for the past nine months running considerably below Estimates, while claims for old-age pensions “greatly exceeded expectation.” Lansdowne, in the Address debate that February, commented severely on the “amazing” old-age pension figures from Ireland. In Ireland itself the Act was of great benefit, though figures early in the new year suggested that many beneficiaries had in fact no claim.
The cost of non-contributory pensions, together with rising naval Estimates, forced the financial crisis of 1909. Asquith, opening the session of that year, told the Commons that finance must be the first business; that social reform had to be paid for; and that the Old Age Pensions Act was “only the first instalment.” The peoples-budget-1911 of April 1909 was framed to meet that bill — land-value duties, super-tax, and heavier death duties — and the constitutional struggle that followed was inseparable from the decision of 1908 to put a non-contributory pension charge on the Exchequer.
Germany, Insurance, and the Next Instalment
Even as the pensions Bill passed, Lloyd-George was looking beyond it. In August 1908 he visited Germany to study workmen’s insurance, and allowed himself to be interviewed by the Neue Freie Presse of Vienna advocating an Anglo-German understanding. The trip linked the non-contributory pension experiment to the contributory health and unemployment insurance that he would introduce in 1911. Asquith, at Glasgow in April 1909, already sketched labour exchanges, the reduction of boy labour, and unemployment insurance as “the next stage of social reform after old-age pensions and debt reduction.”
Clayton, writing in 1911, listed old-age pensions with Workmen’s Compensation and the Trade Disputes Act among the labour legislation of the previous twenty years that demonstrated “the value of parliamentary representation to the working class.” The Act of 1908 did not create a universal right; it selected by age, means, and character; it left friendly societies and Labour critics unsatisfied. But it established the principle that the State would maintain the aged poor from general taxation, and it committed Liberal finance to a permanent social charge that Tariff Reformers and Free-Trade Unionists alike had to confront.
Aftermath and Significance
By the opening of 1909 the Act was already a settled fact of public finance and of Irish and British social life. An amending Bill in 1911 relaxed qualifications and removed the pauper disqualification that had been the most contested feature of the original statute. When Asquith, returning from Dublin in July 1912, spoke at Port Sunlight of the benefits secured by the Old Age Pensions and Insurance Acts, he treated both as achievements that Ministers would have betrayed their trust not to force through under the Parliament Act.
The political significance ran deeper than the weekly payment. Pensions were the first large-scale demonstration that the 1906 majority intended to use the State for social security rather than for Tariff Reform or for the defence of the house-of-lords. They made the People’s Budget necessary; they prepared the ground for National Insurance; and they gave Labour and Liberal members a concrete achievement to set against the industrial unrest that would mark the years 1911–14. The “colossal liability” Lansdowne had denounced became the foundation stone of Edwardian social-reform.

events/outbreak-of-the-great-war.title: The Outbreak of the Great War (July–August 1914)
events/outbreak-of-the-great-war.content:
The Outbreak of the Great War (July–August 1914)
The Great War came upon Great Britain with a suddenness that belied years of naval preparation, yet it closed a political year already darkened by the irish-home-rule-crisis, bye-election losses, Labour and Nationalist pressure, and the Ulster and Army crises of the spring. Within twelve days the Cabinet that on Friday, 24 July 1914, was still debating Fermanagh and Tyrone found itself at war with the German Empire; the Fleet concentrated for a test mobilisation stood at war stations in the North Sea; and Parliament, cheered by a Vote of Credit of one hundred million pounds, placed the resources of the Empire at the disposal of a struggle which Mr. Asquith described as one of the greatest in history. The unfinished Irish and Welsh measures were disposed of only by wartime suspensory arrangement; Sir Edward Carson transferred Ulster energies, under protest, to the national cause; and Earl Kitchener of Khartoum took the War Office as the recruiting and military organisation of a long war began.
The Austrian Note and the Crisis in Cabinet
Churchill’s later narrative of the Admiralty places the Cabinet of Friday, 24 July, still immersed in the Irish boundary question when Sir Edward Grey brought in the Austrian note to Serbia. The note was clearly an ultimatum of a severity seldom seen in modern diplomacy; its arrival cut across the domestic quarrel at the very moment when the Curragh incident, the Larne gun-running, and the Buckingham Palace Conference had shown how thin was the line between constitutional agitation and force in Ireland. The Irish crisis had divided Cabinet and Army while Europe moved toward war, and had delayed decisions on any continental commitment.
Within hours the European capitals were in motion. Serbia’s acceptance of nearly all the Austrian demands seemed for a moment to open a path of escape. By Sunday, 26 July, Austria was not satisfied; the First Sea Lord, Prince Louis of Battenberg, had already, on Churchill’s instruction, told the Fleet not to disperse after its practice mobilisation; and Grey viewed the situation very gravely. At Grey’s and Sir William Tyrrell’s insistence the Admiralty published a communiqué announcing that the First Fleet at Portland would not disperse for manœuvre leave and that the vessels of the Second Fleet would remain at their home ports. The notice appeared in the Monday papers under the heading “British Naval Measures” — the first public signal that Britain was holding her sea power in readiness under the doctrine of command-of-the-sea.
The Cabinets which now met daily or twice a day found an overwhelmingly pacific majority. Churchill estimated that at least three-quarters of the members were determined not to be drawn into a European quarrel unless Great Britain herself were attacked. Against this current Grey held to two fixed points: the obligation involved in Belgian neutrality, and the danger that would arise if France were left to face Germany alone. Churchill pressed the naval precautions which the Fleet’s concentration made possible. On 30 July he obtained authority for the Fleet to pass the Straits of Dover by night and take up its war stations, and the great ships moved north in secrecy and darkness.
Finance Collapses as Diplomacy Ends
The Chronicle of the last days of July and the first of August fixed the sequence of financial and diplomatic collapse that closed the old order. On 31 July the London Stock Exchange was closed by order of the Committee, and the Bank rate raised to 8 per cent. On 1 August the Bank rate was advanced to 10 per cent.; the National Penny Bank suspended payment; Germany declared war on Russia and France. On 2 August German invasion of Luxemburg and France began; prayers were offered for the nation throughout the United Kingdom; the Admiralty called out the Naval Reserves; there was a patriotic demonstration before Buckingham Palace; and a partial Moratorium was decreed by Royal Proclamation.
On the verge of war the Cabinet met twice; divisions of opinion previously existing among Ministers disappeared in the course of the day almost entirely. The King held a Council at 4.30 p.m.; the Government took control of all wireless telegraphy; a moratorium of a month was established for certain bills of exchange; and the Admiralty called out the Naval Reserves, including naval and marine pensioners under fifty-five, and the Royal Volunteer Reserve. On the announcement of that last step a crowd of some 6,000 marched up the Mall to Buckingham Palace and sang the national anthems of Great Britain and France.
Next morning London awoke to a new kind of Bank Holiday. The morning papers announced the Germans’ violation of Luxemburg, their invasion of France, and their ultimatum to Belgium; crowds gathered outside Buckingham Palace and Whitehall, impartially cheering Ministers and Unionist leaders. A large section of Liberal opinion was still uncertain. Many condemned all wars as criminal; many more held that the Foreign Office was prejudiced against Germany, and abhorred fighting to preserve the balance of power or to strengthen Russia. Protests against departure from neutrality were specially noticeable in the Manchester Guardian and the Daily News; manifestoes came from the Bishops of Lincoln and Hereford, the British Neutrality Committee, and a Cambridge group who called war against Germany in the interest of Russia and Servia “a sin against civilisation.” Those divisions, the Annual Register records, were rapidly closing as knowledge of the real position grew.
Grey, Belgium, Ultimatum, and Declaration of War
On 3 August came the abandonment of Cowes Regatta by special desire of the King; a German ultimatum to Belgium; Royal Proclamations authorising the Admiralty to requisition British ships and forbidding the export of warlike stores; and Sir Edward Grey’s statement in the House of Commons.
The decisive turn had come with the German violation of Luxemburg and the German ultimatum to Belgium. The appeal of the King of the Belgians that the guaranteeing Powers should uphold the sanctity of the Treaty regarding Belgian neutrality settled the issue for the majority of Asquith’s colleagues. By Monday, 3 August, most of them regarded war as inevitable, though resignations were still expected. Formal sanction was given that morning to the already completed mobilisation of the Fleet and to the immediate mobilisation of the Army. No Cabinet decision was taken, Churchill insists, to send an ultimatum to Germany, to declare war, or to despatch an army to France; those supreme acts “were compelled by the force of events, and rest on the authority of the Prime Minister.”
That afternoon Grey informed the House that the Germans were willing to comply with the British demand that no German warships should be sent into the English Channel; then, with the sombre march of his argument, he carried the assembly with him. Outside the Chamber Churchill asked him what would happen next. “Now,” Grey said, “we shall send them an ultimatum to stop the invasion of Belgium within 24 hours.”
On 4 August an Order in Council placed the railways of the United Kingdom under Government control; the British ultimatum to Germany was delivered; British Army mobilisation was ordered by Proclamation; British Ministers resigned; and the German invasion of Belgium began. Throughout that day the Admiralty lived under the double strain of the expiring ultimatum and the chase of the German battle-cruiser Goeben and light cruiser Breslau in the Mediterranean. Churchill sought authority to engage if the Goeben attacked French transports; the Cabinet adhered formally to the view that no act of war should be committed before the ultimatum expired. “The moral integrity of the British Empire,” Churchill records, “must not be compromised at this solemn moment for the sake of sinking a single ship.” The order was cancelled. The Goeben escaped into Turkish waters.
At 5.50 p.m. the Admiralty warned all ships that the war telegram would be issued at midnight. Mobilisation was complete; every ship was in its station. At eleven o’clock at night — midnight by German time — the ultimatum expired. Along the Mall an immense concourse was singing “God save the King.” The chimes of Big Ben broke over the sound, and as the first stroke of the hour boomed out the war telegram — “Commence hostilities against Germany” — was flashed to the ships and establishments under the White Ensign all over the world. Churchill walked across the Horse Guards Parade and reported to the Prime Minister that the deed was done. On 5 August the German mine-layer Königin Luise was sunk by H.M.S. Amphion and the Third Torpedo Flotilla. The political year of 1914 had ended; the war year had begun.
Great Britain at War: Empire, Vote of Credit, and Kitchener
The war found a Government prepared to withstand the enemy and a Parliament and people whose divisions — on which the Germans had staked their hopes — were rapidly closing. Promises of help poured in from all parts of the Empire. Austrian and German reservists were detained; enemy ships in British ports and within reach of Allied cruisers were seized — twenty on the first day alone — and German oceanic trade was stopped at once. The Fleets that had been brought together at Spithead took up their stations in the North Sea; cruisers went out to protect the trade routes. Horses and motor-lorries were requisitioned for the despatch of the British Expeditionary Force — the opening of what would become the long narrative of the Western Front in 1914 — and a system of secrecy as to movements, loyally observed by the Press and rigorously enforced by authority, settled over the country.
The first day of war in the Commons brought the announcement of ministerial resignations, of the violation of Belgian neutrality, and of the impending Vote of Credit of £100,000,000, which was loudly cheered. Two war measures passed almost without debate: one amending Prize Court procedure, the other empowering the Crown to impose restrictions on aliens with a view to the removal or detention of spies. Late that evening a White Paper (Cd. 1467) was published containing nearly 160 documents of correspondence respecting the European Crisis. It eventually enabled the British people to form their own opinion as to the responsibility for the war.
On 5 August Asquith moved the Vote of Credit. After tribute to Grey’s unremitting efforts for peace, he quoted the German Chancellor’s appeal for British neutrality — free licence, as regards France, to annex French possessions overseas if successful; as regards Belgium, bartering away Britain’s obligation to keep her plighted word. He characterised the proposal as infamous. “The war has been forced upon us.” The Government had thought it both the duty and the interest of Great Britain to go to war — first, to fulfil a solemn international obligation; secondly, to vindicate the principle that small nationalities were not to be crushed by the arbitrary will of a strong and overmastering Power. He asked for £100,000,000 not only for naval and military operations but to assist food supplies, promote trade and industry, relieve distress, and meet all expenses arising out of the state of war. He had taken the War Secretaryship temporarily; Lord Kitchener, with great public spirit and patriotism, had now undertaken it. Kitchener was not a politician; his acceptance did not identify him with any set of political opinions.
The War Council of 5 August, as Churchill records, debated whether four divisions or six should go to France; and Kitchener’s vast recruiting task began at once. In an early military statement he reported rather more than six divisions of British troops and two cavalry divisions in the field, further Regular divisions being organised from units withdrawn from oversea garrisons and replaced where necessary by Territorials who had volunteered for service abroad. Troops were coming from India and the Dominions, and the response at home to the call for recruits had afforded a remarkable demonstration of the energy and patriotism of the young men.
Irish Home Rule Suspended
When the European crisis absorbed the nation, the unfinished Irish and Welsh measures still had to be disposed of under conditions which the Opposition denounced as an abuse of the war emergency. In the House of Lords the second reading of the Home Rule Bill was moved, but ultimately adjourned by 93 votes to 29. Crewe said that any expectation on the Continent of civil war in Ireland had been encouraged quite as much by the threats from Ulster as by any action of the Government; what was important was that the Home Rule Bill and the Amending Bill should come into operation at the same time. Lansdowne complained that the Government were enabling the Nationalists to obtain without a struggle what would otherwise have cost them a very serious struggle. A similar motion adjourning the Welsh Church Bill was carried by 89 to 27. Lord Lansdowne’s Legislation (Suspension during War) Bill was then passed through all its stages.
Sir Edward Carson issued an indignant manifesto to the Ulster loyalists, attacking the Government for taking advantage of the war to pass the Home Rule Bill, but reminding them that their motto, now as always, was “Our Country First.” But they would never have Home Rule — never! Next day the Commons disagreed with the Lords’ amendments to the Suspensory Bill; the Lords gave way. The political struggle of the session thus closed, not by a settlement on the merits, but by a wartime arrangement which left both statutes on the book subject to suspensory provisions, while Carson transferred Ulster energies, under protest, to the national cause — the suspended irish-home-rule settlement that would later be transformed by the Easter Rising and by the debates of the First Coalition.
The Money Market and Emergency Finance
On the adjournment of the first war sitting, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Lloyd George, made his statement on the financial position. The emergency, he said, was due to temporary causes, largely to the stoppage of remittances from abroad; there was no failure of credit. After conferences at the Treasury it had been decided to suspend the Bank Charter Act in order to economise gold. Condemning the hoarding of gold as helpful to the enemy, he stated that on 7 August Government notes for 1l. and 10s. would be issued, convertible into gold at the Bank of England; postal orders would also be legal tender; the Bank rate would be reduced to 6 per cent.; and the moratorium extended for a month. Mr. A. Chamberlain fully endorsed the statement.
Not a market in the City was unmoved: the machinery of the money-market and the banks, the Stock Exchange, Lloyd’s, the Baltic, the shipping lines, the Corn Exchange — all felt at once the shock of a war for which no peacetime organisation had been prepared. Later work turned on the discrimination of bills, the restoration of the foreign exchanges, and the protection of the Stock Exchange from a forced realisation of securities. Some 70–80 million pounds of securities were hypothecated in respect of pre-war debts; the Government agreed to advance 60 per cent. of their value on 29 July on condition that the banks undertook not to put them on the market till six months after the war. Gold at the Bank rose during the war from 26 to 85.5 million pounds; the loan of 350 million pounds was over-subscribed; in all some 440 million pounds was raised with the Stock Exchange closed. A financial catastrophe, probably without parallel, had been avoided under a system of Treasury control and State guarantee which preserved British credit for the war.
Food prices and the spy danger at once claimed public attention. Sugar jumped from 15s. to 38s. per cwt.; of flour and imported meat there was no shortage. Territorial troops were posted to guard railways, bridges, and waterworks. The Aliens Restriction Act enabled the Government to require all enemy alien residents to register and to restrict their freedom of movement and residence.
Within hours of the war telegram the machinery of a nation at war was thus in motion: Prize Courts, alien restrictions, financial emergency measures, the White Paper, the Vote of Credit, Kitchener at the War Office, the silent preparations for the passage of the Army to France, and the wartime suspension of the Irish and Welsh statutes. The long Victorian and Edwardian peace was over.
