events/passchendaele.title: Messines and the Third Battle of Ypres (Passchendaele) (1917)
events/passchendaele.content:
Messines and the Third Battle of Ypres (Passchendaele) (1917)
The British Flanders campaign of 1917 opened with a carefully prepared success on the Messines ridge in June and then, at the end of July, passed into the prolonged offensive known as the Third Battle of Ypres — a struggle that culminated, on 6 November, in the storming of the village of Passchendaele by Canadian troops. It was the principal British land effort of the year on the Western Front after the inconclusive fighting of the Somme the year before, and it was fought under a War Cabinet formed when the first Coalition of 1915–16 had already given way to Lloyd George’s smaller directing body. The Annual Register of 1917 records the operations in the language of the contemporary official narrative: limited advances under extreme bombardment, heavy fighting east of Ypres through the autumn, and no large geographical change. Hankey’s diary and the War Cabinet minutes of June 1917 place those operations against a darker political background — the first clear warning that French army discipline was breaking, Lloyd George’s desire to abandon the Flanders offensive and seek a separate peace with Austria, and the claim that the Messines mine plan itself had originated with Hankey and been carried out by Norton-Griffiths.
After Arras: The Battle of Messines
After the Battle of Arras and the unsuccessful French offensive in April there was a lull in the fighting. British captures of prisoners during May were small, and only one gun was taken. At the beginning of June the British opened a new offensive, carried out with even greater vigour than had been displayed at Arras. The new operations received the name of the Battle of Messines.
To the west of the small town of Messines the ground rises to a ridge, a long low hill which the Germans then held, and from which their guns commanded much of the British Front south of Ypres. It was this ridge which was the immediate objective of the assault. North-west of Messines the German line, as it existed at the beginning of June, formed a marked salient and ran westward of Wytschaete. After a violent artillery preparation lasting for several days, the infantry of the British Second Army moved to the assault at 3 a.m. on 7 June. The attack extended over a front of nine miles from Klein Zillebeke, just north of the Ypres–Comines Canal, to a point about a mile south of Messines village. The Second Army was under the command of General Plumer.
The attack upon the ridge was preceded by the explosion of twenty enormous mines (Hankey later wrote of nineteen), upon the preparation of which months had been spent. The sound of this explosion was heard in the outskirts of London. The German defence was literally blown to pieces. The whole of the contested ridge was captured in the first rush of the infantry. The villages of Wytschaete, Messines, Oosttaverne, Hollebeke, and Klein Zillebeke were also captured. Five thousand prisoners were taken on this one day, but the number of guns which fell to the British was not large. The advance reached a maximum depth of two miles. In the course of the next week the Crown Prince of Bavaria, who commanded the troops on the British Front, launched a series of violent counter-attacks, but all his attempts to retake the ridge were successfully frustrated. During the remainder of June the British made further slight advances, and by the end of the month the toll of captures increased to sixty-seven guns and nearly 9,000 prisoners — figures, the Annual Register noted, not so large as those relating to the Battle of Arras.
Hankey recorded that the plan of concentrating mines and preparing for an offensive months ahead had been suggested by him and pressed on the soldiers both personally (to General Fowke, the C.R.E. in France) and through Swinton by letter in the first six months of 1915. “I believe the first idea was mine but Norton-Griffiths carried it out.” The purpose of the Messines stroke, as Hankey’s biographer summarises it, was to straighten out the notorious Ypres salient. The capture of the dominating Messines ridge was a heartening, though limited, success. As soon as the Germans had recovered from the initial shock the battle resumed a static form — though with Plumer’s Second Army better placed through possession of the geographically insignificant but tactically vital high ground, and the German “bulge” south of Ypres eliminated. Nothing further was attempted in this sector until the start of the Third Battle of Ypres at the end of July.
The French Crisis and the Question of Flanders
While Messines was in progress, General Henry Wilson brought to the Cabinet the warning that the French would not stick it much longer, and that Pétain had failed in his promise to carry out an offensive on the 10th in support of Haig’s attack on the Messines ridge. The report, confirmed more or less by Lord Esher, made the War Cabinet very anxious. It was the Cabinet’s first clear intimation that something was seriously wrong with the discipline of the French Army. Hankey’s chapter headings for the spring and early summer of 1917 place the same crisis in a wider strategic frame: the failure of the Nivelle offensive and the French mutinies; the Russian Revolution and its effect on Allied strategy; the entry of the United States into the war; and the problems of co-ordination with the Allies. In a Specially Secret Cabinet Minute covering seven foolscap pages in Hankey’s own hand, he recorded that the War Cabinet felt the very grave information communicated by Wilson strongly reinforced Lord Milner’s arguments in favour of a fresh stocktaking of the whole war situation.
Lloyd George took a more sanguine view than Wilson. After harsh remarks about the large number of instances in which the advice of the experts had proved wrong, he emphasised his belief that Britain could achieve both a military and a diplomatic success. Once again he had his eyes on the Middle East, where he hoped that if Syria could be got into British hands both Turkey and Bulgaria might sue for peace. The final decisions of 8 June included the setting up of a Committee on War Policy (Milner’s proposal, with Smuts brought in as a fresh mind) and a resolve that Austria was at least entitled to a reply on peace feelers — despite Italian objections. Hankey recorded the gist of the discussion: Lloyd George now proposed to abandon the British offensive in Flanders and try to isolate Germany by making a separate peace with Austria. Haig and Robertson’s reaction to those proposals would follow in due course. The Flanders offensive, nevertheless, went forward.
At home the same months were marked by the determination, recorded in the Annual Register, that the war must be continued “at whatever sacrifices” until a victorious conclusion had been reached. Man-power and the disposition of the forces continued to occupy the House when the war was under debate. Critics of the Salonika expedition and advocates of fuller use of the Military Service Acts argued over where the next drafts should come from; Mr. Churchill, in a general strategic survey early in the year, doubted whether decisive results could be expected by mere attrition and hoped the Government would not commit its armies to attrition on a gigantic scale unless they were absolutely certain they could pursue it to a decisive point. The Flanders offensive was precisely the kind of commitment that debate had in view.
The Third Battle of Ypres
The next British offensive was carried out with some assistance from the French and was known as the Third Battle of Ypres. During the last ten days of July the bombardment of the German line in Flanders was increased to a pitch of extreme violence, and according to the German account the artillery duel on this occasion exceeded in intensity anything previously witnessed. After the bombardment the infantry went to the attack on 31 July, a small contingent of French troops making a joint attack and operating on the British left wing, close to the sea.
The new offensive suffered the same fate as the other great attacks in the Western Theatre. Advances were made in the initial stages only: the opposing lines were driven back a short distance, but were not broken. The attack extended over a front of fifteen miles, from Steenstraate on the river Yser to La Basse Ville on the river Lys. The French contingent captured Steenstraate and Bixschoote and drove back the German lines to a depth of about two miles. This advance was achieved in the first rush, on the morning of 31 July, and the British advances further south were likewise made on the first day. The British captured the villages of Verlorenhoek, Frezenberg, St. Julien, and Pilkem in the centre, and the villages of Hooge, Westhoek, La Basse Ville, and Hollebeke on the right wing. The British took over 5,000 prisoners on 31 July, and the French captured about 1,000.
The German counter-attacks were prompt and determined. Throughout the night of 31 July–1 August they endeavoured to recapture the ground they had lost, hoping to seize the disputed terrain before the British had had time to consolidate. In this the enemy were frustrated; on 1 August the Germans did succeed in recapturing St. Julien, but they obtained no appreciable advantage at any other spot, and the British once more entered St. Julien two days later.
During the next fortnight the fighting on the British Front was less severe, but on 15 August Sir Douglas Haig again took the offensive. On that day Canadian troops delivered a successful assault upon a dominating height known as Hill 70, near Lens, and on the following day the village of Langemarck, north-east of Ypres, was taken. During these two days about 2,500 prisoners were captured, and a few guns also fell into British hands. The total number of prisoners taken by the British in these offensives from 31 July to 31 August inclusive was 10,697, and about forty guns were captured.
Hankey’s narrative of July–September 1917 centres the same months on the third battle of Ypres itself, his visits to the front, and his impressions of Haig and the commanders, together with the growth of the Cabinet Secretariat and the co-ordination of Allied strategy. The offensive remained Haig’s great Flanders effort of the year; the political doubts of June had not cancelled it.
Autumn Fighting and the Storm of Passchendaele
Although no large geographical changes were brought about, extremely heavy fighting took place in the Western Theatre during the last four months of the year. The Allies had the initiative throughout, and it was invariably they who took the offensive, although the German defence remained powerful and vigorous. By means of very heavy bombardments and desperately hard fighting, the British pressed back the Germans for short distances along the front east of Ypres. On 20 September assaults were delivered along the Ypres–Menin road, and in the successful though limited advance over 2,000 prisoners were captured. The village of Veldhoek was rushed, and on 21 September 1,000 more prisoners were taken. During the next few days the Germans made several powerful counter-attacks, but the British held their new positions. In the month of September the British captured 5,296 German prisoners and eleven guns, and in October they similarly captured 9,125 prisoners and fifteen guns.
On 6 November another assault was delivered east of Ypres, this time a short distance north of the Menin road, and the village of Passchendaele was stormed by Canadian troops. Passchendaele stands on relatively high ground. The name of the village would become, in later British memory, a byword for the cost of the Flanders offensive; the contemporary Annual Register records the storm as one more limited success in a year of extremely heavy fighting that left the Western Front still locked in deadlock. Hankey’s circle would look back on the campaign with the resolve, later attributed in his biographer’s narrative, that there should be “no more Passchendaeles.”
Caporetto, Versailles, and the Close of the Year
Hankey’s October–December chapter places the conclusion of the Passchendaele offensive beside the Italian disaster at Caporetto, the dispatch of British and French divisions to Italy, and the creation of the Supreme War Council at Versailles — inter-Allied machinery in which Hankey himself took a central part. War-weariness and a growing demand for a negotiated peace form the political atmosphere of that autumn in his account, even as the Annual Register recorded at home unbroken public determination to prosecute the war to victory, food restriction and national service experiments, daylight air-raids on London, and the great Representation of the People measure still the central domestic business of Parliament.
The Flanders ridge had been bought in short advances under extreme bombardment; the Ypres salient had been improved by Messines and by the autumn gains east of the town; the German line had not been broken. When the year closed, Britain remained, in Hankey’s phrase for the midsummer months, the cornerstone of the Allied effort — but the strategic situation of early 1918, as his next chapters open it, was already the preparation for the German spring offensives that would test the Western Front more severely than the limited Flanders advances of 1917 had done.

events/peoples-budget-1911.title: The People's Budget & Parliament Act (1909–1911)
events/peoples-budget-1911.content:
The People’s Budget & Parliament Act (1909–1911)
Between the spring of 1909 and the high summer of 1911 the United Kingdom passed through its most serious constitutional conflict since the Reform crisis of 1832. A Finance Bill framed by David Lloyd George as Chancellor of the Exchequer was rejected by the House of Lords; two general elections in 1910 returned a Liberal ministry dependent on Irish and Labour votes; a Constitutional Conference broke down; and the Parliament Act of 1911 stripped the Upper House of its absolute veto. The struggle joined the financing of old-age pensions and the Navy to social-reform, the defence of free trade against Tariff Reform, and the Irish demand that Home Rule should no longer be blocked by an hereditary chamber. It ended only when King George V was prepared, if necessary, to create peers enough to force the Bill through — the same royal instrument that had broken the Lords in 1832.
The Budget of 1909
Parliament opened on 16 February 1909 under King Edward VII with a Speech already signalling the fiscal pressure of the year. An unusually long financial paragraph warned that, owing especially to old-age provision and the increased cost of the Navy, expenditure would rise. In the Commons debate on the Address, Mr. Asquith insisted that finance must be the first business of the session: social reform had to be paid for, and the Old Age Pension Act was only the first instalment. Mr. Balfour charged Ministers with driving capital abroad by rash speech; Labour speakers pressed land-value taxation as a remedy for unemployment.
The Budget was introduced by Lloyd George on 29 April 1909 — the most controversial financial statement of the period. Described by its author as a “War Budget” against poverty, it proposed new taxes on land values: a 20 per cent tax on the unearned increment of land when sold; a duty of a halfpenny in the pound on the capital value of undeveloped land; and a 10 per cent reversion duty on a landlord’s interest at the expiry of a lease — together with increased death duties and a super-tax on incomes above £5,000. The proceeds were to fund old-age pensions and naval construction amid accelerating Anglo-German rivalry. Mr. Balfour declared that the force behind the Budget was “really Socialism.” Great landowners and financiers organised resistance; the Marquess of Lansdowne would later argue that the measure was “not an ordinary Budget” but a bundle of political measures disguised as a finance bill.
The second reading occupied four days in early June. Its rejection was moved on 7 June by Mr. Austen Chamberlain, who indicated that the Opposition alternative was Tariff Reform and insisted that the proposals were collectively confiscatory: more money would be raised than needed; the burden was unfairly distributed, especially on Scotland and Ireland; unearned increment was really deferred interest, taxed thrice; there was no unit of valuation; the undeveloped-land duty would hit agriculture and destroy mortgage margins. Mr. Ure, the Lord Advocate, replied that the Budget taxed superfluities and persons well able to pay; in ten years gross incomes reviewed for income tax had increased 30 per cent. while national expenditure rose only 15 per cent.; land owed its value to the community. The Budget was “a great and democratic Budget.” Mr. Harold Cox condemned reduction of the New Sinking Fund and called the land-value taxes political warfare.
Toward Confrontation with the Peers
By October independent Unionist peers were making the case for rejection. Lord Curzon at Leeds (15 October) attacked Lloyd George as a demagogue, noted some 250 amendments still pending, and insisted that the Lords had only waived, never abandoned, the right to amend a Finance Bill, and had never waived the right of rejection — whether for tacking, as mischievous, or to refer principles to the people. The Budget’s socialistic feature, he said, was that it was intended to “side-track” Tariff Reform. Viscount Milner likewise pressed the constitutional right of rejection. The Edinburgh Review, Old Whig and Free Trade Unionist, strongly deprecated rejection or amendment.
Report stage began on 18 October. An attempt to recommit the land clauses on the ground of 139 new Government amendments was rejected 180–80; Harold Cox’s motion to omit Clause 1 establishing increment duty was rejected 207–89. Revised Budget arithmetic closed near £162,840,000. Reduction of the Fixed Debt Charge from £25,000,000 to £24,500,000 accompanied a further £500,000 draught on the Sinking Fund, making £3,500,000 in all. Lloyd George reported improved death-duty yield, better stamp receipts, and whisky consumption down by as much as 30 per cent. in some places. A contemporary survey observed that the United Kingdom was “saturated with politics.”
The Lords’ Rejection (30 November 1909)
After five months of debate in the Commons, the Finance Bill went up to the Lords in November. On 30 November, by a vote of 350 to 75, the House of Lords rejected the Bill — a breach of the convention, standing since the seventeenth century, that the Lords did not interfere with money bills. The last occasion on which the Lords had rejected a finance measure was in 1860.
The constitutional crisis was immediate. The Earl of Crewe, moving the second reading, faced a resolution from Lansdowne asserting the Lords’ right to reject a Money Bill. Lansdowne argued that “the Commons’ privileges were now interpreted strictly, and ‘tacking’ had increased, culminating in the Finance Bill of 1894,” and declared that the Budget “would merely be reserved for the approval of the people.” The Lord Chancellor (Lord Loreburn) replied that rejection was “legal, but not constitutional. Supply was the exclusive function of the Commons, and rejection was a direct invasion of their privilege and the powers of the Crown.” He warned that the conflict “could only end ultimately in one way.”
The January 1910 Election
The Lords’ rejection forced a dissolution. The general election of January–February 1910 was carried on with unexampled vigour: about 250 meetings were addressed by Peers in the five weeks between the adjournment and the issue of the writs; the Tariff Reform League and Free Trade Union spent lavishly outside the authorised candidate limits. Parliament was dissolved by Royal Proclamation on 10 January; the first pollings followed on 15 January after unopposed returns including Mr. Joseph Chamberlain for West Birmingham.
The election turned on the constitutional struggle opened by the Lords’ rejection of the Finance Bill, on Tariff Reform versus Free Trade, and on Home Rule. Since an obscure sentence in Asquith’s Albert Hall speech of December 1909, no responsible Minister had made any full revelation on Home Rule, and Unionists charged the Ministry with destroying the only machinery which ensured that a Home Rule Bill should be referred to the electors. The result was a hung Parliament:

























PartySeatsLiberals275Unionists273Labour40Irish Nationalists82
The Liberal government survived with Irish and Labour support. A later speaker observed that a transfer of 8,000 Liberal votes to the Unionists would wipe out the existing Liberal majority, while a transfer of 8,000 Unionist votes to the Liberals would double it. The Finance Bill was passed promptly by the new Commons and accepted by the Lords in April 1910 — the Peers having, as they claimed, referred it to the people and now bowed to the electoral result on that measure alone.
Veto, Conference, and the Second Election
The constitutional question — the Lords’ veto — now became the central issue. Parliament was opened by Royal Commission on 15 February 1910; Mr. James William Lowther was again chosen Speaker. Opposition speakers declared that there had never been a deadlock between the House of Lords and the country, and that the Veto resolutions would reduce the Lords to legislative impotence. The Attorney-General (Sir W. Robson) replied that if the Lords controlled finance they could control the Administration and force dissolutions; they would have unlimited power without responsibility; Tariff Reform, once imposed, could never be repealed if the Lords could stand in the way.
The death of King Edward VII in May cast a temporary hush over party warfare. On 17 June the Constitutional Conference opened — an attempt by leading men from both sides to compose the differences between the Houses without a further appeal to the constituencies. Settlement of deadlocks by a Joint Committee had been debated; but an influential section of Unionist Peers held that if they were to be deprived of their powers it should be done by the constituencies and not by a conference. Rumours later attributed the final disruption to Lords Lansdowne and Cawdor and to the numerical strength of majorities required on Bills sent back after rejection. The Conference continued through summer and early autumn without public disclosure; its failure was welcomed by advanced Liberals, Labour, and the main body of the Nationalists. Free Trade Unionists urged that food taxes should be postponed; the Morning Post regarded the constitutional issue as of slight importance compared to Tariff Reform. Mr. John Redmond returned from an American and Canadian fund-raising tour on 12 November with some $200,000 for the Home Rule cause; Unionists made much of “the menace of the American dollars.”
On 18 November Asquith, taking all the time of the House for Government business, insisted that Dissolution was best got over at once. It was now admitted that Liberal legislation did not get a fair chance and that the Lords only forced a Dissolution when the Liberals were in office. The Earl of Crewe announced the Dissolution in the Lords; Lansdowne characterised the statement as astounding and doubted whether a Parliamentary manœuvre had ever been carried out with greater cynicism. Lloyd George, addressing 5,000 men at Mile End on 21 November, said the crisis had been precipitated by the rejection of the Budget; the Government needed money for defence and social reforms by taxing great incomes and fortunes, while the Lords demanded that the burden be put on the bread and meat of the people. The Budget, he insisted, was a complete financial success. At Bury St. Edmunds on 12 December Asquith insisted that the sole issue was the supremacy of the people over legislation. Mr. Winston Churchill at Parkstone declared that the first step must be the abolition of the Veto; after that he hoped for national insurance, education, devolution, and an Irish Parliament for purely Irish affairs. “But the Veto must go now.”
The first polls were taken on 3 December. The balance of parties remained substantially as before: the Ministry still depended on Irish and Labour votes. Unionists held that they must continue to fight the Parliament Bill. The Observer urged that the situation should be allowed to end in absurdity by accepting the creation of 500 “puppet peers.” Less extreme Unionists were divided among submission, a Referendum on the Veto Bill, and hopes of compromise. Unionist speakers insisted that the Parliament Bill was a dodge to smuggle through Home Rule; none of the Ministers had touched on it till 500 seats were decided. The Liberal–Irish–Labour coalition now had a renewed mandate to reform the House of Lords.
The Parliament Bill, 1911
Parliament was opened in state for the first time in the new reign by King George V on Monday, 6 February 1911. Before delivering his Speech the King read and signed the Accession Declaration as established by the Act of 1910. Proposals would be submitted without delay “for settling the relations between the two Houses of Parliament, with the object of securing the more effective working of the Constitution.” The only Bills specified were those removing the pauper disqualification for old-age pensions and for insurance against sickness, invalidity, and (in special trades) unemployment — the programme that would become the National Insurance Act.
The Parliament Bill abolished the Lords’ absolute veto: if the Commons passed a bill in three successive sessions over a period of two years, it could become law without the Lords’ consent. For money bills, the Lords’ power was reduced to a one-month delay. The maximum duration of a Parliament was reduced from seven to five years. After two days’ debate, leave was given on 22 February by 351 to 227 to introduce the Bill. A Referendum Bill was also read a first time; opponents argued that it would be used as an engine of obstruction. Balfour ridiculed the idea that the electorate had given a mandate either for the Parliament Bill specifically or for the other measures suggested, or not suggested, by the Government. The debate was protracted and bitter; the guillotine was applied; Committee stage occupied the greater part of the weeks before the Coronation.
The Lords, the Die-Hards, and the Peer-Creation Threat
Committee stage in the Lords began on 28 June. The Earl of Cromer moved to transfer the decision on money bills from the Speaker to a Joint Committee. Viscount Haldane pointed out that the amendment would restore to the Lords powers it had tacitly resigned. Supported by Lansdowne and the Archbishop of Canterbury, it was carried by 183 to 44; the Lord Chancellor said that nothing would induce the Government to accept it.
The subsequent stages divided Unionist Peers between those who counselled surrender and the “die-hards” or “Halsburyites,” led by the Earl of Halsbury and numbering between 100 and 150 peers determined to reject or emasculate the Bill. Lord Ribblesdale counselled surrender: “the game was up,” and “with dear food round their necks and the House of Lords on their backs” the Opposition were not likely to win a general election. Viscount St. Aldwyn pointed out that if resistance were persisted in the Bill would become law after a prorogation, and that the constituencies were absolutely apathetic. He complained that there had been no full disclosure of what had taken place between Ministers and the King, who had been put in a most cruel position; His Majesty had been bound by his hypothetical promise of November 1910. Lord Willoughby de Broke declared that the Government might win a dozen general elections without altering his opposition; the Dukes of Bedford and Marlborough supported resistance. Lord Newton said that, so far from ridicule killing the creation, “they would have the ridicule and the Government the Peers.”
The crisis deepened when Asquith received — and the House was forced to confront — a guarantee from King George V that the King would create sufficient new Liberal peers to force the Bill through if necessary. Lord Midleton claimed the right of the House to know whether the Government had received that authority; the Earl of Rosebery backed the demand for a clear statement as to the “guarantees.” This use of the royal prerogative — the same method used to force through the Reform Act of 1832 — broke the organised resistance of the party leadership. Lord Lansdowne, following Wellington’s example in 1832, advised Conservative peers to abstain rather than compel the King to swamp the House.
Passage and Royal Assent
On 10 August 1911, after a dramatic all-night sitting, the Parliament Act passed the House of Lords by 131 votes to 114. The Halsburyites were defeated; some 300 Unionist peers stayed away rather than vote against their party leadership or join the die-hard resistance. The Act received the Royal Assent on 18 August 1911. By its terms the Lords’ veto was strictly limited: a Bill might be rejected for two sessions but would pass into law on the third; money bills could be delayed only a month; and no Parliament might last more than five years.
The Unionist party emerged disorganised, torn by dissensions, smarting under severe defeat, and suspicious of its own leadership. In the autumn Mr. Bonar Law attacked the Government’s course since the Act: the country was living under a provisional Constitution; the Government had not reformed the Second Chamber, but only readjusted the relations between the Houses so as to prevent the submission of Home Rule to the electorate.
Significance
The Parliament Act permanently altered the British constitution. It removed the Lords’ power to block legislation approved by the Commons, clearing the way for the Home Rule Bill, Welsh Disestablishment, and the social reforms of the Liberal government — including National Insurance. It resolved a conflict building since the Unionist majority in the Lords systematically rejected Liberal legislation from 1906 onwards: Education, Licensing, and now Finance had each demonstrated that a permanent Conservative majority in one House could nullify a Liberal majority in the other.
By making Home Rule possible without the Lords’ consent, the Act helped drive the Ulster Unionist movement toward extra-parliamentary resistance and the formation of the Ulster Volunteer Force in 1912, setting the stage for the Irish Home Rule crisis that would be overtaken by the Great War. The two elections of 1910 had confirmed that the Liberal ministry could govern only with Irish and Labour support; the Parliament Act made that coalition’s legislative programme enforceable. Finance, once the exclusive preserve of the Commons, had been the weapon that broke the hereditary veto — and the instrument by which social reform and free-trade finance were secured against a second chamber that had never accepted either.

events/representation-of-the-people-1918.title: The Representation of the People Act 1918
events/representation-of-the-people-1918.content:
The Representation of the People Act 1918
The Representation of the People Act 1918 was the greatest single extension of the parliamentary franchise in British history. Shaped by a Speaker’s Conference on electoral reform, carried through the Commons in the critical stages of June and the autumn of 1917, and in force as statute in the early months of 1918, it wrote women into the electorate at the age of thirty, secured the vote of soldiers and sailors from the place of their home, redistributed seats in Great Britain toward the industrial and urban centres, and left Irish redistribution as the chief unresolved anomaly of the settlement. It closed the long Victorian and Edwardian sequence of parliamentary-reform that had run from 1832 through the Second and Third Reform Acts, and it did so under the pressure of a war that had made the old register, and the old exclusions, impossible to defend.
Wartime Register and the Problem of the Absent Voter
The need for a new franchise had become practical before it became comprehensive. In the summer of 1916 the question was agitated whether a General Election could or should be held during the war, and whether a new register could be prepared that would include the soldiers and sailors fighting abroad. The Government determined to appoint a select committee to inquire whether it was practicable and desirable to prepare such a register, with adequate representation of those engaged in the war and in war work, and to conduct an election upon it during the war.
On 19 July 1916 Herbert Samuel moved the appointment of that committee in the Commons. He laid special emphasis on the difficulties of the task — above all on how soldiers at the front would vote while under bombardment — and asked whether there was justification for embarking on an expenditure of £300,000 and the labour of 20,000 persons except in case of overwhelming necessity. Sir Edward Carson took him sharply to task for attacking the very proposal he was supposed to be advocating. The country must have a register, Carson insisted, since a General Election might be necessary at any moment; he branded the proposed Committee as a farce and called on the House to refuse it and compel the Government to do its own business. Many members took the same view. asquith-herbert-henry, hastily sent for, consulted with Samuel and other Ministers and acquiesced in the obvious feeling of the House that the motion should be withdrawn. The Government would reconsider the matter.
From that failure of a narrow, wartime-register expedient the path led toward a full reconstruction of the franchise. The instrument chosen was not a party bill but a Speaker’s Conference on Electoral Reform — a device of all-party composition under an impartial chairman that could produce a compromise acceptable enough to pass in wartime.
The Speaker’s Conference and the Bill of 1917
By the summer of 1917 the Franchise and Representation of the People measure, already shaped by the Speaker’s Conference, was advancing through its critical stages in the Commons. The war itself had altered the argument. Many members declared that the experiences of the conflict had shown that the conscious co-operation of women in the activities of the nation was a source of strength and not of weakness. Sir John Simon insisted that the industrial problem would be more than before a women’s problem, and that its solution could not, in any justice, be attempted by a Parliament with an exclusive male electorate.
The militant and constitutional campaigns for women’s suffrage had suspended their peacetime methods after the outbreak-of-the-great-war; the Bill now before the House was the parliamentary harvest of that suspension as much as of the long pre-war agitation for womens-suffrage. At the end of the sitting Sir Frederick Banbury’s amendment — the principal anti-suffrage challenge at that stage — was heavily defeated.
Women at Thirty: The Clause of 20 June
On the following day, 20 June 1917, the House considered the qualifications which women parliamentary electors must possess. The only substantial point that remained to be decided was the age-limit. The Bill had fixed it at thirty years. Many of the anti-suffragists tried to produce dissension among the suffragists, and an ultimate wrecking of the principle, by proposals to remove or lower the age-limit. Sir George Cave, who was in charge of the Bill, opposed the alteration and declared roundly that if any such amendment were accepted he could not be responsible for the further conduct of the measure. The amendment was rejected by an overwhelming vote. In the end the clause enfranchising women was added to the Bill by a vote of 214 members as against 17.
The age of thirty was thus not an accident of drafting but the price of carrying the principle. It kept the women’s electorate short of a majority of the whole, and it held together a wartime coalition of suffragists and cautious converts that a more sweeping clause might have broken. Women local-government electors and women who met a minimum property or marital qualification within the Bill’s scheme entered the parliamentary nation; the younger women who filled the munitions factories and the transport services would wait for a later Act.
Soldiers, Sailors, Paupers, and Conscience
The House then proceeded to a series of Government amendments securing the franchise to soldiers and sailors. Every soldier and sailor on active service and on full pay was to have the right to vote for the place of his home. The debate was resumed on the 25th, when it was proposed that the voting age for soldiers and sailors who had seen active service should be nineteen, on the argument that if a man was old enough to fight he was old enough to vote. The feeling in the House was so strong that the Government promised to reconsider the matter.
On the following day two further proposals of interest were made. The first was that the pauper disqualification should be removed, which the Government accepted — a quiet but significant breach in the old Victorian association of the franchise with rate-paying independence. The second was a proposal to disfranchise conscientious objectors. Mr. M’Neill, who moved it, declared that the objectors had sheltered themselves from the perils and sacrifices accepted by others, and that after the war they would enjoy immunities and liberties preserved to them by other men’s efforts: were they then to exercise the franchise when the peril was over? Lord Hugh Cecil made an eloquent speech for liberty of conscience, arguing that since conscientious objectors perversely but sincerely adhered to a higher law above the safety of the republic, it belonged to the credit of the country to respect their convictions; he hoped for the honour of the House and the nation that the amendment would be rejected. Sir John Simon also spoke against the proposal. The wartime franchise was thus drawn wide for the fighting man and, in the matter of conscience, refused the path of punitive exclusion.
Redistribution and the Irish Difficulty
Parliament reassembled on 16 October 1917. The main business of the autumn session was the Franchise Bill and a new Vote of Credit; progress was also expected with the Education Bill, so that franchise reform and the reconstruction of popular schooling moved forward together as complementary pieces of wartime social-reform. The Boundary Commissioners had already put forward their plans for redistribution. They proposed to add thirty-one members to the number representing Great Britain, and their scheme provided for a new distribution of political power by which the industrial and urban elements would gain at the expense of the agricultural and rural. Greater London was to have 101 members; Lancashire, sixty-six; Birmingham and its environs, forty-one; Glasgow and its environs, thirty-two. The map that had still carried the weight of the older county and small-borough system after 1885 was to be redrawn toward the cities that had made the nation’s war production.
When the Commons began its discussion of the Reform Bill in the autumn, it was confronted with an Irish difficulty. The Bill, in accordance with the recommendations of the Speaker’s Conference, applied the new franchises to Ireland but confined redistribution to Great Britain. Sir John Lonsdale, the Ulster Unionist leader, pointed out the resultant dilemma. The Bill, he declared, was based on a party compromise involving the accepted principles of “one man one vote” and “one vote one value,” but without redistribution in Ireland the second principle could not come into operation. He suggested a rearrangement of the Irish constituencies that would not prejudice any settlement which might result from the Irish Convention. John Redmond urged that a compromise made by the Speaker’s Conference ought not to be disturbed. Sir George Cave, for the Government, admitted that a strong case had been made out for consideration, and that if the House so desired the matter would receive further attention.
The Irish anomaly was not accidental. It stood at the intersection of the franchise settlement and the still-unresolved Home Rule question, which lloyd-george-david had in May offered to treat either by a limited application of the Home Rule Act with exclusion of north-east Ulster or by a Convention of Irishmen of both parties. Redistribution in Ireland would have prejudged representation under any future Irish settlement; leaving it untouched preserved the Speaker’s Conference bargain at the cost of “one vote one value” across the whole United Kingdom.
The Act in Force and the New Electorate
The year 1917, which had opened with unbroken determination to prosecute the war to victory, closed with the great Representation of the People measure still the central domestic business of Parliament — women already written into the franchise at the age of thirty, soldiers and sailors secured their vote from the place of their home, and Irish representation left as the chief unresolved anomaly of redistribution. Early in 1918 the measure stood as the Representation of the People Act. By 26 February, when the Labour Party met in resumed Annual Conference at the Central Hall, Westminster, the party adopted a new constitution transforming itself from a federation of societies into a national democratic political organisation open to every worker who laboured “by hand or by brain.” The change marked the determination of the party leaders to seize the opportunity given by the widening of the electorate and the enfranchisement of women under the Act, and to make the Labour movement the most powerful political force in the country — the electoral foundation of modern labour-representation completed at last by statute.
The Coalition manifesto issued as the nation turned from war toward reconstruction after the armistice-1918 declared it the duty of the new Government to remove all existing inequalities of the law as between men and women. The franchise Act had opened the gate; equality in the wider law remained a programme. The same manifesto treated housing, education, and the prevention of degrading standards of employment as conditions of social harmony which the Coalition would earnestly endeavour to promote — the new electorate was assumed to demand a new social agenda. In 1919 a Women’s Emancipation Bill appeared among the session’s measures, while the first General Election under the new register returned Labour candidates with nearly 2,500,000 votes — a measure of how far the enlarged electorate had already shifted the balance of party competition.
Place in the Sequence of Reform
The long sequence of parliamentary-reform that the Act completed ran in a single line through the century. The Reform Act of 1832 had transferred power from the landed aristocracy to the middle class while leaving the working class voteless. Disraeli’s “leap in the dark” of 1867 enfranchised male householders in the boroughs and raised the electorate from about one to two millions. Gladstone’s Act of 1884 gave household suffrage to the country districts and enfranchised the agricultural labourer, and the Redistribution of Seats Act of 1885 followed on a basis of single-member equal electoral districts of some 54,000 inhabitants — with the enduring controversy over plural voting and “one man, one vote” still unresolved. Local government had already moved further: household suffrage in municipal elections, and the eligibility of women for town councils, school boards, and boards of guardians, had made the exclusion of women from the parliamentary franchise look increasingly anomalous even before the war.
The Act of 1918 completed that sequence under conditions none of the earlier reformers had imagined. It brought women within the parliamentary nation at thirty, gave the fighting services a vote that could be cast from the place of home, pushed redistribution toward the industrial cities, and left the Irish difficulty — as so often in the politics of irish-home-rule — only half resolved. The war that had compelled the Military Service Acts in 1916 compelled democracy in 1918.
Chronology

1916, 19 July: Samuel moves a select committee on a wartime electoral register including soldiers; motion withdrawn after House opposition led by Carson.
1917, May: Lloyd George’s Irish offer refers to a Conference “on the lines of the Speaker’s Conference on Electoral Reform.”
1917, June: Critical Commons stages of the Franchise Bill; Banbury amendment heavily defeated.
1917, 20 June: Women’s age-limit fixed at 30; clause enfranchising women carried by 214 to 17.
1917, 25–26 June: Soldiers’ and sailors’ franchise; proposal of voting age 19 for men who had seen active service; removal of pauper disqualification accepted; debate on disfranchising conscientious objectors.
1917, 16 October: Autumn session; Franchise Bill principal business; Boundary Commissioners’ scheme (+31 seats for Great Britain; London 101, Lancashire 66, Birmingham 41, Glasgow 32).
1917, autumn: Irish difficulty — new franchises applied to Ireland, redistribution confined to Great Britain; Lonsdale, Redmond, and Cave.
1917, end of year: Women at thirty, soldiers’ and sailors’ votes, and Irish redistribution unresolved, as the measure’s outstanding features.
1918, early: Representation of the People Act in force.
1918, 26 February: Labour Party adopts new constitution to exploit the widened electorate and women’s enfranchisement.
1918–19: Coalition programme pledges removal of legal inequalities between men and women; first election under the new register; Women’s Emancipation Bill in the 1919 session.

Sources

Annual Register, 1917. Chapter II for the Franchise Bill’s critical June stages, the war argument for women’s co-operation, Banbury’s defeat, the 20 June women’s clause (214–17), soldiers’ and sailors’ votes, the age-19 proposal, removal of the pauper disqualification, and the conscientious-objector debate; Chapter III for the autumn redistribution scheme and the Irish difficulty under the Speaker’s Conference recommendations; year-end summary of the measure’s outstanding features.
Annual Register, 1918. Chapter I for the Labour Party’s 26 February constitution, expressly linked to the widening of the electorate and women’s enfranchisement under the Representation of the People Act; Coalition manifesto passage on removing inequalities of the law as between men and women.
Annual Register, 1919. Opening English History material on the post-election Labour poll (nearly 2,500,000 votes) and the appearance of a Women’s Emancipation Bill among the session’s measures.
Clayton, Joseph. The Rise of the Democracy, Chapter VII (“Parliamentary Reform and the Enfranchisement of the People”), for the sequence of 1832, 1867, and 1884–85 against which the 1918 Act completed the democratic franchise.

events/scramble-for-africa.title: The Scramble for Africa and Partition (1880–1914)
events/scramble-for-africa.content:
The Scramble for Africa and Partition (1880–1914)
The Scramble for Africa was the rapid invasion, occupation, colonisation, and partition of the African continent by European powers during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. What Langer calls the “tremendous, almost epic outburst of European interest in affairs that lay beyond the frontiers of Europe” transformed the political map of Africa with extraordinary speed. The British Empire, already the largest colonial power, emerged from the Scramble with vast new acquisitions stretching from Egypt in the north to the Cape in the south — a continuous belt of territory that imperialists dreamed would one day run uninterrupted from Cairo to the Cape of Good Hope.
The partition was driven by a confluence of forces: the strategic imperative to secure the sea route to India through the Suez Canal; the economic pressure of intensifying European industrial competition and the search for new markets; the psychological and ideological appeals of imperial expansion; and the deadlock in European continental politics after the formation of the Franco-Russian Alliance, which redirected the energies of the great powers toward overseas competition. As Langer observed, “the rivalry and competition between the great powers in Africa, in the Far East and in the Near East were, during the last years of the dying century, every whit as important, and perhaps more important, than the shifting trends of purely European diplomacy.”
The Berlin Conference and the Rules of Partition
The Berlin Conference of 1884–1885, convened by the German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck, established the framework within which the European powers partitioned Africa. The conference was called in response to the intense rivalries that had erupted following King Leopold II of Belgium’s claims in the Congo Basin and the expansionist activities of other European powers along the African coasts.
Fourteen nations participated, though no African representatives were invited. The conference produced the General Act of Berlin, which established several key principles for the colonisation of Africa. It declared the Congo Basin a free trade zone and guaranteed freedom of navigation on the Congo and Niger rivers. Most consequentially, it laid down the “principle of effective occupation”: a European power could only claim African territory if it could demonstrate actual control through administration, military presence, or treaties with local chiefs. This doctrine — known as the doctrine of hinterland — became the legal architecture of partition. The conference recognised the International Association of the Congo (Leopold II’s private enterprise) as the legitimate authority over the Congo region, effectively creating the Congo Free State as a personal possession of the Belgian king.
Although the Berlin Conference was ostensibly about free trade and humanitarian principles — including the suppression of the slave trade — its practical effect was to accelerate the partition by defining the rules of the game. Once the principle of effective occupation was established, the European powers raced to plant flags, sign treaties with African rulers, and establish administrative posts to secure their claims. The conference did not divide Africa itself, but it set the diplomatic and legal framework within which the division would be carried out over the following decades.
The Berlin Act was followed by a series of bilateral treaties between the European powers that delimited colonial boundaries. Among the most important were the Anglo-German Agreement of 1886 defining spheres in East Africa, the Anglo-French Convention of 1889 delimiting West African boundaries, and the Anglo-German Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty of 1890, which fundamentally shaped the British position in East Africa.
The British Advance: East and West Africa
Egypt and the Sudan
The British occupation of Egypt in 1882 was the decisive event that drew Britain deep into African affairs. Though the Gladstone government had repeatedly declared its opposition to a permanent occupation, the suppression of the Arabi revolt at Tel-el-Kebir was followed not by withdrawal but by an indefinite stay. Langer observes that the occupation of Egypt was the “initial impetus to British imperialism in the last years of the century.” Gladstone intended to withdraw; even Salisbury expected to make some adjustment. But after 1887, when France and Russia blocked the projected Anglo-Turkish convention, “the chances of evacuation rapidly diminished.”
From Egypt, Britain was drawn into the Sudan. The Mahdist revolt under Muhammad Ahmad swept the Sudan in the 1880s, culminating in the fall of Khartoum and the death of General Gordon in January 1885. For over a decade thereafter, the Sudan was abandoned to Mahdist rule while British attention was occupied elsewhere. The reconquest began in 1896 under General Herbert Kitchener, whose methodical campaign up the Nile — accompanied by a railway built across the desert — culminated in the decisive victory at Omdurman in September 1898. The Sudan was restored as an Anglo-Egyptian condominium in 1899, formally under joint sovereignty but in practice under British control.
East Africa: Kenya and Uganda
In East Africa, British expansion was driven by a combination of missionary activity, commercial enterprise, and strategic rivalry with Germany. The Imperial British East Africa Company (IBEA), chartered in 1888 under the leadership of Sir William MacKinnon, was the vehicle for British claims in the region. Henry Morton Stanley’s “Relief Expedition” to Emin Pasha in 1887–1889 further stimulated British interest in the interior.
The German presence in East Africa posed a direct challenge. The German explorer Karl Peters, acting under the auspices of the German East Africa Company, had penetrated inland and by March 1890 had reached Uganda and concluded a treaty of protection with the King. An expedition sent out by the IBEA arrived in Uganda only a month later. “This race for Uganda and the threat of Peters to cut the British off from the interior and from the Nile created a sensation in England,” Langer records. The Times on 3 April 1890 called attention to the danger of having the Germans on the Nile.
The rivalry was resolved by the Anglo-German Agreement of 1890 (the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty), which assigned Uganda and the territory north of a line running from the southern tip of Lake Victoria to the northern tip of Lake Tanganyika to the British sphere. Britain subsequently decided to retain Uganda as a protectorate (declared in 1894), and Kenya — then known as the East Africa Protectorate — was gradually brought under British administration. The Uganda Railway, begun in 1896 and completed in 1901, linked the East African coast with Lake Victoria and cemented British control over the interior.
Nyasaland and Central Africa
Further south, British influence was extended over the territories around Lake Nyasa. The British African Lakes Company had been active in the region since the 1870s, combating the Arab slave trade and establishing missionary stations. In 1889, Cecil Rhodes began subsidising the company and sent Harry Johnston — whom he had indoctrinated with his imperial vision — to Nyasaland to set up posts between Lake Nyasa and Lake Tanganyika, territory to which the Germans were also laying claim. By 1890, the British Central Africa Protectorate (later Nyasaland) was established.
West Africa: Nigeria, the Gold Coast, and the Niger Basin
In West Africa, British expansion followed the Niger River inland and extended British authority over the territories that would become Nigeria and the Gold Coast. The Royal Niger Company, chartered in 1886 under Sir George Goldie, was the instrument of British penetration of the Niger Basin. Through a combination of treaties with local rulers and military force, the company secured British claims to the lower Niger and the Benue Valley, outmanoeuvring French and German rivals. The Royal Niger Company’s charter was revoked in 1899, and the British government took over direct administration of the territories, which were amalgamated into the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria and the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria in 1900. In 1914, these were unified into the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria.
The Gold Coast (modern Ghana) had been a British possession since the early nineteenth century, but British authority was contested by the powerful Ashanti Confederacy. After several Anglo-Ashanti wars — the most important being the war of 1873–1874 and the final conflict of 1895–1896 — the British annexed Ashanti in 1901 and incorporated it into the Gold Coast Colony.
The Benin Expedition of 1897, following the massacre of a British mission to the Kingdom of Benin, resulted in the capture of Benin City and the extension of British authority over the Niger Delta region. The famous Benin bronzes, seized as booty, were carried to Europe.
The Cape-to-Cairo Dream and Rhodesia
Cecil John Rhodes was the most energetic and visionary of the British empire-builders in Africa. As Langer describes him, he was “the great imperialist” who “was ready at once to take over anything in central Africa between the Zambezi and the White Nile.” His driving ambition was encapsulated in the slogan “Cape-to-Cairo” — the vision of an uninterrupted belt of British territory stretching the entire length of the African continent, from the Cape of Good Hope to Egypt, linked by railway and telegraph.
The idea appears to have been first put forward in 1876 by Sir Edwin Arnold. Rhodes made it his life’s work. As Langer records, “This group, of which Cecil Rhodes was the leading spirit, was wedded to the idea which later became familiar through the slogan Cape-to-Cairo, and which envisaged the ultimate connexion of British territory in south Africa with the new possessions in central Africa and Egypt.”
The British South Africa Company
Rhodes’s instrument for northern expansion was the British South Africa Company (the “Chartered Company”), which was granted a Royal Charter in the autumn of 1889. The charter gave the company “almost unlimited rights and powers of government in the huge area north of the Transvaal and west of the Portuguese possessions, without fixing any northern limit.” Rhodes used the company to acquire vast tracts of land, establish settlements, and impose British administration over the territories that would become Southern and Northern Rhodesia — named after him in what Justin McCarthy called “perhaps the most striking personal tribute ever paid to a British imperial figure during his own lifetime.”
The company’s operations were conducted with a military arm. It fought several wars of conquest against the Ndebele (Matabele) and the Shona peoples. McCarthy observed that “for a long time, all but unknown to the vast majority of Englishmen at home, the Chartered Company was writing out a new volume of history with a big pen, sometimes, it must be allowed, dipped in very red ink.”
Bechuanaland and the British Ultimatum to Portugal (1890)
The road to the north passed through Bechuanaland. As a member of the Cape ministry in 1884, Rhodes had urged the establishment of a British protectorate over Bechuanaland — the territory lying between the Transvaal and the newly proclaimed German colony of South-West Africa — to keep open “the road to trade and territorial expansion towards the north.” This protectorate was established in 1885, preserving the corridor northward.
British expansion also brought conflict with Portugal, which claimed a vast swathe of territory linking Angola on the west coast with Mozambique on the east — the so-called “rose-coloured map” that would have blocked British access from south to central Africa. In January 1890, the British government delivered an ultimatum to Portugal demanding the withdrawal of Portuguese forces from the disputed territory between the Anglo-Portuguese spheres in Central Africa — territory that would connect the British position in Nyasaland with the Chartered Company’s claims in the interior. Confronted by British naval power, Portugal was forced to capitulate, relinquishing its claims to the disputed region. The 1890 ultimatum was a landmark in British imperial supremacy in Africa.
The Rhodesian Settlement
Rhodes’s vision extended to the railway. The Cape-to-Cairo railway and telegraph line was to be the physical embodiment of British dominion. Rhodes planned to buy the Portuguese end of the Delagoa Bay railway line and even the whole of Portuguese territory south of the Zambezi, but these projects proved too ambitious. Nonetheless, the railway was pushed northwards from the Cape through Bechuanaland, with Mafeking as its temporary terminus.
Rhodes’s personal dominance of southern African affairs was checked by the Jameson Raid of 1895, which forced his resignation as Prime Minister of Cape Colony. But his territorial legacy endured: Rhodesia remained under Chartered Company administration until the 1920s, and the Cape-to-Cairo idea, though never fully realised, shaped British strategic thinking for a generation.
Anglo-German Agreements and Rivalries
Germany’s emergence as a colonial power in the 1880s introduced a new dimension to the Scramble for Africa. Bismarck, initially sceptical of colonial acquisition, had authorised the proclamation of German protectorates in South-West Africa (1884), Togoland and the Cameroons (1884), and German East Africa (1885). These acquisitions brought Germany into direct rivalry with British expansion, particularly in East Africa and South Africa.
The Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty (1890)
The most important Anglo-German colonial agreement was the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty of 1 July 1890. The negotiations were driven by the acute rivalries that had developed in East Africa. Langer describes how “the rivalries of the English and Germans had become so acute that Bismarck had already taken up the question of a settlement.” By April 1890, the agitation on both sides had reached such dimensions that it threatened to impair good relations.
Lord Salisbury, the British Prime Minister, took the initiative. He concluded that the growing tension with Germany was dangerous and “would force us to change our systems of alliance in Europe.” He therefore decided “to offer the Germans the island of Heligoland in return for concessions in Africa.” He spoke of the island as “a mere sandbar which would eventually be washed away.” The naval authorities agreed that it could not be defended without heavy fortification. Some members of the cabinet objected, but Salisbury finally induced them to agree.
On the German side, the suggestion regarding Heligoland was received with great enthusiasm. Emperor William II and the new Chancellor Caprivi considered the island of great strategic importance — as a coaling station and protective outpost at the mouths of the German rivers, and to prevent its use by the French fleet in time of war.
Under the treaty, Germany recognised a British protectorate over Zanzibar (which Britain had long regarded as crucial to the suppression of the slave trade) and gave up claims to territory in East Africa north of a line from the southern tip of Lake Victoria to the northern tip of Lake Tanganyika. This ceded to Britain what would become Kenya and Uganda. Germany also renounced claims to the coast north of the Tana River. In return, Britain ceded the small North Sea island of Heligoland — of immense strategic value for the defence of the German coast — and recognised German claims to territory in East Africa south of the agreed line.
The agreement was well received in both countries: “in England because of the extensive gains made in Africa, in Germany because of the sentimental interest in Heligoland, which was inhabited by Germans,” Langer records. Politically, the treaty “checked the growing tension between the two nations.” But it was not without wider consequences: the apparent rapprochement of England and Germany “represented a danger for France as it did for Russia,” and contributed to the urgency with which the Franco-Russian Alliance was pursued.
French Objections and German Ambiguity
The French protested loudly against the Anglo-German Treaty, arguing that “the assumption by Britain of a protectorate over Zanzibar was a violation of an earlier treaty.” They demanded compensation either in Egypt or in Tunis. The British government was in a difficult position but refused to give way.
Anglo-German relations remained ambivalent. The Heligoland Treaty had eased tensions, but German policy in South Africa — particularly the encouragement of the Transvaal Republic and the Kruger Telegram after the Jameson Raid — kept the two powers at odds. In the later 1890s, Joseph Chamberlain’s abortive attempts to negotiate an Anglo-German alliance foundered on mutual suspicion, and the two powers drifted toward the naval rivalry that would define their relationship in the new century.
The Fashoda Crisis and Anglo-French Rivalry
The most dramatic crisis of the Scramble for Africa was the confrontation between Britain and France at Fashoda in 1898, which brought the two countries to the brink of war and resolved the long struggle for control of the Upper Nile.
The Struggle for the Nile
The Fashoda crisis was the culmination of a decade-long rivalry for the Nile Valley. Langer calls it “the great and dramatic contest that ended in 1898 with the Fashoda crisis.” The British position in Egypt, occupied since 1882, required control of the Nile waters. The French, smarting from their exclusion from Egypt, sought to establish a position on the Upper Nile that would enable them to challenge British dominance.
King Leopold II of Belgium, through the Congo Free State, also harboured ambitions on the Upper Nile. The Anglo-Congolese Treaty of May 1894 provided for the lease to Leopold of a considerable area along the west bank of the Upper Nile, extending from Lake Albert to Fashoda. This treaty aroused immediate protests from France and Germany and was ultimately abandoned.
The Marchand Mission
The French government decided upon a direct challenge. Captain Jean-Baptiste Marchand was dispatched with a small force of Senegalese troops to march across Africa from the French Congo to the Upper Nile. His instructions, dated February 1896, were to establish a French presence at Fashoda. The mission, supported by French activity in Abyssinia, was intended to force a reckoning with Britain over the Nile.
Marchand’s heroic journey across Africa took over two years. He reached Fashoda on 10 July 1898, raised the French flag, and established a small fort. Unknown to Marchand, however, the strategic situation had been transformed by Kitchener’s annihilation of the Mahdist army at Omdurman on 2 September 1898. Kitchener was now master of the Sudan.
The Confrontation
Kitchener, informed of Marchand’s presence, proceeded up the Nile with a flotilla of gunboats. He reached Fashoda on 19 September 1898. The two commanders met — Marchand with his small band of exhausted men, Kitchener with the overwhelming force of the Anglo-Egyptian army. The confrontation was conducted with impeccable courtesy but absolute firmness. Kitchener insisted that Marchand must evacuate; Marchand insisted that he had his orders from Paris.
For the next two months, the two governments argued the case. The British position, grounded in the principle of effective occupation and the Anglo-Egyptian claim to the Sudan (derived from Egypt’s historical sovereignty), was unyielding. The French public was outraged, but the French navy was no match for the Royal Navy. The French foreign minister, Théophile Delcassé, who had replaced the more combative Hanotaux, recognised that France could not fight. On 3 November 1898, the French government ordered Marchand to withdraw.
Consequences
The Fashoda crisis was a decisive moment in European diplomacy. It demonstrated British naval and imperial supremacy and confirmed the British position in the Nile Valley. The Sudan became an Anglo-Egyptian condominium under effective British control.
But Fashoda had the paradoxical effect of clearing the ground for a new relationship between Britain and France. The two powers, having faced the prospect of war and recoiled, began to resolve their colonial differences. The Anglo-French Agreement of 21 March 1899 delimited spheres of influence in Central Africa east of the Niger watershed. More significantly, the experience of the crisis contributed to the climate in which the Entente Cordiale of 1904 could be concluded.
The Entente Cordiale — a series of agreements signed on 8 April 1904 — resolved a range of colonial disputes between Britain and France. The most important provision concerned Egypt and Morocco: France recognised the British position in Egypt, and Britain recognised the French position in Morocco. The exclusion of Morocco from the British sphere was a notable feature of the Entente, reflecting the new spirit of compromise. The 1904 agreement, though not a military alliance, laid the foundation for Anglo-French co-operation in the decade before the Great War.
The Boer War and the Consolidation of British Africa
The Scramble for Africa reached its violent culmination in southern Africa with the Boer War of 1899–1902. The collision between British imperialism and Boer independence, personified in the rivalry between Cecil Rhodes and President Paul Kruger, resulted in the conquest and annexation of the Transvaal and Orange Free State. The war — the largest and most costly imperial conflict Britain had fought since the Napoleonic Wars — absorbed enormous military resources, provoked intense international criticism, and generated bitter domestic controversy in Britain.
The peace settlement under the Treaty of Vereeniging (31 May 1902) incorporated the Boer republics into the British Empire, but with generous terms that promised eventual self-government. The Union of South Africa, established in 1910, brought together the Cape Colony, Natal, the Transvaal, and the Orange Free State under a single dominion government, completing the British consolidation of southern Africa.
Legacy
By 1914, the Scramble for Africa was essentially complete. The continent had been divided among the European powers with almost no regard for African political boundaries, ethnic distribution, or cultural coherence. The British Empire’s African possessions formed a vast arc from Egypt and the Sudan in the north-east, through Uganda, Kenya, and Nyasaland in the east, to Rhodesia, Bechuanaland, and South Africa in the south, and across to Nigeria, the Gold Coast, and Sierra Leone in the west.
The partition left a lasting legacy of arbitrary borders, colonial economic structures, and ethnic divisions that would shape the post-colonial history of Africa. The Berlin Conference’s principle of effective occupation — requiring demonstrable control rather than mere claim — had driven a frenzied expansion that transformed the political map of an entire continent in the space of a single generation. As Langer concluded, imperialism in this period was driven by the fact that “much of the globe was an English preserve and the British were not backward in advancing claims to such regions as were still unappropriated” — and the same could be said of the other European powers. The race for Africa was the most spectacular example of the imperial rivalries that characterised the closing decades of the nineteenth century.
