events/second-reform-act-1867.title: The Second Reform Act (1867)
events/second-reform-act-1867.content:
The Second Reform Act (1867)
The Reform Act of 1867 — commonly called the Second Reform Act — was the most dramatic volte-face in nineteenth-century British politics. A Conservative government that had helped defeat a mild Liberal reform bill in 1866 proceeded, in the session of 1867, to carry a measure far more democratic than anything the Liberals had proposed. The bill introduced household suffrage in the boroughs, nearly doubling the electorate, and prompted Lord Derby to describe his own policy as a “leap in the dark.”
The Fall of the Russell-Gladstone Reform Bill (1866)
The immediate background to the Act lay in the failure of Lord Russell’s Liberal government. In 1866, Russell and Mr. Gladstone introduced a Reform Bill of modest scope. Gladstone stumped the country during the Easter recess, declaring at Liverpool that the government had “passed the Rubicon; had broken the bridge and burned the boats behind them.” Yet the measure commanded little public enthusiasm. Conservatives opposed all reform on principle; many Whigs and half-hearted Liberals drifted away. The hero of the anti-reform opposition was Mr. Robert Lowe, a Liberal who attacked the bill with withering sarcasm. Although Lowe had few physical gifts as an orator — a harsh voice, ungainly presence, poor eyesight — his classical allusions and epigrammatic invective delighted the Tory benches. Conservatives made an idol of him, even declaring him the greatest statesman of the day. Mr. Disraeli, by contrast, was thrown into the shade and listened quietly, regarding Lowe’s prominence as a passing episode. The bill was defeated, the Liberal government fell, and Lord Derby formed his third Conservative ministry. (McCarthy, History of Our Own Times, Vol. IV, ch. LII)
Disraeli’s “Ten Minutes’ Bill”
When Parliament reassembled in February 1867, the Queen’s Speech promised a Reform Bill. Lord Derby was frank about the risks: he called the undertaking a “leap in the dark” — a phrase originally used by Lord Cranbourne (the future Lord Salisbury) as a taunt, which Derby adopted as his own. The Conservative Cabinet had prepared two measures: a “comprehensive” bill and a more modest “second-class” bill held in reserve. On Saturday, 23 February, the Cabinet seemed in harmony on the comprehensive measure. But on Sunday, Lord Cranbourne examined the figures and concluded that the comprehensive bill would amount to household suffrage in many boroughs. He tendered his resignation, threatening to bring others with him. On Monday, 25 February, the Cabinet was hastily summoned. With only ten minutes before Disraeli had to address the House, the comprehensive bill was shelved and the “second-class” bill substituted. Sir John Pakington, who later explained the affair at Droitwich, gave the measure its enduring name: the “Ten Minutes’ Bill.”
The Ten Minutes’ Bill was received with universal discouragement. Disraeli saw at once that it could not pass. On 26 February he withdrew it and announced that the government would bring in a genuine measure on 18 March. At this, General Peel, Lord Carnarvon, and Lord Cranbourne resigned. Cranbourne explained that he objected to a bill that would leave political power divided between rich and poor, destroying the influence of the intervening classes. For the second time in ten years, a Conservative Cabinet had split on the question of reform and the borough franchise. (McCarthy, History of Our Own Times, Vol. IV, ch. LII; Annual Register, 1903, Obituary of Lord Salisbury)
The March Bill and the Progress of Household Suffrage
The bill introduced on March 18 proposed that in boroughs all who paid rates, or twenty shillings a year in direct taxation, should have the vote, along with various “fancy franchises” for property-holders, savings-bank depositors, and the educated. Mr. Bright compared the scheme to “offering something with one hand and quietly withdrawing it with the other.” The government, however, had resolved to pass some Reform Bill that session at any cost. Lord Derby frankly admitted that he saw no reason why a monopoly of reform should be left to the Liberals, and Disraeli was determined not to go out of office on a Reform Bill a second time.
One by one the checks and balances were abandoned. The dual vote was laughed out of the bill. The voting-paper principle was dropped. The fancy franchises were swept away. A lodger franchise was introduced. At each stage Disraeli would threaten to drop the bill if an amendment were carried — and when the amendment was carried, he would announce that the government had changed its mind and would accept it. The House came to treat this as mere ceremonial.
The crucial struggle turned on the compound householder — the occupier of a small house whose landlord compounded for the rates. The bill as framed excluded compound householders from the franchise. Mr. Gladstone proposed a compromise: a line below which houses should not be rated at all, but every rated occupier should vote regardless of who paid the rates. He and Bright feared carrying the vote too low, to what Bright called “the residuum of the constituency.” But a group of advanced Liberals — known as the “Tea-Room Party” after the meeting where they resolved their course — refused to support Gladstone’s amendment. They believed that if pressed, the government would yield to anything rather than see the bill defeated. They were proved right: the government undertook to abolish the compounding system entirely, place every occupier’s name on the rate-book, and give every occupier the vote — household suffrage pure and simple in the boroughs. “The Tea-Room Party,” McCarthy writes, “had conquered both ways. They had prevailed against Mr. Gladstone, and prevailed over Mr. Disraeli.” (McCarthy, History of Our Own Times, Vol. IV, ch. LII)
Redistribution and Final Provisions
The bill passed its final stage on 15 August 1867. Its principal provisions were:

Borough franchise: All male householders rated for the relief of the poor, and all lodgers resident for one year paying not less than £10 a year rent.
County franchise: Persons of property of the clear annual value of £5, and occupiers of lands or tenements paying £12 a year.
Redistribution: Eleven small boroughs were disfranchised; thirty-five boroughs with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants were reduced to single-member constituencies. New seats were created for Chelsea, Hackney, Leeds, Liverpool, Manchester, Salford, Glasgow, Birmingham, Dundee, and Merthyr Tydfil. Manchester, Liverpool, Birmingham, and Leeds each received a third member. The University of London was given a representative.
Minority representation: In constituencies returning three members, no elector could vote for more than two candidates (the Lord Cairns amendment, carried in the Lords against the government’s wishes). In the City of London, with four members, each elector could vote for only three.
Incidental reforms: Parliament was no longer required to dissolve on the death of the sovereign; members holding offices of profit from the Crown no longer needed to vacate their seats on moving from one department to another.

The Irish and Scotch Reform Bills were deferred to the following year. The Scotch Bill established a borough franchise equivalent to England’s and a county franchise based on £5 property or £14 occupation, with some new seats created by disfranchising small English boroughs. The Irish Bill merely reduced the borough franchise from £8 to £4 and did nothing on redistribution. (McCarthy, History of Our Own Times, Vol. IV, ch. LII; Clayton, The Rise of the Democracy, ch. “Household Suffrage”)
The “Leap in the Dark”
Lord Cranbourne had first used the phrase “leap in the dark” to taunt the government. Lord Derby adopted it as an honest description of his policy. McCarthy observes that while the government acted sagaciously in settling the question decisively, “one is still lost in wonder at the boldness, the audacity with which the Conservative government threw away in succession every principle which they had just been proclaiming essential to Conservatism and put on Radicalism as a garment.” Disraeli, he notes, had said of Peel that he “caught the Whigs bathing and walked away with their clothes”; now Disraeli had “helped to turn the Whigs out of their clothes in order that he might get into them.”
Lord Cranbourne denounced the surrender with great severity from his place in the Commons and anonymously in the Quarterly Review. Yet he did not lose the confidence of his party; Disraeli admired his invective, and they were soon drawn together by common opposition to Gladstone. (McCarthy, History of Our Own Times, Vol. IV, ch. LII; Annual Register, 1903)
Hyde Park Disturbances
While the bill was passing through its stages, the Reform League convened a public meeting in Hyde Park on 6 May. Mr. Walpole, the Home Secretary, issued a proclamation forbidding it, but the League took legal advice and found the government had no power to prohibit a meeting in advance. The meeting was held peacefully, watched by police and soldiers. However, on an earlier occasion the park railings had been torn down by a crowd that surged in when the gates were closed — the Hyde Park “riot” that convinced the government of the necessity of reform. Walpole, worn out by the thankless troubles of his office, resigned as Home Secretary (though he retained his seat in the Cabinet) and was succeeded by Mr. Gathorne Hardy. (McCarthy, History of Our Own Times, Vol. IV, ch. LII; Clayton, The Rise of the Democracy, ch. “Household Suffrage”)
Impact on Party Politics
The Act’s passage was a masterstroke of Conservative party strategy — what contemporaries called “dishing the Whigs.” The Conservative party, which had in opposition helped defeat Gladstone’s moderate bill, now carried a more radical one. As the Diamond Jubilee volume of McCarthy’s history observes, this was characteristic of Disraeli’s method: he would carry to success measures that the Liberals had been unable to pass, and thereby claim the credit for reform.
The first general election under the new franchise came in 1868. The results confounded expectations. The working-men’s candidates — Mr. Ernest Jones, Mr. Beales, Mr. Odger, Mr. Bradlaugh — all failed. “Either our new masters were not so powerful as they were expected to prove,” McCarthy writes, “or they were very much like our old masters in their taste for representation.” The new House of Commons had a Liberal majority of about 120, larger than the majority of 60 in the previous Parliament. Mr. Gladstone thus had a commanding position for his programme of reform, beginning with the disestablishment of the Irish Church. (McCarthy, History of Our Own Times, Vol. IV, ch. “The Irish Church”)
The Act fundamentally altered the composition of the electorate, increasing it from about 1,000,000 to 2,000,000. The town workman was enfranchised, as the middle-class man had been by the Act of 1832. Mr. Lowe, the great opponent of reform, was elected as the first representative of the University of London — a constituency created by the Act he had fought — and is remembered for his remark: “We must now educate our new masters.” (McCarthy, History of Our Own Times, Vol. IV, ch. LII; Clayton, Rise of the Democracy)
Chronology

1866, June: Defeat of Gladstone’s Reform Bill; fall of Russell government; Derby forms his third ministry.
1866, autumn–winter: Widespread reform demonstrations in large towns; Hyde Park railings torn down.
1867, February: Queen’s Speech promises Reform Bill.
1867, 23 February: Cabinet meets in seeming harmony on comprehensive bill.
1867, 25 February: Cabinet crisis; “Ten Minutes’ Bill” introduced.
1867, 26 February: Ten Minutes’ Bill withdrawn; comprehensive bill promised for 18 March.
1867, March: Resignation of Cranbourne, Carnarvon, and General Peel.
1867, 18 March: Disraeli introduces the comprehensive Reform Bill.
1867, May–July: Clause-by-clause fight; abolition of compounding system; household suffrage established.
1867, 6 May: Reform League meeting in Hyde Park.
1867, 15 August: Reform Bill passes its final stage.
1868: Irish and Scotch Reform Bills passed.
1868, November–December: First general election under new franchise; Liberal victory under Gladstone.

Sources

McCarthy, Justin. A History of Our Own Times, Vol. IV. Chapter LII, “The Leap in the Dark,” provides the most detailed narrative of the bill’s passage, including the “Ten Minutes’ Bill” episode, the compound-householder struggle, the Tea-Room Party, and the final provisions.
Clayton, Joseph. The Rise of the Democracy. Chapter “Household Suffrage” covers the Hyde Park disturbances, Disraeli’s conversion to reform, and the Act’s provisions.
McCarthy, Justin. A History of Our Own Times: The Diamond Jubilee Volume, Vol. II. Chapter XXIII discusses the bill in the context of Disraeli’s political method and his rivalry with Gladstone.
Annual Register, 1903. Obituary of Lord Salisbury (formerly Lord Cranbourne) provides contemporary commentary on the resignations and Cranbourne’s denunciation of the “leap in the dark.”

events/somme.title: The Battle of the Somme (1916)
events/somme.content:
The Battle of the Somme (1916)
The great Franco-British offensive of the summer and autumn of 1916 on the Somme was the principal British land effort of the year on the Western Front. It opened after a prolonged preliminary bombardment, became very largely a British responsibility because of the strain Verdun had thrown on the French army, and continued for four months of extremely heavy fighting in which territorial gains remained small while casualties mounted to levels that shocked London and the Empire. The Annual Register of 1916 and the diary of Maurice Hankey together record the strategic design, the first days of the assault, the later use of tanks, the limited advances of September and November, and the contemporary dispute over the scale of British losses. In the calendar of the Coalition year it stood beside the Military Service Acts, the Irish Rebellion, and the reconstruction of the Government as one of the defining facts of 1916.
Strategic Setting
It was common knowledge among the Allies that some strategists held a great offensive on the Western Front to be a mistake, and that a decision should be sought in another direction. The chances of success, these authorities thought, were too small to warrant so hazardous an undertaking; the loss of life would be terrible in failure and even in success. That was not the view of the responsible military chiefs in France and Great Britain. They argued that if the difficulties were greater on the Western Front, that front was also the area where, for geographical reasons, both France and Britain could exert their greatest force — the same logic that had fixed British strategy since the outbreak of the Great War.
The offensive when at last it came was mainly a British movement. The French co-operated but were allotted a minor part — a reversal of the previous September, when the more important operations had been given to the French. The Germans, the Annual Register observed, feared the British more and had concentrated a much more formidable army opposite the British line; the first French assault therefore gained ground somewhat by surprise. The section chosen for the new offensive began several miles south of Arras, north of the river Ancre, and extended to several miles south of the Somme. Between Arras and the Somme the line was held by British troops; south of the Somme the operations were carried out by the French under General Foch.
The German line ran westwards of the small town of Combles and at that point penetrated deeper than almost anywhere else into French territory, the front lines standing over forty miles in advance of the Belgian frontier. The object of the offensive in its first stage was to smash those front lines, drive the enemy back into the Ardennes about Maubeuge, reconquer the greater part of the industrial district lost since 1914, and threaten the German position near Lille and in the north-west. The line of assault fell naturally into three sections: north of the Ancre (British), between the Ancre and the Somme (almost wholly British, and the scene of the most severe fighting), and south of the Somme (French).
Bombardment and 1 July
On 24 June the great preliminary bombardments started on the Somme front. Hankey, full of anxiety over what would happen when the infantry attacks followed, listened apprehensively to the thunder of the guns, which could be clearly heard at Highstead. That same day he lunched with the Asquiths and compared notes on Jellicoe’s Jutland despatch; the Prime Minister called it “the worst despatch I have ever read,” and Hankey was sent to the Admiralty to have it amended. The guns on the Somme continued. Towards the end of June the Cabinet devoted almost its whole attention to Asquith’s endeavours to resolve the Irish question left by the Easter Rising — so much so that on 30 June the War Committee did not get through its agenda.
On 1 July, at 7.30 a.m., the assault was launched along the whole of the selected part of the line. Successive waves of British infantry went “over the top,” to be met by withering crossfire from the machine guns which had survived the prolonged bombardments. Because of the strain which the German offensive at Verdun had thrown on the French army, the Somme battle finally became very largely a British responsibility. It very soon proved, in a phrase Hankey’s biographer records, “both the glory and the grave of Kitchener’s Army.”
On the left wing, between Gommecourt and the Ancre, the British advanced with the rest and after heavy losses entered the German advanced trenches in many places; but in that section the German guns had never been properly mastered, and before evening the enemy succeeded in killing or driving back the British and recapturing their trenches. Although the British losses were heavy north of the Ancre, it was in the centre that the most fearful fighting occurred. The length of the line between the Ancre and the Somme was about twelve miles. Over the whole of this section the British advanced on the first day, the progress most marked on the right, where it was helped by French successes, and least important on the left, where the troops were liable to be enfiladed owing to the failure north of the Ancre. On either side of the main road from Albert to Cambrai the British pressed forward. The villages of La Boisselle, Mametz, Montauban, and Fricourt were seized in the first rush. For seven miles northwards of the Somme the British advanced to a depth of over a thousand yards; northwards again as far as the left bank of the Ancre smaller advances were made. In the first two days the British captured 3,500 prisoners and the French about 5,000, but few guns were taken.
At first the largest advances were made by the French, whose extreme left wing extended across to the right bank of the Somme and whose immediate objective was Péronne. South of the Somme they were fortunate in finding the Germans relatively unprepared — the enemy having deemed the French army incapable of any really serious offensive after its losses before Verdun. On either side of the main road from Bray to Péronne they pushed forward, and in three days advanced to a depth of three miles on a front of about six miles, capturing Frise, Feuillères, Herbecourt, Flaucourt (three miles from Péronne), Assevillers, and Fay. On the third day the French took over 2,000 prisoners. On 4 and 5 July Foch’s troops gained more ground and on the north bank of the Somme captured Hem — the most rapid part of the offensive, during which the French once more used their cavalry, a striking incident, for no cavalry had dared to show itself for many months. By the 9th, in spite of counter-attacks, the French had advanced as far as Biaches, only one mile from Péronne. By about the 10th of the month it became apparent that neither the French nor the British were advancing at the speed necessary for any dramatic success. Speed, the Annual Register insisted, was essential once a fortified line was to be burst.
War Committee Reaction
On 3 July Hankey recorded a War Committee meeting confined to Cabinet members on a finance question, with very strained relations between Lloyd George and McKenna. After the meeting he talked with Balfour and Lloyd George about the offensive, which, as he had fully anticipated, appeared to have almost completely failed, with very heavy losses. “We had 23 Divisions and the Germans only 6 or 7½; we had about 750 big guns and an equal number of field guns. It always seemed to me to be utter folly. I cannot see a trace of any strategical conception in it. To deliver a frontal attack on an entrenched force provided with every possible defensive organisation violates every military principle.” Lloyd George reminded him of his memorandum of December 1914, in which he had argued that no increase in men would enable the Allies to break the front in the west and that victory was only to be obtained in the eastern theatre.
Three weeks later hard evidence enabled Hankey to assess the results more accurately. Esher had written that he thought the battle “the beginning of the end” — which Hankey considered highly optimistic. In truth, he confided to his diary, the 120,000 casualties already suffered in three weeks exceeded the losses in the whole Dardanelles campaign of eight months. The offensive seemed to him “to involve the maximum of effort and the minimum of result,” though he admitted that more had been accomplished than he had expected, and that if the “Caterpillars” were a success the yield might be even greater. A few days later Churchill circulated a strongly worded memorandum about the futility of the huge sacrifice of life on the Somme: the Allies, he argued, could have held the Germans on the front just as well by threatening an offensive as by making one; once the kick was out of an army, the enemy recovered his freedom of movement. The comments on Asquith’s copy of the paper showed that it was very ill received in government circles.
July to November: Pozières, Tanks, Combles, Beaumont Hamel
At the end of July the British made an advance along the main road to Bapaume and took the village of Pozières, lying over two miles from the spot at which the original British line crossed the road. Longueval, Bazentin-le-Grand, and Bazentin-le-Petit were won in the middle of the month; on one occasion the British used cavalry for the first time since 1914 — detachments of the Dragoon Guards and Deccan Horse. The maximum depth of the British advance in July was slightly over three miles. In the same period the British captured altogether fifty-four guns, sixty-six machine guns, and nearly 11,000 prisoners; the French took eighty-five guns, eighty-nine machine guns, and 12,000 prisoners — figures which, in comparison with the numbers engaged, the Annual Register judged not large. Elsewhere on the Western Front the only severe fighting was at Verdun: the Crown Prince of Prussia continued his offensive through the spring, capturing Fort Vaux on 6 June and Fleury and Thiaumont on 23 June; but the British offensive on the Somme paralysed the German effort on the Meuse and in all probability was the chief means of saving Verdun from capture.
Extremely heavy fighting continued throughout August, September, October, and November. The number of casualties was very high, especially among the French and British, who were almost invariably the attacking parties, but the territorial changes were negligibly small. In early September Hankey visited the front and set down his impressions: the Germans were still very strong, dug better than the British, and the prisoners he saw were fine, well set-up, intelligent-looking men; German artillery fire was very heavy though probably not as heavy as the British, and British losses were considerable. He believed Haig’s tactics quite wrong — “It is no good hammering away at the Somme, where the enemy has accumulated vast numbers of men and guns to resist us. No war was ever won by such methods.” Haig ought to open up a new front as a surprise; the “Caterpillars” would provide the means. Hankey did not think the British would see a decisive success in the west that autumn: the Caterpillars were the only chance, and they were being mishandled.
In the September offensive the British employed a new and formidable type of armoured motor-car, nicknamed “tanks.” These tanks were so heavily built that they were invulnerable to anything except a direct hit from a big gun. The first use took place on 15 September — exactly a week after Hankey’s visit. Only sixty were available, and more than half never reached the starting point; their crews had not been fully trained. In the shell-mangled chaos of the Somme they were thrown away, in the judgment of Hankey and Swinton, for the price of a minor tactical success — the capture of the village of Flers. Small wonder that those who had worked for nearly two years on the new development were bitter about the folly and conservatism which had in a few hours undone that inventiveness. At a War Committee meeting Grey said that Hankey’s name ought to be mentioned when the first employment of the tanks was announced. That same day, 15 September, Asquith’s eldest son Raymond was killed in action on the Somme — a blow from which those closest to the Prime Minister, including Hankey, felt he never recovered.
On the Somme the most notable later advance was the capture of Combles on 26 September. The Germans maintained their hold on Péronne. As summer drew into autumn the offensive continued to produce heavy losses for small gains until, in mid-November, the onset of the winter rains brought it to an end. By that time the men were utterly exhausted, and their transport was bogged down in the all-pervading mud of the devastated battlefield. North of the Ancre, where the failure had been complete in July, the villages of Beaumont Hamel and Beaucourt-sur-Ancre were taken on 14 November, over 5,000 prisoners being captured. On the road to Bapaume some progress was made, and at the end of the year the British line ran eastward of the village of Le Sars. On 16 October the dreadful losses were brought home personally to Hankey by the news that his brother Donald, the “Student in Arms,” had been killed while leading his platoon of the 1st Royal Warwickshire Regiment in an attack.
Casualties and Contemporary Judgment
In the western theatre the casualties of the opposing sides were probably approximately equal — which, the Annual Register reminded its readers, meant that they were very unequal in proportion to the total numbers of the respective armies. The German casualties in the unsuccessful assault upon Verdun were very heavy, but these were counterbalanced by the very serious losses incurred by the Franco-British forces in the precisely comparable offensive on the Somme. The absence of official British statistics, though no doubt necessary, led to exaggerated statements; and it was sometimes forgotten that although the battle of the Somme continued for four months, the rate of losses incurred in the first month, July, was not subsequently maintained. “It was not the case that the British had half a million casualties on the Somme.” The aggregate wastage of the white manhood of the British Empire up to the end of 1916 was certainly not much more than one-third that of the manhood of Germany — the latter country having a population only slightly greater.
The only compensation, and it was certainly not a negligible one, was that the heavy British sacrifices contributed to saving Verdun, where German pressure declined in July. In the last two months of the year the French, by a welcome change of tactics, regained most of the lost ground at surprisingly small cost — Douaumont on 24 October, Fort Vaux at the beginning of November, and further gains beyond Douaumont in mid-December with nearly 12,000 more prisoners and over 100 guns. Hankey had never believed in the Somme offensive, though he held some hope that if the tanks were used skilfully they might bring a substantial success. His old friend Colonel Seely, formerly Secretary of State for War, returned on leave from France and described the offensive as “a ghastly and tragic blunder” in which the British had “lost men out of all proportion to the results,” calling British tactics “antiquated” and the general staff “wooden and unreceptive to modern ideas.” “There is much truth in this,” Hankey commented, but the Red-Hatted Staff were in complete control, and until they could be convinced there was nothing to be done. After the summer of 1916 he himself became a reluctant “westerner,” on the ground that it was better to have a second-best plan which the army had its heart in than a more perfect plan which those who had to carry it out did not believe in.
The battle closed without the dramatic rupture of the German front that its designers had sought in July. Verdun had been relieved; a strip of ground between the Ancre and the Somme, and later north of the Ancre, had been taken at enormous cost; tanks had appeared as a new instrument of war, mishandled on first employment yet holding, for those who had conceived them, the promise of a different method. The strategic deadlock on the Western Front remained unbroken into 1917, when the same front would again be the scene of a great British offensive at Passchendaele.

events/suffragette-movement.title: The Suffragette Movement (1867–1918)
events/suffragette-movement.content:
The Suffragette Movement (1867–1918)
The women’s suffrage movement in Britain — encompassing both the constitutional campaign of the National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies (NUWSS) and the militant direct action of the Women’s Social and Political Union (WSPU) — was one of the most defining social and political struggles of the late Victorian and Edwardian eras. After more than half a century of parliamentary bills, public agitation, imprisonment, hunger strikes, and forcible feeding, the Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised some six million women — roughly two‑thirds of the adult female population — and marked the culmination of the longest sustained campaign for electoral equality in British history.
Origins & Constitutional Campaign
The parliamentary campaign for women’s suffrage predated the rise of the suffragettes by decades. John Stuart Mill, during his single term in the House of Commons, moved an amendment to the Reform Bill of 1867 to substitute “person” for “man” — the first parliamentary vote on women’s suffrage. It was defeated by 196 to 73. The same year, Millicent Garrett Fawcett began her lifelong commitment to the cause; she had married the radical Liberal MP Henry Fawcett, of whom McCarthy’s History of Our Own Times records that he was “a most ardent advocate of women’s claims to the legislative suffrage.” (McCarthy, Diamond Jubilee, Vol. II, ch. XXIII)
A Women’s Suffrage Bill introduced in 1870 passed its second reading in the Commons by 124 to 91 but was later blocked by the government. Another bill reached a second reading in 1884, during the passage of the Third Reform Act, but Gladstone — who had earlier voiced sympathy — refused to include women’s suffrage in the government’s franchise measure, arguing that the question was not ripe for settlement. The Act of 1884, which extended household suffrage to the counties, explicitly confined the vote to male householders.
Throughout the 1880s and 1890s, the constitutional wing of the movement grew. In 1897, the many local and regional women’s suffrage societies were federated into the National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies (NUWSS) under the presidency of Millicent Garrett Fawcett. The NUWSS pursued a patient strategy of parliamentary lobbying, petitioning, public meetings, and the education of public opinion. By the turn of the century, the organisation represented some 300,000 women, yet successive governments declined to bring forward a franchise bill.
Rise of Militancy
Frustration with the slow pace of constitutional methods produced a schism. In 1903, Emmeline Pankhurst, a veteran of Manchester radical politics, and her daughter Christabel Pankhurst founded the Women’s Social and Political Union (WSPU) in Manchester. The WSPU adopted the motto “Deeds, not words” and rejected the patient lobbying of the NUWSS in favour of direct, confrontational action.
The first militant phase began in 1905 when Christabel Pankhurst and Annie Kenney disrupted a Liberal Party meeting in Manchester by demanding a statement on women’s suffrage; they were ejected, arrested, and imprisoned. This act — deliberately courting arrest for maximum publicity — set the pattern for the next nine years. The Annual Register for 1906 recorded that “the agitation by the extreme supporters of women’s suffrage, popularly known as the ‘suffragettes,’ who had caused a good deal of disturbance both in Liberal meetings and in the House of Commons itself,” had spread rapidly. In June 1906, a deputation attempted to force its way to the Prime Minister’s house in Cavendish Square; one leader, “understood to be Miss Billington, assaulted a police sergeant” and was sentenced to two months’ imprisonment after refusing to recognise courts “on the ground that laws were made exclusively by men.” (A.R., 1906)
The Annual Register of 1907 noted that “nearly thirty women’s suffrage societies, representing some 300,000 women,” had held a conference under the presidency of Mrs. Fawcett, passing resolutions that “neither sex nor marriage should disqualify for the franchise.” Yet the WSPU escalated its methods. In 1908, suffragettes chained and padlocked themselves to the railings of 10 Downing Street, shouting “Votes for women,” and were sent to prison for three weeks. (A.R., 1908)
By 1909, the campaign had grown more violent. The Annual Register reported “very bitter feeling” aroused by events in Birmingham and elsewhere; suffragist prisoners in Holloway had “broken windows, assaulted wardresses, and otherwise entered into concerted action to defy the prison regulations.” When additional punishment failed to deter them, they adopted the Russian revolutionists’ plan of a “hunger strike.” (A.R., 1909) The government’s response — forcible feeding — provoked intense public controversy.
The arson campaign began in earnest after 1910, when a promised Conciliation Bill that would have enfranchised women householders was abandoned by the Asquith government. The WSPU responded with systematic attacks on property: letterboxes were set alight, windows of shops and government buildings smashed, and unoccupied houses set on fire. The Annual Register for 1913 catalogued the burning of a large unoccupied house at Ascot, a church at Clevedon, an orchid house at Kew, and numerous other outrages.
Hunger Strikes & Government Response
From 1909, the hunger strike became the central weapon of the suffragette prisoner. As the Annual Register recorded:

“[Suffragists] had declared their intention to be treated like ordinary prisoners… A ‘hunger strike,’ however, compelled the authorities next day to release several.” (A.R., 1909)

The government’s attempt to break the hunger strikes by forcible feeding — inserting a tube through the nose or mouth to administer liquid food — was condemned by medical opinion and gave the suffragettes a powerful propaganda victory. The Annual Register noted that “very bitter feeling had been aroused by the forcible feeding of the ‘hunger strikers’” and that questions were raised repeatedly in the House of Commons. One celebrated case involved Lady Constance Lytton, who disguised herself as a working-class woman to demonstrate that working-class prisoners were forcibly fed while aristocrats were released on health grounds. (A.R., 1909)
The government’s dilemma was acute: letting hunger strikers die would be a public scandal, but releasing them immediately on arrest made the law a farce. The Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Bill — instantly dubbed the “Cat and Mouse Act” — was rushed through Parliament in April 1913. The Home Secretary introduced it declaring that “forcible feeding… was most objectionable, and he desired power to take alternative action.” Under the Act, hunger-striking prisoners could be released on licence when their health was endangered and rearrested when they had recovered. The Annual Register described the Bill’s passage:

“The suffragists described this measure as the ‘Cat and Mouse’ Bill, and it did nothing to moderate the agitation.… Hunger-striking became a matter of course among suffragist prisoners, and even a few ordinary criminals adopted it; and release under the Bill merely gave fresh opportunity for demonstrations.” (A.R., 1913)

Emily Wilding Davison, a prominent member of the WSPU who had been repeatedly sentenced to imprisonment for militant outrages and had always resorted to the hunger strike, became the movement’s most famous martyr. On 4 June 1913, during the running of the Epsom Derby, she ran onto the course and was struck by the King’s horse, Anmer. She died four days later. The Annual Register recorded tersely: “On the 8th, after an attempt to stop the Derby in the interest of militant suffragism, Emily Wilding Davison, B.A. London… repeatedly sentenced to imprisonment for ‘militant’ outrages, and had always resorted in prison to the ‘hunger strike.‘” (A.R., 1913) Her funeral procession through London drew enormous crowds, and her death — whether intended as suicide or a desperate protest — galvanised public attention.
Mrs. Pankhurst herself was repeatedly imprisoned and subjected to the Cat and Mouse regime. In 1913 she undertook an American tour that raised £4,500 for the WSPU’s funds. (A.R., 1914) The Annual Register for 1914 recorded that the WSPU’s receipts for the year ending February 1914 amounted to nearly £37,000, apart from sums raised by local branches. By the spring of 1914, militancy had reached its peak: churches were burned, paintings slashed at the National Gallery and Royal Academy, the aqueduct supplying Glasgow with water was threatened, and a deputation attempting to force its way to Buckingham Palace led to the arrest of sixty-six women. (A.R., 1914)
Suspension & War Work
The outbreak of the First World War in August 1914 transformed the situation abruptly. On 10 August 1914, the government announced a general amnesty for suffragist prisoners and for persons convicted of offences in connection with industrial disturbances. The Annual Register recorded:

“[B]oth the non-militant and the militant groups of the suffrage societies provisionally abandoned their agitation (though a few of the militants made a scene at the Home Office on August 27), and organised themselves for the relief, in various ways, of the women and children sufferers by the war. Admirable work was done in these directions by the National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies, and by the Women’s Emergency Corps; and Miss Christabel Pankhurst, on her return from Paris a little later, repaid the Government by speaking at meetings designed to encourage recruiting for the ‘new Army.‘” (A.R., 1914)

The suspension of militancy was never formally rescinded by the WSPU; it simply ceased as the nation mobilised. Emmeline Pankhurst threw herself into the war effort, organising recruitment rallies and urging women to take up war work. The NUWSS under Millicent Fawcett similarly directed its energies into war relief, while never abandoning the ultimate goal of women’s enfranchisement.
Women’s contribution to the war effort was immense. They filled factory jobs — particularly in munitions — served as nurses near the front lines, drove ambulances, worked on the land, and replaced men in countless civilian occupations. By 1918, women had demonstrated beyond dispute their capacity for labour that had previously been considered the exclusive domain of men. The Annual Register for 1918 noted that some 6,000 women munition workers marched to Whitehall in November 1918 to demand a living wage; the Prime Minister received deputations and promised support for equal pay for equal output. (A.R., 1918)
The 1918 Franchise Act
The Representation of the People Act 1918 — the largest single extension of the franchise in British history — received the Royal Assent on 6 February 1918. The Act’s passage had been under discussion since 1916, when a Speaker’s Conference on electoral reform recommended a comprehensive overhaul. The Bill was introduced in 1917 and debated extensively in both Houses.
In the Commons, the Franchise Bill entered its final stages in December 1917. The Home Secretary, Sir George Cave, steered the Bill through against determined opposition on details such as the disqualification of conscientious objectors and Irish redistribution. The Annual Register recorded that the Bill was read a third time with “congratulations… offered to Sir George Cave… on his conduct of the Bill and its results.” (A.R., 1917) In the Lords, the clause enfranchising women was passed on 10 January 1918 by 134 votes to 71 — a majority of sixty-three. The Archbishop of Canterbury strongly supported the Bill, and Lord Selborne declared that “the enfranchisement of women would bring strength and fresh power to the country and the Empire.” (A.R., 1918)
The scale of the Act was unprecedented. The Annual Register noted:

“[W]hile the Reform Act of 1832 enfranchised 500,000 new voters, that of 1867, 1,000,000 new voters, and that of 1884, 2,000,000 new voters, the Act of 1918 enfranchised 8,000,000 new voters, 6,000,000 being women, of whom 5,000,000 were married, and 2,000,000 being men.” (A.R., 1918)

The Act granted the vote to all men over 21 (with a residency qualification abolishing the old property-based franchise) and to women over 30 who met a minimum property qualification or were local government electors, or who were married to a man who qualified. The age and property restrictions were deliberately calibrated to ensure that women did not become a majority of the electorate — a concession to anti-suffragist fears.
Later in 1918, the Parliament (Qualification of Women) Act — passed on 23 October 1918 — removed the bar on women standing for election to the House of Commons. The motion, moved by Herbert Samuel, was carried by 274 votes to 25. The Annual Register recorded that “the only sound that was heard in the Chamber when the figures were announced was an involuntary burst of laughter from the Ladies’ Gallery.” (A.R., 1918) At the general election of December 1918, Constance Markievicz became the first woman elected to Parliament (though as a Sinn Féin abstentionist she never took her seat), and Nancy Astor entered the House as the first woman to sit as an MP in 1919.
The suffragette movement thus achieved its primary objective — the enfranchisement of women — though at a staggering cost in personal suffering, imprisonment, and violence. The constitutional campaign of the NUWSS and the militant agitation of the WSPU, while divided in method, had been complementary forces. As the Annual Register observed when summing up the anti-suffragist case during the 1914 debates, “The question was not of equality of the sexes, but of fitness to discharge public duties” — a question that the women who had worked in munitions, nursed the wounded, and fed the nation during four years of war had answered decisively.

events/third-reform-act-1884.title: The Third Reform Act (1884–1885)
events/third-reform-act-1884.content:
The Third Reform Act (1884–1885)
The Third Reform Act — consisting of the Franchise Act of 1884 and the Redistribution of Seats Act of 1885 — was the crowning legislative achievement of Gladstone’s second ministry, extending the household suffrage that had been granted to boroughs in 1867 to the county constituencies, and fundamentally redrawing the electoral map of the United Kingdom. The Acts added some two million new voters to the electoral register, enfranchised the agricultural labourer for the first time, and established the single-member constituency as the dominant form of parliamentary representation.
Background: The Anomalies of Representation
By the early 1880s, the defects of the existing electoral system had become glaring. As Justin McCarthy records, “the most flagrant anomalies and injustice were still existing” in the distribution of seats. “In some cases pitiful little boroughs with only a few hundred inhabitants returned as many representatives as some great and important counties. Then there were purely imaginary divisions of constituencies which threw the balance of representation quite out of gear.”
The county franchise had remained far more restrictive than the borough franchise established by the Reform Act of 1867. While the artisans of the towns had obtained the household vote, the agricultural labourer of the countryside — who formed a vast and growing portion of the population — remained disenfranchised. Sir George Trevelyan had brought forward year after year his motion for “the equalising of the county franchise with that which prevailed in cities and boroughs,” but without any actual success. Only a strong Liberal Government, McCarthy observes, could possibly deal with the evils from which the country suffered.
The external circumstances of 1884 were inauspicious for reform. The Egyptian question darkening the air, and the Irish troubles exasperating men’s minds in all quarters of the House of Commons, many sincere Liberals felt that the Government was only courting defeat by venturing on the contentious question of a reduced franchise. Mr. Gladstone, however, was not deterred.
The Franchise Bill of 1884
Gladstone divided his great reform scheme into two separate bills. The first — the Franchise Bill — he introduced into the House of Commons on February 29, 1884. In a speech of remarkable breadth, he declared that the bill was introduced “in fulfilment of a pledge, in obedience to a widely expressed demand, and for the purpose of adding strength to the State.” He declined to argue anew the case of the classes to be enfranchised, as that case had been admitted in regard to borough populations fifteen years before, and had been “completely approved by the experience of those fifteen years.”
“I am not prepared,” Gladstone told the House, “to discuss admission to the franchise now as it was discussed fifty years ago, when Lord John Russell had to state, with almost bated breath, that he expected to add in the three kingdoms half a million to the constituencies. It is not now a question of nicely calculated less or more. I take my stand upon the broad principle that the enfranchisement of capable citizens, be they few or be they many — and if they be many, so much the better — is an addition to the strength of the State.”
The Government proposed to put the county population on the same level as the populations of cities and towns. In boroughs, the ancient rights franchises were left untouched; the household franchise of 1867 remained; the ten pounds clear yearly value franchise was extended to land held without houses or buildings; and a new service franchise was created for persons who were inhabitants of a house but were neither occupiers nor tenants — including the officers of great public institutions and the humbler men who occupied houses as caretakers. In the counties, the franchise was reduced to ten pounds yearly value, and the household, lodger, and service franchises of the boroughs were established in the county constituencies. No one already qualified was to be disfranchised. Everyone who was the head of a household would be enabled to become a voter.
The bill extended to Ireland and Scotland with whatever slight differences of detail might be necessary under the existing conditions of those countries. Gladstone insisted that “England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales were to be treated in this measure on a principle of absolute equality.” Nothing, he declared, would induce the Government to depart from that determination. “I could bear no part in the responsibility of passing, perhaps, a Reform Bill for England and for Scotland, and then leaving a Reform Bill for Ireland to take its chance.” As McCarthy observes, these words “were addressed to the House of Commons, but they were levelled at the House of Lords.”
The first reading was carried without serious opposition. The measure passed through its third reading on June 26 and was at once sent up to the House of Lords.
The Lords’ Challenge and the Autumn Crisis
In the House of Lords, Lord Cairns immediately gave notice of a resolution declaring that, while the peers would be prepared to concur in a well-considered and complete scheme for the extension of the franchise, they did not think it right to assent to the second reading of a bill “having for its object a fundamental change in the electoral body, which is not accompanied by provisions ensuring the full and free representation of the people, or by any adequate security that the bill shall not come into operation except as an entire scheme.” The amendment was carried by 205 votes to 146, and the further progress of the measure was practically stopped for that session.
Unlike the crisis of 1831, when reform had been opposed on the ground that it would invite revolution, the Conservative peers now disclaimed any desire to prevent the passing of a bill for the further extension of the suffrage. “What they contended was, that it was the interest of the people to have a symmetrical scheme before them, in order that they might know whether full justice was to be done to the popular claim.” Some spoke of themselves as “much better friends of the people than Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal Government.”
Negotiations were instantly opened between the Government and the leaders of the Opposition. Meetings were held all over the country, and the negotiations went on day after day, giving rise to “all manner of misunderstandings,” public explanations repudiated, and frequent complaints about unauthorised publication of private interchanges. Still, two great facts were manifest to the public: first, that the House of Lords disclaimed any intention of setting itself up against the popular will; and second, that the Liberal Government was prepared, while surrendering no principle, to invite the Opposition’s assistance in moulding a satisfactory measure. Parliament was prorogued on this understanding.
During the recess, Gladstone declared, “I do not believe that the House of Lords has as yet placed itself in a position of irretrievable error. I believe it to be possible that it may go back, and may go back with dignity and with honour.”
There was some disturbance in Birmingham in October 1884, when a Conservative meeting was held in Aston Park and the Liberals organised a counter-demonstration. The park was broken into, rival crowds came into collision, and there was wreckage and destruction of property. Lord Randolph Churchill endeavoured to fix Mr. Chamberlain with responsibility, and used his memorable expression about “drawing the badger” — compelling Chamberlain to defend himself.
The Winter Session and the Compromise
The winter session of Parliament was opened on October 23, 1884, when the Queen’s Speech announced that the two Houses had been called together “to give further consideration to the great subject of the representation of the people in Parliament.” The Franchise Bill, in substance unchanged, was brought in and read a first time without division or even discussion. On November 6, Gladstone moved the second reading. An amendment insisting on a redistribution bill was formally moved, but as it was now known that negotiations were proceeding favourably, the amendment was not pressed. The second reading was carried by 372 votes against 232 on November 7. On November 11, the bill was read a third time without a division.
The negotiations were conducted on the Government side by Mr. Gladstone, Lord Hartington, and Sir Charles Dilke, and on the Opposition side by Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote. The result was that the House of Lords became willing to accept the Franchise Bill, and Gladstone announced that he would soon introduce his Redistribution Bill.
The Redistribution of Seats Act 1885
On December 1, 1884, Mr. Gladstone brought in the redistribution measure. The bill proposed to increase the number of members of the House by 12, raising the total from 658 to 670. The 12 additional members were given to Scotland, which had been left with an admittedly inadequate representation; Scotland was now to have 72 members. Six disfranchised seats were restored to representation and given to England. Ireland and Wales retained their representation as before — Ireland kept 103 members, a number defended on the ground that the Act of Union provided that Ireland should have not less than 100 members.
The most significant innovation was the adoption of single-member constituencies as the dominant principle. As Clayton records, “the principle of single-member equal electoral districts — on a basis of 54,000 inhabitants — was adopted. Only twenty-three boroughs, the City of London and the Universities of Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin, retained double-member representation.” This represented a fundamental reorganisation of the electoral map.
There was considerable discussion about the proposal to divide nearly all the great cities into different wards or districts, each returning one member. Mr. Courtney, then Financial Secretary for the Treasury, was so strongly opposed to this principle that he resigned his office. Sir John Lubbock moved an instruction to sanction the transfer of votes to provide for the representation of minorities, but the instruction was rejected by a large majority.
The Franchise Bill passed through all its readings in the House of Lords and became law just before the adjournment for the Christmas recess. The Redistribution Bill came on again early in March and was finally carried through both Houses of Parliament without much further trouble.
McCarthy records the outcome with satisfaction: “Nothing seems to us to have been more satisfactory than the principle of practical arrangement which was adopted in this instance by the leaders of the Government and the leaders of Opposition.” While extreme Radicals insisted the Government could have got better terms, and some Tories declared their leaders had sacrificed too much, the great majority on both sides were satisfied. “No serious fault has since been found in the working of this scheme of reform, which was agreed to by the common consent of the leading minds representing Liberalism and Conservatism in the country.”
Significance and Impact
The Third Reform Act completed the work begun by the First Reform Act of 1832 and the Second Reform Act of 1867. As the Annual Register for 1918 would later record in summarising the successive reforms, the Act of 1832 enfranchised 500,000 new voters; that of 1867, 1,000,000 new voters; and that of 1884, some 2,000,000 new voters.
Joseph Clayton, writing in his contemporary survey The Rise of the Democracy, summarised the transformation: “The third Reform Act, giving household suffrage to the country districts, was passed by Gladstone in 1884, and it was followed by a Redistribution of Seats Act in 1885. By these two Acts the agricultural labourer was enfranchised, a service franchise was created for those who were qualified neither as householders nor lodgers, and the principle of single-member equal electoral districts — on a basis of 54,000 inhabitants — was adopted.”
The effect on the balance between the Liberal and Conservative parties was profound, though not immediate or straightforward. The enfranchisement of the agricultural labourer was generally expected to benefit the Liberals, who had championed the reform and who now commanded the allegiance of a vastly expanded rural electorate. In the event, the general election of 1885 — the first held under the new franchise and the new boundaries — produced a hung parliament in which Parnell’s Irish Nationalists held the balance of power. The newly enfranchised county voters proved more independent than either party had anticipated, and the question of Home Rule for Ireland, which Gladstone embraced in the aftermath of the election, came to dominate the next decade of British politics.
The Act also had a lasting constitutional significance. As Clayton noted, when the Labour Party began to send working-class representatives to Parliament in growing numbers after 1900, it was the extension of the franchise in 1867 and 1884 that had “made the entry of the workman inevitable.” The Third Reform Act thus laid the electoral foundation upon which the modern democratic political order in Britain was built.
Yet McCarthy, writing while the memory of the debates was still fresh, cautioned that no reasonable man could suppose it to be a final settlement. “The principle of ‘One Man, One Vote’ was enunciated more than once during the debates, and the time must come when that principle will have to be established in our legislation, and a man will no longer be allowed to have one vote for his house in the West-end, a second for his office in the City, a third for his country house in one of the shires, a fourth for his shooting-place in Scotland, and so on.”

The authoritative contemporary account of the passage of the Acts, including extensive quotation of Gladstone’s speeches, the parliamentary manoeuvring, and the negotiation with the House of Lords.

events/western-front-1914.title: The Western Front, 1914 (Mons to First Ypres)
events/western-front-1914.content:
The Western Front, 1914 (Mons to First Ypres)
After the outbreak of the Great War the first British campaign on the Continent was the passage of a small professional army across the Channel, its collision with the German right wing at Mons, the long retreat to the Marne, the recovery on the Aisne, and the first terrible stand around Ypres that closed the open warfare of 1914 and fixed the trench line for years to come. Parallel with that land drama ran the contest for command-of-the-sea in home waters: the Grand Fleet held its controlling position in the North Sea, while German battle cruisers struck the Yorkshire coast in December and the Admiralty redistributed its forces against further raids. For Great Britain the year on the Western Front was the year of the British Expeditionary Force — the force that, in the contemporary judgment of the Annual Register and in Churchill’s later narrative, played a part out of all proportion to its numbers in denying Germany the six-week victory on which the German design had staked the war.
Passage of the Expeditionary Force
The war found a Government prepared to withstand the enemy and a Parliament and people whose divisions — on which the Germans had staked their hopes — were rapidly closing. Promises of help poured in from all parts of the Empire. Horses and motor-lorries were hastily requisitioned; preparations, perfectly well known in the ports, were actively made for the despatch of the British Expeditionary Force; and most of the papers patriotically suppressed what news of the movement leaked by inadvertence. Then began that system of secrecy as to movements and details, loyally observed by all concerned and rigorously enforced by authority, which was kept up throughout the year by all the belligerents.
The Force crossed mainly by way of Southampton to Havre and Boulogne. Two destroyers and the Eighth Submarine Flotilla watched continuously to attack the German fleet had it interfered. The South-Western Railway Company dealt with the huge traffic. The arrival in France was announced officially in England on 18 August, though French papers had published it ten days earlier on the authority of the French War Office. Disquieting rumours had arisen from the delay; it was officially stated that no casualties had yet occurred among the troops.
At the same time were published a Message from the King and Instructions from Earl Kitchener. The King told the soldiers that they were leaving home to fight for the safety and honour of his Empire; that Belgium, whose country Britain was pledged to defend, had been attacked, and that France was about to be invaded by the same powerful foe. Kitchener’s instructions, to be kept in every soldier’s active-service pay-book, ordered the men to help their French comrades against a common enemy, to set an example of discipline and steadiness under fire, to maintain friendly relations with those they were helping, and to look upon looting as a disgraceful act. “In this new experience you may find temptations, both in wine and women. You must entirely resist both temptations… Do your duty bravely. Fear God. Honour the King.”
Mons and the Retreat
The concentration of the Expeditionary Force in France was completed on 21 August. Hopes raised in England by earlier accounts from France and Belgium gave place to anxiety as the Germans occupied Liège and advanced to Brussels, the French retired in Alsace, and Namur fell suddenly on 25 August. The fall of Namur, it was announced, necessitated the retirement of a portion of the Allied troops from the line of the Sambre to their original defensive position on the Franco-Belgian frontier. The British position was not fully revealed until Sir John French’s despatch was published on 10 September.
On 22 August, French stated, he had moved the troops into position in pursuance of General Joffre’s plans, apparently to cover the French left on the Sambre. They occupied a line of about twenty-five miles from Condé westwards through Mons to Binche: the Second Corps from Condé to Mons, the First from Mons to Binche, the 5th Cavalry Brigade on the extreme right at Binche. After cavalry reconnaissances on the 22nd and 23rd, the actual engagement began at 3 p.m. on the 23rd. Believing himself faced by only one or at most two German Army Corps, French learned at 6 p.m. from Joffre that there were at least three — a reserve corps and the 4th and 9th Corps — while a fourth was engaged in a turning movement on his left flank, and the French on his right were retiring before the Germans, who on the 22nd had secured the passages of the Sambre between Charleroi and Namur.
He therefore began to retire at daybreak to the line Jeumont–Maubeuge, some ten miles farther back, a position previously surveyed but difficult to hold, and reached it before nightfall. During the retirement the Second Cavalry Brigade under General De Lisle attempted a flank attack on the enemy’s infantry, was stopped by a wire entanglement, and the 9th Lancers and 18th Hussars suffered severely. Supported by the 19th Infantry Brigade, the Second Corps under General Smith-Dorrien effected a retreat, but with two German corps on its front and one threatening the flank it suffered great loss. From the new position a further retreat was forced by the enemy’s efforts to outflank the British and drive them on Maubeuge; on the 25th a further retirement was effected to a line some sixteen miles to the south-south-west, running from Cambrai by Le Cateau to Landrecies.
On 28 August the British retirement was followed closely by two German cavalry corps moving south-east from St. Quentin; the Third and Fifth Cavalry Brigades, under General Gough and General Chetwode, respectively repelled the Uhlans of the Guard south of the Somme and routed the eastern German column near Cerizy. Next day the Sixth French Army got into position on the British left; but the German numbers were overwhelming. After a visit from General Joffre, Sir John French agreed to retire towards the line Compiègne–Soissons; and, as his communications with Havre were threatened, the British base was changed to St. Nazaire, on the Atlantic near Nantes, with an advanced base at Le Mans. Joffre ordered a general retirement to the line of the Marne until he could reach a position enabling him to assume the offensive. Rearguard actions were frequent. On 1 September the First Cavalry Brigade, south of Compiègne, were overtaken by German cavalry; they momentarily lost a Horse Artillery battery, but with the help of detachments from the Third Corps they recovered it and captured twelve German guns. The First Corps were also engaged at Villers-Cotterets, the Fourth Guards Brigade suffering considerably.
Panic in London and the Turn of the Tide
On Sunday, 30 August, London was horrified by accounts of the retreat published in the Daily Mail and The Times — the latter speaking of “a retreating and a broken army,” the former of a “pitiful story” and an incessant German advance. The gaps left by the Censor’s editing suggested that the whole truth might be worse; the Daily Mail telegram closed with an appeal for reinforcements at once. For a few hours the news produced something like a panic. Its diffusion was restricted because the day was Sunday; in the afternoon the War Secretary issued a report of the four days’ battle showing that since the 26th, apart from cavalry fighting, the British Army had rested, that reinforcements covering double the loss suffered had already joined, and that the French armies had that day stopped the German advance. A decisive British victory in France, the statement added, would probably be fatal to the enemy; the continuance of Anglo-French resistance on a scale that kept the enemy’s best troops in the closest grip could, if prolonged, lead only to one conclusion.
Next day in Parliament the alarmist accounts were severely condemned by the Lord Chancellor and the Prime Minister, Mr. Asquith, the latter describing them as a regrettable exception to the patriotic reticence of the Press. It appeared, however, that the Press Bureau had actually requested their publication, and that the closing paragraph urging reinforcements was due to the head of the Bureau, Mr. F. E. Smith, himself.
Behind the public alarm the strategic crisis was resolving. Lord Kitchener journeyed to Paris. Correspondence passed between him and Sir John French. Of the retirement to the Marne it was later stated that losses were 15,000, not a third of those inflicted on the enemy; but the spirit of the force was not affected; drafts amounting to 19,000 men had arrived or were approaching, and the interval of quiet since 1 September had been used to fill up the gaps and refit and consolidate the units. The British Army was south of the Marne, in a line with the French forces on its right and left; the enemy was neglecting Paris and marching south-eastwards, having apparently abandoned its flanking movement on the Allies’ left — a change in German plans made about 3 September. The British troops, French reported, had definitely established their superiority to the Germans alike in rifle fire and in cavalry and artillery work; despite the heat, men and horses were in excellent condition; but “we must have more men.”
The Marne and the Aisne
On 3 September, when the British forces were in position south of the Marne between Lagny and Signy-Signets, and Sir John French had taken steps to defend the passage of the river, General Joffre invited him to retire twelve miles farther, to a position behind the Seine. The enemy crossed, and there were several outpost actions. On 5 September Joffre announced his intention of taking the offensive, and, at his request, the British Army changed front to its right, its left coming to rest on the Marne and its right on the Fifth Army. On 6 September the new battle began on a front running from Ermenonville through Lizy, Mauperthuis, Cortecon, Esternay, Charleville, to a point north of Verdun. About noon a German retreat began, and a series of battles followed till, on the evening of 10 September, the enemy, driven back to a line running from Compiègne to Soissons, were preparing to dispute the passage of the Aisne.
French specially mentioned the forcing of the passage of the Petit Morin River (8 September) by the First British Corps, and of the Marne by the First and Second Corps, and of the battle on 10 September, when these Corps, assisted by the Cavalry division on the right and the Third and Fifth Cavalry Brigades on the left, drove the enemy northwards, capturing thirteen guns, seven machine guns, some 2,000 prisoners, and much transport. Some further encouragement was given by the announcement (10 September) that the Fleet had swept the North Sea up to and including the German coasts in certain waters.
A further despatch, dated 8 October but published with the narrative of 19 October, practically completed the history of the fighting on the Aisne. On 12 September the enemy made a stand and prepared to dispute the passage of the river somewhat to the east of Soissons. The river valley ran east and west; the bottom was flat, the hills bordering it were about 400 feet high, with numerous spurs and re-entrants; they were backed on the north by a high plateau with patches of wood, admirably adapted for concealing troops. The enemy held a very strong position on the north of the Aisne — a winding stream, 170 feet wide and unfordable — commanding all the bridges, and with great facilities for concealment.
On 13 September the British forces were ordered to advance and make good the Aisne. Portions of them that day crossed at various points a distance of about twelve miles from Bourg to Venizel (the latter some three miles east of Soissons), with comparative ease on their right, with great difficulty on their left — the Fifth Infantry Brigade, in particular, crossing in single file under heavy fire on the broken and only remaining girder of a bridge. The crossing was not completed till the evening of the 13th, when the enemy (though still holding some points on the Aisne) effected a general retirement and entrenched on the high ground two miles north of the river, leaving detachments of infantry supported by powerful artillery in commanding points on the slopes of the spurs. The river was further bridged, under heavy artillery fire, by the Royal Engineers, and on the 15th there was a general advance, to ascertain whether the enemy intended to hold his position. The bombardment of Reims Cathedral and the announcement that, on the eleventh day of the Battle of the Aisne, the Allies were gaining ground, supplied the public with such encouragement as the secrecy of the time permitted.
Antwerp, Flanders, and First Ypres
The fate of Antwerp next absorbed attention. Sir John French stated that General Paris had handled the British force sent to the city with great skill and boldness; its action had considerably delayed the enemy and enabled the Belgian Army to be withdrawn and regain its value as a fighting force, and had also facilitated the destruction of war material which would have been of great value to the enemy; moreover, the moral effect of this “necessarily desperate attempt” to succour the Belgian Army had greatly conduced to their efficiency as a fighting force. The despatch was virtually a reply to Press strictures on a step regarded as essentially the enterprise of the First Lord of the Admiralty, Mr. Winston Churchill, who had, in fact, visited the city during the British occupation. The Morning Post of 13 October described it as “a costly blunder, for which Mr. Winston Churchill was primarily responsible”; the relief had come too late, and kept the Belgian Army there too long. In other quarters it was pointed out that the despatch of the force must have been the act of the whole Cabinet, and that it had a moral value as a demonstration of sympathy with Belgium.
Meanwhile the Germans occupied Bruges and Thielt, bombarded Arras, and were evidently making a desperate effort to reach the coast at Dunkirk and Calais, hoping to interfere at least with British shipping in the Channel. The capture of Antwerp seemed to increase their means of interference. The defenders had destroyed the stores of petrol, and sunk or disabled the steamers in the port; and to have used it as a naval base even for submarines would have involved the violation of the neutrality of Holland. But it increased the danger of a Zeppelin raid on London; the Mayor of Gravesend issued a warning against hostile aircraft; and it opened the way for a German advance to the more suitable bases, at Zeebrugge and Ostend, for a naval or aerial attack.
The fall was accompanied by a fresh influx into England of Belgian refugees: in four days (7–10 October) some 10,000 landed in Folkestone from Ostend; on Sunday, 11 October, 4,250 landed there from Ostend and 900 from Flushing; by 17 October the total number in England was 100,000. Crowds reached other ports, notably Lowestoft, in sailing craft, amid great suffering. Relief was promptly given by committees at London and Folkestone, and shelter and hospitality were offered throughout Great Britain; numbers of Belgian wounded were provided for in improvised hospitals, private houses being frequently lent and fitted up by their owners. Many German spies were said to be among the refugees, and for that reason they were withdrawn from Dover and Grimsby. The fate of Belgium was a powerful factor in the issue of a Labour manifesto (15 October), signed by twenty-five Labour members of Parliament and thirty-five leading trade union officials, declaring that in view of Germany’s conduct there must be no peace until the enemy had been defeated.
After the Aisne the struggle became a race for the northern flank and the Channel ports. A daring attempt, not fully revealed until six weeks later, was made by Sir John French to outflank the German forces in northern France. The general idea, set out in his lengthy despatch published on 30 November, was to effect a turning movement north of Lille and then, with the French, to press the German right. The British force was transferred from the Aisne between 3 and 19 October. Battle was joined in the Ypres–Armentières region from about 11 October; the first great stage of the struggle around Ypres ran on to about 31 October. The fighting round Gheluvelt, some six miles from Ypres, on 29–31 October became the emblem of the British stand. The professional army that had marched from Mons, diminished and reinforced, held the line against repeated German attempts to break through to the Channel. By the end of November the open warfare of August and September had closed into the continuous trench system that would dominate the Western Front for the next three years — the long road that would later lead through the Somme, Passchendaele, and the crises of 1918.
Home Waters: Command of the Sea and the Yorkshire Raid
While the Expeditionary Force fought its way from Mons to Ypres, the naval war in home waters entered a new phase. With the destruction of Admiral von Spee’s squadron at the Falklands the enemy had no organised squadrons outside his home waters, and command-of-the-sea, judged by traditional standards, was practically done. Yet the Dresden’s escape and the unsolved mystery of the Karlsruhe still occupied cruisers; and in Home waters mining and submarines of increasing range made free movement precarious. Over 150 trawlers and drifters formed the nucleus of the Auxiliary Patrol; the Grand Fleet itself now depended on fishing craft for free movement near its bases. Still the key fact remained that the Grand Fleet held its controlling position. The High Seas Fleet, under the Emperor’s absolute control, was confined to submarines and destroyers for offensive action, with only occasional sorties of heavy cruisers; outside the Baltic Britain enjoyed a command as complete as in the old blockades of Brest. Until Fisher’s new programme of monitors and fast heavy ships for inshore work was forward, the enemy might use the long winter nights for some sudden blow to diminish the blockade or deter further troop movements to France.
By 10 December news of the Falklands had revealed the temporary weakening of the Grand Fleet. Now if ever was the enemy’s moment to strike, and by the 14th reports of an impending attack were so far confirmed that the fleet was put in motion. It appeared to be a cruiser raid, with or without transports; without undue prejudice to concentration it was possible to ensure that the enemy should have no time to land any serious force, or if a mere naval raid, that subject to the chances of the sea he should never get back. The 5th Battle Squadron stood at shortest notice; Tyrwhitt with his Harwich flotillas was directed to get touch and shadow; Beatty was to take the four remaining battle cruisers from Cromarty, joined by Goodenough’s light cruisers from Scapa, with one battle squadron in support.
Ingenohl, fretting at the inaction imposed since Heligoland, took the Kaiser’s limited permission for big-cruiser sorties as a hint and devised a coast raid — stretching his instructions by supporting Hipper with three battle squadrons. Early on 15 December Hipper left the Jade with Seydlitz, Moltke, Von der Tann, the newly completed Derfflinger, and Blücher; the battle squadrons left Cuxhaven in the afternoon and after dark took supporting station while Hipper proceeded on his errand toward the Yorkshire coast. The raid of 16 December was a purely naval, not a combined, operation; yet intelligence made it impossible to relax measures against an attempt to land troops.
Redistribution and the Cuxhaven Raid
The southern areas had been weakened by the loss of Bulwark. On 20 December Beatty was ordered from Cromarty to join the 3rd Battle Squadron and 3rd Cruiser Squadron at Rosyth; Princess Royal, delayed hunting the ghost of the Karlsruhe, was already homeward bound. The new 10th Cruiser Squadron under de Chair in Alsatian completely relieved the Grand Fleet of the north-about trade-route watch. Christmas Day tested the new stations with an air raid on the Cuxhaven Zeppelin sheds — nine seaplanes from Engadine, Riviera, and Empress, supported by Harwich forces, the whole Grand Fleet concentrated in the middle of the North Sea in hope of provoking a fleet action. Dense frost fog frustrated location, but in Schillig roads seven battleships and three battle cruisers weighed in such hurry that Von der Tann fouled another cruiser and both were severely damaged. Of the returning airmen three were rescued by Nasmith in E 11 off Norderney under the approach of a Zeppelin — founding the reputation he completed in the Sea of Marmara.
Those winter dispositions — Beatty at Rosyth, the Grand Fleet still controlling the North Sea, the Auxiliary Patrol watching the approaches — set the scene for the next meeting of battle cruisers in January 1915 at the Dogger Bank, and for the wider strategic debates that would soon turn part of British effort toward the Dardanelles and gallipoli. On land, the professional army of 1914 had held the line from Mons to Ypres at a cost that already pointed to the need for the mass armies Kitchener was raising at home. The Western Front of 1914 closed not in victory but in a continuous trench system; the year had denied Germany its short war and committed the United Kingdom to a continental struggle of a scale no Cabinet of July 1914 had fully imagined.
