The Annual Register 1905
Part I — English History
Chapter I — Port Arthur, Defence, and the Fiscal Campaign
In England, as throughout the civilised world, the thoughts of men in the first week of 1905 were occupied less by any domestic event than by the fall of Port Arthur. Profound satisfaction at this signal triumph of Britain’s Japanese allies was mixed with respectful sympathy for the gallant defenders of the fortress. Lord Selborne, the first Cabinet Minister to speak after the news (Wolverhampton and Handsworth, 5 January), tried to turn admiration for patriotic devotion into support for Mr Chamberlain’s injunction to “think Imperially,” arguing that the future would lie with nations and Empires counted by hundreds of millions and that Britons must work for better Imperial organisation—commercial, naval, and military—at the approaching Colonial Conference.
Anxiety about defence was uneven. Lord Selborne’s naval administration was generally held vigorous and enlightened; his letter of 3 January confirming that Rosyth on the Firth of Forth would be continuously developed as a naval base (subject to financial as well as naval considerations) was accepted with little demur. Military administration was another matter. Lord Roberts’s January article in the Nineteenth Century and After, “The Army as It Was and as It Is,” insisted that national safety required a large scientifically trained reserve of officers, larger forces or reserves, and better-educated privates—conditions that could not be improvised and which, in his view, had not yet been provided. Rumours of dissensions in the Army Council cast doubt on whether the War Secretary could carry through coherent reform.
There was satisfaction at a special Army Order of 5 January giving general effect to the Esher Committee’s reorganisation of military commands: London became an independent district; the rest of the United Kingdom was divided into seven commands (Aldershot, Southern at Tidworth, Eastern with headquarters in London, Irish at Dublin, Scottish at Edinburgh, Northern at York, and Welsh and Midland at Chester), each under a general officer commanding-in-chief with a major-general or brigadier in charge of administration authorised to correspond with the War Office on routine matters.
The terrible grievance of Mr Adolf Beck, wrongly convicted and imprisoned, was finally met by a Treasury offer of £5,000 compensation—only once equalled in similar circumstances—which he accepted though claiming business losses of £40,000 and chronic bronchitis contracted at Portland.
Opinion continued to set against both the Unionist Government and Mr Chamberlain’s fiscal propaganda. On 7 January at Stalybridge, Mr J. F. Cheetham (Liberal) defeated Mr J. Travis-Clegg by 4,029 to 3,078 (majority 951), reversing a Conservative majority of 81 in 1900. Cotton-district Free Trade feeling and accumulated discontents were the simplest explanation. Mr Chamberlain’s Preston speech of 11 January to some 5,000 hearers made no reference to the reverse, but argued that the cotton trade’s “record” 1904 export values (up more than £10,300,000 on 1903) masked relative decline: Britain’s share of the world’s cotton consumption had fallen since 1896 from 41 to 25 per cent., while Germany, Austria, France and the United States had increased their trade more than 50 per cent. over 1892–1903. His remedy remained tariff revision and the power to “pay [foreign countries] in your own coin”; he carefully declared he would under no circumstances tax raw cotton. A carefully worded resolution designed to allow Balfourite “retaliation” and a colonial conference left him, he said, in an “embarrassing position,” for such a conference must attend favourably to colonial schemes of mutual protection.
Chapter II — Opening of Parliament and the Wyndham Crisis
Unionist fiscal dissensions sharpened before the session. The Greenwich Conservative Association, by 46 to 32, asked Lord Hugh Cecil—the most brilliant of the younger Free-Trade Conservatives—not to stand again; he refused (17 February), though Protectionist local opposition had been discouraged from Conservative headquarters. At the same time Lord Lansdowne’s foreign policy increasingly commanded confidence. A Blue-book on the day Parliament opened showed that Russia’s preposterous 1904 claim to decide at pleasure what was absolute contraband had been virtually abandoned for rice and provisions; coal and raw cotton remained contested in principle, but practical interference with British ships had ceased except for undoubted blockade-runners seized by Japan. Parallel firmness by the United States had helped.
Parliament was opened by the King and Queen in person on 14 February. The Speech recorded satisfaction at the visit of the King and Queen of Portugal; strict neutrality in the Russo-Japanese war; continued Balkan anxiety and Austro-Russian reform proposals to the Porte; ratification of the Anglo-French Convention; arbitration agreements with Sweden and Norway, Portugal and Switzerland; and the agreement with Russia for inquiry into the North Sea (Dogger Bank) disaster. Steps toward a representative constitution in the Transvaal were under earnest consideration; the Tibetan Agreement was noted with praise for the civil and military authorities; negotiations with the Amir of Afghanistan were impending. Domestically the Speech put first the Scottish ecclesiastical difficulty; promised economy in the Estimates; electoral redistribution; Alien Immigration legislation; permanent machinery for the unemployed (with the King’s “profound regret and sympathy” for abnormal winter distress); Scottish education; Workmen’s Compensation amendment; improved status for the Local Government Board and Board of Trade and a Minister of Commerce; valuation reform; naval prize consolidation; industrial-accident notification; renewal of Agricultural Rates and kindred temporary Acts; butter adulteration; and Crown Cases Reserved procedure.
In the Lords, Earl Spencer opened for the Opposition, complimenting Lansdowne’s prudence on war questions, pressing Macedonia, seeking more light on South African self-government and Chinese labour, supporting the India Secretary’s Tibet line while defending Sir Frank Younghusband, and criticising gigantic peace expenditure and successive Army schemes. Lord Lansdowne replied that intervention to end the Far Eastern war might bring rebuffs or worse; contraband had been reduced; a wider Russo-Austrian Macedonian reform scheme would be freely criticised; Transvaal proposals were deliberately limited at first; Chinese-labour prophecies had not been realised; Younghusband had admitted exceeding instructions, but his feat would live after the censure was forgotten. Redistribution, he added, was “physically impossible” this session—sharply reducing the Speech’s announcement. The Address was agreed. In the Commons a privilege motion against the new Lord Alington for canvassing North Dorset tenants was met by Balfour’s previous question (287–191), though the Sessional Order against Peers’ interference was confirmed 345–65.
The session’s Irish crisis centred on the MacDonnell–Wyndham affair: the confidence reposed by Chief Secretary George Wyndham in Under-Secretary Sir Antony MacDonnell, and MacDonnell’s association with Lord Dunraven and the Lord-Lieutenant, Lord Dudley, in conversations that had issued in the Devolution proposals of September 1904. Wyndham’s resignation followed; Sir Antony remained Under-Secretary and Dudley Viceroy. Lord Milner retired from South Africa and was succeeded by Lord Selborne. Walter Long became Irish Secretary and, after pressure, affirmed the Under-Secretary’s definite subordination.
The International Commission’s Dogger Bank report, Education Act difficulties, Navy Estimates, Churchill’s fiscal motion, Trade Unions and Trade Disputes, Coal Mines Employment and Workmen’s Compensation Bills, South African war supplies, the Transvaal Loan, Physical Deterioration, and a series of fiscal debates which Ministers boycotted—Opposition resolutions being carried nem. con. and ignored—filled the early months. Brighton’s bye-election was another Ministerial reverse. Lord Lansdowne spoke on Macedonia and on Germany in the Pacific. The Budget, Home Rule, Irish university education, Land Values, Agricultural Rates continuance, and the introduction of Unemployed Workmen and Aliens Bills carried the House to the Easter adjournment.
Chapter III — Aliens, Education Revolt, and Delcassé
Politicians treated the short Easter recess of 1905 as almost a complete holiday; the notable exception was Mr Brodrick at Godalming (27 April), who emphasised the non-Protectionist, self-sufficing character of Mr Balfour’s fiscal views and believed that if Balfour’s policy alone had stood against sheer Free Trade the Government would have had not a minority but a majority at Brighton. A Local Government Board order published 29 April regulated relief to underfed school children under sixteen (not blind, deaf or dumb, living with a father not on relief): applications must come from school managers, authorised teachers, or education officers; guardians were to inquire and grant relief ordinarily or as a loan, never in money, for not more than a month on a single application, preferably through charitable meal tickets—an effort to treat a painful problem on “sound lines.”
The Aliens Bill’s second reading (2 May) revealed that East London Liberals now largely accepted its main purport. A National Liberal Club meeting of East London Members and candidates (27 April), through Mr Sydney Buxton and eight others who wrote to Sir H. Campbell-Bannerman, hoped Liberals would not oppose second reading. Sir Charles Dilke moved that low-priced alien labour was best met by anti-sweating legislation and that asylum for persecution victims must be retained; Major Evans-Gordon denied anti-Semitic motives and called Britain a “refuse-heap for Southern and Eastern Europe.” Mr Asquith admitted excessive alien crime and approved exclusion of criminals, held the new Bill improved on 1904’s, but would not oppose second reading. Home Secretary Akers-Douglas promised boards of appeal including a magistrate (and hoped a poor-law guardian) and denied intent to exclude bona-fide political refugees. Mr Buxton from the front Opposition bench supported keeping out “uneconomic and undesirable” Russians and Poles who lowered wages and worsened East London overcrowding. Mr Chamberlain welcomed the Bill as protecting workers against underpaid immigrant labour and ironically congratulated Liberals on fiscal progress. Dilke’s amendment fell 211–59 (some ten Liberals with the Government); the Bill was then read a second time without division amid Ministerial cheers.
Education administration under the Act of 1902 was in mounting difficulty. The West Riding County Council resolved to dock denominational teachers’ salaries for time spent on denominational religious instruction—contrary to the Act; the Board of Education advised managers not to comply. Merionethshire was declared in default under the Defaulting Authorities Act of 1904 for failing to maintain voluntary schools. Most urgent was East Ham Borough Council’s April resolution refusing to administer the Education Act after May because of rates said to have reached 2s. 9d. in the pound (with another 9d. needed for new schools), threatening some 25,000 children. On 4 May Mr Gray (West Ham, N.) moved the adjournment; Mr Balfour refused to recognise abdication of local duty, noted the State already paid 60–70 per cent. of education costs, and said East Ham had spent £18 per child on buildings where elsewhere £12 10s. sufficed. The motion failed 159–116. East Ham contested his figures (claiming only 48 per cent. State grant) but on 23 May rescinded its “revolt” 12–7; a deputation of overburdened urban districts saw Balfour privately on 8 June.
The Trade Unions and Trade Disputes Bill was altered in Grand Committee and ultimately withdrawn by its promoters; the Unemployed Workmen and Workmen’s Compensation Bills advanced amid criticism. Balfour spoke at the Albert Hall, Chamberlain in Birmingham; a farewell banquet honoured Mr Choate. Scottish Education, Local Veto (Scotland) (defeated), and Land Values Taxation (Scotland) (second reading) occupied the House. Wyndham explained his resignation; Balfour made a major Imperial Defence statement (with a letter from Lord Esher); Lansdowne spoke on German Pacific islands, the German tariff, and the Anglo-Japanese Alliance. The resignation of M. Delcassé was received with regret in Britain. Fiscal debates continued in both Houses; the Scottish Churches Bill progressed; and the Speaker resigned, thanks were voted, and his successor elected.
Chapter IV — Morocco, War Stores, and the Decline of Balfour
The Whitsuntide recess opened with Lord Roberts’s impressive appeal of 12 June that rifle shooting become “a national pursuit” as archery once had been. He held that better shooting would have prevented most of the unfortunate incidents of the South African War and of 1880–81; failing conscription, security depended on national ability as well as willingness to take arms. Miniature ammunition and short ranges had overcome the obstacles of ranges and expense; under an association amalgamating the National Rifle Association and the Society of Miniature Rifle Clubs he sought at least £100,000 to put rifle clubs within every man’s reach. He avowed that conscription in some form could not permanently be avoided unless obligatory physical training and rifle instruction were enforced in schools up to eighteen—but that was for legislation. The Press was sympathetic; the money came in slowly.
The Co-operative Congress (14 June) claimed over 2,200,000 members, loan and share capital of £36,500,000, and annual trade of nearly £92,000,000, and resolved to exercise direct legislative influence; but a proposal to join forces with the Labour Representation Committee was crushed 801–135 as “handing over … bag and baggage, to a body financed by trade unions and controlled by Socialists.” Mr Haldane at Tranent (13 June) said the Government’s fiscal fog had unified Liberals behind Free Trade, and that Liberals would maintain the Japanese alliance as surely as Conservatives.
Foreign anxiety centred on German pressure upon France over Morocco. Delcassé’s retirement was generally believed due, directly or indirectly, to German hostility; the Sultan’s proposal of an International Conference, instead of accepting French reforms, was regarded as German-inspired at Fez. Britain’s obligation under the Anglo-French Agreement of April 1904 to give France diplomatic support seemed plainly engaged. On 15 June it became known that Britain had distinctly refused the Sultan’s invitation—yet not as a final reply, so that if France later accepted a conference after understanding with Germany on its scope, British support would follow. Paris acknowledged British loyalty and dismissed German suggestions that England wished to drive France into collision with Germany.
The same day brought the Report of Sir W. F. Butler’s Committee on sales and refunds to contractors in South Africa. Mr Arnold-Forster’s preface stressed incomplete evidence and that charges remained sub judice; subject to that, the story was startling. After peace a Pretoria sales department under Colonel Morgan (Army Service Corps) sold surplus stores cheaply to contractors who resold the same goods to the Army at high profit. On oats alone a contractor named Meyer was said to have gained £1 on every 300 lb bought and sold back—a gross daily profit of £2,000. The Committee condemned Morgan (and severely noted his brother Frank’s connection with contracting firms) and held successor Colonel Hipwell unfit and culpable; they abandoned mere negligence for an “impression of cleverly arranged contrivance.” The rhetorical style of the report invited discount, but public demand for a full inquiry was intense. Balfour, after first suggesting a Commons committee, then a non-statutory Royal Commission, was driven (22 June) to a statutory Royal Commission from the outset—losing time and reputation for business management. Commissioners named 26 June were Mr Justice Farwell (chairman), Sir George Taubman-Goldie, Field-Marshal Sir George White, Sir Francis Mowatt, and Mr S. Hope Morley, late Governor of the Bank of England. Sir Robert Reid’s vote of censure on stores mismanagement was debated and defeated by the Government’s full majority.
The Unemployed Workmen Bill was read a second time; the Indian Budget brought into the open the Curzon–Kitchener dispute over Indian military administration, the Home Government’s decision, and denials of the Viceroy’s resignation (premature denials, as Chapter V would show). The Aliens Bill passed committee under closure by compartments and was read a third time. East Finsbury inflicted another Ministerial defeat. Lord Roberts in the Lords warned of military unpreparedness; the War Secretary replied. The Churches (Scotland) Bill was carried through the Commons. Ministerial Redistribution resolutions, after an unfavourable reception and the Speaker’s ruling, were withdrawn. A Unionist party meeting failed to heal fiscal wounds. The Government was defeated on the Irish Land Commission vote and decided to ignore the defeat. The Unemployed Bill passed on a reduced scale after episcopal and labour appeals; the London County Council Tramways Bill was thrown out by the Lords. The Duke of Devonshire’s fiscal motion in the Lords was met by the previous question. As the session ended, the Register recorded the failure of the parliamentary machine and a marked decline in the Prime Minister’s position.
Chapter V — Entente Displays, Curzon’s Fall, Peace in the East, and the Change of Ministry
Though prorogation fell on Friday 11 August, Parliament’s corporate life continued one day longer for a crowning courtesy to the French naval visitors. On Saturday 12 August over 220 Peers and MPs entertained Admiral Caillard and about 130 officers of his squadron at luncheon in Westminster Hall—the Lord Chancellor and the Speaker presiding, Balfour toasting the French Navy and John Morley replying for the Houses. The occasion answered the British Atlantic Fleet’s reception at Brest under Admiral May. Parallel with Anglo-French cordiality ran Anglo-German irritation: after French assent to a Morocco conference early in July, Britain agreed (12 July) to attend, but German circles understood British sympathy lay wholly with France. Suspicious German comment on the Channel Fleet’s Baltic cruise was not matched by official coldness; by the Emperor’s order German squadrons interrupted manoeuvres to greet the British ships (28 August), with banquets at Swinemünde and warm municipal hospitality.
In the prorogation week appeared the Royal Commission report on Food Supply and Raw Material in time of war (chairman Lord Balfour of Burleigh; the Prince of Wales a member). Normally the country held about seven months’ raw cotton, two months’ manganese, and seven weeks’ wheat and flour. The main report saw no reasonable probability of serious interference with supplies but feared panic price rises and recommended a guarded national indemnity against maritime capture; only the chairman, the Prince of Wales, and Admiral Bosanquet signed without substantial reservation. Other sections urged free grain storage experiments, or held that a strong fleet made such experiments needless.
Doubt about the Curzon–Kitchener compromise was confirmed on 21 August by Lord Curzon’s definite resignation of the Viceroyalty. The immediate cause was the Home Government’s refusal to appoint General Barrow—whom Curzon particularly desired—as Military Supply Member of the Viceroy’s Council (they preferred him as Chief of Staff, fearing he would not inaugurate the new system “with an open mind”). Curzon read this as want of confidence and as divergence from the modifications he thought had been secured; Kitchener’s latest proposals seemed to him “almost indistinguishable” from the original scheme the Government had rejected. Brodrick at Godalming (23 August) stressed that in such questions the Secretary of State spoke for Cabinet and India Council, not personal whim, while paying tribute to Curzon’s past services. Publication (26 and 28 August) of lengthy controversial minutes by Kitchener and Curzon was widely judged a serious State blunder.
The announcement of 29 August that peace had been concluded between Japan and Russia was received with universal British satisfaction. Japan’s self-restraint in forgoing a large indemnity was admired; the terms were held to embody her success by sea and land and to secure her against recurrence of the dangers that had forced war. Gratification was deepened by the knowledge that the renewed and extended Anglo-Japanese alliance—by then understood to have been for some little time in existence—had facilitated Japan’s moderate temper.
The Trade Union Congress at Hanley (4–9 September), some 450 delegates representing about a million and a half organised workers, noted the mutilation and withdrawal of the Trade Unions Bill and the failure of Workmen’s Compensation, and urged great trade-union efforts. Volunteer discontents, Balfour’s reassurances, autumn fiscal campaigning (Asquith, Sir E. Grey on foreign policy and Chinese labour, Morley on the Japanese treaty, Chamberlain, Lord Hugh Cecil, the Duke of Devonshire, Lord Londonderry, Austen Chamberlain), the Queen’s and the Premier’s Guildhall appeals for the unemployed, and Lord Roberts’s propaganda for universal military training filled the months. The Conservative Conference at Newcastle saw a Chamberlainite triumph despite Balfour’s appeal for unity; Chamberlain’s contrary Bristol appeal and articles in the Times and Daily Telegraph pointed to the Premier’s resignation. After a transient Liberal crisis on Home Rule, a Macedonian Blue-book, and an announcement that the Volunteers were not to be reduced, Mr Balfour resigned. Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman became Prime Minister and formed an administration favourably received by public opinion. Balfour defended his resignation; Lord Rosebery commented on the new ministry; the new Premier set out Liberal policy; a despatch on Chinese labour issued; and an electioneering Christmastide posed the issues before the country.
Chapter VI — Scotland and Ireland
Scotland. The Royal Commission on the great Churches Cause (Lord Elgin, Lord Kinnear, Sir Ralph Anstruther) reported on 19 April. Expressing regret at the “extreme bitterness” between the Free Church and the United Free Church, it held the Free Church, from paucity of numbers and poverty of resources, incapable of carrying on the work of the Church it claimed to represent and thus of putting its enormous endowments to their proper purpose—yet unjust that those endowments should pass absolutely and unconditionally to the United Free Church. It recommended a statutory Commission in which the whole Free Church funds and property as at 31 October 1900 should vest, charged to allocate them primarily to secure “adequate provision for the due performance of the purposes for which the funds were raised,” preferring the United Free Church where the Free Church could not execute the trusts, on equitable conditions and with liberal equipment for the Free Church according to Presbyterian standards. The “Wee Frees” received the report angrily; the United Free Church with satisfaction; Principal Rainy told its General Assembly (26 May) that the Government Bill would follow Commission lines.
The same day the Church of Scotland Assembly, on Lord Balfour’s motion, unanimously sought parliamentary liberty to ease the 1693 subscription formula—leading to clause 5 of the Ministerial Churches Bill, opposed by some English Low Churchmen and Nonconformists as a precedent for Anglican emancipation, and by Campbell-Bannerman and others as out of place, but carried with much Scottish Liberal support. The Act set up a strong executive Commission; the Free Church required unconditional subscription to the Confession’s literal meaning, the United Free a relation determined by its judicatories. Bye-elections, especially the Ministerial defeat in Buteshire, and Liberal triumphs in Edinburgh and Glasgow University elections, showed Scottish aversion to Protection and Unionist unpopularity. Campbell-Bannerman’s Premiership excited the liveliest Scottish interest; Imperialist Liberals felt represented by Haldane and Asquith for Scottish seats as well as by Grey and Fowler. The King reviewed over 38,000 Volunteers in the King’s Park, Edinburgh, on 18 September (estimated 250,000 spectators), including 700 Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve and a motor-car column, and hoped the spectacle would encourage recruitment. Clyde shipbuilding reached a record 540,080 tons; iron, steel, cotton and woollen trades prospered; jute and linen were hampered by raw-material prices.
Ireland. The year’s most striking political fact was the driving from the Chief Secretaryship—within two years of his acclaimed Land Purchase Act—of George Wyndham, a politician of high ability and partly distinguished Irish lineage, by the more vociferous Unionists angered at his confidence in Sir Antony MacDonnell and at MacDonnell’s part in the Dunraven–Dudley Devolution conversations of September 1904. Yet MacDonnell remained Under-Secretary and Dudley Viceroy: no further “human sacrifices” could be obtained without risk of breaking the Unionist Government. The new Chief Secretary, Walter Long, after pressure, affirmed the Under-Secretary’s definite subordination and a firm intention to enforce the law against agrarian intimidation; at Belfast (20 April) he pledged redress of legitimate grievances and “ascendency to no party, but to everybody justice and fair play.” In the summer and autumn the Executive forbade and suppressed meetings summoned to overawe graziers (aimed at breaking up grass lands for small farmers), tried intimidators before special juries under the Crimes Act, and restored Unionist confidence in the South and West. Land Purchase Act regulations of 9 July required Estates Commissioners to inquire into intimidation and postpone tainted applications—right as a penalty, doubtful as a presumption. Operation of the Act as a whole was blocked because agreed transfers already involved purchase money far exceeding available funds.
Supplementary Chapter — Finance and Trade in 1905
By F. Harcourt Kitchin
Few years had been so satisfactory as 1905. A world-wide revival followed the post-war dulness: abundant American cotton of 1904 and bountiful harvests in Canada, the United States and Argentina carried prosperity to Europe. Britain, France, Germany, Austria and Italy had much to congratulate themselves upon; Canada and the United States enjoyed their finest industrial years. Russia remained a black spot from war drain and internal disturbance; Japan must suffer years of financial strain but was coming to be regarded as a “four per cent.” country.
British revival began in foreign trade. Total imports were valued at £565,279,402 (increase £14,240,774, or 2.5 per cent.). Exports of British and Irish produce advanced by £29,312,427 (about 9.7 per cent.) to £330,023,467—passing all records—and re-exports of colonial and foreign merchandise rose by £7,494,240 to £77,798,521. Manufactured exports increased by £26,133,863 (10.7 per cent.), cotton yarn and cloth to India and China far surpassing records; woollens and iron and steel also rose substantially. Imports of manufactures rose only £7,409,339 (of which £1,769,847 re-exported). By the partial test of manufactured export expansion versus import increase, 1905 was one of Britain’s best foreign-trade years.
Internal demand for credit was strong, especially later in the year. The Bank rate did not exceed 3 per cent. for the first nine months, rose to 4 in September on a foreign gold drain, and averaged only 3 per cent. for the year. Rand mines yielded £20,800,000 gold against £16,000,000 in 1904. London Bankers’ Clearing House clearings expanded 16.3 per cent., country clearings 5.2 per cent. Consols closed at 89⅛ against 88⅛ at the start. Japanese Four per cents. rose from 76 to 92½ while Russian Fours fell from 91½ to 82½. Japan borrowed abroad during the war £82,000,000 (£22,000,000 at 6 per cent., the rest at 4), floated a £50,000,000 foreign conversion loan at 4 per cent. (half issued, half retained to convert Sixes in 1907), and raised £48,000,000 internally; completed conversion left war debt about £138,000,000 (foreign £110,000,000, domestic £28,000,000) with annual interest £6,100,000 against normal peacetime revenue of some £23,500,000—yet monetary centres retained confidence.
Lancashire cotton had by far its most prosperous year: American crop over 13,500,000 bales (some 2,000,000 above world requirements); yarn exports up 25 per cent., cloth 11 per cent.; ninety spinning companies averaged 19 per cent. profit on share capital; sixty-six new mills were equipped at about £7,000,000—prosperity that stiffened Lancashire’s opposition to Chamberlain’s fiscal proposals. Woollen and worsted recovered more modestly; exports of yarns and fabrics rose nearly £2,500,000, nearly half from Japanese and Chinese military demand. Shipbuilding set a British record of 1,811,000 tons launched against 1,376,000 in 1904, though rising iron prices later checked new mercantile orders (new steamers ordered in September cost fully 20 per cent. more than a year before). Engineering, machinery (exports up nearly £2,250,000), waggon, motor and cycle trades (output estimated over £10,000,000, nearly all home) were better occupied; coal remained dull and cheap, aiding the revival. British works, Kitchin judged, had been overhauled and made more adaptable to modern requirements.
Part II — Foreign and Colonial History
Chapter I — France and Italy
France. The capital domestic event of 1905 was the Chambers’ vote for the separation of Church and State—long a Radical article always postponed until the Pope’s Nuncio’s absence from the New Year diplomatic reception at the Élysée signalled an impending religious crisis. A campaign against freemasonic delation in the army, channelled through General Février and the Legion of Honour, filled Conservative papers with confidential reports on officers’ politics. The session opened 10 January; M. Fallières was re-elected President of the Senate without opposition, while M. Doumer defeated M. Henri Brisson for the Chamber presidency 265–240 and used the chair against a Ministry he called a scandal. After a two-day confidence debate won only 287–281 (a virtual defeat once ministerial votes and Doumer’s abstention were counted), M. Combes resigned on 18 January. M. Rouvier formed a Government (commission 21 January; list 24 January): Rouvier as Premier and Finance; Berteaux remaining at War; Delcassé at Foreign Affairs; Chaumié to Justice; Etienne (Interior) and Thomson (Marine) among new men. The programme included the military law, repeal of the Falloux Law, Income Tax, Separation of Church and State, and an old-age pension fund.
The Military Law, carried in the Senate 239–37 (17 January–15 February) and later by the Chamber without modification, shortened active service to two years while retaining reservist and territorial training periods and requiring Polytechnique and Saint-Cyr students a year in the ranks. The Separation Bill’s general discussion occupied nine sittings ending 10 April; thirty-six further sittings to 3 July settled thirty-seven clauses regulating French religious life—Aristide Briand, as Reporter, making his name by tolerance and concessions to ministers of religion. The 1905 Budget totalled some 3,603,000,000 francs with a nominal estimated surplus of only 21,000 francs, later improved by harvests and colonial trade; Parliament actually increased expenditure by nearly 20,000,000 francs. Labour violence marked the year: at Limoges (April) a porcelain lock-out of nearly 20,000 followed a strike against Haviland; troops fired, killing two workmen (17 April); the strike ended 22 April. Toulon arsenal disturbances on May Day and a Lyons police strike (ended by Prefect Alapetite’s energetic requisition of troops) further strained order.
Colonial embarrassments—Congo scandals leading to Savorgnan de Brazza’s inquiry, the recall of General Gallieni from Madagascar, Indo-Chinese disorders—coincided with the Moroccan crisis. A German press campaign against the French mission under M. St. René Taillandier led up to William II’s theatrical visit to Tangier. Delcassé, feebly supported, offered resignation about 19 April after Nationalist and Socialist attack; it was not accepted, but he was soon forced from office under German pressure—an event deeply regretted in Britain and central to the English chapters’ account of the summer’s diplomacy. French public opinion, reviewing the International Commission on the Dogger Bank firing by Admiral Rozhdestvensky, held that England’s forbearance and France’s conciliatory rôle testified to the reality of the 1904 Franco-English agreement even as Morocco tested its most important colonial clause.
Italy. (The extract’s Italian section is not preserved in the working file; the Register pairs Italy with France in Chapter I of Part II.)
Chapter II — Germany, Morocco, and the Anglo-Japanese Settlement
German policy in 1905, as seen from the English narrative, was dominated by the challenge to France in Morocco and by friction with Britain. The Emperor’s Tangier demonstration, the forced retreat of Delcassé, and the Sultan’s conference proposal were read in London as a deliberate test of the Anglo-French Agreement. British refusal of the conference invitation (mid-June), later qualified so as not to embarrass a French acceptance on agreed bases, and Britain’s subsequent agreement to attend once France assented (announced 12 July), kept faith with Paris without closing the diplomatic door. Baltic Fleet courtesies in August and municipal hospitality at German ports showed that official Germany did not sustain the full bitterness of a section of its press. Lord Lansdowne’s statements on German Pacific islands and the German tariff, and the continued intimacy of the Entente, formed the British side of a relationship the Register describes as one of irritation without rupture.
The renewal and extension of the Anglo-Japanese Alliance—understood in Britain before its formal publicity—framed the Far Eastern settlement. Port Arthur’s fall in January, Japan’s military and naval triumphs, and the peace of late August were received in England with allied pride tempered by respect for Russian defenders. The alliance was held to have encouraged Japanese moderation on indemnity and to open trade prospects in the Far East that Liberals as well as Unionists meant to uphold.
Chapter III — Russia and the Far Eastern Peace
Russia’s year, in the British record, ran from the humiliation of Port Arthur and the Dogger Bank inquiry through catastrophic defeat to a peace that reversed her financial credit relative to Japan’s. The International Commission in Paris on Rozhdestvensky’s firing upon the Hull fishing fleet, aided by French diplomacy, averted worse consequences; England’s forbearance was noted on both sides of the Channel. Internal disturbance and war drain made Russia the “black spot” of the commercial year; Russian Fours fell heavily while Japanese credit rose. The peace terms, without a large indemnity, nonetheless embodied Japan’s completeness of success and were welcomed in Britain as securing the ally against a recurrence of the struggle.
Chapter IV — Colonies and Dependencies (from the English narrative)
South African questions remained politically explosive at Westminster: Chinese labour, the Transvaal Loan, steps toward representative institutions in the Transvaal (the Orange River Colony deferred), and above all the Butler Committee’s exposure of post-war stores sales and contractor refunds, which forced a statutory Royal Commission. Lord Milner’s retirement and Lord Selborne’s appointment marked a change of imperial proconsul. In India the Curzon–Kitchener controversy over military administration ended in the Viceroy’s resignation after the Home Government refused his nominee for Military Supply Member and seemed to him to reopen the substance of Kitchener’s original scheme. Tibet and Afghanistan appeared in the King’s Speech as diplomatic successes or negotiations in progress. Scottish and Irish chapters apart, the colonial note of the English history is one of administrative scandal, constitutional half-steps in South Africa, and a Viceroyalty broken on Army reform.

The Annual Register 1906
Part I — English History
Chapter I — The General Election
The new year found the country immersed in preparations for a general election which the Annual Register judged the most exciting and startling since 1880, if not since 1832. The positions of the two great parties had been completely reversed. The late Ministers were arraigned on charges of reckless extravagance, misjudgment of South African affairs, the introduction into the Transvaal of “Chinese slavery,” the endowment of denominational education, and the propounding of crude and self-contradictory fiscal reforms.
The Liberals, formerly the party of criticism and obstruction, now posed as reformers and claimed to be the real Free Traders and apostles of economic progress.
Among the issues before the electors, the fiscal question was probably the most important, especially in rural constituencies. Next came Chinese labour; then the modification of the Education Act of 1902. Home Rule, though somewhat unexpectedly revived by Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman, was held by the Duke of Devonshire and others to be an improbable subject for early legislation by the new Government.
The Free Food Unionists occupied a peculiarly delicate position. The Duke of Devonshire, in a letter of 29 December 1905 to the honorary secretary of the Unionist Free Trade Club, declared that the proposals of the Tariff Reform League were “indistinguishable from pure Protection,” that a Unionist majority would almost certainly mean the adoption of that programme, and that Free Trade Unionists should therefore support Free Trade candidates irrespective of party. Some Free Fooders followed this counsel; others clung to party loyalty while repudiating Chamberlainite Protection.
Mr. Chamberlain’s election address attacked the new Ministry as essentially a Home Rule and Little Englander Government which must exist, if at all, by Irish votes, and insisted that the Colonies were awaiting a preferential response from the mother country. Mr. Balfour, in his address to the electors of Manchester, denounced the Liberal programme as surrounded with obscurity and warned that Home Rule, Disestablishment, and the destruction of voluntary schools had lost none of their ancient charm for Radical lawmakers.
Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman’s address contained no specific programme and no mention of Home Rule. He attacked the late Government’s wars and adventures abroad, its reckless finance, and its confused Army reorganisation, and declared that Protection was immoral, oppressive, and corrupting.
Sectional bodies crowded the field with manifestoes. The Cobden Club, the United Irish League, the Social Democratic Federation, and the Free Church Council all issued appeals; the last-named sent ministers about the country by motor car to deliver Liberal speeches, while special prayers were offered in the churches.
Full-page newspaper advertisements defended Chinese labour; cartoons, especially those against Chinese labour, aroused lively indignation among Unionists. At Derby on 3 January Mr. Chamberlain declared that under Free Trade there were a million able-bodied male paupers in the United Kingdom—a statement which Liberals and Free Trade economists immediately and successfully challenged as a misuse of the poor-law figures.
At the Albert Hall on 5 January the Prime Minister, while affirming that the Liberals remained a Home Rule party, announced that they would not introduce a Home Rule Bill in the coming Parliament but would proceed step by step toward the larger settlement.
A Blue-book on Chinese labour, issued 21 December 1905, became a principal campaign document on the Liberal side. Polling began on 12 January. The chapter records a Unionist rout of extraordinary completeness as the returns came in from London, the industrial North, Scotland, and Wales.
The residual strength of Tariff Reform within the diminished Opposition was carefully analysed; Wales returned no Unionists; Scotland became predominantly Liberal; and the prediction that the Government would be dependent on Nationalist votes was falsified by the scale of the Liberal and Labour majority over all other groups combined.
Chapter II — The New Parliament and Early Session
The new Parliament assembled on 13 February. Mr. J. W. Lowther was re-elected Speaker on the motion of Sir Edward Grey, seconded by Mr. Keir Hardie, who thus marked the arrival of Labour as a distinct parliamentary force rather than a mere wing of Liberalism. The King’s Speech promised legislation on Trade Disputes, Workmen’s Compensation, Merchant Shipping, Education, and the reform of Irish government; careful consideration of the social and economic conditions of the rural districts of Great Britain; and a Colonial conference on the question of preference.
The Address debate ranged widely over Chinese labour, the fiscal question, Army organisation, India, Education, women’s suffrage, the Macdonnell controversy, and Home Rule.
Chinese labour was the first great test of the new majority. Lord Elgin’s telegram of 20 January had directed that no further Chinese labourers should be imported into the Transvaal pending the establishment of representative government there. The Prime Minister on 22 February defended this course, and the subsequent debate of 26 February produced a Ministerial majority of 416 to 91.
On fiscal policy Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman reaffirmed Free Trade as the settled doctrine of the Government; Mr. Chamberlain continued to press imperial preference as the true imperial bond; Mr. Asquith, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, warned that a 2s. corn duty would mean a rise of about 2½d. on the four-pound loaf and brushed aside the subtler forms of retaliation as unworkable.
Mr. Haldane, at the War Office, sketched a policy of two-year service with the colours and of carrying out the recommendations of the Esher Committee for the reorganisation of the military departments. Mr. Morley, as Indian Secretary, dealt with the partition of Bengal and with the difficult question of military administration under the new arrangements that had followed the Curzon-Kitchener dispute.
Mr. Birrell, President of the Board of Education, outlined an Education Bill that would place all schools maintained from the rates under the local education authorities, impose the Cowper-Temple restriction on religious teaching in provided schools, and grant “facilities” for denominational instruction under strict conditions—including a four-fifths parental majority where special facilities were claimed for a particular denomination.
Women’s suffrage made its first dramatic appearance in the new House when Mr. Keir Hardie moved an amendment to the Address in favour of the enfranchisement of women; it was rejected by 114 votes, only 46 members voting for it. In Ireland the Crimes Act of 1887 was suspended in the few districts where it still operated; Sir Antony Macdonnell was continued as permanent Under-Secretary for Ireland; and the Government’s Irish policy was described as Home Rule by instalments rather than by a single large measure of the Gladstonian type.
The Navy Estimates stood at 31,869,500l., a reduction of about 1,500,000l. upon the previous year, while the two-Power standard was reaffirmed as the measure of national security. The Army Estimates of 29,796,000l. showed a reduction of nearly 3,000,000l. Mr. Redmond and the Nationalists pressed for an Irish Council and for the speedy restoration of the evicted tenants as the session settled into its legislative work.
Chapter III — The Education Bill and the Budget
The Education Bill became the central measure of the session and the principal battleground between Nonconformists, Anglicans, Roman Catholics, and Jews, as well as between the two Houses of Parliament. Passive resisters continued their campaign against the rates levied under the Act of 1902 even as the new Bill sought to recast the whole settlement of elementary education.
Clause by clause the four-fifths rule, the powers of the local education authorities, Cowper-Temple teaching in provided schools, and the special facilities for denominational instruction in schools transferred to the public authority were fought over in the country and in the House. Anglican bishops and Catholic prelates organised resistance; Free Church councils rallied Nonconformist opinion behind Mr. Birrell; and the Jewish community sought safeguards for its own schools.
Women’s suffrage agitation accompanied the parliamentary struggle outside the chamber. Disturbances at the House of Commons on 25 April and further scenes on 19 May, when the Prime Minister and Mr. Asquith were interrupted by women demanding the vote, advertised the determination of the militant section of the movement and foreshadowed more serious collisions later in the year.
Mr. Asquith introduced the Budget on 30 April. He announced a realised surplus of nearly 3,500,000l.; reduced the tea duty from 6d. to 5d. the pound; repealed the coal export duty which had been a standing grievance of the export trade; left the income tax at 1s. in the pound but introduced a notable relief for earned incomes as distinct from income from property; and raised the fixed debt charge (the new sinking fund) from 9,500,000l. to 13,500,000l., thereby accelerating the reduction of the National Debt swollen by the South African War.
The Labourers (Ireland) Bill and other social measures advanced alongside the Education struggle. The chapter closes with the Education Bill still in the thick of debate, its friends already warning that the Lords would mutilate it beyond recognition and its enemies organising resistance in the constituencies, in Convocation, and among the managers of voluntary schools.
Chapter IV — Committee Struggles, Plural Voting, and the Transvaal Constitution
Through the summer the Education Bill occupied the committee stage day after day. Clauses 1, 4, and 7—the local-authority clause, the facilities clause, and the four-fifths clause—were remodelled under Mr. Birrell’s management. Denominationalists complained that the concessions were illusory and that the Bill destroyed the religious character of the voluntary schools; Nonconformists complained that too much had been given away to the Church and to Rome. Amendments from every quarter thickened the Bill without reconciling its opponents.
On 25 June Mr. Lewis Harcourt introduced the Plural Voting Bill, designed to abolish the plural franchise at parliamentary elections so that no elector should vote in more than one constituency. It obtained a second reading on 2 July by 323 to 96, the Opposition denouncing it as a partisan attack upon property and upon the university seats.
Workmen’s Compensation legislation also advanced as part of the Ministry’s labour programme, extending the range of industries and the classes of workmen covered by the principle of compensation for accidents.
The most important imperial announcement of the year came on 31 July, when Mr. Winston Churchill in the Commons and the Earl of Elgin in the Lords explained the main provisions of the new Transvaal Constitution. The Lyttelton Constitution, devised by the late Government, was declared “stillborn” and unworkable.
Responsible government was to be granted at once; Boer and Briton alike would receive the full privileges and rights of British citizenship; the legislature would be a single chamber of sixty-nine members elected by adult male suffrage, with a nominated Legislative Council subject to a property qualification of 25,000l. capital or 250l. a year; and no new licences for Chinese labourers would be issued after 30 November. The Opposition denounced the measure as a surrender to the recently defeated Boers, who, they warned, would use the vote as a substitute for arms and would dominate the new Colony.
The Prime Minister, rising near the close of the debate, declared that he had never heard a more unworthy speech—his words drowned by Opposition protests—and the resolution approving the Constitution was carried by 316 to 83.
In the Lords the Plural Voting Bill received a second reading on 3 August by 105 to 38, only to be rejected later on principle when the real issue was joined. The Education Bill itself was read a second time in the Upper House on 1–2 August without a division, the peers reserving their strength for the committee stage after the recess. The session then adjourned for the summer, leaving the great constructive Bills incomplete and the constitutional tension between a Liberal Commons and a Unionist Lords already clearly visible.
Chapter V — Recess, Dreadnought, Autumn Session, and the Lords
Bank Holiday speeches and the East Denbighshire bye-election kept party feeling alive after the adjournment. Mr. Churchill predicted a satisfactory Licensing Bill for 1907; Earl Carrington, at an agricultural show at Broughton Castle near Banbury, commended the Land Tenure Bill as a measure of justice to the farming class.
Viscount Milner, replying to an address of appreciation of his services in South Africa—presented privately at his own desire and signed by more than 370,000 adult males, with separate addresses from Natal (some 3,000 signatures) and from Cape Colony (20,000)—warned that the danger in South Africa was disunion and at home the growth of a spirit of anti-nationalism. The East Denbighshire poll on 14 August showed an increased Liberal majority; a Labour candidate announced by Mr. Keir Hardie did not appear.
On 8 August the Court of Appeal, in The King, on the prosecution of the Board of Education, v. The County Council of the West Riding of Yorkshire, decided that under the Act of 1902 a local authority might deduct from teachers’ salaries the proportion estimated to be due for denominational teaching.
The judgment seemed both to defeat the intentions of Parliament in 1902 and to destroy the passive resisters’ grievance. Some magistrates continued to issue distress warrants; others adjourned summonses sine die. The Government took the case to the House of Lords, which reversed the judgment on 14 December.
The Report of the War Stores Commission, appointed in 1905 after Sir William Butler’s committee, was issued as a Blue Book on 10 August. It found a deplorable lack of cohesion and intercommunication between the departments at the War Office; inexcusable carelessness and extraordinary ineptitude in the business of the Director of Supplies in South Africa; and a loss of public money estimated at between 750,000l. and 1,250,000l.
Higher officers were for the most part charged with stupidity and lack of business capacity rather than corruption, though petty corruption among non-commissioned officers was noted. Disciplinary action followed on 16 October: twelve officers were dealt with by methods varying from censure to removal from the army, and nine officers and non-commissioned officers were discharged for misconduct. Mr. Haldane announced that the nucleus of an administrative staff would be trained at the London School of Economics.
Against this administrative blot the construction of H.M.S. Dreadnought stood as a national achievement of the first order. Her keel plate had been laid on 2 October 1905; she was launched in the presence of the King on 10 February 1906; and on 4 August the King and the Prince of Wales inspected her.
She was designed to carry ten 12-inch guns so mounted as to facilitate all-round fire, twenty-seven 12-pounder quick-firers for defence against torpedo craft, and five submerged torpedo tubes; her main armour belt reached eleven inches; her coal capacity would enable her to steam 5,800 sea miles at moderate speed or 3,500 at 18 knots, extendable by oil fuel; her speed was to be 21 knots. She was the first large warship fitted with turbine engines, and the admiral and all officers were berthed forward of the engines instead of astern.
She left Portsmouth for steam trials on 1 October 1906, precisely 364 days after the first keel plate, and both steam and gun trials were in every way satisfactory—proof, the Register observed, that Great Britain could keep well ahead of other nations.
Army reorganisation advanced by the Army Order published 13 September constituting, for the first time, a General Staff for the British Army in accordance with the recommendation of the Esher Committee. It was to be composed of (a) the general staff at headquarters—fifty-seven officers, including three major-generals—and (b) the general staff in commands and districts—114 officers, mostly of the rank of colonel or below.
Members would as a rule have passed through the Staff College and have had eight years’ service; appointments would be for four years. Mr. Haldane insisted that such a staff was necessary not only in war but to make the Army progressive in peace, and he hoped it would become a real bond of union with the forces of the self-governing Colonies.
The Spectator, at the instance of its conductors, embodied an experimental company of working-class lads of average age nineteen for six months’ thorough training; the results were held to show that a good infantry soldier could be made within that time. Considerable sections of the Liberal party, however, remained bitterly hostile to all popularisation of military training, and especially to drill and rifle practice in schools.
Friction between Liberalism and Labour appeared in the Cockermouth contest, in South Wales attempts to coerce non-unionists into the Miners’ Federation, in Clyde boilermakers’ strikes, and in a resolution of the Scottish Liberal Association at Peebles on 5 October, carried by 55 to 34, urging Liberal opposition to all candidates who would not dissociate themselves from Socialism. Unionists, for their part, revived suspicions that their leaders had somewhat relaxed their Unionism in connection with Sir Antony Macdonnell’s appointment and the devolution schemes of 1904–5.
When the autumn session opened, “strangers” in the House, the Plural Voting Bill, the Evicted Tenants question, and above all the Education Bill in the Lords dominated business. Municipal elections, speeches by Mr. Balfour, Mr. Asquith, and Mr. Austen Chamberlain, the Trade Disputes Bill, the Land Tenure Bill, the Town Tenants (Ireland) Bill—with a proposal to expropriate Lord Clanricarde—the Merchant Shipping Bill, land settlement and Chinese vice in the South African compounds, deputations on old-age pensions and the Congo Free State, and naval affairs filled the calendar.
The Lords reconstituted the Education Bill almost beyond recognition on report; rival deputations thronged Westminster; the Plural Voting Bill, having passed the Commons, was rejected by the Lords; the Trade Disputes Bill and the Town Tenants and Land Tenure Bills ran their course under pressure of time; a Licensing Act Amendment Bill, a Workmen’s Compensation Bill, and an Education (Provision of Meals) Bill advanced; and the traditional “Massacre of the Innocents” cleared the Order Paper of measures that could not be saved.
Efforts at compromise on the Education Bill between the two Houses failed. The constitution of the Orange River Colony was announced on lines akin to those of the Transvaal; the writ for Worcester was suspended; a Wireless Telegraphy Convention was debated; other legislation was hurried through; and the King’s Speech closed the session.
The political outlook was one of open conflict between a massive Liberal majority in the Commons and a Unionist majority in the Lords, with the mutilated Education Bill as the symbol of the struggle and the party machines already preparing for the next phase of the constitutional quarrel.
Chapter VI — Scotland and Ireland
Scotland. Apart from its share in the politics of the United Kingdom, Scotland had a quiet year marked by great commercial and industrial prosperity. At the general election only Stirling Burghs escaped a contest—and that through the sudden illness of the Unionist candidate—and of the seventy-two members returned only twelve were Unionists: two of them for University seats, four owing their return to Liberal-Labour rivalry, and two Free Traders.
Scottish opinion thus showed itself decidedly adverse to fiscal reform. Eleven Labour candidatures against Liberals helped to exacerbate the autumn dispute between the two progressive forces. The Scottish Home Rule Association took occasion to urge the need of devolution for Scotland as well as Ireland.
Of legislation specially affecting Scotland, the Fatal Accidents and Sudden Deaths Inquiry Bill and the Statute Law Revision (Scotland) Bill were useful measures of reform; the National Galleries (Scotland) Bill substituted for the old Board of Manufactures a new board of seven trustees nominated by the Secretary for Scotland. A Royal Commission on the expediency of instituting Registration of Title in Scotland was announced on 1 May.
Slight additional encouragement was given to the teaching of Gaelic in primary schools, in order to provide a supply of teachers for some 25,000 Gaelic-speaking children—a measure which provoked some criticism as a waste of time and a possible fosterer of separatism, but which commanded a strong preponderance of Scottish opinion. Acute indignation was aroused in November by the proposal to remove the Scots Greys from Edinburgh and Glasgow and so to deprive Scotland of a cavalry regiment altogether.
Mr. Haldane explained on 21 November that Piershill Barracks had become insanitary for cavalry, that the cost of new barracks would be very heavy, and that the removal might not be permanent; but Lord Rosebery, at a protest meeting in Edinburgh on 3 November, scoffed at the arguments from sanitation and economy and declared that if such treatment were continued the Scottish nation would be compelled to examine more closely the benefits it received from the Treaty of Union.
In ecclesiastical matters the Free Churches Commission proceeded with much inevitable delay in apportioning the property of the former Free Church between the United Free Church and the “Wee Frees.” A report of 19 October stated that about a thousand congregations had then had their cases decided.
The General Assemblies of the three Churches opened in Edinburgh on 22 May, Lord Colebrooke being Lord High Commissioner for the Church of Scotland. The fourth centenary of the University of Aberdeen was celebrated on 25–27 September with great éclat; the King and Queen visited the city on the last day to open the new buildings of Marischal College—laboratories, lecture rooms, the Mitchell Tower and Hall—erected by public subscription at a cost of upwards of 200,000l.; some 120 honorary degrees were conferred upon delegates from universities as far afield as Japan and Ecuador.
In commerce and industry the year was one of great prosperity. The shipbuilding output of the Clyde reached the highest figure on record, the highest estimate being 601,658 tons for the year, with about 500,000 tons remaining for 1907; engineering output measured by indicated horse-power (608,620 i.h.p.) was also the largest recorded.
Among vessels launched were the Cunarder Lusitania; H.M.S. Agamemnon, the most formidable warship ever built on the Clyde; the Canadian Pacific liner Empress of Ireland; and the Pacific Steam Navigation liner Oriana. Of 374 vessels launched, 151 went to foreign and 30 to colonial owners.
A seven weeks’ strike of the “black squad”—boilermakers, riveters, and other ironworkers—in October and November threw nearly 17,000 men out of work before the threat of a general lock-out terminated the strike on 21 November. The jute trade was prosperous; mineral oil benefited from interference with the Caucasian industry by the Russian revolutionists; aluminium, motor-car manufacture, and electrical engineering gave favourable reports; the herring season on the north-east coast was excellent; and the average price obtained for 1,951 shorthorn cattle slightly exceeded 64l. a head—an increase of 250 per cent. on that of about twenty years previously.
Ireland. Politically the year was one of comparative quiet, though Irish affairs still exercised an appreciable influence on English politics. At the general election more than three-fourths of the Irish seats were uncontested, and the balance of parties was hardly changed. The Nationalists lost South Dublin to the Unionists and won West Belfast from them; Liberals were returned in two Ulster constituencies; and of the eighty-two Nationalist members four, including Mr. W. O’Brien and Mr. Timothy Healy, stood independent of the regular Irish Parliamentary party. The Nationalist leaders, while declaring they would be satisfied with nothing less than full Home Rule, avowed their intention of giving the Ministry time to mature its plans for Irish legislation.
The Earl of Aberdeen made his State entry as Viceroy into Dublin on 3 February. Three days later the operation of the Crimes Act, 1887, was suspended in the few districts in which it was still in force; on 13 February new regulations were issued for the inspection of estates under the Land Purchase Act; and on 6 March Mr. Long’s instructions to the Land Commissioners were cancelled and they were directed to frame their own rules. Delay in the restoration of the evicted tenants to their holdings was bitterly complained of by the Nationalists both in Parliament and in Ireland. The Sale of Intoxicants Bill provided for the Sunday closing of licensed premises in Dublin, Belfast, Cork, Limerick, and Waterford—hitherto exempted—and for universal closing at 9 P.M. on Saturdays; it divided the Nationalist party but eventually became law.
The Labourers (Ireland) Bill and the Town Tenants Bill became items in the conflict between the two Houses; the latter was partly occasioned by the eviction at Loughrea of one of the Marquess of Clanricarde’s tenants. Mr. Bryce on 28 May sketched a scheme for encouraging the teaching of Irish in primary schools.
Royal Commissions on Irish Railways, on the working of the Congested Districts Board, on Canals and Waterways, and on Trinity College, Dublin, were appointed and took evidence during the year.
The Irish Land Purchase Acts continued to work satisfactorily. An issue of 7,000,000l. guaranteed land stock at 89 was made in June and was over-subscribed to about nine times the nominal value of the loan. Some agrarian disturbances and outrages were reported from the south and west, partly in connection with attacks on large grass farms and partly due to attempts to force landlords to sell under the Acts.
A few regrettable exhibitions of disloyalty were reported, notably the action of Alderman Kelly of Dublin in cutting down the Union Jack from the steamer conveying the Corporation down the Liffey at the opening of the new drainage works on 24 September; the Corporation declined to take notice of his act. The Gaelic League continued its efforts for the encouragement of the Irish language and the revival of Irish customs.
Supplementary Chapter — Finance and Trade in 1906
F. Harcourt Kitchin recorded that 1906 was one of the best general trade years the world had known. The industrial expansion which began toward the end of 1904 had been assisted by bountiful harvests almost everywhere, and the United Kingdom, the Continent of Europe, and North and South America had shared in a series of trade records—the Americas even more than Europe.
The only grey spots were Russia, still troubled politically but showing an extraordinary power of recuperation; South Africa, suffering from the effects of the late war and a surfeit of party politics; and China, where unsold stocks at Hong-Kong and Shanghai had seriously accumulated. Japan, on the other hand, was picking up after the war drain and threatened to become a more serious competitor in Far Eastern markets than ever before.
Reports from India, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand were most cheerful—almost too much so, since there were doubts whether the boom in Canadian land and railways could last.
Money in the technical sense understood in the Money Markets was scarce nearly all through the year. The autumn saw the Bank of England rate of discount go up to 6 per cent. and stay there for some months; at no time was the market rate of discount in London below 3 per cent. The demand was due principally to the requirements of industry and railway development, but partly also to the waste of wealth by earthquake and fire.
The great disaster at San Francisco in April caused destruction of property exceeding 50,000,000l. in value; with a similar catastrophe at Valparaiso, though on a smaller scale, it threw a heavy strain on the world’s supplies of available capital. British insurance offices were badly hit at San Francisco and ultimately paid about ten and a half millions sterling, but as some little set-off the disaster caused such a demand for cement, steel, and other building materials as to benefit, directly and indirectly, many British industries.
As the prices of high-class securities are much influenced by the current value of money, the year was not a good one for large holders of good securities. Consols fell as much as 3 points to 86; Great Western Railway Ordinary declined by 12 to 133½; London and North Western Ordinary by 8 to 153; Metropolitan Railway Ordinary had a ghastly fall of 27 to 60.
On the other hand, Canadian, Mexican, and many South American securities showed great strength on account of the rapid development proceeding in those countries. The only loan operation worthy of permanent record was the issue of Russian Five per Cents. Of a total of 90,000,000l., the 13,000,000l. offered in London were readily taken up on terms giving subscribers nearly 5 per cent.; the new scrip shortly afterwards, in consequence of internal disturbances in Russia, fell as low as 12 discount, but recovered steadily later when it was seen that the long-prophesied revolution had failed to come off.
There had never been a year during which a greater amount of over-sea trade was carried on. The aggregate imports and exports of the United Kingdom for the first time exceeded 1,000,000,000l. While imports increased by nearly 43,000,000l., or 7.6 per cent., to 608,000,000l., the exports of British and Irish produce increased by no less than 45,800,000l., or 13.9 per cent., to 375,600,000l.
Re-exports of colonial and foreign produce were also 7,300,000l. (9.5 per cent.) higher, at 85,000,000l. The greater part of the increase in imports consisted of raw materials, and the greater part of the increase in exports of manufactured goods, so that the foreign trade of the year was in an unusually healthy state.
One of the most notable features was the advance in metals: raw copper and tin by about 30 per cent., lead by 25 per cent., antimony by nearly 100 per cent.—advances almost wholly due to industrial demand, which revived the Cornish and Devon mining industries. Over 2,000,000 tons of new shipping were put into the water from the shipbuilding yards of the United Kingdom, a record figure; yet the expansion—due principally to excited orders placed soon after the close of the Russo-Japanese War—added to the glut of British shipping seeking employment, and shipping generally had a hard and rather unprofitable time.
Lancashire cotton equalled the prosperous figures of the previous year; some of the heavy engineering trades, as well as motors and cycles, had a wonderful year; the electrical industry was badly hurt by high commodity prices and foreign competition. Broadly speaking, American and German absorption in their own internal demands had for the time almost suspended “dumping,” leaving British manufacturers more of the home market than for years past—an observation Kitchin offered impartially as between the advantages of open ports and of an exclusive home market.
Part II — Foreign and Colonial History
Chapter I — France and Italy
France. Republican France faced, after the passing of the law separating Church and State, the problem which Catherine de Médicis had put to Henry III after the murder of Guise: the thing was well cut, but could it be sewn up? The question affected the elections to the Chambers, the succession to the Presidency, and the completion of the process of separation. The Senate elections of 7 January, concerning Series B and vacant seats, returned 103 senators.
For the first time Socialists succeeded in electing two members—M. Flaissières, ex-Mayor of Marseilles, and M. Delhon, a vinegrower of the Hérault—and for the first time the balance of Right and Left was not appreciably modified, an indication that equilibrium had been reached and that France had accepted separation.
On 17 January the National Assembly met at Versailles to elect a successor to M. Loubet. The Radical and Radical-Socialist groups, and even the Socialists, supported a moderate Republican senator, M. Fallières; the Right supported a Radical deputy, M. Doumer. M. Fallières was elected at the first ballot by 449 votes to 371.
He could not enter on his duties till 18 February, and political life resumed its normal course amid the approach of the electoral campaign—until an unexpected explosion of religious passions broke the monotony. A clause in the Separation Law provided that in every church an inventory should be taken of artistic treasures and church furniture.
Catholics offered forcible resistance, beginning on 31 January in Paris and spreading within days to La Vendée, Brittany, the mountains of Auvergne, and Flanders. Parish clergy protested; the laity prevented entrance to the churches; in the Grande Chartreuse peasants rolled down masses of rock upon the soldiers; in the Loire, La Vendée, and the Loire-Inférieure there was bloodshed.
On the very day of M. Loubet’s retirement (18 February) the Press published an Encyclical embodying an energetic papal protest against the severance of the Concordat. The Vatican designated occupants for vacant French bishoprics without State control, and left French Catholics uncertain as to the lawfulness of forming Public Worship Associations to take over church property.
The Gallican spirit had so completely died out that not a single bishop took the initiative in compliance with the law. On 7 March, after a disturbance at Boescheppe in the Nord in which a demonstrator was killed, a vote of confidence proposed by M. Péret and accepted by the Government was rejected by 267 to 234 through a coalition of Socialists, Radical Socialists, and the Right.
M. Rouvier fell at a moment when the Algeciras Conference was at its most difficult stage, the Budget was still under discussion, and public peace was disturbed both by the inventories and by strikes.
An explosion of fire-damp in the mines of Courrières, near Lens, on 10 March resulted in the loss of more than 1,100 lives. The survivors charged the company with having neglected safety works through avarice; a strike was proclaimed and rapidly spread through the district; anarchist elements were attracted from Paris and from abroad.
M. Sarrien was charged to form a Ministry and by 13 March had succeeded, though by a childish concession to superstition the decrees were post-dated 14 March. M. Sarrien became Prime Minister and Minister of Justice; M. Clemenceau took the Interior—his first office, though long known for skill in overthrowing Ministries; M. Aristide Briand, a Socialist who had once advocated the general strike, took Public Instruction with Public Worship; M. Léon Bourgeois took the Foreign Office; M. Raymond Poincaré took Finance.
The Ministry applied the Cartesian method of dividing difficulties: M. Bourgeois got France through the critical stage of the Morocco question; M. Clemenceau suspended the inventories wherever there was organised resistance, remarking with some humour that the pleasure of counting the candlesticks in a church was not worth the sacrifice of a single human life; M. Poincaré limited his ambition to getting the Budget passed in the form left by his predecessor.
In a single month (14 March–14 April) the Finance Bill passed both Houses, and the Chamber broke up on 14 April for the elections.
The seventh Legislature under the Constitution of 1875 ended amid domestic confusion unparalleled since 1871—miners’ strikes in the Nord and Pas-de-Calais, building strikes at Clermont-Ferrand, general strikes at Lorient and Toulon, and in Paris compositors, excavators, Metropolitan railway men, and even postmen on strike. Threats of a general strike and an assault on capitalism for 1 May produced an unprecedented panic; troops guarded workshops, bakeries, and printing establishments; searches were made at the houses of revolutionists and Monarchists alike.
Amid these troubles the electoral campaign went on with remarkable discipline. Of 591 seats, 433 were decided at the first ballot on 6 May; only 169 were carried by the Opposition. When the new Chamber met on 1 June it consisted of about 175 Reactionaries, Nationalists, and Conservative Republicans or Progressists; 340 Republicans of the Left, Radicals, and Radical Socialists; and 75 Socialists either “independent” or “unified.”
For the first time the majority on the Left was large enough to be independent of the Socialist alliance. France was as resolutely hostile to priestly rule as in 1875 and 1877, and in the main accepted the separation of Church and State—so manifestly that the General Assembly of French Bishops, under Cardinal Lecot, favoured by a large majority the formation of Public Worship Associations and petitioned the Pope for the necessary leave.
M. Henri Brisson was elected President of the Chamber. After a debate of unprecedented range in which M. Clemenceau mercilessly ridiculed M. Jaurès’s Collectivist Utopias, a vote of confidence was passed on 21 June by 400 to 88. On 12 July, after a third trial as calm and dignified as its predecessors had been disturbed, the Full Court of Cassation quashed the verdict of the Rennes court-martial of 1899 against Captain Dreyfus and did not remit the case for trial before another tribunal.
Next day the Government introduced a Bill restoring Dreyfus to his rank with seniority for the whole time of unjust deprivation; Lieutenant-Colonel Picquart was at once promoted brigadier-general and a few months later general of division. Thus ended the Affair which had stirred France so profoundly.
A law establishing a weekly day of rest was forced through; M. Poincaré’s Budget exceeded four milliards of francs (revenue 4,010,922,935 francs); and the Council of State laboured at the rules for apportioning the property of suppressed ecclesiastical establishments and for applying the weekly rest—seen already to bristle with difficulties.
(Extracts for Italy and for subsequent foreign and colonial chapters are not included in the phase-b package beyond this opening France narrative.)

sources/annual-register-1907.title: The Annual Register: A Review of Public Events at Home and Abroad for the Year 1907
sources/annual-register-1907.content:
The Annual Register 1907
Part I — English History
Chapter I — Education Echoes, Party Divisions, and the Irish Outlook
The acute political activity of the autumn session of 1906 was followed by a marked lull, broken at first only by the failing echoes of the controversy on the defunct Education Bill. The Primate, in a New Year’s letter to the clergy and laity of his diocese, pleaded for consideration of the subject without narrowness of mind, and reasserted the demand of Church people for elementary Christian teaching in all schools, coupled with recognition of the toil and expenditure undertaken to ensure an education “on the lines of corporate Christian life.” The Bishop of London formulated the aim of Churchmen as religious teaching everywhere, denominational schools where special circumstances justified them, and the safeguarding of parents’ rights. Both bishops stressed the financial burden of the prolonged controversy; the Bishops of London and Southwark issued a joint appeal for 50,000l. to repair and extend Church schools, while the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Westminster appealed (13 January) for 100,000l. for the schools of his diocese. The Bishop of Hereford regretted the Bill’s failure and outlined in The Times of 24 January a scheme of compromise providing undenominational schools within the reach of all children. The Archbishop of Canterbury, addressing the Canterbury Diocesan Education Society on 21 January, admitted that Voluntary Schools could not go on exactly as they were and that changes must accept popular control and freedom of teachers from denominational tests; Lord Crewe replied next day that it was useless to reopen communications except on the lines already discussed before the House of Lords.
Though Lord Hugh Cecil and other High Churchmen claimed the destruction of the Education Bill as a Church victory, many Unionists shared the Primate’s desire for a settlement on political grounds. Mr Leverton Harris declared that the Conservative party had “made a profound tactical blunder”; Mr Austen Chamberlain’s New Year’s Message to the Outlook urged a constructive Unionist policy of imperial union and social reform, with tariff reform as the means of providing funds “without robbery or jobbery.” Mr Joseph Chamberlain, through the Montreal Star (10 January), told the people of Canada that of all bonds uniting nations the bond of commerce was the strongest, and predicted the ultimate success of mutual preference. Tariff Reformers pressed to put preference first on the Unionist programme; the Daily Graphic suggested a fiscal truce and found little encouragement.
The Liberals were not allowed to forget their own divisions. Impressive Rectorial Addresses by Mr Haldane at Edinburgh (10 January) and Mr Asquith next day at Glasgow drew from Mr Keir Hardie, speaking at Darvel on 12 January, a remarkable attack: both Ministers belonged to the Liberal Imperialist section which had nearly wrecked Liberalism; of the three prominent Liberal Imperialists in Scotland, two were of the Birmingham type and had supported the war, while Lord Rosebery, “the best man of the three,” was the scapegoat. Haldane’s national ideals, Hardie said, were drawn from Japan and Germany; Britain was following the pathway that led Rome to ruin.
Meanwhile the plan for reorganisation of the Field Army, foreshadowed by Mr Haldane in July 1906, was announced at Glasgow on 11 January and embodied in a special Army Order published on 14 January. Its leading feature was abandonment of the continental model of Army Corps and substitution of the Japanese and Indian model of large divisions, each containing three infantry brigades with divisional cavalry and artillery. Organisation for war would be one cavalry division of four brigades, six divisions, army troops, and line-of-communication troops; peace organisation would be four cavalry brigades, six divisions, and army troops, with headquarters at Aldershot, Tidworth, London, Dublin, Edinburgh, and York.
