Chapter IV — The Position of the Chancellor of the Exchequer in the Money Market
The government’s influence on the money market through the management of public deposits. The Exchequer accounts — the balances held by the government at the Bank of England — fluctuate enormously with the collection and disbursement of revenue. When taxes come in, large sums are withdrawn from circulation and deposited at the Bank, reducing the banking reserve; when the government pays out money (for dividends on the National Debt, salaries, or public works), these sums return to the money market and increase the reserve.
Bagehot describes the mechanics of these flows in detail. The collection of the income tax, the customs and excise duties, and the land tax all produce seasonal movements in the Exchequer balances. The quarterly payment of dividends on the National Debt — some £26 million per year — sweeps an enormous sum from the Exchequer into the hands of fundholders, who deposit it with banks, which re-lend it. The management of the National Debt — conversion operations, the issue of Exchequer bills, the timing of dividend payments — gives the Chancellor of the Exchequer “a great and growing influence” over the money market, though he exercises it “involuntarily” more often than by design.
Bagehot argues for greater publicity and predictability in these government operations so that the market can adjust. He notes that the Bank of England could mitigate the disturbance of government transactions by smoothing the ebb and flow of deposits, but that “the Bank does not attempt to estimate the probable duration of these fluctuations,” and the result is “a certain amount of avoidable disturbance.” He calls for the Chancellor to recognise that government finance and the money market are inseparable: “a Chancellor of the Exchequer who does not understand the Money Market can never thoroughly understand his own office.”
Chapter V — The Mode in Which the Value of Money Is Settled in Lombard Street
The determination of the rate of interest and discount. The open market rate — the rate at which bill brokers and other lenders discount commercial bills — fluctuates with the supply of loanable funds and the demand for credit. The Bank Rate (the minimum rate at which the Bank of England discounts bills) stands above the market rate in ordinary times, but the Bank’s rate becomes decisive when money is scarce. “In all common years,” Bagehot observes, “the Bank of England has little or no influence on the rate of interest. It simply follows the market. Its rate rises after the market rises and falls after it falls.”
But in times of stringency the Bank’s rate becomes dominant precisely because the Bank controls the ultimate reserve. When the open market rate rises above the Bank Rate, merchants and bill brokers can profit by discounting at the Bank and re-lending in the market, forcing the Bank to raise its own rate. The mechanism by which the Bank of England’s rate influences the whole money market has two stages: when the Bank raises its rate, it attracts gold from abroad (because higher interest rates draw foreign capital), which increases the reserve and checks the outflow of bullion; when it lowers the rate, the reverse happens and gold tends to leave. The Bank Rate thus operates as a controlling instrument over the foreign exchanges and the internal credit cycle.
Bagehot describes the process as a self-correcting one: “The rise in the rate of discount operates upon the trade of the country exactly as a rise in the price of any other commodity. It lessens the demand.” Higher rates discourage speculative importation, reduce the volume of bills drawn, and encourage export of goods to settle foreign balances — all of which correct the exchange rate and stop the drain of gold.
He also examines the concept of “the value of money” itself, distinguishing between the purchasing power of money in the commodity markets and the rate at which money can be borrowed in Lombard Street. The two are connected but distinct: a fall in the Bank Rate does not necessarily mean a fall in general prices, nor does a rise necessarily mean inflation. The rate on Lombard Street is “the price of loanable capital,” not the price of goods.
Chapter VI — Why Lombard Street Is Often Very Dull, and Sometimes Extremely Excited
The alternation of confidence and panic in the money market. In ordinary times the market functions quietly — bills are discounted, loans are made, credit circulates freely. “Lombard Street is usually as quiet as a plain English market town,” Bagehot remarks, “though in times of pressure it is like a city besieged.” But credit is inherently psychological: “A state of panic … is a sudden and unreasonable want of confidence.”
Periods of commercial speculation generate excessive optimism, which leads to over-trading, the acceptance of bad security, and the extension of credit beyond prudent limits. “The trade of a country,” Bagehot writes, “is not a fixed amount; it varies with the spirit of the times — with the hope of gain and the courage of speculators.” When some signal event — a prominent failure, a political shock, or a drain on the Bank’s reserve — punctures confidence, the market swings violently from excess of trust to excess of fear. Borrowers who were eagerly accommodated become pariahs; sound securities that were taken without question become unsaleable; the machinery of credit, which operates silently and efficiently in ordinary times, suddenly seizes up.
He describes the psychology of panic in vivid terms: “At the beginning of a panic we all believe that we can get £5,000,000 of notes when we need them, and at the end we are all afraid that we cannot get £500,000.” The tendency of borrowers and lenders to alternate between these extremes is “the governing condition of the money market,” and panics, though terrifying, are “as old and as periodic as the history of English commerce.”
Bagehot draws on the experience of the panics of 1825, 1837, 1847, 1857, and 1866. Each followed the same pattern: a period of speculation (in foreign loans, railway shares, or some new industry), a shock that broke confidence, a sudden contraction of credit, and finally, intervention by the Bank of England or the government to stem the panic. The consistency of the pattern is what makes a science of crisis management possible.
Chapter VII — More About the Mode in Which the Value of Money Is Settled in Lombard Street
A deeper analysis of the interaction between the Bank of England’s reserve, the rate of discount, and the foreign exchanges. Bagehot explains the mechanism of gold movements in detail: when England imports more than she exports, the balance must be settled in bullion, draining the Bank’s reserve. The Bank must then raise its rate to attract gold back from abroad — for “gold flows to the market where interest is highest.”
He distinguishes between two kinds of drain on the reserve: an internal drain (caused by a loss of confidence at home, when the public convert deposits into notes or specie) and an external drain (caused by an adverse balance of payments). “A panic is a period in which the two often happen together — in which a foreign drain of gold and a domestic distrust of credit combine to produce a common catastrophe.” The Bank’s rate must be raised high enough to attract foreign gold, but the real difficulty is that an internal drain may continue even after the exchange has turned favourable, because the public’s demand for cash is driven by fear rather than by economic calculation.
The India Council’s sales of bills in London are identified as a further factor affecting the exchanges and the reserve. The Government of India had to remit large sums to London to meet expenses in England — interest on the Indian debt, payments for stores, furlough allowances — and did so by drawing bills on India and selling them in London. These “India Council bills” were a large and fluctuating element in the foreign exchange market, and their sale or withholding could materially affect the supply of loanable funds in Lombard Street.
Bagehot emphasises that the Bank’s reserve must be adequate not only to meet domestic demands but also to withstand external drains. He argues that the Bank should maintain a reserve of at least £12 million to £14 million as a minimum — but that even this may be insufficient in a severe crisis. The Bank Rate is “the proper instrument for correcting both kinds of drain,” but it must be used promptly and decisively, not hesitatingly.
Chapter VIII — The Government of the Bank of England
A searching critique of the Bank’s constitution and management. The Court of Directors is composed largely of London merchants and bankers — “eminent in their own trades” but possessing no special training in central banking. The Governor and Deputy-Governor serve for two-year terms and typically ascend through a prescribed rotation — first Deputy-Governor, then Governor — ensuring that “no single individual acquires commanding experience or authority.” A man typically serves one term as Governor and then returns to private business; by the time he has learned the complexities of central banking, he relinquishes office.
Bagehot is scathing: “The Bank is managed on the principle of having no principles.” The Direction is amateur in character, slow to adapt to changing circumstances, and prone to vacillate between inaction and belated action. “It appears to me that the constitution of the Bank of England is radically bad,” he declares. “The real reason why the Bank of England has been so long managed as it has is that it has never been considered as a national bank — as a bank on which the credit of the country depends.”
The secrecy of the Bank’s proceedings — its refusal to publish detailed accounts, its habit of announcing decisions without explanation — contributes to the instability of the market. “If it were known that the Bank of England would act in the way that I have described, there would be a manifest diminution in the severity of panics. The knowledge that the Bank of England would lend freely in a panic would of itself inspire confidence. But as long as the market is left to guess at the Bank’s policy, panics will be more severe than they otherwise would be.”
The management of the reserve is a direct consequence of this defective constitution: the Bank lends timidly in a crisis (because the directors are afraid of the responsibility) and freely when no crisis exists (because they want to earn dividends). The two-year term of the Governor means that “the management of the Bank is in the hands of men who are always learning and never learned.”
Chapter IX — The Joint Stock Banks
The rise of the London joint-stock banks after the Bank Charter Act of 1833, which permitted joint-stock banking within the London radius. The Act renewed the Bank of England’s charter but removed the prohibition on other joint-stock banks operating within sixty-five miles of London. This opened the door to a new kind of banking institution.
Banks such as the London and Westminster Bank (founded 1834), the London Joint Stock Bank (1836), and the Union Bank of London (1839) grew rapidly. They attracted deposits by offering interest on current accounts — a practice the private banks had generally disdained — and by conducting aggressive lending operations. Their business model was simple: pay interest to attract deposits, lend the money at a higher rate, and keep only a small reserve. Bagehot notes that the London and Westminster Bank had deposits of £2.5 million in 1836, rising to over £14 million by 1857.
“The joint-stock banks early adopted the practice of keeping only a small reserve of notes and coin in their own tills,” Bagehot observes, and relied instead on two forms of liquid assets: money at call with the bill brokers, and deposits at the Bank of England. This made them dependent on the central reserve without bearing proportional responsibility for maintaining it. They competed fiercely with both the private banks and the Bank of England, undercutting rates and offering services that the older banks considered undignified.
Bagehot analyses the dangers of the deposit system in the joint-stock banks: the ease with which deposits can be withdrawn in a panic, the temptation to lend long and borrow short, and the moral hazard of relying on the Bank of England to provide liquidity in a crisis. “A joint-stock bank … may pay interest on deposits for years, and attract an immense mass of deposits, but the moment a panic begins, these deposits may vanish, and the bank may be ruined.” He includes detailed balance-sheet statistics from the London and Westminster Bank covering 1845–1857, showing the growth of deposits, the proportion of cash in hand, and the changing composition of assets.
He also discusses the competition for deposits that drove up interest rates and drove down credit standards. “The payment of interest on deposits naturally leads to a competition among banks to attract them, and this competition tends to lower the quality of the securities on which money is lent, because each bank is anxious to employ its deposits profitably.” The danger was that the system encouraged “overtrading” — lending more and more to less and less creditworthy borrowers — while the banks themselves held insufficient reserves against the withdrawal of deposits.
Chapter X — The Private Banks
The surviving private banks in Lombard Street and the West End: firms such as the Rothschilds, Barings, Glyn Mills, Coutts, Drummonds, Child’s, Hoare’s, and others. These were the historic names of English banking, most of them partnerships in which the partners were personally liable — unlimited liability — for all debts. Their history stretched back to the goldsmiths of the seventeenth century.
Unlike the joint-stock banks, the private banks tended to hold their own reserves more conservatively. “They keep a larger proportion of their deposits in actual cash than the joint-stock banks, because they have not the same power of attracting deposits by offering interest, and because their reputation depends on their known solidity.” They conducted business with a select clientele of wealthy individuals, aristocratic families, and the gentry. Their lending was more personal and more cautious.
Their relationship with the Bank of England was close but informal. The private banks had long maintained deposit accounts with the Bank of England, and many of them kept their entire cash reserve there. “They have no agreement with the Bank of England; they keep their money with it simply because it is convenient, and because it has always been the custom.”
Bagehot observes the gradual decline of private banking as the joint-stock banks absorbed an increasing share of deposits. “The private banks are gradually losing their business. The deposits which they used to receive from the country bankers are now largely taken by the joint-stock banks, and the wealthy people who used to keep their accounts with the private banks are beginning to find the joint-stock banks more convenient.” The concentration of banking into fewer, larger institutions was an unmistakable trend.
He also examines the special position of the Rothschilds, who as both bullion brokers and bankers occupied a unique place in the system. “The house of Rothschild is perhaps the greatest name in Lombard Street, but it is more a foreign than a domestic power; its main business lies in the great loans and the bullion trade of the world.” Barings, by contrast, was more purely a merchant bank, acting as accepting house for international trade and as financial agent for foreign governments.
Chapter XI — The Bill Brokers
The functions of the bill brokers as the intermediaries of the London money market. Firms such as Overend, Gurney & Co. (which failed spectacularly in 1866, an event that hangs over the entire book) acted as the great clearing-house of credit: they borrowed money at call from the banks, often at low rates of interest, and employed it to discount commercial bills at a higher rate, profiting from the spread.
The bill brokers thus linked the surplus cash of the banking system with the demand for credit from the trading community. “The bill-brokers stand between the bankers and the merchants; they borrow from the one and lend to the other.” The banks found it convenient to place surplus cash with the brokers at call, earning some interest on money that would otherwise lie idle; the merchants found the brokers more accessible and more flexible than the Bank of England.
Bagehot analyses the fragility of this system carefully. The brokers’ liabilities are payable on demand (or at very short notice — “at call” in the market’s phrase), but their assets — the discounted bills — are repayable only at maturity, which might be three months or more. In normal times this mismatch is manageable because the inflow of maturing bills roughly matches the outflow of call loans. But in a panic the banks call in their loans simultaneously, the brokers cannot realise their bills except at ruinous loss (by re-discounting at “panic prices”), and the whole discount market seizes up. At that point, only the Bank of England can intervene as the lender of last resort.
The evolution of the discount market from a mere agency business to one in which brokers dealt as principals is a central theme. “Originally the bill-broker was a mere agent; he brought the man who wanted to lend money and the man who wanted to borrow together, and charged a commission for his services. But gradually he became a principal; he borrowed from the lender on his own account, and lent to the borrower also on his own account.” This transformation concentrated risk in the brokers themselves, and the failure of a great broker like Overend, Gurney & Co. could bring down the whole market.
Bagehot provides extensive analysis of the Overend failure. The firm, once the largest discount house in the world, had expanded beyond its traditional business into speculative ventures — shipping, ironworks, and other industrial investments — and was brought down when these ventures failed. Its collapse on 10 May 1866 precipitated the most severe panic since 1825. The Bank of England was forced to lend enormous sums to keep the market afloat, while the government suspended the Bank Charter Act to permit additional note issues.
Chapter XII — The Principles Which Should Regulate the Amount of the Banking Reserve to Be Kept by the Bank of England
The core of Bagehot’s policy recommendations and the classic formulation of the lender-of-last-resort doctrine. This is the most famous chapter in the book, the one that established Bagehot’s name in the history of central banking. He sets out three principles:
1. Hold a much larger reserve than current practice. Bagehot argues that the existing standard — one-third of banking liabilities, as suggested by Governor Weguelin and Mr. Hankey — is inadequate. “No one would now ever be content if the banking reserve were near to one-fourth of its liabilities.” He analyses the composition of the Bank’s liabilities, distinguishing between those that are likely to be withdrawn in a panic and those that are stable. The reserve must be sufficient to meet the worst-case scenario: a simultaneous internal and external drain. He argues that the Bank should aim for a reserve “considerably larger than one-third” — perhaps as much as one-half, depending on circumstances — and that it should be built up by retaining profits and by refusing to force dividends.
2. Lend freely in a panic, but at a high rate of interest, on good security. This is the central principle. In a crisis, the Bank should advance money “without stint” to all solvent borrowers who offer acceptable collateral — but at a penal rate (Bagehot suggests Bank Rate plus a premium, perhaps one to three per cent above the pre-panic rate). The high rate deters speculative borrowing (ensuring that only those who genuinely need money will come to the Bank) and attracts gold from abroad (because foreign investors will send gold to earn the high interest). The free lending calms panic by assuring the market that “anyone who has good security can get the use of money.” Bagehot’s formulation is emphatic: “The only safe plan is to lend money freely, largely, and in the end successfully. A panic is a species of neuralgia in the money market; it must be treated by relieving the pressure, not by increasing it.”
3. Make its policy known in advance. The Bank should declare publicly that it will follow these principles, so that the market knows what to expect. “The knowledge that the Bank of England would lend freely in a panic would of itself inspire confidence.” Uncertainty about the Bank’s intentions compounds panic — borrowers do not know whether help will be available, and this uncertainty itself produces hoarding and contraction. A clear, publicly known policy would reduce both the frequency and the severity of panics.
Bagehot’s crucial distinction is between lending freely to the market at large and bailing out individual mismanaged institutions. “Every great panic brings some destruction,” he writes; it is not the Bank’s duty to save unsound firms. “It is the duty of the Bank of England to prevent the destruction of the whole credit system, not to rescue every individual firm that has been imprudent.” The lender of last resort is there to preserve the system, not to protect individual speculators from the consequences of their own folly.
He also addresses the objection that lending freely might lead to an over-issue of notes and a depreciation of the currency. The high rate of interest charged by the Bank is the safeguard: it ensures that the extra notes go only to those who genuinely need them and that they are withdrawn as soon as the panic subsides. The Bank’s lending should be short-term — discounts of bills with a few weeks to run, or advances against government securities — so that the money returns automatically when the bills mature.
Chapter XIII — Conclusion
A summing-up of the argument and a survey of possible reforms. Bagehot acknowledges the difficulty of reforming so deeply entrenched a system, but insists that palliatives are necessary because the system itself — the single-reserve system under which the entire banking structure rests on the Bank of England — cannot be fundamentally altered. “We cannot do otherwise,” he concludes. “The one-reserve system is fixed upon us. The only practical imitation of the American system would be to enact that the Banking Department of the Bank of England should always keep a fixed proportion — say one-third of its liabilities — in reserve.”
He rejects the French plan of government appointment of the Bank’s directors, which would politicise the institution. “The direct appointment of the Governor and Deputy-Governor of the Bank of England by the executive Government would not lessen our evils or help our difficulties. I fear it would make both worse.” And he rejects the American system of fixed reserve ratios for national banks as too rigid and likely to provoke panic: “if one-third were fixed by law, the moment the banks were close to one-third, alarm would begin, and would run like magic.”
The best available remedies are: the maintenance of adequate reserves (which must be higher than the one-third standard then in use), the timely publication of the Bank’s accounts (so the market can judge the state of the reserve for itself and is not left to guess at it), a clear and publicly stated lending policy (the lender-of-last-resort doctrine announced in advance), and the gradual improvement of the Bank’s internal governance (longer terms for the Governor, more professional management, and a recognition by the Court of Directors that the Bank is not an ordinary joint-stock bank but a national institution). “The Bank must learn to be a national bank, and to act as such; it must learn that it is not only a corporation that ought to provide profits for its proprietors, but a national institution that ought to keep the national credit.”
The book ends with the measured hope that “education and discussion will in the end so far improve the constitution of the Bank of England, that it will act, and will be seen to act, on a true and perfect system.” Bagehot does not expect sudden or radical change — the Bank’s “defects are too old, too inveterate, too much ingrained into the character of the institution” for that — but he believes that the power of reasoned argument, applied persistently, can bring gradual improvement.
Appendix
Note A — Comparative table of the liabilities and cash reserves of the banking systems of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and the United States. The figures are detailed and presented in a standardised format:



































Banking SystemLiabilities to PublicCash HeldProportionBank of England & London Joint Stock Banks£120,000,000£13,500,00011.2%Bank of France£125,000,000£32,000,00025.0%Banks of Germany£88,000,000£41,000,00047.0%National Banks of United States£212,000,000£26,000,00012.3%
The English proportion of 11.2 per cent — calculated by including only the Bank of England’s reserve against the combined deposits of the Bank and the London joint-stock banks — was the lowest of all four systems, though Bagehot notes that the English figure understates the true position by omitting the reserves held by provincial banks and the private banks. The comparison demonstrates the “overwhelming predominance” of English banking resources in absolute terms, but also the thinness of the English reserve relative to liabilities.
Note B — Extracts from evidence given by Alderman Salomons, chairman of the London and Westminster Bank, before the House of Commons Select Committee in 1858. This is the longest appendix note and contains detailed testimony on:

The lending practices of joint-stock banks during the panic of 1857. Salomons explains that the London and Westminster Bank did not withdraw accommodation from its own customers during the crisis; on the contrary, “our advances to our customers on the 31st of December were nearly 500,000 pounds higher than they were on the 1st of October.” The contraction was achieved by allowing bills discounted for brokers and strangers to mature without replacement.
The distinction between discounting bills and making advances on bills deposited as security. Salomons explains that when the bank lends money on bills as security, it is not a re-discount and carries no further liability; when it discounts a bill, the bank’s liability continues until maturity. This distinction was important because the joint-stock banks’ practice of lending on deposited bills rather than discounting them allowed the banks to control their exposure more precisely.
The banks’ confidence that the Government would always intervene. Salomons states bluntly: “If the Bank of England had stopped payment, all the machinery of Government would have stopped with it, and we never could have believed that so formidable a calamity would have arisen if the Government could have prevented it.” He and his fellow bankers “never for a moment” contemplated that the Bank of England might fail, and expected that the Government would issue a letter suspending the Bank Act — which it did.
The competition among banks for deposits and the understanding reached after 1857 to moderate the payment of interest on deposits. Salomons confirms that “all the banks have come to an understanding that it is not desirable, either for their proprietors or for the public, to follow closely at all times the alterations of the Bank.”
A statistical table showing the deposits, cash in hand, money at call, and government securities of the London and Westminster Bank at half-yearly intervals from 1845 to 1857. The table shows the bank’s deposits growing from £2.5 million in 1845 to over £14 million by 1857, while cash in hand as a proportion of deposits fluctuated but generally declined.

Note C — Statement of circulation and deposits of the Bank of Dundee at ten-year intervals from 1764 to 1864. This is a remarkable long-run series showing the growth of deposits in a provincial Scottish bank from nothing (the Bank of Dundee had no deposits at all in 1764) to nearly £685,000 by 1864. The note illustrates the long-term growth of banking intermediation in Scotland, where banking had developed earlier and more thoroughly than in most of England. Bagehot uses it to demonstrate that deposits are not a fixed quantity but can be built up over time as the public becomes accustomed to using banks.
Note D — The full proceedings of the half-yearly meeting of the proprietors of the Bank of England held on 13 September 1866, reprinted from The Economist. Governor Launcelot Holland’s address describes the Bank’s actions during the panic of 1866, triggered by the failure of Overend, Gurney & Co. on 10 May. The Governor reported that the Bank had made “extraordinary advances” totalling some £45,000,000 in the three months from May to July, including £20,000,000 in the first fortnight of the panic. The meeting records the debate among proprietors over:

The suspension of the Bank Act of 1844, which temporarily permitted the Bank to issue notes beyond the statutory limit
The Bank’s decision to pay interest on deposits to attract funds during the crisis
The propriety of the Bank’s lending policy and the conduct of the directors
The governance of the Bank and the question of whether the proprietors should have more control over the direction

Governor Holland defended the Bank’s actions vigorously, arguing that it had done “all that was possible” to meet the crisis and that the suspension of the Bank Act had been “absolutely necessary.” The debate among the proprietors — some of whom criticised the Bank for having lent too freely, others for not having lent freely enough — gives a vivid contemporary picture of the controversies that Bagehot’s book sought to resolve.
Also included is a summary of the financial results for the half-year, showing the Bank’s profits, the dividend declared (which, despite the extraordinary advances, was maintained), and the state of the reserve at various dates during the crisis.

sources/mackinder-british-seas.title: Mackinder, Halford J. — Britain and the British Seas (1907)
sources/mackinder-british-seas.content:
Britain and the British Seas (1907)
Halford Mackinder’s masterwork of geographical synthesis, presenting a complete picture of the physical features and conditions of the British natural region and tracing their influence upon the human societies dwelling within it.
Source
Halford John Mackinder, Britain and the British Seas. Second edition. Oxford: At the Clarendon Press, 1907. First edition published January 1902; reprinted September 1904; second edition January 1907. Volume I in “The Regions of the World” series, edited by H. J. Mackinder.
Mackinder — then Director of the London School of Economics and Political Science, formerly Reader in Geography in the University of Oxford — conceived the book to meet the needs of foreign students visiting Britain. His aim was “to present a picture of the physical features and conditions of a very definite natural region, and to trace their influence upon the human societies dwelling within it.” The book is structured in twenty-one chapters progressing from the physical foundations (position, seas, platform, geology, climate) through the human geography (ethnography, historical geography, the regional geography of England, Scotland, and Ireland) to the applied dimensions (strategic, economic, and imperial geography).
Text
raw/mackinder-british-seas/raw.txt — 17,293 lines, ~698 KB. Extracted from a Harvard University library scan (Widener Library copy, shelfmark DA630.M158x 1907). The raw text includes all twenty-one chapters, the preface, the list of illustrations, and the index. Some minor OCR artifacts are present from the library digitisation.
Contents
Preface
Mackinder explains the book’s origin in the needs of foreign students and his aim to produce a complete geographical synthesis. Britain is “so small, and is known in such detail, that it has been possible to attempt a complete geographical synthesis.” He disclaims exhaustive local description, aiming instead at “a picture of the interaction of human society and natural environment within the limits of a definite region.”
Chapter I — The Position of Britain
Britain’s changing position in the world’s geographical imagination: from the “utmost corner of the West” at the end of the known world before the great discoveries, to the central position in the land hemisphere after the exploration of the Atlantic. Mackinder traces the implications of this shift for British history, diplomacy, and trade.
Chapter II — The British Seas
The physical geography of the waters surrounding Britain: the Narrow Seas to the east and south, the Ocean to the north and west. The contrast between the inner and outer faces of the land — the smooth, low-lying coasts facing the Continent and the jagged, cliff-edged western seaboard with its five thousand islands.
Chapter III — The Submarine Platform
The shallow continental shelf surrounding Britain: the Strait of Dover so shallow that St. Paul’s Cathedral would rise above the water if sunk in it; the hundred-fathom line beyond which the sea-bed slopes suddenly downward. The submarine platform’s significance for fisheries, navigation, and the geological unity of the British archipelago.
Chapter IV — The Movement of the Waters
Tides, currents, and their effects on British coastlines. The shallow marginal sea as the scene of “more vigorous movements than is the deep ocean or a land-girt mediterranean.” How tidal fluctuations have shaped harbours, contributed to shipping, and determined the position and seasons of fisheries.
Chapter V — The Uplands and Lowlands
The rough moulding of the land-surface and its continuity with the sea-bed. The bas-relief character of British topography — broad uplands rising from lowlands “like the sovereign’s head on a coin.” Contrasts between the weathering properties of air and the preservative influence of deep waters.
Chapter VI — The Structure of Britain
The fundamental geological distinction between the soft, recent rocks of south-eastern Britain (sands, clays, chalk) and the hard, ancient rocks of the north and west (quartzites, slates, crystalline limestones, igneous rocks). How the harder, older rocks rise into uplands while the newer, softer deposits have been reduced to lowlands.
Chapter VII — The English Plain
A detailed survey of the varied accumulation of newer rocks in the English plain between London and Chester. The geological strata, their agricultural capacities, and their influence on settlement and communications.
Chapter VIII — The Physical History of Britain
The geological history of the British Isles through successive ages: how “the British polity is made of institutions dating from all centuries” just as “natural features of widely different geological ages” compose the physical landscape. The shaping of Britain by ancient seas, volcanic activity, ice ages, and river systems.
Chapter IX — The Rivers of Britain
Denudation and the river systems of Britain: how “denudation acting upon grained and unequally resistant rocks has shaped the present surface.” The major river basins, their geological history, and their roles in drainage, transport, and settlement.
Chapter X — British Weather
The interaction of geological stresses and atmospheric agencies producing the characteristic weather of the British Isles. The cyclonic systems of the North Atlantic, the influence of the Gulf Stream, and the variability that marks British meteorology.
Chapter XI — The Climates of Britain
Climate as “average weather” and its regional variations: the south-western mildness, the eastern dryness, the northern coolness. How the changeable weather produces different average results in different parts — the distinction between the climates rather than a single “British climate.”
Chapter XII — Ethnographical Geography
The racial geography of the British Isles: how “the lie of the rock features of Britain and the interacting currents of the surrounding sea and air constitute the physical environment of one of the great nations.” The distribution of pre-Celtic, Celtic, Roman, Anglo-Saxon, Danish, and Norman elements in the population, and their relation to the physical regions.
Chapter XIII — Historical Geography
“The organisation of a people only becomes accurate and permanent when founded on a territorial basis.” Mackinder traces the settlement of Britain from the Saxon invasions across the Narrow Seas through the political unification of England, the union with Scotland, and the establishment of the imperial maritime position.
Chapter XIV — Metropolitan England
The concentration of population, wealth, and power in London and the Home Counties. London as the centre of government, finance, and commerce — drawing upon the resources of the whole country and the empire. The geographical factors that made London the natural metropolis.
Chapter XV — Industrial England
The industrial districts of England: “built on a broader scale than Metropolitan England, consisting of fewer and larger natural elements, but having no obvious topographical centre.” The coalfields, the manufacturing districts of the Midlands and the North, the iron and steel centres, and the textile regions. The geographical foundations of the Industrial Revolution.
Chapter XVI — Scotland
The subdivision of Scotland for geographical description: the Highlands, the Central Lowlands, and the Southern Uplands. The geological and climatic factors shaping Scottish regional character, agriculture, industry, and population distribution.
Chapter XVII — Ireland
“The largest single feature in the configuration of Ireland is the central plain,” spreading from the east coast a hundred miles westward. The contrast between Ireland’s central lowlands and its mountainous perimeter, and the implications for agriculture, settlement, and historical development.
Chapter XVIII — Strategic Geography
“Every civilised nation is related in two ways to the land” — the dynamical aspects of British geography. The strategic position of the British Isles in European and world politics: the command of the Narrow Seas, the naval bases, the defence of trade routes, and the geographical foundations of British sea power.
Chapter XIX — Economic Geography
“The most generally distributed element of the British environment is the moist equable climate,” and its consequence for agriculture, forestry, and the natural wealth of the country. The distribution of mineral resources, the geography of manufacturing, the transport system, the ports and their hinterlands, and the economic relations between regions.
Chapter XX — Imperial Britain
“The activities of the British people depend ultimately on the resources of Britain itself” — but Britain’s position as the centre of a world-wide empire is the product of its geographical situation. Mackinder analyses the imperial role of the British Isles as the heart of a maritime empire, the economic interdependence of the mother country and the colonies, and the geographical requirements for maintaining imperial unity.
Chapter XXI — Summary and Conclusion
Mackinder draws together the threads of his geographical analysis. “Britain is a world by itself” — the interaction of physical environment and human activity has produced a unique national character and position. The summary reviews the typical results of British geography and considers what broad conclusions may be drawn for the future.

sources/mackinder-eight-lectures-india.title: Mackinder, Halford J. — Eight Lectures on India (1910)
sources/mackinder-eight-lectures-india.content:
Eight Lectures on India (1910)
Halford Mackinder’s educational lectures on the geography, history, religions, and peoples of India, prepared for the Visual Instruction Committee of the Colonial Office and designed to accompany a series of lantern-slide illustrations.
Source
Halford John Mackinder, Eight Lectures on India. London: Waterlow & Sons Ltd., 1910. Prepared for the Visual Instruction Committee of the Colonial Office (Chairman: the Right Hon. Sir Charles Lucas, K.C.B., K.C.M.G.). Printed for the Royal Colonial Institute. OCLC 13304715.
The lectures were designed for a comprehensive scheme of visual instruction in geography for the schools of the British Empire. Each lecture was intended to accompany a set of lantern slides and dealt with a particular province of India in correlation with a major theme of Indian civilisation: geography, religion, and history interwoven. The book includes a Preface by the Visual Instruction Committee explaining the educational aims of the series, an Introduction by Mackinder on the general geography of India, and eight lectures with numerous references to the illustrative slides.
Text
raw/mackinder-eight-lectures-india/raw.txt — 7,369 lines, ~267 KB. Extracted from the printed 1910 edition. The text includes all eight lectures complete.
Contents
Lecture I — Madras: The Hindu Religion
India introduced as “an empire within an empire” — three hundred million people within the British Empire’s four hundred million. Mackinder begins with Madras, the southernmost and oldest province, and pairs the geographical description with a survey of the Hindu religion: its pantheon, its caste system, its temples and practices, and its permeation of every aspect of life in southern India.
Lecture II — Burma: The Buddhist Religion
Across the Bay of Bengal from Madras to Burma, the easternmost and newest province of the Indian Empire. Mackinder describes Burma’s geography — the Irrawaddy river system, the teak forests, the rice cultivation — and pairs the province with an account of Buddhism: its origins, its doctrines, its spread through Asia, and its distinctive Burmese manifestations in the pagodas and monasteries of the country.
Lecture III — Bengal: The Monsoons
Bengal as the Metropolitan Province of India, the heart of British power founded by Clive. Mackinder describes the rich alluvial plains of the Ganges and Brahmaputra deltas, the dense population, the jute and tea industries, and Calcutta as the imperial capital. The paired theme is the monsoons — the climatic system that governs Indian agriculture and life, the seasonal alternation of wet and dry winds, and the geography of rainfall across the subcontinent.
Lecture IV — The United Provinces: The Mutiny
Northwestward from Bengal over the great plain of the Ganges into the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh. Mackinder describes the heartland of Hindustan, the great cities of Allahabad, Cawnpore, Lucknow, and Agra. The paired historical theme is the Indian Mutiny of 1857: its causes, its course, the sieges and massacres, and its consequences for British rule in India.
Lecture V — Bombay: The Marathas
The maritime gateway of western India. Mackinder describes the great harbour of Bombay, the cotton trade, the Western Ghats, and the railway network. The paired historical theme is the Maratha Confederacy: the rise of Sivaji against the Moguls, the Maratha wars with the British, the career of the Peshwas, and the incorporation of the Maratha territories into British India.
Lecture VI — Rajputana: The Feudatory States
In the centre of northwestern India, a group of large native States — Rajputana, “of the greatest historical interest.” Mackinder describes the princely states of the Rajputs, their martial traditions, their magnificent fortresses and palaces, their desert landscape, and their position within the system of British paramountcy. The paired theme is the nature of the feudatory system and the relationship between the Crown and the native princes.
Lecture VII — Delhi: The Muhammadan Religion
The historic capital of India, seven times built on its successive sites. Mackinder describes Delhi’s strategic position on the Yamuna, its great architectural monuments — the Kutb Minar, the Jumna Musjid, the Red Fort — and its role as the seat of Mogul power. The paired theme is Islam in India: the Muhammadan conquests, the Delhi Sultanate, the Mogul Empire from Babur to Aurangzeb and its decline, and the enduring Muslim presence in Indian life.
Lecture VIII — The Northwest Frontier: The Sikhs
“The British Empire has but one land frontier on which warlike preparation must ever be ready — the Northwest Frontier of India.” Mackinder describes the mountainous borderland between India and Afghanistan, the passes of the Hindu Kush, the turbulent Pathan tribes, and the strategic importance of the frontier in imperial defence. The paired theme is the Sikh religion and people: the founding of the Khalsa by Guru Gobind Singh, the rise of Ranjit Singh’s kingdom in the Punjab, the Anglo-Sikh wars, and the incorporation of the Punjab into British India.

sources/mackinder-geographical-pivot.title: [source] The Geographical Pivot of History (Mackinder, 1904)
sources/mackinder-geographical-pivot.content:
The Geographical Pivot of History (1904)
Halford John Mackinder’s seminal lecture to the Royal Geographical Society, introducing the heartland concept that became the foundation of modern geopolitics — the argument that the vast interior of Euro-Asia, inaccessible to sea-power, is the pivot region of world politics, and that the Columbian epoch of maritime expansion (1492–1900) has given way to a closed political system in which land-power once again asserts its strategic primacy.
Source
Mackinder, H. J. “The Geographical Pivot of History.” The Geographical Journal, Vol. 23, No. 4 (April 1904), pp. 421-437. Read at the Royal Geographical Society, January 25, 1904. Followed by discussion (pp. 437-444) with contributions from Mr. Spencer Wilkinson, Mr. Amery, Sir Thomas Holdich, and others.
The lecture was delivered at a pivotal moment in British strategic thinking — less than two years after the end of the South African War, in the midst of the Russo-Japanese War (which broke out in February 1904, weeks after the lecture was given), and at a time when trans-continental railways were transforming the strategic geography of Asia.
Text
raw/mackinder-geographical-pivot/raw.txt — OCR-extracted text from the original Geographical Journal pages. The paper is accompanied by four maps (Fig. 1: Eastern Europe before the 16th century; Fig. 2: Political divisions of Eastern Europe at the time of the 3rd Crusade, c. 1190; Fig. 3: Political divisions at the accession of Charles V, 1519; Fig. 4: Continental and Arctic drainage — equal area projection) and is followed by a transcript of the discussion.
The Argument
Mackinder’s paper is the first systematic attempt to state a global geopolitical formula based on permanent geographical features rather than the transient configurations of national power. It operates through a series of layered contrasts — forest versus steppe, land-power versus sea-power, the heartland versus the marginal crescent, the Columbian epoch versus the closed system of the twentieth century — each narrowing from the widest historical perspective to the immediate strategic predicament of the British Empire.
I — The End of the Columbian Epoch
Mackinder opens by declaring the Columbian epoch (1492–c. 1900) at an end. The four centuries of European overseas expansion, during which the maritime powers of Western Europe enveloped the globe, have run their course. “When historians in the remote future come to look back on the group of centuries through which we are now passing,” he writes, “it may well be that they will describe the last 400 years as the Columbian epoch, and will say that it ended soon after the year 1900.” The expansion of Europe against “almost negligible resistances” — the defining characteristic of the age — is over.
The world has become a closed political system. “Every explosion of social forces, instead of being dissipated in a surrounding circuit of unknown space and barbaric chaos, will be sharply re-echoed from the far side of the globe, and weak elements in the political and economic organism of the world will be shattered in consequence.” The contrast in effect is that between “the fall of a shell into an earthwork and its fall amid the closed spaces and rigid structures of a great building or ship.”
For the first time, Mackinder argues, the world as a whole can be understood geographically. “I propose this evening describing those physical features of the world which I believe to have been most coercive of human action, and presenting some of the chief phases of history as organically connected with them, even in the ages when they were unknown to geography. My aim will not be to discuss the influence of this or that kind of feature, or yet to make a study in regional geography, but rather to exhibit human history as part of the life of the world organism.”
II — Forest and Steppe: The Physical Foundation of European History
Mackinder turns to the fundamental contrast within Europe itself: the division between the northern forest belt and the southern steppe lands. The vast Russian plain is not uniform: the north and north-west were “forest broken only by marshes,” while the south and south-east were “a boundless grassy steppe, with trees only along the rivers.” The line separating them ran diagonally north-eastward from the northern Carpathians to the southern Ural range, with Moscow lying just to the north (the forest side).
This division was “formerly very coercive of humanity,” though “the clearing of the forests, the drainage of the marshes, and the tillage of the steppes have recently averaged the character of the landscape.” The earlier Russia and Poland were established “wholly in the glades of the forest.” Through the steppe came, from the unknown recesses of Asia, “by the gateway between the Ural mountains and the Caspian sea,” a remarkable succession of Turanian nomadic peoples across the centuries: Huns, Avars, Bulgarians, Magyars, Khazars, Patzinaks, Cumans, Mongols, Kalmuks.
III — The Asiatic Invasions of Europe
Mackinder traces the sequence of nomadic invasions and their profound effects on European political development. Under Attila the Huns established themselves “in the midst of the Pusstas, in the uttermost Danubian outlier of the steppes,” dealing blows northward, westward, and southward. “A large part of modern history might be written as a commentary upon the changes directly or indirectly ensuing from these raids.” The Angles and Saxons may have been driven to cross the seas and found England in Britain; the Franks, Goths, and Roman provincials were compelled to stand “shoulder to shoulder on the battlefield of Chalons” against the Asiatics; Venice was founded from the destruction of Aquileia and Padua; even the Papacy owed prestige to Pope Leo’s mediation with Attila.
“Such was the harvest of results produced by a cloud of ruthless and idealess horsemen sweeping over the unimpeded plain — a blow, as it were, from the great Asiatic hammer striking freely through the vacant space.” The Avars followed the Huns; Austria was founded as a marchland against them. The Magyars increased the significance of the Austrian outpost, drawing the political focus of Germany eastward. The Khazars, contemporaries of the great Saracen movement, held the longest and most effective occupation of the Russian steppe. Finally, the Mongols held Russia tributary for two centuries. “For a thousand years a series of horse-riding peoples emerged from Asia through the broad interval between the Ural mountains and the Caspian sea, rode through the open spaces of southern Russia, and struck home into Hungary in the very heart of the European peninsula.”
Against this land-power stood a rival mobility: the Vikings in their boats, descending from Scandinavia upon both the northern and southern shores of Europe. “Thus the settled peoples of Europe lay gripped between two pressures — that of the Asiatic nomads from the east, and on the other three sides that of the pirates from the sea.” Both pressures were stimulative rather than overwhelming.
IV — The Heartland of Euro-Asia
Mackinder shifts the perspective from Europe to the Old World as a whole. The continuous land-mass of Euro-Asia, measuring 21 million square miles, or half of all the land on the globe, is characterised by a remarkable distribution of river drainage. Six of the greatest rivers in the world — the Volga, Oxus, Jaxartes (draining into salt lakes) and the Obi, Yenisei, Lena (draining into the frozen Arctic ocean) — are “practically useless for purposes of human communication with the outer world.” The core of Euro-Asia, “although mottled with desert patches, is on the whole a steppe-land supplying a wide-spread if often scanty pasture,” and “wholly unpenetrated by waterways from the ocean.”
Here Mackinder introduces his central geographical concept: the heartland. “To east, south, and west of this heart-land are marginal regions, ranged in a vast crescent, accessible to shipmen.” These marginal regions are four in number, coinciding “in a general way” with the spheres of the four great religions: the monsoon lands of Buddhism (turned toward the Pacific) and Brahminism (turned toward the Indian Ocean); Christianity (Europe, watered by Atlantic rains); and Mahometanism (the land of the Five Seas — the Nearer East — in large measure deprived of moisture by the proximity of Africa). The marginal belt contains more than 1,000 million people, or two-thirds of the world’s population, in less than 7 million square miles.
The Nearer East — strategically placed between the heartland and the ocean — “partakes of the characteristics both of the marginal belt and of the central area of Euro-Asia.” It has been “the weakest spot in the girdle of early civilizations,” for the isthmus of Suez divided sea-power into Eastern and Western, and “the arid wastes of Persia advancing from Central Asia to the Persian gulf gave constant opportunity for nomad-power to strike home to the ocean edge.”
V — Sea-Power and Land-Power: The Columbian Reversal
The discovery of the Cape route to the Indies was “the all-important result” — it connected the western and eastern coastal navigations of Euro-Asia, “thus in some measure to neutralize the strategical advantage of the central position of the steppe-nomads by pressing upon them in rear.” The Columbian generation endowed Christendom with “the widest possible mobility of power, short of a winged mobility.”
“The broad political effect was to reverse the relations of Europe and Asia.” Whereas in the Middle Ages Europe was “caged” between desert, ocean, and frozen wastes, and constantly threatened by the superior mobility of horsemen and camelmen, she now “emerged upon the world, multiplying more than thirty-fold the sea surface and coastal lands to which she had access, and wrapping her influence round the Euro-Asiatic land-power which had hitherto threatened her very existence.” New Europes were created in the vacant lands discovered in the midst of the waters. “Britain, Canada, the United States, South Africa, Australia, and Japan are now a ring of outer and insular bases for sea-power and commerce, inaccessible to the land-power of Euro-Asia.”
But the land-power remained, and recent events had increased its significance. “Russia has organized the Cossacks, and, emerging from her northern forests, has policed the steppe by setting her own nomads to meet the Tartar nomads.” The eastward swoop of the horsemen across Asia was “an event almost as pregnant with political consequences as was the rounding of the Cape.” Mackinder draws a striking cultural parallel: “It is probably one of the most striking coincidences of history that the seaward and the landward expansion of Europe should, in a sense, continue the ancient opposition between Roman and Greek.” The Teuton was civilized by the Roman and embarked upon the ocean; the Slav was civilized by the Greek and rode over the steppes. “Thus the modern land-power differs from the sea-power no less in the source of its ideals than in the material conditions of its mobility.”
VI — The Pivot Region in the Railway Age
Steam and the Suez canal had appeared to increase the mobility of sea-power relative to land-power. But trans-continental railways were “now transmuting the conditions of land-power,” and nowhere could they have such effect as “in the closed heart-land of Euro-Asia, in vast areas of which neither timber nor accessible stone was available for road-making.” Railways “work the greater wonders in the steppe, because they directly replace horse and camel mobility, the road stage of development having here been omitted.”
The Russian railways have “a clear run of 6000 miles from Wirballen in the west to Vladivostok in the east.” The Russian army in Manchuria is “as significant evidence of mobile land-power as the British army in South Africa was of sea-power.” Mackinder predicts that “the century will not be old before all Asia is covered with railways.” The spaces within the Russian Empire and Mongolia are “so vast, and their potentialities in population, wheat, cotton, fuel, and metals so incalculably great, that it is inevitable that a vast economic world, more or less apart, will there develop inaccessible to oceanic commerce.”
“Is not the pivot region of the world’s politics that vast area of Euro-Asia which is inaccessible to ships, but in antiquity lay open to the horse-riding nomads, and is to-day about to be covered with a network of railways?”
VII — The Geopolitical Formula
Mackinder states his conclusion as a geographical law. “Russia replaces the Mongol Empire. Her pressure on Finland, on Scandinavia, on Poland, on Turkey, on Persia, on India, and on China, replaces the centrifugal raids of the steppemen.” She occupies “the central strategical position held by Germany in Europe. She can strike on all sides and be struck from all sides, save the north.”
The world is divided into three concentric strategic zones: the pivot area (the heartland, occupied by Russia), an inner crescent (Germany, Austria, Turkey, India, China), and an outer crescent (Britain, South Africa, Australia, the United States, Canada, Japan). “In the present condition of the balance of power, the pivot state, Russia, is not equivalent to the peripheral states, and there is room for an equipoise in France.”
The great strategic danger is “the oversetting of the balance of power in favour of the pivot state, resulting in its expansion over the marginal lands of Euro-Asia.” This would “permit of the use of vast continental resources for fleet-building, and the empire of the world would then be in sight.” Such a catastrophe might occur “if Germany were to ally herself with Russia.” The threat of this event “should, therefore, throw France into alliance with the over-sea powers,” with France, Italy, Egypt, India, and Korea becoming “so many bridge heads where the outside navies would support armies to compel the pivot allies to deploy land forces and prevent them from concentrating their whole strength on fleets.”
Mackinder acknowledges that the particular combinations of power may vary, but insists that the underlying geographical relationship is fixed: “from a geographical point of view they are likely to rotate round the pivot state, which is always likely to be great, but with limited mobility as compared with the surrounding marginal and insular powers.”
He concludes with a caution: “the substitution of some new control of the inland area for that of Russia would not tend to reduce the geographical significance of the pivot position. Were the Chinese, for instance, organized by the Japanese, to overthrow the Russian Empire and conquer its territory, they might constitute the yellow peril to the world’s freedom just because they would add an oceanic frontage to the resources of the great continent, an advantage as yet denied to the Russian tenant of the pivot region.”
Discussion (pp. 437-444)
The discussion following the paper was opened by Mr. Spencer Wilkinson, who described it as “one of the most stimulating papers that has been read for a long time.” Wilkinson identified two main doctrines: first, that the world had become a single political system (a truth “foreseen some years back”); and second, the geography of the pivot region — which he described as new and deserving close study. He questioned whether Russia’s internal social development might limit her capacity to exploit her geographical position, and noted that the pivot’s full potential depended on railway development proceeding without interruption.
Mr. L. S. Amery, later a major figure in British imperial strategy, produced a notably prescient contribution. He extended Mackinder’s framework, arguing that sea-power and land-power were not the only two forms of mobility — air-power was a coming third: “Both the sea and the railway are going in the future to be supplemented by the air as a means of locomotion, and when we come to that, a good deal of this geographical distribution must lose its importance.”
Sir Thomas Holdich and others debated the precise boundaries of the heartland and the significance of mountain barriers. The President, Sir Clements Markham, praised the paper for its originality and breadth, noting that it would “stimulate thought and lead to the fruitful investigation of the relations of geography and history.”
Significance
Mackinder’s paper is the founding document of modern geopolitics. The heartland thesis — often summarised in the dictum “Who rules East Europe commands the Heartland; who rules the Heartland commands the World-Island; who rules the World-Island commands the World” (a formulation Mackinder would refine in his 1919 book Democratic Ideals and Reality) — became one of the most influential strategic concepts of the twentieth century. It directly shaped the thinking of Halford Mackinder’s later work, informed British blockade strategy in both World Wars, and was studied (and misappropriated) by German geopoliticians such as Karl Haushofer. The paper’s central insight — that the permanent geographical features of the Eurasian landmass impose strategic constraints on any maritime power seeking to prevent the domination of the continent — remains a foundational reference in strategic studies.

sources/mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol1.title: Justin McCarthy — A History of Our Own Times, from the Diamond Jubilee 1897 to the Accession of Edward VII, Vol. I (Sixth Volume)
sources/mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol1.content:
Justin McCarthy — A History of Our Own Times, from the Diamond Jubilee 1897 to the Accession of Edward VII, Vol. I (Sixth Volume)
Period covered: 1897–1899
Source
Justin McCarthy, A History of Our Own Times, from the Diamond Jubilee 1897 to the Accession of Edward VII, Vol. I (Sixth Volume), London: Chatto & Windus, 1905. Harvard University Library copy (K.F. 16096).
Text
raw/mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol1/raw.txt — 14,367 lines, 598KB. Extracted from 428 page-level OCR text files from an Anna’s Archive ZIP. Clean scan with readable text throughout.
Contents
Preface — The author states that these two concluding volumes (the Sixth and Seventh) cover the period from the Diamond Jubilee (1897) to the Accession of Edward VII. They aim not merely to record events and dates but to survey life and social progress across the whole span of Victoria’s reign, with retrospect chapters on politics, literature, art, science, and social change.
Chapter I — Colonial Federation — South African Troubles
The Diamond Jubilee of 1897 gives occasion for a review of colonial relations. The Colonial Premiers, Colonial troops, and representatives from Asian and African dependencies figured prominently in the Jubilee procession. McCarthy traces the development of Canadian federation as a model, then turns to the South Africa Committee investigation into the Jameson Raid. The telegrams between Rhodes, Jameson, and Chamberlain’s Colonial Office are examined — including the testimony of Flora Shaw (colonial correspondent of the Times) and the famous “sealed instructions” telegram. The chapter also covers the parliamentary formal censure of Rhodes and the debate on colonial federation schemes.
Chapter II — Greece, But Living Greece Once More
The Cretan revolt against Ottoman rule and the intervention of the European Powers. McCarthy recounts the story of the Greek national movement for the rescue of Crete, the landing of Greek troops, and the outbreak of the Greco-Turkish War of 1897. The European concert (England, France, Russia, Italy, Austria, Germany) attempted to maintain order but was divided in its sympathies. The chapter covers the Greek defeat, the armistice, the Treaty of Constantinople, and the establishment of an autonomous Cretan state under Prince George of Greece.
Chapter III — Employer and Workman
The condition of the working classes in late-Victorian Britain. McCarthy surveys the continuous efforts toward improvement during the later years of the reign: factory legislation, the employer’s liability question, workmen’s compensation, the eight-hours movement, the efforts of individual philanthropists, trade-union activity, and the growing recognition of labour’s claims in Parliament. The chapter discusses the conciliation movement in industrial disputes and the emergence of a more organised labour representation in politics.
Chapter IV — The Death of Gladstone
Ascension Day, 19 May 1898 — the death of William Ewart Gladstone at Hawarden. McCarthy describes the scenes at Hawarden, the Queen’s message, the lying-in-state in Westminster Hall, and the funeral in Westminster Abbey. A full biographical retrospect of Gladstone’s career is woven into the narrative: his early Toryism, his conversion to Liberalism, his great administrations, the Home Rule schism, and his final retirement. The chapter dwells on his character — his devotion to his wife, his religious intensity, his physical vigour even in old age, his love of books and Homeric scholarship, and his moral authority over the nation.
Chapter V — “Another Daybreak in the East”
Eastern affairs in the aftermath of the Greco-Turkish War. The title is taken from Shakespeare. McCarthy examines the condition of the Ottoman Empire, the Armenian question, the continuing unrest in Crete and Macedonia, the ambitions of the European Powers in the Levant, and the complications arising from the decline of Turkish authority in Europe. The chapter also touches on the relations between the Powers and the Sultan, and the growing influence of Germany in the Near East.
Chapter VI — The Far East
China and the Far Eastern question. The Dowager-Empress Tzu-hsi and her system of personal rule. McCarthy discusses the scramble for Chinese concessions — the Russian lease of Port Arthur, the German seizure of Kiaochow, the British lease of Weihaiwei, and the Japanese emergence as a Pacific power. The chapter covers the “Hundred Days of Reform” under the Kuang-hsü Emperor, the conservative reaction led by the Dowager-Empress, the Boxer movement in its early stages, and the growing tension between the European powers and China.
Chapter VII — “How We Have Performed Our Roman Rites”
The Ritualist controversy in the Church of England. McCarthy examines the conflict between the High Church (Ritualist) party and the Low Church and Evangelical parties over liturgical practices — the use of incense, vestments, altar lights, processions, and the eastward position. The chapter covers episcopal charges, the Public Worship Regulation Act, the prosecutions of Ritualist clergy, the imprisonment of some clergymen for contempt of court, and the broader question of religious liberty within the established church.
Chapter VIII — “Here’s a Woman Would Speak”
The Women’s Rights movement in the closing years of Victoria’s reign. McCarthy surveys the agitation for the enlargement of women’s sphere: the struggle for admission to the universities and the medical profession, the Married Women’s Property Acts, the movement for women’s suffrage, the work of women in local government and the poor law boards, and the changing social position of women. The chapter also covers the Queen’s own views on women’s questions, and the emergence of the “New Woman” in literature and society.
Chapter IX — The Old World and the New
The Spanish-American War of 1898. McCarthy describes the outbreak of the conflict between Spain and the United States, beginning with the Cuban insurrection and the destruction of the USS Maine in Havana harbour. The chapter covers the American declaration of war, Dewey’s victory at Manila Bay, the land campaign in Cuba including the charge of the Rough Riders at San Juan Hill, the destruction of Cervera’s fleet off Santiago, and the Spanish surrender. The Treaty of Paris — the cession of Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States, and Cuban independence — is discussed. McCarthy reflects on the emergence of the United States as a world power and the implications for European diplomacy.
Chapter X — Some Deaths in 1897
Obituaries of notable figures who died in the year of the Diamond Jubilee. McCarthy devotes particular attention to Sir John Everett Millais (the painter), the Duke of Devonshire (the seventh Duke, formerly the Marquess of Hartington), Professor J. R. Seeley (author of The Expansion of England), and other figures from politics, literature, and the arts. The chapter is both a record of individual lives and a survey of the generation that was passing away.
Chapter XI — The Death-Roll of 1898
The death of Prince Bismarck receives first place. McCarthy describes the profound impression made on the English people by the passing of the Iron Chancellor, and provides a biographical sketch of his career from the unification of Germany to his dismissal by William II and his retirement at Friedrichsruh. Other notable deaths recorded include Sir William Harcourt (the statesman, though his death actually occurred later), Professor Huxley, Lord Acton, and leading figures in literature and science. McCarthy uses the chapter to reflect on the changing of the European political guard.
Chapter XII — Peace Claims Her Victories
The Hague Peace Conference of 1898–1899. McCarthy recounts Tsar Nicholas II’s Rescript of August 1898 inviting the Powers to a conference on disarmament and international arbitration. The chapter covers the opening of the conference at The Hague in May 1899, the debates on arms limitation (which achieved little), the establishment of the Permanent Court of Arbitration, the conventions on the laws of war (the Hague Conventions), and the declaration against the use of asphyxiating gases and expanding bullets. McCarthy is cautiously hopeful about the conference’s significance despite its limited practical results.
Chapter XIII — The Session of 1899
The Parliamentary session of 1899. McCarthy surveys the political landscape: the Liberal party under new leadership following the retirement of Sir William Harcourt, the growing divisions within Liberalism over imperialism and the South African question, the Conservative-Unionist Government under Lord Salisbury, and the key legislative measures of the session. The chapter also covers the budget, the naval estimates, Irish land bills, and the early parliamentary skirmishes over the Transvaal that foreshadowed the coming war.

sources/mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol2.title: Justin McCarthy — A History of Our Own Times, from the Diamond Jubilee 1897 to the Accession of Edward VII, Vol. II (Seventh Volume)
sources/mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol2.content:
Justin McCarthy — A History of Our Own Times, from the Diamond Jubilee 1897 to the Accession of Edward VII, Vol. II (Seventh Volume)
Period covered: 1899–1901
Source
Justin McCarthy, A History of Our Own Times, from the Diamond Jubilee 1897 to the Accession of Edward VII, Vol. II (Seventh Volume), London: Chatto & Windus, 1905. Harvard University Library copy (K.F. 16076). Printed by Ballantyne, Hanson & Co. at the Ballantyne Press.
Text
raw/mccarthy-diamond-jubilee-vol2/raw.txt — 19,731 lines, 705KB. Extracted from 444 page-level OCR text files from an Anna’s Archive ZIP. Clean scan.
Contents
Chapter XIV — Educational and Philanthropic Movements
The early spring of 1899 and the introduction of Mr. W.S. Robson’s Education of Children Bill, which proposed to raise the minimum age for children leaving school and regulate the employment of children in factories. McCarthy examines the debate: Sir John Gorst’s independent support, the opposition from agricultural interests (who defended field work for children as healthy), the Berlin Conference of 1890 on factory labour, and the eventual passage of the bill. The chapter also covers the growing movement for old-age pensions — the parliamentary committee under Lord Rothschild, the scheme for contributory pensions, the debates on the Poor Law, and the public agitation led by Canon Blackley and Joseph Chamberlain.
Chapter XV — New Ireland
The transformation of Irish Nationalist politics after Parnell. McCarthy traces the reunion of the Irish Parliamentary Party, the emergence of John Redmond as leader of the reunited Nationalists, the replacement of the old landlord-dominated local government by a system of elected county councils (the Local Government Act for Ireland, 1898), the Wyndham Land Act and the beginnings of land purchase, the revival of the Irish language movement, the work of the Gaelic League under Douglas Hyde, and the improvement in economic conditions. The chapter presents an optimistic picture of “New Ireland” emerging from agrarian conflict and political division.
Chapter XVI — Another Death-Roll
The death-roll of 1899. Leading entries include the Duke of Northumberland (Algernon George Percy, 6th Duke), the artist George Frederic Watts, the scientist Edward Frankland, the African explorer Henry Morton Stanley, and the novelist George Meredith — among others. McCarthy uses the chapter to reflect on the changing of generations and the cultural loss represented by these passings. Each figure receives a substantial biographical notice.
Chapter XVII — The Coming South African War
The drift toward war with the Boer Republics. McCarthy describes the re-election of Paul Kruger as President of the Transvaal in May 1898, the refusal of the Volksraad to grant the franchise to Uitlanders, the despatch of Sir Alfred Milner as High Commissioner, the Bloemfontein Conference between Milner and Kruger (May-June 1899), the failure of negotiations, the ultimatum from the South African Republic, and the British decision to send troops. The chapter examines the competing narratives: the British claim to protect the rights of British subjects in the Transvaal versus the Boer fear of being swamped by foreigners and losing their independence.
Chapter XVIII — The War in South Africa
The narrative of the Boer War. McCarthy describes the outbreak in October 1899, the early Boer successes — the sieges of Ladysmith, Kimberley, and Mafeking, the “Black Week” of December 1899 (the battles of Stormberg, Magersfontein, and Colenso) — and the British recovery under Lord Roberts and Lord Kitchener. The relief of Kimberley, the battle of Paardeberg and the surrender of Cronjé, the relief of Ladysmith, the advance on Pretoria, the annexation of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State, and the subsequent phase of guerilla warfare. The chapter also covers the role of colonial contingents, the volunteer movement in Britain, and the financial cost of the war.
Chapter XIX — The General Election of 1900
The “Khaki Election” of 1900. McCarthy analyses the political calculation behind Lord Salisbury’s decision to dissolve Parliament while the war was still in progress. He discusses the campaign: the Liberal split between “Liberal Imperialists” (Rosebery, Asquith, Grey) and the “pro-Boer” faction (Lloyd George, Morley, Labouchere), the patriotic wave that favoured the Government, the Conservative-Unionist victory, the defeat of prominent Radicals, and the results — a reduced but still commanding majority for the coalition. The chapter also covers the new Parliament and the parliamentary debates on the conduct of the war.
Chapter XX — Yet Another Death-Roll
The death-roll of 1900. The chapter opens with Dr. James Martineau, the eminent Unitarian minister (brother of Harriet Martineau). Other figures include Sir John Ruskin (the art critic and social thinker — McCarthy notes his long retirement at Brantwood), Professor Max Müller (the philologist), Sir Henry Irving (the actor), and the Duke of Cambridge (the Commander-in-Chief). McCarthy uses these biographies to reflect on the intellectual and artistic ferment of the Victorian age now passing.
Chapter XXI — Last Years of the Reign
An extraordinary outbreak of regicidal passion in Europe — the assassinations of the Empress of Austria (1898), King Humbert of Italy (1900), and President McKinley of the United States (1901). McCarthy discusses the anarchist movement and its doctrines. He then turns to domestic affairs: the political uncertainty in Britain as the war dragged on, the last speeches and public appearances of the Queen, and the gradual decline in her health. The chapter also covers the social and economic condition of the country — the continuing growth of cities, the expansion of the railway system, the progress of technical education, and the condition of the agricultural labourer.
Chapter XXII — The Death of the Queen
The death of Queen Victoria at Osborne House on 22 January 1901. McCarthy opens with the significance of the new century and then describes the Queen’s final illness, the gathering of the family (including the German Emperor William II at her bedside), the moment of death, and the immediate aftermath. The chapter covers the lying-in-state, the funeral procession through London, and the burial at Frogmore beside Prince Albert. McCarthy reflects on the length and importance of the reign — the longest in English history to that date — and the transformation of Britain through the sixty-three years of Victoria’s rule.
Chapter XXIII — A Retrospect — Political
A comprehensive review of the political history of Victoria’s reign. McCarthy surveys the changes in the constitution and the working of Parliament: the extension of the franchise in 1867 and 1884, the Ballot Act, the reform of the Civil Service, the gradual democratisation of the House of Commons, the decline of the House of Lords, the growth of the party system, and the evolution of cabinet government. He examines the great political movements — Chartism, Free Trade, the Reform Bills, Home Rule — and the leading statesmen from Melbourne to Salisbury. The chapter concludes with McCarthy’s assessment of the political temper of the age: a movement from aristocratic to democratic government, accomplished by gradual reform rather than revolution.
Chapter XXIV — A Retrospect — The Arts of Peace
The material and intellectual progress of the Victorian age. McCarthy surveys the revolution in transport (steamboats and railways), the electric telegraph and submarine cables, the internal combustion engine and the beginnings of the automobile, the great exhibitions (1851 and later), the extension of education, the growth of the press, the development of municipal services (gas, water, sanitation), the advances in medicine and public health, and the improvement in the material conditions of life for all classes.
