The chapter also covers literature (Tennyson, Browning, Dickens, Thackeray, George Eliot, Carlyle, Ruskin, Arnold), science (Darwin, Huxley, Kelvin, Faraday, Lister, Pasteur), painting (the Pre-Raphaelites, Landseer, Millais, Watts, Leighton), architecture, and music. McCarthy concludes the entire work with a tribute to the peaceful achievements of the reign and the sense of progress that characterised the age.
Index
Alphabetical index to both volumes (pp. 377+).

sources/mccarthy-history-vol4.title: [source] A History of Our Own Times, Vol. IV (McCarthy, 1886)
sources/mccarthy-history-vol4.content:
A History of Our Own Times, Vol. IV (1865–1880)
Justin McCarthy’s narrative of English politics from the formation of Lord Russell’s government after Palmerston’s death through the Berlin Congress and the Conservative reaction, presenting the events of the reign of Queen Victoria as they appeared to a contemporary Liberal observer.
Source
McCarthy, Justin. A History of Our Own Times. A New Edition with Copious Index and an Introduction to American Readers, by Elmo. Four Volumes in Two. Vol. II [containing Vols. III & IV]. Chicago and New York: Belford, Clarke & Co., 1886.
Volume IV of McCarthy’s history (Chapters XLVIII–LXVII) covers the period from the death of Lord Palmerston in October 1865 through the Congress of Berlin in 1878 and the general election of 1880 that brought Gladstone back to power.
Digital scan: University of Michigan copy via Internet Archive.
Text
raw/mccarthy-history-vol4/raw.txt — 895,000 characters, OCR text from the Belford, Clarke & Co. 1886 edition. The OCR is generally readable but contains common scanning artefacts (broken words, incorrect punctuation, character substitutions).
Contents
Chapter XLVIII — The New Government
Lord Russell forms a government after Palmerston’s death. Lord John Russell’s age and the question of leadership. Gladstone becomes leader of the House of Commons. The ministry’s programme and the question of reform. The Wensleydale peerage case. Sir George Lewis. The Suez Canal question and Lord Palmerston’s earlier opposition. The Arrow affair and the Chinese war. The end of Lord Russell’s government.
Chapter XLIX — The Troubles in Jamaica
The Jamaica rebellion of 1865. Governor Edward John Eyre’s suppression and the martial-law controversy. The trial of George William Gordon. The Royal Commission. The dispute between the Eyre defenders (Carlyle, Ruskin, Tennyson) and the prosecution party (John Stuart Mill, Huxley, Herbert Spencer). The legal and moral questions surrounding colonial governance.
Chapter L — Driven Back Across the Rubicon
The Queen opens Parliament in person for the first time since the Prince Consort’s death. The reform question and Lord Russell’s resignation. Lord Derby forms a minority Conservative government. Disraeli as Chancellor of the Exchequer and leader of the House. The abortive Reform Bill of 1866. The “Adullamites” and Robert Lowe. The Hyde Park riots. The fall of the Derby government.
Chapter LI — The Reform Agitation
The Reform League and the popular agitation for parliamentary reform. Public meetings in Hyde Park and the government’s response. The collapse of the Derby-Disraeli government on the reform question. The state of public opinion in the country. The brewing crisis over reform.
Chapter LII — The Leap in the Dark
The Reform Bill of 1867 — Disraeli’s “leap in the dark.” The Conservative government takes up reform. The bill’s passage through Parliament: household suffrage, the redistribution of seats, and the doubling of the electorate. The political calculations of Disraeli. The effects of the reform on the party system. The general election of 1868.
Chapter LIII — The Fenian Movement
The Fenian rising in Ireland and England. The Manchester rescue of Fenian prisoners. The Clerkenwell explosion. The execution of the Manchester martyrs. Public feeling in England and Ireland. The effects of Fenianism on English opinion toward Ireland. Gladstone’s declaration that the time had come for Irish reform.
Chapter LIV — Trades-Unions
The trades-union agitation and the Sheffield outrages. The Royal Commission on trades-unions. The question of picketing, intimidation, and the legal status of unions. Public alarm and the reaction against union violence. The growth of organised labour. The legal reforms affecting trades-unions.
Chapter LV — The Example of the New Dominion
The British North America Act of 1867 and the Confederation of Canada. Lord Carnarvon’s speech on the second reading. The principles of colonial self-government and the Durham Report tradition. The strategic and economic arguments for confederation. The significance of the Canadian example for imperial policy.
Chapter LVI — Begins with Soldan, Ends with Prester John
The visit of the Sultan of Turkey to England in the summer of 1867. The state ball and public receptions. The diplomatic significance of the visit. English attitudes toward the Ottoman Empire. The Sultan’s impressions of England and English impressions of the Sultan.
Chapter LVII — The Irish Church
The Irish Church question. The condition of the Protestant Church establishment in a predominantly Catholic country. The general election of 1868 fought on the Irish Church issue. Gladstone’s victory. The disestablishment and disendowment of the Irish Church. Its effects on Irish society and English politics.
Chapter LVIII — Irish Ideas
The Irish land question. Fox’s principle that “Ireland ought to be governed by Irish ideas.” Gladstone’s Irish Land Bill of 1870. The Ulster custom, tenant right, and landlord-tenant relations. Compensation for disturbance. The limitations of the Land Act and its reception in Ireland.
Chapter LIX — Reformation in a Flood
The Education Act of 1870 — Forster’s bill for national elementary education. The compromise between church schools and board schools. The Nonconformist agitation. The abolition of purchase in the army (Cardwell’s reforms). The Irish Land Act. The beginning of the Franco-Prussian War and the change in public attention. Death of Lord Derby.
Chapter LX — The Black Sea Clause: The Alabama Arbitration
The Treaty of Paris (1856) and the Black Sea clause. Russia’s repudiation of the neutralisation clause during the Franco-Prussian War. The Conference of London (1871). The Alabama claims and the Treaty of Washington. The Geneva arbitration and the award against Britain. The settlement of outstanding disputes with the United States.
Chapter LXI — The Tide on the Turn
The declining popularity of Gladstone’s ministry. The Licensing Act and the trade’s hostility. The Ballot Act (1872). The abolition of religious tests at Oxford and Cambridge. The growing opposition to the government. The unpopularity of the Education Act among Nonconformists. The cost of army reforms.
Chapter LXII — The Fall of the Great Administration
The death of Louis Napoleon in 1873. The Irish University Bill and the defeat of the government. Gladstone’s resignation and Disraeli’s refusal to take office. Gladstone resumes office. The general election of 1874. The Conservative victory and the end of Gladstone’s first ministry.
Chapter LXIII — Conservative Reaction — Installed in Office
Disraeli forms his second ministry. The composition of the cabinet: Lord Cairns, Lord Derby, Lord Salisbury. The Public Worship Regulation Act. The agricultural legislation — the tenure and compensation acts. The social reforms of Richard Cross (Artisans’ Dwellings Act, the Factory Acts consolidation). The beginning of Disraeli’s imperial policy.
Chapter LXIV — The Eastern Question Again
The Eastern Question reopens. The rebellion in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Bulgarian atrocities and the public outcry in England. Disraeli’s policy of support for Turkey. Gladstone’s pamphlet on the Bulgarian horrors. The Midlothian campaign and the mobilisation of Liberal opinion. The decline of the Conservative government’s popularity.
Chapter LXV — The Congress of Berlin
Lord Beaconsfield goes to the Congress of Berlin. The Treaty of Berlin (1878). The partition of the Balkan provinces. The acquisition of Cyprus. The return of “peace with honour.” The triumphal reception of Beaconsfield and Salisbury. The costs and consequences of the settlement — the Afghan War and the Zulu War.
Chapter LXVI — The Anticlimax of Imperialism
The death of Lord Russell (May 1878). The Afghan War and the disaster at Maiwand. The Zulu War and the death of the Prince Imperial. The growing unpopularity of the government. The commercial depression and agricultural distress. The general election of 1880 and the Liberal landslide. The death of Lord Beaconsfield (1881).
Chapter LXVII — The Literature of the Reign: Second Survey
A survey of English literature from the Crimean War to the late 1870s. The progress of scientific literature: Darwin, Huxley, Tyndall, Spencer. The historical and biographical works: Kinglake, Froude, Freeman, Green, Lecky. The poets: Tennyson, Browning, Arnold. The novelists: George Eliot, Trollope, Meredith, Hardy. The periodical press and the reviewing quarterlies.

sources/mccarthy-history-vol5-1880-1897.title: [source] A History of Our Own Times, Vol. V: From 1880 to the Diamond Jubilee, with extended chapters (McCarthy, 1897/1903)
sources/mccarthy-history-vol5-1880-1897.content:
A History of Our Own Times, Vol. V: From 1880 to the Diamond Jubilee (1897)
Justin McCarthy’s narrative of English politics from the Liberal victory of 1880 through the Home Rule split, Parnell’s fall, and the close of the Victorian era — written as a contemporary history by a Liberal MP who lived through the events.
Source
McCarthy, Justin. A History of Our Own Times, Vol. V: From 1880 to the Diamond Jubilee. London: Chatto & Windus, 1897.
This volume continues the narrative from the general election of 1880 (when the Liberals returned to power with Gladstone at their head) to the Diamond Jubilee of Queen Victoria in 1897. McCarthy writes as a participant — he was a Member of Parliament throughout much of this period and a leading figure in the Home Rule movement.
Digital scan: Harvard College Library copy (call number Br2165.15.9) via Internet Archive.
Text
raw/mccarthy-history-of-our-own-times-vol5/raw.txt — 900,000 characters, OCR text from the Chatto & Windus 1897 edition (Chapters I–XVII).
raw/mccarthy-history-vol5-extended/raw.txt — 281,000 characters, OCR text from the Harper & Bros. 1903–1905 edition (Chapters XVIII–XXV, extending the narrative into the later 1890s).
Contents
Chapter I — The New Liberal Administration
The Liberal victory of 1880 and the formation of Gladstone’s second ministry. The composition of the cabinet. The difficulties inherited from the previous Conservative government: the Zulu War, the Afghan entanglement, the Transvaal annexation. Gladstone’s Midlothian campaign promises. The return of the Liberals after six years of Conservative rule.
Chapter II — The Bradlaugh Episode
The election of Charles Bradlaugh as MP for Northampton. The controversy over Bradlaugh’s atheism and his refusal to take the parliamentary oath. The committees of the House. The legal proceedings. Bradlaugh’s eventual admission after years of struggle. The constitutional and religious questions raised by the affair.
Chapter III — Inherited Responsibilities — and Others
The burden of foreign policy inherited from Beaconsfield. The Transvaal question and the Boer rebellion. Majuba Hill and the Convention of Pretoria (1881). The retrocession of the Transvaal. The Irish Coercion Act and the Land Act of 1881. The Kilmainham Treaty and Parnell’s release.
Chapter IV — The Irish Question
The Irish land war. The Land League and the No-Rent manifesto. The arrest of Parnell. The Phoenix Park murders (May 6, 1882). Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke. The public horror and the government’s response. The Crimes Act. The National League and the continuation of agrarian agitation.
Chapter V — On Fame’s Eternal Beadroll
The death of George Eliot (December 1880). A survey of her literary career and its significance. The deaths of other notable figures: Lord Beaconsfield (1881), Thomas Carlyle (1881). The passing of the generation of the great Victorians.
Chapter VI — Oh! Whither Hast Thou Led Me, Egypt?
The Egyptian question. The Dual Control and the Khedive Ismail. The Arabi Pasha revolt. The bombardment of Alexandria (1882). Sir Garnet Wolseley’s campaign and Tel-el-Kebir. The occupation of Egypt. The Sudan question and the Mahdi. The fall of Khartoum and the death of General Gordon (1885). The public outcry against the government.
Chapter VII — Some Losses to the World — One Gain, at Least, to Parliament
Deaths of notable men in 1882: Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Charles Darwin. The rise of new political talent. The Reform Act of 1884 — the extension of household suffrage to the counties. The Redistribution Act of 1885. The third Reform Act and its effect on the electoral map.
Chapter VIII — Reform Amid Storm
The passage of the Reform Bill of 1884 against the opposition of the House of Lords. The compromise between the parties. The Redistribution Bill of 1885. The fall of the Liberal government over the budget. Lord Salisbury forms a caretaker government. The general election of 1885.
Chapter IX — Fall of the Liberal Government
The resignation of Gladstone’s ministry. The defeat on the budget. Lord Salisbury’s first ministry. The general election of 1885 and the rise of the Irish Parliamentary Party as a balance of power. Gladstone’s conversion to Home Rule. The Hawarden Kite and the public revelation of Gladstone’s Home Rule policy.
Chapter X — Home Rule
The introduction of the first Home Rule Bill (April 1886). The split in the Liberal Party: the Liberal Unionists under Joseph Chamberlain and Lord Hartington. The defeat of the Home Rule Bill. The general election of 1886. The defeat of the Liberals and the return of Lord Salisbury with a Unionist majority.
Chapter XI — Wrecks of Many Kinds
Lord Salisbury’s second ministry. Lord Randolph Churchill as Chancellor of the Exchequer and leader of the House. The resignation of Lord Randolph Churchill. The “Johnny in the Lot” incident and the rise of Arthur Balfour. The Irish policy of coercion and the Plan of Campaign.
Chapter XII — Parnellism and Crime
The Times’ publication of the forged Parnell letters (April 1887). The Pigott forgeries. The Special Commission on Parnellism and Crime. Richard Pigott’s confession and suicide. Parnell’s vindication. The triumph of the Irish leader.
Chapter XIII — The Year of Jubilee
The Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria (1887). The celebration and its meaning for the British Empire. Arthur Balfour as Chief Secretary for Ireland. The Liberal Unionist alliance. The Crimes Act for Ireland. The growing agitation for Home Rule.
Chapter XIV — Only a Death-Roll
The death of John Bright (March 1889). The deaths of other notable figures: Cardinal Manning, Robert Browning. The Parnell divorce case (1890). Captain O’Shea’s petition. The divorce decree and the moral condemnation of Parnell. The split in the Irish party. The fall of Parnell.
Chapter XV — Home Rule Without Parnell
The Irish Party splits into Parnellites and anti-Parnellites. The struggle for control of the Irish National League. Parnell’s campaign in Ireland and his death (October 1891). The reunification of the Irish Party under John Redmond and Justin McCarthy (the author himself). The general election of 1892 and the Liberal victory.
Chapter XVI — Mr. Gladstone Resigns — Lord Rosebery Succeeds
Gladstone’s fourth and final ministry. The second Home Rule Bill (1893) — passed by the Commons, rejected by the Lords. Gladstone’s resignation (March 1894). Lord Rosebery becomes Prime Minister. Sir William Harcourt as Chancellor of the Exchequer. The weakness of the Liberal government.
Chapter XVII — The Cordite Explosion
The Rosebery ministry and the cordite vote. The defeat of the government on the cordite supply. Lord Rosebery’s resignation. Lord Salisbury’s third ministry. The general election of 1895 and the Unionist landslide. The end of the Liberal ascendancy. Retrospect on the Victorian era as the Diamond Jubilee approaches.
Extended chapters (Harper & Bros. 1903–1905 edition)
The following additional chapters extend the narrative beyond the 1897 edition, covering events through the late 1890s:
Chapter XVIII — The Eastern Question Once More
The renewal of the Eastern Question in 1895. The Armenian massacres in Constantinople and the Ottoman provinces. The European powers and the question of intervention. The Sultan Abdul Hamid and the reluctance of the Great Powers. Gladstone’s final speech on the Armenian question. The Cretan insurrection and the Greco-Turkish War (1897).
Chapter XIX — Venezuela and South Africa
President Cleveland’s message on the Venezuela boundary dispute (December 1895). The Monroe Doctrine and Anglo-American relations. The arbitration of the boundary. The Jameson Raid into the Transvaal (December 1895). The Kaiser’s telegram to Kruger. The diplomatic crisis between Britain and Germany. The South Africa Committee investigation.
Chapter XX — Death — and Dynamite
The deaths of Lord Leighton, Sir John Millais, William Morris, and other eminent Victorians in 1896. The dynamite outrages in London and the police response. The anarchist movement and public alarm. The end of an era in art and letters.
Chapter XXI — The Dongola Campaign
The opening of Parliament in 1897. Lord Kimberley’s leadership of the Liberal peers. The Dongola Expedition and the reconquest of the Sudan. General Kitchener’s campaign. The advance up the Nile. The preparations for the final reconquest of Khartoum.
Chapter XXII — The City of Blood
The Benin Expedition of 1897. The massacre of a British mission in the Kingdom of Benin. The punitive expedition and the capture of Benin City. The discovery of the Benin bronzes and the fate of the Oba. The opening of West Africa to British influence.
Chapter XXIII — Pitman — Spencer Wells — The Appeal of the Prince of Wales
The death of Sir Isaac Pitman (January 1897), inventor of shorthand. Sir Spencer Wells and the progress of surgery. The Prince of Wales’s appeal for the relief of the poor. The growth of philanthropy and voluntary charitable organisation in later Victorian Britain.
Chapter XXIV — The South Africa Committee
The South Africa Committee hearings (February 1897). The investigation into the Jameson Raid. The testimony of Cecil Rhodes, Dr. Jameson, and the Colonial Office. The committee’s report and its conclusions. The political consequences in Britain and South Africa.
Chapter XXV — Blondin — Nansen — The Penrhyn Quarries — The Education Bill
The death of Blondin the rope-walker (February 1897). Fridtjof Nansen and his Arctic exploration. The Penrhyn quarry strike and the labour question in Wales. The Education Bill of 1897 and the question of voluntary schools. The state of English education at the close of the Victorian era.

sources/old-and-new-london-vol1.title: Thornbury — Old and New London, Vol. I: The City, Ancient and Modern
sources/old-and-new-london-vol1.content:
Thornbury — Old and New London, Vol. I: The City, Ancient and Modern
Walter Thornbury (1828–1876) — Old and New London: A Narrative of Its History, Its People, and Its Places. Illustrated with numerous engravings from the most authentic sources. Vol. I. The City, Ancient and Modern. New edition, carefully revised and corrected. London: Cassell & Company, Limited. (Original serial/book publication Cassell, Petter & Galpin, mid-1870s; this OCR set is a later Cassell reprint.)
The opening volume of the six-volume topographic survey of the metropolis. Thornbury writes as a Victorian antiquary-journalist: street by street he piles legend, charter, fire, pageant, and literary anecdote onto the surviving fabric of the City. The plan of the whole work is announced early—to walk London as a living palimpsest, not to produce a dry gazetteer. Volume I stays inside and immediately around the old City core west and centre: from Temple Bar and Fleet Street through the Temple and Blackfriars to St. Paul’s, Cheapside, Guildhall, the Mansion House, and the financial quarter around the Bank, Exchange, and Lombard Street.
Form and text
Page-level OCR from an Anna’s Archive ZIP (University of California library marks appear on title leaves). Concatenated raw: raw/old-and-new-london-vol1/raw.txt (~2.43 million characters, ~618 page files). Running headers, plate captions, and double-column artefacts are frequent; chapter titles in the body are clearer than the scrambled TOC leaves.
About the author and series
Thornbury was a prolific man of letters (art criticism, novels, London sketches) who died in 1876 while the series was still appearing. Later volumes were continued and completed by Edward Walford. The Cassell set became a standard illustrated popular history of London streets, used for local colour and institutional memory rather than as a critical primary archive. For this wiki it supplies contemporary Victorian description of City institutions—Bank, Stock Exchange, Guildhall, Lord Mayors, newspaper and legal Fleet Street—that frame commercial and political London of 1865–1919 even when the anecdotes run deeper into the past.
Content of the volume
Roman and early London; Temple Bar
The book opens with Roman London: buried remains, Caesar and the Thames, the derivation of the name, London Stone, walls, and legendary foundations under what became St. Paul’s. From that deep past Thornbury steps to the western gate of the City at Temple Bar—the ceremonial threshold between City and Westminster, with its history of traitors’ heads, royal entries, and Johnsonian associations—before plunging into Fleet Street.
Fleet Street and its courts
A long run of chapters treats Fleet Street as the artery of printers, lawyers, and taverns. General introduction gives way to successive “continued” walks along the street and its northern and southern tributaries: Shire Lane, Bell Yard, Chancery Lane, Crane Court (early home of the Royal Society, with Newton and later experiments), Johnson’s Court and Bolt Court (Dr. Johnson’s last years), Shoe Lane, and the south-side alleys toward the river. The texture is anecdote-heavy: coffee-houses, printers, duals of wit, and the density of inns of court influence spilling from the Temple.
The Temple, Whitefriars, Blackfriars
The Temple receives a full cluster—general history of the Templars and lawyers’ monastery, the Temple Church, and precinct life. Whitefriars follows as the old Carmelite site turned Alsatia, refuge of debtors and ruffians in Stuart memory. Blackfriars carries Norman fortresses on the Thames bank, the Black Parliament, the trial of Katherine of Aragon, Shakespeare as Blackfriars manager, Puritan and Jesuit episodes, and riverside disasters.
St. Paul’s, Paternoster Row, Baynard’s Castle, Heralds
St. Paul’s occupies several chapters: fabric, legends, the cathedral after the Fire, churchyard life, and the book-trade quarter of Paternoster Row. Nearby stand Baynard’s Castle and Doctors’ Commons (ecclesiastical and admiralty law), then Heralds’ College, with its visitations and ceremonial science of arms.
Cheapside, Guildhall, Lord Mayors
Cheapside is treated as the historic market spine of the City: Westcheap memory, pillory and conduits, goldsmiths’ monopoly, Pepysian gossip, shows and pageants, then central street and north/south tributaries including Wood Street. Guildhall follows as civic stage. Two chapters on Lord Mayors culminate in modern celebrity—John Wilkes, the North Briton, expulsion, and the Gordon Riots—bridging medieval mayoralty to eighteenth-century popular politics still legible in Victorian memory.
Poultry, Old Jewry, Mansion House; Saxon London
Shorter topographical chapters cover the Poultry, Old Jewry (Jewish settlement and later conversion of the quarter), and the Mansion House. A retrospective chapter on Saxon London resets the deep chronology before the money-market sequence.
Bank, Stock Exchange, Royal Exchange, Lombard Street
The volume’s financial heart: the Bank of England; the Stock Exchange; the Royal Exchange (Gresham’s foundation, fires, rebuildings, the ambulatory or merchants’ walk, Lloyd’s and marine insurance). Neighbourhood chapters fill Lothbury, Throgmorton Street and the Drapers’ Company, Bartholomew Lane and Lombard Street, and Threadneedle Street—the same Lombard Street world that Bagehot analysed as system rather than streetscape. Cannon Street tributaries, Eastcheap, and the Monument close the Fire topography; a final chapter on Chaucer’s London folds the medieval city of the Canterbury Tales back onto the walked streets.
Use for this wiki
Best used for place-bound colour and institutional memory of the City: banking and exchange topography alongside money-market; Fleet Street and Temple as legal-literary London; Guildhall and mayoralty as civic theatre; St. Paul’s as national-religious stage. It is not a political narrative of 1865–1919, but it is a dense contemporary map of the capital in which Gladstone, Disraeli, and the money market operated.

sources/old-and-new-london-vol2.title: Thornbury — Old and New London, Vol. II: The City, Ancient and Modern (continued)
sources/old-and-new-london-vol2.content:
Thornbury — Old and New London, Vol. II: The City, Ancient and Modern (continued)
Walter Thornbury (1828–1876) — Old and New London: A Narrative of Its History, Its People, and Its Places. Vol. II. The City, Ancient and Modern. New edition, carefully revised and corrected. London: Cassell & Company, Limited.
Second volume of the series, still under Thornbury’s name and still titled for the City, but the walk has moved east and north from the Bank–Cheapside core of Volume I. The river front, the Tower, the docks, the eastern approaches, then a great swing through Bishopsgate, Moorfields, Islington and the northern villages, and finally back along the Fleet–Newgate–Holborn line of prisons, hospitals, and inns of court, make this the volume of fortress, trade waterfront, and the City’s northern and western skirts.
Form and text
Page-level OCR from Anna’s Archive ZIP (C. K. Ogden / UC Santa Barbara marks on some leaves). Concatenated raw: raw/old-and-new-london-vol2/raw.txt (~2.52 million characters, ~606 page files). TOC OCR is noisier than Volume I; body chapter heads are usable.
Content of the volume
Fishmongers, London Bridge, Thames Street
The volume opens on the bridgehead economy: Fishmongers’ Hall and Fish Street Hill—William Walworth, company wealth and quarrels, Walworth’s dagger in civic myth, Billingsgate’s changing manners. London Bridge follows with wooden-bridge legend (John Overy, “Old Moll”), medieval stone bridge, houses and chapel on the bridge, and the modern replacement. Upper and Lower Thames Street continue the warehouse and wharf city along the north bank.
The Tower and its neighbourhood
A long block on the Tower of London—fabric, officials, locking-up ritual, menagerie, moat, St. Peter ad Vincula, and a catalogue of state prisoners and executions from Tudor and earlier reigns. Neighbourhood chapters take in the Mint, St. Katharine’s Docks, the Tower Subway and London Docks, then the Thames Tunnel, Ratcliff Highway, and Wapping—Victorian engineering and sailor-town crime mythology side by side.
East End approaches; Bishopsgate to Leadenhall
Whitechapel and Bethnal Green push into the eastern working districts. Returning toward the City gates, Thornbury covers Bishopsgate, then the commercial streets of Cornhill, Gracechurch Street, and Fenchurch Street, and Leadenhall Street with the old East India House—Company memory still warm in the 1870s for a readership that had lived the Mutiny and the end of Company rule.
Shoreditch, Moorfields, Aldersgate, Cripplegate, Aldgate
Shoreditch, Moorfields and Finsbury (drained fen, artillery ground, suburban spread), Aldersgate Street and St. Martin’s-le-Grand (including postal associations), Cripplegate (St. Giles, Milton’s grave), and Aldgate, the Minories, and Crutched Friars map the northern and eastern City fringes and their churches.
Islington to Clerkenwell
A suburban sequence—Islington, Canonbury, Highbury, Upper Holloway, King’s Cross, Pentonville, Sadler’s Wells—then Coldbath Fields prison and Spa Fields, Hockley-in-the-Hole, and Clerkenwell (priory, watches, radical meeting memory). These chapters show how far “London” had already climbed the northern slopes by mid-Victorian times.
Bartholomew, hospitals, Charterhouse; Fleet; Newgate and Holborn
Sacred and carceral London: churches of Bartholomew-the-Great and Less, St. Bartholomew’s Hospital, Christ’s Hospital, and the Charterhouse (Carthusian origin, Sir Thomas More, dissolution, educational and pensioners’ foundation). The Fleet Prison and the buried Fleet River and Fleet Ditch restore the sanitary-antiquarian theme. Newgate Street, the Old Bailey, and St. Sepulchre’s cover the criminal processional route; the Metropolitan Meat Market, Farringdon Street, Holborn Viaduct, St. Andrew’s, the walk Holborn to Chancery Lane, and the Holborn inns of court and chancery close the volume on the rebuilt Victorian west–east artery that replaced the old Holborn valley barrier.
Use for this wiki
Strong on Tower and dockland imagery, East India Company topography, prison and Old Bailey process, Holborn Viaduct as emblem of Metropolitan Board-era London, and the northern “new” districts. Complements Volume I’s money-market core; together they frame the capital’s commercial and coercive geography behind imperial and domestic politics of the later nineteenth century.

sources/old-and-new-london-vol3.title: Walford — Old and New London, Vol. III: Westminster and the Western Suburbs
sources/old-and-new-london-vol3.content:
Walford — Old and New London, Vol. III: Westminster and the Western Suburbs
Edward Walford (1823–1897) — Old and New London: A Narrative of Its History, Its People, and Its Places. Vol. III. Westminster and the Western Suburbs. New edition, carefully revised and corrected. London: Cassell & Company, Limited.
With Volume III the series passes from Thornbury’s City to Walford’s Westminster. The preface stance (body text) is explicit: the first two volumes dealt with City antiquities and buried history; this volume turns west to summon the characters and sites of western London. It is the political and ceremonial volume of the set—Strand and inns of court, Whitehall and the execution of Charles I, Westminster Abbey, Westminster Hall, and the Houses of Parliament—written for a public that still lived among those monuments daily.
Form and text
Page-level OCR from Anna’s Archive ZIP (UC library stamps on title leaves). Concatenated raw: raw/old-and-new-london-vol3/raw.txt (~2.45 million characters, ~616 page files).
About the author
Walford, antiquary and editor, completed and extended Old and New London after Thornbury’s death and wrote widely on county families and London localities. His tone is clubbable and accumulative: parish boundaries, theatrical gossip, royal ceremonial, and guidebook survey mixed in long topographical chapters.
Content of the volume
Westminster defined; St. Clement Danes; inns and Strand approaches
Chapter I defines Westminster—name, see, abbey foundation, palace, and modern extent. From Temple Bar’s edge the walk enters Butcher’s Row and St. Clement Danes (Johnson’s church), with continued chapters on the Law Courts rising in the parish and a circuit of local streets. Northern tributaries of the Strand—Clement’s Inn, New Inn, Lyon’s Inn, Drury Lane and Clare Market, and Lincoln’s Inn (mootings, revels, Thurloe papers, Ben Jonson as bricklayer in the anecdote tradition)—link legal London to the Westminster approach.
The Strand
A major sequence: introductory history of the Strand under Plantagenets and Tudors, hackney rules, Taylor the water poet, paving and pageants; then southern tributaries (Thanet Place, old Rose tavern, riverside palaces’ ghosts), St. Mary-le-Strand and the Maypole, Somerset House and King’s College, the Savoy, and northern tributaries including Catherine Street, Exeter Hall/Gaiety associations, and newspaper offices. The Strand is treated as the processional and commercial hinge between City and court.
Charing Cross to Soho and St. Giles
Charing Cross, the railway stations, and old Hungerford Market; Northumberland House and the Percies; Trafalgar Square and the National Gallery; Leicester Square and Soho Square; St. Giles’s-in-the-Fields (poverty, parish regulation, “Old Simon”); Drury Lane Theatre—fashion, art, and rookery within a few minutes’ walk.
Covent Garden
An extended Covent Garden block: market, aristocratic building, theatres, Russell Street and Tom Davies’s bookshop, the first meeting of Boswell and Johnson, Will’s and Button’s coffee-houses, Dryden and Addison, and the theatrical neighbourhood. This is among the densest literary-topographical stretches in the series.
Thames; Scotland Yard; Whitehall
Chapters on the River Thames as spectacle and highway; Scotland Yard and the Metropolitan Police (modern administrative London); then a long Whitehall sequence—palace history, Charles I and Parliament, Cromwell, the trial and execution of Charles I, debates over the executioner, Marvell’s lines, later precinct and gardens. Whitehall is written as the stage of the seventeenth-century constitution still legible in Victorian stone and street names.
Westminster Abbey
Multiple chapters: early history; historical ceremonies; architectural survey; choir, transepts, and famous monuments (Newton, Stanhope, Cloudesley Shovel, Major André, musicians); chapels and royal tombs; chapter house, cloisters, and deanery. The Abbey is both national pantheon and working collegiate church.
Sanctuary, palaces, Parliament, Westminster Hall
Sanctuary and Almonry; the old Royal Palace of Westminster; the New Palace (Barry and Pugin’s Houses of Parliament) and historical reminiscences of Parliament from medieval summonses through constitutional crises; New Palace Yard and Westminster Hall—law, coronation banquets, state trials; the law courts and Old Palace Yard; St. Margaret’s as the parish church of Parliament.
Use for this wiki
Primary topographical companion to parliamentary and monarchical London: Abbey, Hall, Palace of Westminster, Whitehall, Strand approaches, and police headquarters. Useful colour for constitutional crises, coronations, and the physical setting of house-of-lords, cabinet government, and royal ceremonial under queen-victoria, edward-vii, and george-v.

sources/old-and-new-london-vol4.title: Walford — Old and New London, Vol. IV: Westminster and the Western Suburbs (continued)
sources/old-and-new-london-vol4.content:
Walford — Old and New London, Vol. IV: Westminster and the Western Suburbs (continued)
Edward Walford (1823–1897) — Old and New London: A Narrative of Its History, Its People, and Its Places. Vol. IV. Westminster and the Western Suburbs. Cassell, Petter & Galpin (and later Cassell issues).
Fourth volume continues the western survey begun in Volume III, moving from the parliamentary precinct into court and club London, the great West End streets and squares, Hyde Park, and then north across Oxford Street into Bloomsbury and the British Museum. If Volume III is Abbey and Whitehall, Volume IV is St. James’s, Pall Mall, Piccadilly, and the aristocratic square grid.
Form and text
Page-level OCR from Anna’s Archive ZIP. Concatenated raw: raw/old-and-new-london-vol4/raw.txt (~2.39 million characters, ~600 page files). Title leaf in this set explicitly marks VOL. IV.
Content of the volume
Millbank, Tothill Fields, modern Westminster; parks and palaces
Opening chapters survey Millbank and the streets about the Abbey’s south and west (College streets, Abingdon Street, engineers and actors as residents), Tothill Fields, and modern Westminster. Then the ceremonial green and royal belt: St. James’s Park; Buckingham Palace (Mulberry Garden, Arlington/Goring House, tea anecdote, comparison of English and French palaces); the Mall and Spring Gardens; Carlton House (Regent memory); St. James’s Palace across two chapters as working court.
Club-land: Pall Mall and St. James’s Street
Pall Mall and a dedicated club-land chapter—Johnson on clubs, Queen Anne clubbing, Guards, United Service, Army and Navy, and the architecture of the club house—then St. James’s Street continued, with gambling and political clubs in historical layers. St. James’s Square and its distinguished residents, and the immediate neighbourhood, map the residential heart of high politics.
Haymarket, Regent Street, Piccadilly
Waterloo Place and Her Majesty’s Theatre; the Haymarket (old hay-and-straw market, ambassadors’ perils, Addison in a garret, street theatre of trade); Pall Mall East and Suffolk Street; Golden Square. Then the Regency commercial spine: Regent Street and Piccadilly; Burlington House; noble mansions on Piccadilly; northern tributaries (Half Moon Street, Clarges Street, Boswell lodgings, Albemarle Street, bishops of Ely, etc.).
Hanover and Grosvenor Squares; Apsley House; Hyde Park
Hanover Square and Grosvenor Square as aristocratic estates; Apsley House and Park Lane (Wellington). Two chapters on Hyde Park—rural air, gates, Achilles statue, Rotten Row, the Drive, reviews and riots in memory—place the park as both leisure ground and political safety-valve (echoing reform demonstrations treated elsewhere in the wiki’s political sources).
Oxford Street to Bloomsbury and the Museum
Oxford Street and a long run of northern tributaries culminating in Tottenham Court Road form the divide. Bloomsbury—once edge-of-town, later deserted by fashion for farther west—leads into three chapters on the British Museum (collections, reading room, public institution). Square-by-square chapters follow: Bloomsbury Square, Red Lion Square, Queen Square and Great Ormond Street, Russell and Bedford Squares, Gordon and Tavistock Squares—the Bedford estate world of lawyers, physicians, and literary lodgers.
Use for this wiki
Best for court, club, and West End political society: Buckingham and St. James’s palaces, Pall Mall clubs where party and imperial elites met, Hyde Park as public political space, and Bloomsbury/Museum as intellectual London. Pairs with Volume III’s parliamentary fabric and with narrative sources on Jubilees, reform crowds, and Edwardian season.

sources/old-and-new-london-vol5.title: Walford — Old and New London, Vol. V: The Western and Northern Suburbs
sources/old-and-new-london-vol5.content:
Walford — Old and New London, Vol. V: The Western and Northern Suburbs
Edward Walford (1823–1897) — Old and New London: A Narrative of Its History, Its People, and Its Places. Vol. V. The Western and Northern Suburbs. Cassell, Petter & Galpin / Cassell & Company.
Fifth volume leaves the old Westminster–St. James core for the great nineteenth-century expansion: Belgravia and Knightsbridge, the Exhibition and South Kensington museums, Chelsea and Kensington Palace, Paddington and the underground, Marylebone and Regent’s Park, then the northern heights—Camden, St. Pancras, Highgate, Hampstead—and the north-eastern corridor out through Hackney and Tottenham. It is the volume in which “London” becomes the Victorian metropolis of estate building, railways, and middle-class villas.
Form and text
Page-level OCR from Anna’s Archive ZIP. Concatenated raw: raw/old-and-new-london-vol5/raw.txt (~2.38 million characters, ~604 page files). Title leaf marks VOL. V and the western/northern subtitle.
Content of the volume
Belgravia, Knightsbridge, the Great Exhibition
Belgravia—building of the Grosvenor estate on difficult soil, rent-rolls, contrast with Bethnal Green, Tattersall’s, St. George’s Hospital—opens the western fashion district. Knightsbridge follows. A full chapter on the Great Exhibition of 1851 anchors Crystal Palace memory (before Sydenham gets its own treatment in Volume VI) as the spectacle that advertised industrial Britain.
Chelsea, South Kensington, Kensington Palace and Holland House
Chelsea across several chapters: manor history, More and other eminent residents, the Hospital, Cremorne Gardens. West Brompton and the South Kensington Museum (the museum quarter born of Exhibition profit and Albertine cultural policy). Kensington town, Kensington Palace (including Victoria’s childhood associations in the guidebook vein), Kensington Gardens, and Holland House with its Whig-political and literary salon history.
Tyburn, Paddington, underground London
Tyburn and Tyburnia—gallows memory turned residential estate; Paddington. A distinctive chapter on Underground London: railways, subways, and sewers records the Metropolitan and related lines, utility subways, and main drainage as the hidden infrastructure of the modern capital—directly useful background to Metropolitan Board / LCC-era London.
Marylebone north, Regent’s Park, Primrose Hill
Kilburn and St. John’s Wood; northern Marylebone historical associations; Regent’s Park and the Zoological Gardens; Primrose Hill and Chalk Farm—Nash’s park crown and the northern pleasure ground.
Euston corridor, Camden, St. Pancras, Foundling, Agar Town
Railway-age north: Euston Road, Hampstead Road; Camden Town and Kentish Town; St. Pancras; Somers Town and Euston Square; the Foundling Hospital; Agar Town and the Midland Railway—clearance, termini, and working-class displacement beside monumental stations.
Highgate and Hampstead
An extended Highgate and still longer Hampstead sequence: Caen Wood (Kenwood), North End, the Heath and the Upper Flask, the town, literary associations, Rosslyn Hill, Belsize and Frognal. Heath as open space, spa memory, and literary suburb dominates.
North-eastern suburbs
Final stretch: Haggerston and Hackney, Hoxton, Kingsland, Dalston, Stoke Newington and Stamford Hill, Tottenham and Edmonton—ribbon development along the roads into Middlesex, villages becoming continuous town.
Use for this wiki
Essential for suburban and infrastructural London of the later Victorian and Edwardian periods: Exhibition/South Kensington culture, underground railways and sewers, northern railway termini, and the social geography that underlay franchise reform, labour politics, and metropolitan government. Complements political narratives that otherwise stay in Westminster.

sources/old-and-new-london-vol6.title: Walford — Old and New London, Vol. VI: The Southern Suburbs
sources/old-and-new-london-vol6.content:
Walford — Old and New London, Vol. VI: The Southern Suburbs
Edward Walford (1823–1897) — Old and New London: A Narrative of Its History, Its People, and Its Places. Vol. VI. The Southern Suburbs. New edition, carefully revised and corrected. London: Cassell & Company, Limited.
Concluding volume of the six. Walford states at the outset that the work’s last circuit will keep mainly to metropolitan and strictly suburban districts south of the Thames (with a final west-bank coda up through Fulham, Hammersmith, and Chiswick). Southwark and Bankside supply deep history—bridge, abbey church, theatres, bears—before the chapters fan out through dockland, Greenwich, the southern residential belt, Lambeth and the “transpontine” theatres, and the south-western villages absorbed into Greater London.
Form and text
Page-level OCR from Anna’s Archive ZIP. Concatenated raw: raw/old-and-new-london-vol6/raw.txt (~2.98 million characters, ~658 page files)—the longest extract of the six.
Content of the volume
Southwark
Introductory Southwark: geology of the south bank, etymology, Roman settlement, old London Bridge, Knut’s trench, Norman reception, civic annexation to the City, saga material on Olaf and the bridge. Continued chapters: old London Bridge in detail; St. Saviour’s (Southwark Cathedral); Winchester House and Barclay’s brewery; Bankside in the old time—Hope and Swan theatres, Paris Garden, bear-baiting, Pepys and Evelyn, bad repute and royal visits; High Street; St. Thomas’s and Guy’s Hospitals. This block is the volume’s historical deep end.
Bermondsey and Rotherhithe
Tooley Street and Bermondsey trades; the Abbey; Rotherhithe (Redriff), manor descent, fires, docks and sailor parish—downstream working river.
Greenwich and Blackheath
A full Greenwich sequence: town; Hospital for Seamen; parish church; Park and Royal Observatory. Then Blackheath, Charlton; Eltham, Lee, Lewisham—court, naval charity, science, and suburb on the Dover road side.
Inner southern residential belt
Old Kent Road; Newington and Walworth; Camberwell; Peckham and Dulwich; Sydenham, Norwood, and Streatham (including Crystal Palace/Paxton associations after the Hyde Park Exhibition); Brixton and Clapham; Stockwell and Kennington. These chapters chart the filling-in of south London as commuter and middle-class residence.
St. George’s Fields, Blackfriars Road, Lambeth
St. George’s Fields and Bethlehem Hospital; Blackfriars Road with Surrey Theatre and Surrey Chapel; Lambeth—parochial history, manor, appearance from the Adelphi, Lambeth Palace associations, then transpontine theatres and Waterloo Road. Political meetings and open-ground memory sit beside ecclesiastical Lambeth.
Vauxhall to Chiswick; conclusion
Vauxhall and Battersea (gardens, fields, bridges, Red House); Wandsworth; Fulham (Walham Green, North End); Hammersmith; Chiswick (eyot, church, Hogarth and gardening names). A general remarks and conclusion chapter closes the entire Old and New London enterprise—looking back across six volumes of street narrative.
Use for this wiki
Gives the south-bank and suburban metropolis missing from Westminster-centred political sources: bridge and Borough, naval Greenwich, Crystal Palace south, Lambeth as archiepiscopal and theatrical shore, and the continuous town that reformers, railway companies, and the LCC inherited. Read with Volumes III–V for a full Victorian mental map of the capital.

sources/politics-grand-strategy.title: [source] The Politics of Grand Strategy: Britain and France Prepare for War, 1904-1914 (Williamson, 1969)
sources/politics-grand-strategy.content:
The Politics of Grand Strategy: Britain and France Prepare for War, 1904-1914 (1969)
Samuel R. Williamson, Jr.’s foundational study of the Anglo-French Entente as a working alliance — the first detailed analysis, based on British, French, and Belgian archives, of the secret military and naval conversations that committed Britain to continental intervention in 1914.
Source
Williamson, Samuel R., Jr. The Politics of Grand Strategy: Britain and France Prepare for War, 1904-1914. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1969.
Digital scan via the Internet Archive (China-America Digital Academic Library), captured from a Harvard University Press first edition.
Williamson’s book was a pioneering work in the study of alliance politics and entente diplomacy. Drawing on newly opened French military and naval archives (including the deliberations of the Conseil Supérieur de la Guerre and the Conseil Supérieur de la Marine), the British Cabinet and Committee of Imperial Defence papers, the Belgian Foreign Ministry archives, and private manuscript collections including the diaries of General Henry Wilson, Williamson reconstructed the full story of the secret staff conversations and their impact on the strategic options of both powers. The book remains a definitive treatment of how the Entente Cordiale evolved from a colonial settlement into a de facto military alliance.
Text
raw/politics-grand-strategy/raw.txt — 1,315,000 characters (21,338 lines), pdftotext extraction from the 1969 Harvard University Press edition.
Contents
Chapter 1 — The Formation of the Entente Cordiale, 1898-1904 (p. 1)
The Anglo-French colonial agreements of April 8, 1904: the settlement of disputes over Egypt, Morocco, Newfoundland, West Africa, Siam, and Madagascar. The background of Anglo-French rivalry from Fashoda (1898) through the Boer War. The diplomatic negotiations under Lord Lansdowne and Paul Cambon. The nature and limits of the Entente Cordiale as a diplomatic understanding rather than a military alliance.
Chapter 2 — The Entente Challenged: The First Moroccan Crisis, 1905 (p. 30)
Germany’s challenge to the Entente through the Kaiser’s landing at Tangier (March 1905) and the subsequent diplomatic crisis. The fall of Théophile Delcassé. British support for France at the Algeciras Conference. The first test of the Entente’s political cohesion and the emergence of a pattern of Anglo-French diplomatic cooperation against German pressure.
Chapter 3 — The Military Conversations Begin, 1905-1906 (p. 59)
The initiation of unofficial Anglo-French military staff conversations during the Moroccan crisis of 1905-1906. The role of King Edward VII, Sir Edward Grey, and the French attaché Victor Huguet. The informal talks between General Grierson and Colonel Laguiche. The Cabinet’s limited knowledge and the precedent of secrecy. The first tentative discussions about possible British military cooperation with France in the event of a German attack.
Chapter 4 — Preparing for War: British Defense Policy, 1906-1910 (p. 89)
The evolution of British defence policy under the Liberal government. The reforms of the Committee of Imperial Defence and the War Office (the Haldane reforms). The creation of the British Expeditionary Force. The differences between Admiralty and War Office strategic thinking — the “blue water” school versus the continental commitment. The Army’s growing orientation toward intervention on the Continent.
Chapter 5 — French Strategy in Transition, 1905-1911 (p. 115)
The evolution of French strategic planning from Plan XV to Plan XVI. The debates within the French General Staff and the Conseil Supérieur de la Guerre. The influence of General Michel’s proposals for a defensive reserve army and their rejection. French planning for a concentration on the Belgian frontier. The developing French need for British military support to counter German numerical superiority.
Chapter 6 — The Entente Under Stress, 1908-1911 (p. 131)
The strains within the Entente between the Algeciras settlement and the Agadir crisis. The Bosnian crisis of 1908-1909 and its impact on Anglo-French relations. German naval building and the British naval scare of 1909. The growing divergence between British and French strategic priorities. The role of General Henry Wilson as Director of Military Operations and his efforts to deepen the military commitment.
Chapter 7 — Agadir Confirms Britain’s Continental Strategy (p. 167)
The second Moroccan crisis (Agadir, July-November 1911) as a turning point in Anglo-French strategic relations. The German gunboat Panther at Agadir. The Mansion House speech by David Lloyd George. The critical CID meeting of August 23, 1911, at which the Army’s plans for a continental commitment (six divisions to France by M+15) were formally adopted over the Admiralty’s amphibious strategy. The ousting of Admiral Wilson and the triumph of General Wilson’s continental strategy.
Chapter 8 — Joffre Reshapes French Strategy, 1911-1913 (p. 205)
General Joffre’s assumption of command and the reformulation of French war planning: the adoption of Plan XVII. The concentration of French armies on the German and Belgian frontiers. The debates over the use of Belgian territory. The coordination of French railway movement schedules. The Schlieffen Plan and the French response. Joffre’s demands for a British contribution and the integration of the BEF into French defensive plans.
Chapter 9 — The Naval Conversations Begin, 1911-1912 (p. 227)
The beginning of Anglo-French naval staff conversations. The Mediterranean naval balance and the German threat. Churchill’s arrival at the Admiralty and his reorientation of British naval policy. The Anglo-French naval agreement: the concentration of the French fleet in the Mediterranean and the British commitment to guard the Channel and the North Sea. The strategic implications of this division of naval responsibility.
Chapter 10 — The Haldane Mission, 1912 (p. 249)
Lord Haldane’s mission to Berlin (February 1912) as a last attempt at Anglo-German détente. The proposed naval and colonial agreements. The failure of the mission: Germany’s insistence on British neutrality in a continental war as the price of a naval ratio agreement. The diplomatic aftermath and the hardening of British policy toward Germany. The strengthening of Anglo-French ties as a consequence of the failure of Anglo-German understanding.
Chapter 11 — The Mediterranean and the Entente, 1912 (p. 264)
The Mediterranean dimension of the Anglo-French relationship. The Italo-Turkish War and the Balkan Wars. The British decision to withdraw battleships from the Mediterranean to concentrate against Germany in the North Sea. The French assumption of the primary naval role in the Mediterranean. The exchange of letters between Grey and Cambon (November 1912) and the question of “moral obligation.” The political battles within the Cabinet over Mediterranean policy and the extent of commitment to France.
Chapter 12 — The Political Consolidation of the Entente, 1912 (p. 284)
The consolidation of the Entente at the political level through 1912. The role of the radicals and the discovery of the secret military conversations by the radical wing of the Liberal Party. The exchanges of letters between Grey and Cambon and the definition of the Entente as a diplomatic understanding without formal alliance obligations. The politics of secrecy and the limits of parliamentary knowledge.
Chapter 13 — Prepared for War: The Entente Military and Naval Arrangements (p. 300)
The detailed military and naval arrangements completed by 1913-1914. The BEF’s concentration zones in France (Maubeuge-Le Cateau-Hirson). The railway timetables and supply arrangements. The Anglo-French naval conventions for the Channel and the Mediterranean. The role of General Henry Wilson as the principal architect of the military arrangements. The degree of British commitment demonstrated by the specificity of the operational plans.
Chapter 14 — The Entente on the Eve of War, 1913-1914 (p. 328)
The state of the Entente on the eve of the Sarajevo assassination. The CID’s invasion inquiry of 1913-1914 and the debate over compulsory military service. The political vulnerability of the Asquith government. The Curragh mutiny (March 1914) and its effect on the Army’s readiness. The state of Anglo-German relations. The public uncertainty about British intentions and the private certainty of the military planners.
Chapter 15 — The Anglo-French Entente Goes to War: August 1914 (p. 343)
The July crisis and the Anglo-French response. The role of the Entente in shaping British decision-making. The Cabinet crisis of August 2-4. Sir Edward Grey’s speech to the House of Commons. The German ultimatum to Belgium and the invasion of Luxembourg. The British declaration of war. The mobilization and dispatch of the BEF to France. The fulfilment of the secret staff conversations. Williamson’s analysis of the Entente’s role in converting a continental war into a world war.
Select Bibliography (p. 373)
Extensive bibliography organized by archival sources (British, French, Belgian), documentary collections (published diplomatic documents), and secondary works (books and articles in English, French, and German). Key archival collections used: Adm. (Admiralty Archives), Cab. (Cabinet and CID Archives), F.O. (Foreign Office Archives), W.O. (War Office Archives), Archives Guerre (French Ministry of War Archives), Archives Marine (French Ministry of Marine Archives), M.A.E. (French Foreign Ministry Archives), Belg. Arch. (Belgian Foreign Ministry Archives), and RA (Royal Archives, Windsor).
Index (p. 397)
Comprehensive index of names, subjects, and places.

sources/wakeman-church-of-england.title: Wakeman, Henry Offley — An Introduction to the History of the Church of England
sources/wakeman-church-of-england.content:
An Introduction to the History of the Church of England
Henry Offley Wakeman (Fellow of All Souls College, Tutor of Keble College, Oxford) offers a narrative interpretation of the development of the Church of England rather than a mere chronicle. His stated aim is to answer the question “How is it that the Church of England has come to be what she is?” by fixing attention on what has proved permanent and passing quickly over periods of interruption or deterioration.
The book is written from a High Church/Anglo-Catholic perspective, reflecting the Oxford Movement’s conception of the Church of England as a branch of the Catholic Church, reformed of medieval abuses but in continuous historical succession with the primitive and medieval Church.
Sources
Henry Offley Wakeman, An Introduction to the History of the Church of England, from the Earliest Times to the Present Day. Fifth edition. London: Rivingtons, 1898. OCLC 3084052.
The work includes prefaces to the first (September 1896), third (December 1896), and fifth (December 1897) editions. A chronological table (55 BC–1896) precedes the text, and an extensive index follows.
Text
raw/wakeman-church-england/wakeman-church-england.txt — 22,228 lines, ~1.15 MB. Extracted from the New York Public Library copy (NYPL 3 3433 07029946 0) via Anna’s Archive zip, with individual page text files concatenated in numerical order.
Contents
Chronological Table (55 BC–AD 1896)
A detailed timeline from Caesar’s first invasion of Britain through the planting of the Church in Roman Britain, the conversion of the English, the Danish invasions, the Norman Conquest, the Reformation, the Civil War, the Restoration, the Evangelical Revival, the Oxford Movement, and the ritual controversies of the late nineteenth century.
Chapter I — The Church in Britain, 200–597
The planting of Christianity in Roman Britain, the martyrdom of S. Alban (AD 304), the British Church at the Councils of Arles (314), Nicæa (325), and Ariminum (359), the mission of S. Ninian in Galloway (397), the withdrawal of the Roman legions, the Pelagian controversy and the visit of SS. Lupus and Germanus (429), the mission of S. Patrick to Ireland, and the survival of the British Church through the Anglo-Saxon invasions.
Chapter II — The Conversion of the English, 597–655
The mission of S. Augustine to Kent (597), the foundation of the sees of Canterbury, London, and Rochester, the failure of Augustine’s conference with the Welsh bishops (603), the conversion of Northumbria by Paulinus (627), the apostasy after the death of Edwin, the missions of Felix to East Anglia and Birinus to Wessex, the Celtic mission of S. Aidan from Iona to Northumbria (635), and the Synod of Whitby (664) which decided for Roman over Celtic customs.
Chapter III — The Organisation of the Early English Church, 655–735
The work of Theodore of Tarsus as Archbishop of Canterbury (668–690): the organisation of dioceses, the Synod of Hertford (673), the introduction of the penitential system, and the establishment of parochial organisation. The careers of Wilfrid, S. Cuthbert, and the missionary work of Willibrord and Boniface (Winfrid). The death of the Venerable Bede (735).
Chapter IV — The English Church from the Death of Bede to the Coming of the Normans, 735–1042
The Danish invasions and their effect on the Church, the decay of monastic life, the revival under King Ælfred, the Benedictine monastic revival under Dunstan, Æthelwold, and Oswald (tenth century), and the state of the Church on the eve of the Norman Conquest.
Note A — The Papal Supremacy
A note on the development of the doctrine and practice of papal supremacy in the early and medieval Church.
Chapter V — The Norman Conquest, 1042–1087
The effects of the Norman Conquest on the English Church: the replacement of English bishops and abbots with Normans, the introduction of Norman church architecture and organisation, the separation of ecclesiastical and secular courts, and the Gregorian reform movement’s impact on England.
Chapter VI — The Struggle between Church and State, 1087–1176
The conflict between the spiritual claims of the Church and the temporal claims of the Crown: the careers of Anselm and Becket, the Constitutions of Clarendon (1164), the murder of Becket (1170), and the compromise that followed.
Chapter VII — The Church and English Liberty, 1176–1297
The development of canonical jurisprudence, the granting of Magna Carta and its ecclesiastical clauses (1215), the rise of the friars (Franciscans and Dominicans) in England, the growth of the universities, and the confirmation of the charters under Edward I.
Chapter VIII — The Decay of the Medieval Church, 1297–1485
The increasing worldliness of the clergy, the effects of the Black Death, the rise of Lollardy and Wycliffe’s teachings, the suppression of heresy, the decline of monastic discipline, and the weakening of the Church’s spiritual authority in the fifteenth century.
Chapter IX — The Inner Life of the Church in the Middle Ages
A thematic chapter covering the daily religious life of the medieval English Church: the parish system, the monastic orders, the liturgy and worship, preaching, popular devotion, the cult of saints and relics, pilgrimages, church architecture and art, and the educational work of the Church.
Chapter X — The Church on the Eve of the Reformation, 1485–1529
The state of the Church under Henry VII and the early years of Henry VIII: the condition of the monasteries, the quality of the parish clergy, popular attitudes toward the Church, and the limited penetration of Renaissance humanism and early reformist ideas into England. The chapter sets the stage for the break with Rome.
Chapter XI — The Repudiation of Papal Authority, 1529–1534
The divorce question, the failure of Wolsey, the summoning of the Reformation Parliament, the gradual assertion of royal authority over the Church through legislation (the restraint of annates, the restraint of appeals), and the Act of Supremacy (1534).
Chapter XII — The Royal Tyranny, 1534–1547
The enforcement of the royal supremacy, the dissolution of the monasteries, the execution of More and Fisher, the suppression of the Pilgrimage of Grace, and the changes in doctrine and practice under Thomas Cromwell and Thomas Cranmer, including the Ten Articles, the Bishops’ Book, and the King’s Book.
Chapter XIII — The Growth of Protestant Influences in the Church, 1526–1549
The gradual introduction of Protestant theology in England: the influence of Lutheran and Reformed ideas, the work of Cranmer, the publication of the English Bible (Coverdale, Matthew’s, the Great Bible), the beginnings of liturgical reform, and the first Prayer Book of Edward VI (1549).
Chapter XIV — Alterations in Religion, 1549–1559
The reign of Edward VI and the second Prayer Book (1552), the Forty-Two Articles, the reign of Mary and the reconciliation with Rome, the persecution of Protestants (the Marian martyrs), and the Elizabethan Settlement (1559) with its Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity and the revised Prayer Book.
Chapter XV — The Growth of Puritanism, 1559–1604
The struggle between the established Church and the Puritan movement: the Vestarian controversy, the Admonition to Parliament, the rise of Presbyterianism, the work of Cartwright, the efforts of Whitgift and Bancroft to enforce conformity, the Hampton Court Conference (1604), and the failure of the Puritan programme under James I.
Chapter XVI — The Strengthening of the Church, 1604–1662
The Caroline divines and the Arminian reaction under Archbishop Laud, the Laudian reforms in worship and doctrine, the Civil War and the destruction of the episcopal Church, the Commonwealth and Protectorate, the execution of Laud, and the Restoration settlement of 1662 with the Act of Uniformity and the Great Ejection of Nonconformist clergy.
Chapter XVII — The Beginning of Religious Toleration, 1662–1714
The period of intermittent persecution of Nonconformists under Charles II and James II, the Declaration of Indulgence, the Revolution of 1688 and the Toleration Act (1689), the Nonjuring schism, the foundation of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel (SPG), and the state of the Church under William III and Anne.
Chapter XVIII — The Ascendancy of Latitudinarianism, 1714–1760
The Hanoverian succession and the Whig supremacy, the decline of spiritual fervour among the episcopate, the prevalence of rational and moral preaching over doctrinal teaching, the political appointment of bishops, and the general torpor of the Church in the early eighteenth century.
Chapter XIX — Methodism and the Evangelical Revival, 1738–1833
The work of John and Charles Wesley, the rise of Methodism within the Church of England and its eventual separation, the Evangelical Revival under Whitefield, the work of Simeon at Cambridge, the Clapham Sect, and the Evangelical contribution to the abolition of the slave trade, prison reform, and missionary activity.
Chapter XX — The Oxford Movement, 1833–1896
The state of the Church, 1820–1833 — The Church described as materially unchanged from the eighteenth century: bishops as amiable scholars in dignified ease, patronage in the hands of the landowning class, non-residence and pluralities flourishing, ecclesiastical courts bywords for delay, Convocation silenced, cathedrals treated as museums. The clergy divided between a cold Protestantism, a few surviving High Churchmen, and the Evangelicals.
The beginning of the Oxford Movement, 1833 — The movement for Church reform in response to the political crisis of 1830–1833: the repeal of the Test and Corporation Acts, Catholic Emancipation (1829), and the Reform Bill (1832). Keble’s Assize Sermon on “National Apostasy” (July 14, 1833). The first Tracts for the Times. The leadership of Keble, Pusey, and Newman.
The revival of Church doctrine — The Tractarian assertion of the apostolic succession, the independence of the Church from the State, the doctrine of the Real Presence, and the sacramental system. The publication of the Tracts, the growing opposition, and the crisis of Tract XC (1841).
The secession of Newman, 1845 — Newman’s gradual movement toward Rome, his secession in 1845, and its shattering effect on the Oxford Movement. The widening of the movement into a general High Church revival.
The Eucharistic controversy — The debate over the doctrine of the Real Presence and the Eucharistic Sacrifice, the prosecutions of Denison (1856) and Bennett (1871), and the judicial decisions of the Privy Council.
The revival of ceremonial — The restoration of Eucharistic vestments and other ceremonial practices under the ornaments rubric, the opposition of the bishops, and the ritual prosecutions. The Public Worship Regulation Act (1874) and Archbishop Tait’s effort to suppress ritualism. The imprisonment of five clergy for refusing to acknowledge the new court. The Lincoln Judgment (1892) which reconsidered and partially overruled earlier decisions. The end of ritual prosecutions.
The growth and activity of the Church, 1845–1895 — The creation of six new English bishoprics and sixty-nine abroad, the revival of Convocation (1852) and the establishment of Houses of Laymen, the first Lambeth Conference (1867) and the decennial meetings thereafter, the development of the Anglican Communion as a worldwide organisation. The Church’s work in education (voluntary schools before and after the Education Act of 1870), the foundation of new theological colleges, the revival of the religious life for men and women, retreats and quiet days, and the training of souls in confession.
The defence of the faith — The Church’s response to the intellectual challenges of the mid-nineteenth century: the scientific spirit, the critical study of other religions, the higher criticism of the Bible, and the utilitarian spirit. The work of the Cambridge school of biblical scholars and the Oxford school of historians. The estimate of the High Church revival as the restoration of the Catholic balance which the Protestant movement of the sixteenth century had disturbed.
Notes C, D, E
Three special notes following the text:

C. The Eucharistic Controversy — More detailed treatment of the doctrinal disputes over the Eucharist in the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries.
D. The Royal Supremacy — The historical and legal development of the Crown’s authority over the Church.
E. English Orders — The question of the validity of Anglican holy orders, written with the assistance of the Rev. F. E. Brightman of Pusey House.

Index
A comprehensive alphabetical index covering persons, places, events, doctrines, and institutions from the entire work.

sources/warre-cornish-church-19th.title: Warre Cornish, Francis — The English Church in the Nineteenth Century, Part II
sources/warre-cornish-church-19th.content:
The English Church in the Nineteenth Century, Part II
Francis Warre Cornish, M.A. (Vice-Provost of Eton College, late Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge) wrote this volume as Part II of the nineteenth-century Church history within the multi-volume series A History of the English Church, edited by Dean Stephens and William Hunt. Where Part I (presumably covering the earlier decades of the century) left off, Warre Cornish takes the story from the aftermath of the Oxford Movement through the great ecclesiastical controversies of the Victorian era down to the end of the nineteenth century.
The work is thematic in organisation but broadly chronological in progression. It focuses on the great questions that agitated the Church in this period: ritual and doctrine, the revival of Convocation, the Church’s engagement with social problems, the legal battles over ritualism, the revision of the Bible, the education question, the disestablishment of the Irish Church, the development of Church organisation at home and abroad, and the missionary expansion of the Anglican Communion.
Sources
Francis Warre Cornish, M.A., The English Church in the Nineteenth Century, Part II. Being Volume VIII of A History of the English Church, edited by the Very Rev. W. R. W. Stephens, D.D., F.S.A., Dean of Winchester, and the Rev. William Hunt, D.Litt. London: Macmillan and Co., Limited, 1910. From the Harvard College Library copy (James Walker bequest).
The work includes a table of contents, errata list, appendices (dates, accession tables, Indian/Colonial/Missionary bishoprics), and an index.
Text
raw/warre-cornish-church-19th/warre-cornish-church-19th.txt — 21,729 lines, ~992 KB. Extracted from the Harvard College Library copy (shelfmark 32044019384742) via Anna’s Archive zip, with 486 individual page text files concatenated in numerical order.
Contents
Chapter I — Ritual and Doctrine
The theory and practice of ritual as the expression of doctrine. The ceremonial of the Roman Church and the Protestant reaction against sacramentalism. The revival of high eucharistic and sacramental doctrine by the Oxford Movement of 1833. The reintroduction of doctrines and practices long absent from Anglican teaching: the Real Presence, eucharistic vestments, elevation and reservation of the sacrament, extreme unction. The careers of Bishop Blomfield and the early controversies over ritual in London. The work of W. J. Bennett at St. Barnabas’, Pimlico, and St. Paul’s, Knightsbridge. The opposition of the Evangelical and Low Church parties. The development of the ritualist movement through the mid-century.
Chapter II — Revival of Convocation
The revival of the Convocation of the Province of Canterbury after its long suspension. The campaign led by Henry Hoare and others for the restoration of the Church’s ancient synodical body. The opposition of evangelical and erastian opinion. The re-establishment of Convocation in 1852 under Archbishop Sumner and the subsequent development of its role. The establishment of the Houses of Laymen and the growth of Church self-government. The decennial Lambeth Conferences.
Chapter III — Episcopate and Cathedrals
The expansion and reorganisation of the episcopate. The creation of new bishoprics: Manchester, Ripon, St. Albans, Truro, Liverpool, Newcastle, Southwell, Wakefield, Bristol and Gloucester separated. The reform of cathedral establishments. The work of cathedral chapters in education, music, and the promotion of worship. The condition of the parochial clergy and the growth of clerical incomes.
Chapter IV — Sisterhoods: Auricular Confession
The revival of religious communities for women in the Church of England. The foundation of Anglican sisterhoods: Park Village, Devonport, Clewer, Wantage, All Saints’, East Grinstead, St. Mary the Virgin, and others. The work of sisterhoods in nursing, education, and social service. The opposition to and slow acceptance of the religious life. The revival of auricular confession as a regular practice in Anglican devotion. The controversies surrounding the confessional.
Chapter V — The Church and Social Problems
The engagement of the Church with the social questions of the age. The work of the Christian Socialists: F. D. Maurice, Charles Kingsley, J. M. Ludlow, and Thomas Hughes. The foundation of the Working Men’s College. The London and other diocesan societies for moral and social improvement. Church work among the poor in the cities. Temperance and other reform movements.
Chapter VI — Progress of Ritualism
The spread of ritualist practices through the parishes of England. The introduction of eucharistic vestments, candles, incense, and the mixed chalice. The growth of a more elaborate ceremonial in worship. The opposition of bishops and the varied response of the episcopate. Organisations for the defence of ritualist clergy. The impact of ritualism on the ordinary life of the Church.
Chapter VII — Ritualism and the Law Courts (1853-1882)
The legal battles over ritual. The founding of the Church Association to prosecute ritualist clergy. The series of ecclesiastical trials and appeals. The Privy Council judgments in the cases of Westerton v. Liddell, the Denison case, the Hebbert v. Purchas case, and the Clifton and St. Albans cases. The Public Worship Regulation Act (1874) and Archbishop Tait’s effort to suppress ritualism. The imprisonment of five clergy for contempt of the new court. The growing strain between the legal decisions and the conscience of the High Church party.
Chapter VIII — Ritual Commission and Revision of Bible (1867-1870)
The Royal Commission on Ritual appointed in 1867 under Archbishop Longley. Its composition and first report on vestments. More detailed examination of ornaments, the eastward position, the mixed chalice, incense, and altar lights. The second report. The question of the revision of the Authorised Version of the Bible. The appointment of the New Testament Revision Company (1870) and the Old Testament Revision Company. The principles and procedures of the revision.
Chapter IX — Ecclesiastical Legislation (1867-1874)
The legislative work of Parliament affecting the Church. The debates and measures in the years following the ritual controversies. The passage of the Public Worship Regulation Bill in 1874 through the efforts of Archbishop Tait. Lord Shaftesbury’s role. The effects of the Act on the ritualist movement and the imprisonment of clergy under its provisions. The reaction of public opinion.
Chapter X — Liberals and Evangelicals
The two great non-Tractarian parties. The Liberal or Broad Church party: the influence of Coleridge, Thomas Arnold, and the Oriel Noetics. The work of Arthur Penrhyn Stanley, Benjamin Jowett, F. D. Maurice. The Evangelical party: its leading figures after the first generation, its influence on philanthropy and missions, its theological positions and its relation to the rising ritualism. The gradual realignment of party affiliations.
Chapter XI — Essays and Reviews (1860-1866)
The publication of the controversial volume Essays and Reviews (1860). The contributors: Jowett, Mark Pattison, Baden Powell, H. B. Wilson, C. W. Goodwin, Rowland Williams, Frederick Temple. The topics: the interpretation of Scripture, the relation of science and religion, the development of doctrine. The storm of criticism and the ecclesiastical trials of Wilson and Williams. The Privy Council judgment (1864). The publication of Aids to Faith as a reply. The eventual liberalising effect on English theology.
Chapter XII — The Colenso Controversy (1861-1866)
The controversy surrounding John William Colenso, Bishop of Natal. His critical work on the Pentateuch, its denial of Mosaic authorship and strict inspiration. The condemnation of his teaching by the Bishops of the Church of England. His trial and deposition by Bishop Gray of Cape Town. The appeals to the Privy Council and the conflicting jurisdictions of the colonial Church and the Crown. The legal and constitutional crisis over the bishopric of Natal. The long-lasting consequences for the colonial episcopate.
Chapter XIII — National Education (1843-1876)
The Church’s role in the development of national education. The establishment of the Committee of the Privy Council on Education (1839) and the controversy over state inspection of schools. The Factory Education Bill of 1843 and the Nonconformist reaction. The growth of the National Society’s schools. The work of Sir James Kay-Shuttleworth and the training colleges. The rivalry between Church schools and British and Foreign School Society schools. The Education Act of 1870 under W. E. Forster and the creation of school boards. The Church’s response and the continued expansion of voluntary schools.
Chapter XIV — Disestablishment of the Irish Church (1868-1869)
The political campaign for the disestablishment of the Church of Ireland. Gladstone’s conversion to the cause. The general election of 1868. The passage of the Irish Church Act (1869), disestablishing and partially disendowing the Church of Ireland as a state church from January 1, 1871. The commutation of tithes and the compensation arrangements. The reorganisation of the disestablished Church of Ireland under its synodical government.
Chapter XV — Church Organisation
The internal reorganisation and development of the Church of England. The development of diocesan organisation, ruridecanal chapters, and diocesan conferences. The growth of the Church Congress and its role in public debate. The establishment of the Church House and the central committees. The Church’s financial organisation: Queen Anne’s Bounty, the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, and the augmentation of poor livings. The revision of the lectionary and other liturgical reforms.
Chapter XVI — Primacy of Archbishop Benson
The primacy of Edward White Benson as Archbishop of Canterbury (1883–1896). His character and ecclesiastical policy. The Lincoln Judgment (1892) which reconsidered the legality of ritual practices and partially overruled earlier decisions. The end of ritual prosecutions. The growth of the religious life and the development of the Anglican Communion under Benson’s leadership. His death in 1896 at Hawarden.
Chapter XVII — Missions — Part I
The missionary expansion of the Church of England overseas. The Society for the Propagation of the Gospel (S.P.G.) and the Church Missionary Society (C.M.S.) in the later nineteenth century. The growth of native churches. The development of the missionary episcopate. The expansion of missions in Africa, India, the Middle East, and the Far East. Missionary work in the colonies and dependencies.
Chapter XVIII — Missions — Part II
The continuation of the missionary story, with particular attention to specialised and regional work. The Universities’ Mission to Central Africa. The missionary work of Anglican sisterhoods overseas. The development of the native clergy. The growth of the Anglican Communion as a worldwide fellowship of Churches. The expansion of colonial and missionary bishoprics. The rise of the autonomous Churches in the dominions.
Appendices
